With Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, Infinity Ward delivers a particularly well-rounded installment that succeeds in offering an excellent experience across its various game modes. I really enjoyed the campaign, especially for its darker atmosphere, realistic conflict, and numerous spectacular sequences. The multiplayer remains just as solid, with several maps and new modes that add a bit of variety, even though I personally prefer the more classic formats. As for DMZ, it has undergone a major overhaul that makes this mode much more engaging. Of course, not everything is perfect—the menus are still just as complicated, and the vehicle handling lacks realism. However, these few flaws didn’t stop me from having a tremendous amount of fun with this new adventure.

601
After a few underwhelming installments, the Call of Duty series could certainly use a success. With Modern Warfare 4, Infinity Ward finally seems to be turning the tide. A more expansive narrative places players right back in the heart of war, while the multiplayer mode returns to classic, no-frills shooting. Those looking for a bit more risk can also dive into the DMZ mode. Yet, not all the old issues have vanished; in the online experience, in particular, poor spawn points and rigid matchmaking can significantly dampen the fun. Has Infinity Ward finally hit upon the right formula, or does the game itself once again prove to be its own worst enemy?

Modern Warfare 4 is a solid COD game. It's nearly perfect and proves that even if the series misses one year, it can come back stronger than ever with the next one. The story is phenomenal, and it's indeed one of the best stories Activision has ever delivered, bringing back some of that classic Modern Warfare feeling.

After more than a decade, the return of Call of Duty to Nintendo platforms has been handled very well. Despite visual limitations and minor performance issues, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 brings one of the best experiences in the genre to the Nintendo Switch 2, featuring an addictive multiplayer mode that fills a niche rarely seen on the platform. There is still room for improvement, but this initial step shows that Activision is on the right track for future releases.
This is the best Call of Duty I’ve smashed out in years. The rough edges remain, but the series is finally moving in the right direction, and I’m more than happy to follow.

Modern Warfare 4 will be remembered above all for its varied campaign and Captain Price’s concluding chapter. The cinematic level design and unexpected events keep the story engaging, while DMZ offers plenty of content for extraction shooter fans with its expansive map and progression system. Multiplayer continues to rely on the series’ familiar, fast-paced gunplay. However, shortcomings in character development, repetitive missions, and a lack of innovation in certain areas prevent the game from feeling consistent across all its modes.

Modern Warfare 4 returns to Call of Duty's roots with a cinematic campaign, compelling characters, and a more balanced multiplayer experience. The revamped DMZ impresses with its depth and variety of activities, although it still lacks tension. Frustrating spawn issues and aggressive SBMM remain, but they don't overshadow the game's strengths. Rather than reinventing the formula, Infinity Ward proves that Call of Duty still has plenty to offer.

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 marks a strong return for the franchise on Nintendo platforms. Its campaign, the return of DMZ, the solid multiplayer experience, and the excellent performance on Switch 2 make it a complete, fun, and easy-to-recommend release.
Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 marks a convincing comeback for the franchise’s single-player campaign.

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 comes highly recommended because it proves, once again, that you don't have to reinvent the formula to deliver a remarkable game. Its campaign, a full-fledged multiplayer mode, and the addition of DMZ allow players to enjoy the experience in different ways, depending on their preferences. Obviously, there's still room for improvement, but this is a very well-rounded and fun Call of Duty game, with enough content to keep you entertained for hours.
Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 seems to be trying to bring the series back to its former glory, even though that’s practically impossible.

At the end of the day, Modern Warfare 4 is the kind of Call of Duty release I’ve been hoping to see. The campaign delivers plenty of cinematic action; the gunplay feels excellent, and DMZ adds something genuinely interesting to the overall package. Even traditional multiplayer, despite a few frustrations, remains enjoyable thanks to the solid shooting mechanics. A strong return for the Modern Warfare series. Not flawless but definitely one of the more enjoyable Call of Duty experiences in recent years.

Modern Warfare 4 has one of the best Call of Duty campaigns in the last ten years and an excellent DMZ mode for extraction shooter fans. Unfortunately, the multiplayer is one of the worst in the series, which makes the whole package quite uneven.
Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 is one of the best entries in years, and arguably the best Modern Warfare game since 2019’s Modern Warfare reboot.

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 is an absolute must-play for anyone who loves first-person shooters. The game features an incredible campaign that strongly evokes the franchise’s heyday, a surprisingly enjoyable addition in the form of the expansive DMZ mode, and a traditional multiplayer mode that’s virtually flawless in terms of gameplay.

Keep in mind, though, that I’m specifically talking about the complete package here. If you’re only into single-player, this installment won’t do much to draw you toward multiplayer. So if you’re looking for a bombastic story, you might be wise to wait a bit longer for a better price.

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 delivers a very strong multiplayer package that feels entertaining throughout, even if it isn’t particularly innovative. With a delightfully over-the-top campaign and a well-oiled multiplayer mode, this is a COD that feels instantly familiar without straying from the beaten track. The slower time-to-kill and more basic movements ensure a fair, fast-paced online experience. Those who’ve grown tired of the series over the past few years won’t find a rebirth here, but those keen to join the shoot-’em-up extravaganza once more will find this instalment offers a satisfying shooting feast.

The final and best entry among its predecessors. With this, we conclude our review for the finale of the Modern Warfare series in its fourth installment, which delivered the best campaign mode in the series with an exciting storyline, escalating events, elevated character writing and dialogue, stunning direction, excellent visual and audio design, outstanding acting performances, alongside extraordinary cinematic cutscenes, and the return of the DMZ mode in its new and improved form. In contrast, it is hindered by a competitive multiplayer mode with numerous issues regarding map design and repetitive game modes.

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 is an excellent return for Infinity Ward and one of the most compelling packages the franchise has delivered in recent years. The campaign recovers much of the cinematic impact that made Modern Warfare famous, offering varied missions, interesting protagonists, and an impressive audio-visual presentation. Private Park Hyun Jun helps bring a more human perspective to the narrative, while Captain Price maintains the connection to the story built in previous installments, even if his arc could have received better development at times. The gameplay is the main highlight.

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 marks a return to the series' roots, and it does a pretty good job of it. An excellent campaign, backed by great gunplay and controversial moments, is exactly what the series needed. However, the lack of new features in multiplayer, a certain degree of repetitiveness, and a shortage of fresh ideas are shortcomings the developers still need to address.
A cinematic campaign, an incredibly fun multiplayer, and a surprisingly ambitious DMZ. Modern Warfare 4 is one of 2026’s biggest highlights.
Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 has managed to bring back some of the feelings that made me fall in love with the series back in 2007 and 2009.

I love that each mode brings something different to the table, and there's a substantial amount of content to enjoy. Modern Warfare 4 is an easy recommendation and a terrific return for Infinity Ward.

In the end , We're fairly torn because we genuinely enjoy the guns and gunplay this year, but the maps and dodgy spawns really hinder the overall experience. Unfortunately, this year, like many others, delivers an average Call of Duty multiplayer experience, at least so far at launch , but the DMZ mode does make up for some of this. We hope Infinity Ward fixes many of these issues quickly, brings back some classic maps that better suit this year's playstyle, and introduces new maps that can eventually become fan favourites.

Don't even get us started on skill-based matchmaking. That has become a lost cause for COD fans, with every game feeling like we're competing for a million-dollar prize pool.

The campaign earns a strong 9/10 from us. Spoilers aside, there were a few crucial moments we felt were somewhat abrupt, and the mini-boss fights came across as more of a gimmick.

Multiplayer in its current state earns an average 7/10 from us. Collectively, we felt the beta was stronger than the actual multiplayer release, and that's honestly quite shocking to think about.

DMZ Earns a soild 9/10 , as mentiond We genuinely feel DMZ offers a more rewarding multiplayer experience, especially for those of us who enjoy objective-based gameplay, tactical encounters, and having a reason to return for another deployment. Warzone might still attract the larger audience, but DMZ is the experience we'd rather spend our time with.

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 is clearly a step forward compared to last year’s installment. The implementation of a campaign with a more human—and less experimental—narrative focus set on the Korean front, combined with an open-structured mission design and highly refined weapon simulation, gives the title a distinct identity within a franchise that had begun to feel stagnant. Likewise, the consolidation of DMZ as an in-depth—and, above all, accessible—extraction mode provides a lasting gameplay variant.

Despite these successes, the game is not without its flaws. The rigidity of the traditional story missions, occasional lapses in artificial intelligence, and recurring issues with respawn zones in multiplayer maps prevent Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 from reaching the level of polish seen in the franchise’s heyday. Nevertheless, this new entry restores the quality of the series, offering a wealth of well-executed content for fans of the genre.

While Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 may not be able to fully fix the fragmented narrative and wasted character potential of the four game reboot series on its own, as a standalone title it delivers the most powerful, satisfying and entertaining Call of Duty experience in recent years.

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare delivers on its promise of providing three exceptionally high-quality experiences, featuring a cinematic campaign that brings the saga to a spectacular conclusion, a robust multiplayer mode that caters equally to a wide variety of playstyles, and an extremely well-executed extraction mode. Together, these elements put the franchise back on track and establish a solid foundation for future Call of Duty releases.

This year’s «Call of Duty» delivers plenty of content and variety. The strong single-player campaign gives Captain Price’s story a satisfying conclusion, but the real highlight is the story of young recruits caught up in the conflict on the Korean Peninsula. The missions are spectacular and varied, even if they fall short of the series’ very best campaigns. 

The multiplayer has little to complain about. Matches feel more grounded and slower-paced than in recent entries, and the launch lineup offers a solid selection of maps and modes, though not all are equally good.

DMZ is a mixed bag. Its unpredictability is both its greatest strength and its biggest weakness. Between fantastic matches, you’ll encounter plenty of dull and frustrating runs. If you have the patience, frustration tolerance and appetite for grinding, though, there’s plenty of fun to be had in its brutal open world.

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 delivers an incredibly confident shooter that hits all of the right notes across its single and multiplayer action. I’ve always been a fan of the campaign and co-op driven action in the series, and trust me, it’s at its very best here – the campaign is thrilling from start to end and DMZ is wonderful to dive into with friends. The multiplayer suite is more accessible than ever too, and even as someone who sees themselves as a bit of a casual, I had plenty of competitive fun (particularly in ‘Combat Outpost’ which makes for destructive fun).

It’s just a really, really good game, and as someone who felt a little underwhelmed by the previous entry, it’s easy to see this as a true return to form for one of gaming’s most high-profile franchises.

The multiplayer mode in Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 is an excellent addition to the series, featuring nearly flawless shooting mechanics, movement that strikes a balance between tactics and dynamism, and a fun unlock system, while Kill Block and DMZ introduce ideas that have been missing for years.

If you were worried about what they might have in store for us this year, you have nothing to fear. MW4 not only features one of the most interesting Campaign narratives and missions in the series, but also a Multiplayer mode that’s fun at its core (though it could use some improvements in certain areas) and a DMZ that, while not the revolution it seemed to be, manages to be a good complement to the rest of the game. Personally, though, I miss the legendary Special Operations, since we don’t have Zombies either.

A triumphant return to form. Modern Warfare 4 delivers a problem-free package featuring a gripping campaign, a deeply refined DMZ, and kinetic multiplayer. It is easily the crown jewel of the quadrilogy.

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 features a campaign that captivates with its mature tone. The multiplayer remains a gruelling experience due to the aggressive SBMM, whilst the DMZ suffers from an excessive amount of grinding. As if that weren’t enough, the absence of Zombies mode is a major blow to the dedicated community.

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 proves that Activision’s studios still have people who know how to make games and tell a compelling story, but why did we have to endure horrible Black Ops 7 before finally getting a gem like this? That's an awesome question.

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 feels like the series it used to be in its glory days. The story is perhaps the best it’s been in recent titles, with twists and turns at every corner. Multiplayer fixes many of the key issues from previous editions, and DMZ offers a fun way to get more of a narrative experience, even if it gets dull at times.

The campaign is fun, exciting, and serves as a wonderful conclusion to the rebooted Modern Warfare story arc. Multiplayer is engaging and packed with customization options, despite a lack of great maps. When players want a change of pace, DMZ offers a great alternative. While it has a few drawbacks, I believe Modern Warfare 4 is one of the best Call of Duty titles in recent years.

Recapturing much of the franchise's glory, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 delivers a fun experience on all sides. The Campaign features a good story built around three different, interconnected, and engaging plotlines. Multiplayer simplifies systems while maintaining its quality, offering many match types and a competent initial set of content. The DMZ mode shows great potential as an extraction "game." Its robust structure, with a great map, many missions, and rewards, works in its favor, but the competition here is more significant than in Multiplayer. In any case, the game as a whole is a great choice for FPS lovers, whether you're a veteran or a newcomer to this series that is once again a benchmark in its genre.

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 delivers one of the strongest campaigns in the series in years, combining spectacular action with memorable characters, emotional moments, and surprisingly varied missions. Its multiplayer sticks to a proven formula, offering outstanding gunplay, excellent weapon audio, and plenty of content, while the returning DMZ mode adds another engaging experience. Frustrating spawn points, awkward hand-to-hand combat, and an underused villain are disappointing, but impressive visuals and rock-solid performance help make this a more than worthy conclusion to the rebooted Modern Warfare series.

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 arrives with a campaign that places South Korea at the center of a North Korean invasion, while Captain Price carries out covert operations away from official channels. These two perspectives give the narrative a more grounded military tone without abandoning the cinematic sequences that helped define Modern Warfare's identity. After the very different directions explored by Black Ops, I found myself missing this approach, which feels closer to the military conflicts that made the franchise what it is today.


The experience also extends beyond the campaign. Multiplayer introduces changes to movement, combat, and the interface, while DMZ embraces an extraction-based structure with its own progression system, operator management, and upgrades that carry over between deployments. Each mode has a distinct identity, and what stood out to me most was how each one gives players its own reasons to keep coming back.

The campaign recaptures a military identity I had been missing, with memorable characters and missions such as Cut Communications, which stands out for its intensity, soundtrack, and use of night vision. Multiplayer also gets things right with its redesigned interface, faster matchmaking, and greater operator customization across classes. DMZ is another major highlight, bringing together its own progression system, operator management, equipment crafting, and decisions that affect future deployments. Each mode has qualities that make it worth investing time in, and this variety is one of the game's greatest strengths.


Overall, I consider Modern Warfare 4 one of the most complete and consistent Call of Duty games I have ever played. The campaign delivers memorable moments, multiplayer is extremely fun, and DMZ has enough depth to keep players engaged for many hours. I enjoyed how the three modes complement one another without losing their individual identities, creating a package that impressed me on almost every front. It is one of my favorite entries in the entire franchise and, in my opinion, should serve as a model for future Call of Duty releases.

While I wish the multiplayer side of things debuted far better, I’m glad the campaign and DMZ came in strong. Infinity Ward managed to pull off a solid ending out of an inconsistent series, and DMZ now feels like a legit contender in the growing extraction genre. Even with some stumbles, some 20 years later, Modern Warfare 4 shows Call of Duty is still in fighting shape.

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 delivers a spectacular campaign with gripping storytelling, outstanding action, and excellent gameplay. A heartfelt farewell to Task Force 141, it stands as a triumphant return and a love letter to longtime fans of the franchise.
With its mission designs, newly added features, graphics, cinematic storytelling, and sound system, the game has become excellent.
The game has never looked better graphically and the sound captured the moments perfectly.
Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 succeeds because it respects its own rich history while boldly refining its mechanical foundations.

Overall, Modern Warfare 4 is a great game. The sound quality and graphics are a step up from its predecessor. It goes to show that moving on from a previous console generation can make all the difference. It boasts a thrilling campaign that is a far cry in all of the best ways from its predecessors. It also makes for a great sendoff. Additionally, its multiplayer goes hand-in-hand with the fun, making playing against other players the most addictive in a while.

The game is set against the backdrop of a fictional Second Korean War. The storytelling was captivating, delivering an unfiltered showcase of what a blockbuster AAA title should be. While the campaign itself is robust and polished, the familiarity of experiencing Koreans own era and living environment injected an even deeper sense of immersion and engagement. In particular, it is packed with elements that will resonate strongly with Korean players, especially men who have served their mandatory military duty.

With a comprehensive selection of core multiplayer modes, a convincing take on extraction shooters, and the strongest – albeit rushed at times – campaign of this rebooted sub-series, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 is a slam dunk from Infinity Ward and the support studios that proves the franchise is at its best when developers are given extra time to cook.

Modern Warfare 4 is the Call of Duty the series needed after a few weaker years. The campaign finally features missions that really stick with you again. The nightclub and the chase for Makarov, in particular, show just how good Infinity Ward still is at tightly directed action. The multiplayer is back to the pace of MW2019 and many times better than the previous game, Black Ops 7. Of course, not every aspect of Modern Warfare 4 is perfect, and as far as I'm concerned, the open-world mission could have been scrapped without any problems. But as a total package, this is the strongest Call of Duty in years and a convincing final installment for Task Force 141.

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 cements Infinity Ward’s triumphant return, marking a genuine, next-generation technical leap. With stunning visuals and impeccable sound design, this installment demonstrates that lessons have been learned from past mistakes; meanwhile, it delivers an intense narrative that balances action with raw emotional depth amidst a conflict between the Koreas, establishing itself as the most impactful experience of the entire reboot era.
Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 delivers a satisfying campaign ending, a great evolution of DMZ, and fun multiplayer. There are missed opportunities, but it's the best Modern Warfare package in years.
One of the premiere first-person shooter series is back on a Nintendo system, and pretty well no matter what flavor you prefer you should find a satisfying match

Modern Warfare 4 is one of the series' better recent campaigns, supported by satisfying gunplay and a variety of missions. It is content-rich and polished, but repetitive objectives and grinding hold it back.

All things come to an end, and Modern Warfare 4 brings a strong conclusion to one of gaming’s longest-running annual franchises. This is one of the series’ tightest and most enthralling campaigns since the 2019 reboot and delivers a high-octane ride, with a noticeable DMZ training mission in the middle that might irk some players. All in all, Modern Warfare 4 brings a strong ending in a new and refreshing setting that will undoubtedly resonate strongly with players.

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 is a good package when taken as a whole. If you have been waiting for a return to form for CoD campaigns, I believe the single-player here is definitely the best of the rebooted Modern Warfare games. Multiplayer is about as standard as it gets, which may be good for the regular players, but it hasn’t been impressive or surprising for a very long time. In total, Modern Warfare 4 is pretty on par with, or slightly above, Call of Duty releases in the last decade, which isn't a bad thing. It's just not necessarily something worthy of great discussion.

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 does what a Call of Duty game should do: it reminds everyone why we keep coming back year after year—despite the frustrations, the cheaters, and the questionable matchmaking.

Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4 had a lot to fix after the last COD release one year ago. Infinity Ward had to deliver and did so in a back-to-basics way. The game is stunning, action-packed, yet grounded in what Modern Warfare stands for. Its story is personal, and the gameplay is tight and refreshing, with lots of believable places that breathe life and will keep you on the edge of your seat. There’s tons of replay value, with some amazing levels that can extend the campaign by a few extra hours. If that’s not enough, DMZ feels like a free, separate game that is likely to see many updates in the future if you’re into fleshed-out extraction shooters. And then there’s the stellar multiplayer that delivers with Kill Block, a mode that could become its own esports platform, where skill stands above the usual “pay-to-win” loadouts from some other modes. While some later levels, especially the snow levels, lack the visual fidelity of the earlier Paris missions, Infinity Ward shows that it can make a beautiful game that is still action-packed and delivers grounded and solid gameplay. If only they could fix that pesky download mess and optimize the install size on consoles to something more reasonable. But once you’re in, NO MORE RULES!

A brilliant campaign and a surprising DMZ mode rescue a package weighed down by a traditional multiplayer rendered frustrating by SBMM, yet built upon solid mechanics. Without a doubt, the best Call of Duty in recent years.
Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 is, for me, one of the most complete experiences the series has delivered in recent years.

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 marks a convincing comeback for Infinity Ward, thanks above all to a spectacular campaign and a solid multiplayer mode, enhanced by the excellent Kill Block. DMZ is an interesting addition, but it’s still too similar to Warzone to fully realize its potential. While it doesn’t revolutionize the formula, MW4 is a well-rounded, entertaining installment that restores confidence in the series’ future.

The Modern Warfare 4 campaign is what Modern Warfare III should have been three years ago. It has all the ear-ringing spectacle you want from a blockbuster shooter, and it isn’t afraid to show what that spectacle costs the people pulling the triggers.

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 marks a true return to form. The campaign is spectacular, brilliantly written and executed, and the story of the Marines squad, along with the heavy themes it tackles, makes it one of the best campaigns in the series’ history. DMZ has finally become a full-fledged mode that can keep players engaged for a long time, and while the multiplayer is polished and incredibly fun to play, it offers too few new features compared to its predecessors. If you’ve skipped the latest entries in the series, Modern Warfare 4 is the perfect time to jump back in.
As a package, Modern Warfare 4 is unarguably the best Call of Duty has been in some time.

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 marks a triumphant comeback, delivering one of the best campaigns in years, meaningful improvements to DMZ, and exactly the return to the classic multiplayer feel that fans have been waiting for. While the mix of two parallel storylines doesn’t always quite come together, and the new multiplayer maps occasionally lack variety, the game otherwise delivers the kind of entry the series has been missing. For fans of the franchise, this is finally a Call of Duty title they can buy without a second thought.

Very good opus than this Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4. Spectacular, giving choice in his multiplayer without necessarily renewing himself too much. The DMZ mode will convince some players, the others will return to the classic modes that also bring their novelties. You should not be disappointed.
After last year's slump, "Call of Duty" 2026 is back in full force.
With a strong campaign, a standout DMZ mode, and familiar competitive multiplayer, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 is arguably the most compelling entry in years.
Modern Warfare 4 closes Price’s saga with a grounded, well-paced campaign, even if a wasted villain and shaky enemy AI keep it from greatness.

Modern Warfare 4 brings almost a decade of storytelling to a climactic conclusion with its amazing set pieces, strong performances, and surprising moral choices. A new and improved DMZ mode will bring newcomers and series veterans back for more, and multiplayer is as energetic and engaging as ever. Despite the short campaign length, there is a lot of content on offer here that Call of Duty fans can sink their teeth into.

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 brings the series back to form with a thrilling campaign, outstanding gunplay, excellent Italian voice acting, and a strong multiplayer offering. The revamped DMZ adds even more value, making this one of the most satisfying Call of Duty entries in years.

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 finally delivers the return to its roots that I've been waiting for for so many years! With a spectacular single-player campaign, a storyline worthy of a true Hollywood blockbuster, interesting narrative choices, and incredibly satisfying gameplay, this installment has completely won me over.

I loved being immersed once again in that intense military atmosphere, enhanced by stunning graphics, excellent French voice acting, and outstanding PC optimization.

Despite a few imperfections and a campaign lasting around six hours that unfortunately comes to an end far too quickly for my liking, I had an absolute blast playing through this adventure.

For me, Modern Warfare 4 undoubtedly features one of the best single-player campaigns the franchise has delivered in a very long time. An absolute favorite that I wholeheartedly recommend to Call of Duty fans and anyone who enjoys story-driven military shooters.

Many Call of Duty campaigns have struggled to hold my attention for very long, so much so that I had to do previous games in short sessions. Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4’s campaign delivered a memorable, superbly polished experience, which I finished in around eight hours, in one go. Throughout the campaign, I felt like I was living through a cinematic movie and interacting with it. I can confidently say that I haven’t seen anything that looks as stunning as this game on an Xbox Series X yet, and recent games like Gears of War E-Day have also blown me away.

If you’re on the fence about Call of Duty this year, let me tell you that even the campaign alone is seriously impressive. This is without the rest of the package to come, which continues with DMZ on the 20th October 2026, online multiplayer on the 23rd October 2026 and Warzone to follow in November. That said, I am definitely diving in for a second attempt at the story on realism mode. If you want to secure your copy of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 with the Standard or Vault edition, you can grab it HERE.

From the frontline to the shadows, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 has delivered a thrilling dual-perspective campaign that reminds us why Call of Duty remains gaming’s blockbuster king, simply stunning!

I went into Modern Warfare 4 expecting another tired chapter of a reboot that had lost its way, and I came out of it with a campaign I’ll be thinking about for a long time. Infinity Ward didn’t reinvent Call of Duty here; it took everything the series does best, the shooting, the set pieces and the cinematic storytelling, and pushed each of them further than ever before.

"A powerful return and conclusion to the Modern Warfare series"
Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 offers an engaging single-player campaign that blends fast-paced combat, cinematic presentation, and mission variety—even providing players with extra room to explore through the semi-open "Stranded" mission. The experience is further enhanced by detailed graphics, exceptional sound design, and strong voice acting. However, inconsistent narrative quality, the negligible impact of player choices, and certain issues with AI and technical performance prevent the game from reaching its full potential. Its ultimate success as a complete package will depend on the quality and stability of its other game modes following launch.

If, like me, you're still playing the Call of Duty series for its single-player campaigns, I can confidently say that Infinity Ward's four years of hard work have more than paid off. This is hands down the best campaign experience I've had since 2019's Modern Warfare.
Metacritic user score 8.9/10 (513 ratings).

Final Fantasy Resonance brings together everything I love about the series in one extraordinary adventure. Its gripping story, rewarding turn-based combat and flexible Visions system fit together beautifully, elevated by gorgeous HD-2D art and a sublime soundtrack. This game reminded me why I fell in love with Final Fantasy, and gave me new reasons to love it.

Being a Final Fantasy fan has never been easier or more rewarding. While the mainline entries focus on pushing novelty, Final Fantasy Resonance bets on familiarity and years of learned design, delivering an experience that feels comforting yet refreshingly distinct.

Final Fantasy Resonance is the culmination of classic Final Fantasy exploding into a new era of gaming. The game feels both nostalgic and like an evolution of everything that once made Final Fantasy the face of RPGs. This is the game that redefines what Final Fantasy should keep at its core moving forward.

I was shocked by how much I loved Final Fantasy: Resonance. I loved the game so much that I was regularly, randomly getting emotional at the realization that this was something I wanted so badly. To some people, including myself, Final Fantasy: Resonance is going to be a dream come true that fills a void for new traditional JRPGs. It’s not a strategy JRPG, and it’s not an action JRPG; Final Fantasy: Resonance is a perfection of classic story-driven turn-based JRPG tropes. It has plenty of quality-of-life features, but it’s not trying to experiment or evolve the genre. The game is a much-needed and much-desired back-to-basics, made by the giant company that created the genre. Final Fantasy: Resonance is my game of the year right now and is a must-play for all JRPG and Final Fantasy fans.

Final Fantasy Resonance from Square Enix is another wonderful adventure within the Final Fantasy family album. It’s a fun story with great, innovative turn-based action, and it looks gorgeous. One of my surprise hits for 2026.

Final Fantasy Resonance is a giant bowl of pure, unadulterated nostalgia, wrapping Brave Exvius in a gorgeous HD-2D bow and pretending its shameless fan-service is a brand-new JRPG. Turn up the difficulty, sink 70 hours into micro-managing vision builds, and enjoy a surprisingly mature, meticulously paced script that gives every main character and sidekick room to breathe—making side quests so well-crafted you’ll actually want to do them all.
Presentational inconsistencies are the only concern for an otherwise excellent JRPG adaptation. Final Fantasy Resonance is a JRPG for fans old and new, traditional, or mobile.

Final Fantasy Resonance celebrates the series as much as it reinvents the mobile game it's based on. The writing is great, with deep characters and story moments that stayed with me after the credits rolled. Rain and company are great leads, with the villains being just as strong. Combat is a blast, inviting plenty of experimentation with the Visions, even if it can drag in the final hours with similarly lacklustre dungeons. There may be issues, but they get lost in the bombast, gorgeous cutscenes and environments that make full use of the HD-2D art style. Final Fantasy Resonance is fantastic, and I hope we return to this world for the rest of the mobile game's story arcs. It's one I'd be happy to return to.

Final Fantasy Resonance is a love letter to the franchise and a modern take on the classic JRPG, with an engaging story, memorable characters, gorgeous visuals, a fantastic soundtrack and a fresh twist on turn-based combat (random encounters included). There’s plenty to explore and do, although some side quests are a bit of a mixed bag. Still, it’s a hopeful sign that Square Enix is willing and able to deliver great classic turn-based Final Fantasy games again, and if this succeeds, I’ll be first in line for more of this.

Final Fantasy Resonance is a near-masterpiece, delivering fantastic combat, memorable characters, a compelling story, and stunning HD-2D visuals. Minor design flaws and its recycled plot hold it back from perfection, but it’s still an exceptional Final Fantasy experience.

While it still leaves plenty of content from the game that inspired it for future sequels, Final Fantasy Resonance brings one of Square Enix's best games of the last decade to consoles. The title features excellent characters and narrative, combat that captures the best of the series' classics without the limitations of a mobile game, and a beautiful visual overhaul in HD-2D. If you're a Final Fantasy fan, you'll love the experience.

Final Fantasy Resonance recaptures the classic essence of the series with an adventure that combines strategic turn-based combat, world exploration, and an epic story shaped by crystals and the fate of its heroes. Its HD-2D visuals look spectacular, while the Visions add variety and a touch of nostalgia to every battle. Although the difficulty can be challenging and there’s a lack of supporting characters, it’s a must-play tribute for fans.

Final Fantasy Resonance may not reinvent the airship, but it incorporates every mainline Final Fantasy title—directly, as classic characters appear as Visions, or indirectly, through a story that draws from every installment. It’s a splendid celebration of the series ahead of its 40th anniversary.

Final Fantasy’s HD-2D debut is a winning celebration of what made gamers fall in love with the franchise in the first place. While its mobile origins sometimes show, it’s been fleshed out into a wonderful role-playing game with fun fan service and plenty of depth. The brilliant turn-based battle system on display keeps Final Fantasy Resonance engaging from start to finish.

Final Fantasy Resonance is a heartfelt return to the series' classic roots, blending rewarding turn-based combat, flexible character customization, and engaging exploration into a compelling HD-2D adventure. Its memorable cast and inventive Vision system breathe new life into familiar JRPG traditions, even if uneven storytelling, pacing issues, and inconsistent presentation occasionally hold it back. Despite these shortcomings, Resonance confidently demonstrates why traditional Final Fantasy adventures remain so appealing.

Despite its exhilarating gameplay, FF Resonance is far from perfect. At times, it plays things too safe, holds your hand a little too tightly, and feels far too easy before finally showing its teeth. You could pick apart its flaws and draw up a lengthy list of grievances, but then a single battle, a familiar melody, or a beautifully staged cutscene comes along and makes it all seem rather trivial. Not because nostalgia blinds us to its shortcomings, but because the game reminds us, with Bahamut’s might and Shiva’s grace, what Final Fantasy is all about.

Final Fantasy Resonance already had a head start thanks to Brave Exvius's excellent storytelling, and the demo had shown plenty of promise, but we could never have imagined that this adaptation of the original mobile gacha game would captivate us for over 70 hours. Along the way, we rediscovered the grandeur of JRPGs from their golden age, filled with secrets, optional bosses, hidden weapons, spectacular summons, and emotional moments set to unforgettable music. The latest effort from Team Asano and Lancarse is a genuine love letter to fans of Japanese role-playing games and, of course, Final Fantasy itself, a franchise represented here with love, respect, and devotion in every single pixel.

Final Fantasy Resonance does an outstanding job of recreating what made the classic Final Fantasy games so beloved. It captures the feeling of starting a new Final Fantasy game and wanting to see where it leads, with some of the best pacing in any RPG. Square Enix has been refining HD-2D for years, and Resonance is its strongest showcase yet. Most importantly, it is a reminder of just how timeless the foundation of Final Fantasy really is. The series has changed enormously over the decades, but Resonance shows that Square Enix can bring the best of the classic and modern eras together. This is truly a Final Fantasy for RPGamers.
Final Fantasy Resonance won't change anyone's mind about turn-based RPGs, but it will remind fans why they fell in love with Final Fantasy over 25 years ago.
There is a lot to love about Final Fantasy Resonance. Its charm is undeniable. Its great cast of characters, fantastic combat, and in depth customization help it stand out in a crowded field.
Final Fantasy Resonance is an addictive, mechanically deep, and gorgeous role playing game.

Final Fantasy Resonance is an incredible reimagining of a beloved mobile game. While some parts can be frustrating, it’s not enough to diminish the overall stellar experience, and it’s easy to recommend to Final Fantasy and retro JRPG fans.

Final Fantasy Resonance takes a discontinued mobile game and reinterprets it as a fluid, fast-paced RPG you shouldn’t miss. The leveling curve for the game’s Visions can be a little wonky, but the turn-based gameplay, party customization, and stellar presentation make that a trifle moot, as it both appropriately lionizes Final Fantasy and offers a new experience for those who missed the mobile game.

By far the franchise's best spin-off, feeling like a lost mainline entry from the SNES era with the best turn-based combat the series has to offer, even if it still carries traces of its mobile game origins in some of its visuals and presentation.

Square Enix has launched a parallel path for Final Fantasy—one that we hope marks the beginning of a revival, which is not only possible but highly desirable, given the series' storied history and the weight of the name it carries. Resonance effortlessly embraces the stylistic hallmarks of the past, breathing new life into them to satisfy the many fans who felt disappointed—and, in a sense, betrayed—by the direction taken by the numbered entries following Final Fantasy X. With this brilliant installment, the saga proves it can simultaneously nurture its two distinct identities: one defined by constant experimentation—straying from its core genre to reach new audiences—and another that proudly and consciously honors the brand’s origins, as well as the fans who helped make this flagship franchise from the Japanese company a global success.

Final Fantasy Resonance is a great remake that shows just how good smaller-budget projects can be for the series. It’s just missing some of the depth we’ve come to expect from Square Enix’s bigger projects. [Issue#376, p.46]

From its very classic structure to all the familiar faces popping up throughout the adventure, not to mention a famous summon making an appearance right from the start, this new Final Fantasy clearly knows how to play on nostalgia. And honestly, it does it so well that it's hard to complain. The turn-based combat doesn't really bring anything new to the table, but it works like a charm. The HD-2D visuals are also looking better and more dynamic than ever. And there's enough here to win over players who aren't necessarily fans of the series. Newcomers can jump straight in and enjoy a really solid JRPG. As for longtime fans who can tell you which game each of the 26 visions comes from without even thinking about it, well, they'll be in heaven.

A Crystal-led quest and a close-knit party give Final Fantasy Resonance the feel of an earlier Final Fantasy adventure. Its turn-based battles carry that old-school appeal forward, with a satisfying cadence that makes dismantling a tough boss especially rewarding. The story leaves some of its more interesting ideas unexplored, but the characters provide much of the journey's heart and soul. Seeing Brave Exvius get a second life in such gorgeous HD-2D makes me want Square Enix to give more of its forgotten adventures the same treatment.

Resonance's stunning blend of 2D and 3D visuals, majestic soundtrack, engaging combat, and hours of rewarding content helps bring these elements together in an adventure that feels quintessentially Final Fantasy.
Featuring turn-based combat, HD-2D visuals, and plenty of returning characters, Final Fantasy Resonance is a nostalgic treat perfect for old-school Final Fantasy fans.

Final Fantasy Resonance is a perfect entry point for newcomers and a celebration of the franchise for longtime fans. The turn-based combat is the real star: the Vision system offers endless depth, especially when you mix Visions with characters they weren’t designed for. The HD-2D visuals and soundtrack shine, but the clichéd story and generic main cast can’t match the legacy heroes who appear as Visions.

Final Fantasy Resonance is an excellent old-school RPG that blends a
gorgeous HD-2D visual style with turn-based combat packed with strategic
depth. The Stagger system, extensive party customization, and Visions,
which let players tap into the abilities of familiar characters from
across the franchise, keep battles engaging and reward careful planning.
The main story takes around 30 hours to complete, while those looking to
see everything can easily spend twice as long with the game. That said,
the slower pacing may not appeal to everyone, and some uneven difficulty
spikes can be frustrating. The lack of Brazilian Portuguese text support
is also disappointing. Even with these drawbacks, Final Fantasy
Resonance remains a strong adventure for fans of traditional RPGs.

Final Fantasy Resonance manages to transform its nod to the past into something more than a mere nostalgic exercise. The return to turn-based combat, the Stagger and Visions systems, and a highly refined HD-2D art style deliver a classic JRPG experience that feels anything but dated. Certain design choices—such as random encounters, backgrounds that don’t always hit the mark, and, most notably, the complete absence of Italian-language support—prevent the package from being flawless; nevertheless, the end result remains a compelling celebration of Final Fantasy’s historical identity.

It would be easy for the game to feel awkward or like it wants to be something else. It doesn’t. And nothing about it feels like a retooled gacha game. Instead, Final Fantasy Resonance’s masterful presentation, along with its understanding of why people yearn for a return to those games, makes for a fully realized, confident experience that stands on its own, originality be damned.

Final Fantasy: Resonance transforms a discontinued mobile game into a genuine single-player, turn-based JRPG. Its enhanced HD-2D pixel-art presentation brings greater emotional impact to a traditional tale of crystals, while a combat system that combines turn-based strategy with classic Final Fantasy mechanics, alongside the freedom to mix and match Vision abilities, delivers over 30 hours of enjoyable gameplay. Although its mobile game origins leave some shortcomings in side quests and exploration, that long-missed flavor of golden-era Final Fantasy is a rare treat these days.

Ghost of Yōtei: Echoes of Sekigahara is a DLC that expands Atsu's journey without altering the base game's core formula. Its storyline, new region, side activities, and the Most Wanted mode deliver compelling content for players eager to return to this world. While it doesn't reinvent the original experience, it stands as a worthwhile expansion for those craving more.

Final Fantasy Resonance might not be a true HD-2D game, but makes up for that by delivering in almost every other way. A good story, great characters, music, quests and fantastic combat system make this a Final Fantasy you need to play.

Final Fantasy Resonance makes the most enjoyable possible use of the series' 40-year history, while delivering fantastic gameplay built around its brilliant Visions system and satisfying Stagger combos. One of the best JRPGs of recent years, and an absolute must-play for fans of the series.

Final Fantasy Resonance brings classic turn-based combat and HD-2D visuals together in a promising RPG that celebrates the franchise's legacy. Its Vision system adds tactical depth, while Espers and iconic characters give exploration a rewarding purpose. However, some unbalanced mechanic and visually inconsistent CGI sequences hold a little back an otherwise compelling experience.

Final Fantasy Resonance is a visually stunning HD-2D adventure that combines turn-based combat with a nostalgic and flexible character progression system. This makes it an easy recommendation, but a predictable storyline, underdeveloped characters and the occasional pacing issues prevent it from reaching the heights of some of the series’ finest entries.
Final Fantasy Resonance is a great game, especially if you feel the strong sense of nostalgia needed to truly draw you in.

The mix of new and old in FINAL FANTASY RESONANCE makes for an engaging story with a visceral battle system and a world that's a joy to explore. However, I wish the visions mechanic was more central to the game and its writing can be eye-rolling at parts.

Final Fantasy Resonance is a gift to fans who have been looking forward to a new Final Fantasy title crafted in HD-2D. From its visuals to its systems, the game is filled with elements that evoke nostalgia for the series' past. It also delivers an almost flawless remake experience. However, those hoping for something truly different may find themselves a little disappointed.
A gorgeous 2D-3D love letter to the franchise for its 40th anniversary, Final Fantasy Resonance is a nostalgic joy that all long-time fans should experience.

Final Fantasy Resonance is a good game, featuring beautiful graphics, a solid story, and an excellent soundtrack. It falls far short of being a "great" Final Fantasy title, however—largely because the franchise’s standard, especially in its classic entries, is exceptionally high. Even so, fans will find a game here that strikes the right nostalgic chords and delivers a solid 35 to 40 hours of fun.

Final Fantasy Resonance is a surprising JRPG, both in terms of its meticulous craftsmanship and its exquisite inspiration from Square's 2D-era masterpieces. The Japanese company has managed to create a game that stands on its own two feet, rising from the ashes of the mobile project Final Fantasy Brave Exvius. The turn-based mechanics work very well, as does the Vision system, even if the narrative premise is extremely self-referential. Overall, the gameplay may be very traditional, but it satisfies longtime fans and has the potential to win over younger gamers. The 2.5D graphics are increasingly refined, delivering visuals that are often breathtaking and demonstrating how firmly this style has become part of Square Enix's DNA. The audio is excellent, including the arrangements of several classic themes from the series, but the game lacks an Italian localization. The story holds up, although it loses momentum at times, with the narrative progressing at two different speeds. The same can be said of the characters, some of whom feel all too familiar. Even so, Final Fantasy Resonance proves that when Square Enix sets out to create a great turn-based game, it rises to the occasion and shows that it hasn't forgotten its roots.

What defines Final Fantasy? A fundamental question that is regularly the subject of fiery discussions among fans, as Square Enix's traditional brand has continually reinvented itself over the years. If the recent series direction with its action-oriented real-time combat systems didn’t suit you, Final Fantasy Resonance should be right up your alley. The title pays homage to the games of the SNES era and should make all fans of classic (J)RPG adventures happy. Newcomers also get their money's worth: If you've only flirted with the earlier games in the series from afar, Resonance is a great entry point. The title does an exemplary job of charmingly combining numerous series influences into a modern, best-of experience.
Gradually, this RPG of craterous lows and wondrous highs coheres into a work of compelling theatricality and mechanical intensity.

If you’re a Final Fantasy fan who enjoys retro-style JRPGs, then Final Fantasy Resonance will absolutely be for you. It does a fantastic job of paying homage to everything that’s preceded it while not being afraid to introduce modern ideas into the gameplay. However, I can’t help but feel like Square Enix has done better in this department before, and while I still very much enjoyed Resonance, I think if it pushed the boat out a bit more visually and narratively, it could’ve been something truly special.

Square Enix has hit on something surprisingly special with Final Fantasy Resonance. While its story and characters struggle to break away from being all too predictable at times, its old-school, turn-based gameplay is fantastic.

Final Fantasy Resonance is well-suited for both veterans of the franchise and newcomers to the JRPG genre. The gameplay is entertaining and varied. Visually, however, the stylishly designed HD-2D graphics alternate with 3D sequences that seem somewhat out of place.
It serves as a means to preserve and breathe new life into the original work, while simultaneously offering a highly enjoyable adventure for fans of more classic Final Fantasy titles.

All of this combined with the best usage of the HD-2D art style to date makes Final Fantasy Resonance a triumph. For those wondering if there's still juice in Final Fantasy as a 2D RPG, this is the game that proves that the series is still the gold standard.

The experiment of imagining how an old-school Final Fantasy might evolve has been a success. Square Enix took the mobile game Brave Exvius and, from its ashes, built a title that revives a narrative formula faithful to the traditions of the past, with well-developed characters and good plot twists, even if it doesn’t offer anything truly original. At the same time, it recreates an entire world to explore, just like in the JRPGs of yesteryear: in some cases, it does so perhaps a bit hastily, but the overall result is truly excellent, thanks above all to one of the best implementations of HD-2D graphics ever seen.

Final Fantasy Resonance is a tremendously enjoyable adventure, with fast-paced combat that encourages experimentation and a very well-balanced progression system. Its spectacular HD-2D presentation and magnificent soundtrack round out a JRPG that knows how to make the journey a constant pleasure.

Final Fantasy Resonance weaves a richly textured journey on PS5, anchored by nuanced character progression and atmospheric world design. Despite occasional narrative lulls and familiar conventions, its thoughtful mechanics and emotional resonance deliver a memorable experience that genre fans will thoroughly appreciate.

Final Fantasy Resonance is a solid, unapologetically classic turn-based JRPG that successfully adapts the mobile gacha title Brave Exvius into a full-fledged single-player experience. Its HD-2D visuals and strategic combat, built around elemental weaknesses and the flexible Visions system, offer genuine depth and satisfying party customization. The world map is a joy to explore, packed with secrets and quality-of-life conveniences that respect your time. However, the narrative feels rushed and thinly sketched, never delving deeply into its cast, while inflated enemy HP turns many battles into tedious endurance tests rather than tactical puzzles. The result is a game that nails the feel of a classic Final Fantasy but struggles to tell a story worthy of its mechanics. For genre veterans craving a lengthy, strategic adventure, it's an easy recommendation, just be prepared for some padding along the way.

Final Fantasy Resonance deserves every single minute of the player's attention. Whether through the dialogue, excellently performed by the voice actors, or the engaging battles, the game constantly pours its heart out. Yes, there are plenty of genre clichés, but here they serve more as great references to the franchise itself, which is one of the precursors of RPGs. Crafted with immense love for its past and for the stories yet to come, this is an adventure everyone will love, even in its simplest moments.

Like nostalgic ride through the old neighborhood, Final Fantasy Resonance is a breezy and charming entry to the expansive saga that doesn't quite rank up there with the all-time greats. Still, it's more Final Fantasy, and that's always a good thing.

Final Fantasy Resonance captures the spirit of the older entries in this emblematic JRPG series, delivering an engaging tactical-based combat system and an expansive world to explore. Its nostalgic appeal is perfectly captured through the beautiful pixel art and the variety of its locales. However, the overall experience is dragged down by clichéd characters and a rather flat overarching story.

Final Fantasy Resonance is a fantastic return to the series’ roots, featuring excellent turn-based combat, an engaging Echoes system, and perhaps the best HD-2D visuals to date. It may not be the new classic hardcore fans were hoping for, but it’s a great reminder of what Final Fantasy once was and what it could become again if its developers focused on the right things.

Final Fantasy Resonance is a fun JRPG releasing just when I personally needed a classic turn-based experience, but in a world with HD-2D releases of classic Square Enix games and Pixel Remasters of the first six Final Fantasy games, Resonance just isn’t an essential experience. Final Fantasy Resonance doesn’t have to do anything new to be a good game, but something fresh could’ve made it a great one.
Final Fantasy Resonance rises like a phoenix from the ashes of Brave Exvius - but the resurrection wasn't wholly without issue.

Final Fantasy Resonance is not only the first entry to use 2D-HD graphics but also brings back turn-based combat and many classic heroes.

Throughout this analysis I have been critical of several aspects because it is my job and the objective of any video game analysis, but let it be clear that I have enjoyed Final Fantasy Resonance like I haven't enjoyed a Final Fantasy game for a long time .

If you're left cold by the modern Final Fantasy games, Final Fantasy Resonance returns you to a simpler time, offering old-school action and a decent narrative, while wrapping it in a delightful visual wrapper.

Final Fantasy Resonance marks a triumphant return to the series' turn-based roots. Final Fantasy Resonance is a full-fledged RPG in its own right, with a solid story and a charming cast.

I've pined for years to see this beloved series return to its roots, instead of leaning into genres that don't really represent what Final Fantasy is. Final Fantasy Resonance is a loving homage to the series' classic virtues, with a charming story, strong gameplay and beautiful presentation, even if it deliberately doesn't reinvent the genre and its dungeons are somewhat uninspired.

It’s easy to see why Brave Exvius became a fan favorite, with an incredibly likable cast and a charismatic take on Final Fantasy’s classic setup of light vs. dark over the world’s natural forces. The long-awaited HD-2D Final Fantasy game absolutely delivered.

The return to pixel art is a great one. Final Fantasy truly feels like Final Fantasy again. Players who miss the old days of turn-based pixel RPGs will love this title. It is a solid return, but the lack of hooks to keep players in for longer sessions feels a bit disappointing.

A full-fledged fantasy. While it could easily fall into the trap of being just another mobile game remake, the truth is that this adventure feels like a true-blue Final Fantasy. Final Fantasy Resonance once again brings turn-based combat into the spotlight and makes excellent use of the series' legacy, but its story fails to match the quality of its gameplay.

The HD-2D RPG Final Fantasy Resonance awakens warm feelings in me for a video game series that has only grown close to my heart in recent times. It feels wonderfully classic, with a great many elements that are essential components of the series.

The new JRPG from Square Enix is a trip down memory lane, with cameos (or rather Visions) from previous games in the storied franchise. Final Fantasy resonance has one of the best iterations of the HD-2D aesthetic to date, it features gorgeous environments, expressive character sprites, and dynamic camera angles. Final Fantasy Resonance is a game that knows exactly what it wants to be: a bridge between the glorious past of the series and the present of Square Enix, a turn-based JRPG that does not reinvent the rules but executes them with taste, competence and a surprising amount of heart. Its combat is the real triumph, a system that starts simple and grows into one of the most customizable seen recently in the genre, while the HD-2D presentation turns every screen into a small interactive painting. If the story had been given the same level of care as the mechanics, we could be talking about an essential chapter of the saga. Final Fantasy Resonance delivers a wonderful return to the series’ classic roots, combining stunning HD-2D visuals, engaging strategic combat, and an enchanting soundtrack. Despite some shortcomings, particularly random encounters and occasional pacing issues, the game successfully revives the magic of classic Final Fantasy with a modern touch, offering a memorable adventure for fans of the series.

Final Fantasy Resonance is a blast from the franchise's past with its gorgeous HD-2D style and addictive turn-based combat, but more importantly, it feels like a celebration of Final Fantasy that's a must-play for long-time fans.

Final Fantasy Resonance successfully recaptures the classic flavor of the franchise. Its turn-based combat and striking art direction stand out as its greatest strengths, whereas its story and musical score fail to reach the same heights. A enjoyable and charming, if somewhat uneven, return that proves there is still magic left in this formula.

Final Fantasy Resonance was a throwback to the older games in the series and a step into the future. With the gorgeous mix of 2D and 3D art, I would love to see more games adopt this stunning art style. The story will actually make you feel something, and I love a game that makes me feel something all around.
Final Fantasy Resonance is one of the best Square Enix games that I’ve played in two decades.

Final Fantasy Resonance delivers an engaging turn-based RPG with strategic combat, rewarding exploration, and plenty of nostalgia for longtime fans. It's a love letter to the franchise while still delivering something that stands on its own.

FINAL FANTASY RESONANCE isn’t a groundbreaking video game, it’s a comforting nostalgia play. It takes the best of the games I grew up with and polishes it for a modern audience, but importantly, doesn’t buff out its retro charm.

Final Fantasy Resonance is a playable work of art that lets us control familiar characters within a shared world, where they coexist harmoniously alongside Rain and Lasswell, two endearing protagonists who honor the legacy of the franchise.

Final Fantasy Resonance works because it knows what makes a classic RPG appealing and adds enough modern touches to keep it interesting. Final Fantasy Resonance is a love letter to classic JRPGs, combining satisfying turn-based combat, gorgeous HD-2D visuals, and a soundtrack full of nostalgia. Its predictable story keeps it from a perfect score, but this is still an adventure worth experiencing.

Final Fantasy Resonance is a heartfelt, beautifully built turn-based throwback with deep Vision builds and satisfying stagger combat. If you love classic Final Fantasy, this is an easy and rewarding pick.

Final Fantasy Resonance is a wonderful return to the series' roots, with gorgeous HD-2D visuals, rewarding turn-based combat, and an outstanding soundtrack. Uneven storytelling, repetitive encounters, and the lack of Italian localization hold back an otherwise captivating RPG.

Final Fantasy Resonance isn’t a game that reinvents the series, but nor does it need to. The combination of nostalgic pixel art, 3D backgrounds, smooth turn-based combat and the Vision system results in an adventure that’s, above all, a real pleasure to play. The downside is that the story takes few risks and the gameplay rarely surprises. Nevertheless, with its charming presentation, strong soundtrack and loads of fan service, Resonance effortlessly puts a smile on my face. Those expecting innovation may sometimes be left wanting. But anyone simply looking for a lovely classic Final Fantasy will find a tasty meal here, topped with extra Chocobo sauce.

FINAL FANTASY RESONANCE transforms Brave Exvius into a gorgeous HD-2D RPG, trading mobile gacha systems for a memorable story and deeply customizable turn-based combat. Its Visions system is a standout, blending classic Final Fantasy heroes with satisfying strategic freedom, while the soundtrack and world-building shine. Random encounters and backtracking can feel dated, some special animations clash with the pixel-art presentation, and the lack of Brazilian Portuguese localization disappoints. Still, its polished battles and affectionate nods to the series make it a new classic.

Aside from the uninteresting stagger system, this is indeed an interesting game. The story is simple, but fun enough to play through. The characters are not original, yet charming enough. There is plenty to do, and the most enjoyable challenges lie in the optional missions. It is just a bit of a shame that the battle system lags behind somewhat. A demo is available featuring the complete first chapter. If you like that, you can essentially purchase this game without any problems.

A stunning HD-2D adventure that proves Final Fantasy magic is alive and well.

As someone who had never really found the right place to begin with Final Fantasy, Resonance proved to be a wonderful introduction to the series. Its memorable characters, engaging combat, stunning visuals and incredible soundtrack kept me invested from beginning to end, making this an adventure I won’t forget anytime soon. In fact, after finishing Resonance, I find myself wanting to explore more of what the Final Fantasy series has to offer, which may be the biggest compliment I can give it.

I think Final Fantasy Resonance is a fine game, fun even, and a wonderful celebration of the franchise. The whole thing feels like a love letter to both the series as a whole and to fans of the oldest games, especially. It’s just in service of a format that isn’t really for me, and that’s okay. The game doesn’t try to shy away from its turn-based JRPG roots but instead embraces them, attempting to present the best version of those old systems as they could. Ironically, I feel like the Resonance design has a potential future in itself for combat systems that aren’t this, and that has me more excited than anything else. It feels weird to say but I like Resonance more for the potential it represents than the celebration that it is. Still, if you’re a lifelong or diehard fan of the series, there’s a lot here to love and I’d still recommend it.
Who knew a more straightforward, nostalgia-fueled experience was all that was needed to get us to enjoy an RPG? Final Fantasy Resonance more than satisfied our itch for a good old school adventure.

Final Fantasy Resonance recaptures the fantasy of classic RPGs in an adventure filled with crystals, friendships, and turn-based combat. While the HD-2D visuals impress during action sequences, a predictable narrative and some drawn-out battles hold the experience back.
Final Fantasy Resonance turns a failed gacha into a solid RPG, with great combat and charm, even if its story mostly repeats Brave Exvius beats.

HD-2D gives Final Fantasy Resonance the old-school charm I’ve wanted to see from the series, while its Vision system and stagger-based combat add welcome depth to familiar turn-based battles. The story is fairly forgettable, but the adventure itself makes a convincing case for more classic-style Final Fantasy games.

FINAL FANTASY RESONANCE is a pleasant surprise that captures the best elements of the franchise, delivering an engaging RPG with strategic, enjoyable combat, deep customization, and plenty of opportunities to experiment with Visions and Espers. Its beautiful pixel art, rewarding exploration, side quests, and hidden secrets kept me invested for over 50 hours, despite some predictable plot twists, repetitive late-game battles, occasional performance issues, and the lack of Brazilian Portuguese localization. More than a nostalgic tribute, RESONANCE offers a complete RPG experience filled with memorable references, satisfying mechanics, and plenty of content for both longtime fans and newcomers. Ultimately, it is not just a gift to fans, but a great FINAL FANTASY in its own right.

Final Fantasy Resonance is an engaging RPG that captures the charm of classic JRPGs through rewarding exploration, strategic turn-based combat, compelling characters, and a polished HD-2D presentation complemented by a memorable soundtrack. Despite some pacing issues and repetitive encounters, its strengths outweigh its flaws, proving that the traditional Final Fantasy formula can still deliver a captivating experience. Balancing nostalgia with thoughtful execution, Resonance is a worthwhile adventure for fans eager to explore fantastical worlds and enjoy challenging turn-based battles.

Resonance looks at elements that Final Fantasy abandoned or modified over the past few decades and asks what would happen if they were simply produced again with modern technology, budget, and expertise. The answer is an extraordinarily well-executed traditional JRPG. I missed picking four characters, looking at a turn order, and spending a few seconds thinking before taking action. I missed coming across a new town, chatting with residents, buying equipment, and heading out to wander across the overworld map. I missed that feeling of getting an airship and realizing that previously inaccessible places were suddenly part of my route. Resonance gives all of that back.

Final Fantasy Resonance is a title that could very well reshape the series going forward, if enough people get behind it. The turn-based combat is fantastic, and while the Vision system could use a bit of a refresh, it celebrates the legacy of this storied franchise in remarkable ways. Rain's adventure is one that is typical of the series, but the attention given to every single character here does elevate that typical story to new heights.

With a unique blend of classic and modern elements, Final Fantasy Resonance features a combination of a linear campaign, an impactful story, and extremely fun combat. It is an exceptional JRPG that revives the most classic style of the Final Fantasy series, while simultaneously evolving the formula in new directions.
Final Fantasy Resonance is a glorious and gorgeous throwback to classic Final Fantasy, with plenty of modern twists and delightful story to tell.

Once you've gotten through the first few hours and the game finally unfolds its full potential, most of these criticisms turn out to be nitpicking. Nevertheless, there was certainly more potential here, and one shouldn't expect the innovative spirit of an "Adventures of Elliot".

Final Fantasy Resonance is a triumph in recreating and repurposing an almost decade-old mobile game. While it can stumble a little in the process, such as dungeons often being too small, or optional encounters being too repetitive, my issues with the game seem to revolve around simply wanting more. Resonance is a celebration of the traditional Final Fantasy formula and a reminder of just how damn well that formula still works.

With a surprisingly deep cast of characters, a combat system full of variety and choice, fantastic visuals and a grand soundtrack to bring it all together, Final Fantasy Resonance isn’t just a worthy game in the series; it’s one of the best in the franchise.

Final Fantasy Resonance is a true “celebratory title” that not only honors and pays tribute to the classic era of Final Fantasy, but also brings the beloved story of Brave Exvius to life in a format that everyone can enjoy.

In a time where video games are so often divisive and trying to please everyone seems impossible, Final Fantasy Resonance might just be the closest game in a long time we’ve gotten to pulling that off.

Final Fantasy Resonance captures the appeal of classic Final Fantasy with strong writing, beautiful presentation, flexible Visions, engaging summons, and rewarding nostalgic connections. Limited maps, repetitive dungeons, delayed encounter controls, unclear dialogue choices, and overly forgiving early combat hold it back, but never overshadow its strengths. For me, it feels like the team’s best work—an adventure absolutely worth your time, with the potential to become a cult classic and one of its biggest successes outside Octopath.

While avoiding being outright bad in any regard, Final Fantasy Resonance does little to captivate the player. The combat system is by far the best element, but largely seems like a reworking of an idea more successfully executed in the Octopath franchise. And while moments of characterization are charming and well written, the actual narrative only pinballs between tropes until it winds up at a rote climax. Despite being positioned as a celebration of the series, it does little but half-heartedly play a couple of the hits and ask you if you remember the good old days.

Final Fantasy Resonance builds on the foundation of Final Fantasy: Brave Exvius, transforming its source material into a fully realized console RPG while adding enough new ideas to stand on its own. The Vision system and Stagger Battle System add meaningful depth to both combat and progression, strengthening the connection between the game's narrative themes and its gameplay mechanics.

Ultimately, Final Fantasy Resonance is both a celebration of Final Fantasy's storied legacy and a compelling RPG in its own right. With its engaging combat, expansive world, memorable cast, and stunning presentation, it delivers an adventure that feels both nostalgic and refreshingly modern.

Final Fantasy Resonance masterfully delivers on its promise to bring the Final Fantasy franchise back to its roots, offering an emotional story filled with memorable characters alongside a fun and rewarding combat system. It lays an excellent foundation for the franchise's future, both for the HD-2D formula and for potential mainline entries that may embrace turn-based combat.

If you miss the FINAL FANTASY RPGs built around crystals, magic, abilities, and turn-based battles, RESONANCE deserves your attention. And even if your preference lies with the modern chapters of the series, there's a great adventure waiting for those who decide to get to know Rain, Lasswell, and Fina.

Final Fantasy Resonance turns the foundations of Brave Exvius into a richer, more ambitious traditional JRPG. Solid combat, the freedom offered by the Visions, gorgeous HD-2D visuals, excellent sound, and respectful fan service sustain an adventure of over sixty hours. The story is slow and uneven, and the lack of Italian localization weighs more than expected, but it remains a fun, rich celebration of the saga.
Final Fantasy Resonance is an unforgettable return to the golden age of turn-based RPGs and HD-2D at its absolute finest.

Final Fantasy Resonance is a glorious celebration of Final Fantasy's illustrious history, with fanfare in abundance, and a blend of modern and retro ideals. Boasting pristine pixel-art, a typically superb score, and nostalgia-fueled battle systems, Resonance is a game for Final Fantasy purists that want to revel in all the franchise has offered us down the years.

You can't ignore the fact that this new Final Fantasy game is cleary showing its "resurrected gacha game" aesthetics even with the new HD-2D touch-up. Its story is also pretty standard and hits all the familiar notes despite its charming heroes and side characters. Nonetheless, Final Fantasy Resonance scratches that turn-based JRPG itch you need, albeit in a familiar package.

Final Fantasy Resonance is a purrtastic love letter to classic Final Fantasy, delivering an entertaining journey with gorgeous pixel art, a fantastic soundtrack, and strategic turn-based combat. It’s a must-play RPG for longtime fans and newcomers are welcome to ride this chocobo.

Final Fantasy Resonance proves that looking to the past can be the best way to rediscover a franchise's identity. Square Enix delivers a rewarding JRPG packed with nostalgia, deep combat, and vast exploration. Despite minor narrative flaws and localization limits, it's a triumphant return to classic airships, crystals, and turn-based battles. Sometimes, to move forward, you must remember where you started.

Final Fantasy Resonance shines by balancing the franchise's rich heritage with a modern and exciting pace. The title goes a bit beyond a beautiful HD-2D presentation, delivering agile combat that respects the player's time. The game ensures you care about your team, making Rain and Lasswell's journey an easy recommendation for both nostalgic veterans and those discovering the magic of the crystals for the first time.

Final Fantasy Resonance is a game that stirred up a lot of different feelings in me. While I feel that it stands completely on its own and could be a numbered entry in the series, I also feel that half of the affection I had for the game is due to the weight that the entire franchise carries. These somewhat contradictory thoughts ran through my entire experience, during which I really enjoyed the game, but also had some low points with it.

«Final Fantasy Resonance» feels like coming home. It delivers everything I’ve missed since «Final Fantasy X»: turn-based combat that makes me think and a story that makes me feel like I’m part of it rather than just watching from the sidelines. On top of that, it boasts the most beautiful HD-2D visuals I’ve seen yet.  It’s essential for fans of classic Japanese RPGs – and the best «Final Fantasy» in 25 years, as far as I’m concerned.
Final Fantasy Resonance is easily one of the best turn-based RPGs of recent times and a standout Final Fantasy title, a love letter to the legendary franchise.

Everything in Final Fantasy Resonance works and fits as it should. The best part is that this can be your first Final Fantasy game, and it'll be a great place to start. Resonance's characters are likable, and the battle system is easy to learn but has enough depth for min-maxers to enjoy. I'm really trying to think about things I don't like about the game, but I can’t. It doesn't get much better than that kind of praise.
By remake attested, by port revealed, their tale can now be told (on PC).
