Gears E-Day proves that looking back can, indeed, help you look forward, too.

The legendary cover-based shooter returns with what might be its swan song; while it exhibits all the genre's flaws, it nonetheless delivers a solid, visually stunning military sci-fi experience—one that is perhaps longer than it should be, yet somehow you end up forgiving it. However, if you are expecting a major evolution or simply don't enjoy shooting from behind cover, steer clear.

It's far from flawless, but after seven years away - and a full two decades since the Locust first smashed through the ground - The Coalition has succeeded in making this particular forever war feel fresh again. [Issue#430, p.96]
A prequel that looks and feels far too similar to the 20-year-old original and while it’s a vastly more entertaining experience in co-op, it still feels worryingly old-fashioned and overfamiliar.

Gears of War: E-Day delivers some of the most spectacular large-scale action sequences in recent memory, but is held back by an irritating cast of characters and unnecessary padding between the firefights.

Gears of War: E-Day is an excellent-feeling third-person shooter. It’s gorgeous, runs well (even in split-screen), and is a ton of fun when it focuses on firefights. It lacks an interesting take on being both a prequel and an invasion day story mechanically, slipping back into classic Gears a little too quickly. The open zone levels are dull, checklist-filled areas that create unnecessary downtime. Multiplayer is sharp and well executed, but also doesn’t rise above being more Gears. Horde Siege takes on the faults of the open campaign levels and becomes too focused on meta upgrades, losing sight of having fun in the current match, not the next one. It’s well-crafted, but ultimately feels at its best when it’s trying the least.

Gears of War: E-Day can be placed on two sides of a coin. On one side, the campaign is lackluster and fails to create a meaningful, lasting impression. On the other side of the coin, the multiplayer, both PvP and PvE, are some of the best you can get within the third-person shooter space. Horde mode feels perfectly refined for what The Coalition built, and PvP remains highly satisfying, especially with the addition of all the new weapons. In the end, it’s a matter of what the player is coming for. The campaign is the weakest link, while its multiplayer helps propel it into a lasting experience. In the end, Gears of War: E-Day is something that could have been so much more.

While the campaign in Gears of War: E-Day doesn’t quite win me over due to its structural weaknesses, the game demonstrates the potential of its new mechanics in its solid multiplayer mode. Personally, I see this as the main reason to buy the game—especially if you play with a regular group so you can coordinate your tactics more effectively. The new Horde mode will certainly take some getting used to for fans. But especially given the larger map, I see a lot of interesting possibilities here for future expansions, provided Xbox gives the game the support it needs. Ultimately, while I’m somewhat torn about the overall package, I’m optimistic about the future of the series.

While Gears of War: E-Day delivers a solid online multiplayer experience, its single-player campaign plays it safe, offering little new in the way of storytelling or level design, and despite a 20-year gap between the original Gears of War and E-Day, the gameplay shows no meaningful evolution, let alone two decades worth of progress.

Gears of War: E-Day is a prequel, which doesn't feel like the next big chapter in GoW universe. Still, nimbler movement, weapon mods and excellent Horde Siege mode freshen up the familiar formula a bit.

There's no point pretending otherwise: we're living in a post-Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine 2 world. Up against the brutal generosity of its direct heir, Gears of War: E-Day simply doesn't measure up. And it would be a lie to say my feelings didn't turn from disappointment to anger over these 14 hours of play. Watching the series that once dictated terms to an entire industry turn into a sluggish follower—bloated with loot and filler—is heartbreaking. The worst part is that Act 3 and the sound design serve as a reminder of what Gears of War could still be. The rest just highlights what it has become: a franchise on autopilot with little left to say, except to cling to memories of its former glory. We tried everything to love it. It did precious little to make us.

Gears of War: E-Day has become a clear embodiment of the modern problems of American game development and of Microsoft in particular. An inadequately large production budget forced the developers not to take risks, and as a result we got a rather boring story and gameplay that in certain aspects has even degraded. Sorry, but rewriting the origin story of the chainsaw gun for the third time doesn't amount to a breakthrough.
Gears has never felt better to play, or more creatively stagnant.
For better or worse, E-Day is distinctly Gears, and I had a good time with it, even if the story is disappointing and the open areas are fairly dull.

Gears of War: E-Day brings the series back to its literal roots, delivering all the blood-soaked action and characters that made it a hit. Filled with expansive maps, tons of thrilling enemy encounters, a slew of weapon modifications, and a truly gripping action-movie narrative, it's the must-own Xbox exclusive of 2026.

Gears of War excels when it leans into humanity versus monsters, is painted with a brush drenched in blood, and offers vicious, savage gameplay that belies surprisingly rich stories and heartfelt characters.

Gears of War: E-Day hits all the right notes for veteran Gears and newcomers alike. Witnessing the fall of Kalona is terrifying, but it's filled with the level of action you'd want from a Gears title.

Gears of War E-Day's campaign offers balls-to-the-wall action and rarely lets up, but that means the story takes more of a back seat than I'd like. It's good that time is given to the backstories of new protagonists Mags and Lucas, but given that the game is literally the playable Marcus and Dom backstory fans have been waiting decades to see, more time could have been spent on their relationship. In terms of pure gunplay, however, very little beats it this year.
E-Day boasts the best combat in 20 years of Gears games – but everything surrounding it is disappointing
Gears of War: E-Day is a good entry point.

The Coalition modernizes movement and cover mechanics without sacrificing the series' hallmarks-such as its sense of weight and brutality-delivering a spectacular campaign, a Versus mode that intelligently revives old-school multiplayer, and Horde Siege, an ambitious and compelling evolution of the classic Horde mode. Add a top-tier technical presentation to the mix, and the score speaks for itself.

Gears of War: E-Day has been promoted as the most ambitious game ever made by The Coalition, but to be honest, it feels like a step back from Gears 5 in several ways. The narrative is a lot less memorable, and the side content is forgettable. Its saving grace is that the third-person shooter gameplay is better than ever, thanks to improved movement and fluidity, making combat encounters generally a lot of fun. Still, it's not the kind of masterpiece that sells a console like the original did.

Gears of War: E-Day is the best game in the series. The story gives us an up-close and personal look at the events of E-Day, providing a horror-filled and harrowing experience. Meanwhile, the enhancements to movement are very welcome, and gunplay feels more varied with a great roster of weapons and the inclusion of mods.

Though fault can be found with its meaningless side quests and examples of knuckleheaded dialogue, Gears of War: E-Day gets so much of its core loop right. It's hard to recall a game nailing the desperate, helpless feeling of invasion quite like this, and E-Day sets a new benchmark for Gears' iconic gunplay. More than anything, E-Day is a technical crown jewel that delivers an audiovisual experience that, on Xbox, is unrivalled.
Gears of War: E-Day is here, bringing with it what feels like a new push for Xbox and one of the best entries into the long-running third-person shooter franchise.

Gears of War: E-Day is everything I wanted from a prequel and more. It finally delivers the Emergence Day story fans have waited two decades to experience, while deepening the relationship between Marcus and Dom and returning the series to the darker, horror-inspired tone of the original trilogy. With the best gameplay the franchise has ever had, incredible visuals, excellent pacing and memorable characters, E-Day isn’t just the best Gears game yet; it’s one of Xbox’s strongest exclusives in years.

Gears of War: E-Day successfully fulfils its mission of returning to the roots of the series, whilst offering noticeable improvements over all previous instalments and reminding us once again of the horror of the Locusts. Unfortunately, it also suffers from issues with pacing and enemy AI, while pushing Marcus into the background in favour of a new character. Nevertheless, this dynamic, emotional and extremely brutal shooter should appeal to fans of the series – and many others as well.

Gears of War: E-Day feels like an old series deliberately recreated with modern technology while preserving its aged character. Fans of Gears of War are unlikely to mind going through another adventure that feels familiar from start to finish.

Gears of War: E-Day is The Coalition's best campaign to date; an intense, spectacular experience that remains faithful to the franchise's roots. Its gripping story, dark atmosphere, industry-leading visuals, and satisfying arsenal make the return to Emergence Day an unforgettable roller coaster that honors the legacy of Gears.

Gears of War: E-Day may have a few shortcomings in its story, character development, and the overall depth of its Versus mode, but these issues don't take away from what is otherwise a fantastic experience. When it comes to gameplay, E-Day stands as one of the best entries in the franchise. Its 15-hour campaign delivers an exceptional level of excitement, backed by brilliantly designed levels. Meanwhile, Siege Horde offers hours of entertainment and has the potential to keep players engaged for the long run with the right content updates. Combined with stunning visuals and high-quality sound design, these elements make E-Day a worthwhile experience for Gears fans and a triumphant return for the franchise. It's a comeback that lives up to the series' legacy and one you shouldn't miss.
A gritty combat adventure with a tragic atmosphere.

As a complete package, Gears of War: E-Day is very good. The campaign may not be all that exciting, but it works fine and is elevated by the solid gunplay, especially if you play with real people rather than AI teammates. The adversarial multiplayer is fine if you can adapt to sticking with the one accepted play style. It is the PvE that really breathes life into the game and makes it a solid multiplier contender for a good while. While the game can be brutal for newcomers, it fits fan expectations well enough that they'd be happy to see this title in their libraries.

Gears of War: E-Day takes the series back to Emergence Day and the beginning of the Locust War through the eyes of Marcus and Dom. The campaign shows a peaceful city gradually turning into a devastated war zone while revealing the origins of several iconic elements of the series. Familiar cover-based combat has been refined with smoother movement and faster encounters, while multiplayer remains close to the classic formula and adds the more dynamic Horde Siege mode. Combined with impressive UE5 visuals, E-Day is a very good return to the roots of Gears.

Gears of War: E-Day marks a brilliant return for one of Xbox’s most iconic franchises, allowing players to experience E-Day and witness the beginning of Marcus and Dom’s story from a completely new perspective. The Coalition isn’t revolutionising the familiar formula, but in a way it’s building on it – improving mobility, shooting and exploration, offering a varied campaign, and in the process showcasing the immense capabilities of Unreal Engine 5. It’s a modern Gears game that never forgets its roots.

It's definitely a step in the right direction for the franchise. With its story, the way it's presented, and the gameplay, a solid GoW game is waiting for us. They've kindly reminded us once again why we love this series. We can easily overlook a few minor flaws.

Gears of War: E-Day is more than I could have hoped for: a focused, tightly contained, action-packed story filled with memorable characters and moments that deliver an emotional rollercoaster for those brave enough to witness the horrors of the first days of Emergence Day. E-Day is what a Gears of War game should be: relentlessly fun, engaging from all angles, and best experienced with friends.

With E-Day, the Gears of War saga delivers a dramatic and profound story centered on Marcus, Dom, and their traumas-but above all, on a humanity that was ready for peace and suddenly finds itself, overnight, in the midst of a war against a ruthless and brutal enemy. The gameplay has returned to the exceptionally high standards of the original trilogy, retaining its foundational elements while expanding every aspect to further enhance the experience-including weapons, enemies, and maps.
Gears of War: E-Day is a bold new step forward for the franchise, while looking backward to the core of what made this franchise so great.

Gears of War: E-Day is a phenomenal action triumph of the highest calibre that doesn’t let players catch their breath for a single second. It captivates with both its melancholic, raw and deeply tragic story campaign and its devilishly addictive yet exceptionally fair multiplayer. For me personally, it’s currently a shoo-in for Game of the Year, and I already know that I’ll be happily spending hundreds more hours in the ruined streets of Kalona. Look past the occasional technical glitches and join the front lines without hesitation, because the Locusts are breaking through to the surface and the relentless battle for humanity’s very survival has just begun.

Gears of War: E-Day delivers the franchise’s classic identity with hard-hitting gunplay, refined cover mechanics, diverse weapons and a dark atmosphere. Its prequel setting also makes for a friendly introduction for newcomers, while delivering the brutality that long-time fans expect.

E-Day is a major victory and a dream comeback for the studio, Microsoft, and most importantly, Gears fans. Smartly blending the dark, terrifying, and bloody atmosphere of the classic entries with a fully modern gameplay system, smooth animations, and graphics that push the boundaries of this generation, it delivers on every front. Whether you're a longtime fan of Marcus Fenix who misses the sound of a Lancer chainsaw, or a newcomer looking for pure, visceral, and flawless action, E-Day is a title you absolutely shouldn't miss.

Gears of War: E-Day is the game fans have been waiting for for many years. A return to the dirty, mean origins of the franchise, which recovers its most visceral identity with far-sighted and absolutely spot-on changes. Marcus and Dom's first adventure is spectacular and adrenaline-fueled, thanks to fun gameplay that respects the legacy of a twenty-year-old series modernized by greater dynamism in movement, cover and shootouts. While we wait to test the multiplayer, an absolutely distinctive feature of the series, The Coalition takes home a clear and evident success. One that some may find a bit too faithful to a game design born of another gaming era. But for everyone else it will be a warm homecoming.

Gears of War E-Day feels like an unnecessary prequel, and a bit of a cop-out to avoid addressing Gears 5's cliffhanger ending. It's a competent but forgettable campaign that's too long for its own good that wastes its new gameplay and mechanics on uninspired level design. That said, I'm sure playing this with 3 other friends can still be a blast.

A fantastic revival of the series, revisiting Emergence Day through Marcus, Dom, and the rest of the squad’s eyes. With evolved gameplay and epic visuals, it delivers an excellent experience for fans of the series.

Gears of War: E-Day takes players back to Emergence Day, the pivotal Locust invasion that defined the franchise, and while this prequel modernises its gameplay for some of the most fluid action seen from the series to date, it loses the spark that makes it a Gears experience in the process.

The Coalition delivers a visually breathtaking and atmospherically uncompromising action epic that takes the series back to its brutal roots through the raw story of a young Marcus and Dom. Despite occasional recycling of urban environments and minor pacing hiccups, it is an absolute triumph of the cover-shooter genre and an unforgettable ride that no gamer should miss.

With Gears of War: E-Day, Microsoft has unequivocally demonstrated its desire to restore the series to its former glory, and that The Coalition is the perfect studio to do so. From the campaign to the multiplayer modes, from the gameplay to the graphics and aesthetics, everything reflects the creative and developmental richness of a major production done right—not just thanks to a massive budget and many years of work, but also to good intentions, excellent ideas, and exceptional execution. At the same time, there’s no denying that there are a few minor issues here and there: the campaign suffers from some slight narrative, structural, and audio mixing shortcomings (including lip sync), while Versus and Horde Siege lack content volume—evidently in anticipation of substantial post-launch support.
If you're a Gears fan, you'll turn your nose up at the annoying new character early on, but you'll enjoy taking part in Emergence Day and learning how it all began.
An engaging story, tied together with some nifty new features that make for smoother gameplay, and more robust PvE and PvP multiplayer modes make this an absolutely irresistible package.

Gears of War: E-Day was a pleasant surprise for me, for XBOX, and for 2026 as a whole. While no Gears game has ever been a disaster, there's no denying that the franchise has been on a downward trajectory since Gears of War 4, struggling to recapture the appeal of the original trilogy. With E-Day, The Coalition has managed to restore the feeling that Gears is once again a flagship XBOX franchise, delivering a high-quality product packed with action from start to finish, meaningful gameplay innovations, breathtaking visuals, and a traditional multiplayer experience, even if there's still room for improvement in some areas.

Gears of War: E-Day is a highly solid entry in the Xbox franchise that successfully recaptures the series' core gameplay identity, horror, and visual grittiness. Although it stumbles in terms of narrative pacing, enemy variety, and certain artificial intelligence issues, its graphical performance and the evolution of its combat system more than make up for these shortcomings.

Gears of War is back with a guns-blazing attitude. If you love the good old mechanics from previous games, now further improved, this package has everything you need. The solid multiplayer and a campaign that strives to deliver an epic experience may still be overshadowed by narrative issues that should have been handled differently.

Gears of War: E-Day tells the story of a legendary event that has been talked about for years. It does so without shying away from grand storytelling or graphic violence. Getting almost everything right in terms of presentation, E-Day also delivers rock-solid gameplay with its fast-paced, menacing action. After taking a few hits with its recent entries, the series is back with a game that recaptures the grandeur of its glory days.

Ultimately, Gears of War: E-Day is a compelling reminder of what makes the franchise endure, even if it falls short of fully realising the potential of its return to the past. The Coalition has recaptured much of the series’ defining identity, from its uncompromising brutality and visceral combat to the emotional bond at the heart of its story. What it has not quite achieved is turning those strengths into a consistently memorable campaign.

The most successful aspect of the prequel is undoubtedly the relationship between Marcus Fenix and Dom Santiago. Their friendship gives the narrative its emotional heart, bringing back the humour, camaraderie, and underlying vulnerability that helped define the original trilogy. Tai further strengthens the connection to the series’ history, while Carlos and the references to established events give the story a broader sense of continuity. Crucially, E-Day does more than invite players to revisit familiar ground: at its best, it reminds us why these characters and their world mattered in the first place.

That same understanding extends to the gameplay. The return to the franchise’s brutal origins restores some of the menace that made the Locust such formidable adversaries, while the familiar arsenal and cover-based shooting remain as satisfying as ever. The combat has weight, the weapons retain their distinctive character, and well-executed encounters demonstrate that the foundations of Gears of War remain remarkably resilient. There is no inherent need to reinvent a formula that still works this well. The challenge is to keep it engaging over the course of an entire campaign, and this is where E-Day proves less convincing.

Its shortcomings become increasingly apparent as the hours accumulate. An overextended campaign, larger environments that too rarely translate into meaningful gameplay variety, and supporting characters who struggle to leave a lasting impression all dilute the experience. Boss encounters frequently favour endurance over ingenuity, while an intrusive interface and severe performance drops in demanding areas further compromise the action. Individually, these issues vary in significance; collectively, they prevent the game from achieving the consistency its strongest moments suggest is within reach.

For all its merits, E-Day is not the triumphant return that could have reasserted Gears of War at the very forefront of the genre. Nor does it recapture the impact of the original trilogy in its entirety. Yet judging the prequel solely against the legacy it seeks to revisit would mean overlooking a more encouraging truth: The Coalition understands the foundations on which that legacy was built. The problem is not a loss of identity, but an uneven ability to translate that identity into an experience that remains compelling from beginning to end.

The distinction matters most when the game returns to Marcus and Dom. Their relationship gives the campaign something that spectacle alone cannot provide: a personal stake in the unfolding catastrophe. Through them, Emergence Day becomes more than the beginning of a war; it becomes the defining experience of two soldiers whose friendship will shape the future of the series. It is in these moments that E-Day comes closest to recapturing the spirit of the original games, reminding us that beneath the armour, the chainsaw bayonets, and the relentless violence, Gears of War has always been a story about survival, friendship, and sacrifice.

That is ultimately what makes this prequel worth experiencing, despite its shortcomings. It does not deliver a uniformly successful return to the series’ origins, but it does reaffirm the value of the characters, the world, and the combat that have sustained the franchise for so long. Its strongest elements provide a solid foundation; its weaker ones make clear how much further that foundation could have taken it.

For The Coalition, the next challenge is not to rediscover what makes Gears of War distinctive, but to build on it with greater ambition and discipline. E-Day proves that the series still has a compelling story to tell and that Marcus and Dom remain at its heart. Whether that promise can be transformed into something truly exceptional will depend on what comes next. For now, this is a worthwhile return to the battlefield: one that honours the past, reclaims much of the franchise’s identity, and leaves room for a more assured future.
Gears of War: E‑Day shows the franchise’s enduring strength, delivering a visceral look at Emergence Day with new threats and classic, weighty combat.

Gears of War: E-Day is a stunning comeback with fun, fast-paced cover shooting, smart enemies and the best visuals in the series, held back only slightly by stiff NPC animations and some ragdoll glitches.

Gears of War: E-Day is precisely the turning point this storied franchise needed after years of trial and error—a glorious, dark, and visceral return to the authentic roots of a series defined by raw brutality and grueling combat. By reviving the heavy, terrifying weight of warfare, seamlessly blending modern movement with a dynamic, destructible cover system, and delivering one of this generation's most breathtaking visual showcases via Unreal Engine 5, The Coalition once again elevates the standard for third-person shooters. While underdeveloped chemistry between young Marcus and Dom, repetitive side quests, and a slight dip in late-game enemy variety hold it back from absolute perfection, the harrowing fall of Kalona alongside addictive gunplay, exceptional pacing, and a rich multiplayer suite make E-Day a gripping, bone-chilling triumph. It is a masterclass in gunpowder and gore that proves the Gears name still demands absolute reverence

Gears of War: E-Day is an absolute masterpiece and the perfect return to form for the franchise. Xbox and The Coalition made the brilliant decision to plug a massive narrative hole that fans have been wondering about for nearly two decades: how did Emergence Day actually happen? E-Day answers that question flawlessly. Thanks to smart mechanical tweaks and new traversal options, the gameplay is never dull; it is constantly engaging, always pushing you to see what horrific set-piece comes next. Because of all this, I firmly believe this is yet another massive win for the Xbox exclusive lineup.

Fans that played the original games on launch will appreciate just how dark and gritty Gears of War E-Day is, and the way the campaign develops with the Locust Horde gradually becoming more of a problem, the environmental destruction and level of detail around every bend definitely cements this game as one of the best looking exclusive Xbox titles

The longest Gears of War Campaign succeeds in entertaining gameplay, intriguing open world chapters with side objectives, and plenty of content to enjoy. The Campaign embraces co-op like no other game does these days and you could argue it's one of the best games that we have witnessed in the series.

E-Day understands that Gears of War has always been about more than shooting monsters. It is about the people standing beside you while you do it. Whether that person is sitting beside you on the couch in split screen, joining you online from across the country, or simply standing beside Marcus as an AI companion, E-Day constantly comes back to the idea that surviving this world is easier when you never fight alone.

Gears of War: E-Day was my first encounter with this popular series, and to be honest, it didn’t encourage me to check out the other games in the series. Don’t get me wrong—it’s not a bad game. Not at all. It’s just incredibly uneven. It’s a game full of extremes, where great, well-thought-out solutions are interspersed with ideas that are outright bad or suffer from poor execution. The latest Gears game offers a spectacular, almost cinematic adventure, accompanied by superb graphics and an incredible, dark atmosphere. Unfortunately, behind all of this lies, well, a terrible story and poorly written characters. Moving on, on the one hand, we have beautiful, detailed locations; on the other, however, we have tedious exploration and places that, despite their polished appearance, are completely forgettable. The same goes for the gameplay, which can be a lot of fun but at the same time grows tiresome due to its repetitiveness and, at times, is downright frustrating because of its uneven difficulty.
Gears of War: E-Day is a shot in the arm for the franchise. It pushes the franchise while returning to its roots and finding what is core to the heart of the series.

Gears of War: E-Day is more than just an attempt to revive past glories or recreate previous successes; it is a heartfelt tribute to the fans that lives up to their expectations. A cinematic and tactical experience that brings together all the right elements, cementing the franchise’s place among the best shooters of this generation and successfully marking the rebirth of a legendary combat saga.

Gears of War: E-Day is a must-play title because it recaptures the essence of the series while introducing significant improvements to its formula. Its campaign is the perfect way to experience E-Day firsthand and gain a deeper understanding of how the relationship between Marcus and Dom began to take shape, all set in a world brimming with detail and in constant flux. It may feel a bit repetitive at times, but beyond that, this is a game that proves that going back to the roots doesn’t have to mean getting stuck in nostalgia.

Gears of War: E-Day is exactly the prequel the franchise needed. The Coalition harks back to the horror, the tension and the brutal action of the first games. But they’ve tweaked the gameplay with smarter enemies and more verticality. The story surrounding Emergence Day also delivers a wealth of emotion, whilst Kalona emerges as one of the most impressive locations the franchise has ever seen. At its core, it remains good old Gears, but this E-Day is undoubtedly one of the strongest and most impressive Gears games ever. Full stop.
E-Day is the Gears game newcomers and hardcore fans have been waiting for, with a spectacular city-wide collapse and real heart.

Gears of War: E-Day is a brutal, atmospheric return to form that reminds us why this franchise became legendary in the first place. It may not reinvent the formula, but its terrifying take on this war’s bitter beginning makes for one hell of a comeback.

Gears of War: E-Day delivers a powerful return to the franchise’s roots, combining intense combat with a darker, horror-inspired atmosphere and an emotional story about Marcus and Dom. The campaign offers satisfying gameplay, well-designed semi-open environments, and impressive visuals, while its expanded movement mechanics modernize the classic formula. Although enemy variety is limited and some exploration elements become repetitive, The Coalition delivers a memorable adventure that captures what makes Gears of War so compelling.

Gears of War: E-Day is a bloody, confident return to the series’ roots, turning the city of Kalona itself into the real star while its human cast, caught in the shadow of a scene-stealing newcomer, never quite rises to the occasion.
Gears of War: E-Day takes the things that made the original games so good, throws in some modern bells and whistles, and reminds us why this series became such a big deal in the first place.

Gears of War: E-Day feels less like another attempt to modernize Gears and more like a reminder of why the series became important in the first place. It keeps the heart of Marcus and Dom's relationship, brings back the fear of the Locust, and adds enough new ideas to make another trip through Sera worthwhile.

In the end, I believe that Gears of War: E-Day has largely succeeded in recapturing an important part of the series' spirit that we loved in the original trilogy, whether in terms of atmosphere, the feeling of combat, or that distinct character that defined the series in its early days. Although it is not the best game in the series, its true value lies not in merely being a return of the Gears of War franchise after an absence, but in its ability to bring back that feeling that made us love the series in the first place, and reminding us of what made Gears games special and beloved by players from the very beginning.

Gears of War: E-Day is an extraordinary production and a powerful return to a world I have loved since that time when I finished the first Gears in that arcade place. Its characters, atmosphere, and collapsing city stayed with me, even when its combat outlasted my enthusiasm. Fans who still love that rhythm will find plenty to celebrate. I came away wishing it had pushed further, but also deeply impressed by how much care went into bringing this nightmare to life.

The way it masterfully tells the story of Emergence Day with its devastation and destruction, watching as the city of Kalona gradually becomes more war-torn was amazing. It was also amazing to have Marcus and Dom back in action again without it feeling like nostalgia bait, and the character development of Mags and Lucas was well paced and meaningful. While I do have a few nitpicks here and there, and I would have liked to see more Versus launch content, there aren’t many AAA games giving this much content with this much quality.

An atmospheric, beautifully optimized return to the series’ roots, E-Day pairs a memorable Emergence Day story with satisfying co-op, detailed environments, and excellent PC performance. Its familiar cover-based combat still hits hard, but bullet-sponge enemies, an underwhelming arsenal, and unreliable squad AI hold the campaign back. Even so, it’s a strong prequel and an easy recommendation for Gears fans—especially through Game Pass.
Gears of War: E-Day takes the franchise back to its roots with a brutal, emotional and spectacular experience that reminds us why the Locust War remains one of gaming’s most memorable conflicts.

Gears of War: E-Day is a brutal and visually spectacular return to the series, combining incredibly satisfying gunplay, excellent audiovisual feedback, oppressive atmosphere, and strong environmental storytelling with some genuinely effective horror elements. Its larger areas occasionally dilute the campaign’s pacing, enemy AI can be inconsistent, and a few encounters frustrate more than they challenge, but the relentless action and polished presentation make this one of the year’s biggest surprises. Jsem Gamer

I love the linear segments of E-Day, they deliver on rioting action and awesome set-pieces. This gets derailed by the dull open zones in the map and some to spongy enemies. But the highs outweigh the lows for sure.

Gears of War: E-Day understands perfectly that going back to the past doesn't mean living on nostalgia alone. The Coalition uses characters, enemies and elements that any fan recognizes right away, but places them in a completely different moment. One where the Locust are still terrifying and where Marcus Fenix is not yet the practically indestructible soldier we all know.
Gears of War: E-Day is, as expected, a real treat, both in single-player and in co-op mode for 2 to 4 players.

Gears of War E-Day achieves exactly what it set out to do: breathe new life into a legendary franchise without betraying its essence, while giving it something new to say. It does so with an opening act that hits like a punch, technical prowess that sets new standards for the generation, and gameplay that’s finally more in-depth, blending verticality with loadout customization. The only real drawbacks lie in an open world that’s still a work in progress and exploration that’s too guided, which dampen the sense of discovery but don’t undermine the beating heart of the experience. The result is an exceptionally solid game that will satisfy the hardcore community and throw open the door to newcomers; by the time the credits roll, you’re left with the feeling that The Coalition and People Can Fly have rebuilt an excellent foundation from which to move forward. It remains to be seen where the series will go from here, and to find out, it will likely take another two or three years.

Gears of War: E-Day is arguably one of the best Gears games in the decorated franchise, portraying Emergence Day as both terrifying and spectacular, capturing humanity's darkest moment through unforgettable set pieces, emotional stakes, and a renewed focus on Marcus and Dom's brotherhood. While the narrative occasionally treads predictable ground, the game's exceptional presentation, stunning visuals, and atmospheric depiction make for a compelling campaign from start to finish.

E‑Day is the good old Gears we know, but pushed to its peak. With the best gameplay in the series, an atmospheric story, and an excellent Horde Siege mode, this is the return to form the franchise has been waiting for.
Gears of War: E-Day pulls off a feat that seemed impossible: looking back without missing a beat, delivering a prequel of the highest quality.

Gears of War: E-Day doesn’t try to be anything else. It’s the same old formula, but executed with confidence and solidity. The campaign is intense from start to finish, finds room for moments of terror that remind us just how frightening the Locust can be, and provides more context for the relationship between Marcus and Dom. New features, such as the open-world sections and the customisation of weapons, armour and abilities, add to the experience without detracting from its essence. And with Horde, Multiplayer and co-op campaign with open lobbies, the package guarantees hours of gameplay long after the final credits roll. Those looking for a revolution in the genre won’t find it here. But for those seeking Gears of War at its best, look no further.

Gears of War: E-Day is just fun comfort food to go back to shooter-wise; like a village hometown dish you grew up with back again in your mouth after years of abstaining. The best kind of beef rendang and hearty rice combo if we're talking literal Malaysian comfort food.

Gears of War: E-Day is a brutal and confident return to the series' roots, with satisfying combat, strong atmosphere and welcome weapon customization. Its story plays things too safely and the open areas lack focus, but this is still Gears at its most enjoyable.
Gears of War: E-Day successfully returns to its roots.

"The series returns to its darkest day"
Gears of War: E-Day successfully returns the franchise to its roots, preserving its signature combat style while introducing more fluid movement and deeper weapon customization. The story and the bond between Marcus and Dom lend a powerful human element to the experience, while Kalona offers one of the best environments in the series' history. Despite some pacing issues and repetition, E-Day stands as a strong comeback, proving that the classic Gears formula can still deliver a modern, standout experience.

Gears of War: E-Day doesn't completely reinvent the series, and it doesn't need to. Its biggest changes come from movement, encounter design, customization, and the decision to focus the campaign around a single city and a short period of time. Those changes work because they strengthen the parts of Gears that already mattered.
Gears of War E-Day brings the series back its dark visceral roots with elevated levels of horror but everything outside of the campaign suffers.
In conclusion, I've had the privilege of playing one of the best installments in the series—if not the best—set in a very well-crafted world, with mission design that...

Gears of War: E-Day feels like a confident reminder of what made this series Xbox royalty in the first place. It’s nasty, ridiculous, surprisingly funny and occasionally horrifying, all while giving Marcus and Dom another jaunt to share that feels worthwhile rather than merely nostalgic.

With enhanced graphics, 'Gears of War: E-Day' successfully implements the heavy and metalic combat characteristic of the series and effectively portrays the horrors of Emergence Day. However, the monotonous game structure and repetitive combat patterns leave a tedious impression in the second half, and the boss fights also become drawn-out battles in later chapters. While it is a welcome title for fans, it is difficult to strongly recommend to newcomers.

Gears of War: E-Day is the best game The Coalition made! As it was an exceptional experience and one of the strongest (and the boldest) in the franchise's history, while staying true to its core identity. The game delivered a rich story filled with emotions, heartbreaking moments, and excellent environmental storytelling. Alongside interesting dynamic encounters, masterful weapon and gear handling, and refined movement and gameplay mechanics. All of this blends with top-tier visual effects, exceptional animation quality, stunning graphics, and an expressive, powerful soundtrack. It is truly the greatest third-person action game of all time and the undisputed ruler of the genre.

Playing Gears of War: E-Day felt like playing the original trilogy on the Xbox 360, not in a technical sense, but in the feeling of being back in this world. Getting a new adventure with Marcus and Dom is a real treat, and the story surrounding them is incredible.

Gears of War: E-Day feels like the return to Gears that we’ve all been waiting for, bringing back the brutal cover-based combat, dark atmosphere and Locust while still adding enough new ideas to move the series forward. The story of younger Marcus and Dom hit harder than I expected.

Gears of War: E-Day brings back the series’ brutality from a more human perspective, placing Marcus and Dom at the heart of Emergence Day. The Coalition returns to the beginning while expanding the formula through exploration, upgrades and less restrictive areas, without losing the core identity that defines Gears of War.

Ultimately, Gears of War: E-Day is an enjoyable campaign wrapped inside an exceptionally impressive technical package. It is a pleasure to look at, the combat remains satisfying, and the return of Marcus Fenix and Dom Santiago is exactly what many longtime fans wanted. Unfortunately, the forced DEI character writing, unnecessary social commentary, excessive dialogue, questionable level-design decisions, technical stuttering, and underwhelming ending prevent E-Day from becoming the definitive Gears experience I was hoping for after such a long wait when it comes to it's single player campaign portion.

Gears of War: E-Day is set during Emergence Day, fourteen years before the events of the original Gears of War, as Marcus and Dom, along with a host of other Gears, face off against the first wave of Locust. They’ll have to fight and survive against the unknown as they scramble to save civilians scattered throughout the city.

Gears of War: E-Day is a third person action shooter where players will be able to use a myriad of weapons to take the fight up to the Locust. Returning players will notice that The Coalition have made a few tweaks in terms of controls. Given that our protagonists are younger, their movement is a bit more nimble. Running has been delegated to pressing the left joystick instead of holding A. Marcus and company can now jump and climb up reasonably high surfaces. There’s also a useful slide mechanic to dodge enemy projectiles.

Kalona is the real star of «Gears of War: E-Day», transforming so dramatically throughout the campaign that it feels like the game's main character. The story and characters are less memorable, but the weighty, satisfying gunplay and improved movement make for a solid «Gears» experience. It gets repetitive, but fans of the series should feel right at home.

Gears of War: E-Day is not simply the return of a historic franchise, but its definitive consecration in the modern gaming era. The Coalition has pulled off a courageous and surgical feat, stripping away the unnecessary bloat accumulated over the years to return the series to its purest, most ruthless, and visceral essence. The single-player campaign, clocking in at nearly twenty hours, stands as one of the finest narrative achievements in the action genre. It flawlessly blends intimate human drama with a cinematic spectacle of enormous proportions, all supported by an Unreal Engine 5 technical showcase that sets new standards for the entire industry.

Coupling this majestic adventure with an incredibly fluid and entertaining multiplayer suite (despite the natural need for fresh content in the short term) and a Horde mode that is deeper and more customizable than ever, the result is an absolute masterpiece. In a 2026 already packed with outstanding releases, E-Day stands tall as one of the best games of the year, rightfully claiming the title of the best shooter of 2026 and finally giving fans back the true Gears of War they have been dreaming of for far too long. The war for survival on Sera has only just begun.

Gears of War: E-Day not only revives one of Xbox's greatest franchises, but also manages to restore much of the identity that seemed to have been lost in its last two installments. The Coalition understands what made the original trilogy special: the brutality of war, the depth of its characters, an oppressive atmosphere, and spectacular action that doesn't have to sacrifice emotion

Gears of War: E-Day marks the return of Marcus and Dom in an excellent campaign, with renewed gameplay, impressive graphics, and a few issues that don’t overshadow the game’s major achievements. One of the best Xbox titles of this generation, worthy of all the attention.

Following Marcus and Dom on Emergence Day is an action-packed rollercoaster ride. Gears of War: E-Day shines on the PC with stunning graphics and addictive combat, with the weapon customisation adding an extra touch. Unfortunately, the pace drops off in the final third of the campaign, let down by a dull ending and an uninspired boss.

Gears of War: E-Day does not disappoint; the story starts strong and only gets better. For players who have experienced the previous entries in the franchise, there are plenty of easter eggs scattered throughout. Any graphic and audio-related glitches I ran into were very minor and did not detract from the experience overall. For me, this game is in the running for my Game of the Year.

'Gears of War: E-Day' returns to the series' starting point, Emergence Day, bringing back its darkest atmosphere yet and the core appeal of Gears. If you've been missing the explosive, hard-hitting battlefields of the original trilogy, 'Gears of War: E-Day' is sure to be a satisfying choice.

Gears of War: E-Day marks a return to the series’ roots, without, however, feeling like a typical “reimagining” of the past. The Coalition took the core elements that made Gears of War special and rebuilt them masterfully, into a satisfying game that isn’t groundbreaking or the best shooter you’ve ever played, but is certainly capable of entertaining fans of the genre.

Gears of War: E-Day modernises the series without losing its trademark weight, pairing brutal combat and meaningful weapon customisation with strong character work, smart exploration and only a handful of frustrating solo-play shortcomings.
This prequel once again raised the bar for the series and the genre, delivering one of the year's most brutal, jaw-dropping shooters.

Gears of War: E-Day returns to the series' roots with an intense, well-executed campaign and refined combat. It plays it safe rather than innovating, but it's an easy recommendation for veterans and newcomers alike.

Gears of War: E-Day injects new life into the franchise and sets a new tone moving forward. It captured the spirit of the original Gears of War with putting just enough of a new spin on things. It’s definitely a highlight of the series. A perfect reload, indeed.

Gears of War: E-Day’s campaign is a real emotional rollercoaster when it comes to gameplay, but a major disappointment in terms of its story. No wonder Marcus Fenix wasn’t the focus of the game’s marketing.

Gears of War: E-Day delivers a visually stunning and emotionally intense campaign that captures the chaos of Emergence Day. With brutal combat, organic exploration, strong side content, and some of the best visuals Xbox has delivered in years, it deserves serious Game of the Year consideration, even if the Marcus and Dom connection could have been stronger.

Even in a silo, Gears of War: E-Day delivers a rollercoaster of action and emotion that ranks alongside the series’ best campaigns. The Coalition grounds the global devastation of Emergence Day in a deeply human story, letting players watch Marcus and Dom’s friendship forge into an unbreakable brotherhood. It retains the franchise’s signature brutality while completely reinvigorating the moment-to-moment combat. While the narrative plays it safe compared to the tragic finality of Halo: Reach, it sticks the landing and beautifully sets the stage for a new trilogy. Gears of War: E-Day serves as the perfect entry point for newcomers, and explores the devastating, series-haunting history veterans have waited twenty years to experience.
Gears of War: E-Day is firing on almost every cylinder - a fantastic back to basics prequel that makes the Locust Horde scary again while delivering weighty, brutal gameplay that keeps you hooked.

With two decades of expectations on its shoulders, The Coalition succeeded in crafting another classic Gears game with E-Day. Its technical brilliance is matched by strong character development and modernized gameplay, resulting in one of my favorite experiences of the year.

Gears of War E-Day may have the best gameplay the series has ever delivered, but between bullet-sponge enemies, co-op-focused design and a story with little to say, this may well be the weakest Gears campaign to date.

Gears of War: E-Day is a good shooter and an excellent introduction to this universe for those who, like me, have spent years following the franchise only from the outside. There's a long, very well-produced campaign, visually impressive, and one that probably gains another dynamic when shared with friends.
Metacritic user score 7.7/10 (577 ratings).
93.7% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (161 reviews).

After a long hiatus, Castlevania is back and better than ever. Konami's trust in Evil Empire as the stewards of a new 2D era has been well-placed, with a modern and fresh-feeling take that builds on what's always made the series so iconic while carving out its own identity. Rose Belmont is a fantastic protagonist that lends Belmont's Curse a compelling story and heightened exploration. This is an instant classic.

A bold evolution that redefines the future of the franchise, Belmont’s Curse delivers the finest exploration and gameplay systems in Castlevania’s history, setting a new standard for this legendary IP.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is an amazing return to the series’ 2D roots. By blending tight combat and fluid controls, satisfying mechanics via Sypha’s Tarot cards and relics, and punishing platforming, Evil Empire has crafted a Metroidvania experience that honors the franchise’s legacy while also creating its own identity.

The Castlevania series is one that’s near and dear to my heart. I’ve spent decades playing these games since the very first one, and the balance that Belmont’s Curse strikes between being an incredible platforming adventure all on its own and respecting the series’ myriad directions and gimmicks, good and bad, was impressive start to finish. Stellar gameplay, music, scenery, characters (new and old), and a great set of options for altering the intensity make this the easily one of the highest-quality action-platformers I have ever played. When the dust settles, I think there’s a case to be made that Belmont’s Curse might be the best Castlevania game of all time.

Exceptional in every way, Castlevania: Belmont's Curse is a one of 2026's must-play titles. In a year of great games, it's hard to stand out, but Evil Empire has crafted a bonified masterpiece in one of the game's most historic franchises.

Castlevania: Belmont's Curse is not just one of the best games this year; it's one of the best Castlevania games ever made. It is a challenging, consistently engaging, and superbly designed adventure epic that reminds us why this series defined an entire genre in the first place.

None of the tiny qualms I’ve listed mar the fact that Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is an incredible experience from start to finish. It looks, sounds, reads, and plays with sleek style, while asking a thoughtfulness of the player not typically seen in this genre. Taken alone in another game, any of this game’s elements would stand out. The fact that every element blends so perfectly here makes me confident to say that Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is the best Metroidvania I’ve ever experienced. It’s sure to go down as an all-time classic.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is an absolute dream come true for everyone who loves this series. I can’t believe what Evil Empire, Motion Twin, and Konami are bringing to the table. It’s almost as if we, the fans, had sat down and simply asked for everything we wanted to see in a new 2D Castlevania game in 2026. It’s hard to find any significant flaws in this game, which pushes the genre that the series itself helped define to new heights, making it clear that its importance goes far beyond the historical contributions we’ve talked about so much. The return of the Belmonts is more than just a triumph for the legendary Japanese publisher; it’s a celebration of everything that makes our beloved video games so special.

With a storied past, Castlevania: Belmont's Curse sets up the franchise for a bright (but also dark) future. Rose is a fantastic heroine with a deep, compelling story, and she wields some of the genre's most enjoyable combat mechanics. Add a few key accessibility options to make the game less punishing, and I think you have a standout title heading into the final months of 2026. Belmont's Curse is one of the best ways Konami and Evil Empire could have pushed the franchise and the genre forward.

Castlevania: Belmont's Curse masterfully marks the return of the franchise by delivering the finest Metroidvania experience since Symphony of the Night. Combining a narrative that honors the Belmont family legacy with an innovative Tarot card skill-absorption system and a striking art style, the title overcomes minor mechanical flaws to establish itself as the start of a promising future for the series.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is an excellent metroidvania that loses points due to frustrating mechanics and a lack of guidance. Its rich world, great soundtrack and tight controls makes challenges feel rewarding, especially after multiple tries. I just kept coming back for more, and reaching 100% completion during the busy review season might just be the biggest compliment that I can give Belmont’s Curse.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse has successfully captured the series’ classic gameplay elements in terms of its combat and exploration. The game shines brightest through its unique art style, its whip traversal system and of course a diverse array of weapons and abilities. To top it all off, the introduction of Arcana cards adds a new layer of fun gameplay ideas. On the other hand, the save points throughout the game could have been better and some scenes tend to be oversaturated with shades of red, which makes it frustrating to spot enemies and discern details in the environment.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is a strong return to the franchise’s roots. The combat is excellent, the traversal feels fantastic, and player-driven exploration is a big part of why it works. The music is easily the weakest part, but it does not drastically diminish what is otherwise a near-perfect revival.

Overall I love Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse. When it was first announced I was simply thrilled that this legendary series was finally making a proper comeback, and after experiencing the sheer quality of this successor I’m convinced that it’s here to stay. Evil Empire shows an obvious love and admiration for the Konami series and while I’d liked its difficulty to have a bit more of a kick, I think it’ll be fine for most players.

Even when Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse had me in Bloody Tears and praying for mercy, I never stopped grinning from ear to ear and jumping right back in to see what else was hiding in Dracula’s Castle. Thanks to an engaging story, stellar exploration and combat, and a near-perfect blend of new and old, Castlevania’s return just about makes up for the decade-long wait.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is the perfect resurrection for the franchise. Not only does the game capture the spirit of the series, but it expands on elements to create one of the finest examples in the genre. With its tight combat and wonderful world design, this is a killer comeback for the legendary series.
Castlevania returns to 2D with a visually stunning experience packed with great ideas. With Rose Belmont wielding the whip, the legacy of the vampire-hunting family is in very good hands.
Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse has everything a Metroidvania should have: tight gameplay, challenging combat, and a world you’ll love exploring every nook and cranny of in search of secrets.

Overall, I wish there was more interaction with certain Arcana, in spite of the game’s simple plot. This small nitpick doesn’t take away from how lovingly crafted this game is, from its story to its level design and gameplay. It’s clear to me that Evil Empire deeply treasures this franchise, a fact many understood with their Castlevania DLC for Dead Cells some time ago. This title is not just a return to form for the series, but an evolution of its past through modern refinements that make it a perfect entry point for new audiences. I can’t recommend Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse enough, as its eternal night will hook into you like a vampire’s fangs and refuse to let go until the blood has run dry and the curse lifts.

Castlevania Belmont's Curse marks an excellent return for Konami's beloved franchise, preserving its iconic essence while modernizing its gameplay with a more open ended approach. Combat offers plenty of variety, featuring enemies that encourage experimentation and spells that challenge players to use them strategically. Meanwhile, its captivating exploration delivers a constant sense of discovery across environments that are both haunting and beautiful. It truly feels like the foundation for a bright future for the Belmont family.

Despite an 18 year absence, it feels like 2D Castlevania never left. Belmont's Curse is an excellent return to this hallowed series - standing tall with some of the best Metroidvania entries in the franchise. If this is just the start of a Castlevania renaissance, I can't wait to see where it goes.

Castlevania: Belmont's Curse marks a triumphant return for the franchise, delivering a modern 2D Metroidvania that honors its roots while injecting fresh dynamism. The game excels with fluid combat, innovative whip mechanics for traversal, and a deep arsenal of weapons and Arcana spells. Protagonist Rose Belmont's journey is bolstered by an engaging narrative and a rewarding sense of discovery. While challenging, comprehensive accessibility options ensure broad appeal. Minor issues like constant backtracking and lack of explicit map markers are easily overshadowed by its many strengths, making it a must-play for fans and genre enthusiasts.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is a labor of love that draws on all of Evil Empire’s expertise to create a solid, dynamic, explosive, and intense game. Rose is a fantastic protagonist, and—combined with brilliant combat, highly immersive exploration, and breathtaking battles—she transforms the game into a masterpiece worthy of the entire Symphony of the Night legacy.

After many years of the legendary Castlevania series lying dormant, Konami resurrects the IP with an excellent new sequel. Belmont's Curse delivers on all fronts that matter in a Metroidvania, offering excellent exploration, myriad secrets, and plenty of worthwhile items to discover. Meanwhile, the combat is fast-paced and tactical, with a satisfying variety of weapon choices. Fans of Metroidvania games, especially those who appreciate Castlevania's gothic aesthetic, should not miss it.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse feels like a franchise entry that revives the best of the genre, blending the classic with the modern. It delivers a more elaborate story, a protagonist who carries her family name's legacy with poise, and gameplay that demands sharp precision. It might be tougher than previous installments, but that is precisely part of its charm.

Castlevania: Belmont's Curse marks the return of one of gaming's most iconic franchises. With challenging combat, rewarding exploration, memorable boss fights, and an excellent soundtrack, the game honors the series' legacy while carving out its own identity. Evil Empire delivers an engaging metroidvania packed with content and personality, appealing to both longtime fans and newcomers alike. One of the standout games of 2026, it shows that Castlevania still has plenty to offer.
After years of absence, Castlevania returns with a bold, challenging Metroidvania that honors its legacy while confidently moving forward.

Regardless of what the future holds, the fact that the new Castlevania turned out so well is already cause for celebration. And let’s hope we don’t have to wait another 12 years for Dracula’s next return. The Belmonts might not be too thrilled about it, but I’ll be waiting for him with open arms... and a whip in hand.

I’m generally pleased with the end result of Castlevania: Curse of Belmont. It’s a metroidvania that manages to balance keeping the old-school Castlevania thematic alive and well while simultaneously refining platforming and combat mechanics that haven’t yet been possible. Knowing that Evil Empire, Motion Twin, and Konami are seeking to reimagine the now-40-year-old franchise for new players, it feels like they made a valiant effort to retain what longtime fans love most while giving new players just enough to enjoy a Castlevania title for the first time.

Here’s what fans of the legendary Castlevania series want to know: Belmont’s Curse is as good as you hoped, maybe even better. It is a rollicking throwback to the side-scrollers that were so formative they helped launch a genre—the term “Metroidvania” owes half its portmanteau to this series—while still feeling clearly made by modern, brilliant developers.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is a particularly distinctive return for the series, but one that rises to the occasion. Its clue-based exploration goes beyond what we’ve seen in other games of the genre, making the discovery of secrets a real pleasure. Its boss fights are challenging, but also deeply satisfying.

After an 18-year hiatus for the vampire-hunting series' traditional style, Castlevania: Belmont's Curse both slakes the thirst of long-time fans and offers an entry point for a new audience. It is an adventure that plays it safe—taking a somewhat understated approach to the Metroidvania elements and facing some limitations—yet its strengths ultimately shine through, making it well worth playing. Here's hoping Rose Belmont's journey breathes new life into the franchise's future—and that the current low-resolution textures get adjusted for 4K screens.

Castlevania: Belmont's Curse has all the elements necessary to attract both historical enthusiasts and those looking for a solid, modern Metroidvania. The Parisian setting, the centrality of the whip, the gameplay systems, and the ability to customize combat outline a project that doesn't seek to live solely on nostalgia, but rather clearly shows that a bright future is still possible for the series. This new chapter also demonstrates that there's still room for evolution, and that perhaps the lack of boldness in overhauling was ultimately a wise and correct choice, because what the series needed at this moment in its history was to reaffirm that this familiar and recognizable path is ready to be explored again. Belmont's Curse may not be perfect, but it's undoubtedly very good, and it forcefully reaffirms that Castlevania is still alive and well, ready for a second lease of life.

After a twelve-year slumber in his coffin, Dracula deserved a comeback worthy of his legend. By sacrificing the pure RPG format in favor of a more condensed adventure, Belmont's Curse risked tarnishing the myth. While the experience is far from innovative or groundbreaking, it is expertly crafted, driven by exemplary exploration and a spellbinding atmosphere. Rose proves she is far more than a mere heir: she has the mettle, the whip, and the grit needed to worthily carry on the lineage of vampire hunters. The legacy is in good hands.

It feels more like a modern Metroidvania than what you'd expect from a game in the series but there's no denying that Castlevania: Belmont's Curse is a must-have action-packed adventure for anyone who enjoys either the genre or the series.

Marking the 40th anniversary, Castlevania's comeback is a welcome sight for fans, and although Belmont’s Curse leans heavily into contemporary Metroidvania design, sometimes at the expense of the series' distinct identity, it delivers enough highlights to keep us optimistic about the franchise's road ahead.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is not a perfect game, but its flaws do not manage to overshadow the excellent experience it provides overall. It is a great game, featuring a rich combat system, an excellent exploration experience, an enjoyable movement system, and an interesting storyline.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is an alluringly gorgeous, polished and expressive comeback of the series. It plays things mostly safe across the board, which is a design philosophy that’s bound to alienate more expectant Castlevania veterans. For most other players, Belmont’s Curse is a gorgeous, rewarding and deeply engaging adventure that introduces the Belmont Bloodline and the series’ legacy wonderfully. It resulted in a return to form that hopefully serves as the foundation for braver titles, but until then, Belmont’s Curse is a powerful resurrection worthy of Dracula himself and a great Metroidvania all the same.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is a confident return for the legendary series, offering excellent exploration, precise platforming, memorable bosses, and a rewarding selection of weapons with tarot-based magic. Its uneven enemy distribution, audio glitches, and lengthy loading times hold it back just a bit, but Evil Empire has created a compelling metroidvania worthy of the Castlevania name.
Castlevania: Belmont's Curse is a must-have title for fans of the series and Metroidvania games, featuring outstanding gameplay and a solid narrative that fully lives up to the franchise's legacy.
Much like Dracula, Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse brings the series back from the dead. It’s different from previous games, but that doesn’t mean it’s bad. Evil Empire has knocked this out of the park.

It would be an overstatement to say that Belmont's Curse has become the classic Castlevania of our dreams in every single respect. However, while the story is merely solid, we really appreciate the visual style and animations. Above all, the game world is exceptionally well-crafted in its Metroidvania design, complemented by great platforming and a highly entertaining combat system that becomes increasingly multifaceted. Here you get a genuinely good 2D action-adventure and a successful series revival that genre enthusiasts and Castlevania fans really shouldn't miss.
Castlevania is back, trading its usual stone-carved ruins for the burning streets of 15th century Paris
A long-awaited return that brings the series into the modern era with a fast-paced focus on action first.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is proof that any franchise, if given the right team and opportunity, can make magic again. With exhilarating combat and platforming alongside great graphics, the decade-long wait for Belmont’s return, while not perfect, keeps the bloodline alive and well.

Castlevania: Belmont's Curse is an enjoyable and polished revival with excellent combat, rewarding exploration, and flexible customization. However, repetitive enemies, overly talkative storytelling, safe traversal abilities, and an underwhelming soundtrack keep it from fully capturing the identity and atmosphere of the series at its best.

There's a lot here for Castlevania fans to enjoy, with everything from charming series staples to brilliant new ideas capable of sparking genuine joy. More than anything else, Castlevania: Belmont's Curse is incredibly fun to play. At the end of the night, when Dracula is finally dead once more, isn't that what Castlevania is all about?
Despite some uneven difficulty and some iffy vice work, Castlevania: Belmont's Curse doesn't disappoint.

Overall, Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse proves that Evil Empire knows exactly how to honor a legacy without being stuck in the past. It has its flaws—namely in its subdued soundtrack, uneven boss design and somewhat slow start—but its atmospheric world, deliberate combat, and rewarding exploration make it a a standout experience for Metroidvania fans.

The heart of Rose’s arsenal is a grappling whip that can both pull her to foes and latch onto anchor points in the environment, sending her swinging over pitfalls in parabolic curves. Though the whip’s targeting suffers from occasional wonkiness, there’s immense pleasure to be had in the smoothness of the arc Rose traces in the air, and in the momentum she amasses in flight, smashing foes in her path with the weight of a wrecking ball. More than a decade may have passed since the last entry in the Castlevania series, and Belmont’s Curse certainly takes liberties in its interpretation of the material, but some things don’t change: Pity the demon who squares up to a Belmont.

Castlevania: Belmont's Curse is a fantastic return for the series buoyed by stellar exploration, puzzles and a wealth of secrets to uncover. Evil Empire was the obvious choice to bring the series back, and it has paid back that trust in spades, creating a game well worthy of Castlevania's 40th anniversary.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is undoubtedly an excellent revival of the long-running series. Returning to 2D has proven that Konami’s legendary IP still has plenty to offer, even to modern players, when placed in the right hands. Evil Empire has demonstrated not only a genuine passion for the franchise, but also a thorough understanding of what sets Castlevania apart from Metroidvanias that attempt to imitate it.

Castlevania: Belmont's Curse is the glorious comeback the franchise desperately needed. Evil Empire successfully blends their fast-paced combat philosophy with the traditional igavania structure, delivering a thrilling and fluid adventure. While the weapon variety feels a bit shallow and some platforming checkpoints are frustratingly placed, the surprisingly deep narrative, the clever Tarot mechanics, and a bold electronic/orchestral soundtrack make it a highly satisfying experience. A must-play injection of vitality for the iconic series.

There is no doubt that Konami has marked the franchise’s grand return after a long twelve-year hiatus with a highly successful new entry. While Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse may not be the most complex or original Metroidvania seen in recent years, it nonetheless boasts a distinct personality and charm that will easily win over fans of the genre. Developed by Evil Empire, the title also serves as an excellent entry point for newcomers to the series, potentially making it the ideal starting point for a genuine Castlevania comeback in the years ahead.

Castlevania is back [...] The core framework is flawless, and Evil Empire used it to build a game that fits wonderfully into the franchise. I had a lot of fun finally polishing Dracula’s fangs with a whip again, and sincerely hope I won't have to wait another umpteen years for the next opportunity.

The game they have delivered is excellent, considering the price point. It could be a great opportunity to revitalize the series, and based on the feedback this title receives, Evil Empire will likely create something even better for their next Castlevania game. Castlevania fans will undoubtedly pick it up, but I recommend that anyone interested in this genre give it a try.

Castlevania: Belmont's Curse is a brilliant modern platformer that has moments that feel like Dead Cells. As a Castlevania title, it's competent, but one may look at the Bloodstained franchise for a proper successor to Sympony of the Night. Belmont's Curse is extremely challenging and fun, filled with vibrant artwork and features design concepts from the best games in the series. It offers a lot of game time and the ability to customize the gameplay experience. The zoomed-out camera may attempt to add immersion, but it ends up taking away from the details of the world. This is a solid experience all-around, but manages to offer some of the best platforming out there thanks to the whip mechanics. If this is your first Castlevania experience, this particular version may be difficult, but it is a good way to get into the entire series.

The Castlevania series is back. There are lots of things to love about Evil Empire's Castlevania: Belmont's Curse, from its rewarding, interconnected world to its brilliant soundtrack, but issues with the game's balance might bring the experience down for some.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is a confident return, balancing gothic roots with modern platforming and satisfying combat in a varied Parisian setting worth exploring. Its cryptic clues and aimless backtracking will test your patience if the demanding boss fights haven't already destroyed your will, but mastering its mechanics makes the struggle worthwhile for those who enjoy a challenge.
While its combat and level design could be even, Belmont's Curse is fast-paced, deeply colorful and chock-full of fun content. Castlevania is back at long last, and what a treat it is.

Castlevania: Belmont's Curse recaptures the essence of the classic Metroidvania with engaging exploration and a card system that has its own unique identity, although its slow and clunky movement requires more patience than reflexes.

It’s certainly not for lack of effort. Developer Evil Empire shows a solid understanding of the metroidvania fundamentals, making this a must-play for fans of the genre. Unfortunately, for a true Castlevania fix, we’ll have to wait for Bloodstained: The Scarlet Engagement. [Issue#376, p.50]

Belmont’s Curse is a solid enough return for such a long-running series after such a lengthy absence, and it becomes an enjoyable experience if you give it some time. However, with no new ideas to bring to the genre, it never manages to be more than a good Metroidvania.

Castlevania: Belmont's Curse gets a lot of stuff right, but in a world where Metroidvanias are a dime a dozen, it doesn't do quite enough to really stand apart. Decent combat gets the job done, while level design and some lovely art and animation are areas where the game really shines. The game can feel a little unresponsive, leading to some frustrating deaths. It's ultimately a good Metroidvania and a valiant effort to resuscitate Castlevania, but there's little new to see for anyone who's been keeping up with the genre over the last decade.
After a long dormancy, Castlevania makes a welcome full-fat return to its 2D roots, even if you can't help but wish it would stand out more among the many modern competitors inspired by its legacy.
The long-awaited return of Castlevania offers little in terms of innovation or surprises, but it’s a competent Metroidvania with some fun platforming challenges.

Castlevania: Belmont's Curse is a gorgeous metroidvania that breathes new life into the legendary series with several inventive gameplay mechanics. The acrobatic use of the iconic whip and the tarot system, which connects the story with combat, are particularly compelling. However, uneven difficulty undermines the experience, straying from the traditional approach of its predecessors. Dracula's hunters deserved better.
Evil Empire has made a positive mark on both the format and flavour of Castlevania. All told, it's a pretty good night to have a curse. [Issue#430, p.112]
Ambitious, aggressive, and accomplished, Belmont's Curse whips out some of the best Castlevania highs you can experience - but can all end in bloody tears.

Castlevania: Belmont's Curse might not challenge the current kings of the genre for the top spot, but with a distinct artstyle and solid gameplay foundations, it succeeds in bringing the legendary franchise into metroidvania's modern golden era.

A decent enough experience hindered by inconsistency, Belmont’s Curse sadly doesn’t hold its own against the games it inspired. It’s not a bad time, but it is a frustrating and ultimately forgettable one.

Every element in Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse works so well both independently and as part of the whole: flexible combat, beautifully acrobatic traversal, fine-tuned environmental puzzles, wide cast of interesting characters, and eye-catching visual panache–all wrapped within a smart tarot system that lets these ideas complement each other.

Belmont's Curse may not be wildly original, but its planning and execution are superb, its combat and whip-integration thrilling, and its sense of exploration and reward on-point. It wholly delivers that all-important progression-reward feedback loop, tripping every time you come back stronger.It's an unapologetically hardcore affair, and that's welcome. It's one of the best Castlevania games in a long time thanks to its combat variety and smart whip integrations. While nicely balanced, extremely addictive, and with tons to do, those less familiar with the format may find its difficulty frustrating. But, if you play games to feel an elating sense of accomplishment, on that front it will do you right.

Castlevania: Belmont's Curse is an incredibly entertaining game and a wonderful return to form for a series I've loved since forever. While it isn't an echo of the entries I love the most, it's still a fantastic game. The game is pure Castlevania in the best way, and the story and voice acting are sublime as well. If you like any Castlevania games at all, you'll adore this.
There are buzzsaws and blood pits, bats burst into blood and demons burn to cinders. The series' new emphasis on twitch-based action may annoy purists but you can't call it dull

It's great to see a new side-scrolling Castlevania game after all these years, but the genre has evolved and thrived in the series' absence, and Belmont's Curse finds itself in a world where there are a wealth of solid alternatives. While it looks and sounds excellent, the core gameplay hasn't evolved alongside it, making it feel rather outdated. That's not a terrible thing, it's still fun enough, but stand-out moments are few and far between as a result.

Whether you’re a long-time series fan wondering what’s next or a Metroidvania diehard looking to scratch that particular itch, Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is a grand return to form that packs in plenty of twists and surprises.

Castlevania: Belmont's Curse marks a convincing return to Konami's storied series, striking a happy balance between exploration, challenging combat, and a movement system that provides some of the most satisfying gameplay of the entire adventure.
