The sheer amount of exploration here is incredible, and I loved the tarot card system and optional bosses. This is a triumphant return for the franchise, and easily on my list for best games of the year.
Castlevania: Belmont's Curse , I can say that it has exceeded my expectations at every turn. A well-rounded game that serves to return the Castlevania name to its former glory .

“Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse” represents a nice return to old-school form for the franchise with a surprisingly affordable price tag. From its hand-drawn style to its side-scrolling action and exploration, it just evokes classic Castlevania while adding its own new spin on the series. The action-platforming mechanics have some wonky moments and folks who prefer their Castlevania to be even more old-school with just straight up, linear action might not be as pleased. But if you loved the exploration in Symphony of the Night and the Castlevania games on portable Nintendo systems, then you’ll likely take to this game like vampire fangs to an exposed neck.
Belmont’s Curse is a tightly crafted, enjoyable modern Metroidvania, even if its Castlevania branding distract from its strengths.
Castlevania: Belmont's Curse has excellent presentation and style, but some frustrations lead to a fairly uneven experience until it eventually finds its footing.

Castlevania: Belmont's Curse unfurls like a tapestry of mysteries. There are so many secrets to discover, and it'll constantly tug at your curiosity, beckoning you to explore its darkest corners. Powerful spells and satisfying weapons anchor a robust combat system, and certain boss fights are a real treat. However, the difficulty is a little inconsistent, sometimes to a frustrating, punishing degree.
To say that the Castlevania series is long-running wouldn't be quite right. True, it began in 1986, and has kept us more or less stocked ever sinc...
Our Castlevania: Belmont's Curse review explores its gorgeous visuals, excellent soundtrack, satisfying combat, and a solid return for the series.
Castlevania: Belmont's Curse is a must play title and a return to form for one of video gaming's most prominent franchises.
Castlevania: Belmont's Curse is a worthy revival of the franchise and whose foundation could easily sustain the next big entry. However, it's own fundamentals need some serious work.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is a welcome return for the series, combining responsive controls, satisfying combat, and flexible character builds with striking gothic visuals. Its demanding but largely fair challenges reward experimentation, although occasionally confusing progression and frustrating save-point placement hold it back. My main issue with Belmont’s Curse is that it remains ONLY a very good example of its genre:it is a polished, compelling metroidvania that successfully brings Castlevania into the modern era.

If this is the level of game we can expect from Konami and Evil Empire's collaboration, I'm waiting with bated breath to see them team up for even more Castlevania goodness in the future. Let's just hope we don't have to wait almost 20 years this time.

I can appreciate what Castlevania: Belmont's Curse does well, and I genuinely enjoyed returning to Castlevania. But overall, it feels like a game that inherits both the strengths and the flaws of modern indie Metroidvanias, resulting in something that looks like a natural fit on the surface but never truly feels like one.
Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is a gorgeous game, and it will make any Castlevania fan feel right at home after being away so long.

Castlevania: Belmont's Curse is a solid new entry into the Castlevania franchise. This proves yet again that reformed Konami are excellent at choosing developers to carry their original IP forwards. It's fun just running around, sliding and climbing through the playground the developers have crafted, seeing all their cool shortcuts open up. Combat might be fairly simple but it's challenging, fast and satisfying, amplified by gorgeous visual and sound designs. This is a great entry point for new players and a better than expected new game for returning fans. Get this one; the curse is broken!

Castlevania: Belmont's Curse is a must-play if you like metroidvania games, a solid continuation for the legendary series, and it offers a serviceable, fun story and a massive map for you to check out.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is a superb return for one of the best franchises in the Metroidvania genre. With an excellent blend of engaging combat against enemies and bosses, rewarding exploration, stunning art direction, and challenging yet enjoyable platforming, the game delivers a thoroughly satisfying experience. It’s an easy recommendation for both longtime fans who grew up with the classic entries and newcomers looking to discover Castlevania for the first time. If you enjoy the genre, this 15-hour adventure is well worth your time.
Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is a far more modest effort to kickstart interest in the series again, and I do think opinions on it will be divided.

The Belmont clan seeks to finally break their curse and rid themselves of their arch-nemesis once and for all. But it won't be easy'far from it. The default difficulty recommended by the developers is very high; while you can adjust it, the game remains a tough challenge. Certain sections are exceptionally demanding, and the advanced controls feel clunky.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse marks a triumphant return for a franchise that has been absent from the Metroidvania genre and the gaming world for many years. The developers demonstrate a strong understanding of the series’ unique characteristics in most areas, delivering an experience that is deep, engaging, and at times downright addictive. The gameplay mechanics are remarkably rich, the interconnected level design encourages deep exploration, and the platforming sections seamlessly bring these elements together. While the Western-inspired art direction and distinctive soundtrack may stray somewhat from the franchise’s traditional identity, the gameplay retains the essence of what makes Castlevania so special.

Castlevania: Belmont's Curse is a fantastic return for the franchise. Mixing old and new together, it feels at once like a fresh game and something distinctly and undeniably Castlevania. It does a great job of threading the needle between the many different versions of the franchise. There are some inconsistent difficulty spikes, occasional moments of meaningless friction, and the Switch port is a little lackluster. For fans of the franchise who are looking for a return to Dracula's castle, this is exactly what it should be, and it hopefully represents a new life for the immortal franchise.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is a superb return to the legendary series, combining Rose Belmont’s surprisingly compelling, personal story with excellent exploration, demanding platforming challenges and satisfying combat. Evil Empire doesn’t set out to revolutionise the genre, but it makes brilliant use of its tried-and-tested foundations, offering stunning visuals, fantastic enemies and superbly balanced gameplay. This is exactly the kind of Castlevania that fans have been waiting for for years, and proof that Konami couldn’t have chosen a better team to bring the Belmont clan back.

I'd love to see what this team could do with a follow-up in the same vein, one that irons out some of the rough edges related to exploration and respawning. Rose is a compelling character in her own right, but the interactions between her and the souls she's captured add a nice degree of levity and charm to the story moments. It may not fly as high as some of its Castlevania predecessors, or even modern genre standouts like Silksong and Bloodstained: Ritual of the Night, but Belmont's Curse provides a dozen-plus hours of entertainment leading up to the height of spooky season.

Belmont’s Curse is a solid enough return for such a long-running series after such a lengthy absence, and it becomes an enjoyable experience if you give it some time. However, with no new ideas to bring to the genre, it never manages to be more than a good Metroidvania.
It’s by no means a bad game, but it’s a pretty lackluster Castlevania game.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is an adventure that proves the series still has plenty to offer without needing to repeat old formulas. Its blend of combat, platforming, and exploration along with its excellent ties to the classic universe won us over from start to finish. While some challenges might make you sweat a bit more than expected, few things are as satisfying as overcoming those hurdles and uncovering every secret. And yes, of course it’s a Castlevania game.

Castlevania Belmont's Curse is a return to form of the beloved franchise after a long hiatus, and a great one at that, but a lack of identity when compared to other Metroidvania games and some jank makes it hard to stand out as well as its 20 years old predecessors in the DS era.

In the 13 years since we've received the last Castlevania title outside of mobile devices, it's probably fair to say that Castlevania: Belmont's Curse is launching in a crowded genre. Metroidvania's have blown up over the last decade with the release of titles such as Hollow Knight, Nine Sols, and even a spiritual successor to the series in Bloodstained: Ritual of the Night. Even before I'd picked up my controller, I have to admit I was concerned whether or not Belmont's Curse was up to the task, and if Evil Empire's take on the formula could stand out from the crowd. If you're just here to know the answer to that question, you can feel secure in the knowledge that it was up to the task. Belmont's Curse is a great game that keeps up with its peers, and continues Konami's trend of successful series revivals. Belmont's Curse picks up the reins from the Igavania titles of the past with a focus on multiple weapon types, unlockable spells, and more - but I think the first thing to note about the game is that if you're looking specifically for an Igavania, you may find yourself wanting.

Castlevania: Belmont's Curse captivates with its stunning gothic atmosphere, engaging combat, and fantastic boss fights, especially in the excellent second half set in Dracula's castle. However, it suffers from the excessive caution of the Dead Cells developers, who bring no genre innovations to the table, as well as frustrating grappling hook controls. It's a very solid action platformer for both fans and newcomers, but one that falls short of perfection due to a lack of ambition.

Castlevania: Belmont's Curse is a return I appreciated, above all for its ability to carry the legacy of a historic saga without simply rehashing its formulas and mechanics. Evil Empire's work shows a good understanding of what made the franchise great, but also the courage to introduce different solutions, capable of giving the gameplay an identity of its own.

The level design is probably one of the strongest aspects of the entire production. The structure of the areas, the backtracking, the secrets and the use of the whip during exploration deliver that sense of discovery you expect from a Metroidvania.

Add to this a combat system that is solid, fast and responsive, in which Rose's mobility, the variety of weapons and the use of Arcana and relics make encounters dynamic and interesting. The bosses too, while falling short of the quantity and variety of Symphony of the Night, offer convincing combat design.

There are, of course, some omissions and choices that might raise eyebrows among fans more attached to tradition. The RPG component and the handling of equipment are slimmer than in some historic chapters, while the soundtrack, though it accompanies the adventure adequately, does not always manage to leave a mark. Some combat and healing mechanics likewise mark a distance from the classic canons, but they represent a reinterpretation that, on the whole, I found coherent with the direction taken.

Belmont's Curse is not Symphony of the Night and, fortunately, does not try to be. It is a chapter that looks to the past with respect but tries to build an identity of its own through a good balance of exploration, combat and interpretive freedom.

Not every choice is necessarily one I agree with, but the result is a convincing return, one that proves the saga still has something to say.

Castlevania: Belmont's Curse is an excellent piece of fan service that pays homage to the series' history, all wrapped up in a stylish package. It doesn't break new ground in the genre, but that isn't its goal anyway.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is an excellent metroidvania, but is it an excellent Castlevania game? I’ll let the true fans decide that one. With an expansive game world, tonnes of exploration and joyous whippin’ action, this is a truly indulgent experience. Hopefully we don’t have to wait another 18 years for another one of these!
Castlevania returns in a triumphant new adventure, proving that the Dead Cells developers were the perfect choice for the job.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse delivers a promising and solid Metroidvania experience worthy of the franchise's rich legacy, featuring a massive, meticulously crafted world and an unforgettable epic adventure for the protagonist, Rose Belmont. Despite a few shortcomings, including inconsistent boss encounters and a lack of enemy variety, the overwhelming joy of exploration, clever puzzles, and enchanting art direction make this an exceptional journey for fans of both the genre and the series.

Even though it physically follows centuries of fictional lore and decades of real-world gaming history, Belmont's Curse undeniably represents a fresh start. While it may not introduce anything wildly revolutionary to the genre mechanically, the French development team has highly successfully dragged Castlevania kicking and screaming into the modern era.

The wait was worth it. But we hope the next one won’t take this long. Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is everything we hoped for in a new title. The game retains the same magic as the other titles in the series and even takes it to an incredible new level. In fact, we can even say that this game ranks among the best Castlevania titles ever released. This is partly due to the controls, which are fast and modern. There’s also the game’s faithful adherence to the franchise and everything that comes with it—exploring the world and the surprises that unfold along the way. In short, if you love the series, there’s absolutely no reason not to give this one a try. And don’t be surprised if you have a smile on your face from start to finish.

Castlevania: Belmont's Curse gives the series' fans clear reasons to be interested: whip-wielding action, customizable abilities, and an art show that reinterprets the world of Castlevania, with a vast Metroidvania world to explore.

It's easy to consider it one of the best Metroidvanias of the entire generation, an essential game for lovers of the genre, but it's not so automatic to list it among the best Castlevanias due to its kaleidoscopic nature, as it successfully draws on so many inspirations but ends up overshadowing the original.

Castlevania: Belmont's Curse is the return fans have long been waiting for. Evil Empire and Motion Twin's title respects tradition without being trapped by it, with the whip as a means of movement, a tarot card system, and a rich world to explore creating a solid and satisfying experience. The lock-on hitboxes could use a rethink and some enemies that are too similar to one another are flaws that don't detract from the overall experience.
Ultimately, Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse feels like a meaningful new direction for the franchise rather than a simple return to familiar territory.

The return isn’t without its rough edges, and it will hardly please every nostalgic fan, but it represents a convincing new beginning. Rather than trying to recreate the Castlevania of the past, Evil Empire attempts to imagine what the franchise can be today and perhaps in the future. And when Dracula’s castle once again looms over a doomed city, the feeling is that this story still has plenty left to tell us. All things considered, we have a solid and ambitious return on our hands, one capable of combining Castlevania’s classic legacy with modern movement, satisfying combat, and exploration full of secrets. A few superfluous mechanics, inconsistent difficulty, and some divisive artistic choices keep it from reaching full excellence, but the foundations for a new tomorrow in the vampire-hunter saga are absolutely there.
Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is an absolute whirlwind of a fun ride traversing through a ravaged Paris, led by the threat of the great Dracula himself.

Castlevania: Belmont's Curse is a triumphant return for the franchise, proving that the Igavania formula can evolve without losing its identity. The collaboration between Konami, Evil Empire and Motion Twin has produced a title that meets the expectations of the series' veterans while welcoming new players with accessible mechanics and a well-calibrated difficulty curve. Rose Belmont proves to be a charismatic protagonist, and the innovative use of Tarot Cards adds depth to both the story and the gameplay. The combat, with its emphasis on mobility and timing, recalls the best moments of Symphony of the Night and Aria of Sorrow, but with a modernity that makes it immediate and engaging. Technically, the game is solid on PS5 Pro, with stable performance (apart from a few rather crippling bugs) and an audio side that enhances the gothic atmosphere. In the end, the overall experience is of high quality and consistent with what you would expect from a main chapter of the series.

Belmont's Curse is a good game worth playing, with a strong visual identity, powerful atmosphere and notable ideas, but it is let down by inconsistencies in its controls, level design and rewards. It is neither a failed Castlevania comeback nor a game that sets a new benchmark for modern Metroidvanias. It deserves respect for its strengths, but its limitations keep it from fully shining.

Belmont’s Curse is a very good modern take on the series that helped define the Metroidvania genre and has been absent from the mainstream for more than a decade. It’s fast, it’s beautiful, and it has the confidence to be different while still respecting where it came from. If you’re looking for a fun Metroidvania, don’t miss Belmont’s Curse.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is by far a great comeback for Konami to bring back the series. After having the great Castlevania anime series, just getting the game is great! I was on edge thinking this would be something subpar or meek. But, man am I glad this proves me wrong in more ways than one. This is a great game respecting the classics and growing the story from there. I’m hoping for more of this from Evil Empire in the future or any Metroidvania projects they have in store for us.

I give Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse the Thumb Culture Platinum Award

By incorporating two decades of metroidvania evolution into the old Castlevania mould, Belmont's Curse manages to rise above many of its franchise predecessors. High production values and all the best parts of Celeste, Dead Cells and Ori, make this new entry a welcome return to Dracula's castle, and long overdue.
Dracula has returned, and Evil Empire must prove that the legacy of Castlevania is still as powerful as the Dark Lord himself.

Belmont’s Curse is a great game, that sacrifices some of the series identity for a new and fresh approach to the modern gaming space. While the game isn’t Symphony of the Night, it still has a unique and recognizable identity nonetheless, with great care in both its aesthetic and gaming aspect.
Belmont's Curse is a beautiful and fun Metroidvania that has a lot to offer, but in the genre it helped create, today it follows in the footsteps of others more than it leaves new ones of its own.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse delivers an enjoyable Metroidvania experience with satisfying combat, varied boss fights, and a progression system that ties exploration and combat together. Rose Belmont’s story also offers plenty of connections to the franchise’s history, giving longtime fans something extra to appreciate. Some areas can be confusing to navigate, while the art style and soundtrack feel quite different from the series’ classic gothic atmosphere.

The game they've put out for the price they're asking is quite good. This game could be a great opportunity to revive the series, and Evil Empire will use the feedback from this game to create something even better in a new Castlevania game.
Castlevania: Belmont's Curse does the job of bringing back the series well enough, but it struggles to reach its full potential due to a combination of some odd design decisions and technical issues.

Belmont’s Curse has a curse of its own: it will always be compared with its grandfather, Symphony of the Night, which, much like Dracula himself, seems immune to the passage of time. That is quite a legacy to live up to. The fact that there is a debate to be had about which game is better is a testament to just how strong a return Belmont’s Curse is. On its own merits, Belmont’s Curse has shaken up the genre primarily through its refined combat and a different approach to structure, starting as a straightforward platformer before gradually introducing familiar Metroidvania elements and eventually embracing the genre in full. It is a masterclass in balancing a Metroidvania, and its numerous difficulty options also make it one of the most accessible. For now, we declare Belmont’s Curse the rightful heir to the Castlevania legacy and a worthy claimant to the modern day Metroidvania throne.

Despite some performance hiccups, Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is the most fun I've had in a metroidvania game since Metroid Dread. It's exceptional value for money and an easy recommendation for lovers of the genre.

Belmont’s Curse brings Castlevania back to its Metroidvania roots, with satisfying exploration, a versatile whip and abilities that make revisiting old areas worthwhile. Clumsy controls, uneven difficulty and an underdeveloped lead character hold it back, but the fundamentals are strong enough to make this a welcome return.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is a much-needed return, updated yet retaining that classic charm that will delight both fans of the genre and those venturing through the gates of Count Dracula’s Castle for the first time.

Castlevania: Belmont's Curse is a strong comeback and a genuinely fresh 2D Castlevania, with the whip as weapon and grappling hook, fast and punchy combat and a fun relic system, despite a delayed jump and sparse save points.

Although the boss battles in Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse may be lacking and the story, predictable, other aspects like its game design, soundtrack, combat, and characterisation outshine its flaws and make them insignificant. The game is a delight to play and doesn’t shy away from letting players take their time unravelling the mysteries of 1944 Paris. It’s safe to say that Konami can boldly bring on the next chapter of House Belmont in future titles.
“Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse” brings a franchise that seems as immortal as Count Dracula himself back into the spotlight.

In an era with so many new releases and so many excellent Metroidvania games, the fact that we spent so many hours on *Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse*, trying to clear every room and uncover every secret, speaks volumes about its quality.

Wielding a whip, discovering hidden mana and health upgrades, and exploring vast Gothic structures are all part of Castlevania’s DNA, and Belmont’s Curse faithfully preserves these elements. Longtime fans will feel right at home, while new additions demonstrate how the developers have learned from their previous projects and other games in the genre. After years with few major releases beyond mobile gacha games and projects in other media, this marks an excellent return for the series on consoles. Even 40 years after its debut, Castlevania still has plenty of potential to deliver outstanding gaming experiences.

I enjoyed almost all of my time with Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse. The art, music, and story kept me immersed throughout my playthrough. While I was a little skeptical about combat due to the trailers I’d seen making it look more like a 2D Soulslike, the game handles it well. Instead of the departure I expected the combat to be, the fighting felt more diverse and fast-paced while still straightforward enough for a Castlevania game.

Castlevania: Belmont's Curse feels like a love letter to a beloved series, while also managing to maintain its own distinct identity. Great platforming elements, fun and snappy combat and some great nods from the games of the past, this is a game that's incredibly easy to recommend!

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is a romp through a ravaged Paris beset by monsters and led in narrative by the threat of the great Dracula. With excellent art design, challenging platforming and tough bosses, all of the ingredients are here for this Metroidvania. Does it stand against the best? I believe if there was as much content as say a Silksong, potentially. The combat is a blast and the options really provide options. Any chance of remaking the old ones, too? I’d be there day one.

After 18 years, a genre pioneer returns with rewarding exploration, engaging combat, and a compelling story. Yet punishing platforming and shallow progression hold it back. A fine Metroidvania, but one that has lost some of its distinct Castlevania identity.
While some issues do hold it back from its true potential though, Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse still feels like a bloody great time that’ll at least leave you pleased with its taste, if not ecstatic.
While it has the essential elements of the Castlevania series, and a great mix of weapons and exploration, its tuning and Switch performance could have used more refinement

By the end, Castlevania: Belmont's Curse leaves you feeling that the series is in good hands. Combat, traversal, puzzles, characters, and visuals all work well on their own and even better together. The tarot system acts as the glue, turning signposting, lore, spells, and dialogue into one connected loop.

The Castlevania franchise has seen a resurgence in popularity in recent years with the success of the two animated series on Netflix and various older games being made available on modern platforms, so it’s exciting to see what’s in store in its future. Rose Belmont is a solid new protagonist, and Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is an epic new entry in Konami’s long-running series.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse delivers a strong return to classic 2D action, with satisfying combat, striking gothic visuals, and an excellent soundtrack. While its exploration and platforming play things relatively safe, it remains a highly enjoyable adventure for fans of the series.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse makes a triumphant return with an entry that grips you from the start and refuses to let go until the credits roll, where every single enemy encounter is an absolute joy to experience.
Castlevania: Belmont's Curse provides satisfying combat and rewarding exploration but is marred by inconsistent movement, repetitive enemies, and a forgettable soundtrack.
Belmont’s Curse is the Castlevania we’ve been waiting for: fluid whip combat, bosses that push you to the limit, and a castle that feels like the real thing.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is a smart modern refresh of the Metroidvania design, taking modern mechanics, fluidity and speed and pairing that with a traditional Castlevania adventure that fits into a popular part of the timeline.
Belmont’s Curse isn’t just the game that Castlevania needed, but easily one of the best ones in the franchise.

A unique action-platformer for both longtime Castlevania fans and those looking to dive into the series for the first time. This is a game that we highly recommend not just within the series, but within the platformer genre as a whole.

Belmont’s Curse delivers a traditional Castlevania-flavored metroidvania, with a versatile whip, varied boss encounters, and plenty of weapons and abilities to discover. But uneven difficulty, frustrating projectile-heavy fights, and softlocks can turn exploration into a chore. Long stretches of backtracking, sparse checkpoints, and inconsistent visuals further dull the adventure. Customizable settings offer some relief, but they can’t fully make up for the missing quality-of-life features. It’s enjoyable in moments, though best approached on sale.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is a worthy return for the franchise, featuring fast-paced combat, creative bosses, and rewarding exploration. While some aspects, such as weapon variety, traversal, and music, could be improved, its fresh take on the gothic aesthetic and modernized gameplay make for an enjoyable adventure. Although it may disappoint fans expecting something closer to recent 2D entries, it successfully preserves Castlevania’s identity while offering a fun blend of action, exploration, and well-designed challenges.

Evil Empire understands what makes Castlevania tick. The combat strikes a satisfying balance between challenge and a versatile tactical moveset that turns every fight into a dance of blades. The level design guides me without holding my hand, always keeping the next milestone just out of reach. And just when I think I’ve got the hang of things, the next boss absolutely wrecks me and proves me wrong.

Castlevania: Belmont's Curse is Konami's trump card for bringing one of its most legendary franchises back to life. It is a modern Castlevania adapted to the latest mechanics of the Metroidvania genre, featuring classic touches and meticulous attention to detail.

Castlevania returns to the 'Metroidvania' genre it helped popularize. It doesn't takes the crown, but it proves it can still put up a serious fight. Belmont's Curse is a great 2D action game featuring excellent level design, a fantastic atmosphere, and some of the best platforming challenges we've seen in a long time. The combat pacing takes time to get a hold on, but once you learn to control Rose, you won't want to stop until you've defeated Dracula.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse doesn’t return to lecture the industry on how to make a Metroidvania. The market has had plenty of time to figure that out on its own. That is likely the biggest difference between this comeback and what would have happened had the series never faded away. In 1997, Symphony of the Night could write the rules. In 2026, Belmont’s Curse has to fight for attention against games that spent years polishing the very ideas Castlevania helped pioneer. Even so, it manages to carve out its own space.

Castlevania: Belmont's Curse is the return I’ve been waiting for from one of the most important franchises in video game history. Evil Empire managed to capture the essence of classic Metroidvanias while also introducing excellent new ideas. With stunning artistic direction and unforgettable boss battles, Rose Belmont’s journey is one that makes you want to explore every last corner of the map. For those who, like me, have always preferred Castlevania in its 2D roots, the feeling is wonderful: the Belmonts are back, and may many more games follow!
With Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse, Evil Empire has brought the series back to life with an excellent Metroidvania that easily outshines much of the 2026 competition.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse delivers where it matters most and gets the fundamentals right. The gameplay is fun, encouraging you to explore Paris and Dracula’s castle, and we actually kept playing until we had uncovered 100% of the map and found every secret. In our view, that’s all a Castlevania game really needs to do. That makes it easy to forgive the merely decent soundtrack and somewhat generic story. The only real downside is the limited replay value, as there are no extra game modes to keep you coming back.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse delivers a promising return for the series, combining fast-paced combat, a diverse arsenal of weapons, and an interconnected world full of secrets. Its strength shines in the clever utilization of the whip, special abilities, and boss encounters within an experience that respects its classic roots while giving them a modern touch. Although some of its elements feel familiar to fans of this genre, it possesses the necessary components to deliver an enjoyable and distinctive adventure for action and exploration enthusiasts.
Castlevania: Belmonts Curse is an excellent return to form for one of gamings most enduring franchises ever and worthy of the legacy.

Castlevania: Belmont's Curse is, in large part, the revival of the franchise I had always hoped for. Introducing many fresh ideas and advancing the series' legacy—without being tethered to the past or merely copying what came before—the new title features masterful level design and delivers a highly competent Metroidvania experience on all fronts, even if a few details stray slightly from the core Castlevania formula.

I think Konami and its development team hit the right notes with Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse, especially when it comes to reintroducing a long dormant franchise to a wider audience. It’s a game of three distinct acts: a somewhat generic opening third, a middle portion that gradually picks up the pace, and a truly mesmerizing final stretch that finally feels like good old Castlevania at its finest.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse stands as one of the best 2D and Metroidvania gaming experiences, thanks to its distinctive artistic identity and gothic atmosphere. With rich exploration and varied, enjoyable gameplay that blends combat and movement, it delivers an adventure well worth experiencing.

Castlevania Belmont’s Curse is a great game (and ridiculous price) whether you are fans of the license or newcomer. This is one of the titles of the year. Irreproachable in its realization and its staging, we will evaluate our pleasure not to the martial victories on the bosses, but to discover the passages and secrets of the map and the level design. A grand cru.

Evil Empire continues to impress by adding a drawn art style and impressive visuals to the game overall. Not just from character designs but bosses, enemies, and environments too. And while its soundtrack is not the best part, the rest of the sound design fits well into the game. If you are a Castlevania or Metroidvania fan, or even a newcomer, it’s a strong entry for a titan of a series. And one that all players should try to experience as soon as they can.

Evil Empire’s Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse draws heavily from the lore, characters, story, and presentation, but the gameplay has shifted away from many of its RPG roots.  This shift is met with tightly polished execution; however, there is a lingering sense that this isn’t what some fans were expecting.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is the comeback fans have been waiting for for over a decade: a metroidvania that is classic in structure but modern in sensibility, crafted by a studio that knows the genre inside out and proves it with incredibly rich traversal, memorable bosses and outstanding art direction.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is a compelling return to its roots for Konami’s legendary series, drawing on Evil Empire’s expertise to deliver a 2D Metroidvania that masterfully combines exploration, challenging combat, and an art style brimming with care and charm. Rose Belmont’s adventure won us over thanks to a deep combat system and the Arcana, which enrich both progression and the narrative. The gothic recreation of Paris and Dracula’s castle is stunning, accompanied by a compelling soundtrack, though perhaps not quite on par with the splendor of Michiru Yamane’s work. Some limitations in enemy variety and inconsistent difficulty prevent Belmont’s Curse from reaching perfection, but they in no way detract from the overall quality of an adventure that proves just how much the Belmont family still has to tell.
All in all, Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse marks a particularly welcome return for a franchise that richly deserved to be back in the spotlight.

Castlevania: Belmont's Curse marks a triumphant return for the legendary series, with outstanding level design, satisfying combat and a magnificent soundtrack. Its visuals feel somewhat dated and a few difficulty spikes frustrate, but this is a wonderfully crafted metroidvania.

It’s almost mind-blowing to me to be sitting here, typing up my thoughts on a new Castlevania 2D game in 2026. I never would have called this series coming back. Or if it did, I would have expected Konami to try another big-scale 3D reboot. But seeing Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse on my hard drive and being able to play it makes it feel like one part of the gaming world is working as intended. This game feels incredibly good to play, and I’d recommend checking it out as soon as possible.

How do you bring back one of the most legendary video game franchises after a nearly two decade hiatus since its last 2D Entry? With a twenty-five hour symphony of the classics retaining everything that made the series iconic, but reworked to make the experience feel modern with gameplay inspired by one of the most successful indie games of all time. Dracula, Belmont's, demanding platforming and enemies, gothic aesthetic, whips, sub-weapons, layered map, secrets, it's all here.

Belmont’s Curse is a sublime fusion of Castlevania and Dead Cells that blends classic and modern elements effortlessly to make it feel like a natural progression for the series without losing sight of the origins that made Castevania legendary. Purists might disagree with the new feeling being too much of a departure, but for those who appreciated the series revolution that Symphony of The Night was in 1997, they will appreciate the revolution that Belmont’s Curse is in 2026.

Ultimately, Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse doesn’t just mark the end of a twelve year mainline game drought, it answers the question posed at the very beginning of this review with a resounding yes. It is an emphatic, confident return to form. While a few weapon categories fall into redundancy once you have the iconic whip in hand, that minor imbalance is easily eclipsed by how thoughtfully Evil Empire has built the rest of the game.

Castlevania: Belmont's Curse is a treat for fans of the franchise or Metroidvanias in general, and also a great entry point for those who have never wielded the Belmont's whip or for those looking for something fun to play and pass the time. Whatever your case, you can go for it without fear!

The music, gameplay, levels, bosses, &a; looks are all incredible. It's classic old-school Castlevania in many ways, for good and bad. A handful of modern conveniences, some devilishly tricky level design, and a decent story combine for something well worth your time.
Castlevania: Belmont's Curse retains the soul of the Castlevania series perfectly intact, thanks not only to a well-written story but also to its art style and fun gameplay.

Castlevania: Belmont´s Curse combines metroidvania exploration, demanding combat and a story where Rose Belmont proves she has a personality of her own. The Arcana system adds both abilities and narrative depth, while a well-balanced difficulty makes every defeated boss feel genuinely rewarding.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is a classic metroidvania in the best sense, featuring excellent combat, superb level design, and outstanding acrobatic platforming. A lack of artistic ambition and a sense of disorientation in the second half keep it from reaching the genre’s recent heights, but it remains an essential experience for metroidvania fans, made all the more significant by being the first new Castlevania in many years.
Despite its minor shortcomings, Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is a successful title that brings the series’ magnificent gothic atmosphere together with outstanding gameplay.
Not a new pinnacle of the genre, but a worthy comeback for Castlevania with fast combat, creative plattforming and a great world that motivates me to master each challenge and open every chest.

Castlevania Belmont’s Curse is a game that feels thoughtfully designed from beginning to end, constantly finding ways to reinvent itself. With a better balance between boss fights and regular enemies, along with a more streamlined approach to revisiting previously explored areas, it could have been close to perfection. Even so, I think it’s a more than solid comeback for a franchise returning to the spotlight after so many years. As long as Konami maintains this level of quality, I’ll continue to look forward to all its upcoming releases. Hopefully, this game marks the definitive return of Castlevania.

Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is not just a great Castlevania title, it is one of the best Metroidvanias I have played in recent years. The movement feels spot-on, the combat is challenging without being unfair and the visuals are fantastic. The story kept me fully engaged and the game frequently mixes interesting puzzles between fun platforming and combat sequences, all while equipping you with a variety of useful tools.

Castlevania: Belmont's Curse may not play exactly like an Iga-vania, but that doesn't mean it's not a Castlevania title. It truly is in spirit, ambition, action, and overall structure, with a few new twists to the rules that make even veterans wary and up their game. [...]

Even if its music direction may leave you in bloody tears, everything else about this new search action title is as golden as the Alchemy Lab music track in Symphony of the Night.

"A promising return with a revitalized legacy in the heart of Paris"
Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse successfully revitalizes the series through an experience that blends a compelling story, Deep Exploration, and a deep combat System-Supported by Arcana abilities and an innovative whip. Distinctive art design and polished technical performance further elevate the experience, while boss encounters offer a genuine challenge that rewards skill and strategy. The game delivers a complete adventure that honors the Castlevania legacy while evolving it with a modern touch.

An unexpected gem in almost every way. I don't think many were crying out for a Hellraiser game, but everyone will be demanding a sequel to Revival, as Saber's horror show delivers a compelling, rich journey through pain and pleasure.

Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival is a fantastic game that’ll satisfy both franchise and horror survival fans. Depending on whether or not you can stomach it, of course. It really doesn’t hold back, as it shouldn’t. Between the intense cinematics and the gut-wrenching narrative, this game pulls on every string. The Cenobites of Clive Barker’s world are known for two things: pain and pleasure. And this game showcases it all. There were many times when, while adventuring through the cultists’ underground lair, the world at large, or through the sex club, I had to scrape my jaw off the floor. It is a spectacle, and if you can handle a metric ton of body horror, this game should be on your radar.

Hellraiser: Revival is a faithful adaptation of the universe created by Clive Barker, combining an oppressive atmosphere, grotesque visuals, and genuinely tense moments with a structure heavily inspired by games of the genre, most notably Resident Evil 4 Remake. Although the puzzles are simple and the difficulty decreases considerably as the player masters its mechanics and abilities, the campaign manages to hold its own thanks to the excellent setting, intense chases, and creative use of the Lament Configuration. It's not revolutionary, but it's an interesting and authentic survival horror game for fans of the genre and, especially, of Hellraiser.

Those unfamiliar with Barker’s work who are looking for a strong title in this genre will find one that offers plenty of variety and a striking visual identity. It may not reinvent the wheel, but it knows how to combine its gameplay elements in a highly effective and engaging way.
Hellraiser: Revival is at its best when its horror gamification takes a back seat, providing a world that is equal parts depraved and disturbing, scary and thrilling.
Clive Barker's Hellraiser: Revival is not for those with weak stomachs. It's also got a lot of painful imagery. If you can power through that, there's a solid survival horror experience underneath.

I am pleasantly surprised at how much I enjoyed Hellraiser: Revival. Its respect for its source material is apparent throughout, with the Labyrinth, the Cenobites, and the Genesis Configuration being standout pieces of the puzzle. The rest of the game isn't reinventing the wheel for first-person horror, but the "don't fix what isn't broken" approach works just fine here. The squeamish need not apply, as there are moments made to make your skin crawl, but even the most horror-averse people can have a great time in this Labyrinth. Saber Interactive has such sights to show you, and thankfully, there's more pleasure than pain.

Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival delivers an excellent adaptation by expanding the franchise's mythology and book lore, bringing back the classic voice of Pinhead alongside a bold Unreal Engine 5 art direction. Although it stumbles confusedly between deliberate survival horror and action FPS, the title establishes itself as a worthy adaptation of the series' cultural impact.

Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival succeeds above all where it matters most: atmosphere, visual identity, and fidelity to the franchise’s aesthetic. The Genesis Configuration adds personality to a fairly traditional survival horror framework, though issues with balancing, AI, and protagonist writing hold back its potential. A successful adaptation, even if not without its rough edges.

It has some issues than can annoy, such as difficulty spikes and a couple of troublesome forced stealth sections, but these don't stop Clive Barker's Hellraiser: Revival from being a thrilling rollercoaster of a survival horror experience. Sexy, gory and grotesque are perhaps the best words to sum it up.

It’s shocking in 2026 that Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival is a single-player game rather than an asymmetrical multiplayer title, but it’s even more surprising that a game in the Hellraiser franchise is actually great. Seeing a team put time and care into creating a new story for a series that naturally belongs in the mythology and is actually fun to experience feels like a minor miracle, even with some occasional frustrations. Fans of the franchise can rejoice that this title is worthy of Barker’s creation, but newcomers may find that the taste of Cenobite pleasure being offered has them hooked.
Clive Barker's Hellraiser: Revival is incredibly faithful to the source material, creating a horror game filled with some strong puzzles and a stunningly beautiful world.

Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival is a good survival horror game that finds its greatest strengths in its atmosphere and in the distinctive identity of Barker’s universe. It does not particularly innovate within the genre, and some of its mechanics feel all too familiar, but its linear structure, solid resource management, and especially its visual and audio presentation come together to create a cohesive and enjoyable experience from start to finish.

Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival doesn't attempt to revolutionize the survival horror genre, but its blend of horror, action, exploration, and an aggressive, violent, and evocative atmosphere delivers a memorable experience. It has a few rough edges to polish out, but for fans of the genre and the author's work, this is a game well worth checking out.

Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival delivers an entertaining yet somewhat generic survival horror experience, borrowing familiar mechanics from other games in the genre without adding much depth or innovation. While its premise is intriguing, the narrative relies too heavily on shock value rather than fully exploring its potential. The result is an enjoyable but ultimately forgettable horror adventure that falls short of its ambitions.

The strength of Clive Barker's Hellraiser: Revival lies in its refusal to apologize for the carnal violence and discomfort it puts on display. Even as the gameplay struggles to balance survival horror with action, the compelling narrative and relentless art direction smooth over its rough edges, proving that the pain and pleasure of Barker's creation remain just as fascinating in video games.

It’s a game that’s consistently harrowing and very much “for adults only” with its blend of extreme violence, references to sexual bondage, and nightmare fuel creatures who want to rip you apart before you die. This game very much wants to tear your soul apart.

An unexpectedly successful survival horror game that does justice to the
Hellraiser franchise. It’s a bit of a stretch, and there’s no shortage
of bugs, but it’s hugely satisfying, whilst offering visuals that are
rarely seen in games.
An uncompromising and faithful adaptation of Clive Barker’s Hellraiser universe, where the horror pleasures are let down by the pains of its combat.

I have complicated feelings about Hellraiser: Revival. At its heart, Hellraiser: Revival is a well-paced, competently-made survival horror experience that feels incredibly authentic to its gritty source material. But it's also an experience that's currently hampered by immersion-breaking bugs, enemy AI issues, and uninspired boss fights. As a Hellraiser fan, Revival had more than enough underlying substance and quality to pull me through its labyrinth, but I'm not sure I'd be so ready to recommend the journey to a series newcomer.

Clive Barker's Hellraiser: Revival isn't a perfect outing. Some of the creative choices, like adding in explorable sections, add more bloat for the sake of gameplay variety without adding significant substance. To boot, enemy AI in these parts of the game is very simple and offers little challenge. With that said, the true potency of this game comes from the more focused, linear areas, where the concepts and scares get the chance to really show themselves. There are some cool ideas in Hellraiser: Revival, and every Hellraiser fan needs to check it out.

Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival was a tough game to critique, as the pieces were all there, they just didn’t all mesh together in the right way. I’d still recommend it to Hellraiser and horror fans alike though. My only advice would be to knock it down to the story mode to alleviate some of its more frustrating elements.

Hellraiser: Revival doesn't reinvent the immersive sim template it borrows, but a visually arresting, Brutalist-inspired Labyrinth, a story that respects Clive Barker, and a gleeful run of one-off ideas make it an authentic, unapologetically extreme horror.

Clive Barker's Hellraiser: Revival does the iconic horror franchise justice with its story and atmosphere, both of which are top-notch and enough to justify its existence. Its metaphorical plot and incredibly detailed locations make this horror adventure tough to put down, constantly encouraging you to push forward to see what else it has up its sleeve. However, its lousy combat system and excessive number of trial-and-error chase sequences may be a deal-breaker for those who believe "gameplay is king."
Clive Barker's Hellraiser: Revival is an interesting game, but it doesn't excel at anything. However, its recreation of the films' atmosphere makes it perfect for fans of the franchise.

Hellraiser Revival was a pleasant surprise. The atmosphere and characters born from Clive Barker’s imagination are brilliantly rendered, and the game doesn't shy away from depicting extreme events without censorship. The gameplay calls to mind various entries in the Resident Evil saga—a series that is frequently paid homage to, or even outright mimicked in certain mechanics. Ultimately, it all works, offering an entertaining and fun experience... were it not for the heap of bugs and glitches plaguing the game. None of them are game-breaking, but they do disrupt the pacing and hinder the player's immersion in the story's twisted, unsettling atmosphere.

Clive Barker's Hellraiser: Revival is an honest attempt to create a solid survival horror game set in the Hellraiser universe. The story is impressive while also being canon in the series. The Labyrinth is unique and helps deviate from a progressively mundane survival horror experience. The game starts out insane, but begins to fall off more and more. Performance-wise, the game struggles, but performance mode works well enough on PS5 Pro. Fans of this type of horror and the series will enjoy the story and the lore of the world, but this game isn't for casual horror fans. While it comes off as late-stage Resident Evil at home, the flow of the game just doesn't work well. It becomes more taxing to play.

Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival marks the franchise’s debut in the video game industry, and while it juggles a few too many ideas without fully mastering them, it still delivers a solid package. The potential is undeniable, and the future looks bright for the series—so long as the developers narrow their focus and find a clear direction.

At the very least, Hellraiser: Revival succeeds in delivering a faithful adaptation and continuation of the famous body-horror franchise. It's commendable that the developers don't hold back on the S&M, sexuality, depravity, and violence, allowing the game to remain true to Clive Barker's horrific universe. That said, once the initial shock of its extreme presentation wears off, cracks begin to appear in the gameplay, which feels overstuffed with ideas borrowed from much better games.
Hellraiser: Revival is an original yet faithful adaptation of Clive Barker’s long-running franchise. Its unapologetic explicitness is only held back by its AA jank and lack of any replayability.

Hellraiser: Revival is a decent game and a rather good Hellraiser story. Made with evident reverence for Clive Barker’s kinky chicanery, it’s a commendable attempt at an action horror that could have been terrific with some meanginful depth and refinement. Saber did nothing wrong in borrowing BioShock and Resident Evil’s ideas - what it did wrong was fail to borrow more of them!

Revival is not for the faint-hearted, and possibly not the stout-hearted either, given its graphic depiction of torture, body horror and full-frontal nudity. But adult fans of Hellraiser’s brutal fiction will find the descent into the moral abyss true to the Barker brand.

Few horror video game experiences are as graphic and unrelenting as Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival. The vivid displays of torture and a presentation soaked in sin definitely help this resurrection stand out from its contemporaries. The mix of stealth, firearm action, puzzles, boss fights, and escape sections keeps you on your toes, though the repetition is undesirable. The story is easy to follow and approachable for newcomers, yet it can be too reliant on cutscenes to a detrimental point where it seems to prefer telling rather than showing. Still, it works well enough as a backdrop to all the hellish action. As a straightforward narrative experience, you can do a lot worse than Hellraiser: Revival, yet its gameplay and A.I. kinks leave much to be desired.

Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival combines numerous ideas; however, not all of them come together seamlessly. The game thrives when placed in a vulnerable position, but when you gain more strength and action takes over horror, it loses the sense of danger. Each location captures a dark, sadomasochistic ambience, which is where Revival feels most at home. Alas, some bugs and performance issues ultimately tarnish an otherwise atmospheric experience.
While the studded scalp of otherworld antagonist Pinhead absolutely looks the part, it’s a shame that little else in Hellraiser: Revival has been nailed to anywhere near the same extent.

My main takeaway from Hellraiser: Revival is that this could have been a phoned-in release. A first-person shooter with some famous characters, linear levels - bish, bash, bosh. The fact we’ve got a sort of Resident Evil-light, and a fairly competent one, is a big surprise. This isn’t a clever game, and it’s merely OK for most of its campaign, but its ambitions for its budget price are hard to be too down on.

Hellraiser Revival has all the blood, sex and grotesquerie you’d expect, almost perfectly capturing the Hellraiser experience in video game form. But it struggles to carve out an identity of its own, mimicking plenty of horror greats without quite understanding what made them so great. Regardless of its flaws, Revival tells a story that Hellraiser fans should enjoy, even if its uneven gameplay makes it a much harder sell for everyone else.

Clive Barker's Hellraiser: Revival reminded me of the second movie in the series, but not so much for its plot and atmosphere (well, partly for those, too) as for its ability to alternate between interesting situations and others that are decidedly more mundane. We’re dealing with a game driven by two distinct voices that don’t mesh well, especially on a structural level: on the one hand, there’s the labyrinth with all its whimsical touches, mythology, and so on, while on the other, we have a clumsy attempt to blend the mechanics of the latest Resident Evil games with those of Half-Life or BioShock, without bothering to balance all the elements or adequately explore the different gameplay perspectives. The result is an amorphous and disjointed work, lacking a clearly discernible structure capable of adequately justifying the transitions between the various dimensions of the adventure.

Clive Barker's Hellraiser: Revival is a video game with a charm of its own, one that comes mostly from the novella and the film Barker wrote and directed in 1986 and 1987 respectively. It has that raw patina, that grime, that violent, inexplicable and fascinating sex that lived in the original work. After all, Barker himself supervised the game's script. However, much like the Cenobites, Hellraiser: Revival inflicts pleasure and suffering in equal measure: alongside an unhealthy (in the best sense) and well-realized atmosphere and a few well-crafted moments, the rest is plagued by bugs of every kind, sometimes so severe that they compromise the experience. At the same time, the game suffers from a whole series of flaws and naivetés that make it anything but perfect: sudden difficulty spikes, tedious and uninspiring boss fights, stealth sections best forgotten, and an endless recycling of mid-bosses, enemies and situations. A real shame, because this imagery deserved far more; instead, it too has remained a slave to the hell it was born from.

Clive Barker's Hellraiser: Revival had all the components to become a hit. However, stylish design and well-written characters are unable to save mediocre gameplay and irritating puzzles combined with outdated mechanics. On top of that, in 2026 what's happening on screen is incapable of scaring an audience that has lived through a pandemic, an AI boom, and numerous military conflicts.

Ultimately, if you’re a fan of the franchise, this is a great entry into the series lore, and a horror experience you’ll find lots in to enjoy, but you’ll need to be willing to look past it’s inconsistent pacing and spotty gameplay experience. If you’re not a huge Hellraiser fan, then it might be that bit harder for you to push through, but it’s by no means a bad game – just one that, perhaps fittingly, offers some pain with its pleasure.

Clive Barker’s Hellraiser Revival is a frustrating experience, as for every one thing it does really well, it does two things that will annoy the life out of you. Part of me was willing to see past the jank, as you have a pretty niche horror title coming to life in a new medium, and I certainly respect it for giving it a go. However, too often its design choices would irritate me, hold me back from progressing, or just straight up make me not want to play. While it’s got little sparks of something special in there, Hellraiser: Revival is more pain than pleasure.

Clive Barker's Hellraiser: Revival starts with a promising, faithful depiction of its gruesome source material, delivering a striking aesthetic and an unforgettable introduction to the Cenobites. However, the illusion shatters right after the prologue. Plagued by an unbalanced combat system, frustrating resource management, and a massive amount of bugs, Saber Interactive's survival horror quickly devolves into a tedious chore rather than a compelling descent into madness. The narrative attempts to appear mature through excessive gore and explicit themes, but lacks genuine psychological depth. The chilling, perfect geometry of the Labyrinth sections, are not enough to redeem an overall wasted opportunity.

After watching Hellraiser: Revival’s finale stumble through the same visual and audio potholes plaguing the rest of the journey, I was angry. But upon taking time to cool down and reflect, my ire shifted to disappointment and relief that I didn't have to play more. During the rare moments Hellraiser: Revival isn't on fire in some way, it's a halfway respectable take on the popular horror franchise. I just wish playing it didn't so often feel like enduring the twisted machinations of Pinhead himself.

As a longtime Hellraiser fan, I really wanted to enjoy Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival, and there were moments where it captured what made the original film so memorable. Unfortunately, those moments were few and far between, and the underwhelming story, clunky gameplay, and technical issues made it difficult to stay invested. There’s plenty of gore here, but not nearly enough of the psychological horror that makes Hellraiser so interesting in the first place.
Metacritic user score 8.2/10 (484 ratings).
Hellraiser: Revival may not be great action horror but it does win the prize for most unique fetch quest.
The Labyrinth is calling

Whether I'm hunting a legendary animal, participating in a story mission, playing a game of poker, or just exploring the world I've absolutely adored every moment I've spent with the game. It more than fulfills every hope and desire I'd garnered as my anticipation for it grew over the last several years. The phenomenal narrative and performances are emotionally impactful, and the depth of interactivity embedded into the pristinely polished gameplay is nothing short of groundbreaking. Rockstar have outdone themselves with Red Dead Redemption 2 as it ushers in a new era of what the medium is capable of achieving. At this point, I can't wait to start again to explore a different playstyle and especially jump into Red Dead Online.
Red Dead Redemption 2 aimed high in delivering players a living, breathing world, and it has surely hit its mark as Rockstar’s deepest, most immersive experience yet.

Criticisms often come easier than compliments, but in the case of Red Dead Redemption 2, I am at a loss. This is one of the most gorgeous, seamless, rootinest, tootinest games ever made, and if you voluntarily miss out on it, you’re either not a gamer or in a coma.
Red Dead Redemption 2 is the most ambitious open world ever made. A new starting point for the genre, and an incomparable masterpiece.

The astounding thing about RDR 2 is that there's not only a staggering amount of story, side quests, and places to explore but that it's all high quality and doesn't feel tacked on. The high level of craftsmanship in this game is evident in all its aspects, and it's genuinely one of the best games of this generation of gaming.

Red Dead Redemption 2 is a triumphant open world experience that has plenty of engaging content in terms of whacky activities and side quests, while all the same while delivering constant cinematic and believable human drama. This is so much more than «just a cowboy game» – it's a game whose many systems and rich universe feel quite unlike anything else.

An astounding triumph that will certainly stand above the pack this season, Red Dead Redemption 2 is a unique game about unique people. The writing, visuals, and gameplay combine to make an absolute standout of a title, one that has been well worth the wait.
There was never any doubt that Red Dead Redemption 2 was going to be good, but this is something special. A masterpiece that many will be talking about for decades to come.
Red Dead Redemption 2 is a game of rare quality; a meticulously polished open world ode to the outlaw era.

A titanic videogame, a masterpiece that, like everything, will have passionate lovers and other players who will not get too caught up. Everything also depends on thematic genre and preferences. Maybe not everyone likes stories of 'Indians and cowboys'. But this interactive universe created by Rockstar tells a fantastically-constructed story and allows us to live a unique adventure. And for that reason, we believe that this production touches excellence. And for that, it establishes the first 10 in the history of IGN Spain. Good trip, cowboys!

Red Dead Redemption 2 is an absolute masterpiece, a true unique gaming experience. With its realistic and lifelike open world, Rockstar Games redefines what's possible in terms of interactive environment. Better yet, RDR2 is almost perfect on the technical standpoint with mesmerizing graphics, incredibly rich gameplay and one of the best stories ever written. An instant cult classic. [Actual score = 21/20, or 105]

Rockstar's eye for detail, presentation and tongue-in-cheek-storytelling makes this one an instant classic. Red Dead Redemption 2 is the ultimate Wild West sandbox-experience everyone has been waiting so very patiently for. It gives us more of everything we loved about the original and then takes it to a completely new level.
Victory of gaming as an art and the pinnacle of creativity in the gaming industry. A true, impeccably-polished masterpiece that will set standards for a decade to come.

Red Dead Redemption 2 redefines the open world genre. Arthur Morgan's journey through the late 1800s American frontier never reveals the stitches at its seams. Whether you're engaging in a massive shootout in a saloon or quietly enjoying a moment of reflection while fishing on a lake, it all feels like a part of Morgan's life. The level of detail is unsurpassed, and it's a game that wants you to take it slow and enjoy those small details. Rockstar took some risks in eliminating traditional gaming conveniences, but everything pays off in service of the greater experience. Red Dead Redemption 2 sets a new benchmark in detail, immersion, and cohesion that will be heralded for years to come. It's just about as perfect as a game can get.

Red Dead Redemption 2 not only lives up to expectations, but it smashes them and feels like the missing half of a story we never knew was incomplete. Improving on its predecessor in every way that counts, it also reignites interest in its landmark prequel, enhancing the overall experience to an epic scale and giving gamers an odyssey quite unlike any other.

Red Dead Redemption 2 is a triumph in world-building, character craft and downright skulduggery. Being bad has never felt so good as Rockstar toe the realism line while still keeping their sharp, trademark tongue in cheek. It’s the keen attention to detail where Rockstar succeed and this outlaw prequel comfortably outperforms their best works and in time, I believe, will be regarded as a once in a generation game.

Red Dead Redemption 2 is Rockstar's best game, and it's gripping from start to finish. It sets a new bar for open world interaction, providing an absurd level of detail across the board. It's an immaculately polished release that pulls no punches in its delivery, pushing both brutally mature themes and perfectly placed satire. While its clumsy controls and convoluted button layouts can ruin the fun on occasion, it's easy enough to look past these flaws when everything else is of such a high quality. Red Dead Redemption 2 is a modern masterpiece.
Rockstar Games continues to prove that when it comes to creating games, it’s the master at pushing the boundaries of what can be achieved.

The hype being created for Red Dead Redemption 2 and the expectations of the passionate fan-base made a part of me believe that Rockstar Games could never deliver on all of their many promises. They did, and then some. From the feeling of a realistic living world they've created to the emotional bonds you build, Red Dead Redemption 2 is the video game experience of this generation.

Red Dead Redemption 2 is a landmark title for storytelling, open-world design, voice acting, and immersion in video games. It is certainly among the best games of this console generation, but that's not all. It should eventually go down as one of the greatest games of all-time.

RDRII is a masterpiece —a game everyone who even slightly enjoys video games should play. It is not very innovative, but it excels at everything it does, creating a world and characters that will remain with us for a long, long time.
Red Dead Redemption 2 is an immense, breathtaking experience that will be treasured for years to come.
One of the best open world games ever, with the single best story ever written for a videogame.

Rockstar Games has outdone itself again with Red Dead Redemption II. The up-close portrayal of the outlaw Van der Linde gang’s unraveling is a compelling companion story that blends seamlessly with the original game, and depth and breadth of the open world is a technical triumph that every gamer should experience.

Red Dead Redemption 2 is a shockingly amazing game. A big world, an intriguing story, relatable characters and an unparalleled scope for, may be, the best and biggest game of this generation of consoles thus far.

Red Dead Redemption 2 is, without a shred of doubt, a new masterpiece brought to us by Rockstar. The new entry by the company has managed to achieve excellence in gameplay, storytelling and technical aspects. In the end, Rockstar has been successful in pushing the franchise to its limits in order to create one of the most complete games of all time.

What it comes down to is Rockstar’s intent to build a strongly realized and true to life facsimile of the 1890s — which they’ve done extraordinary well. So well, in fact, that I can’t ever go back to the first game anymore because I'm completely spoiled by this game’s offerings. Red Dead Redemption II is video game escapism at its finest and you’d be hard-pressed to find anything else this year that comes close to matching its accomplishments.

Overall, Red Dead Redemption 2 is the perfect gaming experience, and what you were hoping for in the next iteration of the series. It has a rich story, deep gameplay, unrivaled visuals, and plenty of plains to explore.

Red Dead Redemption 2 isn't just a great game. It's a game that sets an impossibly high new bar for how open-worlds can be handled. Its depiction of late 19th-century America feels both historically accurate yet abundantly open-ended, slow-paced and yet alive, grim and yet majestic. It makes the original Red Dead Redemption feel like a warm-up, the doodles on the page before the real thing has come to life.

Red Dead Redemption 2’s elusive, mysterious quality may be just that… it feels like every character in it has a soul. Considering the number of people across Rockstar’s entire studio roster that poured their blood, sweat and tears into this game it is no wonder that it actually feels alive.

Red Dead Redemption 2 brings to life the most vivid, immersive and alive Game World we’ve ever seen. The realistic gameplay mechanics, the smooth interaction with the NPCs and the game’s atmosphere send the gaming value of this title sky high. No matter the hype, no matter the wait, no matter the promotion, this game gives back to the gamers the lost hundreds of hours of contemporary repetitive gaming. In RDR2, every hour is pure gold.

Red Dead Redemption 2 takes everything that made the first so spectacular and elevates it to a new level. It boasts an enthralling story, coupled with rock solid gameplay, and is perhaps one of the best games ever made.
Once again, Rockstar Games has achieved a new goal and standard when speaking of modern gaming development.

Red Dead Redemption 2 tests the boundaries of interactive immersion. Few games look this good, play this well, and have this much to offer. It begs you to slow down, turn every page of its dramatic tale, and savor every last breathtaking detail. It challenges you to be prepared for anything, and make the right decisions when your choices matter most. Arthur Morgan is the lead, but the world takes center stage to pull you in. With a list of challenges left to finish and an online mode launching soon, we plan to spend a lot more time in Rockstar’s unparalleled recreation of the old west.

There's a new sheriff in the open-world action game genre in town. Red Dead Redemption 2 is sure ambitious but it succeeds everywhere he travels: exploration, gunfights, stealth, main quest, characters, side quests, customization, acting, hunting, fishing... Name one element, it delivers. And it sure looks like one of the best looking games ever seen and has many secrets yet to be discovered. And so it can be considered as a masterpiece, an extraordinary, legendary game that we will talk about with sincere admiration for ages.

Rockstar launches the best video game in its history thus far. A titanic development for a first category product that presents a gigantic world, with an unprecedented depth and an interaction that marks a step forward in the electronic entertainment industry. Top notch.

A game of unparalleled scope and ambition, with breathtaking visuals, a broad-ranging but intimate story, and an incredible sense of identity and purpose, Red Dead Redemption 2 will go down as one of the greatest games of the generation, and perhaps video game history.

This is a powerhouse of a video game, one of the finest, built by people at the top of their game and under intense pressure, lest we forget. As it is, they remind us of what games can be, creating a majestic sense of place and time and allowing you to play your role in the way only this medium allows. So, if you’ll excuse me, I have another train to, er, ‘catch’.

It is an incredible achievement in open world gaming, an intricate machine that disguises its machinery better than just about anything else that's come before. In addition to its lengthy and engrossing campaign, it delivers moments of emergent storytelling more compelling than anything I can ever remember playing. Graphically and aurally, it is top-to-bottom stunning.

The new North Star for Open-world games. Details, narrative and basically everything, are impressive. With Red Dead Redemption 2 Western setting had its first real huge tribute since the golden age of the classic movies.

Red Dead Redemption 2 is a magnificent open world game and one of the greatest games of all time. Its world offers unmatched attention to detail, the combat is excellent, and the story is among the best in a AAA game.

Red Dead Redemption 2 is the game that I would like to keep playing for years. The wild west is marvelous and full of interesting events. The story is both solid and attractive. What's more, the interactive system makes a great progress and you can interact with nearly everyone in various ways, and it feels really real. RDR2 definitely will be one of the greatest video games of all time.

If only I could give Red Dead Redemption 2 a higher score that 10, I would. This is by far the best open-world game that has ever graced the face of Earth. No other sandbox can even dream of holding a candle to Rockstar's newest gun-blazing, incredibly detailed Western epic. I envy all of you, who are yet to embark upon this fantastic journey and discover all the secrets this game holds. Truly, I could wipe my memory clean just to be able to experience that world once again. A true gem of the most noble kind.

There can be no doubt that this is a landmark game. It is a new high water-mark for lifelike video game worlds, certainly, but that world is also home to a narrative portrait of the wild west that is unexpectedly sombre and not afraid to take its time.

There is a constant question as to whether or not games are art. Red Dead Redemption 2 is a game that is going to be used as evidence for that argument from here on out. It is quite likely everything people who played Red Dead Redemption would want or need it to be. This game is, at times, a power fantasy that allows people to give in to baser instincts and revel in chaos. It is also an examination of honor and morality in a man who is callous and hardened. There are even times when it explores and embraces downtime in the same way a Studio Ghibli does, practically begging players to savor the vistas, watch wildlife, and enjoy the ride.
Red Dead Redemption 2 is an absolute undisputed classic and a legend in the making, plus with Red Dead Online on the horizon, it looks like our adventures in the wild west are just beginning.

Imagine an arthouse movie with summer blockbuster production values, as if Terrence Malick had been given a Star Wars movie. Imagine if Ubisoft had made Gone Home. Like Arthur Morgan himself, Red Dead Redemption 2 is meditative, laconic, a slow burn, drawn out and unhurried, sometimes even morose, more concerned with characters than spectacle. Let us go then, it suggests.

Red Dead Redemption 2 will most likely be looked upon as a another title that pushed what can be done in an open world, and be marked as one the developer’s most crowning achievements in their long history making video games.
Red Dead Redemption 2 is the best game of the current generation of gaming, and one that will definitely enter the pages of history.

Rockstar has done it again. Red Dead Redemption 2 has surpassed all the reference titles of its genre, becoming a masterpiece of video games. A title that marks a before and after in how the effort and dedication of a studio are able to take a generation of consoles to a new exponent, demonstrating that excellence is only reserved for a select few. If you like to get lost in an unforgettable world, this title is a must on your bookshelf.

Without being groundbreaking or revolutionary, Red Dead Redemption 2 does almost everything perfect. The level of polishing and the amount of content makes its “the beauty” and “the beast” at the same time. No matter what you decide to do in Red Dead Redemption 2, it's impossible not to notice the amazing level of detail.
My cousin told me that the game made him feel glad to be alive. I couldn’t agree more.
Unprecedented. A big, flawless game with a great story. One of the best titles, and not only for this generation of consoles.

It's a game of restraint, but with some brutal sucker punches; the tale of a one-man cowboy army who is nothing without the people around him.
