These are places that constantly shift in the way that they challenge you, and I suspect that better racers than me will spend an awfully long time working out the optimal strategies for handling each one.

Star Wars Galactic Racer is a Star-Wars-authentic thrill rush that may be the best racer in a decade. It’s such a wonderful, engaging experience that literally does everything right. Just be warned – as a roguelite – the on-ramp can take time while presenting a higher difficulty level.

While the lack of local multiplayer is unfortunate, the decision to drop the mode so that the game is kept at a locked frame-rate is the right one. The game is so fast-paced that you need every millisecond possible. The tracks are all excellent, the music and sound effects are jaw-dropping, and both gameplay and customization have a ton of depth. The single player campaign is surprisingly good and has a lot more under the hood than I was expecting. Its roguelike elements are well-thought out, and will keep you coming back for more well after you beat the game. Online multiplayer has a variety of modes, from traditional arcade style races to entire tours across the galaxy, so that every type of player can find something to enjoy. Overall, Star Wars: Galactic Racer has just the right amount of nostalgia, and is a true evolution of the podracing experience. It’s frenetic, bombastic, and above all else, incredibly fun.

Star Wars Galactic Racer is a spectacular surprise and a must-play for racing and Star Wars fans. It shines with exhilarating speed, excellent online support, a smart build system, and a fantastic dose of Podracing nostalgia. While its roguelite structure may not appeal to those looking for a traditional campaign, the quality of its racing and combat makes it one of the best Star Wars games in recent years.

Fuse Games have truly given Millennial gamers like myself that spiritual successor to Star Wars Episode I: Racer that we never got. And to them, I give them all the grace that a post-Empire galaxy allows us.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is a spectacular and surprisingly thrilling racing game that delivers an excellent Star Wars experience through its run-based gameplay, strategic choices, and spectacular crashes.

Star Wars Galactic Racer is the perfect racing game. Fast, furious and frenetic gameplay makes every corner and turn feel such a matter of life or death. A superb unique campaign full of great characters and moments, addictive gameplay loops and a plethora of content make this a game for the ages. The first time you podrace will stay in my memory forever, like being transported into the films. It will take some doing for this game to be displaced as my game of the year. In a year of heavyweight developers flexing their muscles, it’s a brand new team from Guildford who have captured my attention. Fuse Games, congratulations on a superb effort. Besides the fact I dream of yet more planets and tracks, this is the ultimate Star Wars racer. I already long for a sequel!
Its cinematic story is genuinely top notch, and one of the best I’ve seen in modern racing games.

I’m sick of roguelikes and even growing a little tired of Star Wars lately, yet Star Wars: Galactic Racer is easily one of my favourite games of the year. Screaming through the salt flats of Crait in a ramshackle speeder, red dust kicking up behind you as you swiftly snap from your afterburner to your ramjet is just an exquisite sensory experience. It’s a game I’m going to be coming back to for years to come, whether it gets any further content updates or not.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is one of the strongest racing games to release in the past few years. While it stumbles a bit in the story due to its weak villain, it more than makes up for it with charming side characters, both new and old. From fantastic in-depth customization to the jaw-dropping visuals and music and incredibly strong gameplay, this is easily the new gold standard for Star Wars racers.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer manages to combine speed, stunning visuals, excellent sound design and interesting mechanics, while capturing that nostalgic Star Wars feeling without being afraid to do its own thing. The run-based campaign is easily the star of the show, cleverly revealing new conversations and story details with every run, although the content outside of it feels less substantial. The year may not be over yet, but Galactic Racer has already made a serious case for being my Game of the Year 2026.

Fuse Games’ debut is spectacular, thrilling, and inventive in the right places. At its core, Star Wars: Galactic Racer is a throwback to simpler times, but it’s got both the ingredients and the execution to become a modern racing classic.

Every moment feels joyfully fast. Every decision carries the weight of tension. And every run is a rewarding chance to learn, improve, tinker, and adapt, whether it ends in success or failure. I can't wait to keep playing what's been my favorite racing game in years.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is a fantastic racing game that perfectly captures the breakneck speed of the source material’s iconic vehicles. The story and abundance of modes make for a unique racing experience, and though a couple of small rough edges exist in how it’s presented, this is a brilliant title that had me frequently jolting to the edge of my seat. Whether you like Star Wars, racing games, or both, there’s lots here for you to sink your teeth into.
The best Star Wars racing game ever made, which nails the high-speed fantasy while delivering depth, flexibility, and a surprisingly great campaign.

Although a roguelike racing game seemed strange to us at first, Fuse Games took one of the most beloved elements from the prequels and found an interesting way to make it their own. The speed is hard to control, the crashes are satisfying, and the feeling of racing through a wild landscape in a galaxy far, far away is immediate. Whether you’re a veteran player or just curious, this title is definitely a must-have for your collection.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is a thrilling blend of high-speed arcade racing, vehicular combat, and roguelike progression that makes excellent use of the Star Wars universe. Its varied builds, satisfying risk-reward structure, strong presentation, and surprisingly engaging story keep each run exciting, while extensive customization and polished performance round out an impressive debut. Some tracks can become repetitive over time, and the multiplayer experience remains untested, but Galactic Racer still stands out as both a fantastic racing game and a rewarding treat for Star Wars fans.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is an arcade racing game with surprisingly few real weaknesses. The sense of speed is fantastic. Each vehicle handles uniquely, and the mix of boosts, ramjets, bumping, and abilities ensures that there’s always something happening on the track. This works especially well for Star Wars fans. Galactic Racer manages to recapture exactly that special charm that already set Episode 1: Racer apart. The pod races, in particular, are among those moments that simply make a fan’s heart sing. Galactic Racer is fast, aggressive, and wonderfully arcade-style. And whether you were tearing through Mos Espa 25 years ago or are just in the mood for a really good futuristic racing game: there’s a hell of a lot of driving fun to be had here.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is a thoughtfully designed triumph. The excellent handling and eye-popping presentation would be enough to recommend the game alone, but I also love its buildcrafting aspects and roguelite campaign. With a breathtaking sense of speed and planets that demand you think differently about your approach, this is one of the better racing games available on the PS5. I think the release could be a little quicker at getting you behind the wheel, and of course more planets would always be appreciated. But minor nitpicks aside, I really can’t recommend this highly enough.
The thrills of podracing made accessible and versatile in true high-speed racing style. A clever combination of exciting races and a take on the roguelike progress loop that just works.

Star Wars Galactic Racer is the best arcade racer in years. It mixes compelling racing action, an addictive progression system, and excellent world building while stringing a narrative through it all. It’s very fast, and very dangerous. It’s also very, very good.
STAR WARS: Galactic Racer is a great game that has a lot of content. Racing feels amazing, and the enemies are ruthless.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is the Star Wars racing game I've always wanted and has sparked a competitiveness I never knew I had. Fuse Games has designed an exhilarating, highly engaging roguelike racer with amazing buildcraft customization that offers endless possibilities on the track.

Although the title lacks a traditional Grand Prix mode and players are at the mercy of Fuse Games, it is undeniable that Star Wars: Galactic Racer offers one of the most entertaining arcade racing games of recent years. The progression system, ramjet mechanics, track design, and vehicle variety combine to create an experience that shouldn't be missed. Star Wars: Galactic Racer is pure magic for fans of the series and, finally, allows us to race directly against Sebulba.

Even when it was pissing me off, Star Wars: Galactic Racer made me feel alive. Every gravity-breaking boost, every panic-inducing malfunction, every slow-motion, Burnout-style wreck, was thrilling in a way I haven’t often experienced. It almost feels like playing Wizardry with cars, pushing ahead and feeding on the rush of risking life and limb, each deadly opportunity for a shortcut or risky boost like kicking open a door and knowing what’s behind it could wipe your party, but doing it anyway. I had some mixed feelings about the campaign’s roguelike structure, but ultimately the way that structure built upon and enhanced the risk-savoring and thrill-seeking intensity made it fit like a thematic glove. I can feel myself coming back to this over and over just for the vibes any time I feel like I need a little shock to my system to get my blood pumping.

Galactic Racer is a lot more than just a racing game set in the Star Wars universe. Fuse Games has been bold enough to put itself out there on its first outing in a game using an IP that has fans who are incredibly quick to criticize if something doesn’t feel right. From its runs-based racing and compelling new characters to a multiplayer mode that will keep you playing long after you’re done with the campaign, Galactic Racer is another example of a studio taking some well-educated risks with the Star Wars IP to create something truly special.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is ultimately a hard game to pin down genre-wise or to put down gameplay-wise. It takes the best of the roguelite genre and fits it into a new format where there's one-part racing, one-part loot-and-build chasing, and two-parts thrill ride. How or if players give this some unique name remains to be seen. What is clear, however, is that Star Wars: Galactic Racer is a must-play (and a must-replay again and again).

Star Wars Galactic Racer seriously impressed me. While the roguelite mechanics initially threw me for a loop when I first played the game earlier this year, after several hours with the game I can safely say they’ve earned their place in the genre. I’d be down to play more racers that adopt the idea. That said, I know they won’t be for everyone, especially since it feels like we can’t move for roguelikes and soulikes nowadays. In Galactic Racer’s case, though, there’s at least the option to ignore it entirely for some more traditional arcade-y fun, and it’s going to make multiplayer a blast too. It’s well worth picking up for any Star Wars fan, and I’m already hoping it’s followed up by a full-on podracing game with customisable rides.

Star Wars Galactic Racer truly blew me away. The game is exhilarating, beautiful, and a real treat for the ears, all while offering a welcome touch of customization. The content is incredibly generous; every race, challenge, and moment of destruction is a blast. It’s all wrapped in an engaging story featuring colorful characters—the kind you love to hate when they overtake you at the finish line. I had an absolute blast—a rare experience for me in a racing game—as it brilliantly balances instant fun with the frustration of defeat. I wish Star Wars Galactic Racer a bright future, and you can be sure I’ll be following it closely.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is pretty much everything it should be. Threading the needle between next-gen Burnout and Star Wars-themed racer, it 's frantic, fun and incredibly enjoyable to play. The arcade-style action is a pure delight, and the run-based nature of the campaign gives it a ton of replay value, even if you don 't intend to dip your toes into the multiplayer. If you 're looking for a next-gen Episode 1 Racer, this is exactly what you 're hoping for.

Fuse Games hits the gas, engages the afterburners, and pushes the engines to the limit to reach the pinnacle of galactic racing, crossing the finish line in first place. Now this is (not just) podracing; this is one of the best racing games in recent history.

Slapping all the switches before a race in a hectic quick time event, firing up the afterburner, and watching the parts of wrecked speeders gracefully tumble through the air all evoke the iconic podracing scene in The Phantom Menace. But Star Wars: Galactic Racer is so much more than a slavish homage to one drawn-out set piece in a terrible movie from 1999. It is instead an expertly constructed racing game designed to push players and force them to make interesting decisions under duress, a tension only heightened by the game’s sensational sense of speed and pervasive roguelite mechanics. It’s been over two decades since the last Star Wars racing game, but Galactic Racer makes for one incredible return to the genre.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer stands out for turning speed into something that’s also built up between races. Its arcade-style driving, the differences between vehicles, and the management of the Ramjet shape an experience in which taking a curve at full speed or gaining a few seconds of boost matters just as much as choosing the parts for your next setup. The trial-based campaign adds personality and gives you reasons to keep racing, while the multiplayer tracks bring that mix of preparation, risk, and rivalry to the online arena. All of this draws on the Star Wars universe to take us to its most athletic and underground side.

One of the best arcade racing games in years, Star Wars: Galactic Racer is a stunning debut for Fuse Games. With its thrilling racing action that feels like a cross between WipEout and Burnout and its engaging runs-based campaign mode, this is a triumph. The only let-down is that it doesn't have a more standard Arcade mode to let you set up your own events.
With thrilling, high-speed races and a ridiculously addictive campaign, Star Wars: Galactic Racer is an absolute winner, and a must-play for fans of arcade racers.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is an absolute treat of a racing game. The rogue-like element feels fresh in the genre, even if they aren’t the first to ever adopt it. The campaign mode and characters are genuinely great to watch, sprinkled with surprises and Easter eggs for fans. Racing itself is a masterpiece; grappling with handling and acceleration makes for an awesome learning curve and the audio experience is incredibly enthralling. This is probably the very best time to be a Star Wars gaming fan and Galactic Racer deserves a lot more hype than it received pre-launch. Don’t sit on the fence, Star Wars: Galactic Racer is exceptional and a must have.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer combines precise arcade handling, distinct vehicle classes, and meaningful customization with a campaign built around risk, repetition, and gradual mastery. Track hazards, aggressive collisions, and the Ramjet system keep races tense, while the different vehicle types significantly change how each course is approached. The roguelite structure can become punishing, especially when unclear track design or abrupt difficulty spikes end a long run, and the lack of split-screen is a notable omission. Even so, its speed, mechanical depth, and strong audiovisual presentation give it a distinct identity among Star Wars racing games.
Not only one of the best Star Wars games in a long time, but one of the wildest racing games you'll play this side of the galaxy.

We seem to end every session of Galactic Racer a good few inches closer to the screen than we began, suddenly aware that we've been clenching our jaw the entire time, but deliriously happy, even if the result of the last run isn't quite what we'd hoped, just to have survived the experience. [Issue#430, p.108]

Setting aesthetics aside, Star Wars: Galactic Racer makes no attempt—not in the slightest—to erase Episode I Racer from our collective memory. It takes the original concept of wild, galactic-scale racing, infuses it with the destructive DNA of Burnout, incorporates elements of the environmental brutality and multi-vehicle competition found in MotorStorm, and channels the arcade philosophy that flourished during the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 era. The result offers a flavor that has been missing for a long time. Blisteringly fast, loud, intentionally over-the-top, and just as enamored with spectacular crashes as it is with daring overtakes, Galactic Racer serves as a reminder of why, for many years, racing games weren't just about simulating the act of driving—they were about turning it into a spectacle. And perhaps that is its greatest achievement: it transcends both the *Star Wars* universe and the genre of racing itself, reminding us just how exhilarating it could be to wreck a vehicle at breakneck speed—and immediately feel the urge to jump right back in and do it all over again.

The recent movies and series have been of mixed quality, but gamers are in for a treat. Just a few weeks after the strategy game Zero Company, here’s another top-notch game set in the Star Wars universe. Galactic Racer has enough depth to still surprise you after dozens of hours, looks amazing, and plays just as well as the best racing games on the market.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer revitalizes the franchise's racing genre with a fresh, roguelite-inspired arcade experience. Developed by Fuse Games, it blends visceral speed with a procedural campaign, offering dynamic and tense gameplay. The game excels in its core racing mechanics, leveraging Afterburner and Ramjet for tactical depth, influenced by diverse atmospheric conditions. While the narrative is light and some features like a minimap or split-screen multiplayer are absent, the addictive loop of risk-reward, strategic upgrades, and authentic Star Wars underworld atmosphere delivers dozens of hours of intense fun for those seeking a challenging, fast-paced racer.

What a surprise this Star Wars Galactic Racer is. Right from its initial releases, it looked promising, but now that we’ve put it through its paces for a long time, we’re even more surprised by the overall quality Fuse Games title. A delightful mix of Burnout and F-Zero, spiced up with roguelite elements that aren’t intrusive at all, in fact they raise the bar for fun even higher. With the exception of a few tracks "reading" issues - which, with practice, tend to resolve themselves anyway - we’re looking at one of the best arcade racing games of recent years: fun, challenging, and rock-solid in both single-player and multiplayer… a must play for Star Wars fans and everyone else.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is the best racing game in the franchise’s history. Each contest is a tense ride to the finish, requiring you to use everything in your arsenal to overcome your competitors. The sense of speed is exhilarating, especially as you navigate the tight environments and race across the stunning landscapes. While it can be challenging, reaching the top spot feels earned. With its excellent campaign mode, this is a thrilling return to the world of podracing that delivers an exhilarating racing experience from start to finish.

Fast, spectacular and packed with arcade thrills, Star Wars: Galactic Racer delivers a highly entertaining mix of high-speed racing, satisfying progression and strong Star Wars atmosphere. A weak story and some repetition hold it back slightly, but the excellent handling and exciting track design still make it an easy recommendation for arcade racing fans.

Galactic Racer is a Star Wars game, and that might be enough for some, but not for me. Fortunately, it’s an even better racing game, one filled to the brim with courses, vehicle builds, and characters that keep me coming back to the track for one more race.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer not only brings the best features of my favourite arcade racing game, Burnout 3, into the modern era, but also blends them with elements from my second favourite – Motorstorm. What’s more, the whole thing is wrapped up in a roguelike campaign with serious stakes, enough to stir up real excitement and ensure great replayability. Though easy to learn, the game’s driving mechanics prove to have considerable depth. The only downsides are the lack of split-screen and the poor layout of some tracks, but even so, the breakneck driving pace is incredibly fun.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is the space racing game you've always dreamed of, with a rewarding driving experience, a run-based roguelite campaign structured to always offer something new, and a solid multiplayer component. Getting behind the wheel of a speeder is fun right from the start, but you'll need the right amount of practice to get the better of your opponents, hitting insane speeds without exploding at every turn. I would have liked to see a couple more planets, and I think there was room to make the tracks more readable from the get-go, but ultimately it's only fair that anyone brave enough to climb aboard a Landspeeder, Speeder bike, Skim speeder or Podracer should be prepared to face the dangerous consequences.
Star Wars: Galactic Racer is a worthy successor to Episode I: Racer. A very solid and fun racing game.

Driven by blistering speed, distinct vehicle handling, and varied events, Star Wars: Galactic Racer revitalizes the arcade racing formula through a rewarding campaign structure. While it stops short of turning its roguelike framework into lasting replayability once the credits roll, the magic of that first run makes it one of the franchise's finest video game outings.

We’ve had a blast with Star Wars: Galactic Racer, and it’s one of those games we know we’ll keep playing even after wrapping up our review. Fuse Games has managed to recapture some of that instant fun we’d been missing from titles like Burnout and MotorStorm, without simply copying them. The roguelike structure is the big surprise; it makes upgrading our vehicle, choosing routes, and starting over far more engaging than we ever expected from a racing game.

Star Wars Galactic Racer combines exhilarating speed, spectacular collisions and vehicles with distinctly different handling. Its extensive customization and near-roguelite campaign bring real depth to the racing, making every risk matter. Strong visuals and sound create a particularly convincing sense of immersion in the Star Wars universe. However, repetitive environments, on-foot sections that slow the pace and several missing features hold the overall experience back. Despite these shortcomings, Fuse Games delivers a very good arcade racer, with foundations that make you eager to see the Galactic League broaden its horizons.
If you miss the days of Burnout, classic Need For Speed games, Split/Second: Velocity and BLUR, then you’ll be wonderfully surprised by Star Wars: Galactic Racer.
Star Wars: Galactic Racer is one of the most exciting racers in recent memory, blending the Star Wars universe with gameplay that feels both fresh and intelligent.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer features an excellent single-player campaign and very good gameplay in its races, with different aspects influencing the challenges to overcome. The online multiplayer is also enjoyable, although there is no offline mode. The problems lie in a few minor aspects of the gameplay itself and the limited variation in biomes (planets).

Star Wars: Galactic Racer successfully brings the franchise into the fast-paced arcade racing genre. It delivers a thrilling, polished driving model and an engaging roguelike structure that adds real tension to every race. While a limited number of planets and a frustrating late-game difficulty spike hold it back from perfection, it remains a highly addictive and refreshing racing experience in a galaxy far, far away.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer scratches an itch I didn’t realize I had for this kind of stupidly fast arcade racer, largely thanks to a roguelite campaign that injects adrenaline into every run. Managing risky builds and chasing the high of that big payout makes it easy to get carried away, and even easier to crash and burn. It is repetitive in the same way a classic arcade cabinet is, but that magnetic pull remains; it leaves you frustrated for all of five minutes before you’re right back at the starting line for another tour.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer proves that a heavyweight license can still produce a game with a identity of its own, as long as it has the courage not to merely repeat the formula of the past. Fuse Games has taken a genre the industry had shelved and put it back on the track with a roguelite structure that works, a speed that takes your breath away and a care for its worlds that reminds you how a beloved universe should be treated.
Despite a few questionable design choices, Star Wars: Galactic Racer is a fast-paced and incredibly fun racing game with some really unique hooks.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is a thrilling ride. Filled with exciting challenges and a roguelike structure, this game has more depth and content than I expected. I went in expecting a pretty standard racing game, but there are enough twists that every race feels like a thrill all the way to the finish line. Wins and losses are emotional, and hitting max speed and needling the final-lap obstacles while watching the Ram Jet's redline is unlike anything I've played, and it pairs so well with the Star Wars series.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is the fast and furious racer Star Wars has long deserved. It’s stuffed full of fun content, whether you want to hop into fun Scenarios, participate in some quick races or hop into multiplayer.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer brings the carnage-filled arcade racing of the 2000s into the modern day, with slick and exhilarating high-speed racing that mixes perfectly with a run-based format and roguelike elements.

Star Wars Galactic Racer is an impressive effort from Fuse Games that reminds us why the Star Wars universe can be so much fun. It delivers an exciting and highly enjoyable racing experience with a strong foundation that we hope continues to grow and evolve over time.
The game reaches new heights for the entire racing genre while also serving up a fairly good Star Wars yarn.

STAR WARS: Galactic Racer is fast and dangerous ‘runs-based’ game with surprisingly deep mechanics, without losing sight of what makes an arcade racer fun. But it’s the world around the racing that gives it that special Star Wars charm, filling its dusty planets, paddocks and racing leagues with the strange characters that make the galaxy feel bigger than the Skywalker saga. Sci-fi arcade racers should be ridiculously quick and feel like your vehicle might fall apart at any moment, and for me, that's what makes this a genuinely impressive racing game in its own right.

Overall this is a racing game that’s brutal, so so fast and full of risk and reward at every deadly turn. It fits well in the Star Wars universe and sets out a stall for a whole new resurgence in sci-fi based landspeeder racing.

A strong run-based design philosophy, combined with fantastic arcade racing and a stunning depiction of the Star Wars universe gets Star Wars: Galactic Racer off to a flying jumpstart. Its parts come slightly loose thanks to some repetition in maps, difficulty spike boss races and the odd demoralising run. However, this speeder has been assembled with craft and care, which shines through as it fires its engines to a great victory.

Overall I’m absolutely addicted to Star Wars: Galactic Racer. It’s as close as we’ve ever gotten to the thrills of the original N64 game. While far from perfect, Fuse Games has delivered a uniquely fun, high-speed roguelite racer that any Star Wars fan should pick up and play.

Fuse Games brings the spirit of Burnout to Star Wars in the form of a racing game capable of delivering the same adrenaline rush as that series. The roguelite campaign is an unexpected but interesting take, and the graphics are truly eye-catching.

Pending any potential downloadable worlds, the artistic presentation of Galactic Racer is rich in personality and well-varied, adhering to established conventions while being enhanced by the signature visual effects that evoke the classic trilogy—as well as sound design featuring instantly recognizable audio and orchestral music that perfectly captures the Star Wars atmosphere.

Galactic Racer: Star Wars: Galactic Racer is a fantastic adventure set in the Star Wars universe; it demonstrates that the franchise can continue to innovate and bring a fresh feel to its gaming projects—proving, above all, that not everything has to revolve around Jedi and combat. Sometimes, we just want to race our vehicles at high speed across Jakku, and this game delivers exactly that.

One of the best arcade racers of the generation, with great, fast graphics and smooth arcadey controls, wrapped in a roguelite mode that extends its life with its alternate paths and extensive customization options.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is a title capable of surprising the player, though not entirely. Combining a roguelite structure with the frenetic pace of an arcade racer set in George Lucas's galaxy was a risky move, yet the gameplay loop is a fantastic idea that proves highly addictive right from the very first races. Unfortunately, the game loses its way in the medium to long term: while the planets offer diverse settings, the tracks themselves are few in number and repetitive. It is a title for die-hard fans of pod-racing in the Galaxy Far, Far Away, but we had hoped for a bit more spark.

We really enjoyed our time with Star Wars: Galactic Racer. Its roguelike campaign kept us hooked from beginning to end, while its driving mechanics make every race incredibly satisfying. Although the lack of track variety eventually takes its toll, particularly in the secondary modes, and the absence of local multiplayer feels like a missed opportunity, these shortcomings don't overshadow its strengths. Fuse Games has managed to capture the essence of Star Wars and deliver a deeper campaign than expected. So, while there's still room for improvement, we're confident it will be an enjoyable experience for fans who have been waiting years for a new racing game set in the franchise.

For all Star Wars: Galactic Racer’s quality when out on the tracks, it’s hard not to feel that a few more back to basics game modes and a fully fleshed out Podracing section would have made for an all-round more enjoyable experience. I’m not a fan of criticising a game for what it’s not, and there’s no denying each of the vehicles here have their pleasant nuances and thrilling moments, but for whatever reason it always feels like Galactic Racer is trying to keep me from having the brilliant fun the racing gameplay is capable of providing.

Star Wars returns to the racing scene with Galactic Racer, a game that rewards both speed and adaptability. It’s a comeback that feels somewhat underwhelming due to the lack of track variety, but it’s also a lot of fun, even as it challenges players time and time again.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is a fabulous looking and frantically fast anti-grav racer that gets a little repetitive thanks to its heavy reliance on repeatedly revisiting the same slim selection of planets, but has successfully lit the afterburners on a long-dormant slice of the Star Wars universe.
As a way of shaking up the racing game format, the run-based structure of Galactic Racer is more successful than the open world of Burnout Paradise.
Star Wars: Galactic Racer is a great game. Everything I'd usually complain about – games going stale, failing to motivate me long-term, horrible pacing – has been taken care of.
Star Wars: Galactic Racer is a daring and experimental racing game which tries something new and succeeds for the most part.
Star Wars: Galactic Racer is a tenacious thrill ride, and its unique run-based risk-and-reward structure is its defining feature.
Terrence does some futuristic racing in the past.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is a wonderful gift for players who have grown bored with the 'realism' of Gran Turismo 7 and the search for any remotely interesting activities in Forza Horizon 6. Fuse Games has offered a chance to go back to the second half of the 2000s, when arcade racers were at their peak popularity and offered unusual gameplay solutions. Few are capable of that nowadays, so this chance is not to be missed.
Star Wars has been in desperate need of a new racing game for a while now, and Galactic Racer delivers a hugely impressive experience.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is a fast-paced arcade racing game that truly captures the feel of racing in the Star Wars universe. Supported by roguelike elements to keep you coming back for more, there is a lot to like here, with very few pitfalls.
Star Wars Galactic Racer brings high-octane, death-defying competition back to the galaxy, and it doesn't stop for anyone - or anything.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer exceeded my expectations to the highest degree and provides a dream combination of Star Wars Podracing and Burnout. With an engaging Campaign Mode, an interesting usage of Podracers, plenty of characters to meet and interact with, tons of customization, cross-platform multiplayer, and beautiful visuals and music; this game is everything I could have hoped for and more! Star Wars: Galactic Racer did more than bring racing back to the Galaxy, it made me believe there’s nothing faster or more dangerous than Podracing.
Star Wars: Galactic Racer provides excellent, exhilarating racing gameplay, a cheesy but enjoyable underdog story, and some clunky roguelike trappings.
Well it's about time. Star Wars games have always taken on narrow assignments. The Jedi. The Soldiers. The Space Battles. Not since 2002, and the re...

STAR WARS: Galactic Racer nails the high-speed, high-stakes podracing DNA with flair. Its approach to innovation via roguelike progression broadens its appeal while doing away with some archaic practices found in longstanding racing games. Don’t worry if you’re not the biggest fan of STAR WARS, you’ll have a hell of a time and quench your thirst for an explosive racing title that features racing, combat, and more.
STAR WARS: Galactic Racer is a great game that has a lot of content. Racing feels amazing, and the enemies are ruthless.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is a fast-paced thrill that successfully captures the spirit of the Star Wars racing classic and delivers it in droves. While the story is drab and the longer runs can grow frustrating, everything else makes up for it. The unique rogue-lite structure, excellent handling and constant risk-reward choices make every run feel worthwhile and addictive, even in the face of failure. It's this perfect combination that makes Galactic Racer anything but - it's a strong success in every sense of the word.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer not only brings the best features of my favourite arcade racing game, Burnout 3, into the modern era, but also blends them with elements from my second favourite – Motorstorm. What’s more, the whole thing is wrapped up in a roguelike campaign with serious stakes, enough to stir up real excitement and ensure great replayability. Though easy to learn, the game’s driving mechanics prove to have considerable depth. The only downsides are the lack of split-screen and the poor layout of some tracks, but even so, the breakneck driving pace is incredibly fun.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is a polished and highly enjoyable sci-fi racing game that successfully captures the thrill of the iconic Mos Espa race. There are few obvious flaws, but some aspects could use more content, better balance and further refinement. It is very good overall, even if it falls short of fully realizing its potential.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer will capture the hearts of not only franchise fans but also enthusiasts of brutal space racing. You can sense the vibe of Burnout here, along with the spirit of Episode I and the races on Tatooine.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer, at its core, is an amazingly well-designed Star Wars racing game. Despite its limitations and flaws, there was never a moment when its high-speed, high-stakes races became dull. Its tracks are impressively designed, capturing the look and feel of each location in the Star Wars universe, while the runs-based structure makes every race feel like there’s something at stake. Combine that with responsive controls, excellent sound design, and the sheer thrill of racing at breakneck speeds, and Galactic Racer delivers the kind of Star Wars racing game I’ve been waiting years to play. I can’t wait for the servers to go live and race against more players to see just how far my racing skills can take me in a galaxy far, far away.
Star Wars: Galactic Racer is a solid futuristic racing game that will delight fans of the series, but it also deserves a special mention for fans of the genre.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is an incredibly pleasant surprise that isn’t afraid to experiment whilst providing plenty of entertainment for players of all kinds. If you’ve felt that the good old-fashioned arcade racing genre is slowly fading into obscurity, you should definitely give this new release a go. Fans of a galaxy far, far away will be in their element thanks to the authentic atmosphere, but people who have no deeper connection to the famous universe will enjoy this wild ride just as much, especially when it comes to competing for the best times.
Star Wars: Galactic Racer is a thoroughly entertaining racing game; it may not have the sparkle we remember, but it has substance and delivers exactly what it promises. -

Star Wars: Galactic Racer existing at all is a real surprise, but the fact that it's such a fantastic and fun arcade racer is the true miracle here. While the game is indubitably difficult, and will challenge your abilities and patience, there's a genuine masterpiece of a racing game under the hood that deserves your attention. While I wasn't a fan of the implementation of roguelike mechanics, Galactic Racer outshines those complaints for me, and presents a fantastic, high-octane experience that should delight any fan of Star Wars racing games.

A strong run-based design philosophy, combined with fantastic arcade racing and a stunning depiction of the Star Wars universe gets Star Wars: Galactic Racer off to a flying jumpstart. Its parts come slightly loose thanks to some repetition in maps, difficulty spike boss races and the odd demoralising run. However, this speeder has been assembled with craft and care, which shines through as it fires its engines to a great victory.
With numerous skirmish and multiplayer modes to complement the campaign, there’s plenty here for race fans, whether they’re into Star Wars or not.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer delivers thrilling, high-speed arcade racing with satisfying controls, attractive visuals, and surprisingly engaging roguelite elements. Vehicle customization, varied tournament routes, and Sebulba's involvement add welcome depth. Unfortunately, the excitement is frequently interrupted by awkward pacing, unnecessary crash animations, repetitive progression, and frustratingly inconsistent AI. The underwhelming story and uneven difficulty further hold it back. Despite these shortcomings, Galactic Racer remains an entertaining Star Wars racing experience with plenty of untapped potential.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is a brilliant Star Wars racing game. It has the racing gameplay and sense of speed absolutely nailed with the roguelike elements adding to the game’s longevity.  If you’re a fan of racing games, miss playing Burnout or want to race a podracer again like we did in the old PlayStation 2 days, Galactic Racer might scratch that itch.
Fuse Games have an incredible starting position to be able to add new features and content to Galactic Racer over time, but even now, for Arcade Racers Star Wars: Galactic Racer takes first place.
STAR WARS: Galactic Racer is one of the best racing games, let alone Star Wars games, I’ve played in a long time (ago in a galaxy far away).

The return of racing in a far-off galaxy is finally here. This action-packed ride through wild paths and crowded tracks is even accompanied by an interesting story. However, a slight feeling that the content outside of the races and planet variety is a bit lacking prevents it from being ranked among legendary racing games.
Star Wars: Galactic Racer is a welcome and refreshing change of pace for the series, delivering a racing adventure that puts skill and speed ahead of lightsabres and Force powers

I’ll admit, I’ve had a few surprises thrown my way in 2026, but Star Wars: Galactic Racer might just be the biggest surprise of them all. It’s downright fun to play, no matter the mode, and it looks incredible at every turn.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is more than you might be expecting from a Star Wars racing game, not only carrying the torch for the venerable Burnout series, but also creating its own unique ‘runs-based’ genre for racing. It’s a system that can feel equally frustrating and fun at times, although the more time you put into it, the more you undeniably get out of it, making for an ultimately very rewarding racer, albeit one that takes a bit of time to get into gear. I’m happy to report that, yippee, Galactic Racer is indeed, so wizard.

Being completely honest with you, I normally zone out when playing circuit racers because they don’t do much to hold my attention. Doing laps of the same track over and over isn’t usually my jam. So  games like Forza Motorsport, whilst impressive at what it does, don’t scratch my itch. Open-world racers tend to do a bit more for me. However, STAR WARS: Galactic Racer really sunk its claws into me from the get-go. Whilst some of the environments did feel a little repetitive, the racing itself is versatile and spontaneous enough to make every single race feel thrilling.

You can see the love the developers have poured into all areas of this game, whether it’s ploughing through the campaign with its roguelite mechanics, beating your mates’ lap times or diving into the scenarios or online multiplayer. Progression feels meaningful, and it converts to dozens of hours of gameplay. Whether you’re a hardcore Star Wars fan or just someone who simply loves racing games, this is one of the surprise hits of 2026 for me.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer turned out to be exactly the kind of surprise I didn’t expect but had been hoping for in the arcade racing genre. Fuse Games brings back the instant thrills we’ve missed from Burnout and MotorStorm, but rather than simply copying their formula, it adds something genuinely new to the genre with its roguelike campaign structure. With every decision carrying weight and a single mistake potentially ending an entire league run, the game had me saying “just one more race” time and time again. I simply couldn’t put it down.
There is no need for a team or a crew when rockets propel the ships at breakneck speed.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer ultimately succeeds because it takes the most exciting part of Star Wars racing and builds an entire game around it. The speed feels immediate, the vehicles handle differently, the planets force you to adapt, and the run-based progression gives you a reason to keep improving. It is not simply another attempt to recreate Episode I: Racer.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer successfully brings back the kind of racing experience the franchise has been missing for years. It draws on Star Wars Racer and the developers' Burnout background, then combines those ideas with modern progression, branching runs, vehicle customization, environmental hazards, and a campaign that encourages repeated playthroughs.

«Star Wars: Galactic Racer» takes me back to the golden age of sci-fi racing games. Blistering speeds, plenty of action and a motivating career mode are all the right ingredients. The excellent sound effects deserve special mention. Unfortunately, the game lacks variety in the long run, with too few tracks and upgrades that make little difference.

Galactic Racer makes every race matter with a clever risk-and-reward campaign, responsive arcade handling, varied vehicles, and thrilling high-speed battles. Its distinctive planets, immersive sound, and smooth 60fps performance make the first journey a blast. The roguelite structure loses steam after the campaign, though, and repeated runs offer too little variety. Still, the racing is strong enough to keep you chasing one more win.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer, at the very core of its experience, has a solid racing game. Driving the limited vehicle selection is fun, and most of the tracks are well designed with enough personality to get you through. Then you put this roguelike loop on top of the experience, and everything goes haywire. A run can be perfect for 3 hours, then you veer into a wall on one course, and all that progress is undone. This also makes the technical gripes I have all the more pronounced because there are moments you crash for, like, no reason, or one bad attempt to slipstream ends in a forfeit. It’s an interesting idea, but to quote Game Dev Tycoon, Racing and Roguelike are not a good combo, and it hurts the whole thing overall.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is an invaluable addition to the racing game canon precisely because it is excellent, and because it is a game wholly different in style than each of the Forza, Gran Turismo, Need for Speed, and Mario Kart franchises before it. It is important and healthy for the continued development of the art form to experience innovation not only in licensed property but also in the very ways in which we play our favorite games, in genres we falsely believe to have already traversed their creative limits. With a stronger narrative, Galactic Racer wouldn’t just be making a case as one of the better games of the year; it would be in the conversation for one of the best Star Wars IP releases this century.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer delivers exhilarating arcade racing, excellent vehicle customization, and a surprisingly engaging roguelite structure. Repetitive environments and a forgettable story hold it back, but Fuse Games has created a thrilling return to racing in the Star Wars universe.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer delivers a fast, chaotic and surprisingly addictive arcade racing experience, blending classic Star Wars nostalgia with roguelite mechanics that keep every race fresh and challenging.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is an absolute triumph of arcade racing, and I genuinely didn’t expect to love it this much. It captures the impossible speed and raw aggression that made Burnout 3 so special, while still feeling like its own game. The roguelite structure works surprisingly well, giving every race meaningful stakes without compromising the skill-based racing at its core. A few multiplayer limitations and the lack of control rebinding hold it back from perfection, but they’re minor blemishes on an otherwise fantastic package. Galactic Racer is an easy recommendation and the closest any game has come to filling the Burnout 3-shaped hole in my life.

Light-speeding to 2026, FUSE Games has delivered a racing experience worthy of the Star Wars legacy. For Star Wars and racing game fans alike, racing around the galaxy is an exhilarating experience like no other. For me, Star Wars Galactic Racer takes a top spot on the scoreboard as one of my favourite racing games of all time.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is a title capable of surprising the player, though not entirely. Combining a roguelite structure with the frenetic pace of an arcade racer set in George Lucas's galaxy was a risky move, yet the gameplay loop is a fantastic idea that proves highly addictive right from the very first races. Unfortunately, the game loses its way in the medium to long term: while the planets offer diverse settings, the tracks themselves are few in number and repetitive. It is a title for die-hard fans of pod-racing in the Galaxy Far, Far Away, but we had hoped for a bit more spark.
Star Wars: Galactic Racer is a lovely surprise and, above all, an excellent arcade racing game.
Fast, action-packed, and incredibly fun: "Star Wars: Galactic Racer" brings "Burnout" to a galaxy far, far away.

At the start of the game, I was actually quite skeptical that the rogue-like approach might eventually get on my nerves. But now, after almost 40 hours of gameplay, my enthusiasm hasn't faded one bit. Even though I've finished the story! I think it's simply because I find the gameplay so fantastic that I can actually enjoy the rogue-like concept even more than with other games in the genre.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer delivers wizard racing, unique vehicle customization, and plenty of reasons to keep playing beyond its campaign… Fuse Games has made Star Wars racing worth getting excited about again, and I hope they don’t have to wait another generation for the chance to build on it
Thrilling, pure, unadulterated racing with incredibly deep systems and a highly addictive gameplay loop – or, in other words, how to breathe new life into old formulas while exploring new identities.
Star Wars: Galactic Racer captures the speed, aggression, satisfying crashes, and constant risk that made the best Burnout games all-time racing classics.

STAR WARS: Galactic Racer is a very pleasant surprise that succeeds above all because it has a genuine racing game identity. The tournament-based structure, the various vehicle configurations, the contracts, the upgrades, and the many types of events prevent the campaign from becoming a mere succession of races. There are some signs of repetition toward the end, and the lack of French voice acting is a shame, but the excellent soundscape, the sense of speed, and the variety of environments more than make up for it. The multiplayer mode will still have to prove itself once the servers open to the public, but the content on offer already gives players plenty of reasons to continue the adventure.

Fuse Games brings the spirit of Burnout to Star Wars in the form of a racing game capable of delivering the same adrenaline rush as that series. The roguelite campaign is an unexpected but interesting take, and the graphics are truly eye-catching.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is a solid arcade racing game whose best moments take place right on the track. The driving experience is impressive, each of the three vehicles has its own distinct character, and the game runs smoothly. If you're looking for fast-paced, enjoyable races above all else, this game delivers exactly that.

I honestly have little to complain about. This is exactly the kind of racing game I’ve been salivating for the past decade or two. Star Wars: Galactic Racer manages to convey the feel of the classic Episode I: Racer game, as well as Burnout, with improved physics, a somewhat engaging story, a ludicrous amount of content, brutal but rewarding difficulty curve, and a roguelite campaign which won me over in an instant. More than just a game for fans, or an admittedly nostaglic trip down memory lane, this is a must-have for racing enthusiasts, and one of the most pleasant surprises of the year.

Fuse Games‘ Star Wars Galactic Racer is bold, spectacular, and offers incredibly satisfying gameplay chops in single player and multiplayer alike. It’s high difficulty and relentless intensity might scare some casual Star Wars fans who just want some spectacle, but if you’re looking for a killer track-based arcade racer, you’ve found it. The force is strong with this one.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is an entertaining racer that makes every defeat count. Its dangerous tracks, crash camera, and upgrade system reward players who learn from their mistakes, even if the lack of local split-screen is a missed opportunity.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer delivers a fast and visually impressive galactic racing experience with a variety of challenging courses, vehicles, and fun runs-based mechanics. Get past the learning curve of studying the courses, and there’s plenty of galactic fun to be found.

Galactic Racer is a well-designed arcade racer that's tightly built with an excellent single-player structure that rewards players focusing on repeat runs. Additionally, the multiplayer adds another layer of reward for players who are actually fans of the podracing culture in Star Wars. I would recommend Galactic Racer to almost every Star Wars fan.

Star Wars Galactic Racer is the best Star Wars racing game in nearly a quarter of a century. This is unequivocally and objectively true, because Galactic Racer is the first release since the heyday of licensed Star Wars games that came alongside the cinematic prequel trilogy around the turn of the century. Galactic Racer is a reinvention of the pod racing classic that captures the magic of the N64 icon. It’s also one of the best arcade racing games ever that belongs alongside icons like Burnout, Mario Kart, Forza Horizon, F-Zero, Wipeout, Outrun and small handful of others.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer stands out for its addictive "run-based" structure (reminiscent of the roguelike genre) as well as its clever track design and a thrilling sense of speed conveyed through impeccable graphics, technical execution, and sound design. Despite some shortcomings regarding the protagonist's characterization, a lack of offline game modes, and a multiplayer component that could use some polish, Fuse Games’ title successfully brings the racing genre back to the franchise, delivering a fun, challenging experience that is highly recommended for fans of the saga.

Fuse Games has taken the foundational joy of Star Wars racing and wrapped it around a surprisingly deep arcade system, branching rogue-lite campaign, meaningful vehicle differentiation and enough customisation to keep the garage interesting.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is especially worthwhile for those who enjoy both futuristic racing games with a bit of dirty tricks, and the universe created by George Lucas. The big surprise is realizing that the game doesn't rely exclusively on this combination.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer brings back the saga’s arcade racing spirit with a fast, aggressive and highly replayable formula, combining speed, abilities, upgrades, different pilot styles and several modes for solo or multiplayer play. Its controls are accessible, but mastering each vehicle and track demands much more than simply holding the accelerator.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer delivers impressive long-term value through its progression systems, vehicle customization, racer archetypes, and wealth of unlockable content, blending accessible racing mechanics with an inventive runs-based structure and delivering an experience that can appeal to both newcomers and longtime fans of Star Wars and racing games alike. Simply put, Star Wars: Galactic Racer is a must-play title that deserves to be experienced firsthand.

Despite it occasionally making me want to use a very different kind of Force to propel my controller into a wall, Star Wars: Galactic Racer is one of my favourite games of the year so far. Its thrilling combination of roguelite structure—a genre I thought I was tiring of—and proper balls-to-the-wall arcade racing repeatedly had me leaning towards the screen as I barely made it around bends, blasted down straights and got into dogfights with the other racers.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is one of the best games in the series and a racing arcade game that I absolutely loved. Its roguelike campaign is addictive, the handling has more depth than it seems, and the tracks are amazing. If you like racing games, you should give it a try, even if you're not into Star Wars.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer’s modernizations of the arcade racing formula have their upsides and drawbacks, but fundamentally it is one of the most thrilling racing games released in years, with a compelling arsenal of systems, mechanics, modes, and even some pretty well-written characters. Moreover, it’s a reminder of how fresh and bold the racing genre can feel when explored to its limits.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is, for me, the Star Wars racer I have been waiting for since Episode I: Racer. The racing is lightning-fast, chaotic, and accessible, yet there is enough depth in the various systems, vehicles, and tracks to really get better at it. The campaign, in particular, manages to pleasantly surprise by constantly introducing new choices, challenges, and systems. Even after defeating Sebulba, there turns out to be plenty more to come. Arcade mode and scenarios subsequently provide hours of extra challenges, and the multiplayer is also a nice addition, although the lack of split-screen is a real shame. The sections between races could have been a bit more lively, but once you get back into a vehicle, that is a minor detail. Star Wars fans and lovers of fast arcade racers can therefore confidently add this game to their wish list.
Utterly thrilling during its best moments, Galactic Racer is the racing game that Star Wars fans have been waiting decades for.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer manages exceed all expectations and deliver on the decades awaited return of racing to the galaxy far, far away. Between gorgeous visuals, and thoughtful, highly addictive gameplay this is something both Star Wars fans and racing fans in general will have a blast with.

STAR WARS: Galactic Racer doesn’t just respect the legacy of its forebears, it takes the baton and runs with it much further than I ever anticipated. By committing to a high-stakes, run-based structure, Fuse Games has injected a level of white-knuckle tension that is completely unmatched in the genre. They possess an innate understanding of both the visceral thrill of arcade racing and the rich lore of the STAR WARS universe, flawlessly blending them into an essential, tactile experience. With its pristine performance, breathtaking sense of speed, and masterful risk-reward mechanics, STAR WARS: Galactic Racer is a stellar and exemplary modern classic.
A worthy successor to Episode I Racer that we’ve been waiting over two decades for. Harder than it looks, but the driving feel is incredible!

Star Wars Galactic Racer has everything it needs to make us shout ‘Now this is Podracing,’ but it manages to be even more than that, establishing itself as one of the best, most complete and most entertaining racing games in recent years.

Star Wars Galaxy Racers is a VERY fast and furious racing good time if you'd rather trade asphalt and wheels for Land Speeders and crater-turfed race courses. It's not every day you get a Star Wars racing game that has both a meaty single-player campaign and replayable multiplayer options, so revel in it!

Ultimately, Star Wars: Galactic Racer surprised me. I expected an enjoyable Star Wars racing game, but what I got was something with far more depth, progression, and staying power than I anticipated. The roguelike campaign structure occasionally gets in the way of its surprisingly ambitious story, the similarities between tracks on individual planets can become noticeable, and some of the walking sections feel unnecessary from a gameplay perspective.

None of those issues change the fact that the actual racing is exceptional.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is an almost unique title in the gaming landscape thanks to its mix of roguelite and racing, and for this alone it deserves a try. Whether you are Star Wars fans or lovers of speed and adrenaline, it has everything it takes to keep you glued to the screen for hours. If you can't stand roguelites and their punishing structure, though, it won't change your mind and may often lead to frustration.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is uncommonly good in a number of categories. It has a raw yet polished racing feel and sense of speed, bringing racing back to the Star Wars universe in a big way and iterating on how it all functions in ways that encourage player expression and experimentation. Most importantly, I've just been having so much damn fun, smiling ear to ear each race and growling in frustration when I come up short.
91.6% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (167 reviews).
Metacritic user score 7.6/10 (1234 ratings).

Housemarque is back with yet another fantastic fast-paced third person shooter. Saros builds on Returnal, delivering deeper and more enjoyable gameplay, as well as a new permanent progression system and modifiers which allow you to tweak the difficulty to your preferences. All in all, it's Housemarque's best game yet.
As a follow up to Returnal, Saros is excellent. It builds on the foundations of Selene’s adventure is a sensational slice of bullet-hell shooter goodness.

Housemarque enhances their already lofty reputation with a title that even surpasses their efforts with Returnal. The prospect of putting down the controller is almost as terrifying as the world of Carcosa.

A blistering, rapid-fire epic without peer, Saros confidently
delivers a dual masterclass in third-person shooter design and roguelike
sensibilities all wrapped in a delectable veneer that elevates it to one
of the best looking games on PlayStation 5. To quote the kids -
Housemarque cooked here. This is their masterpiece and it is next the
must have, utterly essential PlayStation exclusive. Carcosa beckons.
Saros finds a perfect balance amidst its chaos. The same game that makes your heart race will also take advantage of the slow-paced segments to tell a surprisingly deep and sensible story.
A perfect marriage between difficult and accessible, Saros is a brilliantly designed and majestic sci-fi nightmare that is as compelling as it is challenging.

Saros is a bold, confident realization of 30 years of Housemarque. It builds on the mystery and exceptional gameplay of Returnal with an excellent lead performance, and changes to the formula mean even more players will come to realize that Housemarque is PlayStation's secret weapon.

Saros is a triumphant successor to Returnal, delivering an outstanding sci-fi experience. Its excellent visuals bring the planet Carcosa to life, while its fast, fluid combat remains consistently satisfying. Special praise should be given to the meticulously crafted audio, with an eclectic soundtrack and impactful sound design. Moreover, Housemarque demonstrates a clear evolution over its predecessor, refining an already memorable formula into one of the strongest experiences in the Sony Studios lineup.

Saros might not be perfect, with the storytelling in particular showing some rough edges. It takes a while getting up to speed but when all systems are in place, it's an exceptional arcade shooter and an extraordinary spectacle.

Advancements in progression, narrative delivery, and player engagement, as well as refinements made to a near-perfect set of gameplay fundamentals, see Saros eclipse its predecessor and ascend to a throne above all others in the genre.

The developer didn’t turn a blind eye to the shortcomings of its predecessor, Returnal. Saros has kept the best parts—the controls are wonderfully responsive, your character runs and jumps at a brisk pace, and the atmosphere is delightfully dark—and made adjustments where necessary. Still, you’ll inevitably die while playing; that’s just part of the genre. But with every session, you get better and stronger, and you’re better equipped for your next run. The dopamine rush this creates makes the game—at least for us—incredibly addictive. Saros plays it safe and, while challenging, is perhaps less daring and revolutionary than Returnal, but that makes the game more accessible to a wider audience.
This is a great showcase for the PS5 and well worth a look for those seeking a sci-fi epic packed full of challenge.
The end result is a top notch when gameplay, entertainment value, and difficulty level are perfectly tuned to the same pitch.

The narrative may not be as convincing as that of Returnal but Saros one-ups its predecessor in almost every facet. It’s a seat-of-the-pants thrill ride that escalates the spectacle with every chapter and will haunt your dreams with walls of coloured missiles.

Saros pushes the envelope on multiple fronts, changing the roguelike genre in ways that’s more player-friendly than ever while taking advantage of the PS5’s DualSense controller in novel fashions. It’s near perfect in several ways, even if its story lacks the satisfaction that its gunplay otherwise provides.

Saros is a masterpiece. Not only does Housemarque successfully build on the foundations of Returnal, but it refines them to create a more accessible experience without losing its core principles. The combat system encourages aggression, making each encounter a tense and enthralling battle where risk-taking is rewarded. While the story is much more present than its predecessor, it never interrupts the action, complementing the deep and complex systems. With more options to personalise your adventure, this is not just a Game of the Year contender, but one of the defining games of its generation.

SAROS is head and shoulders above Returnal, which was already a stellar reinvention of the bullet-hell genre, thanks to a richer story, tougher enemies and gameplay systems that tailor the game to the player.

Saros is Housemarque at its best. It nails the roguelike formula, with each run feeling completely different than what came before thanks to changing areas and a variety of weapons. The story grips you and doesn’t let go, with Rahul Kohli’s fantastic performance at the heart of it.

Saros is Housemarque's ultimate creation; the culmination of years of hard work and experimentation. Returnal is Game of the Year quality, no doubt. But Saros has taken what Returnal offered and refined it, only adding to the formula until the end result is Housemarque's finest release yet. In a sea of great April games, Saros' excellence stands out as another Game of the Year contender.

Saros is brilliant from every angle, even if it isn’t the bold, risk-taking, and highly innovative bet that Returnal once was. Its highly sophisticated gameplay fits perfectly with a beautiful level design and its entire roguelite structure. On top of that, it presents one of the most visually and audibly impressive titles you can currently find on PS5—without even mentioning its deeply crafted science fiction story that keeps you engaged throughout a surprisingly long runtime. Yes, we’re looking at one of those games that will undoubtedly appear on “best of the year” lists, and it could even earn a spot among those competing for Game of the Year.

Saros masterfully delivers on everything it sets out to do. Although the game doesn't yet have any extra content to enjoy after the ending, it manages to entertain the player for a long time simply through the curiosity of testing all types of weapons and searching for audio recordings of past crews. Saros is the kind of homework a student is proud to show to the teacher.

Saros is an utterly sizzling romp through a sci-fi cosmic horror show that showcases Housemarque’s pedigree for spectacular, arcade action. Not only is Saros a user-friendly evolution of Returnal's core systems, which were already near-perfection, but it’s an exceptional, technical showpiece for a console that makes faultless performance seem magical. If Returnal was a reason to invest in next-gen, Saros pays that belief off again in what is currently a one-horse race for Game of the Year.

Saros stands tall as a bold evolution for Housemarque, proving the studio wasn’t content with simply recreating the magic of Returnal. Instead, it refines and expands on it in meaningful ways by pairing its punishing bullet-hell combat with smarter progression systems, broader accessibility ideas, and a narrative that trades clarity for intrigue. Arjun’s relentless, emotionally driven journey through Carcosa gives the experience a fiery contrast to Returnal’s isolation, while the “come back stronger” philosophy is felt in every run, every failure, and every hard-earned breakthrough back at The Passage. It can be overwhelming and at times unforgiving, but that tension is exactly what makes its victories so intoxicating. And by turning struggle into growth and persistence into something deeply rewarding, Saros cements itself as a serious GOTY contender and a lot more than just a sequel in spirit.

Saros is an extraordinary game—bordering on perfection within its genre—and a masterclass in how to fully harness its own strengths. Its gameplay is entirely at the service of the player; featuring polished mechanics, a palpable and customizable progression system, and the genuine sensation of playing a title with infinite longevity. It stands as a magnificent display of strength from the team at Housemarque—a studio that is no longer the underdog—having successfully delivered two of the very best exclusives of the PlayStation 5 generation: Returnal and—indeed—Saros.

Just as the moon covers the sun, with lost Carcosa awash with golden yellow, Saros eclipses all in its wake. Boasting a deep and synergistic core gameplay loop evoking Returnal, premium difficulty balancing options, emotionally-driven character writing, and the newest look cosmic horror has seen in decades, you wouldn’t be driven mad by playing this game; you’d be mad not to. Strange is the one who cannot fathom the greatness of Saros, but stranger still is lost Carcosa.

Housemarque pulls it off again. Saros is a remarkably gripping roguelite that preserves the best elements of Returnal while improving on its weaker points. The combat is chaotic, but you never lose control and are less at the mercy of luck. A compelling mystery also unfolds along the way. Only the characters… well, who were they again?

Moving, shooting, improving (both in stats and skill), winning, and even losing is an unequivocal joy in Saros, and I only wish I could write this sentence faster so I can hurry up and get back to planet Carcosa and attempt another run.

Saros marks the peak of Housemarque’s craft. Moving away
from a more traditional roguelite structure, it adopts a slightly less
punishing approach without sacrificing challenge or its highly addictive
nature. Built around a strong sense of progression, the game delivers a
rewarding feeling of evolution throughout the journey. With a
well-crafted sci-fi universe and sharp, responsive gameplay, Saros
strikes a compelling balance between demanding encounters and an
inviting overall experience.

SAROS takes what made Returnal such a epically awesome action game and turns the dial way up while simultaneously offering such a distinct and immersive game world that it'll haunt your dreams even long after the end credits roll.

Saros has become one of my favorite shooters of the past few years, honestly since Returnal. I appreciate Housemarque for giving both the more hardcore and the less hardcore among us the chance to see the world it's crafted in its entirely. My hands hurt a little, and I'll probably need a new controller sometimes soon, but it's a cycle I'm willing to be stuck in for a bit longer.

Housemarque’s Saros feels like a proper evolution of Returnal’s mechanics. It’s bold, it’s exciting, thrilling even. Each time Arjun heads out in search of answers yields clues to the truth behind Carcosa and those burdened by its existence.

Saros is a brilliant evolution of Returnal proving that less can truly be more. It's a gameplay machine, polished to perfection, paired with a distinctive tone, narrative, and story all its own. One of those rare gems that feels timeless, no matter the years. Saros is utterly addictive.

Saros is Housemarque at its best, delivering an intense sci-fi roguelike with stunning visuals, strong storytelling and exceptional use of the DualSense. Its fast, tactical combat evolves the Returnal formula with color-based mechanics, high-risk encounters and rewarding permanent progression. Despite some frustrating progression bugs, Saros stands out as one of the most polished and challenging experiences on PlayStation 5.

SAROS stands out confidently and without a shadow of a doubt as one of the best PlayStation 5 exclusives, the result of an extremely polished and intelligent effort by Housemarque. It's not simply an evolution of Returnal, but a bold step forward that finds its strength in a remarkably well-achieved balance between challenge, depth, and accessibility. The game manages to make a typically demanding structure more readable and manageable, without ever truly simplifying it. The progression is smart and rewarding, the gunplay precise and satisfying, while new mechanics add complexity without ever feeling frustrating. Everything is designed with one clear goal in mind: to guide you through the experience in the best possible way. The result is an excellent experience on every level — solid, polished, and perfectly balanced. SAROS doesn't just improve on what came before; it demonstrates that it's possible to elevate a genre while keeping the challenge intact, making it at the same time more modern and accessible.

Will Saros appeal to everyone? Probably not—and if you didn’t enjoy the gameplay of Returnal, this one won’t hook you any more, as it relies on the same core foundation. That said, Housemarque has done such a thorough job with difficulty tuning that one can only commend such a precise response to the criticisms previously aimed at the studio. In terms of gameplay, Saros holds up admirably despite its tiny flaws, and the whole experience feels perfectly cohesive—whether in its enemies, its biomes and their variations, or the many mechanics and weapons that keep enriching the experience throughout the adventure. Add to that a gripping story, with an allegory that is far less cryptic—and therefore far more engaging—and you’re looking at the very top tier of the PlayStation 5. As far as I’m concerned, it’s the console’s best exclusive, and it’s never leaving my system.

Saros is a fantastic example of just how much good can come from giving a razor-sharp developer the time and freedom to create the game they want from a clear vision. For whilst Saros is, in scope, Housemarque's biggest game to date, it still feels laser-focused in its desire to bring bullet hell into a 3D space and equip the whole thing with an engaging sci-fi story set in a fantastic world.

Saros is one of the strongest Game of the Year contenders of 2026. While it features typical roguelite frustrations, it never feels unfair and instead rewards persistence. Housemarque refines what made Returnal great while making the experience more accessible. The result is an intense, atmospheric shooter that stands out in the genre.
Saros stands out as a must-play for fans of the genre and a worthy successor to Returnal, pushing roguelike shooters forward with confidence and style.
Saros refines Returnal’s formula with intense combat and smart improvements. A must-play PS5 shooter and strong Game of the Year contender.

Overall, Saros feels like a natural evolution of what Housemarque achieved with Returnal, but with enough ambition to try to surpass it. The game refines the genre and takes it to interesting and exciting new places through smart design choices that aim to balance challenge and accessibility without compromising its core essence.

Housemarque builds on everything that made Returnal great, pushing the intensity and bullet-hell chaos to even greater heights. A well-crafted progression system ensures players can dive into the action with confidence, without worrying about wasting their time.

Saros is a fiercely focused hybrid of bullet-hell, roguelite, platformer, and horror sci-fi whose demanding but fair combat and aggressive risk-reward loop easily outweigh its flat supporting cast and static hub.

Like Returnal before it, Saros didn't need to be a roguelike at all. That the experience holds up so confidently regardless is a testament to the game's quality, largely because the core gameplay is once again every bit as tight as you'd expect from Housemarque.

Saros is a brilliant third-person shooter that takes what worked in Returnal and streamlines it for an even smoother game without diluting the fun. The core gameplay is the star attraction; complex yet intuitive, and a perfectly judged challenge that's so satisfying to overcome. With compelling permanent progression, flexible ways to modify your experience, and an intriguing story to follow, this is another step towards Housemarque's planetary takeover.

SAROS delivered a top-notch Rogue Like experience with gameplay that keeps you on the edge of your seat and a pretty challenging combat. Furthermore, the game provides a fantastic utilization of DualSense features that takes you in even deeper levels of immersion. The end result, a title that is one of the best PS5 exclusives this year.

Housemarque strikes back with another thrilling expedition into the unknown. Saros is masterfully expanding the studio's roguelike gameplay in the compelling world. The fast-bullet action, the sense of discovery and playing cycles stick to your mind. One of the best sci-fi voyages of the decade.

Saros builds on the excellence of Returnal, furthering Housemarque's blend of third-person action, bullet hell and roguelite with a more broadly told and ambitious story, a subtly more accessible path for newcomers, and still plenty of challenge for those that crave it. Echoing the game's tagline, Housemarque has come back stronger.

Overall, Saros is a fantastic experience that should not be missed. Housemarque has taken what worked for them previously and made it better. More importantly, they’ve taken the negatives from previous releases and assessed them honestly, allowing them to turn said negatives into positives.

It might not be a direct sequel, but decisions like this and others elsewhere address every issue I had with Returnal. Housemarque's previous game is fantastic in its own way. Yet Saros elevates the studio's roguelite formula to another level. Its structure is surprisingly malleable, combat is deeper and more rewarding, and I couldn't resist being wrapped around the finger of its mysterious and foreboding narrative. I find roguelites hit-and-miss, but it didn't take long before I was utterly infatuated with Saros. It's an incredible game that does more than just refine what worked before. Even after rolling credits, I can't wait to dive back in.

Without straying from the excellent formula they gave us in Returnal, Housemarque has delivered a spiritual successor in Saros that achieves the rare feat of improving in almost every aspect.
