Demon Tides is an addictive open-world platformer that excels through its deep, expressive movement system and vibrant art style. While the corny dialogue and minor technical jank occasionally distract, the sheer freedom and charm make it a standout indie gem, that speedrunners won’t want to miss.

Demon Tides makes platforming easy with a large world to explore and various ways to interact with it. The freedom to explore the world as you wish while slowly improving your abilities is genuinely rewarding. It takes lots of time to learn with lots of methods to get through different challenges. It’s a great platformer that is welcoming to newcomers and challenging for veterans.
Demon Tides’ unique, memorable style and its abundance of gameplay elements to explore and experiment with will bury itself in many hearts.

Demon Tides feels like a confident step forward. It expands the scope, refines the controls, and delivers a more polished experience overall. The platforming is responsive, creative, and satisfying. Exploration feels great, exploring every corner of the world.

While the story and humour won’t resonate equally with everyone, the gameplay carries the experience easily. And if you weren’t completely sold on Demon Turf, this sequel might be the one that clicks.

There’s also a free demo available, which makes it easy to test the waters before committing.

For fans of 3D collectable platformers, this is absolutely worth checking out. It’s energetic and clearly built by a team that understands how good movement should feel.

I had a great time with it, and I suspect many others will too.

Demon Tides is a very good game for an independent company. It takes chances with size and freedom, gives you a lot of ways to move, and gives you one of the most fun open-world platforming experiences in recent memory. If you want an exciting, fun, and mechanically rich trip, this is the one you should go on.
Demon Tides is a stylish and ambitious platformer that shines in bursts, , but is too often held back by its mechanical and technical shortcomings.

I may harp about Demon Tides’ issues, but that’s only because I want this game to succeed. Fabraz continues to create some of the most interesting collectathons on the market, and not since A Hat in Time have I found myself so enthralled by a game’s frame-by-frame platforming mechanics. 

Like A Hat in Time, though, the jank is real. I wish the game’s colorful visuals and open-world design could shine properly, but performance issues and bugs often drag down the experience. And yet, the game offers far too much fun for me not to recommend it. I 100%’d everything in about 25 hours, and I’d be lying if I said I didn’t enjoy every second.

Demon Tides packs a bombastic punch of peak platforming power that easily justifies its approachable price tag of $24.99 MSRP. You’ll get exactly what you’re looking for if the trailer piques your interest, and if campy convos and stylish schmovement sounds like your cup of tea, developer Fabraz brews an excellent cuppa with Demon Tides.

Demon Tides has some small flaws, but they don’t stop the game from being an excellent platforming escapade that gives a glorious sense of freedom to the player. The core loop of exploring a vast sea, tackling platforming challenges, and customising Beebz’s diverse moveset in your own little ways is immensely rewarding, with everything coming together perfectly to make for a wonderful platforming experience that constantly rewards player creativity.

Demon Tides is a very fun platformer with charismatic characters and smooth movement. It’s the perfect spring or summer game to play just to get into the season and remind everyone to sit back and enjoy the waves sometime.

Demon Tides is a triumph—an ambitious 3D platformer that not only meets but exceeds the high bar set by genre legends. The movement mechanics are mechanically satisfying in a way that rewards skill and creativity, the level design stays fresh across dozens of hours, and the surprisingly dark narrative unfolds through well-written dialogue and memorable characters. The soundtrack perfectly captures the tropical adventure vibe while delivering genuinely hype moments. Features like Talismans add insane depth to the gameplay, the speedrunning integration is seamless and offers near-infinite replayability, and additions like graffiti tagging and photo mode add community and personalization that fit right in. It lacks polish in some areas, such as performance in certain areas and sporadic voice acting, but that’s a trade-off I’ll gladly accept for a game this mechanically deep and content-rich.

This is Fabraz’s magnum opus, a game that legitimately pushes the genre forward and establishes the studio as a serious force in the indie space. This is now my frontrunner for 2026’s Game of the Year and could give a potential next-gen 3D Mario a run for its money. For fans of 3D platformers hungry for the freedom and creativity that defined Super Mario 64, Sunshine, and Odyssey, Demon Tides is an essential experience. This is the new Queen of 3D platformers, and her reign has only just begun.

Demon Tides is another example of how good tributes to older games can be, this time in the 3D action-adventure space. While the graphical fidelity is a little rough around the edges at times, the core game is a vibrant, sea-hopping adventure that I can’t get enough of. I absolutely love exploring every inch of the sea and bouncing my way through all kinds of platforming challenges. If you are someone that enjoys games like A Hat in Time or Bowser’s Fury, I can’t recommend this game enough.

Demon Tides tries to emulate bits and pieces of many 3D platformer favorites, and while it doesn’t nail it all perfectly, it still turns out a very fun and engaging adventure. Outside of some minor annoyances, the movement and traversal techniques feel good, and the growing list of challenges to grab your next golden gear keeps things interesting. I wouldn’t say it’s a hell of a good time, but there is plenty to like as you go bursting off for the next island.
Demon Tides is an ambitious, often janky platformer that does its best to show inspiration from some of the greatest games in the genre, and ends up feeling a little bit bland because of it.
A few technical issues and camera problems aren't going to detract from the fact that Demon Tides is a 3D platformer fan's wet dream.

Demon Tides builds on the strengths of its predecessor while introducing fresh ideas: I love the moveset of Beebz, the islands constantly offer new challenges and the freedom it gives you makes the game a truly unique 3D platformer experience. With talismans and outfits plus loadouts you can create your own personalized gameplay experience, the fast travel feature makes exploring and completing the various islands even easier and the leaderboards provides additional motivation to replay certain sections. A few minor technical issues occasionally interrupt the flow but thanks to the manual checkpoints, which you can set yourself at any time, there are never any major frustrations.
A new King's Field-like emphasises horror to brilliant effect.
85.7% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (42 reviews).

Tenebris Somnia is a survival horror adventure featuring not only spectacular FMV sequences, but engrossing tension-fueled combat and thoughtful puzzle design. Immersing myself within this grotesque, yet emotionally compelling, multimedia experience was uniquely captivating. While there are some small shortcomings here and there, these are vastly overshadowed by the sheer spectacle of the audiovisual presentation and the reliably engaging gameplay. Fans of horror games and films alike owe it themselves to check out this standout triumph of a multimedia experience.

Tenebris Somnia stands out for it's innovative combination of survival horror and live-action filmmaking. With a gripping story that had me invested from start to end and an atmosphere oozing creativity and passion, it's an experience that has left a lasting impression. What a great reminder of the nightmarish charm of indie horror, and the wonderfully weird experiences that can come from developers willing to take risks.

Tenebris Somnia is a pleasant surprise that blends classic survival horror, rewarding puzzles, and striking live-action sequences into a nightmare with an identity of its own. Its influences are easy to recognize, yet its mix of pixel art and practical effects feels distinct. Stiff combat and occasionally vague clues interrupt the pacing, but its strengths make it an excellent pick for the Halloween season.
Tenebris Somnia proves that creativity and attention to detail are the two most powerful tools in this industry.

Tenebris Somnia mines the enjoyable nostalgia of playing the horror games of yesteryear without feeling dated in the worst way. Weaving a solid indie horror film adds to the experience rather than feeling like a gimmick. The result is a captivating, well-executed survival-horror romp that maintains a hair-raising atmosphere with a fraction of the pixels of other genre giants.

Tenebris Somnia is a refreshing take on survival horror, blending nostalgic pixel art with brilliant FMV sequences and practical effects. Fans of retro horror and experimental FMV games, especially those who enjoyed FAITH, should definitely give this one a shot.
Tenebris Somnia recaptures the forgotten classic feel of the survival horror genre and reminded me why it is still foundational to contemporary greats.

It's difficult to make a pixelated 8-bit game scary, but that hasn't stopped Tenebris Somnia from trying. With Tobías Rusjan's creative brain and Andrés Borghi's eye for cinematography combined, Saibot Studios has managed to deliver a compelling retro horror adventure, complimented by some stellar FMV cutscenes. The only things keeping me awake at night were the clunky controls and the huge difficulty spikes in bossfights, throwing a somewhat damp blanket on an otherwise ingeniously designed experience.

Tenebris Somnia is a real labour of love, showing the developer’s affection for both classic survival horror and cinema in equal measures. The slow drip of story and tension through the excellently produced live-action cutscenes contrasts with the pixel graphics, while the ways the world opens up to explore Ivan and Julia's relationship create a compelling story. In a golden period for horror gaming, Tenebris Somnia is yet another excellent entry, showcasing a different aspect of the genre.

Tenebris Somnia crafts an unsettling horror experience on PC, using tension and moody visual direction to keep players constantly on edge. While pacing hiccups occasionally dilute the dread, its atmospheric sound design and intense set pieces deliver a chilling descent into psychological tension.

Tenebris Somnia is an Argentine survival horror game that blends pixel art with live-action cinematics produced with a level of professionalism that rivals much larger productions. Its well-connected puzzles keep the experience flowing without holding the player’s hand. However, the imprecise combat, due to the way the pixel art is rendered, and a few quality-of-life shortcomings take away some of its shine, though they never dull the experience entirely.

For me, Tenebris Somnia was a very interesting and refreshing game. It has a unique presentation, and those FMV scenes add a lot of intensity to the game. The story, while it does have its ups and downs, felt compelling overall and quite disturbing during certain scenes. Since there are 4 endings in total, you can replay the game or use the different save spots to try and check them all out if you want. It took a bit to get used to the controls and combat, but after that, things felt smooth. The puzzles were a tad obtuse, and some boss battles had quite the difficulty spikes. But overall, I found the game to be enjoyable, and the retro flair combined with the FMV excellence made it a compelling experience, to the point that I was able to finish the game in a single sitting.

Tenebris Somnia excels when it uses its fantastic horror movie sections to carry the story forward and reference in-game events. It does less well when it comes to the game’s often-obtuse puzzles and occasionally clumsy combat. Play it for the high production values of the FMV side, and stay for the deep story that pays tribute to filmmaking.

As a lover of movies and horror games, as well as classics, Tenebris Somnia has been a truly surprising experience. That delightful blend of worlds used to tell a story makes it a unique adventure. And while it isn’t original in terms of mechanics or action, that actually works in its favor thanks to the nostalgia factor.

Tenebris Somnia is an intriguing game. It takes players back to simpler time, where mechanics were more unforgiving, and while it does suffer in some ways because of it, it still managed to be compelling. The narrative and unique FMV cinematics are its biggest boons, and while I did enjoy some of the puzzles, the combat, movement, and a few illogical sequences tarnished the experience. This feels more like an interesting experiment and conversation piece than something I’d willingly choose to play again.

Tenebris Somnia introduces itself to an overcrowded horror genre with a novel concept, juxtaposing pixel art with full-motion video. It's one that carries the experience, but only to an extent, with uneven design decisions and obsession over some of the genre's worst tropes obfuscating its potential.

Unlike the recent Silver Pines, it’s not a new classic, but with a compact length of 6-8 hours, it’s perhaps short enough to entice curious genre aficionados to find the time for it in a busy fall schedule. The gameplay might not be all that compelling but I guarantee you that the innovative presentation and narrative make it a game unlike anything out there.

Like most horror survival games, the horror itself reflects our humanity, relationships, and responsibilities to one another. It elevates our worst fears, anxieties, and darkest experiences, and asks us to face them head-on. Tenebris Somnia, Latin for dark dreams (or visions), pulls us into the horrific world of dreams and memories, and makes those fears manifest. That said, I did find the FMV portions and the overall concept of Tenebris Somnia to be its strongest features. The point-and-click side-scrolling pales in comparison to the overarching narrative and serves more as a means to an end than a strong foundation, and the narrative is muddy and needlessly complicated. If this classic-style horror retro game is a game you enjoy, then you will love Tenbris Somnia. The back-and-forth between 2D and FMV can be a little jarring and certainly isn’t for everyone, but the mystery and story are strong and make for an enjoyable weekend adventure.
If you’re a survival horror or point-and-click adventure game fan, then Tenebris Somnia is likely a game of the year contender for you.

Tenebris Somnia's blend of eras makes for a remarkably effective fright fest. Its use of FMVs give tangible life to the otherworldly horrors of its pixel art, all worked into an esoteric point-and-click framework that should only isolate a few.

Tenebris Somnia is a memorable horror game with a distinctive visual style, creative puzzles, and an excellent blend of pixel art and live-action filmmaking. Its atmosphere and creature designs make a strong impression, while the occasional combat and puzzle frustrations add some rough edges that can make the journey less smooth, yet also contribute to its tension and challenge. The early story revelations weaken some of the mystery, and the slower movement can make certain boss encounters more awkward than they should be. Even so, the game's artistic direction and commitment to its unusual presentation make it stand out among modern horror releases. As someone who appreciates creative horror games, I found plenty to enjoy here, and I would recommend it to fans of retro survival horror who want something with a different look and feel. There is room for improvement in its storytelling and combat, yet Tenebris Somnia remains an intriguing journey into a disturbing world that is worth exploring.

That being said, if you do enjoy horror in general? One hundred percent — Play it. This is one of the, if not the, best horror game of the year, and at minimum top three, in my personal opinion. Still hard to say where it goes overall in the GOTY discussion, if that matters to you, but again, outside of the industry itself, it’s been an amazing year for games so that’s not a mark against it at all.

Tenebris Somnia doubles as a great game for survival horror fans and film heads. It's wholly original and doesn't lean on its influences obnoxiously. Using filmmaking as a storytelling element while having beautifully shot FMVs is a stroke of genius. The intentionally minimalistic survival horror gameplay isn’t so simple that it loses its appeal, but rather, it emphasises the elements that made it great from the start.

With a few caveats, this is a magnificent indie game that bursts onto the survival horror scene, bringing fresh ideas to a genre that’s already been done to death. It’s one of the games that has surprised me the most on the indie scene, alongside others such as, for example, the great *Crow Country*. Its original blend of pixel art and live-action footage—with meticulous attention paid to both aspects to deliver the best possible result—struck me as spectacular. Plus, the sense of terror is spine-chilling throughout, with a story that hooks you from start to finish and more than a few puzzles that will leave a lasting impression. The combat is a bit clunky, yes, but it also adds a level of difficulty that’s perhaps necessary.

Tenebris Somnia is one of the biggest surprises of the year, and one of the best survival horror games of the year. It's a unique and rare experience, proving perfectly how realistic scenes can be combined with pixel art.

The creators had a clear vision, which they brought to life in a truly original way. The retro-inspired Tenebris Somnia is an undeniably memorable horror experience that isn't afraid to tackle even the darker and more difficult aspects of life. A word of warning for the more sensitive players.

Tenebris Somnia is a creative concoction of FMV story telling with retro survival horror gameplay that ultimately isn't great at doing either. Both are commendable efforts and work as a whole package to deliver something unique, but its ambition is better than its execution.
With clever puzzles, tense encounters, and a unique FMV-retro style, Tenebris Somnia is a horror adventure genre fans can confidently put their faith in.

Tenebris Somnia is a truly fascinating little horror adventure that doesn't always get everything right, but its creepy atmosphere, intriguing story and wonderfully bizarre presentation make it well worth a look.

"Tenebris Somnia" is yet another outstanding example of the horror games currently being produced in South America, boldly reimagining a classic format through innovation, blending seemingly opposing styles into a complementary whole, and establishing itself as one of the genre’s standout releases of the year.

Here, we have a game that shines brightest when it engages in a dialogue with itself and embraces a layer of metanarrative that is exceptionally well executed. This approach enriches every aspect of the experience, from the storyline to the gameplay, but especially the immersion, a key element in all the artistic forms that the game pays tribute to and reveres.

Tenebris Somnia combines classic survival horror in pixel art with live-action cinematic sequences, practical effects, and a supernatural story. It is an adventure with a striking audiovisual identity, despite some inconsistencies in its puzzles and combat.

Tenebris Somnia deserves a very special place in the library of anyone who appreciates good survival horror. It's an adventure that respects the player's intelligence, demands attention, and rewards curiosity. The experience manages to captivate from beginning to end, mainly due to the way it transforms seemingly simple situations into moments of pure discomfort.

TENEBRIS SOMNIA brings a horrifying breath of fresh air to the survival horror genre. With an immaculate story, thrilling classic gameplay, beautiful pixel art game design, and of course haw dropping beautiful cinematic cutscenes...it might just be my favorite horror game of the year.

Tenebris Somnia blends pixel art and live-action cinematics into a classic horror adventure that feels fresh and interesting. The puzzles are very satisfying, and Julia’s story keeps you hooked from start to finish.

There may be more value in Tenebris for someone with nostalgia for the long gone era of the adventure game but for anyone else, even someone as open minded as me, it struggles to be anything more than a novelty.
An interesting mix of old-school adventure and pretty slick modern horror video production
Tenebris Somnia isn't the most polished or innovative survival horror game of recent years, but it is one of the games with the most distinctive personality.

Tenebris Somnia is an ambitious video game—perhaps too ambitious for the tools at its disposal. The experiment of combining pixel art and live-action works fairly well, although the poor quality of some cutscenes—especially in terms of special effects and the actors’ performances—risks failing to achieve the desired effect at all. The game effectively creates an unsettling and frightening atmosphere, but the combination of puzzle-solving and survival elements isn’t quite as successful: a combat system that’s clunky, to say the least, and puzzles that are sometimes too easy and sometimes too difficult don’t contribute to an optimal experience. Tenebris Somnia therefore succeeds better in its narrative goals than in its gameplay objectives, but overall it gives the impression of trying to prove too much compared to what it can actually deliver.
Tenebris Somnia is an imperfect creature, but like all bizarre beings, it has a charisma all its own.

Tenebris Somnia is a beautiful work of art in the survival horror genre. All its elements —combat, puzzles, narrative, and aesthetics— work in perfect harmony to deliver a fantastic horror experience. It is one of the best games of the year and a source of pride for Latin America. No horror lover should miss it.

Tenebris Somnia is unusual, and I think that’s a good thing. In promotional materials, the most boasted accolade is that of the award-winning film crew behind the cutscenes. The team did a wonderful job of making the live-action segments feel cinematic and synchronizing them nicely with the actual gameplay sections, but on occasion the other parts of the game can feel neglected as a result. The game advertised was an incredibly scary experience, but I found the fear factor a little underwhelming. 

If you want a game that feels almost like a digital escape room with the way its puzzles are presented, Tenebris Somnia is the game for you. But if you’re looking for a genuinely horrifying experience, fumbling to survive while fighting something straight out of a nightmare, maybe give the game a pass or at least temper your expectations.

Tenebris Somnia is one of the most original horror games of the year. Complex puzzles in the style of classic adventure games, stunning pixel art, and superbly executed live-action scenes come together to create a combination you won’t find anywhere else, and the story—about a cult, filmmaking, and a relationship falling apart—keeps you glued to the screen until the very end. However, the game lacks precision in combat, and the lead actress’s emotionless performance takes away some of the tension. If you’re a fan of classic survival horror games and enjoy giving your brain a workout, this title is definitely worth checking out—preferably around Halloween.

I came away from Tenebris Somnia appreciating what it was trying to do, even if I don’t think every part of it works equally well. The live-action scenes are easily the most distinctive feature, and the practical effects give the horror a different feel from what you’d normally expect from a pixel-art game. The atmosphere is creepy, and the story gives you a reason to keep going. The gameplay is a little less impressive. Some puzzles are confusing, combat could be smoother, and a few sections feel rough around the edges. These issues stop the game from being as good as it could have been.

While the puzzles were occasionally gratifying, the live-action cutscenes stuck with me most, as the game wears its love for film on its sleeve. Tenebris Somnia treats film with the respect it deserves and shows the toll it can take on one’s life when devoted to one's craft.

Tenebris Somnia is a really cool horror experience thats brilliant presentation and storytelling are only let down by some poor combat and the occasional iffy puzzle. Don’t get me wrong, I had a really good time playing the game, and when everything clicks, it’s a real horror treat. It’s just a shame that there were a couple too many tedious moments in the game.

However, whilst it has some flaws, Tenebris Somnia is still a fascinating nightmare worth experiencing (if only for the jaw-dropping presentation alone). It won’t be the best horror game that you’ve played, but it’s still an impressive experience that’ll be unlike anything else you’ve played before.
Tenebris Somniais a memorable survival horror experience that combines retro pixel art with unsettling live-action sequences to create a nightmare that feels both familiar and deeply disturbing.

Some investigation sequences can interrupt the pacing when we cannot immediately identify which item we need to use or combine. Although most puzzles are intuitive, I found myself stuck at certain points, trying to figure out what the game expected from me and revisiting areas that had nothing to do with the situation at hand. It is also difficult not to question some of the protagonist's decisions, especially given Ivan's disappearance and the lack of answers. Overall, these are minor limitations, accompanied by an additional consideration for those seeking to complete everything: missable achievements require careful attention to save files and campaign progression. These aspects could have been handled better, but they do not compromise the experience.

On the other hand, Tenebris Somnia makes excellent use of its investigation mechanics. The ability to collect and combine items, discover new ways to interact with the environments, and tackle specific situations, such as the battle in the dark room, provides enough variety to maintain interest throughout the campaign. The narrative also gains momentum as we descend through the building's floors and learn more about Ivan's memories. Although combat plays a secondary role, boss encounters introduce distinct moments into the progression, while exploration and puzzles sustain most of the experience.

The biggest highlight is the integration of gameplay and cinematic sequences. The live-action actors, practical effects, scene direction, and sound design contribute to an atmosphere that also works in the 2D sections, where the game demonstrates its ability to inspire fear without relying on filmed footage.

The story, which revolves around a troubled relationship, cults, and disturbing events, gains strength by presenting conflicts that feel tangible. This is a testament to a script that sustains curiosity until the most unsettling moments, even across its multiple endings. Tenebris Somnia is an exceptionally competent production that delivers on its vision, featuring a distinctive visual identity, well-executed investigation mechanics, and a cinematic presentation that makes the experience particularly memorable.

In my humble opinion, Tenebris Somnia is a masterpiece. It won't be everyone's cup of tea, but anyone who enjoys a strong, dark story and doesn't mind a bit of horror will feel right at home. It may not be the most technically brilliant game, but it's certainly the most memorable game I've played all year.

Tenebris Somnia seamlessly blends 90s FMV adventure with pure survival horror dread. While combat has clunky moments, its stunning cinematics, smart puzzles, and gripping story make it a new horror classic.

Tenebris Somnia manages to stand out in a sea of samey, repetitive indie horror games thanks to its intriguing premise, solid writing, and genuinely unique presentation. While its gameplay isn’t particularly groundbreaking, it’s far from bad, and I loved the contrast between its 8-bit, Amiga-era visuals and its shockingly well-shot, if occasionally off-putting, live-action cutscenes.

Unless you're really not into the 2D stylings of a retro-fitted horror game and don't like getting lost and stumped at tricky brain teasers, as well as mostly avoiding monsters to get ahead and survive, Tenebris Somnia is an immaculate time that thrives in its unique presentation.
100.0% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (11 reviews).

A top-down soulslike was still relatively new territory for me, but Tombwater proves the perspective is well worth exploring. It offers a compelling narrative, varied combat, and an engaging gameplay loop, with meaningful upgrades and tools introduced at a steady pace to keep momentum strong, while its distinct environments reinforce the game’s grim tone. Navigation can be a bit unclear and the controls take some getting used to, but thanks to its stability and many strengths, those flaws are easy to overlook.

Zelda meets Dark Souls, Tombwater is a fantastic action adventure set in a Lovecraftian reimagining of the Wild West. Tricky combat is king here, but thanks to difficulty options you can choose to focus on exploring the rich world around you and uncovering its secrets. This is a real hidden gem, and one that really should be on any action-adventure fan's radar.

All in all, Tombwater is one of my favorite Soulslikes, if not one of my favorite games, period. I’m not usually a fan of Zelda-likes, but I could barely put this one down. And only part of that was because I kept getting lost and wandering into a new miniboss arena.

Tombwater is very good at mixing two very different inspirations into a coherent experience. Bloodborne, moved into two dimensions, supplies the core combat mechanics, the feeling of eerie transformation, the magic system, and the fire. The Wild West brings in the characters, the dusty town, and the taciturn main character. Anyone who loves both will have a lot of fun exploring this world, discovering its past, conquering its many challenges, and developing their combat abilities. It helps that players have the option to make the game easier in the Settings menu once they start their adventure. Tombwater can be frustrating at times, but its core combination of ideas is very good.

Tombwater is a well-crafted blend of top-down soulslike, horror, and western setting. Even though its limited map doesn't offer much help for planning backtracking, the diversity of locations and how they intertwine to form a greater whole, dotted with secrets to discover, makes exploration one of the highlights of this fun pixel art eldritch adventure.

Along its 15- to 20-hour playthrough, what makes Tombwater hard to put down is its level design. Smartly placing shortcuts that are unlocked once a difficult boss or area is advanced through, it is purposeful in its ravaged layout. Obtaining new abilities, such as rock climbing and a special shot from your gun to light torches, incentivizes you to explore every cursed nook and cranny.

Tombwater is a perfect addition to the Metroidvania soulslike genre. It did a phenomenal job of bringing Eldritch Horror to the wild west and making it a truly immersive and fun experience. Even with the issues with controls for non-mouse and keyboard users and the sometimes questionable sound choices, this game has absolutely stolen my heart with its storytelling and beautifully horrifying art and atmosphere.

Tombwater sets up an intriguing space in the current indie game landscape. A Western horror game disguised as a Soulslike is a brilliant sale, but Tombwater is so much more. It is a triumphant realization of the 2D Zelda formula in a non-medieval, Bloodborne-esque setting. I hope I get to return to this world sooner than we’ll likely return to Yharnam.

Good Western games are few and far between and great ones are even more of a rarity. There have only been a few handfuls of truly great westerns like the Red Dead series, Oddworld: Strangers Wrath, Outlaws, Oregon Trail and a small selection of others, but now Tombwater needs to be placed in these hallowed halls alongside these icons. 

Tombwater features gameplay inspired by The Legend of Zelda and Bloodborne that gets paired with a faithful western story revolving around an anti-hero trying to live an honest life, who becomes forced to pursue frontier justice in this Eldritch universe. The result is an experience that would make Clint Eastwood proud as Tombwater is one of the greatest Westerns games ever crafted.

Tombwater captures the soul of a soulslike game and wraps it in a retro-western inspired skin, while offering a deeper focus on story without short-changing the mechanics you’d expect from the genre. The basic map definitely hurts exploration, and the lack of accessibility will mean the game is unplayable for some people, but even then, it’s impossible not to recommend Tombwater to fans of soulslike games and retro games alike.
93.5% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (31 reviews).
The Super Bomberman Collection is a genuine celebration of the SNES era of Bomberman games. Five amazing games, tons of goodies, what more could you want?

Super Bomberman Collection showcases some of the best Bomberman gameplay the franchise has ever seen. If you have friends or family for local co-op or competitive play, there are a lot of options, stages, and features to explore. While I will continue to bang the drum for thoughtful compilation releases, of which this is definitely one, more online connectivity would have been a great addition to the package. Perhaps best enjoyed in short bursts, Super Bomberman Collection is the best Bomberman release since the Bomberman 64: The Second Attack!
The Super Bomberman Collection is a wonderful bundle of games, whether you were a Bomberman kid or want to try something new.

If you’re someone like me who wishes to re-experience these really great titles from Hudson Soft, then I certainly recommend you give Super Bomberman Collection a try. And hey, maybe if this sells well, then Konami might consider finally bringing more of these older titles, either as another collection or as titles to Nintendo Switch Online.

Super Bomberman Collection is the most complete and confident celebration of Bomberman’s early years to date. It blends preservation with modern polish, offers a wealth of content across seven games, and captures the joyful chaos that made the series iconic. Minor technical quirks and limited online features hold it back slightly, but they do little to diminish the overall achievement. This is Bomberman at its most generous, its most accessible, and its most enduring.

With this Super Bomberman Collection, fans will finally find a complete way to relive the golden age of the series; new players will have the perfect opportunity to discover why Bomberman remains a video game icon more than thirty years after its inception. A blast from the past for one of the longest-running and most beloved series in gaming.
An excellent compilation of seven games from the heyday of Bomberman, but it’s a shame it doesn’t have more online options, to make joining in the multiplayer fun easier.

Super Bomberman Collection showcases some of the very best gameplay that Bomberman has to offer. Between the various games on offer, there are dozens of hours of exciting couch multiplayer battles to be had, demonstrating that it doesn’t take the latest and greatest tech for a game to simply be fun to play with others. Though the lack of native online is disappointing, the great gameplay coupled with some robust museum content that honors the legacy of these games makes this one a no brainer—especially given the relatively cheap price. If you’re looking for another game you can pull out on game nights with friends, I’d highly suggest you pick this one up.

There’s nothing out there in video games quite like multiplayer Bomberman. And with the Super Bomberman Collection, we’ve righted a historical wrong, with over half this series previously unavailable in North America without importing carts that wouldn’t fit in a Super Nintendo without taking a pair of pliers to the poor thing. This is a respectable collection that includes multiple new localizations, high quality museum assets, and a dope, new unboxing feature. It doesn’t have the same production value as Konami’s other collections, and it’s a bummer the big sign of that is no online play. But if you can get your friends together in a room, I guarantee you’ll have a megaton blast.

While other compilations are more robust, Super Bomberman Collection is still a blast with its seven games on offer. The solo gamer in you will have fun in smaller sessions, and grab some friends for a local battle or couch co-op (no online play), and you’ll have an even better time.

The display issues, input lag, and little bugs here and there detract from what is otherwise a rather well put-together assortment of games. Super Bomberman Collection might not have your favorite Bomberman game in it, but there’s plenty here for any fan to find some fun with. I really appreciate all the extra touches in the UI, and having two newly-translated games is nothing to sneeze at. The GameShare option is a natural fit here, provided you have Switch-owning Bomberman fans in your vicinity. I wish the actual play experience was a little better than it is, but I’d imagine most players will find this to serve their needs well enough.
Hudson Soft's classic franchise returns in Super Bomberman Collection, offering many hours of fun retro action.

Super Bomberman Collection is a must-own for anyone who has ever enjoyed this franchise. With a grand total of seven games, including many that are reaching US shores for the first time, snappy presentation, and tons of behind-the-scenes goodies, you really can't go wrong.

Ultimately, this isn't a lazy emulation but a true work of historical memory, restoring dignity to a series that helped define the canons of a genre that continues to inspire modern titles. Super Bomberman Collection is not only a gift for nostalgic fans to relive a glory of the past, but a bridge for new generations to discover how a simple bomb laid the foundations of the video game.
