As a remaster, Fighting Force Collection does exactly what it needs to do. Both games run well, look as good as possible, and are presented in a way that respects their original form. There are no game-breaking issues, no lazy emulation shortcuts, and no technical excuses. This is a competent, respectful revival. Where the first Fighting Force remains the clear highlight: still fun, still chaotic, and still best enjoyed with a second player on the couch. It’s proof that good core design can outlast technical limitations. The second game? It’s… fine. Functional. Interesting in a historical sense. But also a strong example of why some games are better remembered than replayed. And that’s okay. Not every classic needs to be reinvented, and not every sequel deserves the same reverence as its predecessor. The Fighting Force Collection succeeds because it lets you experience both and decide for yourself. So, what you get is a solid, enjoyable remaster anchored by a genuinely fun original game, slightly dragged down by a sequel that time hasn’t been kind to. Yes, it’s worth playing, worth remembering, just maybe not worth revisiting everything.

It's easy to see why it made such an impression back in '97—the choice of path, the differences between the characters, and the environmental destruction. It's a shame there had to be a sequel, which is dynamic but has aged very poorly. And let's be honest — nothing/little was done here. These are just two old games preying on nostalgia.

I was really looking forward to the Fighting Force Collection, but after playing, a part of me wishes I had left this one in my memory. Fans of the series will know exactly what they are getting here, nothing more, nothing less. Unfortunately, as a fan of the original game, I cannot help but feel disappointed. The first game feels much shorter than I remembered, and the sequel drags on for far too long.

Fighting Force Collection resurrects two failed 3D experiments that have not aged gracefully, pairing clunky combat and awkward design with a bare minimum remaster effort from Limited Run Games. While the historical curiosity of a lost Streets of Rage 4 prototype may intrigue genre historians, weak emulation, poor presentation, and fundamentally sluggish gameplay make this a tough sell for anyone beyond preservation purists.

What we have here is a bare bones remaster of Fighting Force and its crummy sequel, featuring only the most obligatory of modern conveniences. The paltry options menu, meager archive material, and total lack of border imagery demonstrates little of the love shown to other Limited Run releases. Fighting Force itself still has something to offer a very niche audience, but as a member of that audience I already have a version of Fighting Force, one with more options for fine tuning and without a $19.99 MSRP

The definition of insanity is doing the same thing over and over again and expecting a different outcome. Fighting Force Collection didn't reinvent the wheel here, and I really wish it had. It's the same game. Take that for what it's worth.
Is this collection worth it? The first game is still fun, but the sequel remains a bad game with little reason to revisit. €20 for two basic ports with minimal improvements is too much.

Fighting Force Collection has the merit of bringing two games of the late 1990s in a way that’s as close to the original experience as possible. Unfortunately, there is little else going for it. If the first game can still provide some shallow but fun beat’em up action, the second game falls flat due to terrible camera and controls, featureless characters, and a failure at attempting to deliver a stealth action experience. Nostalgia has its value, but the Fighting Force games should rather have been remade instead of ported to this generation.

In the end the Fighting Force Collection is more of a curiosity than a compilation of classics. Some people have nostalgia for the first game, it was decent. The second game, however, should have remained forgotten. Core Design started strong and ended with a whimper and I would rather remember them for titles like Tomb Raider and Soulstar, and not the travesty that is Fighting Force 2.
Pair of classic 3D beat ’em ups that are definitely showing their age
Is this collection worth it? The first game is still fun, but the sequel remains a bad game with little reason to revisit. '20 for two basic ports with minimal improvements is too much.

Without any significant innovations, additions, or improvements that go beyond the norm, Fighting Force Collection carries with it, without compromise, the qualities, such as setting, simplicity, and objectivity of the purest digital beat 'em up; and the limitations of its time, visually and mechanically speaking, which will certainly bring a nostalgic smile to older players, but will hardly seduce subsequent generations.

Despite the production following all the remastering standards we appreciate, I can only recommend Fighting Force Collection to die-hard retro gamers and fans of the franchise who remember the PlayStation titles with a sense of nostalgia and would like to revisit them on modern consoles. If you don’t fall into either of these categories, there’s very little here for you in this two games, which, it has to be said, were rightly forgotten.

Fighting Force Collection functions more as a nostalgic throwback than a true update of its two games. The first Fighting Force remains the pack's biggest draw, with a simple yet effective co-op mode that can still provide some enjoyable moments. The second, however, falls far short and highlights more clearly than ever the series' uncertainties in its evolution. It's an honest collection, but one that relies heavily on historical value rather than current gameplay.
A faithful collection and a useful window into a strange era for the genre, but also proof that some classics age better as memories than as games.

Fighting Force Collection is a faithful port of a long-forgotten PS1 series. Those who grew up with these games will find some nostalgic fun, but anyone else will struggle to find many positives to pull from this collection.
Fighting Force Collection introduces the beat ’em up cult classic to a new generation while letting old-school gamers reconnect with their youth.

Fighting Force Collection is a good little set that brings two influential 3D brawlers back into the spotlight. Despite story issues, awkward mechanics in the second game, and some dated design choices, the core fighting still feels great. Smashing up furniture, blowing up vehicles, pulling off combos, and battling through waves of enemies remains fun, and the collection does a solid job preserving what made these games stand out. It is a nostalgic, chaotic, and enjoyable return to a pair of games that helped shape the 3D beat ’em up genre.

Fighting Force Collection is a curious title. It seems solely aimed at people who enjoyed these titles back when they were released. Neither of them are particular cult classics and while I was happy enough to play both of them again, not enough has been done to bring in a new crowd . I feel the lack of different versions of the games or much in the way of other bonuses really just makes it feel like a bare bones product just thrown out for the few people craving their next retro fix.

If you enjoyed the Fighting Force games back in the day and have a hankering for jumping back in, I would say go for it. But in a market full of retro rereleases, Fighting Force Collection doesn’t even scratch the top dogs of the market. Much like the original releases, there isn’t enough here for it to be a true standout.

Fighting Force Collection is less than the sum of its parts (which aren't amazing on their own). The first game is more appealing and easier to pick up, as its beat 'em up premise, despite being simple, works well, especially when played with a friend. The second title shifts to a secret agent-style adventure, with more weapons and missions that are more complex. Both are entertaining for a while, but their mechanics are practically outdated for current 3D games. That is where the collection could have improved things, with more technical enhancements, interesting materials about the games, and gameplay options. Considering the complete package, it is worth for nostalgia or curiosity reasons, but very little beyond that.

Fighting Force Collection brings two late-1990s games back mostly as they were, with a few modern touches to keep them playable now. The original Fighting Force still has a solid brawler gameplay loop, especially with co-op and a tolerance for its older design quirks. Fighting Force 2 slows things down and never finds the same pull, which makes the difference between the two hard to ignore. This collection makes the most sense if the first game is the main reason you’re here.

The original Fighting Force is the far superior game of the two games, but having both included is a great way for fans to relive a hidden gem and a bad game if they wish, and for newcomers to experience two lesser-known titles from back in the day. Fighting Force Collection may not be the most feature-rich compilation, but it brings back a long-forgotten franchise to modern consoles and some fond memories for longtime fans.

A faithful but uneven collection. Fighting Force 1 remains fun with modern conveniences, while Fighting Force 2 drags everything down. Best suited for nostalgic fans who know exactly what they are getting.
While neither game is necessarily a classic of the beat ’em up genre, there’s plenty of nostalgia and charm to be had revisiting them in the Fighting Force Collection.

Fighting Force Collection is a love letter to a specific slice of gaming history, and while the gameplay is undeniably dated and might struggle to win over a modern audience without those rose-tinted glasses, the nostalgia factor here is certainly strong. If you grew up smashing up these blocky environments, this collection is definitely a fun trip down memory lane.

The only people who will have some kind of enjoyment with Fighting Force Collection are those who grew up with those games and have a borderline die-hard nostalgic attachment towards them. I can’t criticise the folks at Implicit Conversions for their porting skills, as there’s nothing wrong with their remastering efforts. The problem lies at the fact these games have simply aged poorly. In fact, I don’t think they have ever been that good, even for their time.
14.7% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (34 reviews).
The Relic: First Guardian may never escape its technical shortcomings, but its melancholy world is well worth saving.

The Relic: First Guardian is an undeniably ambitious title, but it heavily suffers under the weight of expectations, ultimately trying to do too much and doing it poorly. There are certainly positive aspects: excellent environmental design, dynamic and intuitive gameplay, and an equipment management system that integrates seamlessly with the lore.  However, these qualities are not enough to offset a series of poor game design choices. Enemies prove to be ultra-aggressive, while the 80 bosses—supposedly the flagship feature of the game—turn out to be flaw-ridden "damage sponges" that are often mere copies of one another. The game world is vast, varied, and boring—immersed in a cosmic void, with design decisions that destroy any sense of discovery. A visually well-crafted technical presentation is undercut by frustrating camera management and visibly dated NPCs. So many times in my reviews I find myself writing that "more could have been done," but The Relic: First Guardian is the first game that made me think that, perhaps, less should have been done.

There are things about The Relic: First Guardian that I absolutely loved. The game's exploration also leaves something for you to find, and the game's combat is satisfying and rewarding. It's just a shame I had to suffer through major bugs that kept me from progressing or finishing quests.

The Relic: First Guardian is a game that dared to be different and suffered for it. In the pursuit of challenging what has been tried and tested, it put forth a plethora of great ideas: equipment-based tactical combat, non-respawning enemies as progression, and genuinely great boss battles. Unfortunately, it also revealed why those ideas weren’t the norm. Poor animation implementation, questionable camerawork, and forgettable narratives all end up making this a much lesser product than the sum of its parts. In fixing what wasn’t broken, it only revealed the cracks within itself.

The Relic: First Guardian is a game of stark contrasts, where immense developer passion clashes with severe technical shortcomings. While the anachronistic PS3-era graphics and early framerate drops make for a frustrating start, the game redeems itself through a magnetic exploration loop, a surprisingly deep RPG progression without inventory clutter, and a staggering roster of over ninety unique bosses. Once the technical performance miraculously stabilizes in the latter half of the adventure, a genuinely solid and rewarding action-RPG emerges from the rubble. It’s a heavily flawed journey, but one crafted with enough heart and solid mechanics to earn a passing grade.

The Relic: First Guardian* is certainly an ambitious debut project from the studio Project Cloud Games, promising a vast open world, eighty unique elite enemies, and a simple yet conceptually strong story. However, that ambition ultimately hindered development, resulting in a product that fails to deliver on any of its initial promises in a polished state. This forces those who have already purchased the game to wait for numerous fixes before it reaches the level of quality promised by the trailers and promotional material.

I think I could write about 4000 more words of complaining about The Relic: First Guardian, but I’m eager to simply wash my hands clean of this game and forget it ever existed. If you love Souls-likes or action RPGs, there are dozens of other experiences you’re better off playing. This one’s not even worth your curiosity.

The Relic: First Guardian has plenty of promising ideas on paper, from its Korean mythology setting to its fast-paced combat and variety of Brutals, but few of them truly stand out in practice. The fragmented storytelling, uninspired voice acting and lack of meaningful combat depth make both the lore and the battles feel less engaging than the trailers suggest. Despite being marketed as a soulslike, its challenge comes more from clunky controls than memorable encounters, leaving the overall experience feeling underwhelming.

The Relic can be summarily described as disappointing and a chore to play. It's one of the weaker AA soulslike games from a developer that is clearly trying to punch above their weight. There was no reason to include an open-world environment where assets are repeated ad nauseam and enemy variety is virtually non-existent. Technically, the game is all over the place, with a camera that often proves to be the worst enemy and a highly inconsistent frame rate. Lastly, the advertised 80+ boss fights are, for the most part, humanoid enemies that are frustrating to fight rather than exciting encounters.

The Relic: First Guardian feels like a case of a smaller developer overextending itself. It brings an aggressive twist to combat and features a host of bosses to battle, but that's not enough to overcome the game's flaws and weaknesses. A flurry of patches have arrived since launch, but you're currently still better off waiting to see if they can address more of the core issues.
The Relic: First Guardian is one of the worst games to come out in 2026. With so many other titles worth your time and money, this one is an easy skip.
Between rough gameplay feel and mechanics, The Relic: First Guardian doesn’t present itself with a bang, but with a wimper.
The true dark fantasy of The Relic: First Guardian is all of the potential it squanders; an energetic action game marred by its own shambolic state and broken in too many inexcusable ways.

The Relic: First Guardian is a game with good ideas, but it ultimately fails to execute them. Performance issues, recurring bugs, and the lack of essential navigation features make the experience feel unfinished, leaving the impression that it needed more time in development.

The Korean studio doesn't quite hit its stride. Despite this, and provided the technical aspects are quickly fixed, The Relic: First Guardian is a dark ARPG that rewards initiative without ever becoming too frustrating or punishing; it's not a mere imitation of FromSoftware's work.

Relic: The First Guardian is not so messy as to be unplayable. In fact, the game’s combat can be excellent at times, and the use of Korean folklore twisted into a dark narrative is an interesting idea.
Soulslike adventure through the apocalyptic wasteland of the once-prosperous realm of Arsilthus that could benefit from a patch or two

Despite the time that has elapsed and the patches applied on other platforms, The Relic: First Guardian remains a mess that can't address some of its shortcomings on the technically weaker platform it is running on. The combat seems decent until you reach one of the game's numerous boss fights, where the fighting suddenly feels messy. The story isn't that engaging, and it's actually made worse by the side stories, whose endings and constant repetition of facts overshadow some of the fairly intriguing narratives you would've found along the way. The presentation is also quite terrible in parts, especially the voice acting, which makes the game's long length all the more agonizing. There is still a kernel of a good game, and there is a chance that enough patching can make this a decent title, but with so many Souls-like games already on the system, even if you discount the ones created for the original Switch, there's not much reason to give this title a look.

Relic: The First Guardian has the foundations of a solid action RPG, with an impressive roster of over 70 unique bosses and a respectable variety of Relic-based abilities that keep major encounters engaging. Unfortunately, those strengths are constantly undermined by shallow combat mechanics, clunky animations, inconsistent voice acting, poor audio design, technical issues, and surprisingly amateur translation errors. Rather than a true Soulslike, this is a straightforward action game weighed down by an overwhelming number of avoidable flaws. With more polish, it could have been a pleasant surprise. Instead, it ends up as a frustrating experience that rarely allows its best ideas to shine.
The Relic: First Guardian is a work of violent contrasts, a crossroads where an almost moving authorial passion collides head-on with undeniable production and technical limitations.
"A game that perhaps could have shown considerable potential, but ultimately ended up buried under the weight of its own shortcomings."

Evaluating a work like The Relic: First Guardian always presents an ethical and critical dilemma. Behind the flaws of this project you can glimpse the enormous heart of a small team that tried to bite off more than it could chew, putting together a content package beyond its real means. But passion alone cannot justify a product that reaches the market in a truly too approximate technical state. Focusing on quantity instead of quality was the final blow to a project that, in different conditions, could have made its mark among soulslike games. In its current state, the adventure is a problematic journey with the taste of a wasted opportunity. One that, despite all its rough edges, shows the seeds of intriguing and quite stimulating ideas. Therefore, while waiting for massive corrective patches (which we hope will arrive soon), it is a dark fantasy odyssey meant only for the most devoted fans of the genre.

The Relic: First Guardian may not reach the heights of the genre’s best titles, but it can still appeal to action RPG fans looking for challenging combat. Its strengths lie in its dark fantasy setting, combat system, and attempt to offer its own take on the Soulslike genre. If you can overlook some of its weaker aspects, The Relic: First Guardian can still provide a decent amount of fun.

The Relic: First Guardian is an engaging new action game that takes cues from the Soulslike genre while incorporating medieval and Korean folklore into the mix. With its enjoyable combat mechanics and difficult but fair boss fights, The Relic: First Guardian offers many systems that will make Souls fans happy. However, its technical issues take away from the beautiful vision that the game sets out to achieve.

The Relic: First Guardian is messy, buggy, with a bad story, bad voice acting, it should be the kind of plucky Z-tier game I fall in love with. Instead it is marred by a lot of (presumed) clanker nonsense. There are better bad games to spend your time with.
The Relic: First Guardian shows clear ambition, but repetitive enemies, weak technical presentation, an awkward camera and inconsistent framerates run too deep for patches alone to fix.
The Relic: First Guardian is one of my personal disappointments of the year. And perhaps the worst part is that I don't think it's a game completely devoid of good ideas—it does have some.

The Relic: First Guardian has been available on PC and PlayStation for a while. Accordingly, I’ve been waiting patiently to give this a go on Xbox. With Souls-like elements, unusual mechanics, and a rich and dark lore-filled story, this appealed to me. However, there are plenty of performance issues and bugs that hold it back.

Project Cloud Games has developed this action-adventure, Souls-like title. It is a semi-open world game that encourages you to investigate every building, ruin, and cave you encounter. However, you must stay frosty throughout as monsters roam everywhere and danger is around every corner.

This single-player affair focuses on bitty lore, impressive passive abilities, and seamlessly never-ending boss battles. The huge and often hideous bosses test your skills as you dodge, weave, block, and slice your way to victory.

The Relic: First Guardian is hardly a bad action RPG, which makes its failures all the more aggravating. Its fierce fighting, exciting parries, occasional exploration surprises and tougher boss encounters hint at the potential of a far greater game.

The Relic: First Guardian delivers an accessible mix of RPG and soulslike elements, backed by more than 80 bosses, dynamic combat and beautifully crafted environments. However, chaotic group encounters, a clumsy camera and repetitive mission design hold back an ambitious adventure that still needs further refinement.

After trying to give The Relic a fair shot I just could not continue. The bosses are unbalanced, and combat is just too janky to really enjoy it. Statues effect are very punishing with some of the first few bosses you will encounter. I’m not sure why the game decided to riddle the world with notes, and make them right next to each other at that. With me even counting 11 notes exactly one after another, that just led to a boss fight. An empty, lifeless world with side-quest that end up feeling like just filler. But honestly from the 8 hours I spent with The Relic, the whole time has felt like useless padding.

A very large amount of my frustration comes from just how bad the hit boxes are. Tie that with the severe dropping in frame rate over nothing going on in the world. And even worse when you actually fight one enemy let alone a group or boss.

Everything is just a chore, and I just couldn’t push through. I really don’t have any praise for The Relic: First Guardian. It’s definitely the Thumb Culture Bronze Award.

Unfortunately, The Relic: First Guardian disappointed us. It has plenty of ideas, quests, and bosses, but everything feels a bit slapdash and poorly polished. You can sense the passion and dedication, but productions of this scale require more structured teams and a significantly larger budget. It would have been better to lower the bar a bit, reducing the quantity of content in favor of higher quality—both in terms of the combat system (the game’s core) and the technical aspects. We hope this first project will serve as a learning experience for the developer to understand where they went wrong, because there’s no shortage of ideas, passion, and love for the genre.
either a soulslike nor an action RPG, The Relic: First Guardian is a huge wasted potential due to its lack of technical polish and severe stability issues.

The Relic: First Guardian is a solid addition for Soulslike fans, offering fast combat, engaging lore, deep weapon skill trees, and great boss design. However, weak visuals, unstable PS5 performance, and a generic art style drag the experience down significantly, preventing it from reaching greater heights.

The Relic: First Guardian is best described as an action RPG that blossoms despite its clear limitations. It is far from a perfectly well-rounded game, with awkward animations, imprecise controls, and underwhelming character models standing out as obvious flaws. Even so, its stylish combat, built around carefully timed attacks and defenses, delivers a thrilling sense of catharsis that keeps you coming back.

The Relic: First Guardian is not only one of the worst Soulslikes I have ever played, but a prime candidate for the worst game of 2026. It's a game that crumbles under the weight of its own ambition, aiming to be the next Elden Ring and missing the target wildly. Not one aspect of this game warrants praise, and in its current state, it is an affront to the Souls genre as a whole. It's time I will never get back, but hopefully through my suffering, you won't suffer the same fate.

The Relic: First Guardian is Project Cloud Games debut title. It has some issues, like performance issues and a lack of some basic mechanics like jumping, but the world-building, the skill tree, the combat, the bosses and the feeling of wonder we all need and love from Soulslike is present. It has jank sure, but it has heart, and it’s one of my favourite experiences of the year, and something that I will continually be heading back to for the next few months.

The Relic: First Guardian lives in a constant tension between ambition and reality. Its intense world‑building, melancholic Korean‑folklore micro‑stories, and surprisingly layered combat show Project Cloud Games’ clear vision and uncommon talent. But an overload of bosses, abrupt difficulty shifts, technical problems, and some awkward design choices keep it from reaching its full potential. What remains is an imperfect yet heartfelt action game, capable of striking moments for those willing to accept its roughness and sink into its ruined world. If the team can refine this first effort—cutting excess and aiming for greater cohesion—the future could hold something truly exciting. For now, it’s a dark, troubled journey, still worth taking for anyone seeking something different in today’s action landscape.
20.0% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (10 reviews).

If you enjoy detective stories, narrative-driven games, or mysteries that reward careful thinking under pressure, this game is shaping up to be a compelling experience. Clue: Murder By Death understands the appeal of a good mystery and respects the player’s ability to solve it. Placing strict limits on time and information, it creates a sense of urgency that makes every choice feel meaningful. It is not about finding every answer, but about finding the right one before time runs out.

Clue: Murder By Death will disappoint those looking for a direct adaptation of the very popular boardgame. It will also fail to deliver the level of humor and kitsch of the movie. But, with its simple mechanics and extensive storytelling, it does deliver a pretty cool murder mystery that starts off pretty slow and then delivers plenty of surprises. The presentation will be the biggest obstacle for detective game aficionados. Put on a crime-focused podcast and take breaks when the simple graphics start to grate. Clue: Murder By Death’s more than 100 rooms don’t all pack surprises, but they create a fictional universe with a ton of storytelling potential.

Clue: Murder by Death seems perfect for a niche audience, as it offers a mystery that requires player commitment and meaningful deduction skills to solve, with very few tools to make it easier. For a general audience, however, the game is likely to feel slow, awkward to play, and full of distracting load times, which come together to make a game that’s hard to engage with.

Should Clue: Murder By Death ever add in some quality of life basics, even just labeling the rooms, or allowing you add markers, this could be a wonderful mystery. For now, unfortunately, it's one where it feels fine to leave quite a few stones unturned.

Clue: Murder by Death oozes charm and nails the whodunnit vibe, with clever companion mechanics and a ticking clock that keeps the tension high. Sadly, the bloated mansion, limited inventory, and forced repetition drag the experience down. The game is brilliant in concept, yet flawed in execution. However, for under twenty bucks, mystery fans might still find it worth the sleuth.

Clue: Murder By Death fully immerses the player in a thoroughly realised 1930's era country estate murder mystery with the welcome addition of cute, cartoony visuals. Sadly, the game is somewhat let down by a frustrating two-hour real-time playthrough limit that collides with tedious character walking speeds and frequent clunky load screens.

Clue: Murder by Death is a modern take on the classic board game, bringing 3D graphics and open world exploration to the mystery solving. Investigate the scene, interview suspects, and eventually present your case, all within only two hours. Unfortunately, there are numerous bugs within that timeframe.
Will you be able to solve the murder of Lord Anderson?

Clue: Murder by Death on Xbox is a solid detective experience that modernises the classic formula with atmosphere and immersion.

Its early hours are genuinely gripping, and its presentation — especially in audio and environmental design — creates a satisfying sense of suspense. The move from board game abstraction to explorable mystery is a smart evolution.

Clue: Murder By Death has a great framework for a video game. Appropriate graphics and a clever use of different dialogue give the game an authentic feel, more than just a remake of a classic board game.

However, with slow loading times and character movement, it misses the mark and leads to cumbersome and frustrating gameplay. Clue: Murder By Death would have benefited from more user testing and proofreading to capture the typos and grammar mistakes. Although I initially liked the game, the game-breaking crashes mean I really can’t recommend it at this time.

Unfortunately, the experience wasn’t much fun for me. There’s a decent foundation here, but it’s weighed down by too many rooms to explore, too many suspects who start to blur together, and far too many objects to sift through. Combined with a poor map system, limited inventory space, slow character movement, unclear objectives, and noticeable input lag, the game quickly became frustrating.

Instead of feeling like a clever mystery to unravel, I felt overwhelmed. The sheer cognitive load turned what should have been an engaging investigation into something that felt more like work than enjoyment. That said, if you have a few hours to spare and enjoy obtuse mystery games that demand a lot of patience, this might still be worth a look.
While it has some decent ideas and story beats at its core, mechanically it plays slowly and in a pretty clunky manner, detracting from the overall experience

the-walking-dead-streets-of-survival.title: The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival

reviews.excerpt: 23.1% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (39 reviews).
If you're a fan of the TV series or just love a solid, retro-style brawler, The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival is worth your time despite a few hiccups.

The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival is one of the better games based on The Walking Dead, being a side-scrolling beat 'em up with surprising RPG and adventure elements. It's just a shame that its combat feels a little basic in some areas, and its abundance of firearms can result in some frustration.
The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival is enjoyable especially if you're a fan of the show, however, combat can get repetitive and targeting is frustrating.

The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival isn’t a game I’ll be returning to over and over again. There simply isn’t enough mechanical depth or variety to make repeated playthroughs particularly compelling. But what it did do was remind me of one of Daryl’s old supply runs: get in, grab what you need, and get back out before you have time to overthink it. Streets of Survival isn’t particularly spectacular, but it’s short, straightforward, and easy to digest.

Streets of Survival is clearly not the best beat ’em up out there, but it’s not the worst Walking Dead game we’ve had either (Overkill’s The Walking Dead and The Walking Dead: Destinies have already been there...). The pixel art works really well here, and the different levels follow the story arc of the second half of Season 8 quite closely. So both old-school gamers and fans of the TV series will feel right at home. That said, both groups will probably be frustrated by how limited the game feels, with a campaign that can be completed in just three hours, as well as the publisher’s greed, with a simple endless mode locked behind a DLC that costs almost as much as the base game.

Despite being a fan of both The Walking Dead and the beat ‘em up genre, I can’t fully recommend Streets of Survival. It has a few standout moments, and I did enjoy wreaking havoc as Michonne, but the short 12-level, 3-hour campaign just isn’t unique enough to justify picking up any of the many better beat ‘em ups available.

If you’re a fan of The Walking Dead, you’ll undoubtedly enjoy revisiting one of the most interesting periods in the series’ history. Judged purely as an old-school 2.5D beat ’em up, The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival is rather mediocre, feeling a little clunky and repetitive. But if you’re a fan of the franchise, there’s some decent old-school fun to be had here, at least for a little while.

The Walking Dead: Street of Survival features an appealing retro aesthetic, but falls short due to repetitive gameplay, a limited move set, and a lack of enemy variety. The narrative fails to capture the intensity of the TV series, the story mode is too short, and the game lacks replay value given its limited character selection and absence of co-op functionality.

The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival is more Walking Dead than Streets of Rage. The fan service will delight fans with nods to the series scattered throughout the adventure and several iconic characters.
Arcade-style 2D beat 'em up based on AMC's The Walking Dead
The clunky controls, the problematic behavior of ranged enemies, some unfair spikes in difficulty, the short playtime, and—above all—the lack of co-op prevent it from truly standing out

Overall, The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival is a side-scrolling brawler with an interesting concept and strong appeal for fans of the series, but held back by unrefined combat, a repetitive structure and a short duration. It works as an occasional experience and as a pixel-art tribute to AMC's universe, but it does not manage to establish itself as a reference title in its genre.

The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival takes an incredibly strange concept, turning the grounded human drama of the titular franchise into an arcade-style beat-’em-up. Unfortunately, the execution does not save the odd premise, as the game is mechanically underwhelming, unbalanced, short, and tone-deaf. Furthermore, an essential game mode that gives the game its only real replayability is locked behind a deluxe edition upgrade, giving the impression that the game is nothing more than a cash grab made to milk whatever is left of the TWD fanbase.

"It must be said that The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival is a worthwhile title; despite lacking a fresh, new narrative, it manages to carve out a coherent path for itself in its story mode, and its gameplay offers a varied and engaging experience, so much so that the game's pixel art design doesn't feel out of place or inconsistent with The Walking Dead universe and is well received by its audience. While the absence of the Walker Pit mode in the standard edition and the short length of the story for a $20 standard-edition title are undeniable flaws, overall, The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival keeps its audience properly entertained for its roughly two-and-a-half hours of gameplay."

This beat ’em up adaptation of The Walking Dead franchise had all the ingredients for a fun game, but it falls short in many ways. While The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival brings a fresh survival-horror twist to the beat ’em up genre, its core gameplay falls short. Frustrating combat mechanics and a disappointing lack of multiplayer overshadow its innovative genre-blending approach.

The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival has brought back a bit of that magic I felt whilst watching the series. This beat ’em up through and through is both a tribute to the series and simply an enjoyable, well-made game. It isn’t limited to mindlessly bashing and shooting your way around. Odaclick Game Studio delivers a good story and well-thought-out gameplay. The talent tree and ‘The Walker Pit’ mode are a nice bonus. Even though Streets of Survival has its minor flaws, its entertainment value more than makes up for them.

Sadly, I feel The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival misses the mark in some key areas. While the combat is fine, and fans of the show will be glad to reunite with the core main characters, the lack of voice acting and general atmosphere I associate with The Walking Dead meant it didn't quite engage me as much as I'd hoped.

I honestly can't recommend The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival to anyone but hardcore fans of the show, and even then it's a hard sell. While visually a gorgeous game, that is nowhere near enough to save it from the poorly designed gameplay. Committing some cardinal sins of beat ‘em ups of a single combo to execute and no multiplayer unfortunately has left Streets of Survival surrounded by a zombie horde, doomed to be turned into the one thing they swear to fight.

The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival works well as a nostalgic experience of moments from the TV series. But for those looking for a new great Beat 'em Up, however, the limitations of a production that presents good ideas but doesn't always manage to fully develop them become more evident.

The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival is about as relevant as The Walking Dead series is in 2026. At its core, it’s a title that doesn’t really understand its own genre, and while it attempts to introduce new elements and experiments, they don’t work particularly well. The result is something so ordinary and uninteresting that not even gallons of spilled blood and dozens of walkers can save it.
For fans of The Walking Dead and retro brawlers, there's fun to be had here. It just needed a little more polish, a little more content and, perhaps most importantly, a second player.
While there may be some mileage here for die hard Walking Dead fans, newcomers may feel a bit lost, and the gameplay can have a tendency to get tedious at times

The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival delivers exactly what it promises. Whether you are a fan of the comics, the TV series, or classic Beat 'em Up games, this title is an easy recommendation. With a frantic pace from start to finish and finely tuned mechanics, the game offers a fun and enjoyable experience.

Unremarkable. It isn’t a flawless game, nor does it set out to be. But to be honest, it could have been so much better. It fulfils the basic function of entertaining without any great fanfare, but it falls a bit short in terms of depth and, above all, in its gameplay. The gameplay feels clunky, awkward and unsatisfying. This is almost a fatal flaw in a game where the emphasis on action is practically absolute. There’s no better news on the graphics or audiovisual front either, as these are also fairly basic and don’t quite hit the mark. In short, if you’re a fan of the series, you’ve got an excuse to play it; otherwise, I wouldn’t recommend this title, even as a fan of the genre
The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival is an okay game that has the foundation of something that could have been made so much better.

The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival delivers nostalgic pixel-art action, recognizable characters, and satisfying progression, but uneven combat and limited content keep this enjoyable adaptation from becoming an essential beat ’em up.

A short and highly polarizing experience that successfully captures the atmosphere of The Walking Dead through its charming retro presentation. While repetitive combat, limited progression, and the lack of co-op hold it back from reaching its full potential, it remains an enjoyable experience for dedicated fans of the franchise.

Streets of Survival does add a few wrinkles to the mix, such as the gunplay and skill system, but what's in the final product quickly wears out its welcome, with an experience that has some extremely frustrating moments, and is over quickly.

The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival brings AMC’s iconic universe to the beat ’em up genre with enjoyable combat, firearms, RPG elements and a highly replayable cooperative experience. Its short levels and limited character differences hold it back, but the faithful pixel-art presentation and accessible gameplay make it an entertaining new take on the franchise.

For Walking Dead fans, this is still a decent way to spend a few hours revisiting the show’s characters and smashing heads. The pixel-art presentation looks great, Michonne is fun to play, and the early combat has a satisfying snap. Just be ready for a game that becomes more frustrating and repetitive the longer it goes on, especially once every other enemy decides to pull out a gun.

The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival is a pretty mid run of the mill beat’em up that feels a bit slow, outdated and 10 years too late. I really did try to like this, but the issues kept killing my enjoyment. This game should’ve released about 8-10 years ago during the peak of the franchise. While the upgrade mechanics are a nice touch to the genre, there’s really no reason to buy this. There are so many better, more fluid beat’em ups than this. Unless you’re a die-head fan of The Walking Dead or you must play every beat’em up in existence, this is an easy pass.

Streets of Survival is a fun use of The Walking Dead IP, a much better use of the license than some past games. It’s a serviceable side scrolling romp that is perfect for newbies, but may lack depth that veterans of the genre are used to.
The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival offers enjoyable brawling and a solid retelling of the Saviors War, yet its brevity and familiar beats make it best suited for franchise or genre loyalists fans.

Streets of Survival has a foundation for a great series, but the lack of some quality of life features in its combat, and a lack of co-op make this hard to recommend, given the genre has so many other options that are simply better games. The Walking Dead is perfect for videogames, but few games have really hit that high mark, and despite enemies having near perfect aim here, Streets of Survival can't quite say the same.
The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival” offers a fast-paced, accessible, and entertaining arcade experience...

The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival had a concept that intrigued me, turning the franchise into a beat ’em up with some resource‑management strategy. Unfortunately, the execution undermines almost everything that could have worked. The controls are clunky, boss fights are poor, progression barely impacts gameplay, and replay value is virtually nonexistent. Daryl and Negan are fun to control, and a few sound effects land well, but they’re not enough to save an experience that wore me out long before the credits rolled.

The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival is an enjoyable beat ‘em up that brings with it some genuinely unique ideas. Sure, it can feel a little clunky in places and the lack of multiplayer is disappointing, but the satisfying combat, authentic survival horror vibe, and fun gameplay loop ensure it’ll keep both fans of the genre and The Walking Dead show entertained.

The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival is an interesting genre-blending experiment tarnished by an occasionally poor performance and button responsiveness. I was really impressed with how seemless the mixture between beat ’em up combat and survival horror elements felt. When you manage to get a groove of the controls, as well as the uneven difficulty curve, this becomes really enjoyable, and incredibly tense at times. With a few patches and fixes in its pacing, this might even become one of the best Walking Dead-themed games out there. Let’s wait and see.
The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival takes the side-scrolling beat-'em-up genre and modifies it to fit perfectly with the The Walking Dead series, though it could have done more.

The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival is an interesting take on the ‘All Out War’ storyline, and it’s nice to see main characters from the TV show represented well in pixel form. There’s some clunkiness and frustration with the combat, and the campaign is fairly short, but there’s still some fun to be had.

The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival is an okay beat 'em up based on AMC's version of the series. While the game employs some nice and unique ideas, its unbalanced difficulty and sometimes awkward gameplay hold it back. Fans of the show might enjoy a single playthrough or two, but others have little reason to look its way.

The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival maintains a competent level of quality throughout the experience. It doesn't have any major hits, but it also doesn't make any serious mistakes, despite some frustrations involving the hitboxes of enemies and the player themselves.

The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival is a solid 2D beat 'em up that makes good use of its license while retaining the survival elements that define The Walking Dead. Its satisfying combat, character variety, challenging encounters, skill progression, and Walker Pit mode provide a good amount of entertainment, while the scarce ammunition and healing resources add an appreciated layer of tension. However, combat can feel rigid, enemy variety is limited, and the restrictive character selection and lack of substantial content outside the main missions hurt its replayability. The pixelated presentation also struggles to capture the atmosphere of the source material. Despite these shortcomings, Streets of Survival delivers an enjoyable beat 'em up experience, particularly for fans of The Walking Dead and the genre, even if it starts to feel repetitive once you have seen most of what it has to offer.

jay-and-silent-bob-chronic-blunt-punch.title: Jay and Silent Bob: Chronic Blunt Punch

reviews.excerpt: 18.2% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (11 reviews).

Jay and Silent Bob: Chronic Blunt Punch is a fun homage to the world of Kevin Smith. Packed with jokes that capture the spirit of the stoner duo, it blends elements of the View Askewniverse into an enjoyable beat ’em up. With its surprisingly deep combat, the game keeps you engaged throughout its short runtime. Even though bugs and the conventional level design prevent it from feeling essential, fans of Smith will still find plenty to love.

Jay and Silent Bob: Chronic Blunt Punch hits the mark with its visual style and fidelity to the humor of the universe created by Kevin Smith, delivering vibrant graphics and a very distinctive identity that, in itself, is quite eye-catching. However, the experience is ultimately hampered by technical problems, as well as repetitive and shallow gameplay that can quickly become tiresome. Although it works better in multiplayer and appeals to those looking for something more casual and straightforward, the game leaves the feeling that it could have gone further, especially in the refinement of its mechanics and the overall pace of progression.

Jay and Silent Bob: Chronic Blunt Punch is a game of strong contrasts. On one hand, it shines with its excellent hand-drawn 2D art direction and an irreverent humor that perfectly captures the soul of Kevin Smith’s View Askewniverse, bringing great joy to longtime fans. On the other hand, unfortunately, it falls apart heavily right on the gameplay front: clunky controls, input lag, imprecise hitboxes, and repetitive level design turn the 3-to-4-hour campaign into a frustrating experience. The total lack of checkpoints and the need to resort to tedious tactical exploits to survive make it unable to compete with the true heavyweights of the beat ‘em up genre. Despite the affordable price, it is a purchase recommended exclusively to the most die-hard fans of the dynamic duo.
Jay and Silent Bob are back in another side-scrolling beat 'em up. Though while Chronic Blunt Punch looks absolutely fantastic and is genuinely humorous at times, its gameplay lets it down.

Sadly, the combat in Chronic Blunt Punch is so bland and lifeless, and is an absolute technical nightmare. Fans of View Askewniverse will likely crack a smile at the game's absurd story, but that's where the good times come to an end.

Jay and Silent Bob: Chronic Blunt Punch has some charm in its characters, visuals, and humor, but it's currently held back by technical issues and rough design. Even fans of Kevin Smith's work may find the experience frustrating in its current state. It has potential, but it's best to wait for patches before jumping in.

Jay and Silent Bob: Chronic Blunt Punch is fine. The combat is good, especially after the week's worth of patches that have fixed things, like missing invincibility frames and toned down the strength of the enemy hits. The game clocks in at a decent length, and the difficulty is fine if you're OK with only having one life per character and fairly long levels with no checkpoints. There's just nothing that elevates the title into being more than a game you play once. Fans of the duo might dig it, but genre fans will find this to be a filler game that briefly satisfies a craving before moving on to more substantial fare.

It's somewhat wild to me that Jay and Silent Bob: Chronic Blunt Punch is basically the arcade version of the 2020 pseudo-NES release of Jay and Silent Bob: Mall Brawl. They feel incredibly similar in that they're both totally fine beat-'em-ups that are good enough to stand on their own but work best with a familiarity for the characters and worlds. With a sea of brawlers out there, this isn't one of the best ones, but it's the only one that will offer you chocolate-covered pretzels after going to the bathroom. Snoogans.

Jay and Silent Bob: Chronic Blunt Punch comes down to missed potential. The game shows flashes of what it could be, but never sustains it.

The combat can feel satisfying, especially once you build momentum and access its full set of tools. The concept fits perfectly for short sessions.

But the structure works against all of it. Poor checkpointing, unclear systems, and repetitive progression turn what should be a quick, fun experience into something frustrating. That consistency across platforms makes the issues stand out even more. Its co-op limitations, inconsistent combat, and visual issues all point to the same problem: the game never fully supports its best ideas.

When everything lines up, it briefly becomes what it should have been all along. There is a better version of this game. This just is not it.

At the end of it all, there isn’t a lot of replay value to Jay and Silent Bob: Chronic Blunt Punch. I didn’t expect them to change gears and make an epic RPG, but players have been waiting for ten very long years for this game to arrive. Now that it’s finally here, it looks fantastic and that’s it. It handles pretty poorly and can be wildly frustrating.

Jay and Silent Bob: Chronic Blunt Punch is a game defined by stark contrasts. On the one hand, it shines thanks to its excellent hand-drawn 2D art style and irreverent humour that perfectly captures the spirit of Kevin Smith’s View Askewniverse, bringing great joy to long-time fans. On the other hand, unfortunately, it falls flat when it comes to gameplay: clunky controls, input lag, imprecise hitboxes and a repetitive level structure turn the 3–4-hour campaign into a frustrating experience. The total absence of checkpoints and the need to resort to tedious tactical workarounds to survive mean it cannot compete with the true heavyweights of the beat 'em up genre. Despite its affordable price, it is a purchase recommended exclusively to the most die-hard fans of the dynamic duo.
Jay and Silent Bob: Chronic Blunt Punch is a true love letter to the works of Kevin Smith.
27.3% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (11 reviews).
Backyard Baseball may lack the depth of today’s more sophisticated baseball games, but the gameplay experience remains consistently engaging.

Backyard Baseball does what I feel it sets out to do. It took me back to yesteryear and the fond memories of pickup games with my friends at a dusty lot behind the park. It also reminded me of how charmed I was when a humble desktop computer game tried to capture that very spirit way back when. This 2026 version of Backyard Baseball isn’t perfect. Some computer behavior could be tightened, I wish they’d made some new kids to go with our faves, and we need online multiplayer, stat. That said, the strategy, depth, and, most importantly, vibes are all there in respectable fashion. Whether you want to introduce a young fan to baseball sims or pick this up for some fond memories, Backyard Baseball will serve up good RBI for the price of admission.
It has its ups and downs and the lack of the promised online play at launch is disappointing, but Backyard Baseball's return is an overall good time no matter your age.

Backyard Baseball (2026) is not struggling in terms of being a modern-looking reimagining of a ’90s classic. And it is rounding the bases easily as a bridge between generations. However, the gameplay experience needs some more time in the batting cage before this new experience receives the title of being a hit. Clunky controls and a batting situation that is either far too easy or inexplicably hard are currently holding things back. And with a $52 price tag, this is just as expensive as seeing an actual baseball game, which is wild for the current entertainment proposition. There’s a Hall of Famer here; it’s just not quite here yet.
A reboot that passes the eye test, but falls short of home plate on the things that really matter.

I really wanted to like Backyard Baseball, but it can’t overcome its core mechanical failures. A cute art style and a sharp-tongued commentator only carry games so far. Once it gets going, it immediately falls on its face. Fielding breaks down more often than it functions. Base running drags every inning to a crawl. A thin mode list leaves little reason to push through the frustration once the novelty wears off. The comeback is dead. Now, where’s my copy of Ken Griffey Jr. Presents Major League Baseball?

I like Backyard Baseball. In an era of realistic simulation sports games, it stands out with its art style and animations, giving it a personality that so many other sports games wish it had. While fielding can be a bit of a struggle, going up to bat is always great. However, it’s also like the early 2010s Philadelphia Phillies. Overpriced, as £33 for a game with no extra modes and no online gameplay is a lot to ask. I would say if you’re a big fan of Backyard Baseball, or Backyard Sports in general, it’s probably more worth it to you, but I would say wait for a sale otherwise.

Backyard Baseball hits both of its main targets, the fastball and the breaking ball, if you will. It effectively channels the memories of playing the original games for longtime fans while also being a fairly approachable game for a new generation of kids, especially on the lower end of the difficulty choices. For older players who didn’t play the original games, it’s still a pretty chill, arcadey baseball experience that promises to not get as sweaty as the more sim-style baseball games out there. It’s not going to the hall of fame, but it makes solid contact more often than not.

Backyard Baseball doesn't aim to be the deepest or most realistic baseball game, but it nails the pure fun factor. It’s one of those classics that puts a smile on your face from the very first minute and remains highly recommended today thanks to remasters on Steam (such as Backyard Baseball '97 or '01). If you're looking for something lighthearted, nostalgic, and perfect for playing with kids—or simply for unwinding—this game is a home run.

I could recommend Backyard Baseball to nostalgic super-fans of the franchise or sport, but I'd struggle to suggest it for new players, especially given the price point and the fact that the 1997 remaster is available for $9.99. I myself am going to put Backyard Baseball (2026) down and come back later if/when there have been some patches. 

Backyard Baseball (2026) still has a long way to go to be ready for the big leagues, but it's a new season for the franchise. I'm so happy it's making a return. These games taught me a lot about strategy, statistics, and teamwork; more young people deserve to get to play games like this. I wish the team all the luck in the world as they take the plate.

This charming reboot successfully modernises the franchise's iconic style with impressive 3D visuals while preserving its accessible, character-driven arcade gameplay. However, the lack of direct control during fielding makes defence feel like a chore, and the lack of polish at launch, along with the absence of online multiplayer, prevents this nostalgic return from truly hitting a home run.

Backyard Baseball is still a breeze to recommend if you’re looking for a casual sports game built around personality instead of realism. It perfectly captures the freewheeling spirit of neighborhood baseball, reminding us that sometimes the most straightforward games are still the ones you'll want to revisit long after the last inning is played.

Backyard Baseball is a steal compared to most major sports releases and a polished version of a beloved classic. No infinite customization, huge online ecosystems, or hyper-realistic simulation mechanics. It delivers just what it promises, though: a fun, accessible baseball game packed with personality and replayability. If that's the experience you're looking for, the asking price is easy to justify.

k-pop-idol-stories-road-to-debut.title: K-pop Idol Stories: Road to Debut

reviews.excerpt: 41.2% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (17 reviews).

Road to Debut proves there's more to K-pop stars than catchy songs and meticulously synchronized dance routines. While its behind-the-scenes management can be compelling for a while, the repetition of time and financial management keeps the game from reaching superstar status.

Overall, K-pop Idol Stories: Road to Debut tells a linear story about a manager preparing a K-pop idol group for debut. The gameplay is a mix of a visual novel, minigames, and a management simulator, and it encourages replayability by letting your choices affect how you reach the end of the game. This feels like an homage to the 2nd and 3rd generations of K-pop, which isn’t a bad thing considering many beloved groups debuted during that era. While not much happens unless a minigame or story event triggers, it does give you a taste of what it’s like to work behind the scenes in the industry without turning into a critique of it.

K-Pop Idol Stories: Road to Debut offers a solid foundation for fans of idol management sims, combining resource management, training, and light social mechanics into an enjoyable progression loop. While its core management systems can be engaging, shallow storytelling, repetitive gameplay, and underdeveloped competition mechanics prevent it from reaching the heights of the genre.

K-Pop Idol Stories: Road to Debut is frustrating because it just ends up feeling like a bunch of ideas tossed together without actually understanding what makes each piece work. Your choices don’t carry any impact, your schedules are so RNG focused that you just hope your group gets better, the story entirely drops plotlines for seemingly no reason – it all feels disjointed and disconnected. The story has a throughline of a stalker following your group that genuinely goes nowhere and is resolved with a line of text. The writing is so stiff and awkward that it feels like it was written in another language and machine translated to English. It’s littered with grammatical issues and spelling mistakes. It also ends right after debut, leaving all of your work to get your idols together ending on such a random note. There’s no way to keep playing to support your group and help them navigate stardom, it’s just over. K-Pop Idol Stories: Road to Debut ends up feeling like an experience carried by references and some early enjoyment out of the simulation aspect, before tripping and falling flat for the rest of the ride.

I really enjoyed K-pop Idol Stories' glossy presentation and breezy introspection into the K-pop industry. There are better management and tycoon games out there, but if like me you're a little obsessed with K-culture, it's hard to look past this effort.

Yes, it isn’t groundbreaking. Yes, it isn’t Game of the Year material. But it is what it is, and it knows exactly what it wants to be: a fun, six-hour management, lifestyle, and music simulator that lets you relax and enjoy some K-Pop fun.
Do you have what it takes to take your trainees to the top of the charts?
Fans of management games will find this product to be different from what they're used to.

I don’t understand the power of K-Pop, and K-Pop Idol Stories: Road to Debut did nothing to entice me down that road. It’s a complex and interesting simulation game, sure, but it feels like it’s full of broken glass and really confusing notions that you can only justify/make peace with if you’re eyeballs deep in stanning. If you really want to know what it’s like to have a group of women gradually sell their souls and pretend you’re not the Devil incarnate, then definitely pick up this game, pretend you’re one of the good ones and go make fleeting stars out of strangers you may be grooming.

K-POP Idol Stories: Road to Debut is no K-POP Demon Hunters, but that is obviously an unfair comparison. I was hoping this might maybe become a companion piece to the music, the movies, the TV shows, and everything else K-POP, and in that regard I don’t think it fails, just fails short.
K-pop Idol Stories: Road to Debut successfully captures the excitement and pressure of managing aspiring idols, even if its repetitive structure holds it back over time.

K-Pop Idol Stories: Road to Debut works because it understands that becoming an idol is a marathon, not a sprint. Wisageni Studio’s work is a nice management simulator with endearing characters, significant progress, attractive presentation, and intelligent storytelling.

This may not be the first K-pop management simulation game and doesn’t do anything overly groundbreaking, but it manages to stand out on its own. There’s a lot to be mindful of in the game, but once players find their rhythm, it becomes an enjoyable experience with various stories to discover. Treating your group well feels rewarding, and they show their appreciation. K-pop Idol Stories: Road to Debut may not live up to its full potential, but it still has a lot of content to make managing an up-and-coming K-pop group a fun and pleasant experience.
K-Pop Idol Stories: Road to Debut might well appeal to fans of simulation games and K-Pop if they’ve got nothing else to hand, but they’ll still have to put up with quite a few flaws.
Perhaps for people who’ve dreamed of managing their own group this could have enough appeal, but the degree that chance feels like it often plays in success can be aggravating

Unfortunately, the first thing that stands out in K-pop Idol Stories: Road to Debut is the large number of bugs and game crashes affecting the Nintendo Switch version. Auto-saves are rarely as important as they are here, even though it’s not always possible to resume playing smoothly even then.

Wisageni Studio nails the visuals and soundtrack, capturing K-pop culture's vibe perfectly. The management systems, story, and dialogue show some weaknesses, though — activities and events repeat too often after a few hours, and choices offer limited variety. Still, the randomness gives the game solid replay value, especially since your decisions can lead to different endings. At €19.99, it's a solid package for anyone who enjoys visual novels and wants an easy entry into the management-sim genre.

K-pop Idol Stories: Road to Debut is an engaging management simulation game with beautiful music and art design. More clarity regarding its mechanics would go a long way toward fulfilling its promise.
K‑pop Idol Stories: Road to Debut does a solid job with idol management, but its RNG‑driven stories and lackluster New Game+ make the enjoyable training cycle lose steam on repeat playthroughs.

Even though everything is in the right place, the bugs are unacceptable and can cost you your run. This undermines the game's potential; however, if these bugs are fixed, *K-pop Idol Stories: Road to Debut* is a must-play for anyone wanting to experience firsthand the dream of forming their own K-pop group—complete with blood, sweat, and tears.
19.0% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (21 reviews).

Copa City brings a refreshing take on football management by focusing on an aspect of the beautiful game that gets overlooked elsewhere. Planning and executing the matchday experience for a club and its city works fits snugly into the various sub-genres the game employs, but be ready to face a frustrating lesson or two if you’re playing on console.

Copa City stands out with its original concept and detailed micro-management, but a clunky interface and awkward controls often get in the way. Some mechanics also feel too shallow, especially when it comes to satisfying fan needs. Still, the combination of stadium operations, marketing, logistics and fan-zone planning can be rewarding. Fans of complex management games should give it a look, while those expecting a traditional football manager may be disappointed.

Copa City offered an unconventional concept but stumbled by being more complex than fun. A game focused on managing fanbases had the potential to appeal to both soccer fans and strategy enthusiasts; however, the difficulty involved in setting up routines—which quickly become repetitive—results in a game where the fun peaks early and fades just as fast.
Idee und Leidenschaft leiden an zahlreichen Design-Fehlpässen
Copa City has great ideas. However, a poor user interface, tutorial, and progression system within each game make the experience unnecessarily frustrating.

Copa City is a genuinely promising game that, through updates, could be great. The unique setting and interesting mechanics (once you figure them out) are let down by various bugs, poor - sometimes zero - explanation of objectives and game mechanics due to shoddy translations and poor design, and what does end up being a lack of replay value due to the one-match nature of the setting. Were this an early-access launch, it would be laudable that it's in the state it is. As a full launch, at £30, this is a wait and see.

If you're still craving that World Cup atmosphere, it looks like you're going to stay hungry for a while. Because Copa City isn't the game that's going to satisfy that craving. Then again, it's not exactly a finished game either.

Copa City has plenty of potential by combining sports games and management games into a unique experience. Unfortunately, it still falls short in too many areas. The tutorial is confusing, the gameplay lacks real depth, and the selection of licensed teams and stadiums feels sparse and somewhat thrown together. The voice acting is painfully awkward, and while the game looks decent, it never comes close to matching the quality of the genre's biggest management games. Some players may appreciate its straightforward approach and won't miss the added complexity, but Copa City ultimately feels like an empty trophy that could have been solid gold.

Copa City has potential and with regular updates it could become a really good tycoon management game surrounding football events. However, it needs issues to be addressed like performance and for things to be better explained so players are not overwhelmed with quests that introduce new things without a heads up.
Interesting management sim experience that has you working on organizing a major football event

Copa City delivers an engaging football concept and an enjoyable atmosphere, but its execution falls short of realizing much of that potential. While the game initially feels deep and promising, it quickly reveals limited systems, noticeable repetition, and a progression path that is largely linear.

Copa City moves the action off the pitch and into the behind-the-scenes world of football, delivering one of the most original concepts in the genre. Managing the entire infrastructure of a major sporting event is both engaging and rewarding, thanks to its solid management systems and immersive atmosphere. However, a confusing interface, insufficient tutorials, and a steep learning curve prevent its excellent concept from reaching its full potential. Even so, it's a creative experience that simulation fans should keep on their radar.

Copa City is our biggest disappointment of 2026 so far. While the idea of managing the logistical and urban side of a football event is fresh and fascinating, the execution is disastrous. Clunky controls, a confusing interface, severe technical issues, and a lack of content completely ruin the experience. It's a huge missed opportunity, made even worse by a too-high price tag.

Copa City has a brilliant concept, turning football into a tycoon about fan zones, crowd management, stadium preparation, and the hidden logistics behind match day. When the city comes alive and fans start filling the streets, its unusual perspective really works. Too often, though, unclear tutorials, weak feedback, rough navigation, and an underwhelming match payoff get in the way of what could have been a much smoother management experience.

In its current state, I believe the purchase is worthwhile mainly for those who appreciate the genre and are willing to overlook some rough edges that still need refinement in future updates. After all, behind the finishing issues lies a creative idea that has the potential to become a benchmark within a virtually unexplored niche.

Copa City turns everything that happens before kick-off into a fresh management game, focusing on fan zones, security, services and stadium logistics. Its concept feels genuinely original and engaging, even if the tutorials and interface still need refinement.

Copa City brings a refreshing twist to the management genre by putting players in charge of organizing every aspect of a major sporting event. Its deep simulation systems and charming presentation make for a rewarding experience, but the lack of guidance after the tutorial creates a steep learning curve. With a few quality-of-life improvements, it has the potential to become a standout management game.

Copa City takes a refreshing approach to the football management genre by shifting the focus away from what happens on the pitch. It instead puts you in charge of everything that surrounds matchday. Organising transport, entertainment, security, and fan experiences creates a unique challenge that helps the game stand out from the crowd.

That said, issues with the interface and camera controls can make the experience more frustrating than it should be. Even so, Triple Espresso deserves credit for taking a risk on such an original concept that feels genuinely different. While it ultimately wasn’t a game that clicked with me personally, fans of management sims and football culture may find plenty to enjoy here.

For its solid foundations, ambition and originality, I’m awarding Copa City a Thumb Culture Silver Award.

Copa City looks at football from a fresh angle, focusing on fan zones and stadium logistics instead of the action on the pitch. Unfortunately, clunky controls, repetitive objectives, and a lack of meaningful long-term progression hold it back. The result is an original management game that never fully lives up to its promising concept.

Copa City uses its football theme like a jersey one puts on just to somehow be part of the football world because there’s something to celebrate right now. But it cannot convey the emotions that millions of fans around the world connect with the sport.

Copa City offers a solid level of challenge and even a higher degree of complexity for fans of management-focused titles. However, the console version could benefit from controller optimizations to better handle the volume of information players need to process, alongside some general performance improvements.

COPA CITY succeeds in an area that very few football games attempt to explore: looking beyond the pitch and transforming it into something genuinely playable and occasionally even mesmerizing. The sensation of watching a city come alive under your control, with the right crowd in the right places and the chaos managed, is rewarding in a way that this genre rarely matches.

Copa City delivers a concept rarely seen in the market. By shifting the focus from the soccer field to the backstage of a major sporting event, the game offers an impressive level of management and makes the player feel responsible for every detail surrounding a football match.

We did not necessarily place great expectations around the title of Triple Espresso mixing construction, management and organization of football events. We still start bluffed from the number of options and the depth of the management mechanics, their consistency and the clarity of the menus that make it easy to take control of the game. It must be said that Copa City offers a new look and an unprecedented experience for the players. We have the impression that the history of the game is written before our eyes and that we have contributed to it, and it is a very pleasant feeling. If you are a fan of city management game, you could very quickly hang on. No need to love football in particular, even if it’s a plus, since it’s more of the sports event management that could even be associated with other sports.
38.6% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (44 reviews).
R-Type Dimensions III may be one of the toughest shoot 'em ups ever made but the amount of fun to be had in this striking remake is superb.

R-Type Dimensions III is a great remaster of an Super Nintendo classic. Challenging and rewarding gameplay will need your full attention and more, but it is fully worth it. The stage design is one of the best in the series, while the new 3D graphics are well done as well. However, the new music by Eric Krause steals the show – it is absolutely fantastic.

R-Type Dimensions III preserves the challenge and satisfaction that made the series a shoot 'em up classic. The core gameplay remains highly rewarding, and the optional visual enhancements offer a fresh way to experience it. However, the new features feel somewhat limited, making the overall package harder to justify at its current price despite its enduring quality.

R-Type Dimensions III is a good remaster of a classic game that comes with a few issues and strange changes that might put off some players. I do see new players and casual shooter fans having fun with this port, but some seasoned veterans might be turned off a little. Not a terrible release by any means, but the addition of a classic 2 player mode, patches for the hitbox/weapons issues and perhaps some more unlockables might have made it better. If you are a horizontal shooter fan of any skill level, you should give this one a try but don’t expect a perfect experience. It’s good, but not as great as it could have been.
The classic SNES shooter gets a 3D remaster, making R-Type III both brilliant and frustrating.

R-Type Dimensions III is a faithful restoration of a classic shoot 'em up, featuring local co-op, alternative soundtracks, and real-time graphical overlays. In the end, R-Type Dimensions III is a prime example of how a remake can turn a beloved classic into a frustrating and exhausting experience. What could have been a bridge between nostalgia and modern standards collapses under poor design, unfair difficulty, and odd gameplay choices. R-Type Dimensions III is an undeniably faithful restoration of one of gaming’s most influential shoot-’em-ups. The ability to switch between classic and modern visuals is a genuinely cool feature, the presentation is polished, and longtime fans will likely appreciate the preservation effort. But faithfulness can be both a blessing and a curse. For all its historical significance, R-Type remains trapped in design philosophies that have aged poorly. The difficulty frequently crosses the line from demanding to exhausting, progression relies heavily on memorization, and the overall experience feels more punishing than rewarding. I genuinely wanted to enjoy this, and I gave it chance after chance, hoping that persistence would reveal the magic that made R-Type a legend. Instead, I came away with respect for its legacy but little desire to ever return. For hardcore retro enthusiasts, this may represent a nostalgic trip back to arcade glory days. For everyone else, it’s a reminder that not every classic benefits from being preserved exactly as it was.
Despite its flaws and technical issues, this is clearly a project created with passion, featuring beautiful presentation and a genuine desire to honor the source material.

R-Type Dimensions III is the definitive way to experience a notoriously difficult classic, blending a full 3D visual overhaul with essential modern quality-of-life additions like Infinite Mode and local co-op. In the end, R-Type Dimensions III is a return built on contrasts: meticulous restoration and modern options on one side, and on the other a design that still carries the uncompromising difficulty of its era. It’s an experience that can fascinate fans of classic shoot ’em ups, yet may push away anyone looking for a more contemporary rhythm. It’s a video game that builds on the franchise’s foundations, featuring good level design, a distinctive art style, and a well-paced gameplay experience. However, its fate is uncertain, and the current release schedule may have overshadowed this title too much.
