The lack of players in its early days is a sign that something isn’t right, and—as unfair as it may seem—it’s almost a death sentence for a title that’s so much more enjoyable when played with others, especially on the higher difficulty levels. In any case, Sam Stone is back in his most retro form, taking down anyone who stands in his way.
Serious Sam: Shatterverse is a fun and surprisingly natural evolution of the franchise.

Serious Sam: Shatterverse has a genuinely promising roguelite foundation, with satisfying gunplay, chaotic action, varied builds, and co-op that suits the series extremely well once everything starts opening up. Unfortunately, it takes far too long to get there, with sluggish early progression, repetitive environments, limited initial variety, and technical issues making the opening hours much weaker than the game eventually becomes.

It’s hard to believe Devolver Digital decided to invest in a project as mediocre, predictable, and hollow as Serious Sam: Shatterverse, which forces a classic series into something it simply isn’t: a co-op roguelike with sluggish progression, uneven difficulty, and uninspired gameplay that gives us very little reason to return to this half-baked multiverse.

Serious Sam is one of those games you can just load up, hit a few rounds of killing aliens, and feel satisfied with what you have achieved. Shoot, punch, heal, kill it’s simple and fun, a great way to end or start your day. The sheer fact that we are still making this type of game in 2026 is just a testament to what a solid community can do when you make something fun. If you’re a fan of the series, this entry will satisfy your inner Sam.
Serious Sam: Shatterverse had potential but falls short. It is a playable title—and fun when played with others—but it falls far below the standards set by the series.

There is nothing inherently wrong with Serious Sam: Shatterverse. It ticks all the boxes. It’s a perfectly serviceable first-person shooter / roguelite hybrid that uses its source material well enough to conjure up a half-decent excuse for a plot, and a varied arsenal of weapons for you to use against hordes of familiar enemies. I guess my main issues with it are how grindy it is, requiring you to play multiple runs before being able to unlock anything worth giving a crap about, and the simple fact that it is yet another roguelite in a sea full of painfully similar competitors.

This new Serious Sam offers a side of the franchise we haven't seen before. I seriously doubt whether that is the right direction. You’ve seen the environments at some point, the enemies become very recognizable after a while, and the gameplay is too much of the same to become truly addictive. After quite a few loops, you’ve seen it all pretty quickly. The progression you make slowly but surely is the most attractive aspect of the game, but it is too slow. Co-op is where the game is most fun, and it is practically mandatory to play it. In that regard, however, I would rather see the good old campaign return instead of this roguelite approach that has now been chosen.
“Serious Sam Shatterverse delivers a chaotic and refreshing roguelite experience that captures the franchise’s trademark humor and frenetic action.”

My early impression of Serious Sam: Shatterverse was not all that positive – felt like a “Serious Sam at home” that lost the uniqueness of the original games, while also simplifying the game formula, losing the wacky easter eggs and more. And yet, despite some repetition of the stages, a couple hours in the game truly shines, thanks to the vast array of stage modifiers, the depth of the loot game and class builds, and the intensity of the gameplay on higher difficulties, making for quite the exhilarating FPS roguelite experience – especially in co-op. While we wait for the next mainline Serious Sam, Shatterverse shall keep us busy with its intense and highly replayable roguelite scenarios.

Shatterverse is surprisingly shallow for what it offers, but its fast paced combat does retain its signature feel. The multiverse appeal may be exhausting for some players, given its overuse in multiple forms of media at the moment, but a lack of creating your own Sam is an omission that is bizarre to me. Still, the cast here is fine enough, and at the end of the day, if it looks like Serious Sam and plays like Serious Sam, then I'm glad that the series is still kicking around, some 25 years later.
20.0% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (36 reviews).

Disgaea Mayhem is a fun new Disgaea action RPG spin-off with Musou-like gameplay qualities. Despite the change in genre from Disgaea's strategy RPG roots, Disgaea Mayhem retains many of the core features that Disgaea fans know and love, including the grindy Item World and leveling and gear systems. However, the short story runtime may leave gamers wanting more here.

Disgaea Mayhem, even with the large variety of side experiences, is a pretty short game, with a campaign that can easily be completed in under ten hours. There are certainly lots of systems that players can dive into to extend, especially for those to wish to reach the maximum possible level. There is no real post-game content, however, though there will be some downloadable content available after launch. That said, the game is still a pleasant experience. Battles are fun to blast through, and power-leveling a character before cranking up the difficulty can be a blast. Like the main series, it’s not something that everyone will enjoy, but fans of Disgaea will find it an enjoyable spin-off that stays true to the series’ fundamentals.  It may not ultimately be as delicious as the dessert it revolves around, but it is a tasty experience while it lasts.
Disgaea Mayhem feels more like a spin-off proof of concept than an evolution or new direction for the series, and a proverbial monkey’s paw that will make me careful what I wish for in the future.

Playing Disgaea Mayhem almost feels like peeking into an alternate universe where NIS’ flagship series began life as an action RPG, rather than a tactical one. Plenty of the franchise’s iconic, over-the-top RPG systems are present and accounted for, and they graft surprisingly well onto Mayhem’s core hack-and-slash loop. The problem is that said loop isn’t fleshed out nearly enough, with shallow and repetitive combat that loses its lustre quickly. Couple that with a forgettable story and a bizarrely short runtime, and Disgaea Mayhem barely ends up making much of an impression at all. It’s an interesting novelty, but I’m fine staying in the timeline where Disgaea keeps tactical battles as its bread and butter.

Disgaea Mayhem is so close to being a decent game. It's held back by the most mindless and unimaginative battles ever conceived in a Dynasty Warriors clone. There are no generals to protect or outposts. No compelling winning or losing conditions. There aren't even that many foes to beat. The only thing N.A. has to do is slap around 100 cartoon monsters, and he's won. The core Disgaea elements work perfectly for character progression, and even the staple democratic features remain fun and make sense in Mayhem. However, the lacklustre presentation, barren gameplay, and lifeless combat keep it from meeting the standard of quality. At least it was over quickly.

Disgaea Mayhem is an attempt to create a Musou-style fighting game in the Disgaea universe. The story captures the whimsical DNA of the main series to the fullest, but the gameplay feels lackluster. Battles feel repetitive and button-mashy, especially because you have to play every map four times without any change to the gameplay. Since you can get strong quickly, you don’t really need to engage with the side modes. Truly a shame, because waging large-scale war as an Overlord with demon armies could be so awesome, dude!

Disgaea Mayhem does a great job of presenting the loveable Disgaea vibe in an action RPG setting. But that setting is pretty thin and unrewarding, especially considering the limited content provided for the asking price.

Everything about Disgaea Mayhem is disappointing, especially if you love Musou style beat’em ups. It is short. There’s no main character variety. There’s little enemy variety, and only small groups to cut through instead of hordes. The combat system feels clunky and doesn’t encourage smooth, satisfying combos. The story is bland. It’s all short. Fortunately, there’s a demo so you can at least test and see for yourself how far this spin-off has fallen.

Disgaea Mayhem had a chance to bring the irreverence and originality of the Disgaea series to the Nintendo Switch 2. Unfortunately the result is a game that falls very short of expectations. While Disgaea Mayhem keeps loyal to the spirit of the series, its execution and performance are very disappointing, the new action RPG gameplay mechanics are excessively repetitive and uncreative, and the visual presentation is very outdated. It's a shame that such a quirky and fun series has been treated to such a subpar effort, more so when it's sold for a high retail price.

"There's an old joke. Two elderly women are at a Catskills mountain resort, and one of 'em says: "Boy, the food at this place is really terrible." The other one says, "Yeah, I know, and such ... small portions." Well, that's essentially how I feel about..." Disgaea Mayhem. A game lacking a clear identity. It features tedious combat and repetitive missions - plus, it ends too quickly.
Disgaea Mayhem is an action-RPG that adapts the power grind of the strategy series into something more similar to the Dynasty Warriors games.

Disgaea Mayhem is a solid entry into the action RPG genre for the franchise, successfully carrying over the nonsensical plot, core mechanics, and boundless progression that the series is celebrated for.
Disgaea Mayhem is an excellent Musou game, no question. But as a Disgaea title, this game falls pretty flat.
Disgaea Mayhem is light, breezy, and charming, but that isn't enough to overcome the nagging feeling that it could have been a lot more than it currently is.

Disgaea Mayhem is a spinoff title within the Disgaea series, while in Japan and some other regions, the game is called Makaism: Frenzy, referencing the Netherworld Battle Chronicle or Makai Senki subtitle of Disgaea.

Disgaea Mayhem is a fun time and adds a new gameplay style to the mix of Disgaea. You still work on pumping up your numbers, but in a Musou-style engine. It is a load of fun, but it is not the Disgaea Warriors many Musou lovers might be wanting.

Disgaea Mayhem isn’t broken, and it’s fine for short play sessions. But it plays it incredibly safe, borrowing the series’ style and humor while stripping away most of what made the main games unique.
You got your action RPG in my Disgaea!

Disgaea Mayhem has plenty of nifty aspects going for it such as its cute and colourful visuals and familiar systems that are well incorporated in the new action formula. At the same time, the combat is just so simple and repetitive and I wish there was much more to it. 🐧

Disgaea Mayhem is an insufficient game, even considering it's a Nippon Ichi Software title belonging to a glorious series like Disgaea. The gameplay is bland, the settings are repetitive, and the story, despite having all the series' classic elements, is so short it doesn't allow you to fully appreciate it

Disgaea Mayhem trades the series' signature turn-based strategy for direct action combat, delivering an entertaining if uneven first attempt at the genre. Its varied weapon classes, likable characters, and vibrant anime-inspired presentation make for a fun ride, though a lack of real challenge and repetitive post-game structure keep it from reaching its full potential.

Disgaea Mayhem is a brief action title that doesn't take itself too seriously. Its combat system is simple and accessible, with mission durations and story length just right to avoid exhaustion. Those who crave more beyond the story missions can endlessly grow stronger through the Item World, as long as motivation holds.
Disgaea Mayhem’s humor lands but its shallow challenge, limited enemies, and easily breakable balance make the flan‑driven tale feel undercooked despite some solid combat mechanics.

I was excited to see what Disgaea Mayhem would feel like. I understand NIS isn’t exactly the biggest or boldest studio out there, but they’ve rarely left me unimpressed. This was sadly one of the times I was. The concept on paper works well, but the story mode rarely gives the company a chance to shine. This is on top of having a lackluster, completely uninspired structure.

Disgaea Mayhem stands as an interesting experiment—albeit one with flaws—that nonetheless manages to capture the soul of the franchise while drastically changing the way it is experienced on the battlefield.

Disgaea Mayhem is certainly an interesting experiment, which in itself is not something rare for the series; what is definitely more unusual though is it bearing the Disgaea name, usually reserved for mainline titles, a telltale sign of the importance Nippon Ichi Software places on what is essentially a pivot into a different genre. The experiment can't certainly be defined as a smashing success; Disgaea Mayhem is too much of an action-rpg to call itself a musou and too much of a musou to call itself an action-rpg. Its saving grace, ironically, is the elements more closely resembling its Disgaea roots, such as its exponential character progression and challenging post-game, despite both being severely watered down by having a single playable character.

Disgaea Mayhem ended up being far more entertaining than I expected, especially considering the initial wave of negative reviews it received. I even found myself enjoying its utterly idiotic premise and overlooking some of its gameplay shortcomings. It was quickly becoming one of those perfect “switch your brain off and have fun” kinds of games. Unfortunately, it just doesn’t have enough to offer in the long run.

Disgaea Mayhem is the kind of spin-off that has a lot of potential as a concept. The series, by its nature, routinely produces characters that lend themselves well to the action genre. Unfortunately, limiting the entire experience to a single playable character while carrying over progression systems designed for a full roster strips away much of what makes Disgaea satisfying in the first place. The result is a game that understands the appeal of the grind, but rarely gives you a reason to enjoy it.

Disgaea Mayhem is an action RPG that introduces some new fun ideas and manages to include a few of the series’ signature mechanics, giving it that Disgaea charm for a goofy adventure. However, it feels like the game could use more time in the oven due to its short story campaign and repetitive, patchy presentation.
Disgaea Mayhem delivers a merely mediocre result in what it proposes: it fails as a clone of Musou in terms of gameplay and fails to exude all the charisma of the brand it supposedly represents.

Disgaea Mayhem is ultimately just a mediocre game that gets elevated somewhat by being part of a series with enough charm to carry it. With its $60 launch price and disappointing performance, it's hard to imagine an optimistic future for a game that undermines itself just as much as it shows potential.

Mayhem is a bold new step for the Disgaea series, and even though someone like me greatly enjoys the occasional different genre spin-off, there simply isn't much to be seen here. The game places a lot of emphasis on the Magichange mechanic, but the reality is that it rarely comes up during actual gameplay, as most enemies are pushovers and don't really require you to put in any effort. There's a lot of grinding to be done, something that fans of the series will probably enjoy, but while the stick is present, the carrot is unfortunately nowhere to be found.

At the end of the day, Tichelle and N.A.’s story ended up entertaining me in many ways, and the silly, somewhat "Zoomer" humor the series embraces really engaged me—I certainly didn't expect a Cory in the House reference, of all things. Unfortunately, a game can't survive on humor alone, and this one has aspects that make it hard to recommend—not just in a vacuum, but even to longtime Disgaea fans.

Disgaea Mayhem is a flawed and generic hack-and-slash that will not be for everyone. Those who enjoy grinding and watching their stats go up to insane heights might find themselves sucked into an extremely addictive gameplay loop, but for others, it will simply not be worth the time. The Carnage Dimension is where the game truly shines, but reaching it is a high bar to clear.
Disgaea Mayhem is a good diversion into action for Disgaea fans. Charming characters, swift missions, and addictive number crunching make up for shallow fighting and lack of post-game material.

Disgaea Mayhem is a game which is next to impossible to recommend. While the game's combat fundamentals could have served as the foundation for a fun game, the complete lack of any stage design and incredibly short length make this experience feel very shallow and disappointing. Fans of both the Disgaea franchise and action games in general will find very little to enjoy in this title.

Disgaea Mayhem has its stumbles as it fuses Disgaea’s iconic systems with frantic hack-and-slash gameplay, but it’s a largely worthwhile venture for series fans. Jumping between the different weapon types and leveling yourself and your items to crazy heights make for a solid base, and the charm the series is known for is certainly intact, even with its short playtime. Essentially, if you like the Disgaea series and action RPGs, you’ll likely have a good time with Disgaea Mayhem – so long as you know it won’t be too long a time.

I’m very disappointed in Disgaea Mayhem. I do very much enjoy the combat and the item worlds can be fun since they’re one of the only ways to fight actual hordes, but the game is far too short, the levels are far too simple, and the devs have simply added in a bunch of dull grinding in lieu of anything substantial.
31.1% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (45 reviews).

This cozy masterpiece redefines survival through a brilliant modular construction system and a breathtaking, stress-free atmosphere. It transforms vehicle customization into a therapeutic journey, although solo players may struggle with imbalanced resource gathering. Despite this pacing issue, the stunning visuals and rewarding technological progression create an essential, tranquil refuge.

Outbound is the equivalent of sitting in the countryside during late summer, knocking back a cold drink with ice, and relaxing while watching the sunset. This game may have the guts of the usual survival and crafting games that crop up all the time, but Outbound has done a great job avoiding many pitfalls in the genre.

A cozy exploration game that delivers exactly what it promises, blending relaxing camper travel with light base-building and rewarding exploration. While inventory limits and collectibles can feel a bit restrictive or grindy, they never take away from the overall chill experience. Outbound is a soothing road trip that lets you truly unwind behind the wheel.
Outbound is exactly what it promises. A good mix of discovery, crafting, and building, and it provides plenty of relaxation.

Outbound is exactly the type of game you play after a long day at work and get your energy back, like your eco-friendly car. You don't have to worry about danger and you enjoy relaxation and well-being while playing. The game will also surprise you with its extensive possibilities for crafting, exploring and building your mobile base.
Outbound is a super-cozy trek through the wilderness that prioritizes player freedom, but might be too slow for fans of the genre.

Outbound is a contemplative experience that transforms exploration into a refuge. Amid luminous forests, deliberate construction systems, and a quiet sense of freedom, this indie title turns solitude into a form of comfort, delivering a cozy journey that proves getting lost can sometimes become the best way to find oneself.

For the most part this is a cosy laid back game. There’s no real threat in it (you can get injured but even falling from a decent height is unlikely to kill you… you have to try really hard to do any real damage). I love the idea of being able to use renewable resources, sun, wind, rain etc. The recycling mechanic could have been better implemented and fast travel would be a welcome addition… but overall it’s a decent bit of fun and you can even adopt a dog (though once you do… it’s with you for the rest of the game… even if you tell it to stay somewhere, it will inevitably end up by your side again). Good for those who like gentle gaming.

Outbound is a cozy exploration game that does well on its basics—exploration, crafting, building—but fails to really keep the magic and entertainment after a few hours due to its taxing gameplay loop that feels like it rewards so little for so much effort. Nevertheless, the game is fun in its own right, although more improvements and changes would make it even more enjoyable for a wider audience.

Outbound doesn't reinvent the genre, but it doesn't need to. It knows exactly what it wants to be: a cozy, relaxed journey of discovery where you build a life at your own pace, occasionally accompanied by some frustration.

Outbound is an easy-going survival game that puts risk-free exploration above all else. Its core gameplay loop is satisfying enough to keep you and a friend or three hooked for a couple of hours, but the lack of variety and ultimate purpose wears thin beyond that. Of course, the same can be said about many a cozy game, but the best examples always make the process immensely satisfying. Outbound is still a refreshing antidote to a fast-paced world, but barring any additional content updates, this might be one road trip you’ll want to cut short.

Outbound is an interesting and fun game, one that a lot of people will like because it’s cozy and it brings a great sense of adventure. That doesn’t make it perfect, as you might expect. You need to find blueprints and that can prove to be quite difficult. On top of that, creating a mobile base sounds fun at first, but there are a lot of small things to deal with. However, the traveling experience is fun, and driving the vehicle felt very responsive, which is exactly what sets the game apart from all the other ones out there. It feels cozy and immersive, the music is nice, and the visuals seamlessly serve this experience. I found Outbound to be one of those go-to games where I just want to explore and experience the world at my own pace. And it works great for that, even if it does have its own sluggishness and minor issues.
Outbound is a pretty game with an addictive loop but unfortunately a slow-moving van isn't enough to differentiate in a sea of cosy/survival games.

Outbound is a cozy, visually striking van-life adventure game that nails atmosphere and customization, but struggles to keep its open world engaging. While building a home on wheels is a standout highlight and the picturesque scenery is consistently beautiful, the core exploration loop quickly becomes repetitive, with a world that often feels too empty to sustain long-term interest. It’s a relaxing ride, but one that doesn’t give you enough of a reason to keep driving.

If you are a newcomer to gaming and open-world games, then Outbound is a reasonable first recommendation for you to play. It's simplistic, low-stakes, cosy camping fun with accessible puzzles and foraging elements that are even better experienced as a multiplayer game.

Outbound is a game with a sincere execution, but one that doesn't fully follow through on its ideas. By playing it safe to avoid gameplay that might be too demanding for players, it misses out on a potential that could have made it a true must-have in the cozy gaming scene. Still, it remains a contemplative pleasure for lovers of virtual exploration… one you’ll play through from start to finish before tucking it away in the back of your collection, unsure if you’ll ever pull it out again to relive the same journey.

Outbound is slow, cosy and a good reset from the action-packed games I normally play. No big challenges to overcome, but a satisfying gameplay loop, nice visuals and music makes it a good, albeit repetitive experience.

I don’t want to underestimate the need some people may have to simulate a road trip without having to actually having to go on one – and the act of “going outside and doing stuff” that may entail – but there’s so little here, it’s hard not to wonder what the point of it all is.

The game really does deliver on a beautiful, cozy environment. I found myself pausing at vistas to take screenshots like I might snap a photo while camping in real life. If only that world offered a bit more engagement and a better overall balance of grind and reward, Outbound could deliver on its promise. The good news is, the game itself runs well on PC, and many of the biggest issues here feel fixable in time. As it stands, however, the game left me feeling more frustrated than immersed, and I wanted a bit more from this one.

Outbound had the potential to be one of the biggest hits of the year, but a gameplay loop that hinders more than it invites, a purposeless open world, and endlessly repetitive objectives make this so-called cozy camping sim anything but relaxing.

Although there are lots of ways to upgrade and decorate your van - which, I suppose, is just about the only saving grace of this game - I had absolutely zero interest in doing so. Why should I bother putting the time into making my van look nice when the world is so devoid of character? There are dozens of cozy survival games that nail everything Outbound is trying to do, and go so much further. I do expect another developer to pick up where Outbound has dropped us off though: people want a cozy campervan game, and I’m certain someone else is already cooking one up.

Outbound struggles to justify its own loop. It presents a beautiful, yet empty, isolating space that exists without tension or inscribed drive. Focusing on a purely gentle, slow experience is intentional, but results in a world that does not feel worth inhabiting after a few hours. Base building atop your van is easily the game’s strongest feature, offering a satisfying level of creativity and personalisation. Still, with no strong narrative pull or meaningful pressure to engage, it becomes difficult to justify investing time in what is ultimately the game’s best system.

Despite its appealing premise and relaxing facade, Outbound struggles to justify the time (and price) it demands. The slow pacing, repetitive resource gathering, lifeless world design, and lack of meaningful progression drain the experience of excitement as well as comfort. The campervan customisation and eco-friendly concept attached show promise, yet the gameplay loop quickly turns into a mind-numbing chore rather than a therapeutic past time.

Outbound is a relaxing journey that will please anyone who wants to get away without going anywhere. Extensive exploration and a satisfying gameplay loop make for a joyful experience, and it's easy to lose hours to driving around in your camper, collecting logs and unlocking new biomes. A few visual and control gripes might form bumps in the road, but otherwise this is a fun ride.

Outbound is a gently paced, cosy camper game encouraging creative home building and exploration in beautifully varied biomes. With developer, Square Glade Games, highlighting a roadmap of upgrades and add-ons to come in the next few months, there's plenty of reasons to jump in your camper and join in the fun.
A competent camping and survival game set in an unpopulated wilderness, whose lack of narrative structure, threat, or competitive elements leaves it feeling disappointingly hollow.
In that way, Outbound is kind of like real-life camping. Freed from any burdensome goals, you’re merely soaking in the sights and enriching your experience.

The PC version of Outbound is technically superior. If you have the option, you'll get a significant graphical boost on a computer, as the issues with limited detail and blurry images at high settings are largely eliminated.

Outbound is a game with a sincere execution, but one that doesn't fully follow through on its ideas. By playing it safe to avoid gameplay that might be too demanding for players, it misses out on a potential that could have made it a true must-have in the cozy gaming scene. Still, it remains a contemplative pleasure for lovers of virtual exploration&a;#x2026; one you'll play through from start to finish before tucking it away in the back of your collection, unsure if you'll ever pull it out again to relive the same journey.
‍Outbound offers plenty of pretty vistas to virtually photograph, but very little in the way of meaningful gameplay.

Outbound is exactly the type of game you play after a long day at work and get your energy back, like your eco-friendly car. You don't have to worry about danger and you enjoy relaxation and well-being while playing. The game will also surprise you with its extensive possibilities for crafting, exploring and building your mobile base.
A niche title that certain gamers are sure to love, Outbound is an enjoyable exploration title that can often become too relaxing at times.

Outbound is a laid-back survival game that focuses primarily on freedom, exploration, crafting and building your own home on wheels. It offers a leisurely pace, the chance to customise your van, craft equipment, grow plants, cook and travel either solo or cooperatively. Its weakness may lie in a repetitive gameplay loop, which, over time, begins to rely mainly on gathering resources and crafting. However, if you’re looking for a relaxing road trip without the constant struggle for survival, Outbound might pleasantly surprise you. It’s a game for anyone who’d rather build another shelf than save the world. And sometimes, the chance to park up in a beautiful spot and simply enjoy the journey is the very best thing this game has to offer.
Outbound is a relaxing cozy road trip with a cool, upgradable camper base, even if its world feels rather empty and its sustainability theme isn't fully thought through.

Outbound is a wonderfully cozy survival game built around freedom, sustainability, and the joy of turning a simple van into a fully functional home on wheels. Its building, exploration, technological progression, and relaxing atmosphere are genuinely strong, but the empty world, repetitive crafting, restrictive night cycle, and serious co-op issues keep it from becoming a must-play for cozy survival fans.

Outbound is an exploration and base-building game developed and published by Square Glade Games. Aboard your electric van, embark on a journey through nature, enjoying the scenery and building a retractable base on the vehicle's roof. The Outbound festival awaits you at the end of this trip, but enjoying the journey along the way will make it a lot of fun.

Outbound fulfills its promise with charm and sincerity: it’s a cozy game about freedom, van life, and exploring the world at your own pace. The van customization is genuinely satisfying, the colorful aesthetic works well on the Switch 2, and the absence of pressure or conflict creates a rare space for real relaxation. The problem lies in the depth; the gameplay loop repeats itself without reinventing itself, and playing solo the experience loses momentum sooner than expected. With friends, it’s a different story.

Outbound is a cozy survival game in which you travel through an open world in an electric camper and slowly transform your vehicle into a mobile home along the way. The game combines exploration, crafting and building with a relaxed atmosphere that is mainly about freedom and creativity. Thanks to the strong road trip vibe and the relaxing gameplay, Outbound is a nice experience for players who like to play at their own pace, although the game sometimes lacks some variation in the longer term.
Outbound has charm, good ideas, and a camper that works as a mobile home, but it needs more variety, more life, and more polish to reach its destination.

​Outbound delivers a unique spin on survival exploration by turning an electric camper van into a fully customizable mobile base. Driving through scenic biomes and modifying your rooftop homestead is incredibly charming, and it works wonderfully as a cooperative experience. However, Outbound unnecessarily anchors its blueprint progression behind a slow, repetitive recycling grind that forces you to hunt constantly for garbage. If you have the patience to dig through piles of litter for resource coupons, there is a cozy road trip worth taking here.

Outbound is at its best when it leans into its core fantasy: a peaceful, mobile life based on exploration, sustainability and creative building. The camper van customization system is awesome, with surprising depth and freedom. The world is beautiful and the atmosphere is always soothing.
There is definitely the potential for a great cozy game here, though the developers still need to work on several mechanics and improve the game’s technical condition.
If only that world offered a bit more engagement and a better overall balance of grind and reward, Outbound could deliver on its promise.
For our taste, "Outbound" sometimes takes things a bit too leisurely.

If you're looking for a comfy game that can hold your attention for hours while delivering a relaxing and rewarding experience, Outbound definitely deserves a place on your list. Even with a few stumbles, it manages to offer a quite enjoyable and addictive experience within its genre.

Outbound delivers a relaxed and inviting cozy survival experience that successfully blends exploration, crafting, and base-building at your own pace. Its strength lies in its freedom: there is no pressure, no enemies, and no punishment for experimentation, making it an ideal game for players looking to unwind.

While the crafting system can feel overly granular at times and some quality-of-life features are missing, these issues rarely break the overall experience. Minor technical rough edges and occasional interaction quirks are noticeable, but not disruptive enough to overshadow the core gameplay loop.

Outbound is ultimately a slow-burning survival sandbox that prioritizes comfort over challenge — and largely succeeds in that vision.

Outbound is a road trip that rewards patience over speed. Square Glade Games has built a world worth getting lost in, with a van customization system that keeps you tinkering and a presentation that always makes the next horizon look worth chasing.

Outbound is a game with its own rhythm, and it doesn’t try to please everyone — something that becomes clear within just a few hours. It abandons tension and urgency to focus on something simpler: building, exploring, and living in that world at your own pace.

This design choice doesn’t always work. At times, the experience can feel monotonous, mainly due to the lack of variety in the world, the limited impact of the day-and-night cycle, and a pacing that demands a lot of patience. Even so, the game manages to captivate players in a very particular way.

Outbound is great for all “Cozy Game” fans who dream of living an independent life. The mix of base-building on the go and laid-back exploration keeps you engaged, even if there are a few minor issues with pacing and the overall layout.

Outbound has a lot of great elements to it. It’s fun, it has a lot of cute details, and the whole thing is extremely cozy. There is a lot to love about it, and it encourages you to take you time, sit around, and relax as you slide into your new life.
There were some issues, the stamina being the biggest one for me, but if that doesn’t bother you, you will probably adore Outbound. Overall, it was a good time, and I look forward to completing it in the coming days.
A relaxing open world where exploration and clean energy matter more than survival.

Outbound is a game that, if given enough time, could be good in the future. It has a wonderful world that can be filled with things and people to interact with. A wonderful building system that can be improved with better delivery of blueprints. And a road-trip experience that can be improved with sound. Unfortunately, much like its world, right now it’s a game with a shallow gameplay loop that is difficult to stay interested in. Maybe it’s more fun with friends?

Outbound is a relaxing explore-and-craft game that impresses with its core idea of building your home through a mobile “set up camp” system, blending road trip vibes with surprisingly flexible construction. While the grind, slow movement speed, and occasionally confusing blueprint navigation can be frustrating, the overall experience still feels engaging. Its simple but charming visuals and occasional crafting or terminal mini-games add light variety, and the laid-back atmosphere works especially well in co-op with up to four players—though I only played solo.

There are two-hour games that yield 10-page articles, and 100-hour games that only get two lines of commentary. Worse than a bad, poorly made game, Outbound becomes apathetic, and there's nothing more frustrating than leaving an artistic experience without a strong impression.

Outbound offers a charming and creative sandbox experience centered around building the ultimate mobile home. While its crafting systems and camper customization are deeply rewarding as you progress, the world can feel eerily empty for solo players. It is a journey clearly designed with co-op in mind; enjoyable and cozy, but one that truly shines only when shared with friends.
A cozy open-world exploration game that offers a relaxing, occasionally tedious, but mostly successful escape from the daily grind.

There is fun to be had here for the patient, and perhaps with friends, some welcome life can be injected into the abandoned world. Right now though, it’s hard to recommend this one for the average camper.
23.5% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (17 reviews).

Bus Simulator 27 is the best bus simulation experience that we have right now, and it does a lot of things right. Its visuals are excellent, and you really get to feel like you’re driving a bus. The fleet with over 45 buses is amazing, and each one of those is excellently designed. The game ooze realism, but it does come with a cost. The performance can be quite tricky if you have an older computer, and even on a newer one you will have stutters or hangs, along with a large number of small bugs. Despite that, I think Bus Simulator 27 does a great job at being fun to play, immersive, yet also very intense. They did an amazing job when it comes to setting up your own company and designing routes, even if I wish they offered more liberties when it comes to designing routes or managing employees. But in the end, Bus Simulator 27 is a great bus game, maybe the best I played in the past few years. It needs some more polish, yet as a whole, it has an exceptional framework that I hope only gets better with the planned, subsequent DLC.

Bus Simulator 27 was a frustrating title to review, but not for the reasons you may think. The game delivers on many aspects fans love about the simulation genre, with a huge map and plenty of content. After my more than 15 hours, I still feel like there’s plenty to do in the story. Felicia Bay is an exceptional locale to drive around, with great attention to detail. Passenger interactions, though limited, made me feel like a bus driver rather than a chauffeur. The game also does a great job introducing its systems to newcomers. Unfortunately, despite all these praises, Bus Simulator 27 feels like it needs more time in the oven.

Bus Simulator 27 offers a way to let you customize how you experience the game, giving you the choice between realistic and difficult. While the game has a solid foundation, its current state is flawed in a way that makes it feel like an early access title. With some updates to refine the driver AI in particular, it could become a worthy successor to Bus Simulator 21, and offer a fun way to hang out with friends without the stress that can come with other online gameplay experiences. Right now, it's simply not at that point.

If you hear the title Bus Simulator 27 and your ears already perk up then you will have a pretty good time with it. It offers a good amount of different buses, a relatively deep management system and a nice environment. The story mode does offer something even for newcomers but ultimately this game is made for a certain niche that will probably be able to deal with the many smaller and bigger problems that persist in all the game modes.
Bus Simulator 27 is a half-hearted attempt at a bus company manager, and a decent, yet buggy, shot at a bus driving simulator.
The wheels on the bus go round and round, round and round, round and round...

Bus Simulator 27 is a big step forward for the franchise, offering hours of relaxing entertainment with upgraded graphics, new coach buses and deep management features. Despite some technical bumps and AI bugs, driving along Felicia's coastal roads is hugely enjoyable, especially with friends.
Overall, Bus Simulator 27 has the potential to be a really big hit. What holds it back is the buggy world we drive in. The content within is great, but somehow the game still feels incomplete.

Is Bus Simulator 27 one of the best sim games I’ve played? No, there are far too many issues to put it high up on that list. But did I enjoy the time I spent with it? Mostly, yes! Despite its flaws, I can’t deny that I had a pretty chilled-out experience, with only a few issues that made me mumble swear words under my breath. Although it does need a bit more polish, this is still a decent title that both bus and simulator enthusiasts will probably enjoy.

With all that said, I’ll be giving Bus Simulator 27 the Thumb Culture Silver Award!

Bus Simulator 27 maintains the franchise's high standards, even though it caters to a very specific segment of players. The ability to manage a company — in addition to getting behind the wheel yourself — adds an interesting, complex layer of gameplay that helps break up mission repetition, though it might be overwhelming for casual players. Nevertheless, even without Portuguese text support, it is a worthwhile experience for anyone seeking a simulator that offers a wide range of options.

Bus Simulator 27 delivers an enjoyable driving experience with satisfying vehicle physics, a lively and detailed city, and engaging company management that gives every route a sense of purpose. Post-launch updates have noticeably improved its technical performance and traffic AI, although occasional visual glitches, a functional but unremarkable interface, and limited long-term gameplay depth keep it from fully realizing its potential.

All that said, I have mixed feelings about Bus Simulator 27. Its audiovisual presentation is solid, and the sheer amount of content is impressive, particularly the satisfying selection of buses. However, that currently feels like its only real advantage over the competition. On a technical level, there’s still plenty of room for improvement. Overall, I found Bus Bound somewhat more accessible, even if it wasn’t exactly flawless on the technical front either.

Bus Simulator 27 feels stagnant and lacking in innovation and iteration. Something like this might be forgivable in an annual series, but with six years since the last game, that can’t be pardoned. Simteract burdens new and returning players alike with an overwhelming, poorly designed wall of onboarding tasks up-front, and plenty of bugs to demonstrate that this wasn’t ready for release. If you are a bus simulation enthusiast who wants to drive licensed coach buses through an interesting map with friends, you might find some enjoyment here down the road. But for anyone expecting a true evolution of the franchise, this isn’t it. Now, a bus simulator actually worth playing is the far superior Bus Bound – made by the previous developers, stillalive studios.

In its current state, it’s going to be hard to recommend Bus Simulator. At its core, it’s an incredible Simulation experience with so many different mechanics to master, and I had genuine fun listening to passengers talking about aliens and pyramid schemes, screaming at obnoxious passengers listening to loud music, and navigating political corruption.

However, with all the optimisation and performance issues, it turns what has the potential to be a great game into just OK.

Bus Simulator 27 is an interesting one to score because there are two very different stories surrounding it. One is the launch version, which had more technical and gameplay problems than it really should have. The other is the game sitting on Xbox after numerous hotfixes, where many of those frustrations have already been addressed and the underlying experience is much easier to appreciate.

And it is that second version that matters to me.

What remains is a sizeable, ambitious and surprisingly enjoyable bus simulator with a great selection of licensed vehicles, a varied open world, meaningful company management, multiple game modes, plenty of customisation and an excellent co-op option. It doesn’t reinvent the simulator genre, but it doesn’t need to. What it does is provide a convincing virtual bus-driving experience that can be as relaxing or as demanding as you want it to be.

There are still rough edges. The AI can occasionally make you wonder what planet its drivers are from, the penalty system can still be a little too eager to punish mistakes and the occasional technical or visual oddity remains. But the important thing is that those issues no longer completely overshadow the experience.

Bus Simulator 27 is at its best when you stop worrying about reaching the destination as quickly as possible and simply settle into the journey. Pick your bus, plan your route, watch the weather roll in, collect your passengers and become part of the rhythm of Felicia Bay.

It might have taken a few trips around the block to get there, but Bus Simulator 27 is finally starting to feel like the bus simulator it always wanted to be.

Final Thought
Bus Simulator 27 has had a bumpy beginning, but the road ahead is looking considerably smoother. It isn’t perfect, and there are still areas that need refinement, but the combination of a huge world, excellent bus variety, enjoyable driving and surprisingly deep management makes this an easy recommendation for simulation fans. With the developers continuing to iron out the remaining problems, there is every reason to believe this is a game that will only get better with time.

While they certainly have produced a solid entry here, certain systems and menus leave a bit to be desired. While it certainly is a deeper game than Bus Bound, and that may serve its audience, I simply found Bus Simulator 27 to not always deliver where I wanted from it the most; the driving. And with a few bugs to iron out, the current experience is a tad buggy, to say the least. However, despite my few issues here, Bus Simulator 27 does punch its ticket with deep and rewarding simulation systems that will keep you just as busy in the bus as outside of one.

So, as of today, Bus Simulator 27 has all the goods on paper, and if developer Simteract manage to iterate on it via regular updates and tweaks, it has all the chances of becoming another hit, just like Bus Simulator 21 before it. Few games feature the depth and variety of the latest entry in the series, now it’s a matter of fixing a series of issues that currently limit its potential. I plan to revisit the game in the future, and hopefully it will live up to its incredible potential with time.
Rather than being a satisfying driving experience, Bus Simulator 27 instead chooses to bombard you with non-essential systems and details in a bland and buggy world.
"Bus Simulator 27" is aimed at a very specific audience – and for that audience, the title is certainly quite good.

Bus Simulator 27 is probably the installment in the series that most gave me the feeling of running a real transportation company rather than just driving buses. Creating routes, managing employees, handling different vehicles, and adding coaches all add much more depth to the experience, while the map offers enough variety to keep the many trips from becoming repetitive right away. Unfortunately, some of the progression systems could benefit from much clearer explanations. Not to mention that seeing vehicles stop for no reason and cause a traffic jam that puts you behind schedule quickly becomes frustrating. That said, the developers have already planned content for the coming year, and the game should continue to improve over time.
34.2% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (38 reviews).

Dark Scrolls is an indie 2D platformer featuring auto-scrolling, roguelite, and bullet hell mechanics. The levels are procedurally generated and reminiscent of *Super Ghouls’n Ghosts*, even though the game itself isn't particularly difficult. Despite offering creative and varied gameplay options, the stat system can be extremely overpowered, overshadowing many of the other available choices. The game is worth playing for roguelite fans and deserves the attention of anyone interested in it.

Dark Scrolls revives the philosophy of old-school, forced-scrolling arcade platformers like SonSon and enriches it with a modern roguelite structure. The screen advances relentlessly, forcing players to stay constantly on the move while facing waves of enemies and massive bosses, all while collecting coins to invest in upgrades that activate progressively via a unique "Rage" meter. The roster of heroes—each with distinct abilities and movement styles—ensures plenty of variety, and the local co-op mode is a delight for nostalgia lovers. The experience is slightly marred by the repetitive nature of the procedurally generated levels and somewhat uninspired, conventional enemies. Ultimately, it is a successful blend of past and present—one capable of costing you more than a few sleepless nights.

Dark Scrolls isn’t doinksoft’s most enjoyable or approachable game. But between the references to several Capcom classics, it’s frantic energy, and plenty of little secrets, there’s a lot of plucky personality. It can be punishing, grindy and under-explained at times. But each chaotic attempt offers enough oddball charm to justify another run.

While Dark Scrolls boasts an excellent retro aesthetic and rock-solid platforming fundamentals, it ultimately fails to transcend mediocrity due to a lack of distinct innovation. However, for fans of Ghosts 'n Goblins looking for a reasonably challenging experience, it remains a highly competent homage well worth a casual playthrough.

Dark Scrolls is still a charming game that was clearly crafted with love and is worth checking out, regardless of your interests in side-scrollers and roguelikes. Just be prepared to climb out of that grave and into a solid adventure.
Dark Scrolls is a platformer with roguelite elements where you'll die a lot because of its clunky controls, but it has more depth than it seems thanks to its characters.

Dark Scrolls balances high-intensity platforming with a somewhat rewarding progression system. The boss battles are a highlight, utilizing tried-and-true pattern-recognition mechanics that often reward patience and muscle memory. Coupled with a map full of mysteries, branching paths, and new heroes to rescue, there is an amount of replay value here. The single-player mode is so-so, but if you are looking for a frantic, retro-fueled challenge to tackle with a friend on the couch, Dark Scrolls is an absolute must-play.

Dark Scrolls is certainly fun at times, but it overall feels a bit insubstantial. If you’re looking for any sort of plot, Dark Scrolls proudly doesn’t have any of that. While it does have a fairly impressive number of varied characters to unlock, the oddly variable level of difficulty keeps it from being as mechanically satisfying as it could have been. It’s definitely not worth getting if you want to play it solo, but if you have friends to play with, there is some enjoyment to be had.

Dark Scrolls presents an intriguing concept by blending platforming, shoot ’em up, and roguelite elements within a charming retro-inspired aesthetic. Its diverse cast of characters, enjoyable co-op gameplay, excellent pixel art, and fast-paced action stand out as key strengths. However, the execution falls short of its potential, with imprecise controls, frustratingly unfair moments, uninspired level design, and repetition setting in too early. While there is some fun to be found, these shortcomings ultimately prevent the game from maintaining its appeal from start to finish.

Dark Scrolls is a game which I reckon will be a perfect salve for some people, being a neat call-back to the days of 8-bit gaming and old school shmups, but I just found it to be a bit too samey. It's fun, sure, but it works best in shorter half hour bursts for me. I expect a bit more from my roguelites, but if you approach this as an arcade game instead, you'll be in a better frame of mind.

Doinksoft created a wonderful side-scrolling shooter a couple of years ago in Gunbrella, and I thoroughly enjoyed it. But here, it feels like they missed the mark in many ways. There’s some fun to be had, though; it’s not a complete washout. Characters are varied and goofy in the best ways. I found two that I gravitated towards, and that felt pretty powerful once I got the hang of controlling them. The problems arise in a handful of meaningful areas, from a lack of accessibility and explanation of mechanics to the very minimal roguelike rewards. I don’t think it’s a game everyone will enjoy, but there are some wild retro moments that will still put a smile on your face.

While it has plenty of charm and solid fundamentals, the nitty gritty in Dark Scrolls really weighs it down. Unlocking new perks is really grindy, and actually using them doesn’t feel worth the effort because of all the resource drain and volatility. Co-op is more annoying than additive, and there simply isn’t enough sauce elsewhere to make this game stand out as a shooter or a roguelike. It’s a cute game to mess around with for a little while, but it wants you to lock in for hours in order to see it through to the end. There’s a world in which Dark Scrolls isn’t burdened with its need to be a roguelike, and it’s a much more interesting game without those shackles. It feels like I’m having that kind of thought often lately, and that’s a bummer.

Dark Scrolls looks and plays like an old-school 8-bit game, but it doesn’t have the refinement and diversity of the top games from that era. Even in co-op or multiplayer, the game lacks polish. You can only revive a fallen character after completing a level, even if you fill up your HP bar. However, a fallen player can still pick up lives, which hobbles the other players that are still alive. While Dark Scrolls has the look and feel of a classic side-scrolling platformer, it just doesn’t have fleshed-out technical underpinnings and gameplay variety to make it stand out in a crowd unless you have a real strong nostalgia for that era.
Dark Scrolls is a title I should have loved and instead loathed. It is not offensively bad or poorly made, so you may find some fun here that I did not.

In theory, I should like Dark Scrolls a lot more. However, the cozy atmosphere and strong audiovisual presentation can’t save this auto-scrolling platformer from the simple fact that it just isn’t much fun to play: while there’s plenty of variety on offer, doinksoft expects a significant time investment before you get to it, and the unrewarding progression, floaty controls, dull roguelite elements, and frustrating bugs make that a journey you’d rather avoid. If the developers push through a substantial number of updates in the coming months, it may be worth a look (especially given its modest price tag) but until then, just keep scrolling.

It’s hard to believe that Doinksoft is the studio behind Dark Scrolls. After the retro charm of Gato Roboto and the ingenious gameplay of Gunbrella, I would have thought the studio had found the winning formula, but this new release simply doesn't measure up to their previous titles. Between an alarming lack of information on almost everything—which greatly diminishes the satisfaction of unlocking new items (useful? useless? who knows!)—and run-of-the-mill solo gameplay featuring bosses that are nothing more than HP sponges, the roguelite feels messy at best. At least it’s cheap.

A simple, competent shmup can be a beautiful thing, a collection of different heroes to unlock an easy hook. It isn't that Dark Scrolls lacks outright complexity, with multiple paths through the short game, nuance between characters, and some secret mini-quests to round out its content. But it barely acknowledges success or failure, never challenges you after the first few hours, and can't devise a reward or goal to spur you on after you've seen what little it has to offer. If Dark Scrolls were an arcade cabinet back in the day, a few quarters would be enough to send you off to the next one.

Overall, this game isn’t good. I don’t like the issues it has, and the potential it had. It went like a rollercoaster. From the top to the bottom very quickly. Messy controls, no clear instruction, or story/level elements, bad camera movement and designs. The artstyle makes it unique with its rather spooky soundtrack, but that’s all that’s really going for it.

Dark Scrolls does a good job of balancing the cosy repetitiveness of a roguelike with the challenge inherent to the Soulslike genre. There are so many different ways to play, with six characters unlockable on top of the original three, all with their own unique abilities, movement and attack patterns.For the price, there's very little reason to not give this a shot, especially for those who gravitate towards pixel art or any of the genres encompassed within Dark Scrolls.

If you need a time waster and you're fond of sidescrollers, Dark Scrolls is an OK entry that can keep you busy for a while at a budget friendly price-point. It does the job for which it is designed, but the execution is a bit lackluster.

You can strongly dislike automatic side scrolling platformers and still love playing Dark Scrolls. I am proof in the proverbial pudding – I struggled to put it down. What sets Dark Scrolls apart from other platformers is its focus on simplicity. It's a great co-op platformer that's merely held back by its balance and relatively punishing progression. Its charm and co-op chaos will win you over the next time you want a party game to play with your friends!
Dark Scrolls is retro for all the right reasons, and very few of the wrong ones, and you’ll get plenty of substance considering its budget price point.
Devolver Digital often publishes experimental and unusual games, and Dark Scrolls certainly qualifies as such. But while playing, I'm reminded time and again of another recent release, Ball x Pit.

A bit too much is left up to the player to figure out, and I would have welcomed a bit more transparency while I struggled through my first couple hours with the game. By the time I hit my stride, I was bored of fighting the same enemies and bosses over and over. Short bursts and co-op play feel like the best ways to enjoy Dark Scrolls. Even then, there's really not enough charm or polish to shine through an experience that references the classics without containing what gives them staying power.
As a co-op game, Dark Scrolls offers a whole heck of a lot of fun so make sure you bring a chum along for the ride to get the most out of it. 📜

Dark Scrolls is, in a nutshell, a blast. It hits that nostalgic itch for simple, retro concepts and pulls it off with aplomb. If you're looking for depth and strong narrative, it's not here. No, this is straightforward run-and-projectile with friends, or solo, that has a fair bit to unlock for those that persevere.

Dark Scrolls may not reinvent the roguelite genre, but its satisfying combat, creative scroll system, and entertaining co-op make it an easy recommendation for fans of challenging retro-inspired action games.

Dark Scrolls delivers an entertaining arcade experience that excels in local and online co-op play. Its vibrant pixel aesthetic, catchy soundtrack, and character roster provide plenty of initial charm and fluid gameplay. While repetitive layouts and a grindy progression loop keep it from matching the heights of its peers, it remains a fun, budget-friendly option for fans of quick action sessions.

There's no denying that the game has charm and solid foundations, but Dark Scrolls falls a notch short of Doinksoft's previous titles. Unlocking new perks takes time, and using them isn't worth the effort. The co-op mode is interesting but doesn't offer much beyond chaos. At the end of the day, I'm left with mixed feelings.
#DarkScrolls is pared back and straightforward, but finely crafted.

So: Fun but unbalanced, or unbalanced but fun? I legitimately still cannot decide which part is more meaningful for the Dark Scrolls experience, but I can say this: I did have a good time with the game, and I respect the passion put into the old school vibe. Even the digital game guide filled me with nostalgia!

I really enjoyed my time with Dark Scrolls. If I’m being honest, dear reader, it took a few runs before everything finally clicked, but once it did, I could really see what Doinksoft was going for. In fact, I ended up finding it noticeably easier than Demon Throttle. It’s still a fairly niche game, though, one aimed squarely at players who love the NES era of gaming, and don’t mind a healthy dose of roguelike progression. If that sounds like your kind of thing, the variety between runs does a great job of keeping you coming back for more.

Dark Scrolls brilliantly blends bullet-hell intensity with platforming prowess, delivering a roguelite experience that’s genuinely challenging and packed with personality. The Mixed score at launch is honest about the problems — zero onboarding, run-ending bugs, balance inconsistency, visual clutter — but it undersells what the game is when those problems don’t get in the way. The perk combo system is original and satisfying. The character roster has real depth. Co-op is an excellent use of $7.99. doinksoft clearly has interesting ideas here, and if they address the onboarding and stability issues in post-launch patches, this could shift to a clear recommendation without caveats. Right now it’s a conditional one: buy it if you’re comfortable learning a system by doing, especially if you have someone to play with.

It’s ambitious, stylish and full of promising ideas, yet it never quite finds the balance needed to turn those ideas into consistently enjoyable gameplay. And sometimes expectations are unfair, but this time, I don’t think they were. Dark Scrolls looked like the kind of game I’d happily lose dozens of hours to. Instead, it became a game I admired far more than I enjoyed, and somehow, that’s the greatest disappointment of all.

Un nuevo experimento de Doinksoft, que como pasa con todos sus juegos, les sale bien. Una oda a los grandes arcades y plataformas de los años 80 y 90 y a su vez, y aunque parezca contradictorio, un soplo de aire fresco al catálogo de este tipo de juegos.

Dark Scrolls proves once again that great fun doesn’t require a massive budget. Featuring charming retro visuals, addictive gameplay, and ever-changing stages that keep each run fresh, Doinksoft delivers a challenging yet lighthearted experience. While a few control issues hold it back, it’s an easy recommendation for players looking for a fun and highly replayable adventure.

Unfortunately, Dark Scrolls fails to live up to its immense potential, delivering an adventure that lacks polish in crucial areas and suffers heavily from repetition. Players with friends willing to embark on a new 8-bit-style adventure might find some enjoyment in doinksoft’s latest title, but for everyone else, there are more consistent and entertaining alternatives available on the Nintendo console.
Dark Scrolls is a title that manages to be entertaining, yet it fails to shine in the execution of its core mechanics and often stumbles in the presentation of its systems.

Dark Scrolls isn’t a disaster, far from it. Its fast-paced action, humour, quirky heroes and co-op mode make for a few enjoyable sessions, especially with a friend on the sofa. But the imprecise controls, confusing progression and overly repetitive gameplay prevent the game from becoming truly addictive.

Dark Scrolls is a trip down memory lane that emphasizes more tripping than memories. While charming in its adherence to retro stylings, it’s a lesson in why some of that game design is no longer the standard for roguelikes. For folks itching to relive the glory days of figuring out how to play a game all on your own, Dark Scrolls is a hunk of coarse sand paper to scratch that particular itch.

Dark Scrolls isn't the first to do what it does—after all, roguelikes and roguelites don't keep coming out so frequently by accident, even if there are complaints about genre saturation—but it is very well-executed and excels at it. Not to mention that chaotic co-op has become a staple in games famously known for tearing families apart, like Overcooked (it might sound like an exaggeration, but there’s a grain of truth to it).

Overall, Dark Scrolls is a basic action platformer that stays true to the genre roots. It doesn’t try to reinvent the wheel and sticks to its strengths. The variation of characters and one life will ensure you get a few hours of enjoyment out of this game. If you enjoy this style of game, make sure to check out Doinksoft’s back catalogue, as they have released a number of these types of games, so you’ll never be disappointed!
With a little more time, Dark Scrolls could be a delightful little arcade-style sidescrolling rougelike.
It’s an easy recommendation for anyone who enjoys games that demand persistence, precision and just a little bit of stubbornness
Doinksoft flirts with the party game genre in an eccentric and chaotic tribute to the great classics of the late 80s.

Fortunately, this game features a roguelike progression system. Everything you collect during your walkthrough can be used in your village. Updates and the like are therefore collected gradually, allowing you to become stronger and stronger. As a result, the levels naturally become more bearable and easier depending on the amount of money and points you manage to gather. Dark Scrolls is generally quite good and is a game that is easy to play. Unfortunately, it loses some points due to the not-so-intuitive controls. However, if you enjoy old NES games with fun co-op, then you will likely get something out of this. The full playthrough takes about 6-10 hours. For ten dollars, it is up to you to consider if it is worth it.
The Dark Ages is fun in different ways than its predecessors, but Doom has been better.
40.0% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (5 reviews).

Look, Asdivine Knot isn’t going to convert anyone already tired of KEMCO’s familiar JRPG formula, but its crisis-of-faith story, Nexus Gauge, and customizable airship give the adventure more personality than you might expect. Combat eventually becomes easy and the mobile-style monetization is still annoying, but there’s enough charm and progression here to keep the faithful entertained.
Asdivine Knot is a fairly generic and repetitive RPG, but those looking to kill time and gods will likely still have a fun time.

Asdivine Knot is a decent-at-best mobile game that has potential to be a good game, as it has a decent combat system and an interesting upgrade mechanic, but It's filled with boring characters, a barren world, and microtransactions that may have worked when it was a free game that had ads to break up the action. But as a ported release that's competing with other games to get my attention, spend your money elsewhere.
Asdivine Knot isn't a groundbreaking JRPG, but it does have a fun battle system with colorful characters, a bopping soundtrack, and crisp 2D graphics.

Asdivine Knot is a beautiful game with detailed spritework and captivating music, but it’s severely lacking in the gameplay and story departments. From its derivative plot to its simple (albeit effective) turn-based combat, Asdivine Knot does nothing special that can grab the attention of the most seasoned JRPG aficionados. Fortunately, however, its fast-paced combat and accessible mechanics make it a perfect gateway JRPG for anybody who is interested in the genre and does not want to feel overwhelmed.
Asdivine Knot is a highly entertaining old-school RPG with a wonderful cast and intuitive gameplay so definitely play it if you enjoy retro RPGs. ⚔️

Asdivine Knot is a charming old-school JRPG with a promising story about faith and guilt, an eccentric cast, and enjoyable turn-based combat enhanced by the shared Nexus system. Its rewarding airship progression and convenient quality-of-life features make it an appealing adventure for genre fans, although repetitive dungeons, uneven pacing, poorly balanced difficulty, and lingering mobile-style monetization prevent its strongest ideas from reaching their full potential.
25.0% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (28 reviews).

Halloween: The Game takes full advantage of the best features of the top titles in the asymmetric multiplayer horror genre, but manages to create its own identity, something that other similar games have failed to achieve. The option for a single-player gameplay in a short but very rewarding campaign is a great advantage. The overall package isn't perfect in what it sets out to do because it suffers in some general aspects, including chaotic AI, technical instability, and graphical limitations.
Halloween: The Game is a blast, especially now that players are generally quite good at it as it provides open-ended top-notch thrills.

Halloween needs some massaging. There are bugs galore, its Civilian onboarding isn’t great, and leveling up to unlock new color tints on sunglasses, or a new shirt or hat, isn’t the best motivation. But when I’m actually in a match, all of that fades away. The bugs aren’t game-breaking and blend in with IllFonic’s feature-not-a-bug jank, like one where another player and I hilariously moonwalked when we ran instead of sprinted. Learning what to do as a Civilian doesn’t take too much time, even without any helpful context built in-game, and cosmetics don’t affect how I play. What matters in Halloween is the scares I’m delivering and receiving, and the joy I’m feeling through it all. Death has arrived in IllFonic’s latest, and while the fear is abundant, so too is the fun waiting in the sleepy little town of Haddonfield.

The asynchronous multiplayer is crazy, with vicious murder and stalking on the Michael Myers side, and careful strategizing, influence and steep uphill climb from the neighbours side. What easily could’ve been unexciting and banal, the PVE along with the abilities and teamwork make Halloween: The Game a treat, but be sure to excuse its clunkiness to get the most out of it.

Halloween: The Game truly understands the fantasy it aims to deliver, whether you're controlling Michael Myers or desperately trying to survive him. The campaign is short, yet serves as an effective introduction that recreates iconic moments from the 1978 classic, while the multiplayer sets itself apart through NPCs that push the experience beyond the traditional 4v1 formula. Even while stumbling with progression bugs and shallow structural variety, the end result is a violent, entertaining slasher that delivers a solid homage to the original film.

Halloween: The Game is a title aimed primarily at fans of the films and games like "Dead by Daylight." Michael Myers is a horror movie icon, and this newly released title gives him the chance to leave a lasting impression in the gaming world as well—provided the developers continue to roll out new content, dye characters, and maps to ensure the gameplay doesn't become stale after a month or two. It may not be perfect, but it is nonetheless an entertaining multiplayer horror slasher.

Halloween: The Game resurrects the asymmetrical horror gameplay of Friday the 13th, while carving out its own franchise identity. A campaign mode offers a short, sweet Halloween treat. But the multiplayer is a bit of a mixed bag. Still, its bold stab at prioritizing NPC rescue over player survival mostly slices through the competition.

Halloween: The Game has its issues, from poor onboarding when playing as a survivor to simply feeling rough around the edges. But on the plus side, it perfectly captures the essence of the film it's based on and puts a new spin on the traditional asymmetrical multiplayer horror format, making it fun to play whether you win or lose.

Halloween: The Game does a great job of capturing the atmosphere of the classic 1978 movie. Multiplayer can be a lot of fun once you actually figure out how to play. Unfortunately, the game is also rough around the edges with bugs and glitches that hamper the experience. Halloween: The Game isn't as classic as the original film but I would say it's a very respectable Halloween H20. It has its problems but is still very fun.

Halloween: The Game has a solid and entertaining foundation for those who enjoy the slasher genre. Its biggest hook lies in letting us experience both sides of the massacre, though playing as Michael Myers proves far more satisfying. It has a few minor flaws, and it remains to be seen whether post-launch content will keep the game afloat.

It tries too hard to make Michael Myers the monster compelling, when it’s the man himself who should be terrifying. Repetitive gameplay only makes matters worse, and grisly executions can’t sustain the thrill for long.
IllFonic deserves some props for trying to do things differently but the incessant focus on interacting with NPCs undermines what should be a frantic time with other players.
Halloween: The Game nails the atmosphere but not the execution, undercut by bugs, good ideas not fully realized, and a lack of variety.

Halloween: The Game could've been awesome. It's too bad it's grossly unpolished, and its story mode is a lazily constructed, half-hearted attempt. The core game will probably get better with patches and updates, but it’s still doomed to face the inevitable service shutdown that tends to hit these kinds of games a year or two after release. If it had a substantial offline single-player mode, that would have saved it. Maybe this Halloween it’s better to spend it with Pinhead rather than Michael.

For lovers of IllFonic and asymmetrical multiplayer games, those who loved and felt the immense loss of Friday the 13th: The Game, I have no doubt you will enjoy Halloween to some extent. Personally, I don’t believe these types of experiences are extraordinarily enjoyable. I was hoping that with the game itself being based around the Halloween franchise, it would sway my opinion. IllFonic was trying to rebuild the excitement around the now-shut-down Friday the 13th: The Game, but failed to expand past that. Halloween feels dated and slow, leaning more on nostalgia and the love of horror than on community growth, gaming mechanics, and development. I think they could benefit from a stronger single-player experience to bring more excitement to the multiplayer aspect, but honestly, it’s missing that magic.

But if you have played any of their past games or are even a fan of Dead by Daylight which is so janky I don’t understand how it maintains such a large player bas—sorry, but if you can deal with that stuff then Halloween is probably going to be for you, for everyone else just hold out for some patches.

Illfonic has created a solid foundation for an asymmetrical horror game. It addresses some of the worst offenses committed by Dead by Daylight, and rewards more immersive playstyles. It actually brings the horror back to the genre which has been optimized out of its competitor. Now it’s up to the players to do something with it.

Halloween: The Game has an intriguing premise, but unfortunately, it fails to fully realize its potential. Turning Michael Myers into the centerpiece of an asymmetrical horror game is a solid idea, and Haddonfield’s atmosphere, the overall chase sequences, and certain gameplay moments can be enjoyable for Halloween fans. However, poor tutorials, a weak progression system, a lack of gameplay variety, matchmaking issues, and a range of technical and graphical problems prevent the game from becoming a truly memorable multiplayer experience.

Halloween: The Game is a stab at bringing one of horror’s most iconic villains to gaming, but technical issues, balancing problems and a waste-of-time campaign stop it from being the killer experience it could have been.

As a fan of the film series, I have rarely encountered a game that captures the atmosphere of Haddonfield so convincingly: the faint snap of a twig in the front yard, Michael suddenly vanishing from the corner of your eye, the familiar music playing in the background—it all works. At the same time, it is clear that the game is still in an early stage of development. The focus on NPC rescue missions is a bold design choice, though not always a rewarding one, and the single-player campaign—despite some promising ideas—remains too short and too linear to be truly compelling. That said, those who are already big fans of asymmetrical multiplayer horror games—and the *Halloween* franchise in particular—will still find plenty of hours of entertainment here, especially when playing with a well-coordinated group of friends. Michael Myers is back; his digital home just needs a bit of renovation before it becomes truly terrifying enough for the next generation of horror fans.

Halloween: The Game has its flaws: the progression doesn’t seem great, the single-player is nothing to write home about, and the game can easily hit a brick wall when it comes to long-term updates. However, I do believe it will provide a fun, unique asymmetrical horror multiplayer experience, and I can only hope it succeeds where other single-franchise multiplayer horror games failed.
Halloween: The Game is an atmospheric and tense asymmetrical horror game that captures Michael Myers authentically, even if its short campaign, clunky combat and limited map selection hold it back.

*Halloween: The Game* is an asymmetrical horror title that treats Carpenter’s film with respect and passion. Its greatest strengths lie in its atmosphere, sound design, and the sense of being stalked by Michael Myers, though an overly short campaign, technical issues, and a degree of long-term repetitiveness prevent it from reaching greater heights. Nevertheless, it remains an entertaining and recommended title for fans of the genre and the *Halloween* franchise—especially when played with a group of friends ready to scream and laugh together.

Halloween: The Game is a much smarter adaptation than simply relying on Michael Myers’ iconic image. It understands the horror of the original film, transforms many of its ideas into gameplay mechanics, and manages to establish its own identity within the asymmetrical horror genre.
