It lacks polish and relies too heavily on multiplayer, but there is a very solid foundation here and, most importantly, an adaptation made by people who seem to understand why Michael Myers remains terrifying nearly fifty years later.
Halloween is a solid asymmetric horror game buried under a pile of technical issues and general sloppiness. One day it might be worth playing, but right now it’s absolutely not.

Among the hits and misses of its previous projects, IllFonic shows with Halloween: The Game that it still has plenty to offer the asymmetric horror genre. The title emerges as one of the studio’s most complete experiences for those seeking 1v4 multiplayer matches, blending diverse mechanics, immersive atmosphere, and new strategic possibilities. Despite technical issues that still need fixing, the gameplay innovations make the experience more dynamic and engaging, creating an addictive match cycle that encourages players to experiment with different strategies as they return to Haddonfield.

Halloween: The Game delivers an entertaining asymmetrical horror experience that captures the atmosphere of the classic franchise while adding its own mechanics to the familiar formula. Its story mode offers a useful introduction to Michael Myers, while the multiplayer provides tense chases, environmental interactions and plenty of pressure for both sides. However, limited animations, repetitive actions and a lack of depth in its narrative keep it from reaching its full potential.

Halloween: The Game captures flashes of the original film’s campy slasher atmosphere through Myers’ stalking mechanics, cinematic teleportation, and satisfyingly brutal executions. Unfortunately, frustrating NPC-focused objectives, easily exploitable balance, shallow progression, poor animations, technical issues, and fundamentally repetitive match design make it feel like a weaker reskin of Friday the 13th rather than a meaningful evolution of the formula.

Halloween: The Game is the definitive game based on the cult film Halloween and the killer Michael Myers. The asymmetrical multiplayer mode is great fun and offers plenty of options. Meanwhile, the inclusion of a story mode where you play as Myers will delight fans of the slasher genre and John Carpenter’s cult film. The slow pace of the game, which mirrors that of the film, may not be to everyone’s taste, but once you get into the swing of things, we can guarantee that the game is addictive and you’ll want to play one match after another.

Halloween offers a unique, asymmetrical, horror experience. It captures the essence of Halloween well, and while optimization and longevity are concerns, it's an experience that horror fans will enjoy.

Slasher fans will absolutely love the fantastic movie atmosphere, the great soundtrack, and the generous fan service. The switch between Michael and the townspeople also brings a breath of fresh air.
​On the other hand, sluggish movement, gameplay that quickly becomes monotonous, and annoying animation glitches during the manhunt in solo mode detract from the fun. PC players are also held back by clunky controls. While it’s worth a look for die-hard Michael Myers enthusiasts, the technical shortcomings mean you rarely feel like a powerful boogeyman.
Halloween: The Game offers unique ideas within the asymmetrical horror genre, but the game's technical side is plagued by bugs and performance issues that detract from the experience.

Unfortunately, the game currently suffers from a huge number of technical problems. Performance is far from smooth, and matchmaking proves struggling as well. Hopefully the devs will address these issues over the coming weeks. Then the game will deserve a better grade.

Halloween: The Game doesn’t feel like two separate games thankfully. However it does feel like so much more time went into embodying and becoming one with Michael and not the rest of the cast. There is something really great here, but there’s just a little bit more polish to come that will really make this a killer success. As a note, when provided with a copy for review, we were made aware of a few additional fixes and features that would be available by launch day. Some of these will really bring it home and make it a fuller experience.

It’s a tough one to answer, especially in a genre where a pattern of dead match queues after short-term success is the common narrative. I can’t speak on that future, but what I can say is right now Halloween needs work: on its match pacing, its learning curve, its gameplay mechanics, and crucially…its bevy of technical issues. There remains potential for a solid multiplayer horror title here, and the IP and visuals might be enough to convince some, but as of right now, Halloween is not an easy title to recommend to all but die-hard fans of the genre.

Halloween: The Game has its rough patches, but it’s a good enough time for fans of Michael Myers and asymmetrical horror games. My time with it was bogged down by numerous bugs and really dumb AI characters, but when the game ran as it was supposed to, it was a fun horror experience of cat-and-mouse between killer and survivor. Adding some new elements like the additional citizens that you need to save or Michael’s various abilities keeps things interesting, but I do worry about there being a ceiling for this game’s future when compared to past Illfonic and Gun titles.
37.5% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (8 reviews).

Broken Arms' game delivers exactly what it promises—designing golf courses and turning them into a profitable business—but a single, extended Sandbox session is sufficient to see everything the title has to offer.

Under Par Golf Architect is less than the sum of its parts. Each element of the game feels a little undercooked. Together it just about holds up, but the cracks aren't hard to find. However, the game’s got a pleasant presentation. It’s just a little bit silly, and that works if you can put up with spending a bit of time in the rough.
While I applaud the game’s use of the Switch 2’s mouse control support, there’s an awkwardness and sometimes frustrating lack of focus on enjoyable playability here.

Under Par: Golf Architect captures the charm of Sid Meier’s SimGolf with satisfying course design, but inconsistent simulation systems and technical issues hold it back. It’s a promising experience that gets a lot right, just not consistently enough yet.

Under Par: Golf Architect is charming and very welcoming, and that first golf course you create will be a truly fun process. After that, though, you’ll realise that Under Par has nothing else to offer and is such a disappointing missed opportunity. It’s all the more strange that the developers would do this because the same team previously created Hundred Days, a vineyard business simulation, and that one was genuinely interesting and engaging, and had proper tycoon simulation challenges built into it.

If you’re like me and have been itching for another SimGolf game since 2002, then Under Par Golf Architect will scratch that itch. It’s not as polished, but it also runs on modern systems and isn’t at an 800×600 resolution, so you take the good with the bad. Just know it’s probably best played on PC rather than PS5, which has received a serviceable port but one that never feels quite right.
Cozy and chill experience in which you'll build and manage your very own golfing paradise

Under Par Golf Architect succeeds as a relaxing, creative escape for anyone who ever dreamed of designing their own links. It captures the quiet satisfaction of watching a club grow from humble beginnings into a thriving destination, and the ability to play what you build is a cool addition. If you’ve been waiting for the return of SimGolf, this is worth checking out. Just don’t expect it to eagle every hole.

Under Par Golf Architect brought me back to my childhood days of SimGolf in all the right ways. While they could do a bit more in terms of making the management side of the game having more of an impact, everything else hit like a perfect drive.
Under Par Golf Architect is a real Birdie of a tycoon game, with engaging hole creation and the ability to play the courses you make.
34.3% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (35 reviews).

A lack of mission variety, and an array of bugs of the technical variety bring down the experience, but Coldiron have largely improved upon their first outing in the Alien universe, thanks to a fun class system, satisfying gunplay, and challenge cards that make for interesting difficulty experimentation, while remaining mostly faithful to the overarching franchise.

Although it focuses on a single campaign and adds a fourth slot to the squad, Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 is only a minor advance from the first game. There are some quality-of-life fixes and a bit more variety to loadouts, classes, and enemies. The fundamental rhythm hasn’t changed much, and the writing can be painful. Just like the first game, Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 is fun with friends, and for short play sessions of a few missions and moving the campaign forward. If there’s a third game in the works, it really needs to change up the formula.

This sequel delivers a frantic and atmospheric cooperative experience that successfully expands upon its predecessor's foundations. While the combat feels more refined and the setting captures the cinematic essence of the franchise perfectly, it suffers from a repetitive mission structure and a lackluster narrative. Technical inconsistencies and subpar AI occasionally hinder an otherwise thrilling hunt.

Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 features the same deluge of Xenomorphs being torn to shreds by a competent team of Colonial Marines. While Cold Iron Studios has further refined the mechanics already established, additions like a fourth player slot are welcome. Despite its faithful rendition of the Alien universe, it doesn’t change that the gameplay loop will grow repetitive and stale over time, regardless of how your team clicks with it. Though new modes and more diversity would have been expected in a full-blown sequel, perhaps the formula will be nailed in future content expansions or a possible third entry, hopefully not suffering a fate akin to Alien 3.
I'm happy to keep going back for more

It's undeniable that Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 maintains - and expands upon - the achievements of its predecessor, establishing itself as one of the best action experiences in the franchise. This doesn't mean, however, that it ceases to be a generic game: a title that leverages a well-established brand to deliver a common product, lacking great virtues and of little relevance to the universe it intends to belong to.

Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 is the type of sequel that simply aims to offer more of the same, which is fine as long as you weren't expecting innovation. There are some worthwhile additions here, though, such as four-player teams and the new Specialst class. It's just a shame they're counter-balanced somewhat by technical issues.
Aliens Fireteam Elite 2 takes a step forward from the 2021 release. A solid cooperative shooter that corrects many past mistakes without reinventing itself.

An upgraded arsenal and variety of targets make Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 a more engaging shooting gallery than its predecessor, but the weaponry still feels like you've been sent out to deal with an alien queen with Nerf guns and a dream.

Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 offers satisfying cooperative combat and rewarding progression, with plenty of room to experiment with classes and loadouts. Repetitive environments and performance issues on PS5 hold it back, but there’s still fun to be had with friends.

On the surface, being a better version of Aliens: Fireteam Elite feels like a no-brainer, but the game just constantly does things wrong. From the poor story to the less-than-poor optimization and beyond, the game just never manages to be more than its predecessor. The things the game does right, like combat and set pieces, just can't seem to make up the difference with so many other problems stacked on top of them. With the game being so relatively short, there isn't much to enjoy, and anything beyond the core experience will come from other players. In the end, Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 fails in too many places to be a worthy successor at this point in time.

Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 is average, but stands out thanks to a satisfying arsenal, classes with solid builds, and varied enemies that require distinct tactics. However, the lack of Portuguese subtitles, bullet-sponge enemies, FPS drops, and a scarcity of matches in South America are likely to deter fans.

Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 only provides small improvements over its predecessor. The jump to a four-person squad and the new Specialist class are genuine improvements, and playing with a well-drilled fireteam to clear hordes is still satisfying, at least with friends on the mic. Everything else is buried under cluttered menus, unsatisfying gunplay, a mediocre story, and a handful of bugs. If you’ve got three friends and low expectations, there’s still a fun weekend to be had here, but solo players should let this one drift off into space.

The 2021 original was a decent idea in a thin package that worked at its initial price point. Even though the 2026 sequel addresses critiques of the first by adding 4-player squads, rebuilt classes, Horde maps at launch, and mid-mission checkpoints, it still feels like the same game with more bolted on, at a higher price. Yes, the core gameplay still works, but I’d wait for a few patches to iron out the technical performance and snag it on a sale.

It’s hard to recommend Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 as-is. It has a lot of issues, lacks content, and plays almost exactly like its five-year-old predecessor. I’m hard-pressed to find one thing I particularily enjoy more here than I did when I played Aliens: Fireteam Elite, and despite the campaign being a bit more fleshed out, it’s a bore talking to characters, and more so, the lack of endgame content outside of the horde mode really makes it hard to say this is a game you want to play with friends.
What starts as dumb fun quickly devolves into a dull slog through an uninteresting story. Even if Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 had more polish, it's still a very underwhelming sequel.
As team-based shooter it’s competent if uninspired. As an Aliens game, it’s another in a long series of disappointments.

Ultimately, any time you might spend on Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 is better spent elsewhere. Any momentum built up in enjoying the game is derailed instantly when a bug forces you or a teammate out of the game, and the impressive visuals aren’t enough to make up for it.

Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 is a massive letdown of a sequel. At times it teeters on the so-bad-it's-good territory, with references for fans of the series and some admittedly decent customisation. But it does little to amplify what's at its core: a half-arsed co-op tie-in that, bafflingly, lacks any of the charm that the first game had.
Another (mostly) glorious day in the corps.
Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 should be counted among the few really good Aliens franchise video games that we have; and I say that even with the small issues I’ve experienced.
Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2&a;#039;s narrative starts with a rescue mission that quickly gets messy as it becomes evident that Weyland-Yutani is up to its old tricks, experimenting on Xenomorphs.
However, it doesn't feel like the sequel it could have been.

Your opinion of Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 will largely depend on whether you've played the first game. Newcomers will find a straightforward co-op shooter that captures the spirit of Aliens, albeit with technical issues, repetitive combat, and little reason to continue after the campaign unless they're completionists or simply love blasting xenomorphs. For returning players, the fourth fireteam slot is welcome, but it doesn't make up for the lack of meaningful changes elsewhere. After five years, Fireteam Elite 2 feels more like an expanded version of its predecessor than a true sequel. It's not a bad game, but more substantial gameplay changes, technical fixes, and a sale would make it much easier to recommend.

Fans of the Alien series are often forced to deal with subpar experiences, and this comes in as one of them. Not withstanding various design decisions brought on by the new team, the quality is simply lacking on many aspects. Combat quickly becomes dry, and at how high of a price this game is, it is not recommended, even to fans of the series.

Cold Iron Studios has returned to familiar territory to deliver an intense, cooperative experience in which a squad of marines must face off against iconic monsters. While the sequel shares the style of the original, it boasts better level design and is more fun when played as a group of four. The only downside is the numerous minor bugs.
The most disappointing aspect of Fireteam Elite 2 is the hope it built on the original. Instead, it’s more of the same, with more synths and unskippable cutscenes filled with utter guff.

While Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 does make some improvements from its predecessor, it also takes a few steps back. Player customizability and character builds take a step in the right direction, but enemy balance makes some fights feel like a struggle. The game is much more action-oriented; as an unintended consequence, it deemphasizes the atmosphere the Alien franchise is known for. Bugs and strange NPC dialogue bring Fireteam Elite 2 over the edge as a title that doesn't do much to set itself apart.

Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 is a frustrating sequel because its best qualities are exactly what make its shortcomings so obvious. The shooting is satisfying. The Xenomorphs are fun to fight. But the campaign is repetitive, the story doesn’t get interesting until too late, and there just isn’t enough of an upgrade to the visuals and gameplay feel that the sequel needed.

Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 delivers solid action moments, with interesting classes, a good variety of enemies, and combat that shines when the hordes arrive. The downside is that the campaign repeats its structure far too often, becoming tiresome before the end. Combined with performance issues on PS5, weak animations, and an unengaging story, it becomes difficult to recommend the title.

The story is passable, but the action is capable of nice heights, especially with pals on your side or diving into the unpredictable lottery of public matchmaking. It’s hard to beat the intensity of hearing the ping of your motion sensor that precedes mowing down aliens with a smartgun or pulse rifle, and the game provides candy of that sort and more to indulge in. Genre fans who are more forgiving of prominent flaws will have a good time with it. More critical players may want to wait for some title updates to roll through.

Anyone looking for a co-op game that lets them jump right into the action in seconds and have fun without having to think too hard will find exactly what they’re looking for. A bonus for Aliens fans, who’ll get to do all of the above in faithful settings and an authentic atmosphere.

Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 is a game that focuses heavily on replayability, with rewarding progression systems and a ton of missions. That doesn't mean, however, that the developer has found the magic formula to keep me constantly engaged.

Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 stands out as an engaging and promising cooperative Horde shooter game with significant potential for growth and improvement. While it may not yet represent the pinnacle of the co-op shooter genre, it offers a solid foundation that, with some fine-tuning and enhancements, could elevate it to a top-tier status.
Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 delivers another entertaining blast of Xeno-slaying co-op action, but familiar ideas and a general lack of polish stop this bug hunt from reaching its full potential.
There’s a fun game in Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 for sure; just don’t expect much in the way of originality.

Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 manages to deliver exactly what we expect from a good cooperative game in the franchise: lots of bullets, Xenomorphs coming from all sides, classes that really make a difference, and that delicious feeling that any dark corridor could turn into our last moment of life.

"Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2" promised to improve upon everything its predecessor lacked to achieve mainstream success. However, the game we received manages to regress in many ways to the final version of the original and repeats many of the mistakes that nearly killed the first title.
In the end, there is enough here to keep fans happy, and hopefully future DLC will come similar to the original, which will give players plenty of new missions to enjoy.

If you’ve played Aliens: Fireteam Elite, you’ve already played Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2. It’s nearly the same game down to mission structure, only prettier but with 200% more story and dialogue you do not want to hear. Once the campaign ends, there’s no real endgame content to speak of, leaving you with nothing to do but replay levels on higher difficulties where the core gameplay fails to hold interest. Charging $10 more than its predecessor for an experience that recycles the same formula where you’re retreading previous areas is uninspired. It offers a few hours of mindless action if you just want to turn your brain off, but ultimately, Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 simply isn’t enough to justify the price tag.

Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 rebuilds its classes and adds a genuinely clever Specialist system, but stuttering, crashes, and a campaign that runs out of content too fast keep it from being the leap forward it should've been.

While Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 features visual upgrades and several improvements over its predecessor, it fails to be a highly captivating game due to unaddressed flaws, disappointing optimization, and a lack of Korean localization.
33.3% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (36 reviews).
A great array of distinctive cars, mix of winding country roads and crowded urban highways, and modes that emphasize clean racing help this racer shine.
The third game in the Gear.Club franchise is a total success in terms natural evolution within the genre, but still has points that show some amateurism from its developers.

Gear.Club Unlimited 3 is a great racing game that takes advantage of the Switch 2 hardware to deliver a compelling, immersive, and satisfying experience with smooth gameplay. With a roster of more than 40 car models with 50 tracks across France and Japan, racing game fans have a lot to play with in this content-rich story mode. Although there are a few graphical issues and some missing fan-favorite cars, the game is a great foundation for developer Eden Games to build on.

With Gear.Club Unlimited 3, nothing gets reinvented, but plenty gets refined. The addition of Japan, a tighter Career flow, Highway Mode, and deeper customization give the game more variety and confidence, while Switch 2 finally lets it run the way it should. It’s an accessible racer with enough depth for car fans and competitive players alike, and an easy entry point for families. Not groundbreaking, just solid, polished, and comfortable in its own lane.

There is a lot that you can potentially get out of Gear.Club 3, especially if you enjoy time trial challenges, where you’ll get a lot out of the large number of tracks and online leaderboards. Collecting all the cars and then playing around with them is a lot of fun, and ideal for pick-up-and-play sessions. It might not be a must play, but it’s one of those games that you’ll likely find yourself spending more time with than you realise.

Gear.Club Unlimited 3 brings licensed arcade racing to Nintendo Switch 2, offering an accessible experience across the scenic roads of Japan and France. While the visuals and club management mechanics shine, a lack of launch content and stripped-back multiplayer make it feel like a step backward from its predecessor. It is a solid choice for solo racers, though it still needs post-launch polish to reach its full potential.

While it lacks online multiplayer, you might want to pick up Gear.Club Unlimited 3 if you like the idea of developing your HQ in Japan, competing in races to unlock new features and put together an impressive garage of cars. You'll have to put up with a handling model that isn't all that impressive, however, and some will rue the lack of assist and difficulty options.
Despite its good ideas, which it does have, and technical improvements over previous installments, Gear.Club Unlimited 3 loses steam in practically every aspect. And that's a shame.

Gear.Club Unlimited 3 is a tough game to rate. At its core, the driving is sound, the graphics are decent, the game mechanics are interesting, and the career is meaty enough to bother. It even offers a 60 frames per second mode, something previous episodes did not – at least, on Nintendo consoles. On the other hand, it has various important flaws related to the overall racing, and the lack of online multiplayer is a huge step-down from the previous game which did, eventually, add said feature. What we’re left with is a mostly competent, not particularly memorable arcade racer with a handful of highs, but some baffling lows as well. It is a fun game, and on Switch 2 there aren’t too many better alternatives for this kind of racer. But if it follows the previous episode’s path, it may get new content, proper multiplayer and astonishingly deep discounts before long. Perhaps you’re better off waiting for all of that to happen, before jumping in.

Gear.Club Unlimited 3 is the kind of game I would recommend only with a big, big asterisk. If you just want a realistic looking racer, and to race around and do very little else, you will probably get some enjoyment out of it. If you want a racer that gives you a real reason to keep coming back beyond simply unlocking the next event, this will leave you wanting a lot more.

Gear.Club Unlimited 3 is a title with good intentions and a competent gameplay foundation. However, it accumulates too many technical issues, the driving feel and physics are poor, the AI does not behave well, and the absence of online multiplayer along with the very limited content weigh too heavily.
There are moments where Gear.Club Unlimited 3 nearly comes together, but when other games like JDM and Tokyo Xtreme Racer exist, it becomes clear just how much of a poor facsimile it is.

Gear.Club Unlimited 3 leans almost entirely on its Story Mode, yet even that fails to truly pull you in. Beyond that, frustrations stack up – clunky handling, technical hiccups and rubber banding – though the hub, duels and traffic-filled circuits offer brief flashes of promise. In the end, it falls short of must-have status, and you’re better off firing up GRID Legends instead.

Gear.Club Unlimited 3 offers solid handling, a generous car roster, and welcome two‑player split‑screen support, yet the overall experience struggles to rise above average. Technical inconsistency across both visual modes, dated presentation, rubber‑banding AI, and a repetitive progression loop limit the game’s impact, while the absence of online multiplayer reduces its long‑term appeal. There are enjoyable moments, particularly in short sessions, but the Switch 2 debut of the series falls short of the standard set by Eden Games’ earlier work.

Gear.Club Unlimited 3 offers a solid core racing experience, but it suffers from poor visuals, performance issues, some visual glitches, and a scarcity of content to justify the asking price. It is even harder to recommend Gear.Club Unlimited 3 in a post-GRID Legends: Deluxe Edition world on Nintendo Switch 2. There is potential here, but too many caveats for it to be even close to an easy recommendation.
You want to like Gear.Club Unlimited 3. Unfortunately, the lack of customization, ease of the story mode, AI problems, and laundry list of bugs keep it from being worth your time.

Despite some successes — workshop upgrades and highway duels chief among them — it's a middling sim racer with a monotonous (albeit substantial) story mode, limited multiplayer options, and subpar visuals.
The latest Gear.Club Unlimited, now on PS5

Gear.Club Unlimited 3 comes across as a middle-of-the-road arcade racing game. The arcade style handling and tracks are fine, while the car selection is good albeit tiny when compared to the competition. The story and focus on events are great, but the pacing really wants you to play this game in short spurts versus extended sessions. The circumstances create a game that works fine as an in-between title but not as your main racing game, especially when the platform has a ton of better racing titles.
A great entry on Nintendo Switch 2 that brings the Gear.Club Unlimited series, to Nintendo's latest console

Gear.Club 3 Unlimited does not redefine racing, but focuses on fun in single-player mode. However, split-screen gameplay should be treated as a curiosity. For racing fans who spend a lot of time with Nintendo Switch 2, Eden Games' game is a very interesting proposition.

Gear.Club Unlimited 3 is, therefore, a rather mixed sequel which, whilst offering enjoyable racing in attractive settings, rarely manages to step out of the shadow of its more established rivals. If you’re looking for a light-hearted racing game focused primarily on the pure driving experience, Gear.Club Unlimited 3 might keep you entertained for a while. Nevertheless, many might rightly expect something more spectacular from the creators of Test Drive Unlimited.

GEAR.CLUB UNLIMITED 3 is not a bad game in the end: it starts from a driving system that certainly works, with several tracks and a considerable number of cars, but the story is not great and there are many problems on the technical side. Indeed, on PC, with our configuration, we struggled particularly to reach 60 fps. Moreover, the absence of multiplayer is certainly a significant shortcoming, and in terms of content the game offers only two game modes. In short, GEAR.CLUB UNLIMITED 3 is a passable title that could have done much more.

Gear.Club Unlimited 3 represents an unfinished attempt by Eden Games and Nacon to make the decisive leap to the next level, challenging the giants of the racing genre on PC and consoles. The game undoubtedly has its own identity that will appeal to fans of classic arcade games, thanks to a captivating setting split between France and Japan and the excellent integration of the management aspect tied to developing the club’s headquarters. However, the good intentions behind its development are severely undermined by a series of structural flaws that are impossible to ignore in a contemporary production. The severely flawed artificial intelligence, the inconsistent driving physics during drifting sequences, the underlying repetitiveness of the campaign, and the baffling omission of the online multiplayer component prevent the game from competing on equal footing with the industry’s leading titles.
Gear.Club Unlimited 3 is a straightforward racing game that offers a few hours of fun for fans of the genre. Its accessible gameplay also makes it a good starting point for newcomers.

Somebody once told me that sometimes it makes you feel better if something is irredeemably bad, rather than frustratingly lacking, because with the first one you can just walk away and say Yaeah, they did something bad. With games like Gear Club Unlimited 3, I see the ideas; they are there, bubbling right under the surface. As an arcade racer that feels like my childhood, you have NO FLIPPING IDEA how much I wanted to love this game, how much every good intention hurt when every poor design choice cropped up. This is what they meant when all you can do is dwell on what could have been, because clearly they have something in there.

Unlimited 3 has the foundations of a potentially enjoyable racing game, but it still needs more work and polish to appeal to a wider audience. Players looking for a single-player racing experience may find something to enjoy, provided they are willing to overlook some of its shortcomings. However, there is still a long way to go before it can compete with the biggest names in the genre.

Gear.Club Unlimited 3 is a scrappy, B-tier simcade racer that's the best in a flawed series. Despite no multiplayer and tech hiccups, its great car roster and deep customization offer solid fun. Wait for a sale.
Balancing honest ambitions with some undeniable shortcomings, Gear.Club Unlimited 3 remains a more enjoyable arcade racer than its presentation might suggest.

Gear.Club Unlimited 3 is a racing game with some good ideas and a few genuinely enjoyable moments, but it never quite brings everything together. The Japanese setting is a welcome change, the French Mediterranean coast provides a pleasing contrast, and the highway mode adds a different challenge to the usual circuit racing. The car collection and customisation options also give enthusiasts something to work towards.

Unfortunately, inconsistent handling, opposition that doesn’t always provide a convincing challenge, repetitive progression and a lack of online multiplayer all hold it back. The presentation has its moments, but it doesn’t consistently deliver the level of polish that would help the experience stand out.

There is fun to be had here, particularly if you enjoy collecting cars, upgrading your garage and working through a broad selection of events. Yet the individual elements don’t combine into a particularly memorable racing package, and the experience can begin to feel familiar long before you’ve exhausted everything it has to offer.

Gear.Club Unlimited 3 is a perfectly playable racer with a decent foundation, but one that needed more refinement, greater variety and stronger competitive options to make a lasting impression. There’s a good game trying to get out, but it doesn’t quite make it across the finish line.

Gear.Club Unlimited 3 offers a unique experience, to say the least. But it is difficult to determine whether it represents a force. The racing game published by Nacon stands out for its accessible driving, but which is still far from the realism proposed by the references of the genre. We would have appreciated more content, more madness, but we still had fun, and that may be the main thing

Gear.Club Unlimited 3 delivers a pretty and fun arcade racing experience that shines on the Switch 2 hardware. While the garage management is top-tier, the game is held back by the limited car roster and the absence of online multiplayer. It is a solid, stylish racing game that offers a great experience for casual fans.

Unfortunately, Gear.Club Unlimited 3 doesn't live up to expectations on the Switch 2, delivering a repetitive and unpolished game that fails to justify its temporary exclusivity on Nintendo's platform. It's true that die-hard fans of the genre will find some enjoyment in creating and managing their own car club (as well as customizing the paint or tires of licensed cars), but for all other players, it's worth remembering that there are better options on the market.

Considering how bad its predecessors were, this game is easily the best in the trilogy so far, and a clear indication Eden Games has taken fan feedback seriously. It is obviously hampered by the Switch 2’s lack of analog triggers (and it’s not Gamecube controller compatible), but its physics are decent, its responsiveness is good enough, and its framerate is excellent. It does everything it needs to do, it gets the job done in a decent enough state.

Gear.Club Unlimited 3 provides a solid racing experience with various challenges to keep you entertained. Buying different cars and upgrading them to their full potential is exciting. You need some racing background to play as the game assumes you know how to race. If you like standard racing games, this is worth a look but it might not interest other racing fans.
An ambitious effort that aims much higher than its predecessors, Gear.Club Unlimited 3 offers a generous package, interesting tracks and cars, as well as plenty of customization.

Gear.Club Unlimited 3 is a game of "what ifs." What if the ambitious Story Mode was backed by a stable engine? What if the "weather" actually affected the asphalt?
The Highway Rush mode is a blast, and the 40-car roster (featuring the likes of Pagani, Nissan, and Bugatti) is meticulously detailed. However, the frequent game crashes, the complete absence of online play, and a "Graphics" mode that feels like it’s running through mud make this a hard sell for anyone but the most dedicated series fans. Japan deserved a smoother ride than this.

Gear.Club Unlimited 3 is a fast, stylish leap forward for the long-running saga. It blends high-speed racing with deep customisation and a globe-trotting sense of adventure. While not perfect, it delivers a fun and addictive experience that fans of arcade racers and car culture will enjoy. If you want a road trip that mixes pure speed with personality, this one is worth jumping into.

As it stands, Gear Club Unlimited 3 is a fun, if slightly bland racing game that lacks character but has great fundamentals. 

Eden Games have almost twenty racing games under their belt released over the almost thirty year period of their existence and it would have been really cool for Gear Club Unlimited 3 to have a little something to make it stand out from the crowd with all of this studio experience. 

Again, I applaud that it’s a pretty straight racer available for all ages of gamer, but as much as I enjoyed the racing, I was constantly hoping for a little more from the game for it to really, fully engage me.
What we’re left with is a mostly competent, not particularly memorable arcade racer with a handful of highs, but some baffling lows as well.

Gear.Club Unlimited 3 is a racing game that falls short in terms of gameplay options, visuals, and technical performance. The details of the vehicle models and the stories of car culture are good points and will please fans who love cars, but the repetitiveness, lack of innovation, and uninteresting challenges make the whole experience boring after a few minutes of playing.

Gear.Club Unlimited 3 is a fantastic arcade racer on Switch 2, with impressive visuals, and truly engaging handling as you continue to tinker with your cars as you build your showroom. The Club building system is interesting, and while I wish I could navigate the facilities more like a menu, it nonetheless is a fresh take on the upgrade systems we've seen time and time again. If you're looking for a racer that isn't of the Kart variety, then this is it, and you'll pass the finish line in no time.
26.9% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (93 reviews).

Echoes of Aincrad is not a perfect game, but it has many strengths that allow Sword Art Online fans to experience Reki Kawahara’s work from a new perspective. The idea of letting us live the adventure of an ordinary SAO player is a winning one and gives us the chance to truly become the protagonists of a saga that many of us have loved and that others may come to discover, perhaps right through this game. The combat system is well designed in how it combines basic attacks, skills, and synergy with our companions, making the many battles we face engaging. Character progression is tied to crafting and, between missions, you find yourself managing weapons and materials to strengthen yourself and handle level growth in the most effective way possible, in a system that may not be innovative but is satisfying. The main flaw of Echoes of Aincrad is its inability to simulate the liveliness of an MMORPG, with too many silent NPCs and too few points of interest, which would have provided some variety to the many battles. Technically well made, Echoes of Aincrad has a story that struggles to truly take off and cannot be considered a masterpiece, but it remains a good title that takes home the crown as the best video game dedicated to Sword Art Online.

Echoes of Aincrad is a charming game that has intuitive combat and rewarding character growth. Although its repetitiveness brings down the experience from time to time, I still couldn't help but want to keep playing so I could see where my chums would end up next.

Echoes of Aincrad is a much more entertaining and better-executed installment in the SAO franchise thanks to its gameplay improvements and new graphical treatment. Although it still has some aspects to polish, it offers a challenging and highly customizable experience that fans will love. Ultimately, it is a step forward that followers will appreciate.

Sword Art Online: Echoes of Aincrad is ideal for those who are looking for a Dungeon Crawler Experience regardless of its shortcomings. However if you’re one looking for a more traditional Open World RPG with various exploration elements, this entry in the series won't be a suitable choice.

Echoes of Aincrad works when it lets the swords do the talking: the combat system is varied, managing your companion adds a tactical layer the franchise has long been missing, and the crafting, derivative as it is, gives a concrete purpose to every run through dungeons and cities. The problem is everything else. A world that should pulse like a real MMORPG is instead full of mute background characters, a story that takes its time without ever really earning it, and a design choice, locking the Death Game Mode behind a premium purchase.

Sword Art Online: Echoes of Aincrad introduces a few welcome ideas that help refresh the franchise's video game formula. Its Soulslike-inspired combat and maze-like level design make for an engaging experience at first, but the game quickly falls into repetitive patterns. Both its gameplay loop and narrative struggle to evolve over time, preventing its strongest ideas from reaching their full potential.

While the game starts off well as an original story set in the Sword Art Online universe and boasts a very enjoyable combat system, poor gameplay choices and a tedious "semi-open world" will make it difficult to satisfy players outside of the series' fans.

I must confess I was somewhat surprised by the quality of Echoes of Aincrad. Although it still lacks the production value and scope the franchise deserves, it is the title that best recreates the atmosphere of the anime's first season—even without Kirito in the lead role. The chance to experience Sword Art Online from the perspective of an “ordinary” player is precisely what makes it so special, even if that choice comes at a cost.

Echoes of Aincrad from Game Studio Inc. is a wonderful open-world setup that brings gorgeous graphics, good backend character building, easy-to-get-into controls, and a very solid story. What it lacks is enemy variety and action-adventure elements that keep the gameplay engaging long-term.

At its core, Echoes of Aincrad: Sword Art Online is definitely a good action RPG. However, due to its repetitive game design and its reluctance to fully capitalize on the opportunities presented by this fresh perspective on the story of the hit anime, it never quite lives up to its full potential.
It doesn't excel in any particular area, or offer anything that's genuinely new, but Echoes of Aincrad is an enjoyable single-player action RPG experience once it really gets going.

Echoes of Aincrad is a flawed but fun (re)visit to the flying castle of Aincrad. The choice to make the main character of the game a random player in the world of Sword Art Online might be one of the best decisions in recent anime games. The action RPG combat is standard, with a large focus on the weapon you wield, offering the option to pull off some flashy attacks. However, the world and dungeon design have some odd choices built in, like the inability to venture outside a quest area in the open world or the lack of enemies for large chunks of dungeon and world map. But the moment you let go of the believability of this world, the fun starts to come in the monotony, making the experience oddly relaxing. After all, you’re playing a game within a game.
Echoes of Aincrad stands out as an interesting yet imperfect reinterpretation of Sword Art Online’s original arc, offering a true story within the story.

Echoes of Aincrad offers a visually spectacular tribute that stays true to the original storyline, sure to thrill Sword Art Online fans. Unfortunately, its breathtaking world design is hampered by rigid invisible walls, repetitive quests, and clunky combat mechanics. It is a solid, high-quality action RPG, yet it ultimately lacks the polish needed to transcend the limitations of the license.

Echoes of Aincrad draws in fans of the source material with an intriguing narrative, epic battles, and a wide variety of builds, though it lacks character development. However, limited exploration, uninteresting activities, and repetitive enemies make the duels tedious, rendering the project unappealing to new players.

Echoes of Aincrad is a solid albeit middling new entry that adds some enjoyable elements to the franchise. However, many of its gameplay mechanics make the game more frustrating and tedious, ultimately hindering the overall experience.

Echoes of Aincrad is arguably one of the most ambitious video games in the Sword Art Online franchise. Its alternate storyline, solid combat system, and polished audiovisual presentation combine to deliver an entertaining experience.
It was shaping up to be the definitive Sword Art Online game and while it marks an interesting step forward for the franchise, it still ultimately falls short.

Echoes of Aincrad is noble in its concept, but far too repetitive in its execution. While the title boasts a solid and compelling RPG system capable of elevating stat management and equipment customization, a flat gameplay execution ultimately extinguishes any enthusiasm. The bold choice to rewrite the narrative by sidelining Kirito stumbles over a slow and poorly delivered pace, an unconvincing combat system hampered by a total lack of hit impact, completely unrewarding exploration, and an overall repetitiveness that borders on exhausting.
It could have been a top-tier JRPG, but a host of issues leave Echoes of Aincrad: Sword Art Online as nothing more than a game that’s fine for killing time without thinking too much.

I had hoped Echoes of Aincrad would be more than just another licensed anime game, but it never really rises above that label despite its fun concept, enjoyable story moments, and solid action gameplay. The repetitive filler content and a few questionable design choices make it hard to keep playing for long stretches, which is a real shame. Beneath those flaws lies an engaging combat system and great visuals, making it a decent game if you're willing to overlook its shortcomings.

Echoes of Aincrad is the most refreshing Sword Art Online game in years, delivering an original story, immersive MMORPG progression, and meaningful character interactions that finally move beyond simply following Kirito. While repetitive dungeons, shallow crafting, and underdeveloped systems hold it back from reaching its full potential, its strong foundation makes it an encouraging first step for the series, but whether players will take those first steps remains to be seen.

Echoes of Aincrad has the potential to be a stand-out Sword Art Online game, but it struggles to bear the weight of strangely archaic mechanics and monotonous missions. The story and visuals may be enough to get series fans into the game, but anyone else will likely be hard-pressed to get much out of the game.
Echoes of Aincrad is a half-step in the right direction for games based on Sword Art Online.

It's a shame, because the building blocks are actually there. The combat system isn't fantastic, but it's entertaining enough. The weapon system has some good ideas, the simulated MMO atmosphere is actually quite charming, and the whole "death" premise is still strong, even for a new player like me who doesn't have much prior familiarity with Sword Art Online. But Echoes of Aincrad just drags on for too long. It's not a game where I found myself thinking I couldn't wait to see what happened next, rather it became more of a battle between my patience and my stubbornness, where I eventually finished it simply because I'd already got that far.

I wish Echoes of Aincrad were what it was advertised as. It tries to stand out as what fans expect from a game based on the Sword Art Online franchise, but it fails to capture what makes the franchise special. Instead of focusing on its unique setting and world-building, Bandai Namco instead focused on trends and what they think people want in an Action-RPG.

Echoes of Aincrad isn't a bad game for the franchise; in fact, it has memorable moments that really stand out from the other entries. However, the ambition and fantasy it initially promised are too far removed from the actual gameplay experience, with issues related to pacing, quality of life, and content reuse that overshadow its many strengths.

It’s a shame. In my opinion, Echoes of Aincrad provides the best foundation yet for a game set in the Sword Art Online universe. Both in terms of its concept and the fundamental implementation of game mechanics, it lays what appears to be an ideal groundwork—only to do so very little with it. That doesn't mean the title is a total failure; die-hard fans of the source material will likely still find plenty to enjoy. However, the significant gap between the core idea, the presentation, and the game design ultimately relegates Echoes of Aincrad to the ranks of the usual mediocre Sword Art Online titles. And that is a real pity.
While its ideas and open world don't always come together into a cohesive experience, the enjoyable combat and memorable moments still make it a fun action RPG despite its uneven execution.

If you're a fan of Sword Art Online and like big games with highly variable challenges, Echoes of Aincrad is made for you. For my part, I feel like I've had enough, and I won't remember this game as anything other than a game that could have been a summer favorite if it had made a few very simple changes. Balance the difficulty, and fix the level design. Half the game could have been shredded, with good reason.

Echoes of Aincrad fails to leave a lasting impression, but for the hours you put into this Sword Art Online adventure, it satisfies the need for more games like this one. However, it’s bogged down by areas that are a chore to explore, and there’s not enough content to justify making the world’s hubs big, since there’s not enough to do in each one. With that in mind, there’s a whole list of things wrong, but also, the bones of this game move the needle forward, even if it isn’t by much.

Sword Art Online: Echoes of Aincrad aimed to present a darker side of the franchise compared to previous titles featuring Kirito and his allies. In a sense, it succeeds in this regard, boasting a grimmer art style, more detailed environments, and character models that are more polished and realistic—avoiding the overly glossy look of earlier games. Moreover, for a die-hard SAO fan, the experience is exhilarating: stepping into the game world, starting the epic journey from scratch, and engaging in combat that is more skill-based—and thus less automated—than in the past. However, this promising concept runs up against glaring technical and conceptual limitations, including level and game design that feel lazier than expected. Consequently, the forty hours required to complete the adventure are marked by a gameplay loop that feels highly repetitive and not always fully polished. Ultimately, we believe Echoes of Aincrad is a title suited only for die-hard SAO fans.
Echoes of Aincrad needed more time to live up to its own concept.

Echoes of Aincrad is an action game heavily infused with RPG mechanics, but it fails to match the depth of previous Sword Art Online titles, nor does it fully deliver on the new features promised—and indeed clearly visible—at the core of its design. It’s a game aimed exclusively at longtime fans of the series, who will likely be willing to overlook its many rough edges in exchange for references to elements of the game’s lore that were never truly explored in the first season of SAO, such as the elves, the absence of magic, and certain important characters. Although its mechanics are easy to understand and, all things considered, it’s a game that is fairly enjoyable to play without too many issues, its shortcomings are glaring and, above all, difficult to justify. These include an open-map structure that never really allows you to explore the world in its entirety with complete freedom; an RPG system that fails to reward leveling up and prevents you from assigning skill points during missions; and companion AI that, despite its intended role, is hardly intelligent at all. Not to mention a rather unengaging narrative with outcomes that are easy to predict.

The best thing I can say about Echoes of Aincrad is I no longer feel nostalgic for the PS3 generation. Whatever goodwill I had going in is completely drained. I came in thinking that era deserved another chance. I left reminded exactly why we moved on.
A beautiful but insubstantial Sword Art Online spin-off that even hardcore fans of the anime should think twice about buying.

Echoes of Aincrad understands the tone and appeal of Sword Art Online — and that counts for a lot — but it's let down by undercooked gameplay systems and disappointingly dull quest design. Those looking for a grindy action RPG might enjoy how progression is handled, and hardcore fans of the source material will probably push through for the sake of a mostly entertaining story, but you'll still need to stomach so many issues.

Echoes of Aincrad manages the unenviable task of completely squandering the immense potential of its iconic setting. What could have been a thrilling alternate perspective on the classic death game instead devolves into a tedious and frustrating chore. The narrative is poorly paced and abruptly resolved, while exploration is actively discouraged by a disastrous map system and monotonously flat environments. Coupled with a repetitive, unfairly balanced combat system plagued by infinite enemy aggro and poorly designed boss fights, the gameplay loop quickly becomes an exercise in sheer endurance. Despite decent character models, the game is a massive misstep that will make you wish for a forced log-out long before the credits roll.

It’s just that we’re in the middle of a flood of high-quality JRPGs, from indie through to the big blockbusters, and Sword Art Online: Echoes of Aincrad does limit itself in a way that doesn’t do it any favours. The creative and narrative vision is bold and respectable, but offering a poor aping of what many would consider to be the finest game ever made in service of that creative vision was an ill-advised move.

The game starts off promising, but the remaining 95 percent of Echoes of Aincrad consists of repetition and waiting for a game that never actually begins. Even my love for Sword Art Online ultimately wasn't enough to push through it. Echoes of Aincrad isn't a game that's a complete failure. It's far more frustrating than that. It keeps showing you how great it could have been, only to disappoint you time and time again.

Echoes of Aincrad sadly fails as both a standalone RPG adventure or as a fan-pleasing experience for the Sword Art Online community. Its flaws hold it back a lot, and newcomers or seasoned fans alike would be better served playing any of the other games in the franchise instead of this one.

I feel completely and unequivocally indifferent to Echoes of Aincrad. I feel no hate because that would require the game to connect with me at an emotional level — just indifference. And sometimes, that cold detachment is worse than pure, unbridled rage and hatred. This adolescent mess is one that I wouldn’t recommend even to the biggest fan of Sword Art Online.
With Echoes of Aincrad, Bandai Namco tries to once again dive into the world of Sword Art Online, now from a perspective of different players.

Echoes of Aincrad is easily the most enjoyable Sword Art Online game I've played, largely because it finally understands what fans wanted from this series in the first place: letting you experience Aincrad as a custom avatar rather than someone constantly standing in Kirito's shadow.
In the end I was disappointed by Echoes of Aincrad, the pacing of the story combined with what felt to me like a dull world were the major reasons as to why.

Echoes of Aincrad had the makings of being the Sword Art Online game that people have been waiting for. While it made strides in the right direction, the game shed the “anime game” feel but now wears a “generic RPG” badge.
Echoes of Aincrad's premise is a vaguely interesting one. You're a player in a Sword Art Online VRMMORPG experience, which requires the wearing of...
Echoes of Aincrad gives you customisation tools to forge your own Sword Art Online story, but its repetitive design and lingering pace all but remove your sense of agency.
Echoes of Aincrad opens with your player being among the lucky (or perhaps unlucky) few who have been given access to the Beta of SAO.
If you’re new to Sword Art Online, this may be a tougher sell. But if you’re already a fan of the series, Echoes of Aincrad is still worth playing, even with its shortcomings.

Fans of Sword Art Online can certainly thank Bandai Namco for rescuing their favourite game series from the dark ages, as for the first time ever we’ve been treated to modern, well-made and beautiful digital adventures featuring Kirito and his friends.

Sometimes, the most disappointing thing about a game is realizing that its best moments prove the developers genuinely know what they're doing—only for its most repetitive and tedious stretches to reveal that they never figured out how to tie those great ideas together into a satisfying whole.

Sword Art Online: Echoes of Aincrad is exactly that kind of game. At its best, it has enough strengths to make it worth revisiting in the future, especially once its price comes down, and it could even introduce more players to the world of SAO. Until then, however, it remains little more than another decent release aimed primarily at those who are already dedicated fans of the franchise.

Echoes of Aincrad is a solid addition to the Sword Art Online franchise. While its restrictive world design prevents it from reaching its full potential, the new story, memorable characters, and faithful recreation of Aincrad make it an enjoyable experience for longtime SAO fans. If you've always wanted another adventure in Aincrad, this is still worth playing—just don't expect the open-world experience many fans have dreamed of.
Echoes of Aincrad is the best SAO game so far thanks to genuinely demanding combat, but its okay story and empty world leave it far from a masterpiece.

In Summary, Echoes of Aincrad is what feels like a truly generational fumble by Bandai Namco and Game Studio Inc. They created a game world that simultaneously looks amazing but feels devoid of life. A world that encompasses so many great aspects of Sword Art Online itself but feels as if it’s actively choking you to death because of game mechanics that honestly feel like they belong in the dustbin of history.

Echoes of Aincrad had the potential to be a remarkable title, but after careful evaluation, it ultimately feels as though it reached the market before it was truly ready. While its impressive visuals, powered by modern game engines, make for an eye-catching presentation, the experience ultimately struggles to deliver the substance needed to match its ambitions.

Echoes of Aincrad is by no means a bad game, it’s just not enough “game” I think. Combat could’ve used more fleshing out, the environments needed more to actually care about, and the story is just the story of Sword Art Online. If you’re a more casual gamer and want to experience SAO without watching any anime, it’s probably pretty solid for you, but it’s just not enough.

Echoes of Aincrad offers a fresh look at Sword Art Online, moving away from Kirito to tell our own story inside Aincrad. Its direct combat, companions and setting work well, although the story feels a little short and the maps can become confusing.

As expansive as its environments may be, as accessible as its narrative is, and as much as it draws on the popularity of genres such as soulslikes, Echoes of Aincrad is a collection of ideas that never rises above familiar territory, with not a hint of imagination. It can be enjoyable at times, but is also extremely limited when it should have been a breath of fresh air for fans of the series.
Echoes of Aincrad wouldn't be my first recommendation for RPG or action game fans, but it certainly wouldn't be my last one, either. It's simply solid, and sometimes that's enough.

Echoes of Aincrad feels designed to deliberately waste your time. It’s by no means a bad game, there’s a lot of interesting elements to enjoy including the story, the world, and the combat. However, it does itself a disservice by padding the game out excessively with repetitive missions and forced exploration. With strange restrictions on exploration and questionable design choices, it doesn’t respect the player, and suffers for it.

Echoes of Aincrad feels like the long-awaited promise the Sword Art Online franchise has owed its fans for years - and it comes frustratingly close to fulfilling it, which somehow makes it even more disappointing than if it had never tried at all.

Echoes of Aincrad is an odd one for me; I do like it a lot, but I found myself getting just a little annoyed at the lack of variation in enemy types and the battles getting easier because of this. There is a lot to like about Echoes of Aincrad if you are new to the SAO universe, but fans of the anime might find themselves getting a little frustrated at themes they have seen before. I would recommend this to those of you who enjoy a good RPG and who want to invest in the lore of the SAO universe.

Echoes of Aincrad offers an enjoyable action combat system, satisfying cooperation with companions, epic multi-phase boss fights, and a beautiful world. Unfortunately, repetitive enemies and quests, empty locations, uneven responsiveness, and a gradually stagnating story make the roughly fifty-hour adventure feel underdeveloped, especially at its premium price.

Echoes of Aincrad is a good game with an interesting narrative, a beautiful world, and simple but effective combat. Despite some strange design choices and repetitive elements, there’s a lot to like here for both Sword Art Online fans and newcomers alike. It’s easily the best Sword Art Online game yet.
Echoes of Aincrad had a huge opportunity in its hands and squeezes almost every good idea into a shallow, disappointing execution.

Echoes of Aincrad turned out to be a pleasant surprise. This time, the developers decided to go for a much freer, more 'MMORPG-like' approach, giving players a game that manages to pay tribute to the nature of the work while also being fun and satisfying. This is also thanks to a fast, technical, and entertaining combat system, even if, in the long run, it tends to get a bit repetitive. If I really wanted to nitpick, I’d say I didn’t enjoy the beginning much—it’s just too slow and boring, which could turn more than one player away from a game that actually knows how to entertain and excite.

Echoes of Aincrad captures the thrill of survival within the floating castle through a highly dynamic real-time action combat system with Soulslike nuances, deep avatar customization, and a comprehensive alchemy and blacksmithing system—making it an unmissable RPG adventure for fans of the genre, despite suffering from some repetitiveness in its enemy roster.

Echoes of Aincrad is a title that, at first glance, offers a world full of potential for Sword Art Online fans and even newcomers. But the deeper you go, the more you encounter only repetition and weakness.

Echoes of Aincrad is a prime example of an excellent conceptual vision ruined by a gameplay experience that is unnecessarily drawn out and lacks any real boldness in its design. Although the melee combat system offers genuine moments of fun and the smithy ensures considerable depth in weapon customization, the game collapses under the weight of outdated game design, recycled content, and a narrative progression that drowns its more mature themes in a slow pace. This is a game that may perhaps entertain the most die-hard fans of the universe created by Reki Kawahara for a few hours—those drawn in by the visual fidelity and the charm of an adventure experienced from the perspective of a beta tester—but for any other fan of action RPGs, it will prove to be a repetitive experience that hit the market before it was fully mature.
Echoes of Aincrad delivers one of the most immersive Sword Art Online experiences yet, thanks to its satisfying combat, meaningful progression, and fully customizable protagonist.

I enjoyed my time with Echoes of Aincrad. It successfully does something different with the Sword Art Online formula by allowing players to experience the Aincrad incident through an entirely new perspective, and that alone makes it feel fresh. Strong combat, enjoyable progression, excellent presentation, and a genuinely engaging story make it an easy recommendation for fans of the series.

Echoes of Aincrad faithfully recreates the visual universe of Sword Art Online and offers a functional combat system with extensive equipment optimization possibilities. Its smooth performance—using Unreal Engine 5—and the polished aesthetic of its main environments demonstrate a significant improvement in production compared to previous installments in the franchise. However, this new SAO is limited by a monotonous mission design, an exploration system restricted by invisible barriers, and a marked reuse of enemies and bosses. So, unless you're a die-hard fan of Reki Kawahara's work, it's difficult to overlook some of its shortcomings.
I actually enjoyed the basics and found the story and characters entertaining. But the limited exploration, the sometimes chaotic combat and the unsatisfying ending detract from the experience.

'Echoes of Aincrad' was a title armed with ideas that fans would welcome. Viewing the original work through the eyes of a unique original protagonist offered a freshness distinct from spin-offs. However, compared to such an interesting story and setting, it was difficult to find any appealing aspects in the gameplay. In fact, setting aside its unique appeal, the level design—which should be considered the fundamentals—was so drawn out that it felt disappointing.

Sword Art Online: Echoes of Aincrad successfully shakes up the formula with an engaging, flexible action-RPG combat system and rewarding partner mechanics. Unfortunately, severe pacing issues, a lifeless custom protagonist completely overshadowed by Kirito, restrictive invisible walls, and heavily recycled enemy designs relegate this barebones spin-off to a tedious, budget-strained slog.
Despite various limitations, Echoes of Aincrad is a visually and technically solid tribute that offers SAO fans a unique way to experience the world of Aincrad from a fresh perspective.

Despite my wide array of criticisms, Echoes of Aincrad was still a pretty solid experience, but its gameplay and exploration are the weakest parts of the whole package. With a solid story and interesting characters, the recreation of the Death Game is as good as we've had it so far. Combat is fine enough, but exploration suffers due to invisible walls, and a stumbling in the dark approach to traversing it. Regardless, Echoes of Aincrad does make large strides in the right direction of being “that” Sword Art Online game we've always wanted, I just wish it felt more like the grand MMO it was needing to be.
Echoes of Aincrad is a bland, tedious attempt to cash in on the nostalgia of Sword Art Online fans, offering little more than a dozen hours of boredom.

A somewhat failed attempt to translate the Sword Art Online experience into the video game medium. Kirito and company will have to wait a little longer for the adaptation that finally does them true justice.

Echoes of Aincrad is an incredibly frustrating game because so much of it works, yet doesn’t. Its core combat mechanics, progression, and story all show flashes of what made the original series so enjoyable, yet they’re all tied together by a genuinely frustrating exploration system that repeatedly and severely undercuts their strengths.

Sword Art Online has always had a premise that seemed perfect for video games: living inside an MMORPG where every battle, level gained, and decision becomes part of a fight for survival. Echoes of Aincrad embraces that concept by placing players directly into the world of Aincrad, allowing them to create their own character and experience the early events of the series from a fresh perspective.

Unlike previous adaptations, the adventure is not centered solely on Kirito. Familiar characters such as Asuna, Argo, and Kirito himself remain part of the story, but players take on the role of another survivor trapped inside the game, struggling to grow stronger and find their own path through that world.


The opening hours, however, take a while to reveal the game's full potential. The prologue keeps players confined to enclosed environments for an extended period, functioning almost entirely as a lengthy tutorial while introducing the core mechanics. This approach fits the initial feeling of being trapped inside Aincrad, but it also delays the moment when the game begins to showcase its strongest qualities.

Once that introductory section is finally over and players begin exploring the open areas, towns, and landscapes, it becomes much easier to understand what Echoes of Aincrad is trying to accomplish: transforming one of anime's most iconic settings into a world where players can truly forge their own adventure.
Sword Art Online: Echoes of Aincrad proves to be one of Bandai Namco’s strongest video game adaptations, although it still struggles with some of the common issues found in modern JRPGs.

Boss fights finally made me slow down in Echoes of Aincrad. Instead of cutting through another easy enemy, I had to react to what was happening and create an opening for my partner to counter. The story moved too slowly between those fights, and blocked paths kept exploration tied to the current quest. Repeated enemies made the trip to the next boss drag. This is mainly for dedicated Sword Art Online fans who want another trip through Aincrad and can accept how often repetition gets in the way.
Echoes of Aincrad is a serviceable entry point for most casual fans, complementing the main narrative without ever detracting from it.

Echoes of Aincrad delivers an enjoyable action RPG packed with meaningful progression, satisfying combat, and enough original storytelling to keep even the most die-hard Sword Art Online fans invested.

Sword Art Online: Echoes of Aincrad represents the franchise's most ambitious chapter. With engaging combat, rewarding exploration, good customization, and a story that works for both veterans and newcomers, the RPG delivers a solid experience.
Echoes of Aincrad has real heart in its soundtrack and world design, but empty, linear zones and constant enemy recycling drag it down. Combat is genuinely fun, just not enough to save the pace.
Echoes of Aincrad has the bones of the SAO game longtime fans have wanted for years; it just needed more time in the oven to fill out everything surrounding that skeleton.

Echoes of Aincrad initially seems like an ambitious adventure, especially with its story concept and its beautiful world, in addition, of course, to its relatively entertaining combat. However, the game quickly loses its luster, and a set of design decisions turns it into a mediocre experience.

Echoes of Aincrad is a well-realised RPG about the people behind the avatars. While repetitive exploration and awkward world design hold it back, its excellent characters, satisfying combat, and genuine love for MMORPG culture make it the strongest Sword Art Online game yet,and an enjoyable action RPG even for people who don't care for the anime.

Echoes of Aincrad is a disappointing entry from Bandai Namco. Despite its promising premise, the story falls flat, while repetitive content and a $70 price tag make it hard to recommend. Only dedicated Sword Art Online fans may enjoy it, as its biggest flaws are rooted in the game's core design.

Artistic Style and Performance: Regarding the artistic style, it seems that Bandai has allocated a huge budget for this series; as the game features precise and dazzling details for a game that adopts the Japanese animation (Anime) style. Thanks to the beautiful lighting and visual effects, the game maintains a smooth and stable performance at a rate of 60 frames per second, despite the existence of some slight slowdowns or occasional stutters during battles.
Echoes of Aincrad mixes mismatched genres, sluggish pacing, shallow exploration, and lackluster combat into a dated MMO‑like experience that is helped only by a few genuinely strong characters.

Echoes of Aincrad delivers a promising story, engaging characters, and a solid combat system that offers a satisfying challenge. However, its empty world, weak level design, and excessive repetition of missions and enemies undermine the sense of exploration, causing the experience to gradually lose its charm over time.

If you are a fan of Sword Art Online, Echoes of Aincrad offers a chance to return once again to one of the series’ most beloved worlds. However, if you are entering this universe for the first time, you should know that despite all of its strengths, the game is less a revolution in the JRPG genre and more a faithful and charming experience for fans of the world of Aincrad. Ultimately, Echoes of Aincrad proves that even after all these years, the original idea behind Sword Art Online still retains its appeal: the dream of being inside a game that can be beautiful, exciting, and dangerous all at the same time.
Like being trapped inside a virtual MMO, there’s a great adventure in here somewhere. You just have to grind through a few too many fetch quests before you find it.

Echoes of Aincrad is the Sword Art Online game I’ve been waiting for ever since I watched the anime's first arc and thought, 'Why has no game actually put me inside this world?' The decision to replace Kirito with a player-created character is the most important move the gaming franchise has made in its history, and it completely transforms the emotional equation of the experience.

Sword Art Online: Echoes of Aincrad tells an engaging story that lets you experience the events of Aincrad from your own perspective, with emotional character moments and surprisingly dark themes. While the combat remains enjoyable, repetitive enemies and a highly linear quest structure quickly become monotonous. Its beautiful environments create the illusion of an open world, but exploration is largely superficial, making the adventure feel more like a single-player MMO without the benefits of actual multiplayer.

Sword Art Online deserved better than Echoes of Aincrad is able to deliver. The combat and the upgrade and crafting systems are enjoyable, but they're almost completely undermined by the painfully linear level design, the repetitive mission structure, and the way exploration is rendered virtually pointless.

The game's biggest strength is its story, which remains surprisingly serious for most of the adventure before eventually falling back on the usual "save the world" clichés. Unfortunately, your protagonist still feels like a supporting character throughout the story and could easily be removed from many of the cutscenes without changing much.

We recommend that everyone try the demo first to make sure the gameplay is something you'll enjoy, because otherwise the disappointment could be significant.

Despite being tied to Sword Art Online, Echoes of Aincrad is worth checking out for its own merits, as there is a polished and pristine sheen here that most anime-based RPG games don’t get. While it won’t surprise you, it will give you several dozen hours of exciting action and exploration.

"The long-awaited Sword Art Online adventure"
Echoes of Aincrad delivers the most ambitious take on the Sword Art Online universe yet, giving players the chance to experience Aincrad firsthand rather than just follow its events. With its engaging combat system, expansive exploration, and sophisticated progression system, the game lays a solid foundation that could make it the best game in the series to date. Despite some minor performance issues and the lack of multiplayer, the current experience is very promising for fans of Sword Art Online and action RPGs.

Echoes of Aincrad delivers fun combat and pleasing visuals, making the journey through Aincrad quite engaging. However, the repetitive open world and some design decisions prevent the game from reaching its full potential. Even so, it is a competent action RPG that will certainly appeal to most players

Despite its flaws, I enjoyed my over 50 hours with Echoes of Aincrad. It is an easy recommendation for fans of the franchise and a cautious recommendation for people who enjoy action JRPGs and are looking for an MMO feeling. Developer Game Studio Inc. created a solid foundation that they can hopefully build upon in the DLC or a sequel covering the higher floors of Aincrad.

Echoes of Aincrad ushers in a new era for Sword Art Online games, bringing long-requested elements such as a return to the series most famous arc with a brand-new story, while completely overhauling the series combat and exploration mechanics and establishing a solid foundation for the future of Sword Art Online in video games.

Echoes of Aincrad is great because it lets us bring our own character into the Sword Art Online story. With a beautiful, vast map of Aincrad and smooth, well-paced gameplay, the game stands out not only as a great SAO game but also as an excellent action RPG. The problem is that this deep immersion sometimes comes at the cost of a very slow pace, which takes a while to pick up speed; furthermore, while the immense Aincrad is a feast for the eyes, its level design doesn’t always make exploration fun. This slightly dims the luster of the experience, though it doesn’t completely overshadow it.

Echoes of Aincrad is a classic case of "sometimes less is more". It's a game that dilutes too much of its content in an attempt to look grander than it is. This can be a fun experience for those who value certain gameplay loops and new takes on established combat formulas, but it's frankly unacceptable for a AAA title. Only major SAO fans will likely get something out of this one.

Echoes of Aincrad delivers one of the most fun experiences in the entire Sword Art Online franchise, featuring extremely responsive real-time combat, a good variety of mechanics, and the freedom to create your own character.
