Industria 2 has a great premise and fun gameplay, but it's in dire need of better optimization.
INDUSTRIA 2 feels like a late alpha. It's seemingly playable from start to finish.
The dystopian action returned in a sequel that we expected would learn from the original game's shortcomings. It didn't. But at least main protagonist Nora gets to finish her story.

But for all the care that went into world-building, it didn’t feel like any went into the rest of the game. I haven’t ruled out going back and playing the first game to see if I’ve missed something great, but Industria II certainly makes it hard to want to do that.

Industria 2 impresses above all with its atmosphere, audiovisual presentation and original world. It is precisely in these areas that it demonstrates that even a small studio can come up with a distinctive creative vision. However, when it comes to the gameplay itself, it becomes apparent that a number of mechanics have only been partially refined. Combat tends to become repetitive, the artificial intelligence isn’t particularly convincing, and the technical performance remains inconsistent despite patches.

It is an incredibly charming independent project that shows how even a small studio can create a world with enough depth and aesthetic strength to stand alongside gaming legends. It perfectly understands why people loved Half-Life, giving you the feeling of being in the middle of a vast, mysterious adventure. Unfortunately, all of its strengths are currently buried under technical rough edges. If you do not mind the occasional restart, can tolerate technical bugs, and are looking for an atmospheric story-driven shooter for a couple of evenings, you will not regret picking it up.

From the very beginning, Industria 2 presents a dual image of itself. You can see the developer's effort to create a mechanical world with an intriguing atmosphere that constantly encourages you to keep going and uncover the final mystery. On the other hand, technical issues and numerous bugs prevent this potential from fully flourishing. After going through an Early Access period, we expected a more polished and cohesive title.

If you played and enjoyed the original INDUSTRIA, this is an easy recommendation — the sequel improves on every dimension that matters narratively and atmospherically, and the roughness of the launch is being addressed actively. If you’re new to the series, the 4-6 hour runtime at $24.99 is reasonable value for what’s here, especially with the introductory discount active.

Our honest advice: either grab it now knowing you’re buying into a work in progress, or wait 60-90 days for another patch cycle to clear the most disruptive bugs. Either way, this is an indie team with vision and craft, and INDUSTRIA 2 at its best shows exactly what Bleakmill is capable of when everything clicks. We’re rooting for them to get there.

INDUSTRIA 2 is a work deeply torn between the ambition of its developers and the harsh reality of a production process that has faced formidable obstacles. On the one hand, we are faced with an atmospheric experience of rare power, capable of transporting the player into a dystopian universe, while on the other hand, one cannot ignore the state of technical instability in which the title was released. Nora’s journey remains an experience worth having, but it is a journey that currently requires an excessive amount of patience, pending new patches that resolve these issues.

INDUSTRIA II feels very much like the kind of horror movie sequel that gets rushed to market after the moderate success of its predecessor. The story is continued competently enough, but the gameplay feels abandoned halfway through development. Ideas that the original INDUSTRIA introduced — whether narratively or mechanically — are only superficially touched upon here, leaving them unable to make any meaningful impact in Industria II.

And then there is the technical state of the game, which ultimately becomes the final nail in the coffin and pushes an otherwise merely dull experience firmly into frustrating territory. As things currently stand, I simply cannot recommend Industria II. Perhaps Bleakmill will manage to bring the game closer to a solid state through extensive updates, at which point it might become an easy recommendation for fans of the first title. I certainly hope so.
Industria 2 is the sequel we wouldn’t have wished for even in our worst nightmares. Its release was far too rushed.

There is still a spark of what made Industria intriguing in some of the settings and lore we can find, but the package as a whole just misses the mark for me. It is technically average at best, with slow, plodding, and uninteresting gunplay and a story that feels like a step backwards from the original in almost every regard.

Industria 2 delivers good ideas, a strong atmosphere, and welcome gameplay additions, but its technical issues and inconsistent level design hold the experience back. Some moments successfully capture the magic of the first game, while others feel noticeably weaker in comparison.

Nickelodeon Extreme Tennis: Next! includes much of what you might expect and have seen before, but there’s still plenty of flashy, colourful fun to be had. It all feels good to play, with the real standout coming from the large roster of Nick toons, new and old. It’s pretty great to see Rocko, CatDog, and Invader Zim dash around the courts and all with their own fully voice-acted on-court quips. It’s not the deepest or biggest arcade sports game available, but it’s a pretty fun time.

If you’re looking for a casual sports game crammed to the ceiling with familiar faces, you’re in luck! Nickelodeon Extreme Tennis: Next! is a pure tennis experience that performs its duty admirably. It just couldn’t get its hooks in me somehow.
I’m not going to sugar coat it, Nickelodeon Extreme Tennis: Next isn’t a great game. Sure, there is a few hours of fun to be had but after that you will more than likely never turn this on again.

In the end, Nickelodeon Extreme Tennis: Next! is not a deep or competitive tennis simulation, nor does it aspire to be. Instead, it offers a cheerful, chaotic, and relatively inexpensive cartoon party game that thrives when enjoyed with friends on the couch.
Old Skull Games and Gameloft bring us an alternative take on tennis featuring Nickelodeon characters.

Nickelodeon Extreme Tennis: Next! delivers fast-paced arcade tennis, a charming cast of iconic Nickelodeon characters and plenty of multiplayer fun, even if its simple mechanics limit its long-term appeal.

Nickelodeon Extreme Tennis: Next! manages to provide a few hours of entertainment thanks to its accessible approach and its charming cast of characters from the brand’s famous franchises. The arcade-style tennis gameplay is generally well-executed, the special powers add a bit of personality to the matches, and the co-op mode is a welcome addition. However, the initial fun quickly fades due to extremely repetitive progression, limited content, and a clear lack of variety in the courts and activities on offer. The game constantly gives the impression that it could have offered so much more. I hope future updates will enhance the experience!

Nickelodeon Extreme Tennis: Next! For fans of arcade sports games, Nickelodeon crossovers, or just anyone looking for a colorful multiplayer experience. Next up is a pleasant surprise, with far more depth than you might expect from its mobile origins.

Nickelodeon Extreme Tennis: Next! is a fun arcade tennis game built around quick matches, character abilities, power-ups, and local 1v1 play. Story Mode and cosmetic unlocks put some structure around solo play, but the missing online multiplayer holds it back once couch matches run their course. If you have someone nearby and want a fun Nickelodeon sports game, it’s an easy pick. If you need online competition or deeper tennis, its limits show quickly.

This is another Nickelodeon dud in the video game space in 2026. While the tennis can be fun at times, the overall execution falls short. There’s not enough content, the music is horrible, and some of the gameplay can feel awkward while returning shots. The power-ups are cool for the most part, but it doesn’t save Nickelodeon Extreme Tennis: Next! from mediocrity.

Overall, Dracamar is a lot of fun, but definitely has more to offer players that recall the early days of 3D platforming with fondness. With charming but simple visuals, somewhat stilted dialogue, and fun platforming across expansive levels, Dracamar feels like a moment caught in time in the best of ways, providing players with a taste of the way things used to be. For anyone that loved the heyday of 3D platformers, or is looking for an enjoyable jaunt through a colorful world, Dracamar is one to keep in mind!

If you’re a fan of classic 3D platformers, Dracamar evokes those in all the right ways. It may feel like a lost oddity from another continent and generation, but as far as I’m concerned, that’s all part of its charm.

Dracamar is a bright, colourful, family-friendly game that is easy on the eye and great to play. It makes for a great introduction to 3D Platforming to anyone that is new to the genera. Or anyone that is looking for a more laid-back time. Some gamers might find it too easy. And I feel that the progression system does undermine the accessiblity of the game. Still, a fun time to be had nonetheless!
Overall, I did enjoy the game even though it seemed to be geared towards a younger audience with the visuals and simplistic story and characters.

Overall, Dracamar will not set the world on fire with its gameplay, but if you are looking for a fun and cosy platformer to play over a long weekend, or you are looking for something to get a younger child into gaming with a fun, cute art style, then Dracamar is for you.
PS2-era-inspired 3D platformer that plays it safe

Dracamar is exactly the kind of game you might easily overlook at first glance, but it will surprise you all the more once you give it a chance. Its unassuming style hides a superbly designed 3D platformer full of imaginative levels, a pleasant pace, and the joy of discovery. Thanks to its lower difficulty and approachable tone, it’s also ideal for younger players or family gaming. At the same time, with its variety and thoughtful design, it easily holds its own even among more experienced fans of the genre. Great platformers are still alive and well—and not just on the Switch!

Dracamar has a nice idea of what it wants to be, I just don't think the feel of the game matches its charm. Its platforming is serviceable, and the transformations of Oki can be interesting, but Dracamar chooses the safest path at every opportunity. If you are new to platformers, then I can see someone enjoying this, even if there are countless better examples on the platform, but experienced players can easily skip this one.

Dracamar offers a charming 3D platforming experience that will appeal to players of all ages. While its simple mechanics and exploration elements provide a casual level of entertainment, the difficulty in accessing progression features is the primary factor undermining its potential. Camera-related modeling issues and text input problems stand as areas with room for improvement, particularly in light of the level design.

Dracamar is a humble, simple, and effective platformer. It doesn't stand out for its innovation or for offering a particularly deep experience, but it knows exactly what it wants to be and delivers on that promise.

Dracamar is a solid 3D Jump &a; Run with surprisingly long levels that, due to its low difficulty and straightforward level design, is particularly suitable for younger players and genre newcomers. Apart from a few cosmetic flaws, the whole thing is presented in a successful manner, making Dracamar a quite recommendable genre representative.

Dracamar will appeal to a niche audience despite its colourful and simple design. Although I appreciated the nod to a bygone era, I’m not sure it will attract a large following. This is a shame, as I think the safe gameplay, smooth action, and interesting stage design make this a low-key but great addition to the genre. Accordingly, I enjoyed it and recommend grabbing a copy from the Xbox store!

To round off this review of Dracamar, I have to say that I found it to be a charming and enjoyable game, ideal for unwinding. It’s not a title that’s going to revolutionise anything, but it does the job well as a simple platform adventure. It stands out for its Mediterranean setting and its positive tone, but it falls a little short in terms of depth and originality.
Works as an accessible and family-friendly 3D platformer, but has some design issues

Dracamar doesn’t reinvent the platforming genre. What it offers is a bright, easy going adventure focused on exploration, collecting and helping restore a lively world. It’s accessible, it’s cheerful, and it’s the kind of game you can enjoy without too much pressure.

There are moments where it feels a bit familiar, and players looking for a more demanding platformer might not find what they’re after here. But if you’re after something light, colourful and enjoyable to chip away at, especially on a handheld, this is well worth a look.

Dracamar is an exceedingly simple platformer, with mostly straightforward platforming and level design that holds very few surprises. This simple design is an excellent starting point for children, as the mechanics are not needlessly complex or obtuse, but offers little for adult players beyond mindless time-passing.

Highguard is a top-notch PvP shooter, not your average fare, but rather a highly creative and unique game concept whose main mode blends three phases into a virtually ever-changing gameplay experience. Individual gameplay elements, such as the armor system, might initially seem disconcerting, but prove their worth in practice. Further improvements and new content are also to be expected and could elevate an already strong online action game to an even more outstanding one.

The core gameplay of Highguard is fun, so much so that I can see myself playing it as my go-to multiplayer game for the rest of the year. And as the year goes on, Highguard should become an even better game. As it stands, my biggest issue with the game is its lack of content compared to its competitors, but that should be addressed in future updates.

Highguard is undoubtedly a unique proposition in the world of live service and online shooter games, effectively silencing those who expected something derivative. It's clear that this experience isn't for everyone and lacks the diversity to be truly engaging at launch. This makes it a risky gamble. Nevertheless, Highguard was created with passion and will offer anyone willing to give it a try some truly great moments thanks to its well-crafted gameplay loop. But above all, it conveys the feeling that it was created with care and dedication.

Highguard is definitely not a bad game. But it’s also not the kind of game that opens a new era. And honestly, expecting every game to redefine a genre would be absurd anyway. That’s why you should give this already free game at least a chance, because it does include some gameplay elements that might genuinely surprise you. Outside of those, it delivers an experience that’s fairly close to a classic FPS.
Highguard is a fascinating shooter game that still feels like a construction site: It will need some patches to reach its full potential.
Highguard is a competent shooter that tries to appeal to too many people and thus stumbles over its own feet.

The bones of Highguard are solid: the gunplay feels crisp, traversal is slick, and the rounds can be incredibly tense. But at launch, myriad balance issues, overcomplicated round structure, and repetitive-feeling matches dampen the game. Wait for a few months until it's been chiseled into shape.

Highguard delivers solid shooting mechanics reminiscent of Apex Legends, but it is severely hampered by terrible optimization and disjointed gameplay systems that fail to mesh organically. While it avoids the disastrous fate of Concord thanks to its unique siege and vehicle combat, the experience is currently marred by muddy graphics and poor audio, making it feel like an intriguing but unpolished experiment.

Highguard is a smart, messy experiment. When its two-phase loop hits the right density and coordination, the Shieldbreaker turns matches into tense, goal-driven sieges, and the gunplay has the bite to carry the climax. But that same structure can stretch into long prep stretches and noticeable downtime, especially in 3v3 and solo queue, where timing and intent rarely line up. On PC it holds up well, yet the world and Wardens still lack the kind of personality that sticks. Bottom line: a solid concept with rough edges, best for players who want a deliberate raid shooter rather than nonstop firefights.
Highguard's central mode is genuinely cool, but it's overstuffed with FPS trends that should go away for a while.
Highguard sets a strong foundation for something more interesting to come down the line, if given the proper time and feedback. The core of what's there is solid, it just needs more refinement.

Wildlight Entertainment has actually created a concept with immense potential to revolutionize the industry, combining multiple game modes and elements into something truly unique. However, the whole thing crashes and burns due to a shaky foundation of gameplay mechanics and a multitude of other issues. To put it simply, Highguard was a gamble that was revealed a little too early and needs much more time in the oven to become the next big thing.

Highguard isn't ready for prime time. It's not an awful game that's unplayable. It has extremely fun moments when you're playing with your friends, but they're fleeting. It's not something that I would introduce into my rotation of multiplayer games. In its current state, Highguard is an aggressively okay game that needs a lot of work.
There is definitely fun to be had in Highguard, especially with a group of friends but as it stands I wouldn’t bet on it become the new Apex of the genre because it’s nowhere near that level.

Highguard is a game that demonstrates that a new multiplayer concept alone is insufficient. While the premise is interesting, the developers failed to strike the right balance. The 3v3 battles did not help the game at launch, and there was little content. The game may never recover from its poor start.

While Highguard has received far more hate than it deserves, the game just isn't all that good in its current state. It's a mishmash of genre tropes that never quite come together, and even the odd enjoyable moment isn't enough to make it worth your while.

Highguard delivers an original concept but fails to execute it as well as needed. Attractive yet lifeless maps, an unnecessary opening phase, and weak balancing of weapons and heroes weigh it down. In a coordinated trio, it does deliver some adrenaline-fueled and tactical firefights, yet it excels at nothing in particular. The gameplay mode quickly grows tiresome, resulting overall in a completely forgettable experience, one of many that have come and gone before.
For the moment, however, the original ideas in the details of its design are suffocated by bigger problems in its structure and pacing. [Issue #421, p.110]
Wildlight Entertainment's PvP raid shooter mash-up of multiplayer elements offers a repetitive, uninspired and dull time.
Compelling gunplay and a unique raid mode help this FPS stand out.
Highguard is an unusual combination of first-person shooter trends from the last decade, making for a game that is hard to define.
A new shooter with lots of familiar elements.

Highguard absolutely does not deserve the hype around its release, which was largely stirred up by Geoff Keighley. Instead of a surprise launch, the developers should have conducted extensive testing to identify all the core issues with the gameplay foundation from the start. However, the train has now left the station, and the audience's attention has shifted to other projects.

Highguard has potential, but it's not quite being met yet. As it stands today, this is a fun yet bloated shooter that lacks the spark you'll find in other games in the genre, like The Finals. It'll play to the tactical players out there, and it seems that Wildlight is committed to improving the game. But with a game mode that crams every type of shooter into a single experience, Highguard is a jack of all trades and master of none.

Highguard is a fresh take on the multiplayer hero shooter, featuring balanced gunplay and thrilling raid mechanics that had me saying, "Just one more match." Throw in strong art direction with a high fantasy setting, and it gets an easy recommendation from me.
From minute tweaks to large siege towers, Wildlight's detail-oriented attitude helps lift Highguard above the usual Hero shooter fare.
A free shooter that doesn't make the most of its best ideas: the potential is there, but at the moment it suffers from balance, performance, and repetitiveness issues.
Quote not available

It’s unfortunate that most people reading this have already made up their minds about Highguard, some through playing it themselves, others dismissing it outright due to a number of factors, and the few that just aren’t into this kind of game and are reasonable about it. If you are reading this and there’s a spark of curiosity in you about it, dive in.

Is Highguard a bad game? Debatable. It’s not the worst game ever and the absolutely hateful reviews the game has received from people who haven’t even played it are baffling, but it is… remarkably unremarkable.

However, issues like high cosmetic prices, lacking game modes, and overall feeling of a lack of polish, weigh heavily on the game as it stands. None of these problems feel insurmountable, but they do prevent Highguard from reaching its full potential at launch. Highguard is a good game with flashes of greatness and the possibility of becoming something truly special if its developers continue to build on its promising core.

Highguard is successful because it knows its limits and designs around them. It doesn't try to be too big or flashy to be understood. Besides, it gives you a tightly constructed tactical experience that is based on purpose and clarity. A single design theory is supported by all systems.
31.6% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (19 reviews).

Qliphah in Providence’s Shadow is made for a very niche audience. It’s a horror JRPG with a combat system built to appeal to fighting game fans. The combat is deep and is going to be a dream come true for some. This might even be a great entry JRPG for Arc System Work’s usual fighting game audience. Normally I would be hesitant to widely recommend something this niche, but Qliphah in Providence’s Shadow is most easily compared to Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. There are a lot of people waiting for a game influenced by it, and this is the first great one.

It took me roughly sixteen hours to finish my Qliphah in Providence’s Shadow playthrough, though I imagine it might be a shorter turnaround for those who can master countering quickly. While I do feel the game pads some fights to make them last longer, such as including multiple phases or bosses with huge health pools, they feel brief enough due to how quickly combat flies once you’re used to gameplay. I give Qliphah in Providence’s Shadow credit that I didn’t feel like it was rushed or condensed, as the overall ending felt pretty satisfying for our two protagonists, at least. Adding in a New Game + mode for extra replayability, I could easily imagine being tempted to take a return trip to this post-apocalyptic world, especially if I want to test out my abilities against even stronger foes in its really satisfying and compelling combat style. I think those who appreciate a mixture of VN and RPG, as well as those who might want to try action-oriented combat that’s slightly different than your average RPG, could give Qliphah in Providence’s Shadow a chance to step out from the shadows.

Qliphah in Providence’s Shadow is an unfortunate case of ambition easily being the most compelling part of a game. Its core vision and foundation are razor sharp, but are buried beneath a lack of substance, a faltering and mismatched presentation, and a narrative that fails to match the concept’s lofty ambitions. When Qliphah does double down on what makes it stand out, like the unique combat, charming leads, and gorgeous world, there are signs of a much more interesting game just waiting to be unearthed. Until a potential sequel (which I honestly hope happens, weird name and all) confidently finalizes the game’s strong core identity, Qliphah in Providence’s Shadow is an underbaked title that wears out its ambitious charm a little too fast.

Summary: Qliphah in Providence's Shadow has plenty of interesting ideas, combining visual novel elements, investigation, RPG mechanics, and real-time combat with a striking art direction. Unfortunately, its confusing systems and overwhelming amount of information prevent its gameplay from reaching its full potential, while its story and characters never become particularly memorable. It's a creative experiment with plenty of personality, but one that could have benefited from a simpler and more refined execution.

Qliphah in Providence's Shadow focused all its promotion around its Tactical Counter Timeline RPG battle system, and it certainly wasn't lying, as the game presents a gameplay design unlike anything I have seen before. However, what felt interesting during the first few hours quickly became highly repetitive, poorly explained, and eventually unengaging. Pair that up with a script that cares far more about explaining technical terms and lore than actually telling a story, and the result is a half-baked experience that never finds its footing.

Frustration mounts from start to finish during Qliphah in Providence's Shadow. What could have been a unique, brand-new IP sadly fails to capitalize on its great ideas. Combat is convoluted, and its special mechanics don't always work as intended, and the investigation segments almost unlock on their own. There are glimpses of something good here, but bad design decisions constantly hold it back.

Qliphah In Providence’s Shadow has the ambition to try something different, but in practice it needs better execution. It feels like a rhythm based battle system that has a very slow beat to it if you just focus on counters, with any pace needing you to attack without a care for defence. The battles are repetitive too and once you settle on a build there is no real reason to change it up.

Sadly, Qliphah in Providence’s Shadow is a slog from beginning to end. The combat is repetitive from the start, as every fight becomes the same sequence of counters and finishing attacks. The progression system has plenty of upgrades to unlock, but they all leave the same tedious combat intact. The story has some interesting ideas; the writing fails to make them work, and the decent atmosphere is wasted. The basic visuals and repetitive environments are another drag on the experience. Although there are a few good ideas here, the game is simply not much fun to play. RPGamers who want something different may find Qliphah worth a look, but it is ultimately difficult to recommend.

Qliphah in Providence's Shadow is one of those complex productions that are hard to analyze and even harder to describe. Unite Plus and Arc System Works deliver a curious mix of an RPG with a visual novel narrative structure and a rhythm game in which tactical planning takes absolute precedence over impulsiveness. The originality of the combat system, however, is offset by a narrative and structural approach that is tendentially far too repetitive. The Italian translation is a big point in favor of a title whose most fascinating qualities are its ideas and its style. If you accept the compromise of the inevitable immaturity of an experimental production, it could be among the most peculiar offerings of the 2026 video game landscape.

I can only recommend Qliphah in Providence's Shadow to a niche group of players who are deeply interested in complex yet intriguing combat systems, as that is the only decent thing this game has to offer. Its story is poor, the narrative is handled clumsily, and the art direction is terrible. Hopefully, its more compelling combat mechanics will eventually be put to use in a better game in the future.

Qliphah in Providence’s Shadow is clearly a more modestly budgeted project, with expressive, well-animated 3D character models offset by static, frequently reused environments that quickly create a sense of repetition. Its combat combines several ideas, including timelines, cooldown meters, color indicators, and unlockable abilities, most of which work well, though streamlining certain mechanics could benefit future projects from Arc System Works using a similar approach. Ultimately, it is a promising first attempt at a fresh concept for turn-based RPG combat, and hopefully Rena and Soma will return in a sequel that refines these rough edges and delivers the definitive tactical counter-timeline experience.

Qliphah in Providence's Shadow is an intriguing JRPG experience that doesn't always hit the mark with its ideas and overall quality. However, the deep combat mechanics are enticing enough to make the game a worthwhile use of one's time.

Qliphah in Providence's Shadows delivers an interactive graphic novel with RPG combat, blending an evocative art style with gameplay built around dialogue and battles. Arc System Works surprises with a title that is ambitious and original in some respects, but ultimately falls short due to an underdeveloped and unclear combat system, lacklustre investigative sections that require little actual reasoning from the player, and a technical and visual presentation that feels distinctly low-budget. Worth trying, but with your expectations firmly in check.

Qliphah in Providence's Shadow is a complex and challenging JRPG that blends horror, tactical combat, and anime-inspired aesthetics into a unique experience that rewards players who take the time to master its intricate mechanics.

Qliphah in Providence's Shadow will likely attract a small group of enthusiasts who enjoy digging into its unique combat system and mastering its timeline-based mechanics. However, its chaotic presentation, frustrating design, and repetitive structure make it a hard sell for most, and its lackluster story isn't enough to carry it.

Qliphah in Providence's Shadow is a fascinating and unconventional venture one we can certainly call a success, though not without its flaws. While it bears the obvious hallmarks of a mid-budget production, the game manages to create an intriguing atmosphere, supported by excellent art direction. At the heart of the experience lies a bold combat system that rewards focus and a sense of rhythm like few other games in the genre do. For anyone looking for an unconventional JRPG, Rena and Souma’s investigation in the shadows of Tokyo is definitely worth a try.

Qliphah: In Providence’s Shadow is a game carried by it’s fun combat, solid visuals and two solid leads. Had some things been pushed a bit further, perhaps it could’ve been a hidden standout but for as it stands, it’s a good budget title RPG that’s worth checking out.

Qliphah in Providence’s Shadow brilliantly combines gripping Japanese urban horror through VN style, with an incredibly deep, colour-coded, timeline turn-based combat system. Even though there's no traditional detective gameplay, the dark, apocalyptic narrative of Tokyo 2030 remains super intriguing. Paired with a wholly unique, reaction-heavy tactical combat system, this is a niche title that demands your attention.

Moving beyond turn-based RPGs, real-time combat or hybrid forms of the two, this title attempts to break new ground and shake up the genre with a concept that almost feels like a rhythm game at some points. The developers may have been a bit too ambitious however. A reduction in the number of abilities and tutorials would have probably been better. Yet once players get the hang of it the game offers a rewarding sense of accomplishment. Qliphah in Providence’s Shadow dares to innovate, creating a unique blend of visual novel and RPG featuring a combat system unlike anything I have seen before. Ultimately though a bit more polish and less complexity would have benefited the game in the end.
Qliphah in Providence’s Shadow is an action RPG that dares to be different: intriguing and fun, with polished art direction and a combat system that offers a breath of fresh air.
76.5% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (17 reviews).

Lifted is a special little game that manages to effortlessly charm despite its imperfections. It’s a throwback to classic platforming I didn’t know I was needing, all the while being the Back to the Future sequel I know I have dreamed about for decades. I hope it’s not the last we see of Ari Buktu, and I’ll happily board his time-travelling elevator again—anytime.

There are a few annoyances here and there – most of them centred around the use of a hook you’ll be called on to cross some larger gaps – but nothing that comes anywhere close to being a dealbreaker. It’s just that the rest of Lifted is so well done that I can’t help but wish it was a complete package. Still, it comes close enough to achieving that level that it’s hard to complain too much. If you’re a fan of 2.5D platformers, you’d do well to check it out.

LIFTED succeeds not because it reinvents the genre, but because it executes its ideas with confidence and charm. The endearing cast and entertaining dialogue combine with surprisingly challenging-yet-engaging level design to create a truly memorable experience. While it may not be the most ambitious or groundbreaking platformer on the market, it doesn’t need to be. LIFTED knows exactly what it wants to be, and it accomplishes that goal with style, humor, and a lot of heart.

Despite technical flaws that can be slightly annoying, LIFTED still stands as an enjoyable adventure if you have a little patience to overlook its collision issues. The fast pace and easy navigation make up for the execution errors. In the end, the game delivers a great, fun entry point into the world of video games, making it a solid recommendation, especially for a younger audience.
Lifted is a bombastic platformer full of action scenes and witty one liners, but if you're used to the genre you'll likely find it rather basic.

LIFTED captures the charm of classic family platformers with enjoyable traversal, clever puzzles, and exciting chase sequences, but its predictable story and relentlessly quippy dialogue keep it from reaching the same heights as its gameplay.

Lifted is a game that is full of heart and charm, and it looks and sounds like it. Unfortunately, that heart and charm are buried in a generic action-adventure story spread across overly simplistic gameplay that doesn’t really do enough for long enough to become anything other than just okay. It’s a perfectly okay six-hour experience that is easily accessible and family-friendly, and I guarantee that for that reason, it’s going to have an audience that grapples their way into this experience and never let go, but there’s simply not enough here to recommend this game.

Lifted is a special little game that manages to effortlessly charm despite its imperfections. It’s a throwback to classic platforming I didn’t know I was needing, all the while being the Back to the Future sequel I know I have dreamed about for decades. I hope it’s not the last we see of Ari Buktu, and I’ll happily board his time-travelling elevator again—anytime.
LIFTED is a fantastic PC adventure filled with endearing characters, responsive platforming, a colourful presentation, and lighthearted humour, all at a snappy pace that suits its smaller scale.

This is a very promising debut for Adventure Works. It doesn’t break new ground within the genre, but it manages to create a charming, entertaining adventure with a very distinct identity, thanks to its setting, its humour and its constant journey through different historical periods

Overall, LIFTED shows how you may pay tribute to a favorite work but still maintain your own individuality throughout. You can feel the influence of Back to the Future from the very beginning and throughout the entire adventure, but the game’s great sense of humor, various puzzles, slick platforming and playful art design allow it to retain a personality of its own. In this sense, it offers a good answer to the question asked at the beginning of this review.

Lifted brings together the joy of watching your favorite movie with a simple platformer, and I had a blast playing it. There were a lot of cutscenes that gave the enjoyment of watching a movie, so they didn’t distract from the gameplay. The gameplay itself was simple, but well done for the most part and made the journey enjoyable. While I do wish the game was a little bit longer, I have found that going back for the collectibles feels worth it. While the puzzles weren’t challenging, finding the collectibles can be, and earning the new outfits feels like an achievement. Overall, Lifted focuses on bringing joy to the player. Nothing’s so hard as to cause frustration, and the wackiness of the story kept me smiling for the whole playthrough. If you’re looking for a fun, enjoyable couple of hours, I’d suggest Lifted.

If the overuse of perfect didn’t give it away, I have to give LIFTED the Thumb Culture Platinum Award. This game really is just a nice break from other games that are coming out at the moment. After seeing how highly Stu rated the demo I was a little apprehensive, but I can fully agree that this game definitely deserves to be added to everyone’s Steam library.

As expected from the mind of a Disney Imagineer, Lifted is a retro inspired platformer that feels like a trip to Disney. It's an experience that channels your inner-child with charm, whimsy and fun, but it’s also full of frustrations like long lines, sweltering heat, high prices, rude people and crying kids. In the case of Lifted, it’s unrefined gameplay, minimal challenge, forgettable story, and extremely short runtime. How much you enjoy your adventure will depend on what part of the experience you focus on?

All in all, LIFTED is a charming, funny and, for the most part, laid-back platformer that will particularly appeal to families with children, casual gamers and fans of 1980s films. Whilst more experienced veterans of the genre will have no trouble completing it in a single afternoon – and may not find its mechanical simplicity entirely satisfying – it works reliably as an accessible little game.

LIFTED is a good idea that needed more time to mature. Its short length, simplistic level design, uneven dialogue, and technical problems hold it back from real greatness, but the colorful presentation and accessible gameplay make it worth checking out for younger players or families looking for a short game to play together.

LIFTED is a short adventure, but it makes good use of its just over three hours. The game introduces new ideas, alternates between puzzles and precision platforming, and reaches its conclusion before its structure starts to become repetitive.

Lifted is designed for all players, not just seasoned vets. It's welcoming to even the youngest of gamers, but the settings can be tinkered to make it more of a challenge. The game is created by Jeff Ashbrook, a former Disney Imagineer. With that experience, his goal to make a game that appeals to everyone and tells a riveting interactive story is fully realized. It's a solid choice for any gamer who loves a good adventure, is ideal for families, fans of story-driven platformers, or anyone craving a lighthearted adventure. It's not perfect – it's a little on the short side, has its share of camera glitches, and may be too easy for some, but it's still a fun experience. The game has heart, a lot of feel-good moments, and will keep you smiling from beginning to end.

I want to keep this review short and sweet, just like the game. This isn’t the deepest game of all time. There’s nothing groundbreaking here. But it ran smoothly even on my potato laptop, and I was grinning from ear to ear the entire time, which doesn’t happen much. If you like platformers and a good, silly time, you’ll love this one for sure. The only thing holding me back from a perfect score is that it does play oh so very safely within the boundaries of the genre, so it’s hard to call it a “must play.” That said, this is a very, very fun game, and you are guaranteed a fun time!
29.4% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (34 reviews).

WILL: Follow the Light, without the few negative hiccups I noted, is a 10 out of 10 game. But as it stands right now, the few nits that exist within the game pull away from that score slightly - but only slightly. That being said though, if these updates and needed fixes are made, I can easily see this being a can’t-miss game. The beautiful, yet heart-wrenching story, coupled with the intriguing puzzles and environment of the game itself make for an unforgettable digital experience.

WILL: Follow the Light starts slow but ultimately represents an emotional, cathartic journey thick with sensitive themes, including grief and estrangement. It's not long, but the weight of the heartbreaking story is worth every penny.

Will: Follow the Light is far more than just an ordinary walking simulator; it’s an adventure that draws you in with its mysterious, heartfelt, and immersive story. Setting aside the occasional technical glitches that can be frustrating and moments when the game leaves you without a clue, this is a labor of love that fans of the adventure genre—or rather, those who want to lose themselves in a strong story and world-building—should definitely play. Ah, if only it had been polished a bit more.

WILL: Follow the Light tells a simple story of a man trying to look for his son after a massive storm, and along the way, has to confront the mysteries of his own life. The intimate nature of the core premise is compelling enough to carry this walking simulator throughout its entire runtime.
A heartfelt voyage of grief, grace, and the open seas unravels amidst puzzles and a captivating narrative.

TomorrowHead Studio's debut is technically impressive in its use of UE5's lighting. Will: Follow The Light's execution may be bumpier in other areas, while the story might not linger in the memory for long, but it still makes for a stunning and unforgettable trip to the north in all its desolate beauty.
WILL: Follow the Light is a powerful narrative that offers a combination of realism and some failed ambition.

Will: Follow the Light had a compelling premise that could have set it apart from the sea of walking simulators. In fact, the plot framework remains intriguing, but the execution falls short due to lackluster voice acting that lacks both emphasis and intent, failing to convey the urgency of the situation in which our protagonist finds himself. The puzzles also fail to engage, and when you’re not using a mouse and keyboard, they’re hampered by an ineffective control scheme. Will: Follow the Light remains a personal project by a small team grappling with an intriguing production, but it should be viewed as a starting point from which to build upon for Tomorrow Head’s future works.
The ship voyage is connected to a deeply personal story that will touch you and definitely won't leave you cold. It's a shame, though, that the game uses outdated mechanics and graphics.

With strong presentation and a promising premise, the adventure entertains while it lasts but leaves no lasting impression. Nevertheless—and although it is a shame that the positive vibes of the opening and the navigation sequences don't quite reach their full potential—the game’s reflection on how past trauma shapes our perception of the present, along with its use of light as a narrative device, are elements to appreciate during the five or six hours it takes to reach the end credits. If these themes interest you, it is worth giving the game a chance. Otherwise, it is best to let Will shoulder the burden of his past decisions alone.

WILL: Follow The Light delivers a visually striking and emotionally driven sailing adventure that shines brightest when it embraces the loneliness and danger of the open sea. Its lighthouse routines, weather systems, and immersive boating mechanics create a strong sense of place, while the narrative explores grief, family, and isolation with genuine ambition. However, uneven pacing, awkward controls, and inconsistent storytelling often interrupt the emotional momentum. There is a compelling game hidden beneath the surface, but the journey toward its payoff can feel frustratingly unfocused.

The interface suffers from a serious scalability issue: text and icons are very often too small—at times almost illegible—on a screen like that of the Ally X. This is clearly a major flaw for a title that is so narrative-driven and involves extensive document reading. We are confident that this will be rectified promptly; however, given that this type of adventure game is perfectly suited for on-the-go gaming, we felt it was worth highlighting this issue.

Will: Follow the Light is a frustrating experience because the foundation for something memorable is clearly there. Beneath the repetitive puzzle design, uneven writing, and technical frustrations lies a genuinely interesting premise supported by immersive sailing mechanics and strong atmospheric audio. There are moments where the game briefly captures the emotional and cinematic adventure it wants to be, but it struggles to sustain that momentum for long before falling back into its more exhausting habits. For some players, those stronger moments may still be enough to carry the journey through to the end. For others, the game’s shortcomings will likely overshadow the experience long before Will reaches the light.

WILL: Follow The Light is yet another walking simulator that offers an interesting mechanic of controlling a yacht and a dog sled. However, the authors completely failed in terms of the story and world exploration.
Despite this lovely looking world and a story so driven by mystery, I wasn’t able to get past Will as a character or the obtuse puzzles he has to face.
WILL: Follow the Light’s ambitious mix of sailing, character drama and puzzle-based adventuring shows plenty of promise but often results in choppy pacing and rough implementation.

While WILL: Follow the Light can very much look the part, it simply didn’t hold up for me when it came to the actual gameplay and narrative. The story felt fragmented and poorly delivered, even though a late game twist and a heartfelt message about the time we have and the choices we make felt genuine. While narrative ‘walking-sim’ fans may find some enjoyment and a few bright ideas, it’s not quite enough to make this sailing trip truly worth the journey.

WILL: Follow the Light offers a few glimmers of promise amidst its fog of missed potential, but they are too few and far between to recommend. Stiff delivery, rough writing and uneven puzzles all would have been better served by being thrown overboard so WILL could focus on its atmospheric sailing strengths. Instead, WILL is better left adrift at sea with only its lost promise to keep it company.

WILL: Follow The Light has a lot of potential, with amazing scenery and intricate sailing mechanics. However, the finished product feels a bit unpolished. If an interesting narrative can carry you through, it's worth a look; otherwise, I'd give it a miss.
Barring a couple of all-too-short sections near the beginning, Will: Follow The Light is a bewildering and arduous journey. [Issue#424, p.116]

WILL: Follow The Light shows potential through its opening but doesn't deliver on its premise. What should have been a high-stakes story becomes a dull journey, and the story beats don't hit as they should. The sailing is, at least, excellently done, but more focus should have been on that.
A strikingly moody adventure that knows exactly what it wants to feel like, but never fully works as either a game or a story in the way it needs to.
Story-driven, first-person adventure puzzler that falls flat
The ship voyage is connected to a deeply personal story that will touch you and definitely won't leave you cold. It's a shame, though, that the game uses outdated mechanics and graphics.
As a short film there may have been something memorable about this story. As a game, it feels like a fluffed up experience with something to say, but takes far too long to say it.

WILL: Follow The Light is a debut release that earns real respect for what it achieves and honest disappointment for what it doesn’t complete. The opening hours and the sailing sections represent a genuinely promising vision from a team that clearly knows what it wants to make. The back half of the game, with its puzzle missteps and narrative gaps, suggests the resources ran out before the vision did.

At $24.99 for a 5-6 hour experience with photorealistic arctic visuals, strong voice acting, a clean technical release, and a story that — despite its rough edges — has something real to say about fathers and sons, WILL is worth your time if this is your genre. It’s not Firewatch. But it’s a worthwhile first step from a studio worth following.

When all is said and done, WILL: Follow The Light shines in its particular moments of calmness while sailing through the icy waters of the north. Its pitch-perfect soundtrack, evoking Max Richter’s On The Nature of Daylight, leaves a tinge of melancholy. The story itself does not shy away from the inevitability of death.

WILL: Follow The Light is a beautifully crafted narrative adventure that combines stunning landscapes, a melancholic atmosphere and an emotional story about loss, memories and eventual healing. While the gameplay and puzzles are fairly simple, the game's wonderful soundtrack and excellent story will leave a lasting impression long after the journey ends.

Will Follow The Light is a strong debut from TomorrowHead Studio. It delivers a deeply emotional story, engaging gameplay mechanics, and stunning visuals powered by Unreal Engine 5.

While it does have flaws in voice acting, performance polish, and some visual inconsistencies, it remains a standout indie experience that is well worth playing.

WILL: Follow The Light is a sincere, auteur-driven and – at times – evocative adventure that finds its best balance when it lets the sea and the wind do the talking. Unfortunately, this isn’t enough to achieve the desired result: the gameplay is mostly a walking simulator (characterised by decidedly repetitive and unconvincing puzzles), the narrative – despite a twist at the end and a touching message about the time we have and the choices we make – proved too fragmented and underdeveloped, whilst the audio is convincing in terms of the soundtrack and effects but not in the dialogue (at times disastrous). In short – ultimately – it has some interesting ideas that still manage to give the game an identity, thanks above all to its truly stunning setting and the way it uses the journey as an emotional mirror, which will be most appreciated by fans of narrative walking simulators.
Tomorrowhead Studio has done an exceptional job of delivering a narrative-driven game with a beautifully crafted setting.

WILL: Follow The Light isn’t the most memorable game I’ve played, and I found parts of the game pretty tedious. But there are plenty of great factors to be found here, both in atmosphere and presentation, in the eight hours or so you’ll have with the game. For those on Xbox, you’ll be pleased to hear that the Xbox Play Anywhere functionality is available for this one. So if you’d like to play it on the fly, you can do so on console, handheld and PC. It’s a great first outing from Tomorrowhead Studios, and if you’d like to pick up a copy for Xbox Series X/S, you can do so HERE

The light we followed as Will ultimately turned out to be a will-o'-the-wisp. Will: Follow the Light has some good ideas, and the gameplay variety in particular is not lacking. I could happily have spent an entire game sailing in the way it is implemented here.

But aside from its strong opening and a few recurring motifs that run throughout the game, the narrative leaves much to be desired on almost every level. Above all, the emotional core simply fails to land because the storytelling and presentation lack the necessary craftsmanship. Everything is in part there, but much like the town at the beginning, the remains of a solid story can only be glimpsed beneath a landslide.

WILL: Follow The Light is an ambitious game that had all the makings of an indie gem. However, its excellent yacht-sailing simulation and breathtaking wilderness visuals are dragged down by an underdeveloped story, frustratingly repetitive puzzles, poor voice acting, technical issues, and unattractive character models.

Ultimately, Will: Follow the Light has good ideas and great puzzles, but suffers from pacing issues, unrewarding exploration, and a structure that makes much of the experience more tedious than engaging.

Ultimately, Will: Follow the Light isn’t a game for everyone, but it is a title with a distinct voice of its own. It’s a journey through the cold, filled with loss yet still offering hope, all wrapped up in an impressive audiovisual experience. If you enjoy interactive films, particularly dramas, then this is definitely for you. If you need your daily dose of virtual violence, though, you’d be best off steering well clear of Will.

Aside from its sailing mechanics and impressive story, the game can sometimes feel boring due to its pacing. Even though the gameplay is fun and mixed with puzzles, their frequency may not be enough to keep every player engaged throughout the experience.

Some games try to impress with huge open worlds, spectacular action and endless gameplay mechanics. WILL: Follow The Light consciously opts for a completely different approach: a quiet, narrative experience in which atmosphere and emotion are central. That may not make this game suitable for everyone, but it is precisely because of this that the adventure distinguishes itself from many other narrative games.

WILL: Follow The Light is not a clean hit, but I enjoyed it. It has a strong premise, beautiful locations, enjoyable sailing, and enough emotional ambition to make the journey worthwhile. It also has awkward story transitions, shallow puzzles, and themes that needed clearer focus. If you like slow narrative adventures and do not mind some rough edges, there is something here worth experiencing, especially on Series X.

WILL: Follow the Light puts you in the thick of it by taking on raging storms out in the ocean to search far and wide, all for your missing son. Completing tasks and solving puzzles can be fun or tedious, but the gameplay of sailing treacherous seas helps turn a simple story into an epic adventure. WILL: Follow the Light isn’t just a video game; it’s an experience.

WILL: Follow the Light has a genuinely compelling core: the loneliness of open water, lighthouse routines, and a father's grief searching for his missing family. When it leans into its sailing mechanics and atmospheric coastal design, it gets close to something special. But uneven pacing, stiff controls, and a town full of lifeless interactions keep pulling you away from the emotional story it clearly wants to tell. There's a better game hidden beneath the surface. It just doesn't stay there long enough to matter.

Through all of its faults, Will: Follow the Light still has something to give by shining a light on father-son relationships through an intriguing and sometimes surreal story. Its strong voice cast (including Cissy Jones) aids its pluses, and each gives great performances, but it is hard to ignore its frustrations that let it down quite considerably.

Will: Follow the Light had a compelling premise that could have set it apart from the sea of walking simulators. In fact, the plot framework remains intriguing, but the execution falls short due to lackluster voice acting that lacks both emphasis and intent, failing to convey the urgency of the situation in which our protagonist finds himself. The puzzles also fail to engage, and when you’re not using a mouse and keyboard, they’re hampered by an ineffective control scheme. Will: Follow the Light remains a personal project by a small team grappling with an intriguing production, but it should be viewed as a starting point from which to build upon for Tomorrow Head’s future works.

WILL: Follow the Light presented itself from the very first moment, displaying a bit of all these ambitions and attempting to inhabit that ideal space between the reflective and fascinating solitude of Firewatch and the haunting surrealism of What Remains of Edith Finch.
WILL: Follow The Light has definite problems with pace and accessibility, but it does manage to tell a tight story about family, loss and the burden of responsibility.

Will: Follow the Light is a slow, contemplative experience focused on emotional storytelling and realistic navigation systems. It’s a mix of sailing mechanics, environmental puzzles, and explorative gameplay woven into a story of family, loss, and introspection. Meanwhile, pacing issues, inconsistent puzzle clarity, and uneven character delivery hurt overall buy-in.
48.1% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (27 reviews).

Rivage crafts a compelling sci-fi mystery set aboard a meticulously detailed, gorgeous space station. Its challenging puzzles and rewarding environmental storytelling consistently inspire curiosity. However, restrictive energy management can lead to tedious repetition across time loops, and a clumsy interface occasionally frustrates. Still, unraveling its secrets remains an undeniably satisfying investigative experience.

Rivage sets a ridiculously high bar for virtual escape rooms across the universe. If you’re up for a challenge, prepare to get your puzzle on. You’ll be rewarded for your efforts with stunning visuals and a captivating tale. I only wish I could play it with friends (the very clever ones, please).

Rivage is an intriguing sci-fi puzzle game that uses the ability to loop time as a central mechanic. The game's atmosphere is often cozy, but the emptiness and quiet tend to give it an eerie undercurrent as you dig into the mysteries of Vesta and Station Ares. With a short runtime, you can get through the game over a couple of days, but you want to be prepared to think and be frustrated by puzzles. Your first playthrough is the highlight, as you'd know everything about the mysteries after it, but I think it could be a fun game to try speed running.
Rivage is a fine-enough puzzle game, but some questionable decisions make it a more frustrating than enjoyable experience.

The problem is that it’s a convoluted, frustrating journey to get there, and it’s not one I’m entirely sure was even worth it come the end. Every time the power cut out, or I ran into a dead end, or needed to back track, I started to really dislike that arcade machine. Come the end, I began to hate it. Like I said – a brave choice for the developer to make.

Rivage is a beautiful simulacrum of an immersive, sci-fi puzzle game. It is an impressive feat, given that it is a two-person studio’s first project. On the surface, it looks like it accomplishes everything it should. Everything is there: puzzles, immersive storytelling and time-loops. However, in execution, the bad overshadows the good. Good puzzles are drowned out by aimlessly chasing around puzzle pieces. Fascinating mechanics don’t enhance the experience, but are actively hostile to it. The premise is unique and interesting, but is driven by one-note character, bad writing and poorly communicated goals. Underlining all of this is the ever-present anxiety that what you’re experiencing isn’t the work of a real person, but generative AI. Unfortunately, I cannot recommend Rivage.
Rivage is a new first person puzzle game set on space station that's not only running out of power but is suffering from a time loop.

Rivage is a very good looking game and has some great talent in its voice acting which, alongside the written messages, emails, and notes, all goes to give depth to characters that are not present. However, the puzzles are hit and miss. While most are a decent challenge, some outstay their welcome and feel padded out along with the multiple barriers placed in front of players.
Rivage has an interesting premise but struggles to meet its potential.
The very moment we begin our journey in Rivage, it's clear that we're in quite familiar sci-fi territory. Stranded and alone aboard the ARES space...

If you're not puzzle-minded, Rivage is going to be an absolute nightmare with its lack of handholding and direction. But if you've got an analytical mind and thrive when challenged, you're going to absolutely love this immersive sci-fi experience.
First-person sci-fi puzzle adventure set aboard the A.R.E.S. space station in which you’ll have to escape from a time loop

Rivage presents an impressive puzzle adventure in a jam-packed yet uninhabited spaceship with tons of challenging puzzles to solve. However, it has its frustrating moments in the later stages so it's tough to recommend to anyone other than diehard escape room fans. 🛰️

Rivage stands out in the landscape of sci-fi puzzle adventures for its ability to turn the time loop into an investigative tool instead of a simple punishment mechanic. The choice to tie the reset to the station's energy, together with the K9 system that preserves solutions, creates a unique pace of play: every cycle is an opportunity to push a little further, with the concrete feeling of progressing not only through space, but in understanding the story and the mechanisms of A.R.E.S. The narrative side – though without epic ambitions – works thanks to a patient construction of the mystery and a series of clues distributed coherently throughout the environment. The puzzles, despite some roughness in the handling of controls and the linearity of progression, offer a mechanical density that is rare for the genre, with puzzles that require observation, deduction and a good deal of planning. Overall, Rivage is a title made for those who love getting lost in richly detailed environments, where every object can hide a clue and every system can become part of a bigger puzzle. It does not try to amaze with spectacular effects or a highly emotional plot, but builds a solid and coherent experience, where satisfaction comes from understanding, step by step, the rules of a broken world and finding a way to make it work, at least enough to discover the truth.
Rivage is a puzzle game about a time loop and a power limit, with a detailed station and a K9 that saves progress. Lighting, characters, and a few chores need work. Suits patient players.

Rivage is a mysterious and visually beautiful experience, but its puzzles can feel tedious and difficult at first. Despite some technical and audio issues, it remains a good experience for fans of exploration and puzzles.

Rivage is a classic narrative puzzle game—a pleasant way to spend a quiet afternoon—but it doesn’t bring anything revolutionary to the table. The plot, while derivative, manages to draw the player in, serving as the driving force behind further exploration of the space station. It’s a game worth playing, thanks in part to its solid graphics and audio, even if there are a few optimization issues.

Rivage is a smart sci-fi puzzle adventure that combines a mysterious space-station setting with a wide variety of escape-room challenges, clever use of its K9 information system, and a time-loop mechanic that adds an extra layer of planning. Some puzzles can become frustrating, the loop may feel repetitive for certain players, and the lack of a more detailed progress journal can make navigation confusing, but puzzle enthusiasts should find plenty to enjoy.
Rivage combines challenging puzzles, time-loop mechanics and a compelling mystery to create a rewarding sci-fi adventure that constantly makes you think.

Rivage requires willing on the part of the player to really get invested in the world, but let it sink its hook in you and it’ll be an immersive adventure that you won’t soon forget. Excellent stuff all round, and another notch in the already impressive bow of Raw Fury’s output.

In the end, I had to place Rivage on a list of games that, in the long run, didn’t bring me as much enjoyment as I’d hoped. It’s not all doom and gloom, though: some of the puzzles are quite ingeniously designed, but the moments when I truly appreciated the task at hand were few and far between.
An interesting puzzle game, but too inconsistent to be entirely convincing.

Overall though, Rivage is a solid puzzle game from ‘Exnilo Studio’ &a; ‘Raw Fury’. If you are looking for a fully immersive science fiction puzzle game then look no further. While it can be frustrating at times I found myself thinking about the game and coming back for more time after time. Just have patience and the game can be so rewarding.

A game you can’t simply rush through, and that’s exactly why it keeps you hooked for entire evenings. Eleven hours of reading, listening, and taking notes on a station that someone clearly designed with genuine care. A wonderful game!

This year was strong for sci-fi fans- we had a lot of good books being published, new seasons for a lot of sci-fi series (including Star Trek: Strange New Worlds), and of course, some new movies, including the adaptation of Andy Weir’s Project Hail Mary. Rivage fits well with these stories and will offer a few hours of time-bending, space-station fun for true sci-fi fans.

Rivage is definitely not typical walking simulator. It’s a space station packed with puzzles, and if you’re just looking to walk through beautiful environments and listen to the story, you’ve come to the wrong place. However, if you want to put your brain to the test with well-designed puzzles, despite its flaws, Rivage is a competent title, even if it doesn’t really bring anything new to the table.

Rivage isn't perfect—it has its low points and moments where boredom bubbles close to the surface—but the core blend of loops, investigation, and cosmic solitude is original enough to justify the hours it demands.

Rivage is an ambitious groundhog day puzzler that presents a compelling mystery, and rewards those that dig deep into the finer details. However, despite some good world building, and interesting ideas. The puzzles aren't all that satisfying to engage with, the UI feels cumbersome to work with, and the timeloop format feels like an unnecessary burden at times.
36.5% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (52 reviews).

It has been seven years since Koei Tecmo even indicated that it saw a future in Dead or Alive, so frankly it’s just a relief that Dead or Alive 6 Last Round happened at all. While Dead or Alive 7 was the really exciting recent news, this is the definitive version of a brilliant, funny, sexy, mechanically entertaining fighting game and I’ve loved stepping back into its ring.

With the most interesting new content coming mostly down the line, Dead or Alive 6 Last Round is difficult to fully judge at launch. It looks and plays great, so it should tide over fans as they wait for the seventh entry in the fighting game franchise. However, it’s hard not to be somewhat underwhelmed by most of the levels not supporting the new lighting engine and crossover DLC characters not coming with the base game.

Team Ninja's accessible and explosive fighting action is back in a sort of remaster/expanded version that goes beyond the limitations of the previous generation to fully realize the developer's vision. Even with more fighters, Last Round needed more content, but it remains a lot of fun.

Dead or Alive 6: Last Round is a strong fighter that features a wonderful triangle system, adding an extra layer of depth to battles. Although the story mode lacks the focus and structure of its peers, it makes up for this with the wealth of content on offer. The training mode is particularly impressive, offering clear insight into mechanics and combos for both newcomers and veterans. Fights are tight and fluid, thanks in part to the strong animation, although its age does show, particularly in the texture work. With a free-to-play option available, it’s certainly worth checking out, but it doesn’t quite manage to compete with its biggest rivals when you step into the arena.

Dead or Alive 6: Last Round is more of a promise than anything, as it lacks certain features for a fighting game to thrive in this day and age. While the depth of its core gameplay and noticeable upgrades to its visuals and performance are certainly present, it doesn’t offer any significant gameplay changes since its last update in 2020, aside from added cosmetics for a select few and a new Photo Mode. Players will simply have to wait and see if Koei Tecmo is genuine in its intention to reignite the franchise, as updates will be drip-fed from here on out.
Dead or Alive 6 is still fun, but in its current state Last Round feels more like an expensive update that brings very little new content rather than a true revival of the series.

Dead or Alive 6 Last Round is the definitive version of Koei Tecmo and Team Ninja's fast-paced fighter, but there are some aspects of it that are a little disappointing, such as low quality story scenes and a lack of cross-play.

Dead or Alive 6 Last Round gives Team Ninja’s underrated fighter a second chance with a larger roster, current-gen availability, and a welcome new Photo Mode. While the combat remains fast, flashy, and deeply satisfying, the rerelease stops short of being the definitive edition fans hoped for, hampered by lingering monetization baggage and a lack of meaningful modern upgrades. It's an imperfect package, but the core fighting experience is still one of the most entertaining 3D fighters available.

Dead or Alive 6 Last Round is still a fun fighting game. The combat is fast, the roster is better than before and the new Photo Mode is a great little addition for fans of the series. If you never played Dead or Alive 6 before, this is easily the best version to start with. For returning players, it’s a lot harder to recommend. The new costumes and Photo Mode are nice, but not enough to make this feel like a huge upgrade. The lack of crossplay is disappointing, and the game still carries some of the same problems as before. Dead or Alive 6 Last Round is a better version of a good fighter, but not the perfect final round it could have been.
With no meaningful modern improvements to its online modes, this is easy to skip if competitive play is what matters most to you.

Dead or Alive 6 Last Round brings the fighting game to the new generation with a lackluster offering. There is no discount for owners of the base version, and few items are included in the package — with the rest requiring additional purchases — meaning even those who had already bought all the DLC will have to pay up to complete their collection. Furthermore, the novel features are minimal and not particularly significant. It is still worth a look, however, for the fast-paced, fun combat, which remains the game's greatest highlight.

Dead or Alive 6: Last Round preserves the franchise’s excellent combat and polished visuals, but fails to justify its return as a modern re-release. The lack of rollback netcode, minimal improvements and heavy reliance on paid DLC make the package difficult to recommend at full price. While newcomers may still enjoy the experience on current platforms, longtime fans will likely see it as a missed opportunity for the series.

Although it's still a very fun fighting game, Dead or Alive 6: Last Round brings very few new features to justify its existence and fails to truly deliver technical improvements in its transition to the PS5, being a missed opportunity for Koei Tecmo.

Dead or Alive 6, while providing a few features a modern fighting game should have, also disappointingly leaves out many important elements, offers very little new content, and forces returning players to purchase the title again. As such, while the title is a solid new release, it's only recommended to new players who don't mind the missing features.

Taken on its own, Dead or Alive 6: Last Round is still a solid fighting game. The adjustments to the core combat system improve accessibility without sacrificing depth for more advanced players. The roster is strong, especially now that previous DLC characters are included, but customization feels noticeably thin once DLC costumes are set aside. However, the requirement to repurchase characters like Kula and Mai, combined with the lack of meaningful presentation upgrades beyond a single reworked stage, makes this feel like a minor and somewhat underwhelming revision, especially given how long players have waited. If you're new to the series and enjoy fighting games, DoA6 is still worth a look. For anyone who has already invested significant time in the original release, there's little incentive to return unless future updates expand the lighting improvements across more stages or introduce a substantial wave of new characters.

Dead or Alive 6 Last Round is the best version of Dead or Alive 6, a game I enjoy playing even today, but it doesn't do enough all these years later. Maybe it will be an easier release to recommend in a few months, but right now it is hard to even comprehend what made Koei Tecmo re-release the same game with almost nothing of value and not offer any sort of upgrade path. I think if you've managed to disappoint someone who owns basically every season pass on two different platforms, the re-release is a big miss. I enjoyed Dead or Alive 6 years ago, but cannot recommend Dead or Alive 6 Last Round for anyone but those who want a current generation version of Dead or Alive 6 and are willing to deal with every issue that the original had back in 2019.
If you're completely new to Dead or Alive, it's worth giving this a go due to the fun fighting mechanics, but DoA 6 Last Round does little to improve upon the original.

Dead Or Alive 6 Last Round brings the fighter back to remind the community that there is still a third horse in the 3D fighting game race. The core fighting still works, and knocking someone 20 feet across a stage never gets old. However, this release feels like it is asking players to “pay for potential,” with Tecmo promising new characters and modes later while the current package retains more than it enhances.

Dead or Alive 6: Last Round disappoints as a new-gen release. While the core combat remains excellent, with dynamic stages and accessible yet deep mechanics, the overall package falls short. The narrative is fragmented and unengaging, and the online experience is severely lacking, missing essential modern features like rollback netcode and crossplay. Visual enhancements are minimal, with only one stage receiving significant aesthetic updates. For existing owners, the full-price upgrade is unjustified due to limited new content and the need to repurchase some DLC characters.
Dead or Alive 6 Last Round is bringing back the dormant franchise with its hands empty and its mouth full of promises, instead of unleashing the hidden potential DOA6 has.

This should have been a more generous bundle, with all content included, a tag-team mode, and rollback netcode. Instead it’s a cash grab with scant new features to justify its inexplicable existence. Dead or Alive deserves better.
A great fighting game wrapped up in a very bad package.
Seven years of content only partially wrapped up in one snug package.

For newcomers, Dead or Alive 6 Last Round is going to be an electric experience, and it's guaranteed to be one of the best fighters this year purely by the will of its savage gameplay. For vets, however, it may indeed be DOA.

Forcing fans to re-purchase characters again is just icing on the top. Sadly, I cannot recommend this package, if you already own DoA 6, just stick with that, there is little reason to upgrade to the Last Round version.

Dead or Alive 6: Last Round is a step in the right direction, both to attract fans of the saga and to revive the interest of other players and attract more followers to these ranks (myself included), since with this we await the confirmed new installment in the future.
Try as I might, I can't figure out why Dead or Alive 6: Last Round exists. Upon its release in 2019, Dead or Alive 6 proved to be a perfectly soli...
The definitive way of playing DEAD OR ALIVE 6 on PS5

Last Round adds several previously paid fighters, new graphics settings, faster loading times, and a revamped photo mode. However, the bulk of the game remains virtually unchanged; visual enhancements are limited so far, and certain elements'such as cutscenes and fonts'still feel dated.
But for a fan of the original DEAD OR ALIVE 6, this is a good pack only if you want almost all DLC in a single place, along with the promise of new, free content down the line.

As a longtime series fan that is desperate for Dead or Alive to get back on the right track again, it brings no joy to be criticising this disappointing re-release. Dead or Alive 6: Last Round is a game that struggles to justify its existence by including barely any of the previously released DLC by default, missing features from the original title, adding very little in the way of appealing new content, and lacking in crossplay and rollback netcode. DOA is a brilliant fighting series that deserves way better than this. DOA6LR is still a solid entry, but it is impossible to ignore the missteps taken with this edition.

As a definitive version, I’d say it’s a lukewarm recommendation. “Dead or Alive 6: Last Round” is a good demonstration of how Koei Tecmo and Team Ninja still care about their flagship fighting franchise. They could’ve just dusted off their most controversial entry and rushed straight into the next game, but they gave it a second chance, promising more content (an expanded roster) for a seven-year-old game.

Dead or Alive 6 Last Round is a disappointment on multiple fronts: zero new features, no improvements, and, last but not least, a flawed online component. In 2026, with fighting game competition increasingly fierce, you can't launch a product without rollback netcode and, above all, crossplay, neither between consoles nor between the two versions currently on the market. The combat system is still fun, but the flaws mentioned above can only leave a bitter taste in the mouth.

"Great Combat... and a Late Update"
Dead or Alive 6 Last Round proves that the series still boasts one of the most enjoyable and immersive combat systems in the 3D fighting game genre. Battles are fast-paced, the characters are diverse, and the interactive environments give each encounter a unique feel and a wealth of tactical options. The visual enhancements and stable performance make this the best way to experience the sixth installment yet.

Dead or Alive 6 Last Round may not have been the upgrade we were hoping for. In its current state, not much has changed, aside from slightly improved graphics and faster load times.
