The Alighieri's Circle: Dante's Bloodline is a short and atmospheric walking simulator inspired by Dante's Divine Comedy. With its beautiful environments, intriguing story, exploration, and puzzle solving, the game offers a memorable journey through a visually striking interpretation of hell.

By the time the credits roll on The Alighieri Circle: Dante’s Bloodline, what lingers is less the amount of content contained within its relatively brief runtime than the sense of possibility surrounding it. ONE-O-ONE GAMES has chosen an unusually rich foundation for an independent horror game: taking the legacy of Dante Alighieri, weaving The Divine Comedy into an original mythology, and placing that inheritance in the hands of a descendant who must confront a responsibility carried through generations. It is an immediately intriguing premise, but more importantly, it gives the game a personality that is difficult to mistake for anyone else’s.

That personality is most evident in its atmosphere. Villa Alighieri is a particularly effective setting, its quiet corridors, natural light, family possessions and traces of previous generations creating the impression of a house that has accumulated history over centuries. Exploration consequently becomes more than a means of moving the story forward. Looking through rooms, examining objects and uncovering documents gradually turns the Villa into a fragmented record of the family that once lived there.

The Abyss takes the same underlying idea and tears it away from anything familiar. Its distorted architecture, surreal landscapes and imposing scale provide some of the game's strongest visual moments, while its strange combination of Dantean imagery and unexpected elements gives it a character of its own. The Abyss is at its best when it feels less like a recreation of Hell and more like a place that should not exist at all. It is also where the game's approach to horror becomes clearest: rather than relying on constant shocks, it uses space, silence and uncertainty to create unease.

Dante's presence is equally well integrated. The Divine Comedy is not treated as a convenient collection of references, nor is the Inferno simply reproduced for recognisable imagery. The pages, the ritual and the Alighieri family's connection to Hell form the backbone of the game's mythology, turning Dante's legacy into something inherited rather than merely remembered. It is a strong foundation—and one that ultimately exposes the game's greatest limitation.

There is simply more here than the game has time to fully explore. Gabriele is a good example. His position gives the story a naturally compelling human conflict: he has inherited an ancient responsibility he never chose, yet he must still reconcile that duty with the life he has built outside the Villa. His relationship with Dalila and their daughter Ginevra provides an important emotional counterweight to the supernatural events unfolding around him. Yet the game's compact structure means that these relationships are given only limited room to develop. By the end, Gabriele's circumstances are clear, but his journey could have carried considerably more emotional weight with more time devoted to the person behind the obligation.

The same is true of the wider Alighieri family history. The diaries and documents scattered throughout the Villa are among the most rewarding elements of the exploration because they hint at generations of people who lived through the ritual before Gabriele. They create the impression of an entire lineage shaped by sacrifice, secrecy and duty. But much of that history remains something the player reads about rather than experiences.

That is an understandable compromise for a compact production, and the approach works within the game's existing structure. Still, I found myself wishing that some of those stories had been brought to life through memories, visions or short playable sequences. Seeing even a handful of these events unfold directly could have transformed intriguing background material into some of the game's most memorable moments.

The question of runtime therefore deserves a little more nuance than simply calling the game short. At roughly three to four hours, The Alighieri Circle is not excessively long or short by definition. Its length would be perfectly appropriate if its ambitions were contained accordingly. The difficulty is that the narrative repeatedly suggests a much broader mythology, and the game reaches its conclusion just as that mythology begins to reveal how much further it could go. It does not feel unfinished so much as deliberately compact in a world that seems anything but.

The gameplay follows the same philosophy. Removing combat and conventional progression systems is entirely coherent with the experience ONE-O-ONE GAMES has set out to create. Gabriele does not need weapons, statistics or skill trees. His vulnerability reinforces the psychological-thriller framework and keeps the focus on exploration, observation, environmental storytelling and puzzles.

That approach works best when the player is encouraged to read the environment rather than simply move through it. Some puzzles make excellent use of documents, symbols, objects and details discovered elsewhere, allowing the solution to emerge naturally from the world. Others are more forgiving, while the linear structure occasionally limits the feeling of discovery that the setting itself seems designed to encourage.

Once again, the issue is less the underlying philosophy than the degree to which it is developed. With no combat loop or progression system to provide mechanical variety, the remaining systems need to evolve alongside the player's understanding of the world. The Alighieri Circle does this to an extent, but not always enough to match the scale suggested by its setting. And yet, despite those limitations, the game has something that cannot simply be designed into existence: a sense of place.

Villa Alighieri feels distinctly Italian without turning its cultural identity into a gimmick. Dante's legacy is embedded in the narrative rather than pasted onto it. The Abyss translates that literary inheritance into something visual, spatial and interactive. Even when the experience falls short of the possibilities it introduces, there is a clear creative voice behind it. That matters, particularly within a genre where familiarity can quickly become repetition.

The Alighieri Circle: Dante’s Bloodline is therefore not a game I would remember primarily for its length or mechanical complexity. I would remember it for the idea at its core, and for the moments in which that idea genuinely comes alive. Its strongest qualities (its atmosphere, art direction, setting and use of Dantean mythology) give it a character that many larger productions struggle to establish.

Its limitations are real. The linearity can feel restrictive, several puzzles are less demanding than they might have been, and the compact runtime leaves important characters, histories and locations less developed than their foundations suggest. But those shortcomings never overwhelm the experience. If anything, they make its strongest moments more revealing, because they show what this world might have supported with a broader scope.

That is ultimately where I land with The Alighieri Circle. It is an intriguing, atmospheric and distinctly personal game that feels less like a finished statement than the beginning of a conversation. ONE-O-ONE GAMES has taken one of Italy's most recognisable literary legacies and found a way to make it relevant to an original videogame narrative without reducing it to mere decoration.

For players drawn to psychological horror, environmental storytelling and mysteries rooted in place and history, there is plenty here to appreciate. And for anyone interested in seeing Italian cultural heritage interpreted through videogames, the project is particularly worth a look—not because it provides the definitive version of its idea, but because it demonstrates just how much room that idea still has to grow.

Perhaps that is the most fitting conclusion for a game built around inheritance. What The Alighieri Circle leaves behind is not the feeling that the journey was too short, but the feeling that there was more of it waiting beyond the final door.

The Alighieri Circle: Dante’s Bloodline is an underwhelming experience; one that actually had a lot of potential, but is let down by a short runtime that doesn’t let the players immerse themselves in the story. Whilst there are some solid puzzles here and an interesting visual design, there isn’t a lot of it.

The Alighieri's Circle: Dante's Bloodlines brings a combat-free descent into Dante's Hell, with clever trials and a weird, unsettling and personal atmosphere. However, it never really gets under your skin properly.

The Alighieri Circle: Dante’s Bloodline is a fascinating tribute to the Italian poet, offering an original take on the descent into Hell through striking art direction, well-designed puzzles, and excellent Italian voice acting. Unfortunately, an unengaging story, excessive downtime, and beautiful yet sterile environments hold it back. Still, it’s an intriguing Italian production for walking simulator and puzzle fans.
The Alighieri Circle is certainly atmospheric, but the journey was over shortly after the plot finally got interesting.

It may well be that a better-crafted story could have helped the uncomfortably short The Alighieri Circle, but given the quality of the puzzles and the weightless dialogue, not even a sermon from the pulpit could save it now. What's more, it hardly matters that lavish visuals pour out at our feet if the muddled storytelling fails to evoke any feeling at all.

The Alighieri Circle: Dante's Bloodline is a beautiful disappointment. Its atmosphere carries real craft, and the puzzles occasionally demand actual thought, which I appreciated more than I expected. But the story never justifies the journey, the environments repeat too quickly, and the performances undercut the mood they are meant to sell.

The Alighieri Circle: Dante’s Bloodline offers a dark and atmospheric descent into the underworld, built around challenging and varied puzzles that reward careful exploration and observation. Its strong atmosphere and thoughtful puzzle design make for an engaging experience, although the lack of a hint system and some repetitive sections can test the player’s patience.

The Alighieri Circle: Dante's Bloodline is a successful visual and gameplay experience, driven by clever puzzles and a strikingly hellish atmosphere, but held back by a story that feels too thin and a short runtime.

I’m left with the feeling that this is a game with good ideas, but one that fails to realise its full potential. Its setting is one of its greatest strengths, particularly the design of the villa, the soundscape and the reinterpretation of Dante’s Inferno.

I also think it’s a good move for ONE-O-ONE GAMES to focus on psychological horror rather than combat and cheap scares. On the other hand, however, the gameplay feels far too limited. As well as issues with pacing, the puzzles are uneven

A stylish and atmospheric psychological thriller that trades action for clever puzzles and pure deduction. Despite some underwhelming voice acting and a limited number of puzzles, The Alighieri Circle: Dante’s Bloodline delivers a compact and compelling narrative experience that should appeal to fans of slow-paced, mature adventures.

The Alighieri Circle: Dante's Bloodline is a walking simulator with environmental puzzles that reimagines Dante's world by placing it in a new setting. Despite its strong writing and voice acting, the adventure fails to engage players due to static environments and subpar technical execution.

The Alighieri Circle: Dante’s Bloodline might fumble its storytelling, but it delivers great puzzle design that really makes it worth your attention. It’s just a shame that some of its ideas don’t hit the same standard, because there’s a genuinely fascinating tale to be told here… it just could have done with a little bit more depth to help it stand out.

Still, if you love a good brainteaser and appreciate a gloomy, well-crafted atmosphere, The Alighieri Circle: Dante’s Bloodline is definitely worth checking out.
The Alighieri Circle: Dante’s Bloodline stands out for its ambition and atmosphere, even if it does not quite shine with the consistency its premise truly deserves.

The Alighieri Circle: Dante’s Bloodline is a bold reinterpretation of Dante’s legacy, but in reshaping the Inferno it often loses its emotional force and unforgettable imagery. Solid ideas and good Italian voice acting aren’t enough to lift Gabriele’s brief journey, caught between homage and independence. Interesting and ambitious, yet unable to stand beside the masterpiece it evokes.

The intent here is twofold: to spark interest through association and to provide a loose framing story. And both of these The Alighieri Circle achieves with its template drawn from the literary masterpiece. Yet anyone hoping for more of a "Divina Commedia" (like myself) will be bitterly disappointed. Gabriele's journey into the Inferno is a solid, yet superficially narrated work with clichés and an abstract, but ultimately too monotonous game world. At least the few trials we must face are quite entertaining in terms of gameplay and fit well into the game's atmosphere. However, what's missing are memorable highlights or more courage in exploring the existing elements in order to stand out from the crowd.
28.6% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (7 reviews).

Kejora, despite the occasional flaws that I noted, was a pleasure to experience. The story spoke to matters of protecting those around you and what you would do to ensure the safety of others, and did so in a nice, concise few hour package. And in a world of video games that ask upwards of 100 hours of gameplay to finish (yes, I play JRPG’s if you weren’t aware), a brief tale like Kejora is a welcome experience.
Kejora is like Stand By Me meets Groundhog Day, Studio Ghibli style, in a delightful if slightly unpolished coming-of-age Indonesian puzzle-platformer.

Kejora is an absolutely charming and ambitious indie platformer adventure that has all the necessary narrative bones for a visually compelling experience. In terms of story, it largely hits the mark. However, the shortfalls in its awkward gameplay, lackluster sound design, and noticeable UI blips stagger that experience to a degree, and it probably could have used more time in the oven on those fronts. Nevertheless, if you're a fan of hand-drawn animation in games, especially of the Ghibli variety, I would say to give it the chance it deserves.

Kejora isn’t loud. It isn’t flashy. And it isn’t trying to impress you with scale. What it does instead is quietly tell a story about change, fear, and the comfort — and danger — of staying the same. I do have to say however that although the game’s visuals are fantastic and story meaningful. Kejora is very short. Also compared to other Indie titles I have covered it’s price tag is unfair for ~3 hours of gameplay with no replay value.

Kejora is a visually striking 2D puzzle adventure that leans heavily on hand-drawn, Ghibli-inspired aesthetics and a gentle, melancholic tone. While its atmosphere and story carry emotional weight, the gameplay remains overly simple and sometimes clumsy, with weak audio design and restrictive saving systems. It’s a heartfelt narrative experience, best suited for players who value art and mood over mechanical depth.

Kejora is a short and simple game with an animated art style reminiscent of Studio Ghibli films and the books I read in school to help me learn different languages. Despite its efforts and how much I thoroughly enjoyed the introductory act and the larger themes, questions, and ideas, the limitations of its clunky gameplay, declining quality of its story, frequent bugs, and an immersion-breaking lack of sound effects left me less engaged, indifferent, and bored by the end of it all.

Kejora visually draws inspiration from the works of Studio Ghibli and offers a primarily narrative-driven adventure, with few puzzles to solve and some light stealth sections. While the game is aimed at less demanding players, the overall experience feels bland and far too limited in every aspect. Recommended only if you are a fan of Studio Ghibli’s works and are looking for something light and undemanding.

The latest project from Berangin Creative is a journey worth undertaking for anyone who prioritizes the contemplation of visual art over systemic complexity, yet it demands a certain degree of indulgence regarding its sometimes timid narration and stumbling technical refinement. It is a title that warms the heart with its palette but fails to deeply etch itself into the soul, hindered by an excessively linear nature and a ludic structure that struggles to evolve. For these reasons, while remaining an experience endowed with praiseworthy directorial dignity, Kejora stops just short of the threshold of excellence.

For Berangin Creative’s debut game, Keejora is good first attempt. Even with the game’s problems, there’s still just enough here to make for a worthwhile playthrough, but the game’s unutilised potential brings down what could have been something quite special.
Kejora’s gorgeous art can’t mask a clunky, buggy core that feels undercooked and frustrating far more often than it is enjoyable.

Berangin Creative have set the standard for 2026 with their latest release, Kejora. Published by Soft Source Publishing, Kejora is an immersive tale of cursed magic, bravery, and forgiveness. This side-scroller is an indie gem and surprisingly immersive to play, leaving you reluctant to step away without completing the game.
40.0% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (15 reviews).

Truckful offers a relaxing yet occasionally tense driving experience, combining package deliveries with a mysterious story, side missions, and collectibles. Its engaging narrative and puzzle-based gameplay make exploring enjoyable, although judging the depth of the environment can sometimes be difficult. Despite some grindy Scrap collecting, Truckful delivers a unique and compact adventure.

Truckful is a strange delivery game that shines in its genre mix, blending horror with cozy exploration. However, it also has plenty of speed bumps in its controls and exploration, creating a frustrating driving experience that could use more quality-of-life improvements. Still, once you get past those roadblocks, the game becomes surprisingly heartfelt, with a compelling story and a charming cast of NPCs who stick with you as you unravel the town's mysteries. It’s a bumpy ride, but if you’re willing to stick with it, Truckful is worth taking for a spin.

Truckful‘s flow might be interrupted by frequent loading screens, but it is otherwise a pretty fun, relaxing physics-puzzle about driving through a beautiful countryside delivering packages. That is, until sudden, unexpected but much-appreciated horror elements show up, giving the game a unique and threatening element not present in similar titles.

Truckful has a surprisingly deep, dark story with a lot of enjoyable, entertaining characters. This carried me through the game more than I expected, and I’m glad I got to experience what it had to offer. The physics are hit or miss depending on your driving, but the core mechanics and handling are fun. The game excels in story, world-building, mystery, and, more often than not, the main gameplay loop.

Truckful a game you can easily group in with titles like Dredge and Easy Delivery Co, though it relies more on physics-based safe driving. I do wish MythicOwl didn’t break up the immersion so much with the way it handles the map. And I think perhaps it was a bug, but sometimes even on story mode the physics system seemed determined to eject my packages even when driving slowly. But the idea is still pretty fun, and it’s easy to drive around Deepstone Valley to complete jobs or even just explore.
At times, Truckful feels fun, but that enjoyment wanes with repetitive objective requirements, frequent loading screens, and a just-okay story.

In the long run—much like any video game that simulates a job—Truckful turns into a routine: you end up doing the same things and, for the most part, driving the same roads. You move from one character to another, sometimes just to update them on the situation before speeding off to the next conversation. Car chases become few and far between—save for the showdown with the two ghosts—and the entire cargo-hauling mechanic tends to become monotonous. Ultimately, Truckful is a hard game to pin down: it aims to be "cozy" but fails, as the driving mechanics and camera angles will only frustrate you. It tries to be a thriller, yet that element becomes increasingly muted. It sets out to be a job-simulation game but embraces only the worst possible aspect of the job: the routine. The same faces, the same roads, the same packages—over and over again. At a certain point, you’ll even grow tired of the trees, the tree-lined roads, and the little birds.

Truckful turns something as simple as delivering packages into an entertaining adventure thanks to its physics, cargo placement, and navigation that invites you to explore the valley. Plus, the dark, Dredge-esque vibe is addictive. There are things that could be improved, like the camera, but I’ve enjoyed playing the role of a delivery driver in this quirky world.

Truckful is a fantastic driving adventure that hides an unexpectedly dark and mysterious heart beneath its sunny, charming visuals. Transporting its eccentric inhabitants and their heavy equipment across challenging terrain is a real test of skill, driven by an excellent story that culminates in a brilliant cliffhanger. The perfect game for two or three atmospheric evenings.

Truckful proves to be a bold experiment that stands out strongly in the indie game scene thanks to an original blend of driving simulation, inventory puzzles, and cozy horror storytelling. Unfortunately, the game’s good intentions and excellent art direction clash with some rather obvious structural rough edges, such as the restrictive limit of only three equipment slots, the cumbersome game map, and the occasional frustrations caused by the isometric camera, all of which hinder the adventure’s pacing. Despite these obvious balance issues, Truckful possesses a sincere spirit and undeniable charm.

Truckful is a delivery video game that combines a more relaxing side, where we drive a colorful pickup truck through a small village in the woods, with a thriller, featuring huge ghost vehicles chasing us and a curse keeping the villagers confined to the woods.

In this video game, you play as a delivery driver—the only person with a vehicle in a town cut off by a strange presence lurking in the woods. MythicOwl and Pocketpair Publishing present an engaging, cozy simulation adventure for mobile and PC, where handling transport jobs in your pickup truck becomes an experience filled with constant challenges, mysteries, and dangers.

Truckful, despite its flaws, is a good alternative to traditional driving games. It has a familiar personality, with hauling physical cargo, helping a small community, exploring a remote valley, and uncovering a nefarious mystery. If you’re into cozy games with some light puzzle-solving and the odd moment of horror, there is a lot to love here.

For the hoarders. For the scrappers. And for those who know how to change a tire. I do not know where the intersection lies between a car junky and a paranormal thrillseeker, but this is the perfect game for them. For the rest of us, a solid delivery adventure with ghostly undertones awaits. Just be ready to get stuck in the mud more than you expect.

Truckful successfully draws players into its valley with its mysterious atmosphere and story. Its physics-based mechanics and handling capabilities make for an impressively ambitious piece of work on the mechanical front. However, when tight spaces, dropped cargo and interaction issues combine, they turn what is otherwise simple gameplay into something needlessly complicated. As a result, the game’s core tension element transforms into an uncomfortable source of frustration rather than something to be embraced.

Truckful has lovely handling, a compelling mystery, and an opening I genuinely loved. There is a good game here, but equipment restrictions and repeated lost progress made staying in love with it much harder than it should have been.

Truckful is a delightful delivery experience that’ll offer plenty of fun across its blend of cozy and creepy driving. The endearing storytelling, satisfying packing and delivering, and sudden bursts of vehicular terror make for one heck of a ride, and whilst the occasional camera issue and break in pace with loading screens can let it down, it still manages to stand out as a very memorable trip.

Truckful surprised me with its beautiful design, fun gameplay, and a world that offers more than just a few delivery locations. Loading up, upgrading your truck, and meeting strangers combine to make for a cool experience. The secrets and unexpected dangers also leave you curious about what's to come. However, the game is quite tough on standard difficulty, and the early confrontation with the aggressive truck, in particular, could have been paced better. As a result, this pleasant adventure sometimes feels very bumpy.
Truckful is a uniquely weird physics-based delivery game blending cozy adventure with eerie thrills. Satisfying cargo packing is ultimately weighed down by clunky map navigation and UI quirks.
29.4% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (17 reviews).
A mix of pointed humor, some procedural unpredictability, and what feels like a unique challenge help to at least make this an interesting experience overall.

What ultimately defines The Prisoning: Fletcher’s Quest is its willingness to lean into the messy, unpredictable chaos of its themes. This is a game that thrives on unevenness, unfair boss fights, delightful absurdity, random map generation, and moments that make you throw your controller only to pick it up again with stubborn determination. It isn’t polished to a sheen, nor does it always feel fair, but it understands its own tone and purpose, and the developer acknowledges this throughout the game. Fletcher’s Quest is a game that feels like its own critique: uncomfortably familiar to anyone who’s lived through crunch, burned out, or felt their own creativity turn into an adversary. Well, hello, therapy and burnout, good to see you again, but gamified this time.

The Prisoning: Fletcher’s Quest is a great little Metroidvania, full of wacky antics and charm. Its tight controls and strong design make the journey through perilous areas a thrill, while the catchy themes linger long after the relatively short runtime. Boss battles are varied and there are some genuinely funny moments; however, the mission structure can feel repetitive, and some of the randomness lacks clear context and doesn’t always land. Despite its creativity and polish, it risks being overlooked in an already crowded genre.

You can’t go through half a steam store page without tripping over a Metroidvania. Lots of great experiences to be had exploring wide ranging maps with hard stop gates you can only cross once you get that next special ability. The Prisoning: Fletcher’s Quest decided to step in that pond but stayed in the shallow end of map travel. There’s some comedy that oversteps the bounds of where my humor lies. Bluntly, in these spaces, a little bit of editing could go a long way. That said, when the jokes do hit, they’re really funny. When Elden Pixels tees up a gameplay surprise, it’s pure joy. When you get to that next boss, you’re going to feel good about dispatching them. The Prisoning: Fletcher’s Quest is a game whose highs are in the atmosphere, and is short enough where the flaws aren’t felt for long.

The Prisoning is an interesting and unique game and really goes a long way to justifying the return of Acclaim. It feels familiar enough, yet sprinkling in a host of flavor to make it stand out. I really enjoyed playing through the game. The boss fights are the highlight for sure, and I wish it was a bit more fleshed out, but this is a novel title that breaks the standard on several levels. Definitely worth checking out.

Overall, The Prisoning: Fletcher’s Quest is a fun experience that’s light on the metroidvania aspects. It’s well designed and executed, if a little short. This makes it an easy way to pass a few hours, and it scratches that exploration itch. It might be a little crude at times, but The Prisoning: Fletcher’s Quest was a game I think I’ll remember in a sea of similar titles.

The Prisoning: Fletcher’s Quest on Nintendo Switch is a meticulously built yet curiously lifeless micro-metroidvania, where, despite the controls being super-sharp and its pixel art vibrant, the adventure feels boxed in. Repetitive rooms, shallow exploration, and a brief runtime make it resemble a neat demo instead of the real deal. As for its constant meta commentary, it’s very amusing for about 30 minutes, but ultimately drains the world of its potential to immerse.
I enjoyed playing The Prisoning: Fletcher's Quest and had some laughs but its basic gameplay and small scope certainly make it feel limited.

Ultimately, The Prisoning: Fletcher’s Quest is a solid, compact experience that showcases strong fundamentals. Movement feels good, boss encounters are engaging, and the writing has a distinct voice. At the same time, its most promising mechanics are not explored deeply enough, and its metroidvania elements remain surface level. The procedural component adds replay value in theory, but does not meaningfully expand the scope. For anyone seeking a brief, well controlled action platformer with personality, it delivers. For those expecting a robust, sprawling metroidvania, it may feel underdeveloped. It is a good game that hints at something greater, even if it never fully reaches that potential.

The Prisoning: Fletcher's Quest isn't a bad game, and the handful of hours you'll spend with it will certainly pass the time with a decent level of enjoyment, but there isn't really anything particularly memorable here. The procedural generation means that subsequent playthroughs will feature slightly different layouts, though this undercuts the intricate level design that good search adventure games need. Coupled with the sometimes questionable humour and you have a title that can offer a passing distraction but won't stay with you.

The Prisoning: Fletcher's Quest is exactly as it presents itself. It wants to be more, but I wish it didn't think it had to be. It's regular retro platforming, with a good map, checkpoints, forgettable characters, and cool bosses. It's something to do. You'll probably play it twice, but that's twice the something to do.
Will you manage to find a way to escape from this mental prison?
I think this is a great, short Metroidvania. If you are someone who doesn’t need a well-crafted story, you just want to jump around and shoot monsters, this might be a great weekend play.
“I'd rather to play the NES version of Fester’s Quest.”

The Prisoning: Fletcher’s Quest has the bones of a good game. It features some genuinely great platforming mechanics, a weird but unhinged, visually striking opening, and entertaining core shooting. If you just want a new platformer to double-jump your way through, it might scratch that itch.
 However, outside of the basics, it lacks the punch needed to be truly memorable. The recycling of early-game enemies, a lackluster overarching story after the initial setup, and deeply frustrating boss design hold the game back from reaching its full potential.

This is a game you can easily sink a few hours into. I haven't reached the end yet, as it's quite challenging, and you certainly won't encounter the first boss in the first hour. Seasoned platformers might blast through it a bit faster, but even then, you'll need to learn the patterns and stay constantly alert. All in all, The Prisoning: Fletcher's Quest is a surprisingly strong and solid metroidvania. With its witty humor, strong enemy design, tight gameplay, and quirky presentation, this game is a definite recommendation for both fans and non-fans of the genre.
The Prisoning: Fletcher’s Quest isn't going to light the world on fire, but if you're looking for a platformer without any frills you may enjoy it.
The Prisoning: Fletcher’s Quest is a wild ride. It is a tight and beautiful platformer that is only held back by the randomized maps and some frustrating bosses.
36.4% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (11 reviews).

Prinny Party: Going Overboard! presents a hyper-specific gameplay formula that combines strategy RPG gameplay within a co-op board game so not everyone will click with it but those who do will have an absolutely wonderful time powering-up their characters, dood.

Prinny Party: Going Overboard! has refreshing ideas and pleasant enough presentation, but the lack of a traditional online multiplayer mode really hurts its appeal. If you’ve got local pals who you can play with, you’re likely to have a great time messing with each other and taking on some iconic characters from throughout the main series, but otherwise, it’ll require a bit more patience than you might be willing to expend to get the most out of this one.
Prinny Party: Going Overboard! is a fun and chaotic time. Adding computer players adds another layer, as they seem to hate you making any progress.

While there is a solidly-designed game at the center of Prinny Party!, both the presentation and amount of content are sorely lacking for its price point. Devoted Disgaea fans may find a party game worth the cover charge, but those who would quickly tire of a single board with only a few basic gimmicks may want to search elsewhere.
Prinny Party: Going Overboard is a whole lot of fun with friends, but a lack of online multiplayer will make it a tough sell for many.
Prinny Party: Going Overboard! is a reimagination of Disgaea in a digital board game format.

"Prinny Party: Going Overboard!" can be a fun romp with other players as you cooperate, wheel and deal, plead, and ultimately backstab each other at the first fortuitous opportunity. It’s essentially an experiment in human psychology in game form. The lack of online play hurts for PS5, which is the version I reviewed, so get the Switch 2 or Steam version on PC if you have access to those systems. The game can also become monotonous after long sessions. If you’re itching for a RPG combat party game along the lines of Dokapon Kingdom, however, Prinny Party just might scratch that longing.
Prinny Party: Going Overboard! is a fun party game that makes good use of the familiar characters and unique classes from Nippon Ichi Software’s games.
It's time to give it your all and defeat the Supreme Overboard!

Prinny Party: Going Overboard! has a really interesting premise but doesn't quite provide enough material to justify its asking price. Disgaea lovers with pals willing to spend several hours investigating its mechanics might find something useful here. If, however, you mostly want a classic party game with loads of different boards, activities, and reasons to keep coming back, this edition is hard to recommend.
By utterly failing to get players up to speed on pretty well anything going on, and lacking in variety, this supposed party game dives straight into the rocks
Prinny Party: Going Overboard! offers various ways to play and features a delightful array of fun events and different strategies.

Prinny Party: Going Overboard! is a meowtastic Disgaea-themed party-style RPG board game that blends chaotic gameplay with familiar series elements, delivering an entertaining experience for both solo and multiplayer. There's room for improvement but has a purrfect foundation for a potential new party series!

river-city-saga-journey-to-the-west.title: River City Saga: Journey to the West

reviews.excerpt: 41.7% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (12 reviews).

As a roguelike, the game is naturally not designed to be completed just once. It will take hours of attempts and upgrades to reach the end, but even after finishing it, replayability remains high—not only due to the experimentation with various builds and the addictive quality typical of the best roguelikes, but also because the levels become more complex and a "true ending" can be unlocked by completing the game a second time.

River City Saga: Journey to the West is an accessible roguelite that charms more through its humor and personality than its depth - essentially another likeable Kunio-kun-style adventure but with a twist, though not one of its best entries.

River City Saga: Journey to the West brings together the classic Chinese myth and the Kunio games under the form of an action roguelite and as odd as that may sound, the game's comical approach, quirky visual style and immediate combat satisfaction will make players feel right at home. There's plenty of skills to learn and movements to perform, and the game's formula follows the Kunio legacy. At the same time, there's a feeling of repetitiveness that makes itself felt too quickly, and the lack of cooperative multiplayer is hard to understand. The combat is fun, but a more ambitious depth would work wonders for the game's roguelite structure.

River City Saga: Journey to the West’s skeletal structure should work, but the adherence to the subgenre without the knowledge of how to pare back and adapt it to this type of game makes the gameplay carry too much water with a lopsided play-to-dialogue ratio. Someone might crack the code on this mash-up, but River City Saga isn’t the one to show how it’s done. If you enjoy any brawler you can put your hands on and have a fondness for this style of storytelling, it may be worth a look. Otherwise, this time investment is too much in an ocean of better games.

A very safe roguelite. It doesn't really intend to change anything, or to intrigue players with its builds. And this is a genre where you not only have a high difficulty level to keep players wanting to replay, but also provide variety that's tempting and guarantees something new. This one doesn't have that. Even bosses will also remain in their positions permanently. The combat is dynamic, enjoyable, and Kunio is as likable as ever, but that doesn't change the fact that it's an average roguelite.
All in all, River City Saga: Journey to the West is a flawed but fun experience. I wish the translation was better, but the combat is far more interesting than the narrative anyway.

Although I wish it had a co-op mode and more variation in its campaign, I ended up having a lot of fun with River City Saga: Journey to the West and I'm definitely looking forward to new and improved roguelike Kunio-kun games. This is a solid start! 🐒

River City Saga: Journey to the West is a fun little expedition into something different for the franchise, but it never really hit the heights I was hoping for. If you need a decently priced roguelite adventure to tide you over until the next big thing, you could certainly do worse than picking this up. Franchise fans will get a bit more mileage out of it than others, I think, but I would like to see more things covered by “River City Saga,” and hopefully we get co-op then.

Arc System Works played it a little safe with the usual roguelite difficulty curve in River City Saga: Journey to the West to avoid alienating its core Kunio-kun fanbase. Normally, that sounds like a recipe for trouble. This time, however, sitting somewhere in the middle actually works. Combining 80 Secret Skills to shape your favourite Kunio-kun character creates a roguelite comfort game that is fast, snappy and enjoyable, even if it never sets the gaming world on fire.

​Maybe it’s a mixture of burnout with the roguelike genre of late or the fact I went in expecting a fusion of two genres I really enjoyed, but River City Saga: Journey to the West just didn’t click with me. It felt too basic in all areas, and what was once a strong leader in the beat 'em up genre is now trailing behind the stronger releases from Dotemu.

​It’s still pretty serviceable without any particularly massive issues, there just isn’t that special sauce here that I needed to really enjoy my latest Kunio-Kun fix. It’s cheeky, it’s fast-paced, and it's chaotic, but sadly, it feels like a rare miss in the long-running River City series, eclipsed by its much stronger predecessors in the River City Saga spin-off series.

For raw action roguelite enjoyment, there are better games for sure. As it stands, this is a solid experiment from ArcSys with a beloved franchise. Where does River City Saga go next? Hopefully, the team has some cool ideas for us.

River City Saga: Journey to the West won't convert anyone who's already burned out on the roguelike formula, and it doesn't offer the mechanical depth that keeps the genre's best entries endlessly replayable across dozens of hours. But it is a genuine, energetic tribute to a franchise that has endured for forty years through sheer stubbornness and a lot of punching.

River City Saga: Journey to the West is a fun, charismatic, and solidly based roguelite beat 'em up, but it's limited in depth and ambition. It's a title that's more enjoyable for its personality and immediate combat than for the evolution of its systems, and it fits perfectly into that category of games that perform admirably without truly standing out within the genre.

River City Saga: Journey to the West is a vibrant blend of mythology, roguelike growth, and arcade battling, and there’s enough short-term enjoyment to be enjoyed with it. It’s very colorful, and fighting is so easy that you just enjoy it without thinking much. But it has repeated battles and no long-term purpose to make it unforgettable.
Available for about twenty euros depending on your support, River City Saga Journey to the West is a “small” Rogue Like friendly, easy to take in hand and pleasant to play and follow
River City Saga: Journey to the West is a curious and fun experiment that manages to reinterpret the myth of the Journey to the West through the chaos typical of Kunio-kun.

total-war-warhammer-iii-lord-of-the-end-.title: Total War: WARHAMMER III - Lord of the End Times

reviews.excerpt: 100.0% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (11 reviews).

Lords of the End Times is an expansion focused entirely on its protagonists, all of whom are undeniably well-realized. Thanquol is perhaps the most intriguing, thanks to his grand schemes and risk-taking nature, while Boris Todbringer answers the community’s long-standing requests. Nagash and the Glottkin round out a quartet that feels perfectly suited to this apocalyptic setting. Ultimately, the DLC’s value lies in the sheer volume of content Creative Assembly has prepared for us. And when an expansion makes us look at *Immortal Empires* with the feeling that there is still something new to discover, it means Total War: WARHAMMER III undoubtedly still has a few cards—and turns—left to play.

Lords of the End Times adds a substantial amount of excellent content to an already massive game. Thanks to the new and powerful Legendary Lords and the Devastation System, Total War: Warhammer III feels fresh again. Aside from some balancing issues and Boris Todbringer’s slightly lackluster campaign, Warhammer III, Lords of the End Times is both must-have content for longtime fans and a great place to jump in to an already excellent strategy game.
Lord of the End Times finally brings some of the biggest fan favorites into the game—and does them justice in the process.

That said, it is clear that they do not revolutionize anything—nor do they claim to; they simply aim to add value to a game world whose core characteristics are already well-established. This is evident from a technical standpoint as well, given the meticulous attention to detail across all four packs—from flawlessly animated units and high-quality static artwork and cinematics to new, dedicated musical scores. In short, if you have already played *Total War: Warhammer III* and want to return to it, this is an excellent way to do so; conversely, if you haven't played it yet but are interested in these four factions, you now have a fantastic entry point into what is currently one of the best strategy games on the market.

Total War: Warhammer III - Lords Of The End Times might not be the final DLC of the series, but it delivers worthwhile faction updates, a strong Chaos Invasion, and a solid challenge. However, several factions feel too similar in battle, some End Times scenarios become a slog, and the Glotkin’s campaign suffers from weak vassal mechanics in the base game.

Total War: Warhammer III – Señores del Fin de los Tiempos expands Immortal Empires with Nagash, the Glottkin, Boris Todbringer and Thanquol, four very different legendary lords bringing new units, heroes and mechanics that significantly change how each campaign can be approached.

Lords of the End Times works because it’s more than just a list of famous names. Nagash lives up to every bit of the hype. Thanquol’s campaign might just be the most fun in the whole pack. Boris gets the attention he’s deserved for years, and the Glottkin bring something totally different that rounds everything out perfectly

One of the biggest and most ambitious DLCs ever released for Total War: Warhammer III. The arrival of Nagash would be reason enough for many players to return to the game, but Creative Assembly has gone a step further by adding three additional Legendary Lords, new units, distinct campaigns and a free update that refreshes some key content
Lords of the End Times is exactly what you'd expect : a solid set of content for Total War: Warhammer III fans, looking back at the best DLC already released for the game.

And when an expansion manages to make us look at Immortal Empires with the feeling that there's still something new to discover, it means Total War: WARHAMMER III undoubtedly still has some cards (and turns) left to play.
Lords of the End Times can surprise you at every turn. The sheer scale of the expansion, the variety of new lords, and their unique mechanics make every campaign feel different.

Lords of the End Times is the most ambitious DLC ever seen in Total War: Warhammer III and, without a doubt, one of the most generous as well. Nagash and Thanquol offer two of the most original campaigns in the entire trilogy; the Glottkin are solid without going overboard; and only Boris Todbringer falls slightly short. Between Neferata, the rework of the Vampire Counts, the new endgame content, and an access model that’s finally beginner-friendly, the End Times was truly worth the wait.

Total War: Warhammer III has gained four more Legendary Lords in the new Lords of the End Times DLC pack. The most prominent of them is undoubtedly Nagash and his seemingly endless army of the undead, although he is a somewhat more challenging faction to play than you may be used to. The other Legendary Lords are equally noteworthy, but their campaigns are a little less inventive, as Nagash appears to have received the most attention from the developers.

Although some lords are way more interesting than others, “Lords of the End Times” is, overall, an amazing package that revitalizes “Total War: Warhammer III” and sets new standards for Creative Assembly — both in terms of quality and quantity. A must have for any “Warhammer” fan.

After so many years, Total War: Warhammer III reaches its conclusion with an expansion that truly feels like an event. For me, Lords of the End Times closes out one of the most ambitious trilogies ever created—not only by Creative Assembly, but in the entire history of the industry. Here’s to another thousand hours of gameplay in this wonderful franchise.

Fardust built a great setting here to tell more stories in this world, and the game pairs perfectly with recent deckbuilder Death Howl if you seek more not-quite-a-roguelite pastoral horror vibes. Focused in its vision and flamboyant on the screen, Shards of Order should land with anyone looking for smart dark fantasy storytelling that plays its cards right.

Once you get the hang of it and a feel for how it’s meant to be played… Shards Of Order is a decent bit of fun. The mechanic might take a little to get used to but it’s arguably just a variation of different RPG battles styles, essentially turn based, but where you can alter the way those turns end up by playing with time. Given the very reasonable price… I’d say it’s worth a look if you like deck building games and RPGs with a dark story.

Shard of Order proved to be an excellent addition to the deck-building genre. Unique in its concept, it leaves out the round and action-point mechanics found in almost every game of the genre, replacing them with the concept of time. Simple to grasp yet quite deep, this mechanic remains fresh even after countless battles. The game also benefits from great replayability and a nicely crafted dark-fantasy aesthetic.

Shards of Order initially takes some getting used to, especially while figuring out the party roles, sprawling skill tree and the time-based combat. Stick with it though and there’s an incredibly satisfying deckbuilding RPG waiting underneath.

While Shards of Order maintains a cohesive structural path throughout its campaign, its true strength lies in how dynamically it encourages players to step out of their comfort zones and experiment with diverse strategies for every challenge they encounter. By constantly shifting its tempo and requiring fresh tactics, the game prevents its progression from ever feeling repetitive, rewarding curiosity and creative problem-solving at nearly every turn. Although these sudden shifts in momentum can occasionally introduce friction during high-stakes combat encounters where a steady rhythm feels necessary, this intentional variation ultimately elevates the experience by giving the gameplay exceptional depth, a satisfying learning curve, and immense replay value.

I've had a blast with Shards of Order. I have qualms with some of the narrative presentation and would have loved to see more quality-of-life features in the overworld, but the deck-building and combat are top-notch, as is the art style and overall visual presentation. The  game's linear structure, which creates a purposeful, escalating experience, is also a plus, making this an easy recommendation for fans of the genre.
A gloomy fantasy RPG that clearly wears its passion on its sleeve. Its creative card-based mechanics are pretty addictive, too.

Shards of Order takes the deckbuilder formula and grafts it onto a narrative-driven RPG with no roguelite structure. Its greatest strength lies in combat: cards consume neither mana nor action points, but instead advance a shared timeline, forcing players to calculate how much room they are willing to give their enemies. The deck must be built with discipline and adapted to different encounters, objectives, and monsters. A bleak atmosphere, weighty impacts, and imposing bosses are supported by a strong art direction, although some card illustrations feel visually inconsistent with the rest. The absence of procedural runs reduces both longevity and replayability, but makes the experience more faithful to its soulslike nature.

Shards of Order turns time itself into the cost of every card, creating a tense and rewarding tactical RPG. Its shared deck system, striking dark-fantasy world and memorable battles outweigh the limited card variety, uneven pacing and occasional technical issues.

Shards of Order packs a lot into its short, approximately 10-hour experience, and it did more than enough to keep my attention throughout. Both gameplay and story were highlights in the early game. But it does feel like a bit too much story is trying to fit in too small a package by the late game, with major story beats flying by on the mad dash for the end goal...With that said, I’d do that dash again – and I will. The card battling remains consistently solid, and I’m already looking forward to playing a second time to try out different strategies and deck builds.

Shards of Order is a really good deckbuilding RPG that tells a coherent story, has decent progression, and a battle system that challenges. This is not a game where you can just settle on your initial deck choices, but one that encourages regularly switching approaches until you break through. Sometimes that be frustrating, but overall this is a solid RPG experience that's worth your time.
Shards of Order is an excellent card-based RPG that combines deep combat mechanics with a dark fantasy setting for something genuinely captivating.

A blend of apocalyptic dark fantasy, light RPG narrative choice, and highly tactical deckbuilding that is arguably a must-play at its budget price point. Shards of Order is a striking new IP in an overstuffed genre that deserves fans’ attention and further franchise development.
A gloomy fantasy RPG that clearly wears its passion on its sleeve. Its creative card-based mechanics are pretty addictive, too…

Shards of Order makes a strong case for itself. It has a clear identity, an interesting combat system, a dark setting, and enough character progression to make each battle feel connected to the larger journey.

Shards of Order appeals especially to players tired of roguelike runs but who don't want to give up card-based tactics. For those seeking sustained progression, distinct characters, and a complete story instead of endless repetition, it's one of the year's noteworthy indie RPGs.
100.0% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (10 reviews).

It is abundantly clear that Songs of Glimmerwick gets the cozy game genre spot on. It offers more than just a checklist of chores – a genuine sanctuary. It’s a game that respects your time, your agency, and your need to breathe. In a world full of suffering and struggle, that really feels like magic.
A lovingly crafted game brings the magic of music to every aspect of this cosy sim title. If only it increased in tempo a little sooner to unveil its delights before you get waylaid.

Songs of Glimmerwick is a lovely, inviting experience that pulls you into its world. The graphics and art style are gorgeous and perfectly match the witchy world it creates. The voice acting and writing are strong and keep you engaged. While pacing and some interactive elements falter, they fade as you spend more time in this world. Songs of Glimmerwick is a fantastic cozy experience in a fall packed with juggernauts, making it ideal for sitting with and relaxing. It’s wonderful and worth playing.

Songs of Glimmerwick offers a pleasant, cozy experience. It has a wide range of game mechanics, but they're a little shallow and don't quite slot together, and that cozy atmosphere risks sending you straight to sleep at times.

A beautifully soulful immersion into a world of music and everyday magic, where the worst thing that can happen to you is mice gnawing away the roots of a plant (which you can easily grow again in a day).

From side quests to class, Songs of Glimmerwick’s narrative is told in pieces. I found it felt natural to learn about the world this way, especially when you play as a witch who’s unfamiliar with the magical world. I ended up invested in the world before I realized it, and that encouraged me to keep completing quests. Even side quests fit nicely into the narrative, increasing your knowledge of the Etchery and the nearby town of Wisk.

Songs of Glimmerwick is a charming game that skillfully combines elements of magic and gardening, delivering an enjoyable gaming experience that will keep you entertained for at least 30–40 hours. Despite a few shortcomings, it's definitely a game worth giving a chance.

If you’re looking for a cosy game this autumn, and the wait for Witchbrook has you a bit annoyed, I would very much recommend checking out Songs of Glimmerwick. With a story that’s worth investing your time in, fully realised characters that will utterly charm you, and a colourful world to explore at your own pace, there’s just so much here to love. The game’s length can seem a bit daunting, but once it has its hooks in you, the hours will fly by, and before you know it, you’ll have enjoyed the true magic of a game that holds you like a warm hug.

In Songs of Glimmerwick, we step into a magical school where spells are learned through melodies, a mysterious island awaits exploration, and unusual characters have stories of their own to tell. This cozy RPG stands out with its charming atmosphere, beautiful art style, and a unique musical approach to magic. However, a slow start and occasionally tedious traversal take some of the shine off the adventure.

Songs of Glimmerwick is a charming magical-school RPG that replaces combat with music, exploration, gardening, and relationships. Its slower pace and occasional quest confusion may test patience, but its world and atmosphere are memorable.

Songs of Glimmerwick delivers a charming magic-school RPG built around music, exploration, gardening, and story. Its slower pace and lack of combat won't suit everyone, but the world gives you plenty to discover.

Folktales vividly tell stories that are parallel to our world to remind us of something we may have lost along the way. Part farm-sim, part magical school, all an ode to nature, Songs of Glimmerwick is a remarkable achievement because from the very first moment that you play, you feel its kindness reaching out. Through a lush art style, stellar voice work, and its rustic soundtrack, it is a great example of why magic is all around us. We just need to know where to look.
100.0% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (14 reviews).
Metacritic user score 8.6/10 (13 ratings).
This is a considered, artful game and one that’s so clearly created with love. For any fan of sewing or tactile creativity, it’s a must-play experience.

I adore Dressmaker. It is easily one of my top played games of the year. It’s nostalgic, cozy and the story is so memorable. The concept is so charming and the ability to replay and try new designs as well. For some players, I can see the gameplay loop being a bit repetitive, but personally it’s comforting and adds to the appeal. Sometimes all it takes is a needle, thread and a little nostalgia to leave a stitch on your heart.

There are a few things I would change, particularly the sewing mini-game, the repeated filtering in the emporium, and the performance issues when switching away from the game. The mix of historical fashion and modern designs can also feel a little odd, although I think the freedom it gives you is worth it. Overall, though, Dressmaker gave me exactly the kind of cosy dress-up experience I wanted, with enough story and strange little characters to keep it from becoming just another decorating game.
Wonderful cozy shop- and design-simulator, with endless opportunities for custom creations.

I have no real-world skills with sewing or dressmaking, but I thoroughly enjoyed being able to let loose creatively and make some stunning dresses. The low-stress aspect (after figuring out how to fulfill all the customer-required elements) meant it was easy to just focus on the creativity and really enjoy the process. If you have an interest in dressmaking, then I highly recommend Dressmaker!

Dressmaker feels unique among other clothing creation simulations as a result of the premise, and there are a lot of customization options. The concept feels very different than other games out there. There are a few elements that feel like they need some finishing touches, especially regarding crashes and the zoom function. But after a patch or two, I think it could be a real designing gem.

Dressmaker is a delightful game that can be enjoyed in short bursts or for hours at a time. The cast of characters is unique, and their interwoven storylines make the world beyond the shop feel alive. The dressmaking gameplay is easy to understand and features many accessibility options, and the ability to mix and match many patterns, fabrics and appliqué together allows for endless creativity. While I wish there was a little more substance to the actual store side of things, I believe this is a great title for those interested in costume design, as this could be a super enjoyable way to try new things and get creative juices flowing, while also enjoying a fun story.
Aandacht voor ambacht.

I had high hopes for Dressmaker, and so far it has met every expectation I have for cozy games. Cute design? Check. Easy enough mechanics? Check. Some thinking required? Check. Pet the cat? Check. A pigeon? Not something I expected, but check.
I overwhelmingly enjoyed Dressmaker during the time I had with it. This game can easily suck away hours of your day, but you will never feel like you wasted a minute.

Dressmaker is a brilliant gem of the cozy sim genre, conveying the feeling of creating a work of art as flawlessly as possible. It is a safe, calm haven for creativity to blossom, with every moment full of satisfaction and beauty.

Dressmaker has managed to impress us immensely, both for its ability to create gameplay that is both engaging and realistic, and for the stories of its characters, which never fail to capture our interest.

Dressmaker is a wonderful cozy game that offers a whole lot of gameplay for a relatively low price point. Whilst the gameplay did get a little bit repetitive for me, I can’t deny that this is a game made purely with love. I really did enjoy playing this game and I probably will go back to every so often when I want to switch off. Dressmaker has definitely earned the Thumb Culture Gold Award and I think this will be the perfect addition to any cosy gaming fan’s library.

Dressmaker is comforting and addictive, the kind of game you can spend hours playing without getting tired of it, exercising your creativity and patience. One of the most interesting and unexpected surprises of the year!

I did think that I was only going to put a few hours into this game, but I can see myself coming back whenever I just want a cozy creative moment in my gameplay loop. The story flows so naturally with how things might unfold in that political manner and it really does allow for that creative freedom to satisfy the orders. I also love how the game encouraged me to keep moving through the story so I could unlock more patterns, fabric, and embellishments. Overall, there is so much love towards this game, both from me and the community, that I highly recommend it if you enjoy a good story and love being creative.

Dressmaker has quickly evolved from a potential-filled demo to a delightful, fully fledged game. While there are more things I’d love to see (perhaps in a future update?), it’s a wonderful play as it is, especially for the $15 price point. I’ve had an amazing time with Dressmaker, and I’d absolutely recommend it to anyone with a passion for fashion, design, or creativity.

It was so rewarding to shop for fun fabrics and see my vision come together on the mannequin. My only real complaint is that it would be nice to see your dresses on the characters, but overall this is a small issue that the photo mode and dress log mostly make up for.
100.0% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (7 reviews).

Bigger and arguably better than its predecessor, the long-awaited Tormentum II is a welcome darkly atmospheric psychological horror sequel that will have you constantly questioning yourself, even your own perception of what is real.

The duo behind Tormentum have once again showcased their artistic talent, delivering an immersive, intriguing, and visually distinctive game that truly stands out. They’ve managed to preserve what made the first game so good while building upon it and taking things even further.

Tormentum II is a masterpiece of dark surrealism that ventures into the
realm of dark fantasy, yet is rooted in existential science fiction.
Eight years of hard work by the developers have resulted in a dreamlike,
somber odyssey.

For all its frustrations, Tormentum II has given me plenty to chew on. Like one of its great creatures of the night, I’m not sated yet. I want to see more games by OhNoo Studio. That’s a big ask, I know. I promise I’m not saying I need another eight years of your lives like an ever-twisting ouroboros from one of your drawings. It’s just so hard not to want more when this Tormentum II feels like a step in a longer journey. Perhaps this is simply the type of game the developers are interested in. The puzzles need only be exactly what they are. But if OhNoo Studio is hoping to take that next step, well — I’ll be there day one.

Tormentum II is a straightforward point-and-click adventure whose greatest strength lies in its spectacular, nightmarish art inspired by H.R. Giger and Zdzisław Beksiński. Its puzzles could be more challenging and its story more cohesive, but the oppressive atmosphere, striking imagery, multiple choices and endings make this 8–9 hour descent into darkness a memorable and highly replayable journey.

Thinking back on my time in Tormentum II, I’m glad I swan-dived into its macabre world. As a point-and-click adventure, it wasn’t as taxing as I expected (occasionally a bad thing), and certainly not as bleak (mostly a good thing), but it still managed to surprise.
Tormentum II turns a waking nightmare into one of the most compelling puzzle adventures you'll play this year.

The duo behind Tormentum have once again showcased their artistic talent, delivering an immersive, intriguing, and visually distinctive game that truly stands out. They’ve managed to preserve what made the first game so good while building upon it and taking things even further.

What we get here is a meticulously hand-drawn game with a distinctive visual style, one that truly comes into its own alongside its music. This is its main strength. Its pace is slow. The story is well put together and unfolds steadily; it isn't above average, but it's interesting enough – and vague enough in places – to leave you pondering it. If we don't approach it as an adventure game, I wouldn't count the ease of its puzzles as a negative either. Its replay value, however, is low, even if you're curious about the different endings.

On reflection, Tormentum II is a really hard game to give a final score. I somewhat love abstract and bizarro stories, because it gives me something to mull over after, but I can understand not many people connecting with this title.

Tormentum II doesn’t need to reinvent the wheel, but it doesn’t have to. It knows exactly what made the original memorable and builds on those strengths with confidence. If you’re into atmospheric adventures, psychological horror, and gorgeous, yet unnerving, art direction, there’s probably a lot to love here. Sometimes a sequel doesn’t need to be bigger or louder. It only needs to remind players why they fell in love with its weird world in the first place.

Tormentum II establishes itself as a twisted, polished point-and-click adventure, capable of captivating those seeking an escape from the mundane into the unsettling realm of bio-mechanical surrealism.
100.0% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (8 reviews).
If you’re looking for something to itch that relaxing scritch that you need itched, then Milki Delivery will be the nice morsel you need in your life.
It's a soothing ride with a lot of heart, taking players through a delivery cycle that is more than just a routine, but a gateway into a community that is longing to reconnect and grow once more.

Milki Delivery will provide you with a wonderfully pleasant afternoon of dairy-delivering goodness. Some slower moments feel a tad repetitive, but it’s a well-paced adventure that keeps you invested through its many upgrades and whimsical narrative. Cozy is an apt word to describe this little gem, so I recommend it to anyone in need of a chill night in.
While there are many cozy games these days, few offer the quality that you find in Milki Delivery. If you have any interest in a short and cozy experience, this is definitely a game to pick up.

Milki Delivery is a simple and cozy adventure that wins you over with its welcoming atmosphere, beautiful scenery, and the charm of its small community. Even though its activities follow a familiar structure, the growth of the milk delivery business and encounters with the locals make each outing enjoyable and full of little discoveries. It's one of those experiences that invites you to slow down, take in the scenery, and appreciate life's simplest moments, leaving you with a wonderful sense of tranquility by the end of the journey.
Finding a friend for the last milk cow in existence is an odd concept, but Milki Delivery is a cosy, compelling and friction-free adventure I didn't want to put down.

Milki Delivery quickly establishes a routine in a cute, friendly world, and how much you enjoy it depends on what motivates you in cozy games. It can get tedious, due to a very set rhythm to the gameplay loop. There aren’t major rewards when it comes to the narrative or growth beyond getting to do more of the same in new places and at greater scale. It’s fine and unchallenging, but someone might appreciate that if they want something to wind down with after a long day for a few hours.

Milki Delivery delivers a pleasant adventure for players who appreciate cozy indie games. It may not offer dozens of hours of content, but its small world has a clear identity and a heartfelt purpose.

Milki Delivery is exactly what I was hoping for – a cozy, laid-back game, with enough to explore and see and do, without ever overwhelming me with quests and timers. On top of that, the game looks great and somewhat nostalgic; it has that endless summer feel from old anime like My Neighbor Totoro or Spirited Away. It’s a game you can truly enjoy at a slower pace.

Milki Delivery is a short game, but it is not a small one in spirit. Its cozy management loop, charming cast, gorgeous art style, and heartfelt story come together into something that feels genuinely special. I 10000% recommend it to any cozy gamer looking for something wholesome, relaxing, and full of personality.

Join Neha and Milki on their journey and find out for yourself why this little game touched my heart so much. It is udderly delightful... and easily one of the most charming indie experiences I have played this year.

I’ve now played and reviewed a handful of charming, cute, and cozy games this year, probably the most I ever have in just as much time. Milki Delivery is peak among them, excelling at what it sets out to do, not overstaying its welcome, performing immaculately, and providing an engaging experience throughout its roughly six-hour playtime. For the price and quality, it’s the best way to spend a day or two I can think of. I love Milki Delivery and so will you if you want to spend a considerable amount of time smiling. Lactose intolerant? Pop a Lactaid and enjoy!

Even when the gameplay is slow, Milki Delivery is a good reminder of how we should probably all slow down a bit. It's a very sweet, wholesome, gentle experience, and if that's what you need right now, then you will find what you're looking for here.
100.0% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (14 reviews).

I never seemed to accomplish just one thing in Doloc Town. Every upgrade naturally led to another objective, and soon after, I had spent hours optimizing my farm for efficiency instead of doing what I originally logged in to do. The story occasionally loses its momentum due to its cozy nature, and getting around the world can become a chore at times, though neither stopped me from wanting to see what I could discover next. It's why I kept coming back to Doloc Town, and why it's such an easy farming sim to lose yourself in.
Doloc Town is a genuinely fun and incredibly adorable blend of farming sim and platformer set in a post-apocalyptic world, adding a genuinely unique vibe to the genre.

For fans of farming games, Doloc Town is undoubtedly worth trying. It offers plenty of fresh mechanics, systems, and production chains that constantly give you something to work toward, whether it is building a bigger and better farm or unlocking new technologies that make life easier. However, its rather traditional gameplay loop can feel somewhat tiring by todayâ€™s standards, while some of its finer details and player guidance are not quite as polished as they could be, leaving a few small areas where it falls short of other games in the genre.

Doloc Town is mostly happy to wait while you do your own thing, although there are calendar events on specific days and job board postings that will time out. Still, if players want to take a day to go fishing, there's rarely any reason not to, and while the farm does need some attention, the bulk of it can be automated with sprinklers and, eventually, end-game devices. Exploring, plan the next upgrade, experiment with new crafting stations, hang out in town, focus on gathering a specific resource, or just chill to the soundtrack, Doloc Town is generally happy to let players plot their own course through its substantial adventure. Every new day is an opportunity to max out the farm or poke about a bit and soak up the atmosphere, or maybe a bit of both, but however one chooses to spend the time, one goal leads to another until nighttime falls. And then it's a new day, and the biggest challenge of Doloc Town is not diving straight into doing it all over again as the sun rises on an ever-more-comfortable trash pile that's been re-engineered into a home.

An impressively deep farming sim with a post-apocalyptic twist, Doloc Town offers more freedom than you can shake a pick-axe at. It'll devour hours and days of your life, but you'll love every second of it.

Doloc Town can feel slow and doesn’t always communicate its concepts to the player, but it is still a great entry into the farming sim genre, offering much-needed originality in both its setting and mechanics.

Is it original? No. Is it innovative? Also, no. It’s just very, very good at what it is. So if you’re in the market for the gameplay equivalent of daydreaming, this is the one for you. Shyly energetic when you’re shooting robotic killer bees but chiefly docile and harmless, with no real progression setbacks or debt or due date. Welcoming and liberating like a happy yawn.

Doloc Town is another strong energy in a sub-genre that is currently in rude health, with its side-on view and pixel art style helping the game to stand out. While the gameplay systems may not ultimately deviate greatly from established formula, it nonetheless provides a charming experience with enough depth and farm customisation options to keep players engaged for a significant amount of time. Farming sim fans should find plenty to like here.

A charming post-apocalyptic farming sim with creative survival mechanics and enjoyable exploration, but repetitive dialogue, weak localisation, and shallow-feeling systems keep it from fully delivering on its strong premise.
A unique farming simulator in many ways, it's one of the best attempts to make something as engaging as Stardew Valley.

Doloc Town is an incredibly pleasant surprise and one of the most original additions to the farming genre in recent years. The combination of 2D vertical building, the relentless influence of the weather, deep automation and exploration of the wasteland works surprisingly well together. You’ll easily forgive the game’s minor flaws – such as the lack of clarity in the crafting system and the rather simplistic combat – the moment your makeshift pile of scaffolding transforms into a self-sufficient, technologically advanced oasis in the midst of a devastated world. For fans of Terraria, My Time at Sandrock and Stardew Valley, this is an absolute must-play.
Doloc Town turns an unusual mix of post-apocalypse and cozy farming into a well-rounded, refreshingly original experience and is one of the genre's pleasant surprises of the year.

Doloc Town is a promising farming RPG with a great atmosphere, satisfying progression, and surprisingly fun drone combat. Its rough edges and confusing early game hold it back, but the foundation is strong and worth watching.

Doloc Town is a casual farming game developed by RedSaw Games Studio and distributed by Logoi Games and Pathea Games. In a post-apocalyptic world, our young protagonist finds Doloc, a small village facing difficulties. It is in this situation that our protagonist settles in the town and starts her own farm, helping Doloc to prosper again. Besides farming, you can raise animals and collect resources, as well as control drones that will help you both in battle and in tending to your crops. Help Doloc and its inhabitants so that everyone can live better in a devastated world.

I had fun and continue to have fun with Doloc Town. Each game session is light, in the sense that I don't notice the time passing and I don't feel pressured to rush things, even though there's a lot to do and I end up losing focus several times. However, this doesn't get in the way, and the game itself allows you to tackle larger goals in stages. The game's story falters a bit by trying to explain too much, in a very tiring and unappealing way. It won't excite you, but it doesn't bother you either. It's amazing how you can't stay still in Doloc Town; you'll always have something to do, and I think that's great because it keeps the game alive at all times. Even though things get a little easier as the game progresses, it's rewarding to see things gradually evolving. I was missing a good farming game in my life, and Doloc Town managed to fill that void.

Whatever the world has in store for us, Doloc Town can be ranked up there with the cosy farming sim greats to provide a little bit of happiness. While initially very overwhelming and keeping your inventory organised is rather finicky, the gameplay is exceedingly rewarding. Building up both your farm and Doloc itself keeps you coming back just one more harvesting session. Transport Fever 3 is a fantastic addition to the Xbox simulation and strategy library. It is deep without constantly making you feel overwhelmed, complex without losing sight of what makes it fun, and surprisingly relaxing despite the number of financial disasters you can create for yourself.
