This game has really good bones, with 12 or 13 hours in the game I feel I’ve barely scratched the surface. The good far outweigh the bad in my eyes and the game feels oddly relaxing. It gives me the vibes of those old mobile games like clash of clans. If you enjoyed the settlement system in the fallout games you’ll more than likely like this game as well. I would highly recommend this game.

At first glance, Bellwright might seem like the usual blend of RPG, survival, and sandbox elements already seen in dozens of other indie productions. However, its strong management component helps it avoid the dangerous “more of the same” label, turning it into a deep and enjoyable experience. Bellwright is a rough gem: a sandbox in the truest sense of the word, but also a great role-playing game that genre fans will surely appreciate. Unfortunately, the console port currently holds the experience back, partly due to an interface that is difficult to navigate with a controller and a lack of proper optimization. At the time of this review’s publication, the game is still in Early Access, meaning Donkey Crew still has plenty of time to address these issues and refine the weaker aspects ahead of the full release.

An authentic and complex medieval life simulator that emphasises teamwork and management over individual achievement, and while it’s a slow burn the complexity of options more than makes up for a lack of polish.

Bellwright hasn’t quite managed to realise its full potential, which is hampered by a fair number of issues, both technical and mechanical. However, if you’re looking for a deep medieval survival and management game with highly interactive systems, there isn’t much on the market that’s as distinctive as what you’ll find here.

Bellwright works in a lot of ways. In particular, it allows you to customize your gameplay experience to better cater to your abilities. Plus, being able to just dig into a map and make it your own is a super cool idea. However, the problems embedded in the game's core make it a rather hard pill to swallow. Villager behavior, disproportionate time management, cumbersome building limitations, and unoptimized menu systems bring the game experience down. There's a fun game here, but you need to sift through a lot of frustrating limitations to get to that fun game.

There is a good game buried beneath Bellwright's achingly slow opening hours and UI awkwardness. There's satisfaction to be had in building up a base and seeing your NPCs gather, build, fight and progress for you, but it takes too long to get there and I just think most people will give up before they do.

Bellwright succeeds because it understands what makes management games so rewarding. Every hour invested pays off in visible, meaningful ways. Your village grows, your influence expands, and challenges that once seemed impossible gradually become manageable thanks to careful planning and steady progression.
Bellwright es una de las propuestas más ambiciosas que ha dado el género de supervivencia medieval en los últimos años.

Taito Milestones continues to be a solid compilation of classic games. I do wish they had more history and were available on more platforms, but if you own a Switch, these are easy recommendations. Looking forward to reviewing Taito Milestones 5 next year when it inevitably drops on Switch.

While you may not love every game in Taito Milestones 4, if you even enjoy half of them you’re beating the odds versus buying them as individual Arcade Archives releases. More than that, I think the value in a curated set like this is that it might lead you to games you wouldn’t have singled out on your own. Grab it for the hits you know, but make sure to try out the other included games. There are surprisingly few duds in the Taito arcade library, so you’re likely to have some fun with any given title from the publisher as long as you have a little patience. This collection demonstrates that quite well.

Taito Milestones 4 includes some excellent classics as well as oddities that not everyone will enjoy and overall, retro gamers like me are sure to smile as they explore the included titles and figure out the less conventional gameplay formulas.

Taito Milestones 4 has one classic game, three great games, four good games, and two bad games. That’s a pretty good spread. There are lots of different genres in this collection, and several very original ones. I wish Taito Milestones 4 had more extras. And I wish Taito would focus more on getting out more of their best titles. Some of these games are just unnecessary for any reason aside from game preservation. Taito made tons of classic NES games like Bubble Bobble Part 2 and Little Sampson that aren’t available on modern consoles. Let’s get more of them and less unplayable trash. Still, I’m very happy to have Taito Milestones 4 in my collection, especially for Arkanoid, Syvalion, Don Doko Don, and Cameltry.

Although I consider myself a true retro enthusiast, I’ll admit that I had barely even heard of half of the games featured here, and I had played fewer than a third of them in the past. As a result, it was genuinely interesting to fire up these titles from the Cenozoic era. It may not live up to the third collection in terms of the overall quality of its games, but it does contain a few gems that are sure to surprise you. From a preservation standpoint, it’s definitely worth the price of admission.

Taito Milestones 4 presents ten more classic Taito titles released in arcades during the 80s and early 90s. The selection includes some heavy hitters from Taito's catalog, as well as some lesser-known games, and the compilation's extras are conspicuously absent, just like in previous installments—beyond the configuration options for each game, the save state feature, and the online leaderboards. Nevertheless, these kinds of products dedicated to preserving classic games are appreciated, though they could be given a bit more polish.
22.2% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (9 reviews).

Strange things seem afoot below the surface in Town of Zoz, peculiarties surrounding Ito, their family, and the town itself that will need to be uncovered in order to truly become a shaman chef and provide aid to all those who need or ask of it. These deeper mysteries and secrets add a subtle flavour note of intrigue to the enticing, homemade recipe that makes up Town of Zoz, encouraging players to keep going, keep engaging with the world and its gameplay loop, in a wonderful way. Even with a slow simmer to begin, and some prepwork that takes some adaptation, Town of Zoz is sure to have players cleaning their plates and asking for seconds.
Town of Zoz blends engaging combat, farming/cooking elements, with an interesting story that is easy to get sucked into.
Town of Zoz leaves a lasting impression by centering culture, community, and connection in a vibrant adventure that’s easy to get lost in.

Town of Zoz swings big with its mix of combat, cooking, and community, and while not all of its ideas come together smoothly, there’s a lot to admire in its ambition and personality. It’s a slightly rough but endearing adventure that feels as much about reconnecting with culture as it does saving the day.

Town of Zoz’s combat feels a bit jumbled, but the presentation, general gameplay, and music are excellent and make for a pretty unique title. If you don’t see potentially bumpy combat as a dealbreaker, I think there’s a lot to really dig about this game, as it juggles a number of concepts in a distinct and mostly enjoyable way.

The game is an ambitious debut that wins you over with its personality and cultural depth rather than its mechanical polish. It’s a mostly positive romp that feels like a rough diamond. The Bottom Line: If you enjoy vibe-heavy games like Cuisineer or Hades (but with a much slower, cozy pace), you’ll likely love the atmosphere of Town of Zoz. However, if you have low tolerance for technical jank or slow-starting tutorials, you might want to wait for the first major patch. Town of Zoz needs a little bit of polish to address some crashes, combat system and UI clunkiness. But the core story of community and healing through food is something special.

As it stands, these core design problems, coupled with a host of technical issues (frequent crashes, bugs that softlock the game, textures loading improperly half the time, etc.), leave me unable to give a wholehearted recommendation. Perhaps if the developers tweak the combat system and iron out some of the technical problems, a trip to Zoz will become one worth taking. For now, it’s better to spend your summer vacation elsewhere.

Studio Pixanoh has created a game oozing with potential, weaving cookery and combat with a whole lot of anime. But, like a well-served dish, it’s all about finding the right balance of ingredients and Town of Zoz feels just a touch off-balance.

Despite many of its aspects being underbaked, Town of Zoz is a hearty action RPG with plenty of soul. Picky eaters may want to give this one a miss, but those who can stomach a few bugs and glitches will still find a treat here.

Town of Zoz is a game full of creative ideas. It blends farming, cooking, exploration and storytelling into a colourful indie adventure that clearly had a lot of passion behind it. The combat doesn’t quite match the strength of the rest of the experience, and the pacing can feel slow at times, but there’s still a lot to appreciate here.

The world-building is intriguing, the characters are memorable, and the game’s unique visual style gives it a strong sense of personality.

It’s definitely a game with rough edges, but it’s also one that has a lot of charm. For players who enjoy exploring unusual indie projects and don’t mind a few imperfections, Town of Zoz offers a surprisingly engaging adventure.

I highly recommend trying the free demo on Steam.

Town of Zoz is a hidden gem that wears its GameCube-era inspirations proudly on its sleeve. Studio Pixanoh has managed to successfully blend the satisfying, top-down combat of classic Zelda titles with the wholesome, relationship-building agricultural loops of Stardew Valley. While the painfully slow opening hours and minor UI bugs require a bit of patience, the gorgeous cel-shaded art style, deep cooking mechanics, and lovable cast of characters make the journey entirely worthwhile. If you are looking for a cozy, nostalgic adventure with a surprising amount of mechanical depth, Town of Zoz is serving up exactly what you need.

The Town of Zoz has been a story given magical life. Landscapes and crowded town streets are stuffed to the brim with cultural influence that almost makes you swear you can smell Ito's cooking. Despite its technical flaws, there is a wonderfully unique farming/cooking/adventure game that sets itself far apart from a heavily populated genre.

teenage-mutant-ninja-turtles-empire-city.title: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Empire City

reviews.excerpt: 25.0% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (8 reviews).

Against expectations, Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Empire City turns out to be a genuinely great VR beat ’em up, not just fan service for longtime Turtle disciples. Cortopia Studios delivers fast, flexible combat, light RPG progression, and a strong comic-book presentation that punches well above its price point. It’s not without some padding and design quirks, but the core experience is energetic, accessible, and totally radical. Possibly tubular.

Any issues I had with TMNT: Empire City were overcome by just how fun and breezy the game is to play. If I bumped into anything I didn't care for, seconds later I was on to something else and did not care enough to dwell on it. The glitches I experienced were a nuisance, but easily overcome. Cortopia never forgets that this property is based on a comic book that across forty years has not taken itself too seriously while entertaining fans of all ages. Empire City lives up to that standard. Longtime TMNT fans and newcomers alike will find something to like in Empire City.

Empire City shares the same fate that a lot of ambitious VR games do. They try to mimic the scope of big-budget AAA flat games, but cannot do so because of their much more limited budget. So the game ends up being spread thin with little depth over its six-hour game length. TMNT: Empire City VR is a fun, if thin, game. Just be aware that its chief charms come from playing with friends and moving around the city with the parkour system. If you are a Turtle fan, that may be enough for you.
Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Empire City is a game where the effort is clear, yet as a whole, the game doesn't come together in a way that turtles should when fighting crime in VR.

Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Empire City is a buggy, repetitive, and incredibly barebones adventure that mostly fails to capitalize on its extremely awesome premise. The decent parkour system, amusing dialogue, and co-op joy of hanging out with your friends as dorky turtles can be amusing for a bit, but you’ll have to contend with completely lifeless open-world areas, loads of repetitive and sloppy combat and stealth, and quest objectives or other important interactions breaking on you constantly. A cooperative TMNT VR game has all the potential in the world of being a truly great time, but Empire City only offers an occasional glimpse of what that could actually look like.

Excellent multiplayer game centered around the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles IP. Weapons handled well, there's a great hideout to hang out, and the game is designed to encourage fun. Overall this is a very good game best played with a group of friends who can explore and defeat the villains together.

Is the best TMNT VR game that could realistically be made at this budget, and for the franchise’s VR debut, that’s more than good enough. The parkour traversal is excellent, the Turtle weapon differentiation is smart, the story is legitimately written, and the co-op chemistry — when it works — is exactly the kind of chaotic fun the franchise deserves. The shallow combat, sparse open world, and co-op progress bug are real limitations that keep it from being more.

At $24.99 for VR owners who have friends to play with, Empire City is easy to recommend. Solo players without TMNT nostalgia may find the experience thinner. We’re looking forward to revisiting this on the Steam Frame when it arrives — a more capable headset may push the experience closer to its potential. For more VR and action game coverage, check out our full reviews section.

Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Empire City delivers a fun and immersive VR adventure with fast-paced combat, solid voice acting, and strong turtle personalities. Despite repetitive side content and some minor technical issues, it stands out as a unique TMNT experience that works especially well in virtual reality.

Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Empire City is a game of brilliant highs but also some noticeable lows – traversal is fantastic, the comic-book vibes are immaculate, and the co-op is a joy, but it is dragged down by an empty world and combat that lacks any real challenge. If you love the franchise and have a few friends to play with, you will easily look past the flaws – especially since there’s nothing game-breaking – but I can’t help but to think that a bit more attention on balancing out combat would have made Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Empire City a very special VR experience.
While it has the look and aesthetic, Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Empire City lacks fun with static maps and lackluster mission/level design.

Let’s Sing 2027 absolutely does not reinvent the formula, but to its credit, it is one of the most notable evolutions in the franchise in quite some years. A new mode with mini-games, various new vocal options and more enrich the experience quite notably. It is a shame that the game is no longer available on Xbox, and that the vast majority of songs are still locked behind a subscription service. Still, if you wanna sing your heart out to a vast selection of popular tunes, alone or with your buddies on a party night, Let’s Sing 2027 definitely gets the job done.

Let's Sing 2027 is a fun and competent experience, featuring three modes that offer plenty of entertainment. However, the limited song catalog and the reliance on the VIP Pass significantly detract from the overall package. While it is a solid karaoke game, it lacks enough new features to justify a yearly release; it could have simply been an update with new additions - an approach that might also have benefited the franchise's overall structure.

The series is in desperate need for interesting new modes and innovation which doesn't arrive here, but Let's Sing 2027 is still a competent interactive karaoke and is certain to liven up any party. You'll need to invest in the VIP pass to get the most out of it however, because that's where this title really sings.
Let's Sing 2027 introduces some welcome new vocal preference features and a new Party mode, but a weak playlist means you'll need a VIP subscription to get the most out of it.

Let's Sing 2027 is once again a great choice for a fun karaoke night with friends, thanks to improved avatars, the Party mode and the option to sing along to instrumentals. However, the limited content in Party mode, the lack of game modes and the lack of variety in the tracklist hold the game back. As a result, you're quickly encouraged to spend extra money on the VIP Pass.
Let's Sing 2027 continues the party with the fun, social karaoke experience you know and love, now returning with new energy for a brand-new season.

Let's Sing 2027 is quite entertaining for classic karaoke alone or with up to four people. The songs in the VIP Pass, however, are a bit pushy, and singing with the companion app doesn't always work flawlessly. The vocal support with the option for instrumental tracks enriches the karaoke experience. Unfortunately, the same can't be said of the party mode, which offers far too little to set itself apart from classic mode.

The series is in desperate need for interesting new modes and innovation which doesn't arrive here, but Let's Sing 2027 is still a competent interactive karaoke and is certain to liven up any party. You'll need to invest in the VIP pass to get the most out of it however, because that's where this title really sings.

Let’s Sing 2027 doesn’t reinvent the digital karaoke wheel—and it has no intention of doing so; instead, it refines a well-established formula, introducing improvements and new features that make it more accessible.

I had much more fun with Last Man Sitting than I ever expected I would. Part of it comes from gameplay systems I’m familiar with. The roguelite elements, character and weapon selection, perks, and other unlockables in and out of a match make Last Man Sitting go from decent game to excellent game. When you hit that perfect assembly of weapons, perks, and upgrades that carry you to a victory, it feels excellent. This might look like a silly game about white collar workers fighting a robot uprising from the comforts of their office chairs, but once you add some fire, poison, lightning, and a large caliber rifle to the mix, Last Man Sitting blooms.

Last Man Sitting from developer DoubleMoose Games and publisher Raw Fury is a fun and simple shooter with a ridiculous theme, as well as a bevy of customization and upgrade options. The gameplay is short and repetitive, but the price point helps justify it.
Last Man Sitting is an entertaining Roguelike third person shooter, but after a few long days at the office you'll want to take a holiday.

Despite lacking innovation, Last Man Sitting offers some enjoyable moments through its frenetic combat, interesting abilities, and engaging soundtrack. However, limited weapon variety and weak level design make the experience grow repetitive over time, leaving it behind other games in the genre.

Last Man Sitting has the bones of a fantastic action roguelike, which cannot be understated. I lost track of time during my playthrough plenty of times, but unfortunately, boss encounters, weapon design, and certain mechanics fall short. I had a great time with many parts of Last Man Sitting, but when the clock struck zero and the final stage ended, I was left wanting much more.

Based on an absurd and immediate premise, this title from DoubleMoose Games puts us in the seat of an office chair to clean up an office overrun by robots. I think DoubleMoose’s work is straightforward and loud—a cheap, direct shot of adrenaline that doesn’t try to steal a hundred hours of our time, but instead gives us a few minutes of laughter and destruction after an exhausting day of work in real life.

Last Man Sitting is a love letter to fast, physics-driven arcade games that turns the dull atmosphere of office environments into one of the liveliest and most fun action games of the year. Despite some minor physics issues and a solo loop that becomes repetitive, its creative chair-based movement system, varied weapons and superb co-op make it a very respectable, funny experience that is fully worth your time.

Last Man Sitting stands out much more for its boldness and identity than for its technical execution. The mix of mechanics inspired by rogue survivors and the creative gameplay based on mobility with office chairs creates moments that are genuinely fun and different from the genre's standard. However, clear limitations such as shallow content, a repetitive gameplay loop, performance issues at higher difficulties, and unsatisfying boss design ultimately prevent the game from delivering a truly solid experience. Even so, for those looking for something outside the box, the title offers a chaotic and charismatic experience that, despite its flaws, manages to entertain for a few hours and leaves that lingering feeling of "it could have been even better."

dragon-quest-heroes-torneko-s-mystery-du.title: Dragon Quest Heroes: Torneko's Mystery Dungeon -Classic HD

reviews.excerpt: 27.6% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (29 reviews).

Dragon Quest Heroes: Torneko's Mystery Dungeon -Classic HD- is almost a 1:1 port of the original Super Famicom version. The visuals were revamped, and there are a few new quality-of-life and accessibility options, but the gameplay experience is largely the same, for better or worse.
If you’re interested in roguelikes and gaming history, here’s a rare opportunity to see one of that space’s entry points, especially when it comes to console games.
Dragon Quest Heroes: Torneko's Mystery Dungeon - Classic HD is a welcome addition to the Dragon Quest library here in the West, but it still mostly plays like a game from 1993.

If you’re the type of person who loves old-school challenges, strategic decision making, and isn’t turned off by the risk of losing everything and starting over again you’ll find a lot of enjoyment here. Just make sure you know what you’re getting into, because one more run may just turn into 1,000.
Dragon Quest Heroes: Torneko’s Mystery Dungeon -Classic HD- really only exists as a must-play for retro enthusiasts.

Dragon Quest Heroes: Torneko's Mystery Dungeon is a tough game that only veteran players may appreciate. Though it has plenty to offer those who want to see the game credited with starting the Mystery Dungeon genre, it may feel a little too traditional for modern gamers. Nonetheless, Dragon Quest Heroes: Torneko's Mystery Dungeon is a challenging game with plenty of replayability, but only if you can handle the randomness of it all.

Dragon Quest Heroes: Torneko’s Mystery Dungeon Classic HD is every bit a remastered version of a Japan-exclusive Super Famicom game from 1993. While it may be a white whale that inspired a genre, it does feel somewhat ancient and in need of a few updates.

Torneko's Mystery Dungeon is a faithful revisit to Chunsoft's initial turn-based roguelike crossover that disappoints in its presentation, but more than makes up for that in its tightly designed mechanics.

First released in 1993 on the Super Famicom, Enix&a;#039;s Dragon Quest Heroes: Torneko&a;#039;s Mystery Dungeon Classic HD spinoff brought an addicting dungeon-crawling experience with a distinctive Dragon Quest coat of paint that introduced players to the concept of the Mystery Dungeon genre
The one where the Mystery Dungeon series started, remastered for a worldwide release
A charming Dragon Quest spin-off with an enjoyable Mystery Dungeon formula, though some of its randomness and looping music can become a little repetitive

Dragon Quest Heroes: Torneko's Mystery Dungeon - Classic HD is an excellent, if bare-bones, Mystery Dungeon game that's held back by some awkward porting issues. The core gameplay is still incredibly fun, and it's easy to understand why it became a massive franchise. However, the slow pacing drags it down compared to other games in the franchise and makes it a tad difficult to recommend over a Shiren or similar title unless you're a huge Dragon Quest fan. If nothing else, it's great to play the game that started it all in English, and hopefully a few patches can smooth out the rough spots.

Permadeath rogues and randomised Mystery Dungeons are an acquired taste as is, let alone being a Dragon Quest IV spinoff. However, despite it being one of the first of its kind, Dragon Quest Heroes: Torneko's Mystery Dungeon Classic HD still manages to be engrossing and stimulating. It probably didn't even need the visual overhaul, but it's an appreciated bonus that breathes a bit of life into this belated release.

It's wonderful to be able to play such an influential yet underrated icon and Dragon Quest Heroes: Torneko's Mystery Dungeon Classic HD is super-fun to boot as you formulate strategies and consistently watch your adorable little shop expand. 💰

In the end, Dragon Quest Heroes: Torneko’s Mystery Dungeon feels like a giant missed opportunity to properly celebrate the origins of the Mystery Dungeon series. Though the core original game is there, the updates mostly make the game look and play worse.

Dragon Quest Heroes: Torneko’s Mystery Dungeon -Classic HD- was an unexpected yet pleasant surprise to mark the 40th anniversary of Dragon Quest. Although it introduces very few new features, they are significant in making this old-school title more accessible. The opening is slow, tedious, irritating, and frustrating; however, much like the premise of Torneko’s own ambitions, the game grows and reveals its worth through a fun, repetitive loop of trying, failing, and trying again—wiser and stronger. It is a gentle treasure, though one that requires considerable patience and virtue to reach the good parts.

The game is a niche roguelike focused entirely on methodical strategy rather than fast-paced action. It comes highly recommended for fans of retro-style games looking to put their skills to the test with something akin to a large puzzle. However, if that doesn’t sound like your kind of experience, the current high price makes it difficult to justify the purchase.

It’s hard not to be happy about Torneko's Mystery Dungeon finally becoming available to play on modern platforms. After all, the game is a major historical milestone for both the Dragon Quest franchise and the Mystery Dungeon series as a whole. However, when judged purely as a video game, the adventure clearly shows its age, and this “Classic HD” version could have done more to modernize the experience and attract new fans. It’s an excellent choice for a very specific audience. If you’re part of that audience, you can jump in without hesitation. Otherwise, you’re probably better off sticking with more recent entries in the franchise.

Dragon Quest Heroes: Torneko's Mystery Dungeon is a neat little roguelike, but I struggle to figure out how to recommend this title. For Dragon Quest fans, it's a fun little side quest to enjoy. But for fans of roguelikes, it's hard to think of its place among more modern takes on the genre, such as Dreamscaper or Hades. It is, however, fairly priced, but just go in knowing it's a very difficult game to overcome, no matter how many hours you spend on it.

Dragon Quest Heroes: Torneko's Mystery Dungeon -Classic HD- revives a chapter of the franchise that is little known outside Japan, yet it settles for being a faithful reproduction of the 1993 original without taking any bold risks. The issue is that the remaster doesn't go much beyond that. While the enhanced graphics, official English translation, and stat adjustments are welcome, they don't transform the experience; still, it is a welcome historical revival that will primarily appeal to fans of the "mystery dungeon" genre or those with a genuine curiosity about the original title.

Torneko's Mystery Dungeon retains the tense, methodical appeal of classic roguelikes, with satisfying resource management and meaningful risk. Its straightforward systems, thin narrative progression, and demanding structure may feel dated, but modern quality-of-life options and a faithful Switch 2 presentation make it an engaging archival release.

Torneko’s Mystery Dungeon -Classic HD- is a tough old-school roguelike that still knows how to keep you coming back for one more run, even when the RNG has it out for you. The retro presentation holds up nicely, but the sluggish combat and some seriously punishing luck can make the descent feel like an uphill battle, even when you’re going down.

Dragon Quest Heroes: Torneko’s Mystery Dungeon -Classic HD- is a fun and, above all, intriguing game. Even though I'm not a big fan of roguelikes, I quickly understood what made its formula so interesting and why Mystery Dungeon has continued to exist for so many decades. [...] At the same time, Classic HD never ceases to feel like a 1993 game receiving a new presentation. I don't necessarily see this as a problem, but it's something that needs to be considered before purchase. Its simplicity is part of its charm, just as its difficulty and repetitive structure are part of the package.

Mystery Dungeon has moved onto greener pastures since its first outing, but much of that success was owed to a surprisingly solid first outing. Dragon Quest Heroes: Torneko’s Mystery Dungeon -Classic HD- is an alright look at its humble beginnings. While the overall quality of the port is in need of some elbow grease (particularly in the audiovisual department), a good English localization and generally fun gameplay make it a worthwhile endeavor for any Mystery Dungeon aficionados. The focus on collecting money and rare items is genuinely still a unique factor even when taking the broader franchise into consideration, and although this doesn’t smooth over its relatively thin novelty, a short runtime at least means that it won’t risk becoming too stale. I would not say that this is essential for anyone other than diehards, but I definitely had fun experiencing the ups and downs, the trials and errors, and the great sense of victory that comes with Mystery Dungeon.

Torneko’s Mystery Dungeon -Classic HD- is at its best when every step feels like a small gamble. Its enemies, exploration, and constant curiosity about the next floor kept pulling me back, even if sluggish controls and inventory management often got in the way.

Dragon Quest Heroes: Torneko’s Mystery Dungeon -Classic HD- is the perfect way to experience the game that popularized the roguelike structure in Japan, featuring improvements that don't detract from the original experience but instead smooth out the gameplay itself.

Dragon Quest Heroes: Torneko's Mystery Dungeon may have some bumpy parts that are tough to revisit all these years of iteration later, but it serves as a pleasant enough adventure and a fascinating piece of gaming history. I hope the next couple of Torneko games follow suit, as I’d love to have an excuse to see how each subsequent game builds on the last. Plus, I’ll never say no to more official releases of the past Dragon Quest games that the West missed out on.

Sure, it has aged poorly in a few areas, but the core gameplay remains just as entertaining more than three decades later. This charming game absolutely nails that “just one more run” feeling that every roguelike strives for, yet surprisingly few manage to perfect.
27.8% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (18 reviews).

A classically styled CRPG that is welcoming to newcomers without dumbing things down, Disciples: Domination has both the gameplay and the story to keep fantasy fans enthralled for the entirety of its 40+ hour runtime.

Disciples: Domination does not upend what already works about the series. It moves Empress Avyanna’s narrative in a new direction and adds nuance and depth to all the game’s systems. There are a lot of mechanics at play, from combat to RPG-like elements to diplomacy, and they work together well and add up to a rich experience.
Dark fantasy RPG with highly tactical and intense turn-based combat, but weaknesses in city building and character development.

It’s difficult to fault Disciples: Domination for what it does well. The game delivers a tight tactical experience, supports a wide range of distinct factions, and offers plenty to explore. Its visuals are detailed, and the UI holds up well across long play sessions. Where the game stumbles, it does so in familiar ways: a disjointed narrative, forgettable voice acting, and the risk of loot overload. The game doesn’t push far beyond its predecessor, nor does it significantly shift expectations within the genre; its systems, story, and presentation all feel largely familiar. Like a friend whose dress sense hasn’t changed in twenty years, Disciples: Domination struggles to be truly relevant or fresh, but if you’re willing to dance to her older tunes, this is a queen who will happily conquer your doubts.

In the end, Disciples: Domination stands in its own way and gives the impression that, although it has taken a step forward in some areas, this is offset by setbacks in others. That doesn't make it a bad game, but it's not enough to make it stand out in any way. It can't compete with a genre giant like Heroes of Might and Magic, especially in terms of complexity. However, those who enjoyed playing its predecessor will get their money's worth here as well. The developers could have dared to take it a little further, though.

Although set fifteen years after Liberation, it feels almost identical in gameplay. Fans of the first entry in the rebooted series will enjoy this one as well. Combat can become somewhat repetitive over time, though it remains engaging. The story is decent but not exceptional. While it does nothing particularly wrong, it also does little to stand out, but for those seeking a dark fantasy RPG with tactical combat, it might be worth the time investment.

Disciples: Domination offers a massive new campaign that spans anywhere between 30 and 50 hours depending on your level of difficulty and style of play, plenty of major new features with their own spin on systems and combat, baseline enhancements and QoL features that were patched into Liberation over time. But it still sticks too close to Liberation to be called an entirely new game. If you were looking to experience more of Nevendaar from Avyanna’s PoV or want to spend several evenings in a solid turn-based strategy, you will enjoy the new installment. But if you are waiting for the second coming of Disciples 2, Domination features vastly different vibes and aesthetics.

Disciples: Domination is a sequel that embraces absolute continuity. It corrects some of Liberation's imbalances, increases the challenge, and consolidates the foundations, but it stops there. The combat system works, the factions offer distinct approaches, and the dark fantasy atmosphere remains intact. But it lacks the bold vision that could transform a good strategy game into a memorable one. Where evolution was expected, Domination opts for maintenance. Solid but predictable: it will convince those looking for exactly what they already know, disappointing those hoping for a decisive step forward.

Disciples: Domination offers entertaining and strategic turn-based combat with loads of unit synergy to play and experiment with. Though the plot doesn’t quite deliver on its dark RPG aspirations, it’s still entertaining.

With noticeably less content and few innovations, Disciples: Domination feels more like an expansion than a full-fledged sequel. It's a decent game, nothing more, with a lackluster plot and a generic high fantasy world; a must-have for fans of Disciples: Liberation.

This is an average sequel to a tactical game, with the combat being the best aspect. Graphically, it has improved slightly compared to the last game, but the story and texts fail to attract much attention. Nevertheless, the game will find an audience eager to continue the story from Liberation.

Disciples: Domination can feel slow, tedious, and grindy at times, but fun can still be had in its unique party recruitment mechanic and highly customizable player character. However, it doesn’t change enough from the game that came before to justify its existence as a sequel, and may even feel like a disappointing departure for returning fans.

Disciples: Domination knows exactly what it is and what it wants to do. It's an old-school strategy game with great combat but also frustratingly shallow mechanics in other areas. Fans will love it; everyone else will wonder what the big deal is.

Disciples: Domination is a flawed, by-the-numbers strategy RPG that shows some creativity with its units and certain boss mechanics, but lacks enough depth and variety to sustain the amount of fights it throws at you across its decently lengthy campaign. Its writing lacks a consistent tone, its world fails to grip you, while Avyanna only stands out as one of the most unconvincing protagonists to date, making Domination a functional but rather forgettable second entry in the series.

An uninspired strategy RPG, Disciples: Domination offers an unremarkable experience that fails to stand out in a crowded genre. There are a few flashes of brilliance here and there – primarily with the morally challenging decisions that need to be made in the throne room – but otherwise this latest entry in the Disciples series fails to offer a compelling world to save.

With significantly skimpier content and only a few innovations, Disciples: Domination feels more like an expansion than a full-fledged sequel. It's a decent game and nothing more, with an unconvincing storyline and a generic high fantasy world; only for fans of Disciples: Liberation.
Fun turn-based strategy RPG in which you must try to keep together a crumbling kingdom

This is an average sequel to a tactical game, with the combat being the best aspect. Graphically, it has improved slightly compared to the last game, but the story and texts fail to attract much attention. Nevertheless, the game will find an audience eager to continue the story from Liberation.

Disciples: Domination is a functional but uninspired sequel that feels more like overpriced DLC than a true follow-up to Liberation. With recycled assets, tedious combat from the start, catastrophic technical issues, broken balance, and zero meaningful improvements over its predecessor, it's hard to recommend at full price.

Disciples: Domination sharpens its predecessor's strengths and
adds genuine new ideas with the collision system, corpse mechanic
and flexible Avyanna classes — anyone who liked Liberation will
feel right at home.
Disciples: Domination is an interesting title, with solid mechanics and a well-defined identity. A convincing experience, but which would have needed extra refinement on several aspects.
Disciples: Domination serves as indirect proof that sticking to a specific setting when a series changes developers isn’t always the best approach.

One of the biggest strengths of Disciples: Domination is how it handles choices and consequences. Your decisions as a ruler matter. Supporting one faction may damage another relationship. Ignoring problems can lead to long-term issues. Solving grievances costs resources and sometimes reputation.

I’m a huge fan of RPGs, and I particularly love an isometric viewpoint. This freedom and wide scope of vision complements the large open world. Alongside this, the grid-based system is familiar and makes each combat situation easy to follow. The use of lighting and earthy colours creates a sinister and dark atmosphere. The audio supports this with a blend of moody, minor-toned songs and energetic and dramatic tunes. However, it is the voice acting that truly shines. I was impressed by the quality and how well it delivers the story. Additionally, the sound effects have a nice fantasy edge, and the ambient sounds reflect the journey you are enduring.

There is plenty to learn and loads of elements to understand, but Disciples: Domination takes things slowly. The learning curve enables both hardcore fans and newcomers to grasp the fundamentals. Moreover, you never feel out of control of any situation. Subsequently, this has a nice feeling of inclusivity despite the layers of ideas working away in the background. The branching storylines generate huge replay value. If you want to mix things up, you could tackle the 30 to 40-hour playtime repeatedly.

Disciples: Domination is a great fantasy experience.
I love the genre and the franchise, and despite my small complaints, Disciples: Domination is a great fantasy experience. I love the story and the different protagonists. Moreover, the overworld is interesting, and the relationship between the factions was fascinating. However, it has a repetitive edge that cannot be ignored. Moreover, the slightly un-Disciples moments could annoy hardcore fans. Despite this, it is good fun, and I recommend getting a copy from the Xbox store!
Disciples: Domination is a good game that has its bumps in the road. With a good story and some interesting mechanics the game has a lot worth enjoying if you can get through the slow introduction.
Quote not yet available

I went into Disciples: Domination with no prior knowledge of the series and have come out the other side a fan. Its grievance and resource system builds a solid foundation for a sequel and Nevendaar and its casts of characters is a world I want to see more of.

If Artefacts can flesh out some of the new mechanics to have even more variety and get the combat to require just a bit more strategy they truly have something here. As is Disciples: Domination is a very good RPG that should be worth a look to anyone into turn based RPGs.
28.6% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (21 reviews).

Nitro Gen Omega captures the spirit of explosive 2000s mecha anime while delivering a surprisingly deep tactical RPG beneath its stylish presentation. Its layered management systems, strategic combat flow, and pilot relationship mechanics make every mission feel meaningful, while the fast-paced presentation keeps the experience engaging even during downtime. Though the game demands patience and careful resource planning, players willing to learn its systems will find a rewarding mech RPG where every choice matters.

In short, this is not a video game without its rough edges; yet, it feels well-rounded and focused—built around a few highly polished and deeply explored core concepts—and, above all else, it demonstrates that potential for growth typical of those who are already doing things the right way. *Nitro Gen Omega* is original and satisfying; it manages to remain entertaining for at least thirty hours without ever dragging. It only begins to feel a bit weighed down over the long haul—due to the inevitable tension between its sandbox nature and the sheer scope of content a studio this small has attempted to tackle—specifically regarding the variety of environments, factions, and all the classic elements that serve to facilitate player freedom and emergent storytelling. That said, DESTINYbit’s latest work clearly showcases the results of a continued process of maturation—one that solidifies their standing as one of the most intriguing developers on the domestic scene.

NITRO GEN OMEGA from developer DESTINYbit is a unique open-world turn-based experience that offers more than expected. It’s fast, intense, and requires the player to do one helluva fun mech juggling act.

The core of the experience is an intense strategic puzzle, even if the game occasionally mumbles its instructions like a poorly dubbed transition scene. If you are happy to forgo a deep plot or memorable characterization in favor of a challenging combat system rewarding meticulous min-maxing, this game could easily become your next obsession. For those who live for the tactical dance and the glow of a well-animated explosion, Nitro Gen Omega is a mecha well worth the investment. PJs and Sugar Puffs optional.

NITRO GEN OMEGA confirms the talent and courage of DESTINYbit. The Italian studio sets aside traditional formulas to deliver a ‘handcrafted,’ brutal, and magnetic tactical RPG. Although the narrative never truly takes off and some management routines between battles can feel repetitive, the game’s core is a finely polished gem. It is a technical and profound experience that rewards precision and crew synergy, offering one of the most original interpretations of the mecha genre.

Based on a simple premise, Nitro Gen Omega’s combat is genuinely very entertaining and well thought out, and the fun animations are a nice added value. Unfortunately, grindy progession, a barebones open world, unexciting characters, and a perplexing system for switching mechas end up dragging the entire game down.

Nitro Gen Omega manages to win you over thanks to its strongly defined identity and its ability to blend strategy and storytelling in a coherent and engaging way. Some noticeable limitations remain, however: the depth of the combat system, while interesting and full of possibilities, can feel somewhat hard to read during the more hectic moments, making it difficult to immediately grasp all the variables at play, while certain animated sequences tend to repeat with some frequency, gradually losing part of their impact over time. Despite this, the overall experience remains thoroughly enjoyable, capable of entertaining and leaving a positive impression — especially for those who appreciate the genre and are looking for something with personality.

Overall I think Nitro Gen Omega is going to click deeply with a small group of players. Others who dip their toes in will probably enjoy the novelty before bouncing off to something else. If you choose to spend your time here, please consider that this is definitely not Into the Breach meets anime. It does not feel like combat chess (yet), and the similarity of each combat encounter over time slowly erodes the beautiful graphic art style. Keep an eye out, maybe DESTINYbit will introduce a more varied roster of combat scenes or rebalance enemy encounters in a way that deepens strategy.

NITRO GEN OMEGA is a game about you and your Code Lyoko style crew toughing it out at the end of the world. If you enjoy turn-based anime robot action, you might find that fighting for that end is more engaging than it first appears.

Nitro Gen Omega is a game that still feels a little rough in its 1.0 release, not being as approachable in its multitude of systems as it could have been. It’s not a bad game per se, but one that demands effort to understand and pull through. Nonetheless, its battle systems and animations shine through to the point it can be worth giving it a try for fans of unique RPGs and simulators.
Nevertheless, the top tier teambuilding and social systems really help to push players to care for their crew and with that Nitro Gen Omega manages to rise above the little issues that I had with it.
Nitro Gen Omega was a delightful surprise in 2026, especially since the year’s midpoint hadn’t offered much for fans of this genre to celebrate.
A distinctive work, not always perfectly balanced, but with a personality so strong it's hard to ignore.

Nitro Gen Omega is an exceptional title in many ways. Immersive, polished, graphically captivating, and embodying the unmistakable style of mech-themed shonen anime. Managing emotions and relationships may seem complicated, but it's much less punishing than it seems. The combat system is deep and tactical, with a solid learning curve that keeps you entertained for quite a while.

If I had to sum up NITRO GEN OMEGA in one word, that word would be “cool”. Its effortlessly stylish aesthetics and flashy animations took me back to watching shows such as Gurren Lagann or even Megas XLR. Nostalgia aside, though, this is an entertaining and often challenging RPG that doesn’t hold your hand.

This is a very rewarding title that, despite a lack of an engaging story, had me hooked for the majority of the time. Some pacing issues aside, I’d highly recommend giving this one a try. There’s even a demo available, so what have you got to lose?

For it’s stylish aesthetics, engaging gameplay, and everything else mentioned, NITRO GEN OMEGA receives the Thumb Culture Gold Award!

NITRO GEN OMEGA is a very unusual strategy RPG that will make you think outside of the box while creating emotional relationships with your teammates. If you enjoy mecha anime and complex tactical systems, then this game is absolutely for you, but it is not for everyone, especially if you like easier or quicker-paced RPGs.
Nitro Gen Omega has elements of a deep JRPG whose mechanics are worth taking the time to master.

Nitro Gen Omega is a stylish tactical RPG with a beautiful art design, a slick UI and amazing animations. However, I can see some players being turned away by having to learn the many combat systems it throws at you, even if it’s fun once you get used to it. Overall, I still think this game is worth your time.

Nitro Gen Omega doesn’t hide its ambitions: it wants to be a loud, loving tribute to the mecha that raised us, while still standing as a solid tactical game. And despite some repetition and a story that mostly stays in the background, it hits the mark. The loop works, the combat system is deeper than it looks, managing your mech and crew is addictive, and the saturated, angular art style sticks with you long after you turn off the console. It’s not a game chasing spectacle or plot twists—it knows exactly what it wants to be and embraces it with the boldness of a small team with a clear vision. And if you grew up on giant robots, if you still smile when someone shouts the name of an impossible weapon, Nitro Gen Omega will give you exactly what you’re looking for: the feeling of finally starring in your own mecha episode.

NITRO GEN OMEGA  is one of the most inventive strategic RPGs to hit the past few years. What appears to be a bright anime mech game at first glance turns out to be a surprisingly complex survival management RPG with profound decisions and interconnected systems.

Nitro Gen Omega is a game of wonderful strategic depth hampered by a lack of polish and a rough early progression slog. When the combat clicks and your heavily customised machine is tearing through enemy ranks alongside a crew you have genuinely bonded with, it is an ABSOLUTE joy to play and shows that the game could really be something special. It is just a massive shame that you have to wade through a ton of grinding and clunky menus to get to the good stuff.  

If you have the patience to learn its intricacies and don’t mind a bit of repetition, there is a remarkably deep and rewarding experience to be found in Nitro Gen Omega… just expect a few bumps in the road that’ll really test your patience.

NITRO GEN OMEGA is a testament to DESTINYbit’s talent and boldness. The Italian studio sets aside traditional formulas to deliver a “handcrafted,” brutal, and magnetic tactical RPG. Although the narrative never quite takes off and some of the management routines between battles can feel repetitive, the beating heart of the game is a polished gem. It’s a technically sophisticated and deep experience that rewards precise planning and crew synergy, offering one of the most original takes on the mecha genre.

NITRO GEN OMEGA presents a bold and highly original tactical mech concept built around time-based command planning and deep mechanical customization. Its systems offer genuine strategic depth, and the idea of assembling a personalized crew adds initial appeal.

However, the execution struggles to consistently support its ambition. A steep and uneven difficulty curve, combined with pacing issues in combat, can make encounters feel unnecessarily drawn out. Technical inconsistencies and presentation shortcomings further limit the overall impact.

Despite its strong foundation and creative identity, NITRO GEN OMEGA feels like a game that overreaches its current refinement level. It is an interesting tactical experiment, but not yet a fully cohesive experience.

Overall, NITRO GEN OMEGA is a solid mech tactical RPG. The combat takes a bit to get going, but it is fun and full of hyper-animated moments that look amazing. The team building and social systems are solid, making you care about your motley crew of pilots and their interpersonal relationships. It has some really cool moments that get weighed down by grinding and repetitive battles. It has its moments, and with some rougher patches smoothed out, it has a lot of potential. NITRO GEN OMEGA is a fun adventure for anyone looking for a new, flashy mech RPG.

NITRO GEN OMEGA has established itself as a tactical RPG with a very distinct identity, skillfully blending its original combat system with surprisingly deep crew management. While not always accessible or perfectly paced, when all the pieces fall into place, it delivers an intense and unique experience within the genre. Its arrival on version 1.0 and consoles is a welcome addition, concluding its Early Access cycle with a coherent and ambitious result. It's a title with its own character, one that doesn't try to please everyone, but rather captivates those who can appreciate its particular take on the genre.

mafia-the-old-country-man-of-honor.title: Mafia: The Old Country - Man of Honor

reviews.excerpt: 29.4% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (17 reviews).

Mafia: The Old Country - Man of Honor might be more of the same, and that’s perfectly okay with me. Hangar 13’s nod to the original game is appreciated, as is the narrative flair The Old Country has already. Seeing Free Ride revamped is also a pleasure, alongside a meaty amount of content via Salieri’s introduction to the map. Sure, the gameplay doesn’t see a similar update, and your weapons and vehicles are in the same boat, but this might be the best $10 expansion you could spend money on.

Mafia The Old Country Man of Honor gives fans of the base game a compelling reason to return to Sicily, delivering an engaging new story that fits seamlessly into the established narrative alongside additional activities that make its open world feel more meaningful. While the core gameplay remains largely unchanged and is unlikely to win over new players, the expansion effectively reminds longtime fans exactly what made the original experience so appealing.

Mafia: The Old Country – Man of Honor is a DLC that doesn’t aim to introduce new gameplay elements to the original game; rather, it’s more of the same, offering a narrative episode set during the main story, not after it ends. The new story, starring Enzo, lasts about two hours, and it’s precisely this short playtime that might deter many players, given the €9.99 price tag for the additional content. On the other hand, there are excellent new additions to the “Free Ride” mode, with missions that let you return to the Sicilian countryside and fully enjoy the scenery created by Hangar 13, scenery we loved so much in the base game released a year ago.

For anyone who has finished the main campaign and is hungry for more criminal action, Man of Honor is well worth its $10 USD price tag. Even though the main story wraps up in roughly three hours—depending on whether you prefer a slow, methodical stealth approach or an explosive firefight—the addition of Free Ride activities and collection goals rounds out a solid package.
Man of Honor doesn’t reinvent The Old Country, but its compact story, stronger Free Ride content and connections to the wider series make it a worthwhile return.

Man of Honor works best when it places Enzo next to a Salieri who has already learned how easily a code of honor can bend to personal ambition, creating a meaningful bridge to the first Mafia. The problem is that two hours are barely enough to develop that contrast, while stealth and combat inherit most of The Old Country’s weaknesses unchanged. Free Ride gains better context and more purposeful activities, but some of its content still feels checklist-driven. A solid DLC, but too brief and conservative to rise above.
Cumple con las expectativas, pero te deja con ganas de más

The Man of Honor DLC expansion recognizes that Mafia stories aren't really about guns, cars or crime. They're about loyalty, ambition, betrayal and the price people are willing to pay to be part of something bigger than themselves.
2K is wrapping up content for Mafia: The Old Country with an expansion that, while shorter, is interesting for fans. It also adds an update that expands the range of activities.
Man of Honor is more of a small bonus than a major expansion, with a flat portrayal of young Salieri and a short campaign, though its low price makes the extra hours fair value.

Man of Honor is an honest expansion that lacks any real creative spark, relying almost entirely on the introduction of a young Ennio Salieri for its charm. Narratively speaking, the future Don's characterization works well and delivers great moments for long-time fans of the franchise, even if it ultimately remains a self-contained detour that has no real impact on Enzo’s journey. The gameplay holds no surprises and actually feels downgraded compared to the main game: ditching horses and melee duels turns shootouts into more conventional affairs, while rigid exploration boundaries and barren countrysides lay bare the flaws of the level design—further hindered by a bizarre 'winter' Sicily that sports the exact same spring/summer climate as the base game.

I don't consider Man of Honor a bad deal for those who enjoyed The Old Country and want to spend a few more hours with Enzo, Cesare, and company. For longtime Mafia fans, Salieri alone offers some intrigue. Just don't expect an expansion capable of changing your opinion about the base game. Man of Honor is more of the same, and when it finally threatens to be more than that, it ends.

The DLC dedicated to Ennio Salieri's origins is a natural and necessary expansion for the Mafia: Terra Madre ecosystem . Sold at a more than fair price, it offers two hours of excellent narrative entertainment, showcasing one of the saga's most iconic characters with mature writing, razor-sharp dialogue, and masterful voice acting.

Mafia: The Old Country — Man of Honour adds some new story beats that slot in neatly into the main campaign, and it’s nice to see Sicily again after some time away. However, beyond seeing Ennio Salieri again and where the story intends to take him, it’s worth dropping back in.

It fits seamlessly into the base game's narrative—nestling gracefully between the fifth and sixth chapters of the main campaign—and offers a couple of additional chapters that can be played through in an afternoon and just as quickly forgotten.

Simply put, Mafia: The Old Country - Man of Honor is a solid expansion that doesn't do anything truly groundbreaking. The two hours of story missions are entertaining, and Salieri is a great character, while Free Ride has expanded with some pretty neat challenges and extra options. If you enjoyed the original game, there is little reason not to recommend this new DLC. That is despite the fact that it ultimately could have addressed a few lingering flaws, which didn't quite happen. Even so, it is a pleasant return to Sicily.

Mafia: The Old Country – Man of Honor doesn’t breathe new life into the game, nor does it give those who maybe didn’t enjoy the initial experience a reason to return. But for everyone else, including fans of the base game and those interested in giving this a shot, I urge you to jump on board.

Man of Honor delivers a concise, well-written prequel story with strong character chemistry and satisfying Mafia fan service. Its limited campaign and frustrating stealth keep the expansion modest in scope, but expanded Free Ride activities and new weapons add welcome value for returning players.

Man of Honor proves to be an interesting addition to the game, particularly because of the way it ties into Enzo’s story while also establishing a connection to the series’ origins. Moreover, the new content added to Free Ride mode further enriches the experience, offering new activities and several reasons to return to the game.
Man of Honor doesn't reinvent the wheel, but precisely for that reason, it delivers on its promises: a tight story, richer Free Ride content, and meaningful connections to the Mafia timeline.
In Sicily, women are more dangerous than shotguns, but less dangerous than knives.
30.0% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (10 reviews).

Pro Jank Footy captures the cultural zeitgeist of Aussie Rules football with such charm you’d think it’s an Australian psyop. You can really feel the love for the sport in how well the actual game has been translated into this arcade-style version. Despite some issues with swapping from player to player, overall the gameplay is a blast, especially as it gets jankier and jankier with power-ups. It’s the perfect couch co-op game, something easy to pick up and play with some friends for a good time. It knows exactly what it wants to be, and pulls it off with so much Aussie flair.

Pro Jank Footy achieves what it sets out to do by providing an affectionate, delightfully bizarre tribute to Aussie Rules. While AI positioning and forward line density could benefit from tighter balancing, its creative power-up system, varied venues, and accessible match formats make it a fine addition to any footy fan's off-season rotation.

With that sense of cheeky humour and good fun, Pro Jank Footy is a consistent blast. It’s not the deepest game, but it certainly is one of the most funny I’ve played this year. It derives plenty of charm from its goofiness, and may earn a place in your heart for that reason.

Pro Jank Footy's simplicity is in some ways to its detriment, but the sheer slapstick spectacle of the thing, and the clear reverence for the pixelated sports games of old carry it to greatness. This isn't the sort of thing I'd play on the regular, but it is absolutely coming out at group events.
An absurd take on Australian Rules Football inspired by retro arcade sports games of the past, Pro Jank Footy never really finds its footing.

Pro Jank Footy is a tremendous mess of a game, and I mean that in the most complimentary way possible. It boils down a complicated sport into its purest, fundamental arcade form before breaking it through a chaotic overloading of its simple systems. It's fun, it's hilarious, though its biggest flaw, if it even is one, is that it's best played with mates.
Over-the-top roguelite arcade comedy sports game
It may not always play fair, and it certainly doesn't take itself seriously, but that's exactly what makes Pro Jank Footy such an entertaining surprise.

It might not be the Aussie Rules simulation that people want, but Pro Jank Footy is an accessible sports game, that ended up making me appreciate some of the finer points of the real sport. Perfect for beginners that have no idea about this sport, or any sports for that matter.
While I had high hopes that this wild and crazy take on sports could channel some old-school Mutant League vibes, I’m wishing perhaps they’d stopped the jank at mere amateur status…

Pro Jank Footy is far from the deepest experience out there, but it simply nails the spirit of the sport, along with a fresh burst of Aussie humour, so much so that it’s really hard not to enjoy on some level.

I enjoyed Pro Jank Footy, but it isn’t the deepest sports game. Furthermore, the sense of randomness and the often challenging action make it a frustrating title. Despite this, I found it fun, comical, and enjoyable to play. Accordingly, I like it and recommend grabbing a copy from the Xbox Store!

Pro Jank Footy is a blast in short bursts, especially when competing with friends and family. The wild possibilities escalate as more goals are kicked, creating moments of pure anarchy dabbled with nostalgia for anyone familiar with the sport in its best era. The victory on the scoreboard is never really the focus, for if you keep your sanity through a high scoring match you’re doing something right. This is an easy recommendation for anyone that enjoys AFL. For those enamoured by the style and the crazy combinations, definitely give this game a crack. I’ve followed the sport for 38 years, yet the powerups ensured all I knew quickly went flying out of the closest window.

The true hilarity (and often frustration) comes if you play with mates in local VS. I suspect this fun would also apply to the future online mode, but I do wonder however how much lag will impact the experience. Or would it unintentionally enhance the jank!
30.0% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (11 reviews).

Roman Sands RE:Build is a bizarre, captivating psychological experience that transforms mundane service work into a surreal exploration of routine, survival, and identity. Its striking Y2K-inspired presentation, dark humor, memorable characters, and esoteric storytelling make it unlike almost anything else, even if its uneven second half and deliberately unconventional gameplay won’t appeal to everyone.
A frenetic tale of two realities, both alike in dysfunction, which immerses the player in servitude and struggle.

Roman Sands RE:Build is a strange game, and I mean that as a compliment. Its repetitive work can become a real obstacle, but the atmosphere, mystery, music, and unusual characters kept me invested. I recommend it if you’re looking for a psychological horror experience that leaves you with an existential crisis rather than a traditional puzzle game.

I’m glad I got to see the story through, however, with its not-so-subtle homages to the likes of Danganronpa and Evangelion. It remains one step away from its mysteries and doesn’t take them to extreme lengths. There’s a profound and alluring melancholy etched into this work, a broken and messy world that’s strange enough to foster questions, but smart enough not to provide every answer.
It’s the type of game that folds your brain over on itself, constantly making you question your reality and see the world around you from countless angles.

More of an experience in nature than your classical videogame, but they stick in my brain nonetheless. I've been waiting for this game since its announcement and now that it's here, it's something I'll be thinking about for a long while. A little Danganropa, a little work sim, but a lot to ponder.
Undoubtedly one of the more unusual games I’ve played running this site, it may have some appeal for the right crowd, but it definitely will take patience to see everything it has to offer

Roman Sands RE:Build is a wonderfully bizarre adventure that blends surreal apocalyptic storytelling, dark satire, memorable characters, and striking vaporwave aesthetics with an outstanding jungle and breakcore soundtrack. Its inventive atmosphere and intriguing puzzles make it a fascinating experience, although repetitive time-loop tasks, forced grinding, and less expressive character designs compared to the original hold it back.
Arbitrary Metric and Serenity Forge invite us to play the role of a hotel bellhop under unusual circumstances.

Roman Sands RE:Build was the first narrative title of 2026 to intrigue me, primarily because it recognizes that the defining feature of games as a storytelling medium is gameplay, not text. Text serves merely as a tool to shape the interactive experience; in fact, the dialogue—while pretentious and repetitive—does not negatively impact the adventure, given the nature of its time-based theme, but actually sets a fitting tone for the work.

But when a technical issue prevents the player from experiencing the work as intended, the promise unfortunately cannot be kept. A narrative that seeks to draw an intriguing parallel with Plato’s Cave—in a game of philosophical perceptions that is far from juvenile—ultimately remains trapped by the shadows cast on the wall, with the exit sealed off by a bug.
Roman Sands RE:Build is one of those games that is easier to experience than to explain, and it arrives today with a personality that has become increasingly rare in the indie landscape.
31.2% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (32 reviews).

It’s pretty much “just” the music and bosses I have issues with, the game otherwise works quite well, is extremely well-polished, outside of the otherwise uncharacteristic framerate issue with the fourth stage, as on-rails shooters tend to be!

Wild Blue Skies reminds me why arcade shooters were so much fun. It blends the best bits of on-rails action and Saturday morning cartoons into something nostalgic without feeling dated. The basic story and awkward weapon controls hold it back from greatness, but the tight gameplay and gorgeous presentation make this a hell of a pick-up-and-go, replayable joyride. It doesn’t reinvent the arcade shooter, but I do think it nails the landing.

Wild Blue Skies shines when it deviates from the Star Fox formula with some truly phenomenal missions. But its lacklustre story and presentation, and a reluctance to truly step out of Star Fox’s shadow holds it back.

Wild Blue Skies is a solid homage to Star Fox 64 overall. It's visuals are fantastic and it's gameplay controls well and is fun overall. Unlike other recent rail shooters however, the game doesn't do enough to step out of the shadow of Star Fox, nor does it really seem to try to.

Overall, Wild Blue Skies is a charming, budget-friendly tribute to classic Star Fox that delivers plenty of arcade replayability, colorful locales, and stellar voice work for a modest $15 price point. Sadly, uninspired boss fights, frame-rate hitches, and a heavy reliance on its SNES inspirations keep it from carving out a truly unique identity. Chuhai Labs has crafted a fun, nostalgic alternative for rail-shooter fans. If you’re looking to scratch that Fox McCloud itch without breaking the bank, this flight is well worth taking.

Wild Blue Skies is a tribute to the legendary Star Fox. Its inspirations are clear, from its similar protagonist and crew to the level design and structure. While it delivers a fun homage, it fails to add its own spin, making it feel too familiar to Fox’s adventure. Despite this, its aerial combat, imaginative boss battles and charming presentation ensure it’s an enjoyable ride for fans of the genre, even if it never quite escapes the shadow of the classic that inspired it.

Wild Blue Skies was a bittersweet experience for me. While I am a fan of shooters and enjoyed the adventure, its inspiration from Star Fox goes beyond mere homage; it features moments that replicate patterns so closely they stifle the game's potential originality, from the narrative to the level design. That said, if you have never played the Nintendo title, it is worth taking a chance on these blue skies.

Wild Blue Skies treads an extremely fine line between being an homage to Starfox and a blatant copy of it. However you look at it, the bottom line is that it's certainly a serviceable on-rails shooter, with fun gameplay and charming visuals, but unfortunately, it follows Starfox's structure and gameplay elements so closely that it ultimately ends up devoid of anything new to bring to the table, other than a rehashed version of a better game.

Wild Blue Skies is a game that teeters between homage and plagiarism. It could almost be described as a reskin of Star Fox, as it closely mirrors its story, gameplay, and progression. It’s not a bad game by any means, and it boasts an appealing visual style, but it forgets to copy a couple of key gameplay elements, ultimately making it less fun than the title that inspired it.
It looks fantastic and has a great presentation, but with archaic game design and mediocre combat, this Star Fox clone fails to properly get off the ground.

Wild Blue Skies captures that classic Star Fox charm at a budget price, but lacks the refinement that made Nintendo’s classic so memorable. The often-unfair gameplay can frustrate, yet there’s still some old-school fun to be had for the right price.
Games don't get much less innovative than Wild Blue Skies but there's no denying that it's a solidly-made game so that's cool, I guess.

Wild Blue Skies is mechanically fine. It’s as tepid as you could possibly get for an on-rails shooter. Unfortunately, everything else is a pastiche of something that came far before, and is far greater in the grand scheme. Inspiration is a magical thing, but Wild Blue Skies shows that inspiration is only the first step in creating something new.

Bowie and pals’ adventure successfully impersonates the Star Fox 64 experience, but it’s an underwhelming impression. Nostalgic moments and satisfying action appear occasionally, but it pays homage to a fault and doesn’t find space to present its own personality. It has the unfortunate timing of releasing and being compared to this year’s Star Fox on Switch 2 – an excellent remake of Star Fox 64. But even if I did not have that game in my immediate memory, I would be hard-pressed to identify anywhere that it has improved on the genre with design lessons learned since 1997, or even risen to meet the ones that already existed even 30 years ago.

Wild Blue Skies tries to imitate the classic Starfox formula, but only with middling success. The flying is ok, but issues with difficulty, repetitive arcade structure, and virtually no narrative to keep you wanting to play, it is reduced to a score chaser.
On-rails shooter Wild Blue Skies looks quite nice, but it's extremely derivative of Star Fox, and pales in comparison in just about every way.
With a lack of individuality, Wild Blue Skies forced me to make comparisons in which it lost out almost every time.
Wild Blue Skies is a decent rail shooter when it finds the courage to be itself, but too often it’s simply Star Fox 64 But Worse – worse flying, worse story, worse difficulty tuning.

Wild Blue Skies is what happens when a spiritual successor takes too much inspiration from its predecessor. There is nothing inherently wrong with the game, but if you have played Star Fox 64, or the remake, you have played Wild Blue Skies. As this is releasing on the original Switch, there is an argument to be made that it might tide over Star Fox fans who don't have a Switch 2 yet. But with the original widely accessible on Nintendo Switch Online, it's hard to see that argument holding much weight.Wild Blue Skies is a perfectly average game, but with no originality, it makes for a hard recommendation, even to the most dedicated fans of Lylat's finest.

Wild Blue Skies showed a lot of promise, and I was super excited to get my hands on it, especially with all the recent fervor over Star Fox. Rail shooters are a great time, and this particular brand of rail shooter really lends itself well to having fun at different levels of play, across many runs. But after one run, I was ready to be done with this game forever.
Wild Blue Skies falls way short of the mark, making every attempt capture Star Fox 64's spirit without taking any risk to be original in its own right.

Wild Blue Skies works extremely well as a homage to Star Fox 64. Its old-school approach is refreshing at a time when so many other games are trying to put their own spin on the formula. The mechanics are excellent, the handling is responsive, and the level pacing works well with the game's replayability. For those looking for a nostalgic experience that gets the important things right, Wild Blue Skies is well worth checking out.
While Wild Blue Skies proudly wears its on-rails inspiration on its sleeve, this adventure with the Blue Bombers is well worth taking flight.

Wild Blue Skies tries to imitate the classic Starfox formula, but only with middling success. The flying is ok, but issues with difficulty, repetitive arcade structure, and virtually no narrative to keep you wanting to play, it is reduced to a score chaser.
The Blue Bombers make for a fantastic squadron, and I can't wait to suit up and fly with my new comrades again soon.

So, is Wild Blue Skies worth your time and attention? For the price, I’d say so. $14.99 isn’t asking that much for a Star Fox like adventure that’s available on multiple platforms. There’s plenty here to keep you coming back if this is your type of vibe. Otherwise nothing here is really going to win you over. I enjoyed Wild Blue Skies and it is a fun and addictive time. Which is all it needs to be.

I’m someone that has no real nostalgia or love for Star Fox 64, but Wild Blue Skies is such a pale imitation of that game. This is especially true when a fully remade Star Fox just got released two months ago, it’s hard to find any reason to play this over that. There’s also other games that have done this better that doesn’t have enemy clipping through environments, abysmal enemy AI, lack of mobility, and underwhelming shooting mechanics. Wild Blue Skies is perfunctory and so bereft of originality, it never dares to be a maverick and exist as something wholly unique.

It’s a wonderful thing to see games made with such love and admiration for what came before them. Wild Blue Skies proudly wears its love for Star Fox 64, and for the most part, this is a charming homage to a legendary video game.

Featuring a striking anime-inspired art style, likable characters, and fun gameplay, Wild Blue Skies has a stable flight that I can recommend to everyone eager to explore star-filled skies, even if the performance can be a bit rocky and controls for the All-Range sections aren’t perfect.
Wild Blue Skies looks the part, but shallow design, its barebones story, and noticeable technical issues leave this on‑rails shooter struggling to stay airborne.

Wild Blue Skies is a shoot ’em up game that successfully updated itself for modern platforms, bringing stylish and beautiful graphics along with gameplay that truly satisfies once you master its moderate learning curve.

Wild Blue Skies is a fun and nostalgic trip that successfully scratches that retro rail-shooter itch, even IF there are some areas of its design that feel a little lacking. The clear Star Fox inspiration does mean it can lack originality, whilst the difficulty spike and limited lives can be a headache, but you know what? Wild Blue Skies still manages to offer a good time. It can be frustrating, but with some wonderful level design and satisfying on-rails action throughout, it’s well worth checking out.

Wild Blue Skies delivers a Star Fox experience you have most likely already played. If you haven't, then you get a game that performs and controls well, and is fun. Still, nothing about it is unique compared to its source of inspiration. If you don't own a Nintendo console, you might want to give this one a shot, otherwise it doesn't offer a lot that's new.
