Final Fantasy VII Remake delivers an ambitious reimagining of the 1997 classic, featuring dynamic real-time combat, an expanded narrative, and high technical quality. On the Switch 2, the solid 30 FPS performance, the versatility between TV and handheld modes, and the inclusion of the Intergrade DLC make the package even more complete. With accessibility improvements and significant narrative changes, it’s an experience that appeals to both longtime fans and newcomers alike.

Final Fantasy VII Remake Intergrade delivers an exceptional experience on Nintendo Switch 2, with barely compromised graphics and performance when compared to the original release. The masterful storytelling, hybrid combat, and stellar cast performances will leave new and returning players with little left to desire.

"The Legend Finally on Xbox"
Final Fantasy VII Remake Intergrade offers a thoughtful reimagining of a timeless classic, with a significant expansion of the narrative and a deep refinement of the combat and customization systems. Its complete focus on Midgar gives the characters greater emotional weight. Technically, visually, and aurally, the experience remains robust and polished, delivering one of the best hybrid combat systems in modern Japanese RPGs.

Final Fantasy VII Remake Intergrade makes a surprisingly strong transition to Nintendo Switch 2, delivering a stable and enjoyable version of the acclaimed JRPG. While the visuals show some compromises compared to more powerful platforms, performance remains smooth and the hybrid format suits the game exceptionally well. The combat system and storytelling remain as engaging as ever, and the included Yuffie episode adds meaningful extra content. Overall, this is a convincing portable adaptation that proves the Switch 2 can handle large-scale RPG experiences.

Compared to other ports I've seen, if Final Fantasy VII Remake Integrade on Switch 2 is a sign of what we can expect from Square Enix in 2026, then I'll be very happy. Unlike certain ports that won't be mentioned, this version of Final Fantasy VII Remake was clearly made with a lot of love and care, bringing an experience incredibly close to the PS4 version. And all this at a very affordable price, considering that the price of games in 2026 is exceeding the $70 mark.

However, it's a relatively difficult game to recommend, unless you've never played it before, as none of the features on Switch 2 are “exclusive” to the platform, which doesn't make it stand out that much. But if you need a portable way to experience the beginning of this trilogy's story, then you can purchase it with no worries. Just make sure you have enough space.
Final Fantasy 7 Remake Integrade is a fantastic re-imagination of the classic for newcomers or Final Fantasy veterans. The Switch 2 Edition is the most impressive game so far on the platform.

A well-rounded experience with a compelling story, strong music, carefully written characters, and an enjoyable combat system that blends action with planning. It stands out as one of the notable JRPGs currently available on NS2, offering solid performance with a few minor issues that can be improved through future updates, all at a fair price.
Final Fantasy VII: Remake is a unique experience, which risks changing what is known and going further to make us fall in love with a classic that is part of our history.

FINAL FANTASY VII REMAKE INTERGRADE on Switch2 successfully translates the epic scope and depth of the original remake to Nintendo's new hybrid platform, offering a complete and surprisingly stable narrative and gameplay experience. The technical adjustments are reasonable, and the integration of INTERmission with Yuffie adds extra content that helps to delve deeper into the story. It is undoubtedly a highly recommended version for both new players and those who want to revisit Midgar from a different perspective.

After a long wait for Xbox owners, Final Fantasy VII Remake Intergrade delivers a stunning experience that blends spectacular action with strategic depth and respect for its roots. It expands the original’s world and characters with strong pacing and cinematic flair. A rushed, disconnected finale and heavy reliance on prior knowledge slightly undermine the impact, but it remains a compelling, must-play title.

Final Fantasy VII Remake Intergrade is proof that good things really do come to those who wait - only question now is how long it will be before Final Fantasy VII Rebirth reaches Microsoft and Nintendo platforms.
“FF VII Remake Intergrade on Switch 2 is a solid port, a dream come true for those waiting to experience Cloud's adventure in the palm of their hand.”

INTERGRADE’s PS5 release may still be the greatest in terms of technical performance, but the Switch 2 port is a superb choice that balances story depth, combat depth, and graphic excellence. It’s a great way for new fans of the series to get into it and for old fans to relive their favorites. Once again, Square Enix has brought Midgar to life, but this time it’s in the palm of your hand.

Final Fantasy VII REMAKE INTERGRADE works because it knows how to be careful. The story is told in depth within a single part instead of all at once. Each method helps the characters get better, the plots get more interesting, and the people stay involved. It doesn't feel like too much; it feels planned.

Final Fantasy 7 Remake Intergrade is a technical masterpiece, from the neon-soaked streets of Sector 7 to the buttery smooth combat transitions. Whether you're a returning Soldier or a newcomer to Cloud's journey, this "Intergrade" package is exactly what the Switch 2 needed!

Square Enix delivers an outstanding port of Final Fantasy VII Remake Intergrade with beautiful graphics and a locked 30fps performance target. The Midgar story remains one of the best ever in an RPG and nicely sets up the rest of the trilogy, which is also expect to land on Nintendo Switch 2.

Final Fantasy VII REMAKE Intergrade proves that the Nintendo Switch 2 is indeed capable of hosting large-scale productions without significantly compromising the experience. The recreation of Midgar is immersive, the combat system is one of the most refined in the franchise, and the expanded narrative gives new weight to already known characters and events. Even with minor technical slips and occasional limitations, especially in portable mode, the package delivered is robust, competent, and respects the grandeur of the original work.

Final Fantasy 7 Remake Intergrade is a monumental conversion on Nintendo Switch 2: the perfect way to enjoy a truly mammoth video game, capable of reworking one of the best games ever in a modern key, with some new and perhaps even controversial aspects. It's a shame about the price: after all these years since its launch, one might have expected a substantial discount.

The FF7 Remake is a masterpiece, and the fact that it's actually playable on a Nintendo console is incredible. It's been almost 6 years since the game came out, but it still holds up, and the visuals are stunning in both docked and handheld modes.

Final Fantasy 7 Remake's latest ports are superb on both the Xbox Series X|S and Nintendo Switch 2. Despite the framerate differences, both versions keep those stunning visuals and are finally letting players experience one of the best Final Fantasy games out there.

Final Fantasy VII Remake Intergrade for the Nintendo Switch 2 offers a smooth and enjoyable portable experience. With all the latest content and updates, it’s hard to resist picking this up, even if you’ve already played it before. It’s the most convenient way to experience Midgar on the go.

And so we reach the end of this road and the start of a much, much longer one. As I mentioned before, I went into Final Fantasy VII Remake with little to no nostalgia at all, and I’m glad to say I came away happy with my experience. Yes, I have my complaints, mainly that the game often wasted my time unnecessarily or that the combat took too long to really get going. But I also appreciated the narrow scope of the game and the various story elements (which I won’t spoil or talk about here) had me excited to see what happened next, and of course, what happens next. Would I have been as lenient with the Midgar-centric scope if this was the only Final Fantasy VII Remake game I had for four years? That's not my reality, so who cares!
Final Fantasy VII Remake Intergrade on the Switch 2 is an impressive feat. The game is beautiful, stable, functional, and delivers the complete experience, including the DLC, on a hybrid console.

Final Fantasy VII Remake Intergrade is everything we dream of when playing a game: experiencing a wide range of emotions throughout the journey, building empathy with the story, forming deep connections with its characters, and feeling the adrenaline rush during its action-packed moments. It is touching, it is unique, and it is the reimagining of a gaming legend that returns with grandeur to reaffirm its place among the greatest games in history.

FFVII Remake Intergrade Episode INTERmission (talk about a mouthful) isn't a "must-play." The story can feel derivate until some out-of-the-blue revelations occur as you're reaching the end, and the new gameplay implementations are barely explored due to the relatively short length of the DLC. However, if you're looking for a bite-sized return to Midgar accompanied by a very enthusiastic, lovable main protagonist, and a tease for what's in store once Remake Part 2 (or whatever its name ends up being) rolls around, then you'll find plenty to enjoy with INTERmission.
INTERmission is a tremendous but short addendum that sets up the next installment with many exciting possibilities.

While Yuffie's gameplay style is unique and well fleshed out, it doesn't help that she's the only playable character in a game that's designed around managing simultaneous teamwork. The short length, even for a DLC chapter, hurts it as well. It's worth playing for die hard fans of the base game, but not a big deal otherwise, and even some of those fans might be left disappointed.
Final Fantasy VII Remake Intergrade is a must-have on Steam for fans of the original, regardless of how one may feel about the average port job.

‎Where Final Fantasy VII Remake just missed some points to be a masterpiece in our eyes, the Intergrade DLC elevates quite a bit. Hopefully Square Enix will be able to keep that up, and they will be able to curb the length of the next two games. Still, we enjoyed ourselves for the most part, and the interesting and special story of the base game manages to hold us enough to get us all the way through the game.‎

Final Fantasy VII Remake Intergrade is a port with deleterious issues on several levels. And its narrative restructuring, while better developing some main characters, also follows new directions that leave “fleas behind the ears”, in addition to introducing new characters and some unpublished scenes of little use. However, the balance is much more positive. This RPG is a must for fans of the franchise and the genre in general, and is also recommended, with reservations, for those who are fans of the PlayStation original in particular.

While the pace does drag a bit once you make your way to Shinra Headquarters, things pick up in a big way towards the finale, bringing all of the game's standout features back to the forefront. It all coalesces into a thrilling and heartfelt experience that will satisfy longtime fans of the franchise, and while I do wish there was a bigger emphasis on story and character, at times, I still had a blast returning to this world and spending time with this delightful duo, and Remake's second chapter can't get here soon enough.
Despite a conversion certainly not too elaborate, the PC version of Final Fantasy VII Remake Intergrade becomes the best place to enjoy the new epic of Cloud and company.
A faulty and barebones PC port of Final Fantasy 7 Remake Intergrade, which was originally released on the PlayStation 5.

Final Fantasy VII Remake is a great opportunity to introduce you to one of the most important RPGs in history. The graphic and technical aspect is spectacular and the combat system is a marvel. Some decisions in the level design take it away from being a masterpiece, but it is not far off.

Final Fantasy 7 Remake Intergrade provided an interesting part of the story, as it was telling a side of the character Yuffie, and despite its shortness, the game provided a beautiful experience and an enjoyable addition if you liked the full game, then this addition adds a lot of fun things.

About a year and half ago Final Fantasy VII Remake finally achieved something that the brains behind this franchise have been trying to do for quite some time, make an Action/JRPG game that includes all the beloved elements of Final Fantasy while also providing something totally new and modern. Now PC gamers have the chance to experience the definitive edition of this game (Intergrade) but with the caveat that there are some performance issues and we don't get as much customising options as we like to have in a PC game.

Playing this game in its “Intergrade” form is such a privilege that is truly magnified when you get to experience 60fps and almost no loading times. Anyone who owns a PS5, whether replaying the game or a first-timer, would surely enjoy this release in its most polished state, the way it was meant to be played, fixed doors and all.

As a whole, Final Fantasy VII Remake Intergrade is a complete experience. They’ve improved on the visual fidelity that corrected a lot of the hiccups from the PS4 version while adding the INTERmission side content enables the story to open up to a much larger world away from the Midgar-centric stage.

Ultimately, Final Fantasy VII Remake Intergrade is a better version of Final Fantasy VII Remake. While some of the improvements may not seem noticeable, the ones that are, are great. Saves from the PS4 can be saved and imported into this new version using in-game options, so you can carry over your progress and trophies if you decide to jump back into the game.
In the end, INTERmission is some pretty fun gaming, but it’s not worth spending another $60 on Intergrade unless you’re actually interested in replaying the game on PS5.
I have to say, I enjoyed Episode: INTERmission a lot more than I expected. Yuffie has gone from one of my least favourite to one of my favourite characters.

FFVII Remake Intergrade is a game full of moments both expected and unexpected. It is packed with people you recognize and, unless you went all in on Compilation of FFVII, don’t. Its fundamental gameplay is tight and does enough that it engages you with what-ifs. What could happen this time and how will things change since Square Enix is able to things out more? And with FF7R INTERmission especially, we’re getting hints of how additional stories could go.

Final Fantasy VII Remake was already an outstanding release, but Final Fantasy VII Remake Intergrade SOMEHOW makes it even better. Whether it’s with the improved visuals, the smoother performance, the faster load times, or the additional content that fleshes out the Final Fantasy VII Remake universe further, Final Fantasy VII Remake Intergrade offers something to please everyone. I don’t care if you poured hundred of hours into the base game already… this is one PlayStation 5 port that you simply should NOT ignore.

And by the way, Square Enix… I’ll NEVER stop pronouncing Yuffie’s name as yuff-ee.

Final Fantasy VII Remake INTERmission offers a short introduction into the world of Yuffie Kisaragi, which most players can easily skip. The lack of new elements to the main game and the short and generic trip through midgar, make it really hard to recommend this DLC, even with all the technical benefits from the PS5 Upgrade.

Overall, Final Fantasy VII Remake Intergrade is a great upgrade to an already amazing experience. The main game is even better with sharp visuals, enhanced performance, and speedy load times. We even get an extra photo mode and a challenging new boss fight that digs deeper into the lore. As for Episode INTERmission, the star attraction, it adds a fun new story to enjoy. Yuffie is a joy to witness, adding a charming ray of sunshine to the setting of Midgar. She gives us a small glimpse of the story’s future, but it seems like it’ll be worth the wait. Hopefully, Square Enix can manage to meet the expectations of fans for the next part.

I enjoyed Final Fantasy VII EPISODE INTERmission, in some ways even more than the base game. While it is a shorter experience and doesn’t include all of the same features, it felt more focused. Yuffie is a great character who brought a lot of humor to this INTERmission and who I look forward to seeing in the main series.

The Final Fantasy VII Remake Intergrade Episode Intermission Yuffie ultimately feels more like an appetizer for the eventual full-blown sequel to Final Fantasy VII Remake, which might still be years away at this point. If you’re already a fan of the franchise or Final Fantasy VII Remake, the ending of this DLC alone might be enough to make it an essential purchase.

Final Fantasy VII remake Intergrade Intermission is a must-buy DLC for fans. In addition to completeness, it faithfully performed the role of link with part 2 and the build-up to re-establish Compilation of Final Fantasy VII.

Final Fantasy 7 Remake Intergrade, which includes the main game and the additional package, is more than enough for the original fee. Enhanced images and performance for Playstation 5, the main story where you can play an average of 40+ hours, a pack full of Final Fantasy 7 Remake Intergrade with INTERmission offering approximately 6 hours of content.

Despite some story misgivings, Episode INTERmission makes for an exceptional piece of DLC. It adds thrilling combat, a fun new character in Sonon, and Final Fantasy VII Remake’s best mini-game to date. It also includes a few bonus scenes that—without giving anything away—fans of the base game will want to watch.

At $20, Episode INTERmission isn’t the cheapest proposition, but it’s certainly a worthwhile one. If you’re lucky enough to have a PlayStation 5, do yourself a favor and give it a go. Yuffie fans, rejoice!
Though Intermission reuses assets from the base game, it offers enough new and exciting material to more than justify the price of admission for Final Fantasy fans.

It’s established an illustrious place in the hearts of many that have yearned to see their favourite ex-soldier, and his distinguishable buster carve out another, well deserved place in the annals of Final Fantasy’s vast and revered legacy. Final Fantasy VII Remake Intergrade is an essential.
Metacritic user score 8.5/10 (1140 ratings).
95.2% of OpenCritic critics recommend this game (126 reviews).

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is an ambitious entry for the series, and it delivers a memorable experience that's hard to put down. Between the expansive Flame Lord campaigns, which feed into the Pale Raven campaign, there is a lot of story content to parse through. Many of the characters you meet are worth recruiting, and getting to know them over a meal is one of the better moments outside of training with them at the colosseum. What Nintendo has done with the latest Fire Emblem is nothing short of marvellous.

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is another slam-dunk for the Nintendo Switch 2. A bona fide evolution of what came before it, combining the best elements of its recent entries with spectacular results. Perhaps most impressive, is just how well paced this enormous adventure is despite its lengthy runtime.

With Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave, Intelligent Systems delivers a massive epic for the Switch 2 and one of the meatiest entries in the series. The developer doesn’t shy away from going places with the story! It tries things when it comes to mechanics for the different lords’ stories and abilities.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is the most ambitious game in the series to date, and it executes that ambition with almost effortless elegance. It’s tremendously well-written, very cleverly designed, and one of the most engaging and enjoyable experiences I’ve ever had on a Nintendo console.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is an essential game for fans of Fire Emblem and SRPGs, and if you’re new to the series or genre, there’s no better place to get started. The stories of Dietrich, Theodora, Cai, and Leda are all brilliant, worthy of their own Fire Emblem game, and the fact that we get them all in one is just a bonus. It’s still early days, but I’m confident that Fortune’s Weave will be considered one of the best RPGs in the Switch 2’s library even a decade from now.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is a massively intelligent experience, with deep and rich themes, characters, and gameplay systems. In the same month that Wolverine came out, it is nice to see that one of the three big console manufacturers/publishers still respects the player’s intelligence and is out there trying to do more than endlessly iterate on the same “best practice” game-development-by-numbers slop.
An excellent combination of combat strategy, time management, and compelling stories.

Fire Emblem Echoes: Fortune’s Weave feels like four games in one, such is the scale on show. It might too much for some, but those who fall for it will live and breathe it for a long, long time because this is about as good as it gets for tactics fans.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is a masterful tactical RPG that beautifully combines an engrossing multi-path narrative, addictive turn-based combat, and enjoyable exploration. Dungeon sections help maintain excellent pacing throughout, and the sheer scale of the world means you can easily sink hundreds of hours into this experience without seeing everything. Pair that with solid visuals, a great cast of characters, and an amazing soundtrack, and you’re looking at one of the best Nintendo Switch 2 games released thus far.

Some minor presentational blemishes and slight imbalance to the Overblaze system are about the only drawbacks present in an otherwise exceptional new entry of Fire Emblem which marries the traditional and the modern together to a level of success not reached in other recent franchise entries.
Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave has an obsession with scale, but it never loses sight of the minutiae because of it. Our review of a strategy RPG great.

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is excessive in almost every conceivable direction. It has more story than it strictly needs, more characters than most players will fully explore, systems that disappear for dozens of hours before returning in wonderfully ridiculous combinations, and a campaign long enough that reaching its ending felt like completing an actual journey. Yet almost none of that excess feels careless. After 121 hours, I was exhausted, but I wouldn't wish away any meaningful portion of that time. Fortune's Weave takes the foundations of modern Fire Emblem, stretches them further than I could have ever expected, and somehow makes that enormous ambition feel justified. I wanted it to be the absurdly comprehensive Fire Emblem game its premise promised me. Somehow, it was.

Intelligent Systems continues to tread a delicate balance with finesse: introducing new features to expand the scope, whilst never losing sight of the essence of the series and its core values. Fortune’s Weave is more than just an epic instalment in the Fire Emblem series; it is one of the first epics on the Nintendo Switch 2.

Without a doubt, Fire Emblem: Fortune’s is one of the games that will define the Nintendo Switch 2 generation. Featuring classic gameplay, with just the right amount of new features, it delivers an addictive experience that will make its 100+ hours of playtime fly by. While its encrypted, multi-route narrative, stumbles a bit, it falls far short of making the overall experience anything less than spectacular.

Intelligent Systems took all the ideas it had developed throughout the long and storied history of its legendary saga, refined, expanded, and complemented them with new concepts, resulting in an unforgettable installment that is remarkably difficult to find any significant flaws in. Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is a celebration not only of the series and the genre it represents, but of everything we know as video games. The Switch 2 has surpassed its first year on the market with a catalog that is already impressive, but what this new Fire Emblem brings to the table is not something we get to see every day.

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave brings together the strengths of both Three Houses and Engage to deliver a genuinely absorbing experience. Its tactical battles ramp up in difficulty at a steady pace, giving both newcomers and longtime players plenty to enjoy, while its character progression systems reward repeated experimentation and offer substantial replay value. Taken as a whole, it is easily one of the best Fire Emblem games to date.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave arrives on the Switch 2 as a monumental and ambitious work, featuring an epic three-act campaign centered around four protagonist lords. The game innovates within the franchise by blending refined, classic tactical combat with *Persona*-style time-management systems, real-time dungeon exploration, and a variety of quality-of-life improvements. Despite the significant time investment required and the lack of a Portuguese localization, the title stands as a must-play recommendation, delivering an immersive, colossal, and deeply rewarding experience.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is an exceptionally polished and absolutely massive adventure that offers dozens, if not well over a hundred hours of entertainment. At times, its ambition might prove a little overwhelming for some, and its story occasionally reaches such lofty heights that it gets in the way of the tactical battles themselves. For the most part the game feels like a masterpiece – Its world is fascinating and populated by a colorful cast of characters, while its brilliantly challenging battles had me thoroughly hooked. The impressive visuals, magnificent soundtrack and incredibly addictive gameplay loop have turned me into a full-fledged fan of the series.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is the culmination of the series, bringing together elements from across its history and pushing their potential to almost excessive extremes. By packing in an enormous range of features, from its three-part narrative to character development, exploration, social interactions, and the management of multiple armies, the game also suffers from repetitive busywork, a lack of information, and cumbersome micromanagement. It is far from a streamlined experience designed for everyone, and is difficult to recommend to newcomers. Yet this very excess, in all its sprawling, unwieldy glory, is precisely what makes the game so compelling. For longtime fans, it is a lavish, challenging feast that reimagines the entire history of Fire Emblem—a cult masterpiece that rewards those who make it through every course with a sense of satisfaction unlike anything else.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is easily the biggest and best entry in the series yet. I know that sounds like a cliché, but Intelligent Systems has taken an already polished franchise and elevated it with more impactful storytelling, rock-solid tactical combat, and a staggering amount of content that could easily keep you occupied for 150 to 200 hours if you choose to fully immerse yourself in its world. I have to choose my words carefully, with Ocarina of Time just around the corner, but Fortune’s Weave is quite possibly one of the best Nintendo Switch 2 games of the year. Whether you’re a veteran returning for another adventure or a newcomer looking for your next massive RPG, this is yet another incredible entry in a fantastic franchise, and one that I wholeheartedly recommend.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave makes the impossible possible: It unites four different stories in one game without becoming repetitive. Strategy defines every fiber of the game, no matter if it's inside or outside of the battles, and together with an amazing cast of characters fans can look forward to a genuine beast in terms of quality and scale.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave desires to be the largest and the best title in the series. As Fire Emblem is not only about rich plot and dense battles, you can enjoy a full-fledged game with a large number of activities between battles. Enriched with dungeons, nice world-maps and better balance in the game structure, this is a wonderful experience in the connected world full of top-tier content. You can decide how to manage your army, battle and especially time for everything this game offers.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is probably the closest I’ve come to finding my ideal Fire Emblem game. I’ve been playing the series since the Game Boy Advance days, and I loved what Three Houses brought to it, so getting a game that combines so much of what I enjoyed about both was fantastic. I got completely invested in the four stories, spent hours preparing for battles, and even enjoyed the completely different combat system in the dungeons. There’s an absurd amount to do here, and I certainly didn’t expect to enjoy practically all of it. If you’re willing to sink a lot of hours into this game, you’ll be playing one of the best Nintendo Switch 2 games available.

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is a must-play for fans of strategy games and the series, bringing together the best elements from its various eras to deliver a deep, exciting, and content-packed experience well worth investing dozens of hours in.

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is a genuine classic of a game. It's ambitious beyond belief, filled to the brim of content, constantly exciting and engaging, and I was barely able to put it down. Even with the obviously trimmed content, it doesn't feel like it's lacking anything. If anything, it's the most cohesive and fully featured Fire Emblem game I've ever played. The low difficulty level can be a touch of a drag, but it's the smallest of complaints and absolutely won't get in the way of the game being a true masterpiece.

Fortune’s Weave isn’t just a new Fire Emblem: it’s the series trying to be everything it has been over thirty-six years, all at once, with four heroes, five stories and an entire continent to explore, all held together by a subtle common thread. Not everything flows at the same pace, and those looking for a more immediate experience might get lost among calendars and activities, but those who let themselves ride the wave will find one of the best entries in the saga and one of the most important titles ever to arrive on Switch 2, or perhaps the most important of all on the new console.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is an absolute masterclass in tactical RPG design, brilliantly blending the deep combat lucidity of Engage with the rich, branching narrative weight of Three Houses. Offering unprecedented strategic freedom in team building alongside a sprawling, immersive campaign, it stands as a triumphant capping achievement for the iconic franchise.

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is an ambitious tactical RPG that combines excellent combat, memorable characters, and an interconnected narrative capable of supporting dozens of hours of adventure. Despite uneven pacing, repetitive activities, and a few technical limitations, Intelligent Systems delivers one of the franchise's most comprehensive experiences and a standout title in the Nintendo Switch 2 library.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is a victim of feature creep and massive overscope. With the multiple protagonists and storylines, map traversal, dungeon-crawling, as well as new battle additions like Blaze Arts, the entire game could’ve easily collapsed under all that weight. The only real way to make it all feasible was to drag out the run time to absurd lengths, giving every aspect its proper pacing. Still, all of the threads somehow come together cohesively, and the gameplay is as sharp as a needle. While the sheer amount of concepts and mechanics may dull its point a bit, Fortune’s Weave hits just about every mark it sets its sights on.

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is an amalgamation of many diverse elements which add up to one rewarding adventure that's full of thoughtfully-written characters, unique challenges, and satisfying progression systems.
Fortune's Weave is the right direction for Fire Emblem: the series' most mature and deepest story holding up an unprecedented freedom of play. One of the best entries and probably the most original.

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is not only a great continuation of the series, but an amazing entry point for newcomers. The combat, recruitment mechanics, and story are firing on all cylinders for this 100+ hour Tactical RPG.

If you've never enjoyed a Fire Emblem game, I can promise you'll love Fortune's Weave. It offers the tactical battles of yesteryear mixed with modern options and expanded possibilities, and if it wasn't already obvious that you needed a Switch 2, it will become increasingly clear as Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave hits the shelves around the world. For this is undeniably one of the best titles of the year, and it's also a must-have for all Nintendo Switch 2 owners.

Once I finally got past the anime art style and daunting tactical gameplay, I was hooked. Fire Emblem's somewhat arduous onboarding for a newcomer is a minor roadblock in the way of an epic, sprawling, time-consuming adventure that's fun, challenging, and very enjoyable even for a noob to the series.

Fire Emblem: Fortunes Weave is one of the series’ most ambitious and complete entries yet. Its multi-act story, four distinct protagonists, excellent map variety, and surprisingly dark narrative are complemented by deep tactical systems where time management, recruitment, and progression can have meaningful consequences on the battlefield. Some underdeveloped dungeon mechanics, repetitive music, and scaled-back social elements keep it from perfection, but they do little to diminish an outstanding strategy RPG that successfully pushes Fire Emblem forward without sacrificing what has always made the series special.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is a true colossus of a game, almost always for the better, but occasionally for the worse. The core strategy gameplay is varied and engaging, most of the new ideas work, and the narrative is unprecedented in terms of scope. There’s more admin than I like, and the lack of multiple save files and bird interactions can be frustrating, but outside of that, I doubt I’ll play a better game in 2026.

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is sometimes too big for its own good, but that's exactly what makes it easy to root for. Where lesser games cut their losses, it forges ahead—confident in its ability to win over audiences in spite of its stumbles. Like a jack of all trades, it crowns itself champion through the many shapes it can take and all the things it can do. The daring displayed by Intelligent Systems with this entry deserves a standing ovation, and in a year dominated by Grand Theft Auto VI, Nintendo has come out with a title so massive and ambitious that it may raise the standards for gaming in its own way. Whether it be with its bold storyline, constant genre-hopping, or treasure trove of content, Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is a festival of creativity and spectacle, and players willing to overlook some of its shortcomings will find themselves swept away by all its magic.

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is a towering monument of a game, mixing every flavor of Fire Emblem gameplay from the franchise's 30+ year history with a hugely ambitious three-part, multi-protagonist storyline. While there are a few uneven story moments and people will enjoy some aspects of the game more than others, developer Intelligent Systems have done a pretty admirable job of wrangling this unwieldy colossus of a game while giving players the ability to choose their own path through its epic campaign. Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave will almost certainly burn long and bright as one of the Switch 2's signature experiences.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is a sprawling masterpiece of a strategy RPG, building upon the successes of past Fire Emblem games with new interconnected elements, expertly designed combat puzzles, and an emphasis on flexibility and choice. Nintendo and Intelligent Systems have topped themselves, making this the new high point to beat for future entries.

Intelligent Systems delivers supreme tactical combat in Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave with refined mechanics and a plethora of options to choose from, and a story that is uniquely structured in a way that encourages fans to overturn every stone. It’s sure to delight fans of Fire Emblem: Three Houses, but is also independent enough that newcomers shouldn’t feel lost. Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is the dense, character-rich RPG that I’ve been waiting to play on my Switch 2.
A multi-stranded strategy RPG masterclass, Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is absolutely a part of the conversation for being the very best game in this venerable series.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave builds on the formula that made its predecessors so successful, whilst also embracing innovation. It captivates players with strong characters, intriguing lore, and an engaging gameplay loop, which it develops further as the story unfolds, inspiring both newcomers and veterans alike to hone their troops to perfection. Anyone who can cope with the really long playtime, a few repetitive mechanics, and a story that falters towards the end can look forward to a beautifully presented tactical gem.

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is one of the most ambitious entries in Intelligent Systems' longrunning tactical RPG series that succeeds where it matters most. It delivers an exceptionally deep and content-rich Fire Emblem experience, making it one of the strongest modern entries in the series and an essential exclusive for Nintendo Switch 2 owners.

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave has been quite the odyssey and yet, after 160 hours of playtime, we still feel the urge to return to Dagda and keep fighting. That is a tremendous testament to its value, despite some imperfections born from Intelligent Systems' ambition and audacity. It takes time to piece together the puzzle that is Fortune's Weave, but if there is one constant from the very first hour to the last, it is the quality of its gameplay and combat mechanics. They are, quite simply, the pinnacle of a series approaching its fortieth anniversary — a series that isn't ashamed of a single wrinkle. Quite the opposite: it wears every one of them with swagger and a healthy dose of playful irreverence.

This colossal tactical RPG revitalizes the franchise through its masterful four-route narrative structure, outstanding turn-based combat, and vibrant Mediterranean aesthetic. Although simplified quick battles lack depth and unit recruitment can feel needlessly tedious, the sheer wealth of inventive map designs, charismatic protagonists, and strategic nuance makes it an essential tactical tour de force.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave feels like the future of the franchise because it perfectly understood what to take from Three Houses, respects the DNA of the classic games, and adds elements of its own. It's a massive package, and while not perfect, it's engaging both on and off the battlefield.

Nintendo’s latest entry has absolutely won me over and has made me a true Fire Emblem fan. With a robust combat system, sprawling narrative, and dozens of hours of content, Fortune’s Weave is one of the best exclusives Nintendo has released so far on Switch 2.

With Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave, Intelligent Systems masterfully deliver strategic perfection. What early on felt intimidating in scale went on to become breathtaking in its ambition, science fiction and high fantasy colliding throughout to result in an experience that easily ranks as my favourite Fire Emblem game to date. From its tactical brilliance on the battlefield to its meaningful character development, it’s another Nintendo Switch 2 exclusive that proves itself to be yet another simply unmissable masterpiece.

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is the most ambitious entry in the franchise, and you can feel it in every design decision: four heroes, four perspectives on the same fall of the world, and the rare freedom to experience them in any order without losing a shred of progress. The combat remains among the best on the TBS market, now with more layers, more spectacle, and a risk-reward system that forces you to rethink strategies you'd taken for granted. If it stumbles, it stumbles from excess: the management between battles repeats itself one too many times across four campaigns that are nearly identical in structure, and the final act doesn't always live up to the ambition of the rest, with predictable twists and heroes who deserved more room in a story that ends up belonging only to the protagonist. Fortune's Weave isn't perfect, but it's one of those games you'll remember for years, and that outweighs any rough edge still left to polish.

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave continues the franchise tradition of combining addictive strategy combat with an expansive, complex story in a huge fantasy kingdom. There are elements of Fortune's Weave that are starting to feel a little familiar, and it feels like the franchise needs to do something wildly different soon, but what's here is truly sparkling. The game's design is superb, and it's going to very easily be one of the best games on the Switch 2 this year.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave stands as Intelligent Systems’ current magnum opus. It weaves together elements from across the entire series into a warm, comforting experience filled with nostalgia and affection. It takes the best from each of its predecessors and, aside from a few shortcomings—such as the lack of challenge on Normal difficulty and the occasional character who feels overpowered for the point at which they become available—the game delivers on its ambitions and exceeds them by a wide margin.
Deep, ambitious, and endlessly engaging, Fortune’s Weave is Fire Emblem at its very best.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is an impressive new entry in the series, offering a gigantic experience with significant depth to its elements. It manages to build on top of many systems the series has played with in the past while also finding a fresh approach to the complete experience. It’s the kind of SRPG colossus that will provide fun for hundreds of hours, inviting players to be thorough in their exploration of its massive world.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is one of the best entries in the series and a must-play for fans of JRPGs and tactical games. It draws inspiration not only from Three Houses, but also from earlier instalments in the series, featuring excellent map design, satisfying gameplay and a tremendous amount of content. However, due to its sheer scale, its storyline suffers, offering a disjointed narrative with too many subplots and loose ends. Despite this, it is currently one of my contenders for GOTY.

Crucially, however preposterous the stakes get, amid the gods and monsters and promised ones, it never loses sight of the small threads - the individual stories of human courage, camaraderie and altruism - woven into its sprawling tapestry. [Issue#429, p.110]
Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is the game that finally got me on board with this long-running, excellent tactics series.

Fortune’s Weave manages to draw in both the series’ diverse fanbase and newcomers alike with its grand, lengthy, fantastic campaign. Quite the achievement. Now if you don’t mind, I’m hopping back in to hit a few more turns... [Issue#375, p.52]

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave as a full package is excellent. It recovers from the rocky stories of Three Houses and Engage with a gripping narrative spread across four unique characters. It makes some improvement in battles for arguably the best combat to date across a rather large catalogue of titles, which is a huge plus. With respectable visuals and a fantastic musical score on top of all of that, you’re buying arguably one of the best Fire Emblem games since the GameCube era. The downtime between “missions” could be a little better, but otherwise it’s handled exceptionally. Train your units’ skills, build support ranks to recruit new characters, or just generally explore the map and do sidequests while you bolster your roster for upcoming encounters. You genuinely cannot go wrong with Fire Emblem this time, so if you’re a fan of strategy RPGs, you’re doing yourself a disservice by not at least trying Fortune’s Weave.

Fortune's Weave impresses with its scope, wealth of content, and the way it weaves four campaigns into a single, grand narrative. While not every new idea hits the mark - and aspects like cave exploration or certain narrative issues can be irksome - the foundation remains excellent. It is a massive, incredibly engaging Fire Emblem title that, despite falling short of Three Houses in a few areas, still ranks among the very best in the series.

Ultimately, Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is an absolute winner. Despite some clear evidence that somehow even more than what is currently in the game was planned, the game still feels complete, and the story is more than satisfying. The gameplay is some of the most refined it’s ever been, and the visuals are a massive step up from its predecessors, and the incredible soundtrack elevates the game even further.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is a massive, well-crafted strategy game that makes the most of its fresh ideas. Though the free time periods can get repetitive, the maps, narrative, and character progression more than make up for it, making it one of the best games on the Nintendo Switch 2. I can’t even imagine what the next Fire Emblem will be like, since upping the ante from Fortune’s Weave seems nigh impossible.

Of course, I won’t say it is a perfect game by any means, especially because it does have its fair share of issues. Most of which boil down to the calendar system, but still. The characters of this game are so well-fleshed out, and the story is so engaging that I still highly recommend it for both series veterans and anyone looking to try out the series for the first time.
A grand turn-based strategy game with all the bells and whistles you could possibly hope for.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is, by far, the Nintendo Switch 2 exclusive to get. It’s the culmination of what the series has built up to, and it delivers a satisfying fusion of past and present that we’ve come to expect in every new release of the franchise. It’s one of those games you should simply not miss, whether you’re a massive fan of the genre or only remotely interested in it.

Fire Emblem is a franchise deeply cherished by its fans, and it has recently delivered outstanding titles on Nintendo's hybrid console. Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave upholds the high standards set by its predecessors, offering a rich, compelling story—told in an intriguing and immersive way by an excellent cast of characters—alongside the robust strategic gameplay expected of the series.

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is nothing short of a monument when it comes to plot, characters, combat, weapons and pretty much everything else. The semi-flexible structure allows the player to make choices when it comes to navigating the main events, while the difficulty options and blessings can give much needed relief in the harshest Fire Emblem-typical moments. Beyond the combat and preparation, there's a myriad things to do that shape this into a magnificent tactical RPG with an impressive social management dimension. It's demanding and can get overwhelming at times, but we wouldn't have it any other way.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is a joy to play, and its strong characters and interesting story do a lot to keep you engaged and wanting to stick with it. There’s an absurd amount of content here, and most of it is good, which, in some ways, makes it more frustrating that the developers clearly didn’t get to finish this absolute epic of a game.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is a solid, deep, and highly rewarding entry that preserves the series’ tactical core while introducing time travel, interconnected routes, and additional layers of strategic depth. Its story may draw on familiar tropes, but strong execution keeps it engaging through compelling characters, meaningful progression, relationship systems, and demanding battles. It does not fundamentally reinvent the formula, but it delivers a robust and addictive experience that comes highly recommended for strategy RPG enthusiasts, even if its complexity may prove demanding for more casual players.
The new Fire Emblem has perfected the well-established blend of strategy and RPG gameplay, offering fans of the genre an unprecedentedly massive game.
Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is easily one of my favorite settings and stories in the series' history, with memorable battles and characters, even when repetition and overabundance weigh it down.

There is no denying that its structure is, to say the least, unconventional. It will likely be a tough pill for some to swallow... But if you are strategy die-hards who relish meticulous management and min-maxing to build the ultimate army, then here is a tremendous SRPG—a real time sink. Well, more than just a sink... a bottomless cauldron.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is a massive, ambitious instalment that is initially rather difficult to get to grips with. The four storylines, the shared progression and the multitude of systems centred around battles take time to reveal how all the pieces fit together, but once they do, it’s hard not to get swept up in its ensemble narrative. Not everything maintains the same standard, however: side quests and skirmishes often become routine, creating a noticeable gap compared to the main battles, which are far more polished and thrilling. Intelligent Systems may have taken on too much, and doesn’t always manage to sustain the momentum for over a hundred hours, but Fortune’s Weave remains a richly detailed Fire Emblem title, bold in its deviations from the formula and capable of rewarding those willing to give it the time it demands.
Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is a chapter that solidifies many of the profound changes Three Houses introduced to the gameplay formula.

Ultimately, Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is another characteristically high-quality entry in the series, meaningfully blending elements from various predecessors, both narratively and in terms of gameplay, with entirely new features. While this new installment may not quite reach the contemporary benchmark set by the dye 3DS standout "Awakening," it comes closer to the standard of Three Houses than that of Engage. It is a title that will thoroughly satisfy both, genre fans in general and series devotees in particular.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is arguably the least "Fire Emblem-esque" entry in the entire franchise. Beyond its Mediterranean art style, the game introduces a kingdom-scale management aspect—the core of the gameplay—featuring a highly addictive loop, particularly in the endgame. However, this ambition to do more ultimately drowns out the original formula. Historically, the series has relied on a delicate balance: tight skirmishes, carefully cultivated heroes, and the satisfaction of expanding one's ranks amidst a unique story set in a war-torn kingdom. By pushing these elements to the extreme, the game unnecessarily weighs down a formula that didn't need such embellishment. It disrupts its own center of gravity, resulting in an awkward structure that affects every layer of the game and distances it somewhat from the series' defining characteristics. Nevertheless, Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave remains a tactical RPG that is both accessible and deep, offering endearing characters whose growth is a joy to nurture—and, above all, whose survival matters in battles where every blow could be fatal. The bottom line? It is the least "Fire Emblem" of them all, yet it is still a Fire Emblem game. Undoubtedly.

If nothing else, Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is the grandest and most ambitious entry in the series. With a playtime that surpasses the three-digit mark in hours and enough content to support it, it's nothing short of a must-have for fans of the series, tactics games, and Switch 2 owners in general. We could have done with a bit less grinding, nevertheless, this only becomes an issue during the third and final act, without ultimately hurting what is a truly epic adventure.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave lives up to expectations and carries on the tradition of the franchise, delivering a high-quality tactical RPG that remains faithful to the series’ historical traits while introducing a few new ideas. A great cast, a story divided into four intertwining narratives, and an outstanding gameplay system mark the return of the Fire Emblem series with yet another excellent entry. Turn the difficulty all the way up and enjoy a challenge capable of putting your planning skills to the test, all within a narrative packed with interesting ideas and mysteries to uncover. The only real downside is the range of activities available between battles, which, due to their lack of flair and repetitive nature, can disrupt the pacing a little too much. They should be followed carefully if you want to develop your army properly, but they simply lack the appeal needed to truly engage the player. The new exploration sections and turn-based JRPG-style battles are also rather uninspired, but these shortcomings remain marginal when compared to the overall quality of a game like Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave. Perhaps the series could benefit from a less dispersive approach in the future, but that does not change the fact that, if you love turn-based strategy, Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is a game that deserves a place in every Nintendo Switch 2 library. Once you step onto the battlefield, the qualities of a brilliantly crafted system manage, once again, to keep us glued to the controller, in this fantastic universe where Intelligent Systems continues to hit the mark time and time again.

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave represents another step forward in the direction already charted by Three Houses. This new installment not only expands in scale but further refines, improves, and deepens its gameplay systems, while adding a host of side activities and macro- and micro-management options that will delight fans of the series' modern era. Levelling significant criticism at a magnificent game like Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave should not be viewed as a punitive act that diminishes the developers' monumental effort. On the contrary, it serves as a cautionary note for those who demand that every new entry in a series be "bigger, better, and more badass." Fire Emblem does not necessarily need all of that—at least not to the extent seen here. It does not need to grow into a giant with tentacles stretching as far as the eye can see, only to lose its way in the void. At times, the sheer, excessive scale of Fortune's Weave ends up detracting from what is undoubtedly one of the series' best entries—yet also the only one that let itself get carried away by avoidable delusions of grandeur.

Fortune’s Weave proves that it is possible to experiment with the classic formula without sacrificing the depth that defines the series. It takes the best of previous entries, adds its own touch, and delivers an appealing title for fans of Fire Emblem and the tactical RPG genre.

While Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is occasionally held back by some imperfect features, its amazing combat, overall narrative depth, world-building, and visuals make it one of the best titles in the franchise.
Fire Emblem Fortune’s Weave is a solid Fire Emblem game, but after Part 2, I began to feel the tedium of side activities, aspects that, for me, slightly marred an otherwise delightful experience.

Whether you’re a seasoned veteran of the Fire Emblem franchise or a newcomer, Fortune’s Weave is definitely worth trudging through. The amount of content here is colossal and will keep you busy for many, many hours, and will no doubt immerse you in all of its lore, its fascinating story, and its delectable strategy-heavy combat. It’s definitely not perfect due to some Switch 2 handheld bugbears, and it might seem old-fashioned because it runs at 30 frames per second, but if these things don’t bother you, then you’ll definitely embrace Fortune’s Weave even more. Character depth is a little lacking, but the spirit and vast diversity among them make them stand out, and there’s more than enough lore and legend to sink your teeth into. The fire burns very bright with Fortune’s Weave, and it thus comes highly recommended.

Fortune's Weave is a huge game. The story is epic, you've got four campaigns to play through, and a massive roster of characters. It feels so big that it impacts the pacing, which suffers from time to time. I don't want to do every possible thing every time for every campaign. But if you're patient and persistent, you can smash past all of that and succeed. Even if you have to turn off permadeath to do so. There are an imposing amount of systems to discover and master, but it's a lot of fun doing so. And the battles are all excellent affairs. I struggled at points for sure, but overall this was a fantastic time. If you're any kind of Fire Emblem fan, Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is a slam dunk. Don't miss this game.

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave truly shines in the depth and variety of its combat, delivering moments that stick with you. However, a bit more restraint and clearer differentiation between its four story routes would have been the perfect finishing touch.

Fire Emblem Fortune’s Weave delivers excellent tactical combat, deep character progression, clever terrain mechanics, and four compelling campaigns that explore different perspectives of its ambitious story. The 30-day structure adds an interesting layer of strategy beyond the battlefield, while Classic Mode and Fortuna’s Blessing offer flexibility for different players. However, excessive dialogue frequently slows the pacing, and the 30 FPS cap on Switch 2 makes its technical presentation feel surprisingly conservative.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave offers an interesting new take on the familiar formula, combining classic tactical battles with four unique protagonists and interconnected storylines. While the story takes some time to get going and its many systems can initially feel overwhelming, things gradually fall into place and the freedom to switch between narratives keeps the adventure engaging. Despite some less interesting characters and activities, Fortune’s Weave proves there is still room for fresh ideas within the Fire Emblem formula and offers a rewarding experience for fans of tactical RPGs.
Builds on Three House's multi-path structure, becoming grander and more ambitious
Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave blends classic strategic gameplay with newer, more personal touches.

On the whole, Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is dense, deep, and really rather delightful. It can sometimes feel like a bit too much of a good thing, with the pacing slipping in the later chapters, thanks to an unnecessarily complicated protagonist hierarchy and some grindy map management, but the battles have never felt better, and there’s no knocking the sheer amount to do. It takes a lot for a game to hold my attention for as long as Fortune’s Weave, and with a bunch of content still waiting for me, I’ll be happy to pour even more days into it.

The game takes what we saw in Three Houses to a new level with several playable and non-playable characters whose fates interweave, a dizzying list of activities to take part in, a deep battle system to sink your teeth in taking part over several time periods. The more you engage with, the more it rewards you.

For me, Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave ended up being something of an inversion of Three Houses. I loved the characters and world of that game, and thought the tactical gameplay was just fine. For Fortune’s Weave, I spent so many sessions just unable to put the game down. The time management system has been designed to satisfyingly feed into just about everything you do, and battles feel polished, stressful, and exciting. It doesn't nail everything that it sets out to do, but I think this is an exceptionally strong SRPG for most of the run time. I’ll just need to take a long break from huge RPGs to try to get my sleep schedule back on track.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is a gigantic game, and its vastness only steals a little bit of the spotlight from the tactics that I come to these games for. Thankfully, it finds its footing on that front and delivers some unforgettable battles. An excellent soundtrack, beautiful visuals, and a surprisingly strong gameplay loop that connects one fight to the next cements this as one of the best on Switch 2. All of that is weighed down slightly by a vacuous plot that you will struggle to care about. If you can ignore the writing, though, you’re in for dozens of hours of gaming in an entry that lives up to the Fire Emblem legacy.
The best Fire Emblem game of the modern era and a staggering achievement in terms of the volume of content and the variety of gameplay – with even the plot taking some unexpected detours.

Following in the footsteps of Three Houses, Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave features a four-protagonist structure, though it suffers from some pacing issues in the first half. Fortunately, once it overcomes those hiccups and returns to being a true Fire Emblem game, it delivers some of the best battles in the entire franchise, all set against the most spectacular and varied backdrop the series has seen to date.

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is an ambitious and remarkably rich experience, skillfully blending the solidity of traditional tactical gameplay with a fascinating techno-fantasy universe and an expansive ensemble-driven narrative structure. The cast, art direction, and some intriguing gameplay ideas- such as Burning Arts and the unique traits of the four protagonists -help make this a memorable strategic marathon that can easily surpass one hundred hours. But not everything is perfectly in focus: the structure of Phase Two can feel somewhat unintuitive, while the single-save system ultimately limits a degree of freedom that the game itself seems eager to provide. These are frustrating shortcomings, but they do little to diminish the overall quality of the experience or the personality of a chapter that will undoubtedly delight fans of the series.

While it may lack depth in certain areas, it more than delivers where it truly matters: Fortune's Weave is a massive tactical dream featuring a fascinating concept and bursts of highly addictive gameplay.
Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave tells four distinct and engaging stories through demanding tactical combat at its finest – but buries its best ideas under too much busywork outside of battle.
Fortune's Weave is imperfect, messy and overbloated with things to do. I can't stop playing it.

For one of Nintendo’s longest-running franchises, Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave feels remarkably fresh. Each and every gameplay mechanic and system requires some strategic thought and investment, from the calendarised social sim aspect to the tremendous turn-based battles. This is cohesion in its finest form, even if it occasionally feels a little too staggering in its ambition. Players are rewarded for pushing through any initial sense of being overwhelmed and sticking with it to the climactic end, although some late-game pacing issues do disappoint somewhat. Nevertheless, turn-based lovers and social sim enthusiasts will find plenty to love in what feels like the perfect evolution from Three Houses.

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is a dense, massive game that will easily eat up over 100 hours of your time if you want to see and do it all. The turn-based tactics battles are the best they've ever been, but dungeons and Clash Battles leave a lot to be desired. Existing Fire Emblem fans will completely lose themselves in Fortune's Weave, and it's also a solid jumping-on point for those that may be new to the franchise.

Fortune’s Weave has some fantastic moments linked often to adrenalin-soaked clashes on the battlefield. But you’ll expend too much concentration keeping all those narrative threads from unravelling the game’s rich tapestry.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is a creation of almost unbound ambition. That works in its favor most of the time, but there are stumbles along the way, like a crew of side characters that work as extras to the plot, and a structure which demands too much of the player. All that said though – this is an uncut diamond, which, at times, shines brighter than most competing experiences out there. Intelligent Systems continue to choose innovation instead of a clear, sequential path forward for its games, and perhaps that’s why it’s exciting, and at times heartbreaking, to be a Fire Emblem fan.

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is a monumental tactical RPG that occasionally suffers from its own excesses, but remains faithful to the series where it matters most. The turn-based battles are excellent, varied, and mechanically deep, while the four main protagonists offer distinctly different stories and gameplay possibilities. Weaker supporting characters, overwrought dialogue, repetitive management chores, and disappointing dungeons prevent it from being a flawless evolution of Three Houses. Even so, it's an exceptionally generous game with a superb tactical core that can easily occupy hundreds of hours, though not every one of them will be equally memorable.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave delivers another comforting title, bringing a lot of what worked from recent titles Three Houses, Engage, and Echoes all into one. While its story is grandiose and epic, it’s longer than it needs to be, leading to a massively bloated Part 1 and a weirdly streamlined Parts 2 and 3. It tries to be bigger and better, and only totally succeeds at the bigger part. Still, it’s a great time… just maybe be prepared to take your time.

Unfortunately, Fortune’s Weave flies a bit too close to the sun; while many of its individual parts rival or surpass what the franchise has achieved before, the structure that binds all these disparate parts together melts underneath the heat. While Fortune’s Weave doesn’t quite crash and burn like Icarus, it struggles to stay aloft, proving a stern warning about the limits of ambition and maximalist design.

Fire Emblem: Three Houses ended up becoming my “short term disability” game in early 2020 even before the world became Dagsion for about a year, and when I finally finished my objectives with it, I had put about 700 hours into the game to unlock the full support log. I don’t think Fortune’s Weave will hit that number unless the final part of the Expansion Pass gives four part 1s as it’s threatening to, but I can already tell this will be the longest “time to credits” game of my life. And I do want to see it through… just not all at once. There’s other things I want to play or have for review, after all.

Even though it's probably the most generous entry the series has attempted, Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is a contradictory object. On one side, you'll find a broad three-act structure that finally defuses the multiple-routes problem through fine writing, incredibly endearing characters, and some of the best maps in the series. On the other, this is a game that doesn't dare commit to its own choices, constantly apologizing for its major design decisions with options (permadeath you can bypass, a half-optional hub, a skippable second act...) that only drain them of meaning, the whole thing chopped up by time-consuming repetitiveness during the free-time phases. For anyone with the time (or the patience) to deal with the optimization chore that serves as its backbone, Fortune's Weave still remains a very fine entry in the saga. In fact, it's good, because the foundations already were. But there was so much potential here that you couldn't help hoping for something more concise, more precise, more sure of itself.

Fortune's Weave takes us along for an epic journey that drags along in the final stages. Showing the story from four different perspectives is an ambitious choice that mostly pans out, but the game lacks some polish in other areas.

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is a visually stunning departure that trades the series' beloved tactical combat for heavy JRPG exploration. While the core grid battles are brilliant, they often get buried under clunky real-time dungeons and tedious open-world busywork. It is an ambitious, beautiful experiment, but strategy purists may find themselves left out in the cold.
Coupled with the slightly improved turn-based tactical actions returning players know, and Fortune’s Weave is one heck of a coming out party for Fire Emblem
Fortune’s Weave has set a remarkably high standard to beat and remains an instant classic.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is one of the best strategy games of recent years, brilliantly building on the series’ tried-and-tested foundations whilst adding some brilliant new ideas. Brilliant tactical battles, four intertwining storylines and a wealth of options for developing your team mean you can easily spend over 100 hours in this world. Not all storylines and activities are of the same high standard, and the sheer number of systems can sometimes feel overwhelming, but for fans of the genre, this is an absolute must-play.

Overall, I would say Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave deserves praise and makes up for the mistakes that they learned from the previous Fire Emblem game, Fire Emblem Engage. Now, I would say that if I were to recommend this game to any of my Nintendo gamers and friends who are first-time players, I would say this game is quite good, and I would recommend them that they should try playing Fire Emblem: Three Houses first to get to know more of the lore of what Fire Emblem Engage has to offer.

Ultimately, Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave shows that four separate narratives can not only coexist in a cohesive experience, but be one of the experience’s greatest strengths. The deep character development, engaging strategic combat and evolving gameplay structures combine to make for a remarkably varied and compelling adventure.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave brings its sprawling story to life through varied heroes, rewarding preparation and compelling tactical battles, but repeated campaigns and uneven pacing make the journey towards its impressive finale an exhausting commitment.

Fire Emblem: Fortune´s Weave expands the classic formula with four protagonists, time travel and a campaign that lets players follow different routes in parallel. Battles retain the series’ tactical depth, while management, exploration and progression greatly enrich the downtime between major encounters.

Classic battles are better than ever. Combat animations are truly excellent and with the exception of the more battles you grind on the world map, no two encounters are the same.

Overall, it’s easy to recommend Fire Emblem Fortune’s Weave to fans of the series.

Newcomers will be overwhelmed by the sheer amount of systems and mechanics there is to learn. For that reason, I’d still recommend playing the excellent Fire Emblem Three Houses first.

It's not an easy thing to deliver the most ambitious entry in a long-running series like Fire Emblem. And what is even harder is living up to those ambitions and delivering an experience that surpasses its predecessors. Fortune’s Weave succeeds on both fronts, offering a fantastic, cohesive story across its four routes and deeply satisfying strategic gameplay with varied maps that keep things fresh throughout the adventure. Making it easily stands as one of the strongest RPGs of the year and an experience no Nintendo Switch 2 owner should miss.

The story itself is amazing and quite emotional, and the gameplay is quite fun. Fortune’s Weave does everything right in it’s own way. It has big shoes to fill, and even though they don’t fit the way I would have liked, it’s still a grand experience.

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is an extremely extensive strategy RPG that brings with it an enormous number of systems — though unfortunately these are often tied to trivial yet time-consuming activities. The battles are still a lot of fun and can be set to a high game speed, but in terms of quality and strategic depth they can't hold a candle to the series' recent highlights, Fire Emblem Fates and Engage.

Fire Emblem Fortune's Weave delivered one of the grandest and most beautiful entries in the series, featuring a fantastic story, excellent characters, enjoyable gameplay, and an exceptional soundtrack, alongside a charming visual presentation, an eye-catching art style, and brilliant technical performance, standing out as one of the best games of 2026.
Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave delivers a deep, rewarding tactical combat system alongside an epic story that gives you more than enough reasons to keep playing.
The story pairs beautifully with the gameplay, and its dynamic nature keeps players on their toes.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is already one of the best games on the Nintendo Switch 2, and it will likely maintain the staying power that Three Houses did on the Switch 1 before it. It does need some touching up, and hopefully the incoming expansion updates will be well worth it.

I like to think of Fortune’s Weave as four complete story-driven games tied to a much more gameplay-oriented third act that serves more as an extended catharsis than as a story. I acknowledge that drawing that big a divide between them is a big ask, but if that mindset works for you, you’ll probably come out thinking the game is a masterpiece. Even if you don’t, it will still probably be a ton of fun.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave gives you a different story and gameplay experience across each of its four routes. Between the varied battle map tricks and the fun of gathering and training unique teammates, you rarely get bored, even though the game is huge. Even after you beat it, the game is fun enough to make you want to play it again and try training your characters in new ways. However, compared to Parts 1 and 2, Part 3—where all the different journeys come together—has less exciting battles and leaves quite a few gaps in the overall story. It is a very strange game that somehow feels unfinished, even after you have spent so many hours enjoying it.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is a game so committed to a specific vision that I don’t think it will be for everyone. It’s utterly ambitious in scale and complexity, but this is definitely done in a way that more heavily warps Fire Emblem’s “isms” compared to other games in the series. While I think Fortune’s Weave is a better game than the previous Fire Emblem Engage, the latter title was actually easier to like at first thanks to its leaner and more focused game design. However, between the camp of “love” and “loathe,” I eventually found myself firmly in the former camp. Let it sink its teeth into you, and you won’t be let go for a long time.

Considering the success of Fire Emblem: Three Houses, it would have been easy to make a sequel to it that was just a basic iteration of its formula, but Fortune’s Weave takes a much bolder approach in both design and writing. It not only emboldens what that game was, but it actively interrogates it to inform what I feel were very successful experimentations in writing and design. Given the enormity and length of Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave, I don’t anticipate that I’ll play it again for a long time, but my time in Dagda will not soon be forgotten.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave isn’t a game for everyone—it’s long, repetitive, and somewhat difficult—but its well-told story, memorable characters, and brilliant battles make it a title that any fan of RPGs or tactical video games should check out. If you own a Switch 2, it’s an essential play.
Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is exactly what you would expect from a Fire Emblem game. It is a challenging tactical RPG and a worthy addition to the franchise.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is a confident, content-rich evolution of the series. Occasionally unwieldy and sometimes inconsistent, but ultimately an exceptionally rewarding strategy RPG whose four intertwined destinies make its enormous journey more than worthwhile.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is an ambitious and polished evolution of the series, combining deep tactical combat with extensive RPG systems, character development and four distinct story routes. While its wealth of systems can occasionally feel overwhelming, there’s an impressive amount of flexibility and content here, making it a strong entry for both long-time fans and newcomers.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave isn’t just your typical strategy RPG. It feels like a playable Greco-Roman myth, one where the scope of the story somehow manages to keep getting bigger and bigger as you go, and surprises you at just about every turn. Things only hinted at in Three Houses now take center stage, and the franchise goes places it has never been and succeeds with flying colors.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is the sort of game you need to let sink in for a while. The slow start and the sheer volume of information can leave you feeling a bit lost at first. But once all the pieces of the puzzle start to fall into place, it becomes incredibly difficult to put the controller down. The various storylines, the choices on the World Map, the Support systems, Renown, the tactical Skirmishes and the turn-based Dungeons ensure there’s an enormous amount to experience. Even after twenty hours of play, I was still discovering new elements in the game. And most importantly: I constantly felt that my choices were leading somewhere. *Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave* doesn’t just set out to tell one big story. It lets you experience different stories and gradually discover how everything is interconnected. For me, that’s ultimately the greatest strength of this *Fire Emblem*. To me, it’s clear: *Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave* is a reason to get a Nintendo Switch 2.

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave stays on your mind long after you put the controller down. Even after 105 hours, I’m still planning out teams and classes. A tactical behemoth that’s incredibly difficult to put down.

Boasting exceptional tactical turn-based combat and massive replay value across four distinct hero paths, Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is an epic addition to the franchise that delivers tremendous bang for your buck. While repetitive weekly chores and a pointless dungeon Clash system drag on the pacing, the rich lore and tense, strategic battles make it an easy recommendation for strategy RPG fans.
I went in expecting a good Fire Emblem game in Fortune’s Weave. I came out convinced this truly believing that this is one of the best RPGs Nintendo has published in a decade.
