The lack of Brazilian Portuguese localization is the main issue preventing it from being perfect. If you have the time and patience, and speak English, FE:FW is easily one of the best games on the Switch 2 right now and a real treat for fans of RPGs and Fire Emblem.
As you’ve no doubt realised whilst reading, this episode is particularly well done, even if it’s obviously not perfect.

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is not just a tactical masterpiece, it's one of the best games of 2026 - a content-stacked experience that continues the franchise's winning streak of polished, endlessly addictive JRPGs.
Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is an ambitious tactics RPG that goes far beyond the series' previous scope, rethinking the entire Fire Emblem concept on a bigger scale.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is, for better or worse, the most ambitious Fire Emblem of the generation: a tactical epic that brushes against greatness in its third act, when everything comes together magnificently.

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave emerges as a vast and epic tactical RPG for Nintendo Switch 2, masterfully weaving together four distinct campaigns into a single, complex narrative of time travel and political intrigue on the continent of Dagda.

Although it doesn’t deliver builds as customizable or animations as spectacular as Engage, Fire Emblem Fortune’s Weave still offers some of the best combat in the franchise. Combined with captivating characters, a narrative that truly holds your attention, highly varied maps, and an outstanding soundtrack, it’s easy to see why Fortune’s Weave has become a favorite Fire Emblem entry for so many people—including me. After more than 100 hours of gameplay, I still want more, and I think that says a lot about how much I enjoyed the experience. Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is an intimidatingly large and complex RPG, but once its many systems click into place, it's incredibly hard to put down. Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave succeeds by combining the franchise’s traditional tactical combat with four interconnected stories that come together in a very interesting way. Para mim, talvez o maior trunfo de Fortune’s Weave seja justamente conseguir condensar quase 40 anos de Fire Emblem em uma experiência que equilibra o clássico e o moderno.

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is a great strategy game that sometimes seems determined to test your patience. Its tactical battles are fantastic, and its characters and stories end up drawing you in, but the overwhelming start, excessive management, and uninspired dungeons hurt the pacing.

One of the best strategy games of recent years. Intelligent Systems has created a massive adventure, brimming with possibilities and featuring a story that keeps players engaged thanks to its many protagonists and a very well-crafted narrative.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is the most ambitious entry in the series: four intertwined campaigns, some of the franchise’s best tactical battles and a massive world to explore. Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is massive, confident, and slightly indulgent, but it gets the important things right. Even though I wish it respected your time a bit more, the tactics are the series at its best, and I'd recommend it without hesitation to anyone who loved Three Houses.

Fortune’s Weave gave me exactly what I wanted from Fire Emblem: tense battles, characters I actually cared about, and a ridiculous amount of content. It can drag at times, but when it gets going, it’s hard to put down.
Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave combines four epic stories, strategic battles, and high replayability, making it an essential RPG on Nintendo Switch 2.

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is a massive entry in the franchise that will not be forgotten. With its amazing intertwining plotlines, rich battle mechanics, and solid performance on the Switch 2, this may be one of Nintendo's finest titles to date.

“Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave takes the series’ tactical foundations to a new level with deep turn-based combat, four compelling heroes and a wealth of content. Not only is Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave a fantastic entry point for newcomers to tactical RPGs and Fire Emblem in general, but it also is a must-play for any fan of the franchise. Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is ambitious, occasionally messy and frequently brilliant. The four-way campaign takes some patience to understand, but once the separate pieces begin locking together, it becomes the reason I wanted to keep playing.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is one of the best games the series has ever received. Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is the series' most ambitious entry yet, weaving four genuinely distinct hero stories into a tactical RPG so vast it occasionally trips over its own scale, but rarely stops being engrossing.

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave establishes itself as the ultimate benchmark for tactical RPGs on Nintendo Switch 2. Its flawless combination of strategy, a mature narrative, and an unforgettable soundtrack easily overshadows its minor limitations, rising as an absolute must-play.

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is a sprawling masterpiece that fuses an intricately woven narrative with masterfully designed tactical puzzles and unmatched freedom of approach, setting a new high bar for the series.

'Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave' is a potent follow-up to 'Three Houses' with riveting characters, tactics on top of tactics, and a strong aesthetic throughout. It occasionally buckles under the weight of its scale, but this is the big Switch 2 RPG you've been waiting for.

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is an ambitious strategy RPG packed with memorable characters, deep combat, and time-management systems. Its enormous scope can lead to pacing and grind issues, but there is plenty to keep you invested.

It would take well over 1700 words to detail the qualities of Fire Emblem Fortune’s Weave, and the pleasure I took to discover chapter by chapter the story of our 4 heroes and their companions, how everyone’s plot thickens, the controlled combat mechanics and class customization, and how Intelligent Systems rids us of the usually painful segments of the genre. Despite small flaws that sometimes reduce gaming fun, Fire Emblem Fortune’s Weave can unquestionably aim for a place in GOTY’s status at the end of the year and seduce a new audience just like the regulars to the license.
Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave takes the familiar Fire Emblem formula, enriches it with great ideas, and, above all, manages to create an adventure that really made us want to play nonstop.

Fortune’s Weave is massive in the best possible sense, balancing what fans love about the franchise while maintaining its own identity. Its well-written characters, intriguing campaign, unexpected twists, and connections to Fire Emblem: Three Houses make every decision feel meaningful, while branching paths, rewards, and losses add significant replay value. Exploring the Nabatean gods, their connection to Sothis and Three Houses, and developing the characters are especially rewarding. The game’s many mechanics also keep you engaged, constantly forcing strategic decisions both in battle and throughout the city and World Map. Ultimately, Fortune’s Weave is an immersive combination of strategy, storytelling, and meaningful choices. After years without giving a game a perfect score, I had no hesitation here: Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave deserves it.

Who loves Supports in Fire Emblem as much as I do and misses the more nuanced characters and connections of Three Houses might find Fortune's Weave somewhat lacking. But most of the time it is engrossing strategy fun that will make you wonder how the last few hours have vanished so quickly.

Beyond the sheer amount of story content, Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave also brings with it plenty of the series’ familiar mechanics, which are introduced gradually and have to be managed along the way. The restrictions imposed at the beginning of each of the four Flame Lords’ stories can make their respective openings feel somewhat sluggish, but they reward the player’s persistence once the game opens up again after a few chapters.

Fans of the series, and especially of Three Houses, should find plenty to enjoy here. Beginners, meanwhile, have the advantage of being given multiple opportunities to get to grips with the game’s many different mechanics, and can even use time travel to correct mistakes in individual chapters.

Those willing to push through the repetitions and the somewhat tedious management of relationships and training in the capital will find a solid Fire Emblem experience with plenty of potential playtime.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave successfully combines the strong character-driven storytelling of Three Houses with the excellent tactical combat of Engage. Its four-protagonist structure offers a refreshing way to experience the same world from different perspectives, while the vast map and varied battles provide plenty to explore. Some repetition, tedious recruitment requirements, and underdeveloped dungeons hold it back slightly, but the overall formula works remarkably well.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is the most ambitious entry in the series yet, and it could likely be the best at the same time. With an incredible amount of depth and excellent storytelling, this is yet another Nintendo gem not to miss.

«Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave» is a massive strategy epic with a gripping story, memorable characters, and a unique structure that keeps things fresh even after 100+ hours. Beautiful cutscenes, creative character designs, and a bombastic soundtrack round out an exceptional experience. It is, simply put, the best Switch 2 exclusive to date and one of the best games I've ever played.

I enjoyed every single one of the nearly 170 hours I spent with Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave. The countless times I cursed at my units missing a 99% hit chance while enemies land their 10% shots is just part of the Fire Emblem experience. 

I'm still eager to learn more about the history of Fortune's Weave's world. I can overlook the lack of a New Game+ and the single save slot available to players. Attentive fans have already noticed a mention of in-game purchases in the eShop, though nothing of the sort has been announced yet. We'll have to wait and see what the future holds for Fortune's Weave.

Fields of Mistria is everything I look for in a farming sim, combining a lively village, strong characters, satisfying progression, and an addictive gameplay loop. The 1.0 release builds beautifully on the already impressive early access version, with improved day length, better quality-of-life features, and more room for the story to grow. Minor issues like some post-update lag and a slightly underwhelming museum barely hold it back. For me, Fields of Mistria is one of the best farming sims right now, with gorgeous pixel art, memorable NPCs, and a world I’m far from done exploring.

Fields of Mistria is an exceptional farming game sim that stands tall among titles like Stardew Valley and the best Story of Seasons entries. It’s gorgeous. The gameplay loop is sharp. The characters are lovable. The sense of growth and progression is satisfying. Fields of Mistria is a fantastic way to spend 20, 50, or 100 hours of your life.

Fields of Mistria is a rare farming RPG that manages to improve upon the genre's familiar foundations without losing what made them so appealing in the first place. Its farming, RPG progression, relationships, exploration, and narrative all complement one another, creating an experience where nearly every activity contributes to the larger journey. A few rough edges in combat, resource RNG, and quality-of-life keep it from absolute perfection, but they do little to diminish an otherwise remarkably polished and thoughtfully designed experience. Fields of Mistria doesn't just prove that the genre still has room to grow, it sets an incredibly high bar for what a modern farming RPG can be.
It's a shojo anime fever dream with a level of character writing I didn't know I could find in a farm sim.

While it may seem like just another farming sim, I thoroughly enjoyed my time with Fields of Mistria. Fields of Mistria is in its early stages now, but I can’t wait to see what NPC Studio adds in the future.

The already great farming sim gameplay is uplifted by charming characters, the interactions you can have with them, and the magical town of Mistria itself, all of which come together wonderfully in Fields of Mistria's 1.0 release.

This is a cozy sim your friends have probably recommended at least once or twice while it was in early access. Now in 1.0, the developers have shown that they made the most of that time to create something great. There are no more excuses to be sleeping on Fields of Mistria, not anymore.

To Nintendo fans who haven’t experienced Kingdom Hearts in its full splendor, this is an incredible time to jump in. These games are largely excellent action RPGs that are jam-packed with an out-there emotional story filled with oodles of Disney and Square Enix references.

This new collection cements the Nintendo Switch 2’s reputation as a great console for third-party ports, with a impressive array of games that look and run spectacularly even in handheld mode, particularly the most visually stunning of them all, Kingdom Hearts III.

Kingdom Hearts Collection [I~III] is a massive compilation and, above all, a fantastic opportunity to experience the series natively on a Nintendo console. Kingdom Hearts Final Mix retains the charm of the original; Re of Memories offers a different experience with its card-based system; Kingdom Hearts II represents one of the high points of the classic formula; Birth by Sleep and Dream Drop Distance greatly expands the universe; and Kingdom Hearts III takes the whole concept to a much larger scale.

Overall, Kingdom Hearts Collection 1-3 on Switch 2 is a fantastic package that is so close to being completely on par with the Integrum Masterpiece release. Kingdom Hearts 3 and A Fragmentary Passage’s framerate issues are the only things stopping it from definitively being my new favourite way to play, but the ability to go portable is worth those minor issues. Whether you’re a complete newcomer preparing for Kingdom Hearts 4 or a diehard fan like me looking for an excuse to replay, Kingdom Hearts Collection 1-3 on Switch 2 is a fantastic way to do it.

KINGDOM HEARTS Collection [I~III] is an ambitious, emotionally resonant package that highlights the series’ remarkable highs, messy experiments, and constant reinvention. Its native Switch 2 release finally fixes one of the franchise’s biggest accessibility problems, while Critical Mode, Re Mind, and years of updates make Kingdom Hearts III far stronger than it was at launch. However, uneven world design, inconsistent combat systems across entries, performance hiccups on Switch 2, and the continued absence of playable 358/2 Days, Re:coded, Melody of Memory, and the full χ saga prevent this from feeling truly definitive.

Kingdom Hearts Collection [I~III] is an excellent way to experience most of the Kingdom Hearts franchise, whether for the first time or for the umpteenth. Most of the bundled games deliver essentially perfect performance on the Nintendo Switch 2, while the more recent games still maintain consistent enough frame rates to please most. Being able to play the entire franchise on the go is a thrilling prospect, and I’ll likely be doing so for a good long while to come. This is a great way to get ready for Kingdom Hearts IV, and I’m sure many Nintendo-exclusive fans will be doing just that with this top-notch bundle.

Kingdom Hearts Collection [I～III] is an incredible package that brings nearly the entire saga together in one place. I would have liked to see a performance and frame rate toggle for Kingdom Hearts III, and the $75 asking price is a little steep considering how cheap this collection is on other platforms. At the end of the day, though, it’s Kingdom Hearts finally on Switch 2, and it’s hard to ask for much more.
KINGDOM HEARTS Collection (I-III) gives owners of the Nintendo Switch 2 a fantastic collection of games that all run superbly on the hardware. It is finally here!

Kingdom Hearts Collection [I–III] is the definitive collection of the series, offering everything fans need to know to prepare for the fourth numbered entry. A highlight is the Switch 2 version, which finally allows console owners to run the games natively and with good performance.

The Kingdom Hearts Collection [1~3] is the definitive way to experience the saga, offering polished ports and nearly the entire lore on Nintendo Switch 2. Despite minor performance dips, it’s the best entry point for newcomers and a nostalgic return for veterans.
KINGDOM HEARTS Collection [I~III] is a wonderful bundle of everything Kingdom Hearts, and on the Switch 2 it's just perfection.

Look, the game collection is the best thing that Kingdom Hearts fans have been waiting for. It’s also the perfect start for new players who want to play through the entire storyline without the breaks the game had between productions. Kingdom Hearts is a very complex story, but like I said in the beginning of this review, even though it seems weird in the beginning, everything connects in a logical way. However, the whole story is an element that scares people off, and I do believe this has to be the collection to counter the fear because every chapter has been made better to make the game smoother, fill in the story gaps that some of the chapters couldn’t fill in, and make it more enjoyable. Yes, each chapter in Kingdom Hearts has some flaws, but these don’t take away the joy you’ll have when you’re playing. If you haven’t started the franchise, this is the best way to start it. Just in time for Kingdom Hearts 4. Take your time, organize breaks between the chapters, and enjoy every bit of it.

Nomura’s legacy rolls out the red carpet for Nintendo fans, with everything a native Switch 2 release entails: the unmatched appeal of handheld play, the inevitable performance and frame rate scrutiny, and the ultimate runway setting up Kingdom Hearts 4.

Kingdom Hearts Collection [I-III] is the perfect entry point for newcomers looking to dive into the franchise or veterans wanting a refresher ahead of the fourth mainline installment. It stands as a comprehensive compendium packed with countless hours of content and select visual upgrades, most notably seen in KH III.

Kingdom Hearts Collection I-III offers an excellent way to experience nearly the entire series on Nintendo Switch 2, delivering strong performance across most of its titles and the considerable appeal of playing these adventures in handheld mode. Although Kingdom Hearts III and Kingdom Hearts 0.2 suffer from some technical issues, the collection remains a fantastic package for both newcomers and longtime fans of the franchise.

KINGDOM HEARTS Collection [I～III] finally gives Nintendo players the version the series deserved. Native performance, solid visuals and true portable play make Switch 2 a great home for Sora's adventures, although Kingdom Hearts III has some technical compromises and the Game-Key Card physical release is disappointing.

Kingdom Hearts Collection [I~III] is a very good correction for a host of games that suffered from the initial cloud gaming incarnation. The Switch 2 has once again proven that it can handle games of this caliber without having to sacrifice a great deal, and while Nintendo-only fans will benefit the most from this package, those who mostly play on the go will also enjoy these quality ports. Unless you've already played these games to death or already own them in any of their various forms, this collection is well worth owning.

I am not one of those gamers who lives and dies with frame rates, as you can see from my previous reviews, so you won’t get much of that here. That being said, I did notice some stutter while playing KH3, but nothing that really ruined my experience and I thought it still played impressively well, both docked and handheld. Ideally, I will finally beat KH3 on this play through and hope to continue my collection when KH4 is released on the NS2. If you’ve never played anything from the Kingdom Hearts series and own a NS2 you should absolutely dip your toe into the KH water. Even if you don’t want to get the whole collection, the set is broken out into three separately available packs that break up the releases and make it a not so expensive initial investment. If you’re a diehard fan like myself and you’d like to have nearly all of the KH  games on one console, this is an absolute beast of a collection (but often on sale on Steam if you have that capability as well).

Kingdom Hearts Collection [I～III] is the best way to play the whole saga, in order. The classics show their age and Kingdom Hearts III hovers between 40 and 50 FPS, but Switch 2 still runs the collection well.

This new collection, featuring ten titles, allows us to enjoy the stories of Sora and company leading up to the great adventure they will embark on in the next game. We get to experience almost all of the spin-offs and have a complete overview of what is happening in the world of Kingdom Hearts. These are the best editions available today, and having everything in a single package at a reasonable price makes it one of the best ways to experience the series anywhere.

Kingdom Hearts Collection [I～III] is a largely solid port of pretty much the entire Kingdom Hearts series. The Switch 2 versions of every classic game are largely flawless, barring a strange input latency issue in the first game, while the modern games are a little more mixed in their performance. Despite these issues, the collection as a whole remains one of the best action RPG series in video game history, and will remain a permanent mainstay on my Switch 2’s storage for years to come.

There are tons of reviews of the individual games out there, but the fact that the series is as big as it is says as much as any review probably could. If you have somehow missed out on Kingdom Hearts so far and want to catch up all at once, here you go. It’s tremendous bang for your gaming buck, but be aware that once you get to the later entries in this Nintendo Switch 2 version that you’re going to run into some performance issues. If you’re willing to make that sacrifice to have these games on Switch 2, you won’t be unhappy with what you get here.

While this collection doesn't offer anything new or meaningful upgrades, it's a great place to start for newcomers. It also makes the whole Dark Seeker Saga natively playable on the Nintendo Switch 2, where the games feel at home thanks to handheld play.

Restored Land has transformed Dying Light: The Beast from a very good
game into an even better one. The issues I complained about after launch
have been fixed, and the addition of survival mode offers a great
opportunity to revisit Castor Woods.

A re-release or soft reboot of the latest zombie slasher from Techland is better and more challenging than before, with a new persistent survival mode, new roadkill races and more. The best part: it's a free upgrade.

All in all, Restored Land is a bit of a hit and a miss. But it’s a free update, the biggest Techland has ever done, and arrived a little over half a year after launch. For anybody who plays Dying Light solo and hasn’t played The Beast before, Restored Land would be a great way to experience the story and campaign for the first time. But anybody that’s already gone through Kyle’s vendetta with the Baron before will have to do so all over again.
A more complete version of an already strong game, with enough changes to make it worth coming back to. A no-brainer for survival horror fans.

Dying Light: The Beast Restored Land continues Techland’s tradition of meaningful post-launch content and support for its games. Here, players can tackle Castor Woods with a new hardcore, solo survival mode along with a slew of updates for the base game. Taking advantage of Dying Light‘s signature parkour movement and crunchy combat, Restored Land is a fantastic vehicle to dive into Dying Light: The Beast no matter your experience with the franchise.

Enshrouded is an exemplary entry into its genre, seamlessly combining survival crafting mechanics with ARPG exploration and progression and, in my humble opinion, delivering the best of both. While you can absolutely play the game solo, it’s even more fun with friends, scaling the adventure to your group rather than becoming too easy or outright demanding the extra hands on deck as some other survival-crafting titles do.
With its amazing game world and a building system on par with Minecraft, Enshrouded has joined the elite ranks of the survival genre. On top of that, it has plenty to offer fans of action RPGs.

Enshrouded has evolved into one of the most impressive survival games on PC. Its atmospheric open world, rewarding exploration and incredibly versatile voxel-based building system offer hundreds of hours of entertainment. The sheer freedom, variety and attention to detail make Enshrouded an outstanding survival sandbox.
Enshrouded has benefited immensely from two years in Early Access, emerging as one of the best survival crafting games in the business.

Over the years, Enshrouded has had plenty of new content added, and the 1.0 release has turned out even bigger and better than anyone would have expected. Whether you play it alone or in multiplayer, or unlock the Sparkworks system and design your own dungeons and other challenges to share with the world, there are a decent number of social options available to keep the game lively. Enshrouded is a phenomenal achievement in survival RPGs, and one not to be missed.

Enshrouded 1.0 is an adventure you won't forget. It has come an incredible distance over the past few years, grown considerably, and, most importantly, refined practically every one of its systems. It stands confidently on its own as both an action RPG and a survival game, combining the two into an entertaining mix. It works equally well solo or in a group, offering hundreds of hours of fun either way. Don your armor, prepare your glider, and plunge into the depths of the Shroud, because a fantasy apocalypse has rarely felt so magical.
The fog of war clears around Embervale, revealing a survival crafting masterpiece.
The survival hit matured into a full game bursting with fun — only story purists might still resist its call.

Enshrouded is a good example of the evolution of modern survival games. It places the exploration and player freedom front and centre and puts survival and repetition into the background. The game understands that what many people want is to explore and shape the world and not work a second job. This makes "Enshrouded" one of the best games in the survival genres for fans of Action RPGs and even solo players, while fans of more traditional titles will still find plenty to love and dig into here.

Without reinventing the survival game formula, Enshrouded stands out as the most memorable title in the genre for us, despite fierce competition. It is beautiful, open, and rich, offering a variety of content to explore either solo or with friends. While the combat still lacks a bit of depth and the voxel-based world shows its limitations, the possibilities offered by the building—and destruction—systems more than make up for it. This makes it the perfect title for RPG fans looking to try out a different genre without feeling too far out of their element.

Become a hero who saves a lost civilization and battles a deadly fog. Or focus on architecture and construct unique buildings. The choice is yours. The game doesn't force you into anything, allowing you to enjoy its possibilities and its captivating open world.

More than two years after its Early Access release, Enshrouded 1.0 delivers on everything that was originally promised with flying colours. The result is a survival title which, albeit not quite perfect, rivals other stalwarts of the genre.

Enshrouded is a well-crafted survival action RPG that’s great to play both solo and with friends. Exploration lets you gather resources, which you use to upgrade your gear, allowing you to open up new paths and improve your base, which grows a little larger after each adventure. Even the beauty of the landscape contributes to the success of this cycle, encouraging us to stray from the planned path to discover what lies hidden elsewhere. Of course, there’s still room for improvement. Resource management could be less fragmented, the graphics are sometimes inconsistent, and some boss fights could use more polish. These aspects, however, only partially affect the overall enjoyment. In the end, what remains above all is the feeling that you always have a good reason to explore. Another dungeon, a new region, and maybe gathering one last resource for the workbench. And when the day draws to a close in Embervale, you often find yourself already atop a cliff, admiring a magnificent landscape, ready to take flight toward the sun.

The full release of Enshrouded delivers a fairly impressive experience for players who have waited over two years. If you love freely shaping landscapes and constructing grand buildings but have grown tired of the lack of clear goals in traditional survival crafting games, or if you want a fantasy open world with a proper main storyline and deep build customization without sacrificing the freedom to reshape the world and build your own base, Enshrouded offers the best of both worlds.

While some elements of Enshrouded are genuinely impressive – like its hand-crafted world – the way progression is structured, favoring rushing to the hardest biome you can get to and grinding its respawning chests rather than gradually climbing in power as you reach a new biome, ends up doing the game more harm than good.
Almost three years after its early access debut, Enshrouded steps out into glorious 1.0. The building mechanics are still best in class, the combat's improved, and the world is wonderful to explore.

Like a flame burning bright against an encroaching mist, Enshrouded shines resplendent despite its flaws. Through the sheer vastness of its scale and the utter complexity of its systems, it captures the hearts and minds of the adventurous and ambitious. Through its epic retelling of Embervale’s rise and fall, though scattered, it entrances the curious. It is truly an epic of epic proportions that doesn’t maintain its quality evenly throughout its monumental run—forgetting its main mechanic at times and punishing solo players just for existing—but it is nonetheless so huge an adventure that one can’t help but remember it.
Exciting survival exploration with a slew of Early Access kinks to work out.

Enshrouded is my favourite of the recent raft of survival games. It's distinctly unique, what with the Shroud occupying parts huge parts of the map, and the insane building potential is excellent, arguably making it the best survival game of the year.

Enshrouded has been a fantastic experience despite crossplay not being active yet. Enshrouded showcases an excellent fusion of survival elements and creativity, establishing itself as a notable title in the action role-playing game scene. While players eagerly await the full launch, the early access version already provides a significant glimpse into the game’s potential.

Enshrouded is a game that gave me a bit of a rough first impression but fairly quickly charmed me with its clever adventuring and fun decision-making for your character's build. The more I spent with it, the more I wanted to go back and continue my journey in the Embervale.

A few words aren’t enough to describe the experience of Queen’s Domain—in fact, even four times as many wouldn’t suffice. You simply have to launch the game and play it. Setting aside its retro visuals, this title stands as one of the best RPG-adventure experiences out there. It’s brutal in its approach—offering no map or guidance, and featuring truly formidable enemies—but once you find your rhythm within its gameplay design—blending a Metroidvania sensibility with deep, secret-filled exploration—you’ll find yourself immersed in an extraordinary gaming experience.
An adventure of unusual depth, Queen’s Domain is a classic RPG in more ways than one and delivers an exploration game that is unmatched in either past and present.

Queen's Domain is something special, and of all the King's Field inspired RPGs in recent memory it clearly establishes itself as the best in its class. If you're willing to play to its rules, Queen's Domain isn't just one of the best RPGs of the year, but a genuine must play.
An unforgiving reminder that it can feel really good to get lost, die repeatedly and be humbled.

Queen’s Domain feels like a rich and bountiful flavor we haven’t had in a good, long while. As much as it leans into the classic styles that inspired it, it doesn’t forget to be compelling and satisfying for much of its 30+ hour runtime. It keeps some annoyances of those classic games that I’d rather it went without and isn’t shy about reusing enemy types deep into the adventure, but the discovery of any new weapon, the dives into rich and vast biomes, and the never-ending surprises along the way make this an incredibly satisfying single-player RPG. I came for the King’s Field vibes, but I stayed well past the initial novelty for the grand adventure that is Queen’s Domain.

Queen’s Domain is a curious paradox: it feels old, yet manages to be new. It draws upon King’s Field—recalling the freedom found in early 3D RPGs—incorporates influences from The Elder Scrolls, and adopts a PS1-era aesthetic to craft something that very few developers today would have the courage to present without making compromises. It doesn’t constantly hold the player’s hand, it doesn’t point out every secret, and it doesn’t demand that everything be discovered. It simply presents a world and invites the player to step inside. In the—by now almost surreal—wait for the next great journey from Bethesda, it’s hard not to realize that an experience like this was right there, in plain sight all along.

Queen’s Domain is a King’s Field-inspired Souls-like first-person action-combat RPG developed by Freshly Baked Games LLC (love the logo). Leaning heavily into a retro art style from the ’90s—which hurts terribly to label as retro—it’s a brilliant indie release that might only be limited by how well it pays homage rather than carving its own path.

Queen’s Domain will knock you around, but its wonderfully strange island and flying sword make it hard to remain resentful. The slow fights and aimless wandering can wear thin, so bring plenty of patience and remember to save early and save often.

Over the roughly thirty hours spent in its company, it must be admitted that Queen’s Domain managed to deliver some truly striking moments of exploration. Thanks to a level design that puts many games costing four times as much to shame—along with hundreds of secrets that are often a delight to uncover—this title from Freshly Baked Games is a diamond in the rough, whose true brilliance will only be revealed to the most persistent players. It is a game that is far from perfect, yet, oh, how satisfying it proves to be.

Getting lost is part of the fun in Queen’s Domain, where a wrong turn can lead to a hidden area or a new shortcut. But frequent enemy respawns and manual-only saves make backtracking tedious, and with so little guidance, seeing every ending takes a lot of patience.

Freshly Baked Games has released what could be one of the quintessential old-school action RPG’s of the last decade. And while it may not be everyone’s cup of tea and it could use some more accessibility options, the game as a whole is incredibly impressive. Once I gelled with the way it wanted me to play, Queen’s Domain became a title I could not stop thinking about. If you’ve wanted to venture back into the adventure games of 90s PC gaming and you have the drive to hack and slash your way through some very difficult fights, this is a solid choice that stands out among a crowded 2026 release schedule.

Queen's Domain captures the magic of classic action RPGs like King's Field, offering an unforgettable adventure built around exploration, discovery, and player freedom. Its atmospheric world, rewarding secrets, and creative traversal make getting lost part of the fun, but cryptic progression, easily missed items, and tedious combat occasionally undermine an otherwise excellent experience.

More than just a tribute to an important piece of FromSoftware’s history, Queen’s Domain is an action RPG that is as fun to explore as it is to master. In short, for those who enjoy getting lost just as much as they enjoy finding their way in fantasy worlds, the Switch 2 has gained a unique gem that is well worth checking out.

Queen's Domain is one of the best surprises of the year, coming out of nowhere and asserting itself as one of the most satisfying action-adventure games in recent memory.The rewarding character progression, challenging combat, lo-fi visuals, and thrilling sense of mystery all combine to make this one an easy recommendation to anyone looking for that old-school FromSoft style that recaptures the magic of playing older Zeldas and doesn't hold your hand. It'll likely win you over if you give it a fair shot.
Queen's Domain is the latest attempt to recapture and revitalize FromSoftware's early formula for a modern audience

Queen's Domain uses its seemingly obtuse nature to lure players into an intricate world of discovery. Though firmly rooted in the past, its sense of freedom is expressly modern and rewards player curiosity and intelligence.
Excellent old-school-inspired first-person fantasy action RPG set on the Isle of Neasied
The game may not be for everyone, yet if you are down to dip into classic hardcore adventure, you will be amazed by how brilliant Queen's Domain is.

Queen's Domain is an indie masterpiece and a remarkable feat for a two-person studio. Everytime I thought I had done everything, some new path would open. This world is impossibly dense and endlessly compelling. If challenging and somewhat esoteric action RPGs appeal to you, Queen's Domain will likely be one of the best you've played in a long time.

Queen’s Domain has won me over with its exploration, fantastic level design, and the sheer number of secrets it hides. Queen’s Domain has been one of the biggest surprises of the year for me. It had been a long time since a game had managed to bring back that sense of adventure and exploration, that urge to look beyond the main path to see if something worth discovering was hidden there.
You can tell this two-person dev team poured their hearts and souls into Queen’s Domain. This indie gem is so impressive it can easily be deemed as the spiritual successor to King’s Field.

Queen’s Domain showcases how a good level design can elevate an RPG to heights I rarely see it nowadays. Pair it with good combat, unique mechanics and a world filled with secrets begging to be found and you have an instant classic on your hands. By far one of the best RPGs I played in 2026.

Queen’s Domain is one of those games that reminds us that you don’t need a lot of bells and whistles to deliver an entertaining and challenging adventure.
Queen's Domain doesn't just honor the classics that inspired it, it surpasses them with challenging combat, rich exploration, and unforgettable adventure.

Queen's Domain is a slow, atmospheric, King's Field-style adventure with great exploration and a harsh save system. Patient fans of retro RPGs will love it; players wanting speed or checkpoints may struggle.

Queen’s Domain is a truly excellent and entertaining retro-style RPG, with very few flaws and many strengths.

Its combination of deep stat customisation, high-stakes combat, and rewarding exploration makes it one of the most charmingly punishing indie titles you can pick up on PC. This game clicked with me in every way, and I could not put it down.

People have called Welcome to Elderfield the spiritual successor to Graveyard Keeper, but I think it deserves the accolade of being called the spiritual dark successor to Stardew Valley. Stardew Valley is considered the gold standard for narrative-driven farming sims, and in my opinion, Welcome to Elderfield has shown that it has what it takes to stand alongside the greats.

Welcome to Elderfield surprised me as a delightfully spooky, terror-filled take on the cozy farming sim genre. Depicting small-town life as full of unexplainable phenomena and horrors that become the mundane, Welcome to Elderfield easily shines as one of the most unique titles in its genre, while still delivering the familiar mechanics and gameplay loops that fans have come to expect.

Welcome to Elderfield draws you in with its slimy tentacles and grim aesthetic, but it is the challenging gameplay that truly keeps you hooked. Chris Cote masterfully combines humor, horror and tranquility, creating an experience that feels both relaxing and deeply unsettling. Elderfield may be impossible to leave, but after playing it, I wouldn't want to anyway.

The secrets of the town, its residents, its mysteries, and its atmosphere are meticulously crafted. Welcome to Elderfield succeeds at making horror and cozy farming-sim comfort coexist without either one undercutting the other. Its art direction is distinctive, its atmosphere is relentless in the best way, and its willingness to treat the abnormal as mundane gives it a personality unlike anything else currently in the genre. Some rough progression clarity and a few lingering bugs are the price of its ambition, but they’re minor blemishes on what is otherwise one of the most confident and original debuts of the year. If you’ve ever wanted your farming sim to also make your skin crawl, Welcome to Elderfield delivers that in spades.

It is very hard to stand out in video games as a whole, let alone in the farming sim genre. Welcome to Elderfield takes the main gameplay loop of the genre, dips it in grimdark horror, adds a dash of excellent sound and aesthetics, and the result is something that feels truly impressive.

Welcome to Elderfield from developer Chris Cote and publisher Kwalee is a horror-filled cozy game that offers plenty of questing content, a well-designed farming and crafting system, and features just enough turn-based combat to deliver a cornucopia of fun. While it has a few minor, correctable issues, it’s an enjoyable overall gameplay experience.

Welcome to Elderfield is a game worthy of the Lovecraftian title. It makes the mythos feel like a dark fairytale that you can take part in, and the weirdness of the whole experience is brilliant. Every little task feels rewarding because you get information, items, or access to resources. I put hours into this game, and I still don't know how I'm supposed to feel about it. If you're like me and enjoy both horror games and cozy games, then you definitely need to give it a try.

Welcome to Elderfield is impressive due to how many layers it contains. From the weeks I have spent with the game, I am still nowhere near uncovering all its secrets. The way that it juxtaposes wholesome activities, such as fishing and farming, with creepy elements and humour shows how much time solo developer Chris Cote has put into making Elderfield feel as alive as possible. Though some elements of the game need to be better explained, and some extra support may be needed due to the size of the playable spaces, the positives, such as how expansive the town and its secrets are, the dialogue and the creepy/cute aesthetics, make up for the confusion I experienced. Though I have written this review, I know my time with Welcome to Elderfield isn’t over yet. There is still a lot of world for me to be creeped out by…

Welcome to Elderfield is a game that proudly celebrates the things that inspired it. From its sense of exploration to its visual design and subtle storytelling, it’s clear that it was created by people who genuinely love this kind of thing. If you’re a fan of the mysterious and supernatural, this town will feel like your second home.
The words horror and cosy really shouldn’t go together and they absolutely shouldn’t work, but in Welcome to Elderfield they somehow find a horrifyingly happy medium.

Welcome to Elderfield will be an interesting case for fans of the genre who flocked to its revival with Stardew Valley. What the hell is cozy? Much of the enemy art has clear inspirations from Junji Ito. The sheer density of the town’s supernatural happenings and resignation also feel akin. However, it never feels as hopeless or helpless as Ito’s most famous works. Welcome to Elderfield is a game where you can summon the unearthly and smash it with a big hammer.

This is more of a cursed life sim than a cozy one, to be sure. You’re in constant danger, making progress is a nasty grind, and the vibes are utterly rancid. But every victory is a sweet one. The life you build here is hard-fought and well-earned. The people you meet look like the scribblings of a deranged inmate, but they’re part of the mystery and charm of this place. If you can stomach it, Welcome to Elderfield is an endearing escape from the normal world we’re all forever trapped in. I couldn’t get out of there fast enough, but who knows? Maybe you, like the other denizens, will never leave once you arrive.

Welcome to Elderfield looks like a farming game, but it isn’t. Or at least, not entirely. The farm is, of course, important, but no more so than combat, exploration or interacting with the world. They are the four legs of a terrifying table that will attack you when you go to sleep. But four legs that carry an equal weight, after all. None of them is any bigger than the others.

Welcome to Elderfield is best understood as a horror RPG wearing the clothes of a farming game. If you approach it expecting only a peaceful place to plant crops and decorate a farm, the darker systems may surprise you. But if a bit of danger and mystery thrown into your routine sounds appealing, the combination of cozy activities mixed with unsettling discoveries gives Welcome to Elderfield an identity of its own.
Welcome to Elderfield blends cozy farming with creeping horror, offering constant surprises even as late‑game grind and flat character reactions and romance hold it back.
Welcome to Elderfield, which blends cozy farming with dice-driven RPG combat and Lovecraftian dread into an addictive, uneven mix; thin on romance, but endlessly worth exploring.

Welcome to Elderfield is an addictive (and unsettling) experience that successfully marries the satisfaction of farming with the tension of cosmic horror. It’s a ton of fun to play – especially with its satisfying blend of farming and turn-based combat – whilst the eerie (and sometimes grotesque) world really helps give it a unique vibe that really, REALLY appealed to me.

If you’re looking for a release in the farming sim genre that does something genuinely different and like the idea of marrying a skeleton, Welcome to Elderfield is a must-play.

Welcome to Elderfield, where horror fans and farming sim enthusiasts will feel right at home. A wide range of activities and friendly locals await you, along with terrifying monsters and dangerous places that few dare to venture into.

Welcome to Elderfield’s greatest strength is the way it blends the ordinary with the unsettling. Its farming, strange characters, eerie atmosphere, and mystery work well together, even if the language barrier and RNG-heavy combat can get in the way.
