For fans of Japanese RPGs, the changes and trade offs in Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection are largely welcome. Its combat and progression systems offer impressive depth and strategy, making the moment you finally overcome a powerful enemy feel especially rewarding. At the same time, its fairly straightforward story and solid world exploration keep the experience relaxed and enjoyable as you go about stealing eggs and completing quests.

Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection feels just like a turn-based Monster Hunter game. For the first time in the Stories series, they’ve nailed the feeling of every fight feeling like a boss battle.

It is hard to shake the feeling that Monster Hunter Stories 3 is going to slip under the radar, and that would be a real shame. This is not merely a charming sidestep for Monster Hunter fans. It is a confident, ambitious JRPG in its own right, with strong storytelling, smart systems, and a clear identity. For the first time, the spinoff feels every bit as essential as the main series.
Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection is definitely the most ambitious, prettiest and most mature instalment in the series, which finally rises above the label of a ‘small spin-off’.

Overall, Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection is best described as a refined and improved Monster Hunter Stories 2. It doesn't really change the core concept, but pretty much every change in the game is for the better. The new story is easier to engage with, the combat system is more fun than ever, and in general, it's a great leap forward without losing anything that made the previous games fun. Only some minor frame rate issues drag down the Switch 2 experience, and they're not enough to sour an otherwise fantastic game.

The story wound up being a highlight, but even the streamlining of monster dens couldn't solve the heavy-handedness of monster collection and enhancement. If you want to painstakingly tweak the dials on habitats and splice monster genes while dealing with an acquired taste of a combat system, you'll find a better time than I did in this game. Maybe at the end of the day, the twisted reflection was a metaphor for the entire game.

Monster Hunter Stories 3 Twisted Reflection deserves to be studied as a benchmark for how to craft a spin-off. It fully embraces the DNA of the traditional experience while confidently iterating on its formula with creativity to make a sick JRPG first and a great MH experience second

Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection captivates players with its powerful story and charismatic characters. The combat is taken to the next level with a complexity that moves away from the simplicity of the first two installments, offering many possible options and strategies. At the same time, its changing and explorable world allows us to exploit all possible tools to get the Monstie of our dreams. The result? A new installment that improves on its predecessors in every way and can be enjoyed like an anime once you get the hang of its combat.

Third time’s the charm. Building on the best parts of its identity, Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection is ambition done right, blowing expectations out of the water and showing that, sometimes, fortune favours the bold.

The only time I didn’t have much fun was towards the end trying to get a particular gene to spawn so that I could get past the final boss. The many systems of the game feel rewarding and the combat is super enjoyable once you get a handle on it and there are plenty of ways to extend your run time if you so choose.
For fans of Monster Hunter and JRPGs in general, Twisted Reflection represents the highest point Capcom's spin-off has reached so far.

Monster Hunter Stories 3 is a masterpiece that redefines the modern JRPG. Capcom has masterfully combined a deep strategic combat system, fascinating digital wildlife and its rich ecosystem, and heartfelt personal stories that truly resonate with players. It is a game that honors its roots while boldly innovating where the genre needs it most.

y the time the credits rolled on Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection, I was genuinely surprised by just how ambitious the game turned out to be. The series has always had a strong foundation, but this entry finally realises its full potential.

Twisted Reflection reaches the series' definitive form: a perfect balance of exploration, strategy, and collecting that keeps you hooked for dozens of hours without ever wearing thin. Simply extraordinary.
Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection is a deep, intricately crafted, and beautifully rendered game that stands as the series’ highlight in terms of story.

I feel like this was less of a review and more of an ”I love Monster Hunter Stories“ declaration, but somehow, Capcom managed to take what was already a brilliant game series and elevate it in a way I didn’t think was possible. The nuance of the story, the environmental elements and the new monster types could teach people in our world a lot. If you played two and enjoyed it, then you need to play Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection.
A rich and strategic JRPG that turns Monster Hunter’s creature-driven world into a thoughtful adventure about history, identity, and reconciliation.
Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection successfully builds on proven JRPG foundations, combining an approachable yet satisfying level of complexity with a memorable genre experience.

Although I have been a Monster Hunter fan from day one, my exposure to the Stories series had been sporadic—until now. That is about to change, for with Twisted Reflection, the spin-off reaches a level of quality that is simply impressive. Whether it’s the consistently cohesive — and at times bombastic — presentation, the characters bursting with heart, the gripping storyline, or the deep progression system — it all comes together beautifully. Add to this the combat and crafting systems, which wonderfully translate the core Monster Hunter feel into a turn-based RPG format. All of this is delivered on a scale vast enough to keep you glued to your screen for months on end. 

While you have to look hard to find its flaws, they do exist. In particular, if you have an aversion to grinding, the final 5% of the story can become a true test of patience. Furthermore, many side quests are absolutely tedious, and the dialogue can sometimes be unnecessarily long-winded. However, since these elements can largely be ignored or skipped, I am more than willing to overlook this minor shortcoming. For these reasons, I can wholeheartedly recommend Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection to any JRPG enthusiast —and especially to fellow Monster Hunter
 fans.
Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection is undoubtedly the best chapter in the series. It introduces interesting ideas and offers an addictive gameplay loop, despite some imperfections.

Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection marks an unmistakable turning point for Capcom’s spin-off series, which, with this third installment, sheds its status as a minor title to establish itself as a standalone experience of the highest caliber. The cycle of exploration, gathering, and upgrading has been refined to achieve an almost flawless balance, capable of keeping players engaged for dozens and dozens of hours without ever feeling repetitive. A few narrative missteps do not prevent this title from establishing itself as one of the best turn-based RPGs of recent years and, without a doubt, as the best installment ever released in the Stories saga.

Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection is everything I’d hoped for in a follow-up to the second game, so seeing it realized so well is nothing short of fantastic. With excellent characters, a decent story, an enjoyable gameplay loop with as much grinding as you want there to be, and a really gorgeous appearance and world, it’s a genuine must play for fans of turn-based RPGs.

Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection is a spectacular evolution of the series, delivering a surprisingly mature story, excellent exploration systems and deep monstie customization. Capcom once again proves it is at the top of its game with one of the strongest JRPGs of the year.

In total, it took me almost 66 hours to get through the credits once. It could certainly be done a bit faster, since I occasionally let myself get sidetracked by fighting monsters I wasn't quite ready for yet, or by grinding levels.

Most of the time, though, when I reached a new area, I ignored the story quest marker for the time being and explored the new area.

Monster Hunter Stories 3 delivers an exceptional RPG experience that combines a deep story with a stunning anime-inspired art direction, highlighting the beauty of its monsters and environments. Its gameplay is built around enjoyable tactical combat, searching for monsters and rare eggs, and crafting powerful gear from materials discovered throughout the world. Therefore, fans of the series should absolutely play it and not miss this complete experience, especially with the game’s great Arabic localization.

Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection, with its original mechanics of breeding, combat, and exploration, makes it one of the most complete JRPGs. It’s a shame that technical issues on PC prevent it from reaching perfection.

Monster Hunter Stories 3 represents a significant evolution for the spin-off series, as Capcom has successfully integrated an epic narrative with a deep strategic combat system that transcends basic mechanics. The game offers expansive content that satisfies long-time enthusiasts with the inclusion of monsters such as Lagiacrus and Archfield, while simultaneously attracting newcomers with its enchanting visual style and the innovative 'Habitat Restoration' system, which adds value to every creature collected. It is a comprehensive role-playing experience that masterfully balances strategic planning with the joy of exploration. In short, for fans of the franchise or those interested in it, the game provides a unique character that stands apart from the traditional formula we have come to know and cherish.

Ultimately, Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection marks a significant evolution for the series, which has grown in maturity and depth, though at the cost of being slightly less accessible than before. Driven by a more engaging narrative, a rich gameplay system, and particularly polished art direction, the game manages to stand out as much more than just a simple spin-off. This increase in complexity, combined with some occasionally abrupt spikes in difficulty, may, however, surprise—or even discourage—players less familiar with its mechanics. Despite this, the game remains solid and highly satisfying over the long haul. For me, it is undoubtedly the most accomplished entry in the franchise to date.

As a newcomer to the Monster Hunter Stories series I was absolutely delighted to have enjoyed my time as much as I did. Comparing this to Pokémon isn’t even right. This is what I’ve always wanted Pokémon to be, a deeper RPG with an important story that was a bit more mature in theme. I absolutely loved my time with Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection and there is even more I can go back and do with the ecosystem gameplay. I’m happy I finally decided to give this a chance, because in some way I almost prefer this over the regular Monster Hunter series.
Meanwhile, the Monster Hunter Stories series can place itself neatly next to its bigger brother with Twisted Reflection and manages to deliver a beautiful story with in-depth gameplay.

Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection represents the culmination of a remarkable journey that few would have predicted when it began nearly a decade ago. Capcom has pulled off yet another feat in a gaming generation worth celebrating, elevating a spin-off series born from a successful IP to the very pinnacle of excellence. A sumptuous JRPG, as mature in its storytelling as it is layered and satisfying in its gameplay, it’s already a contender for one of the best games of 2026. We don’t know what the future holds for this series, but one thing is certain: missing out on this adventure would be a mistake as big as a Rathalos.

Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection is a good game that I’m ultimately left conflicted on. While it’s the biggest, most polished, and most mechanically thoughtful a Stories title has ever been, it’s also at the cost of what I feel was the series’ unique personality. While the series has been aging with its audience ever since the previous game, Stories 2 struck a much more resonant emotional balance, embracing something more somber and thoughtful while still respecting the oftentimes silly and satirical nature of the original Stories game. Stories 3, in its push to appear as more grown up, abandons a lot of that in favor of an okay but more generic narrative that doesn’t manage to leverage what makes the Monster Hunter series tonally unique.

On the gameplay side of things, Stories 3 is broadly a success. Changes to combat keep its simplicity, while the more punishing boss battles still push it towards being something where you really have to think more than before. It’s also perhaps the most beautiful Monster Hunter game ever made, with tasteful watercolor visuals applied to superb modeling and animations. There is plenty of good here, despite my prior complaints. That said, Stories 3 only feels like half a victory, where it has its own accomplishments but feels dragged down by some of the same things currently plaguing the mainline games. It doesn’t feel finished, performance is wonky, and despite the want for a more involved narrative, in the end it misplaces what made Monster Hunter really work in the first place.

MHS3 is a great game for anyone who wants a slightly chill version of Monster Hunter after the nice teleporting Rathalos. Sure it’s a single player experience, but know that it’s a cozy more laid back version of Monster Hunter. I honestly felt like I was doing the world a favor with not only bringing back extinct creatures. But assisting with creating new combos or creatures with some pretty useful skills. It helped a lot with certain invasive monsties which get more difficult with each species.

I give Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection the Thumb Culture Platinum Award

Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection seamlessly blends Monster Hunter's classic combat systems with traditional turn-based RPG mechanics, complemented by a compelling story and an exploration system that encourages players to scour every corner of the world, making Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection the definitive RPG entry in the franchise.
Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection builds on what came before - a more mature, mechanically satisfying and emotionally engaging adventure.

Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection feels like it prioritizes story, characters, and combat in a way that makes the game feel even more like a JRPG. Switch 2 version reviewed. Review copy provided by company for testing purposes.

Capcom, as it turns out, hasn’t lost its knack for making great RPGs featuring dragons and/or dragon-like creatures. If you liked the previous games in the series, this is an easy recommendation. Those new to the franchise just looking for their next RPG fix might as well jump in here, as you don’t really need any prior experience to have a good time with this.

Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection is the pinnacle of a good story within a ‘catch monster’ game that explains and gives meaning to the ‘breed’ mechanics and truly makes the whole world come alive. Fun, well localized, providing many hours of gameplay with a lot of agility and possibilities, it is undoubtedly the best game of the genre so far! If you don’t know the others, you can start with this one; if you already know them, don’t let this one pass!

I’d say that Monster Hunter Stories 3 Twisted Reflection perfectly captures the magic of blending two beloved concepts into one cohesive whole. It delivers the thrill of Monster Hunter’s iconic creatures alongside the charm and strategic depth of a monster-collecting RPG. Thanks to this you get a game that feels both nostalgic and refreshingly new. For me personally, this is easily the best entry in the Stories series to date and It’s the kind of game that reminds me why I fell in love with Monster Hunter in the first place.

Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection was an incredible experience from start to finish. Its technical highs soar well above its predecessor, with few issues or gripes to address. That said, the series' online play has been a staple across the previous two games, so it does feel quite a strange choice to remove it entirely. Regardless, this is a must-play adventure, with stunning cinematic story beats, the engaging habitat system, and a collection of monsties so massive that you’ll never run out of moments to gush over.

With a resonant story, incredible visuals, deeply satisfying combat and monster nurturing systems, Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twister Reflections delivers the goods, and it’s a must for everyone yearning to scratch that monster collecting itch.

Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection, folks, really surprised me. I admit I approached it with some caution, given that it's a spin-off of an action saga, but the final result pleased me greatly and easily captivated me.

If you want a parallel experience to Monster Hunter, with monster-tamer mechanics, a bit of the tension of being approached by a monster you're afraid will see you, or just want a satisfying turn-based combat with lots of strategy, play Monster Hunter Stories 3.
Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection delivers a darker tale, stronger characters, and engaging combat, offering a gorgeous and rewarding evolution of the spin‑off series

Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection is an undeniably fun and instantly addictive turn-based title based on the world of Monster Hunter. This title follows a unique storyline with the ability to raise dragons and restore the natural balance of their presence in the entire world. The open world gives a lot of opportunities to be lost for hours exploring, but the story is well delivered to keep you hooked until the end
A Capcom conseguiu uma forte evolução sobre os anteriores, que estão a anos luz do que aqui é feito. O combate ficou di…

Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection successfully balances a brilliant and engaging narrative with an addictive, creature-collecting gameplay loop that is incredibly hard to put down. The combat finally packs a proper punch and demands real tactical thinking and adaptability in order to survive, while the deep DNA channeling and new Habitat Restoration systems ensure you will be happily tweaking your perfect team of Monsties for hours on end. It’s just really, REALLY good. 

Add to that the gorgeous visuals, flawless performance, and a tantalising world to explore, and you’ll quickly see that Capcom has delivered a turn-based masterclass in the monster-taming genre that feels like more than just a Monster Hunter spin-off. If you’re a turn-based RPG fan, you won’t want to miss out on this.

Monster Hunter Stories 3 feels like a prematurely released game that could have been truly great. It’s got everything from the series’ signature monster collecting mechanics, the gritty turn-based combat, and much, much better audiovisuals than its predecessors. Unfortunately, beyond the bloat of grinding for stronger monsters and watching filler, there’s not much content to actually engage in.
Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection delivers a near-perfect monster-collecting and combat experience.
Quote not yet available

Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection refines the series' formula by offering more Monsties, a slightly larger world, and combat that remains as accessible as it is strategic. It doesn't take too many risks, but what it does, it does very well. If you enjoyed Stories 2, this is a very solid sequel.
Quote not yet available
Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection is the most ambitious entry in the sub-series to date.

The world of Monster Hunter is best known for big battles against gigantic monsters and collecting materials. However, the Stories series has been taking a different approach for years. Instead of pure action, the emphasis here is more on a story-driven RPG, in which you collect monsters, work with them and experience a great adventure. Developer Capcom continues this with Monster Hunter Stories 3 - Twisted Reflection. The result is a game that clearly builds on previous parts: colorful, accessible and full of familiar elements for fans. At the same time, the game also tries to bring enough novelty to draw players back into the world.

“Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection” is a game about connections. Yourself with nature, to the ones you love and matter to you, extending your hand to the ones in need and forming a bond. Saving endangered species, restoring once fractured or severed ones. Does it always hit the spot? As I stated multiple times above, no. But at the end of the day, it does come from a place of love, of good intentions. And, to me, it is what matters the most.
Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection is the best game in the Stories arc and one of the best RPGs of the last few decades.

Monster Hunter Stories 3 manages to scratch several itches all at once, all in bite-sized, manageable amounts. With a renewed focus on story than other elements, it provides a focused, well-structured challenge that fans of the series will appreciate. Getting lost in its beautifully crafted world is never an issue, since there is always something to do. If you can ignore its minor quirks and slightly outdated systems, Monster Hunter Stories 3 will offer you countless hours of fun.

Powered by the RE Engine, Twisted Reflection is a breathtaking anime odyssey that matures the spin-off series with a fully voiced, politically charged narrative. By refining its tactical "Rock-Paper-Scissors" combat and adding an addictive habitat-restoration loop, Capcom has crafted a high-production JRPG that stands tall alongside the mainline franchise.

Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection is the strongest this spin-off series has been so far. Its story finally gives the adventure real pull, the combat asks more from you in the right ways, and Habitat Restoration gives the whole game a better sense of purpose. The political side of the story could have used more room through the middle, and the Nintendo Switch 2 version has pop-in and frame drops that are hard to ignore. Even with those issues, this is the Monster Hunter Stories game that pulls everything together best.

Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection is a highly qualified game—I would even say a strong contender for game of the year. With beautiful visuals, rich and creative settings, diverse and customizable monsters, and a mature and well-written story, the game also features well-developed and charismatic NPCs. Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection shows that the series has found its definitive identity and delivers the best adventure in the franchise so far.
Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection is the most beautiful, biggest, and richest Stories yet, with a wonderful story, an extremely deep combat system, and endless exploration possibilities.

Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection does well where it matters most, despite having some problems with pacing, menus that don't work smoothly, uneven tutorials and late-game grind spikes. It makes you want it. It wants to hatch one more egg, improve one more build, fight off one more invasive threat, recover one more habitat and see one more part of its world open up because it is curious.

In a world where JRPG’s are on the rise, it’s impressive to see the Monster Hunter Stories series continue to improve upon each installment. And the leap from Stories 2 is significant, putting the series on par with other juggernauts in the genre. Using deep turn-based combat mechanics, a strong narrative, and impressive production values, Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection stands tall in what is a landmark year for Capcom as a publisher. Challenging difficulty, uneven level scaling, and minor performance problems do little to sour what is one of 2026’s best JRPG adventures.

Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection” isn’t flawless. The story drags, most characters barely register, and too many cutscenes feel like filler. But the combat and progression? Pure satisfaction. The fail‑learn-master loop is addictive, and exploration always rewards you. This one’s for players who live for deep gameplay over cinematic storytelling.

Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection is the installment that finally establishes the sub-series as more than just a niche spin-off. It is more ambitious, more mature, and much closer to the spirit of Monster Hunter, both in the challenge of its combat and in the construction of its world.
The latest game in the Monster Hunter Stories franchise brings together everything fans love in an excellent package.

If you’re keen to get back into the Monster Hunter universe, but with a focus on a well-told tale, addictive gameplay and a fresh approach to combat, Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection is an expedition worth embarking on.

This is the best Monster Hunter Stories game to date. Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection outclasses Wings of Ruin in narrative depth, visual fidelity, combat complexity, and world design. The game has a high learning curve, but once you get a hang of it, it holds its own in a stacked 2026 JRPG lineup.

Monster Hunter Stories3 sheds the juvenile tone of its predecessors, delivering a profound narrative and deep progression through its new 'Rewilding' system. By adding strategic depth to the classic rock-paper-scissors combat, it has finally transcended its spin-off roots to fully realize its identity. For fans of monster-taming RPGs and hunters seeking a fresh take on the hunt, this is the definitive choice.

Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection uses the incredible storytelling potential of the Monster Hunter universe to tell a unique, excitingly dark, and political narrative with great animation and gorgeous music. Its turn-based combat is excitingly cinematic, and if you can handle awkward flying mechanics and general JRPG pacing, you should definitely enjoy what this game has to offer.

Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection leaves behind the youthful tone of the spin-off for a much more adult one, along with a complex combat system and an impressive level of presentation that makes every hunt spectacular.

Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection doesn’t aim to completely reinvent what’s been established in the previous two entries in the series. Instead, it smartly tweaks and iterates on what worked and what didn’t work to create a much more refined and enjoyable monster-catching experience.
Its combat cycle has never felt better, and with more to see and do, this is undeniably the best of the trilogy of Monster Hunter RPGs.

I love the different take on the Monster Hunter universe offered by the Stories sub-series. Its themes of ecological preservation fit much better than the indiscriminate hunting for better gear in the main saga, and its Game of Thrones-esque story of warring kingdoms adds a lot of points. But it's the monster breeding and enhancement systems that will keep you glued to this title for hours. Some mechanics don't work perfectly and the story loses steam over time, but it's undoubtedly an excellent creature-catching JRPG.

"The most ambitious installment in the series"
Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection offers a complete JRPG experience that combines strategic combat, open-world exploration, and team building in a deep and enjoyable way. Despite some technical complexities and the difficulty some newcomers might face in learning certain systems, the game provides a sense of control and enjoyment of diverse strategies and building a strong team, making it an excellent choice for fans of both tactical and story-driven games.

Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection is a mechanical masterpiece struggling within a hollow narrative. While its deep genetic breeding and the innovative Habitat Restoration system offer an unparalleled level of monster customization, the story fails to capitalize on its own high-stakes premise of wartime diplomacy and ecological ruin.

The turn-based combat remains a brilliant translation of the series' signature rhythm, but the experience is occasionally marred by punishing late-game difficulty spikes and static, underdeveloped companions. It is a dream come true for theory-crafters and "Monstie" enthusiasts, but those seeking a compelling RPG narrative may find themselves chasing a ghost.
Absolutely stunning visually, packed with cool ways to upgrade your monster game, and stands again as a more friendly inroad to overall franchise
Despite not shaking off all of the series’ gameplay issues, Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection benefits from a huge graphical boost and a more mature story.

Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection is another standout title from Capcom, which has been on a tear with a string of outstanding releases. This is not an exception and shows how a spin-off can proceed to evolve and become successful in its own right. The habitat restoration system is superb, encouraging players to interact with the world in many ways and get rewarded for it.

The game performs splendidly, looking and playing well at the same time, making for an enjoyable experience that even newcomers to the Monster Hunter series will appreciate. Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection is an essential experience and the best installment in the series.

Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection delivers a visually stunning RPG with deep strategic combat, an engaging story, and exploration that rewards players for their efforts. While its complex mechanics may be challenging for newcomers, its beautiful presentation and gameplay systems make it a standout and a contender for the best RPG of the year. It’s pawesome!
It’s pricy at $70, but it’s as good as many of the other turn-based RPG’s and monster catching games that came out recently.

We embarked on an enjoyable JRPG adventure in the vast world of Monster Hunter Stories 3, featuring stunning visuals that deliver a beautiful visual experience. The game offers a massive amount of content within an explorable world filled with exciting events, alongside a deep gameplay system that may initially feel complex for newcomers, but becomes easier to grasp over time. All of this makes MHS3 a clear evolution compared to the previous entries in the series, making it an excellent choice for players looking for a world they can immerse themselves in for long hours full of challenges.

Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection offers a refreshing personal narrative and engaging turn-based combat, though it’s frequently bogged down by repetitive filler quests and a somewhat lifeless open world.
Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection takes players on a mystical journey through a world they may find familiar, but from a different perspective.

Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection is a lovingly intrepid take on the series' conventions. There's a palpable whimsy to its character-driven moments and punchy, elephantine vigor to its action that rivals the greats. All series fans need to give this a go, even if you were repulsed from the spinoffs before.

Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection represents the evolution that the spin-off series needed to stand on the same level as the main Monster Hunter titles and in many aspects, it even surpasses them. With its perfect combination of a compelling story, a gorgeous art style, and addictive, highly refreshing gameplay, the game delivers an exceptional JRPG experience. It sets a new standard for creature-collecting games within the genre, and many titles that focus on gathering and raising creatures should look to it as a reference and learn from its design.

My experience with Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection is an odd one. I love the vast majority of the gameplay it offers, but having played a clearly inferior version on Nintendo Switch 2 really soured me on its otherwise incredible visual presentation. The story and its characters are better than you'd expect if you've played or even glanced at previous Stories games, but it's not the sort of tale you'll be reminiscing about once you put the game down.

Monster Hunter Stories 3: Twisted Reflection isn't just the evolution of the series, but of the genre. It's in-depth systems, memorable story, and plethora of Monsties to hatch will draw in Riders and Hunters alike.

metal-gear-solid-master-collection-vol-2.title: Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2

reviews.excerpt: Metacritic user score 8.9/10 (92 ratings).

It's hard to think of a better collection of games than those on Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2. Even if Metal Gear Solid 4 wasn't such a prize for players who haven't been able to revisit it for so long, the game, divorced of that context, is still excellent. While they're less headline grabbing, Peace Walker and Ghost Babel both sit alongside the very best of the franchise. An unmissable collection for Metal Gear fans.

Metal Gear Solid Master Collection Vol. 2 perfectly achieves its goal: bringing Guns of the Patriots and Peace Walker — formerly exclusive to Sony consoles — to modern platforms. The inclusion of Portuguese subtitles and a price point that aligns with the volume of content offered represent major wins for Konami with the Brazilian audience.

Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Volume 2 continues the high quality established by the first collection in the series, though slightly slimmer in the content it offers. That being said, you’ll be more than treated with a fantastic new version of Metal Gear Solid 4, and the handheld frays of the series to make for a whole tapestry that everyone can now enjoy, alongside the first volume.

Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 is a faithful preservation package that finally frees Metal Gear Solid 4 from the PS3 while giving Peace Walker and Ghost Babel another chance to shine. It does little to modernize the games beyond making them accessible, but strong ports, worthwhile extras, and the enduring quality of the originals make this an easy recommendation for longtime fans.
Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 brings with it two fantastic games, including one of PlayStation 3's best exclusives brought back to life like a shot of nanomachine suppressors to the leg.

A masterclass in game preservation, Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol 2 triumphantly rescues Hideo Kojima’s Guns of the Patriots from its PS3 hardware prison. Combined with the sprawling, essential Peace Walker and retro gems like Ghost Babel, this collection isn't just a phenomenal value; it's an essential piece of gaming history finally restored for modern players.

Metal Gear Solid Master Collection Vol.2 finally frees Metal Gear Solid 4 from PS3 prison, and being able to re-experience that brilliant-but-flawed game again is worth the price of admission alone. Packaged with the fantastic Peace Walker and overlooked spinoff Ghost Babel, this is a phenomenal collection. This time around, the games are at their absolute best too, with Vol 1’s technical issues nowhere to be seen.
Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol.2 includes two fantastic games that still hold up all these years later, along with some great content for fans that want to dive even deeper.

Rather than focusing on what Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2—and MGS4 in particular—does right or wrong, this is more about how necessary and cathartic this closure feels. Releasing the collection is practically a gesture to the fans, and if you know how to appreciate it, it’s perfect. But even judged as a modern game, completely out of context, we could still say it’s the best of all nine.

Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection – Volume 2 finally frees Guns of the Patriots from the PlayStation 3, bringing with it several very welcome visual upgrades. The bonus games are a nice touch, though they aren't exactly the most substantial part of the package. If you are a fan of the series—or want to see how the story concludes—this is a release that belongs in your collection.

Metal Gear Solid Master Collection Vol 2 is a valuable compilation for both longtime fans and newcomers looking to rediscover two essential entries in the series. Its greatest achievement lies in finally freeing MGS4 from the PS3 and bringing it to modern hardware with solid performance, while Peace Walker retains its excellent gameplay despite showing its age more noticeably on a visual level. Overall, the collection provides an accessible, nostalgic, and highly recommended way to revisit an essential part of Snake's legacy.

METAL GEAR SOLID: Master Collection Vol.2 offers 2 must-play titles in the series with one being a brilliant conclusive story while the other is an exciting prequel to the couple of games that are bound to be featured in Vol.3.
Less extensive than its predecessor, but hardly less important: an excellent collection spearheaded by the historic return of Metal Gear Solid 4.

Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 features some of the best games in the series. MGS 4 is without doubt a masterpiece, and this port improves on the original by adding a locked frame rate. While Peace Walker is the same as the previous port, it’s still a brilliant game that offers a co-operative spin on the formula. The GBC adventure tops off the package, highlighting the diversity of experiences that have defined the franchise. Even though each title is a separate icon, cluttering the dashboard, it’s a brilliant collection that is essential for fans of the series.

METAL GEAR SOLID: MASTER COLLECTION Vol. 2 succeeds in its mission, though it suffers from the same issues as the first volume regarding content management and access. The focus is clearly on Guns of the Patriots, and it is evident that this title demanded the most resources, as it is far from a simple port. Nevertheless, that alone is enough to warrant a positive rating and keep spirits high despite the omissions—gaps that could well be filled in a third volume. In the meantime, it is time to enjoy a game that spent 18 years locked away on a single console. Long live Metal Gear Solid and the work of Hideo Kojima!

Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Volume 2 from Konami brings back some solid games to add to an already budding Metal Gear Solid collection. Of course, the star of the collection, Metal Gear Solid 4: Guns of the Patriots, is the real reason why players will want this, and it doesn’t disappoint with its story and perfect PS3 translation.

Bringing two major Metal Gear games to the present day, especially freeing MGS4 from being confined to a single console, is fantastic. Now you can play the entire series from start to finish on modern platforms and bid it a heartfelt farewell. Even just for MGS4, it's a package worth buying; I think it's worth taking advantage of this opportunity.
Despite a light content line-up, Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 is worth purchasing for one reason alone: Metal Gear Solid 4 is no longer trapped on the PlayStation 3.

Master Collection Vol. 2 is a rescue operation carried out with respect rather than boldness, and it should be judged above all for what it manages to give back to the community. A landmark chapter like Guns of the Patriots finally escaping an unjust exile that lasted almost two decades, a Peace Walker that regains its entire online suite and its narrative weight within Big Boss's arc, and a Ghost Babel that turns out to be the loveliest surprise of the whole package.

MGS 4 is the star and makes the collection worth buying, but the absence of Metal Gear Online, the recycled Peace Walker HD Edition, and relatively thin extras stop Vol. 2 from feeling like a truly comprehensive collection.

Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 is an essential collection for the most die-hard Metal Gear fans, especially for bringing Guns of the Patriots off its original platform, the PS3. It is not the most generous compilation due to the small number of games it offers, but both keep their narrative and gameplay virtues intact for modern hardware thanks to the implemented technical improvements.

After nearly twenty years chained to the proverbial radiator that is the PlayStation 3, Metal Gear Solid 4: Guns of the Patriots finally arrives on PS5. The nanomachines, the fashion model robot monsters, the flamenco dance battle, the fried eggs, the cigarette smoking underpants monkey, and that ridiculous final boss, all running at 60 frames-per-second and looking better than ever. This is good, isn't it?
I see no compelling reason to pass this up, as the games were solid from the start; the only potential letdown is their presentation.

Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 is by no means a perfect compilation. It could have benefited from packing in one or two more titles. There’s still no unified front-end, which means that you’ll need to bounce between half a dozen standalone applications instead of launching into a single game with an all-encompassing menu. And just like its predecessor, there’s a noticeable lack of video and behind-the-scenes material. That being said, if you’re looking for a way to play through two of the franchise’s best entries without fiddling with emulators or digging your aging PS3 or PSP out of the closet, it’s hard to take issue with what’s on offer.

Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 isn’t the flawless archive this legendary series deserves, but the return of Metal Gear Solid 4 after eighteen years is an event in itself. Guns of the Patriots has aged nowhere near as badly as its protagonist and still ranks among the absolute best games in the series, while Peace Walker and the unfairly forgotten Ghost Babel are valuable additions to the package. For Metal Gear fans, finally having these near-lost gems together on modern platforms is reason enough to celebrate, easily outweighing most of the collection’s shortcomings.

MGS4 remains an ambitious, gloriously excessive finale, and Vol. 2 gives it the modern platform it deserves, despite some dated design choices, lengthy cutscenes and uneven representation. Ghost Babel, Peace Walker, and deep-cut extras round out a good package.

Featuring another three games from the much-loved Metal Gear Solid franchise, finally being able to play Metal Gear Solid 4: Guns of the Patriots on something other than PS3 makes Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection worthy of your attention alone.

Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 brings together two of the saga's most beloved titles from the modern era. If you aren't familiar with these two games, you are morally obliged to experience them; they are living history in the world of video games, having cemented their legacy on systems as significant as the PS3 and PSP.

Despite including the bare minimum amount of extra materials, Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 is worthy because of its inclusion of MGS4. This history of this important PS3 game has been annoyingly hard to fully explore because of 18 years of exclusivity to a long-dead console that’s notoriously hard to emulate. MGS4‘s silly yet poignant story and rewarding stealth gameplay have aged well and are even easier to appreciate, given how the game now finally runs at a smooth frame rate and has been touched up to look fantastic on modern displays. Peace Walker has its strengths, too, and is, despite its repetitive nature and lack of crossplay, an important entry in its own right that deserves a more modern port. Modern ports may be frustrating to see because these Metal Gear games beg for more, but freeing MGS4 from PS3 purgatory is noble and the main reason this collection is more than solid enough.

Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 successfully preserves two excellent games from one of the industry's most influential franchises, bringing them to modern platforms through solid ports with a handful of welcome extras. However, while the additional content is appreciated, the collection ultimately feels more adequate than definitive, falling short of the comprehensive celebration Metal Gear Solid deserves.
Whilst not offering as many games as Vol.1, METAL GEAR SOLID: MASTER COLLECTION Vol.2 is still an essential for franchise fans, and a great way to replay Guns of the Patriots again.

In short, MGS Master Collection Vol. 2 is a must-have package for anyone who bought and enjoyed Vol. 1. When to buy it, however, depends much more on your attachment to or curiosity about these titles than on a recommendation to play them immediately. Otherwise, it's best to wait for a sale.

Altogether this collection is all about that MGS4 golden goose, but all the additions make it worthwhile, even if there’s an uneven level of attention given to non-Guns of the Patriots content. Still nab it as it’s priced pleasantly enough, but grab it with the intent of playing MGS4 and see the rest of the collection as a bunch of generous extras.
The games included can easily be included in the top of their respective consoles, but the overall experience of this pack feels a little careless and empty of content.

While the first collection combined great games with minimal improvements and a plethora of extras, this one offers weaker games and far less compelling bonus content. At least it has one major advantage: MGS4 the most sought-after title of the bunch is finally accessible to a newer generation. While the game has certainly aged poorly in terms of pacing, it remains a must-play for any fan of the series.

Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection 2 is truly just a vehicle for a remaster for Metal Gear Solid 4: Guns of the Patriots. Konami slotted Metal Gear Solid Peace Walker, one of the best PSP games ever to be released, as an added bonus, along with Ghost Babel, but the real meat and potatoes come in the form of Solid Snake’s final adventure. This is a game that hasn’t seen past its PlayStation 3 release eighteen long years ago, so it’s no surprise it’s the highlight of the package. And for the most part, it delivers.

Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 might not seem as important as Vol. 1 at first glance, but Guns of the Patriots and Peace Walker are both essential entries for entirely different reasons: MGS4, free from its PS3 shackles, wraps up an incredible narrative in style, while Peace Walker is a huge, addictive experience that's perfect for handheld play on Switch 2.With the addition of Ghost Babel and a dense database of extra information, I have no qualms in recommending this for folks who enjoyed the first collection, even if Peace Walker perhaps should have made better use of the Switch 2's power. Now bring on Vol. 3, Konami – Metal Gear Rising, Ground Zeroes, and The Phantom Pain would round it out nicely.
Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 is packed with two of the most important Metal Gear games of all time.

The addition of Peace Walker and Ghost Babel are great, and the encyclopedia rounds out the package. I know what I want for Volume 3 but cannot fathom getting the rights to Twin Snakes would be easy. I am guessing we see something like MGSV and Rising with perhaps bonus titles including the Ac!d series. For now Metal Gear fans are eating good, and I am here for it.

This collection might have fewer games than the first volume, but it feels more substantial and respectful. MGS4 is the star, finally accessible to everyone, and the overall polish proves Konami is serious about preserving Kojima's legacy. It's not a flawless celebration, but it is a vital step forward for one of gaming's most influential sagas.

Metal Gear Solid Master Collection Vol. 2 delivers definitive versions of two franchise classics. It looks and runs great, making it an easy recommendation for returning fans and newcomers alike.

Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 is not a overhauled remaster filled with rebuilt assets and major mechanical improvements. 3. I'd love to have a native version of MGS V on the go, yet it also shows that Konami is running out of things to spice up these collections with. Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol.2 offers the chance to experience two important and classic entries in the Metal Gear series under improved conditions, which is appealing in its own right. This package comes in at $50, and despite some enhancements, you're ultimately still dealing with the same original versions of the games, especially in the case of Peace Walker, which could have greatly benefited from graphical upgrades. I may be a bit biased as Metal Gear is one of my favorite franchises but I recommend Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 to anyone out there that has played the previous games. Metal Gear Solid 4 finally being available on every major current platform makes this collection worth it alone in my opinion but Peace Walker and Ghost Babel both add a lot more playtime to the collection. Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 really stands out thanks to Guns of the Patriots. The rest are really just curiosities. Peace Walker has its moments, but after Phantom Pain it won’t surprise anyone. The rest is just cosmetic tweaks and nostalgia. Boxed editions are becoming a thing of the past, so buy them whilst they’re still affordable.

Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 is a good compilation overall. It is also nice to finally have a way to play the majority of these games on one platform at a time when some franchises still leave their biggest titles scattered across multiple inaccessible systems. Fans won't need much coaxing to pick up this compilation, but it is reassuring to know that some care went into putting it together rather than simply treating it as a quick-and-dirty ROM dump.

METAL GEAR SOLID: MASTER COLLECTION Vol. 2 is an essential Collection above all for the presence of Metal Gear Solid 4. The transfer to PS5 and PS5 Pro (as well as PC, Xbox Series and Nintendo Switch 2) does not reach the ambition of a remake, but offers the most practical and technically advanced way to play the last chapter of Solid Snake's story today. Support for up to 4K and 60 fps concretely improves the quality of the experience, even though the frame rate is not always stable and PS5 Pro does not seem (unfortunately) to have received an exclusive graphics mode. Peace Walker adds depth with Mother Base, recruitment and co-op, while Ghost Babel completes the package with an interesting testament to the versatility of the series. The result is less rich in quantitative terms than Vol. 1, but more significant for the value of the games included. Some conservative choices and the absence of a deeper technical overhaul keep the collection from being definitive in an absolute sense; however, its historical weight and the quality of its content make it a release that is hard for enthusiasts to ignore.

Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 is a bundle of three games. It includes Metal Gear Ghost Babel, Metal Gear Solid: Peace Walker, and Metal Gear Solid 4. The games remain true to their original form, with only the necessary, minimal adjustments made to ensure playability. It delivers exactly what you would expect from a collection like this.

Metal Gear Solid Master Collection Vol. 2 is a package of great value, perhaps less rich than the previous collection, but finally freeing Metal Gear Solid 4 and bringing the whole saga to XBOX. Its gameplay still feels ahead of its time, and Peace Walker's progression is addictive. Konami's lazy remastering work and thin extras disappoint, but after eighteen years, the wait was worth it.

While there’s less in the way of content than Vol. 1, I’m still a massive fan of everything on offer. It’s simply nice to have two previously inaccessible games on modern hardware, both treated to much nicer 4K/ 60 FPS facelifts.

Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 is a nostalgic trip whose stealth gameplay and atmosphere still hold up, even if imprecise gunplay, blurry comic cutscenes and visible age make it hard to win over a new generation.

The Master Collection Vol 2 doesn’t feel quite as big as its predecessor; certainly, there are fewer than half the titles of that first lot. highly recommend *Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2*. However, both Peace Walker and MGS4 suffer from some issues, such as audio and visual bugs that need to be patched out to give these games the definitive versions they deserve.

Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 brings together three memorable entries, with Metal Gear Solid 4 finally receiving a modern remaster at 4K and 60 FPS. Peace Walker retains its engaging base-building and cooperative mechanics, while Ghost Babel is a welcome surprise, although the absence of Metal Gear Online and limited story guidance hold the collection back.

Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 is a particularly important compilation for bringing back Metal Gear Solid 4 and allowing us to enjoy it outside of the PlayStation 3 for the first time. Konami is back with another pretty interesting compilation—and one that's even more appealing to fans of the series.

Metal Gear Solid - Master Collection Vol. 2 breathes new life into two of the greatest classics in video game history, allowing millions of fans of Hideo Kojima’s work to finally experience the conclusion of the saga by delivering the definitive version of Metal Gear Solid 4: Guns of the Patriots and a newly enhanced version of Peace Walker, featuring fully functional online features.
A nostalgic yet uneven compilation that celebrates the series’ legacy while showing its age in technical execution.

It’s worth buying, if only to discover or replay MGS 4 (which can be purchased separately, by the way). Don’t expect major additions or changes to the titles it includes, because there aren’t any. Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 is a great addition to the Master Collection series. It finally brings MGS4 out of its PlayStation 3 jail and brings it up to modern standards. Until then, Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 is another solid compilation of classic era-defining games that can now be relived on modern consoles.

Master Collection Vol. 2 is an incredibly valuable package. It may not be the most complete Metal Gear collection, but it finally gives MGS4 the excellent modern release it deserved.

This pack is an essential part of the franchise and it's notable to see MGS4 finally available in more systems. There's a legacy preservation effort and the pack is full of extras, but there's a feeling that, as a collection or a new way to present these games, it could still be more.

A significant portion of Metal Gear history, once spread across three different hardware generations, can now coexist under one roof on modern systems. Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 offers an opportunity to revisit some of the series’ most notable titles on modern platforms while preserving the stories and gameplay that shaped its identity. Although the collection does not always deliver the level of technical enhancements expected from a modern release, the quality of the games themselves remains evident, especially for those who never had the chance to experience them before. Ultimately, this collection may not be the ideal upgrade for everyone, but it remains an important release for Metal Gear fans and those looking to experience one of the most distinctive stories in video game history.

Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 fails to capture the same sense of completeness offered by the first collection. It is less generous in terms of content, more disorganized in its presentation, and the two major games included here are among the most debated entries in the series. Nevertheless, it is not a package that anyone who loves the series could easily turn down. Because the real value here lies not so much in offering a compilation, but in rescuing games that have long been buried on dusty shelves.
A faithful, technically solid port that finally frees Guns of the Patriots from the PS3 and proves both games have aged far better than expected.

Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 offers one of the most significant re-releases in the series' history, especially with Metal Gear Solid 4 finally leaving the PlayStation 3. Despite the deconstructed interface, limited DLC, and some signs of age, Guns of the Patriots remains a solid stealth and combat experience, while Peace Walker adds important strategic depth, and Ghost Babel delivers an excellent surprise for fans of the series. The collection isn't perfect, but it remains a valuable opportunity to explore a key chapter in Metal Gear history on modern consoles.

It might have fewer titles than Vol. 1, but Metal Gear Solid Master Collection Vol. 2 is a lot more polished out of the gate and is historically important for freeing both Guns of the Patriots and Ghost Babel from their years of isolation locked on their respective release systems. Guns of the Patriots in particular now gets a chance to be remembered by new generations as a key part of the Metal Gear franchise and one of Hideo Kojima’s most unique entries in his oeuvre. If there is going to be a Master Collection Vol. 3, you’d hope it would include not only a complete version of MGSV: The Phantom Pain with Ground Zeroes incorporated, but also releases of the leftovers of the franchise, specifically Metal Gear Solid: Portable Ops (another PSP title), as well as Revengeance and I guess might as well throw in Metal Gear Survive for completionists. The Metal Gear series continues to be one of the most unique, strange and memorable franchises in video game history.

METAL GEAR SOLID: MASTER COLLECTION Vol.2 finally frees MGS4 from PlayStation 3 jail, delivering excellent performance alongside two preserved classics, making it essential for longtime Metal Gear fans.
Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 is a near-perfect collection for those seeking two iconic games that can finally be appreciated by modern audiences.

This collection is worth it purely for MGS4. It still lives up to modern standards due to amazing artistic attention to detail when it was made, and the visual approach is still remarkable. It needed very little attention, and simply breaking it free from PS3 is enough to be excited to pick up Volume 2. That being said, outside of MGS4 there is no real added or additional benefit to the new collection which is a slight drawback.

Even if it features fewer games in absolute terms, and basically no extras to speak of, Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 somehow feels less “lazy” than its predecessor, even though that collection was already pretty great to begin with. The inclusion of a fully remastered Metal Gear Solid 4: Guns of the Patriots, which has never looked or played better, is worth the admission ticket alone. Master Collection Vol. 2 does not reinvent Metal Gear’s past. It finally gives two essential pieces of it the modern home they deserved.

Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 brings MGS4 beyond the PS3 alongside Peace Walker and Ghost Babel, offering a valuable preservation package that reconnects some of the franchise's most important chapters on modern platforms.

Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 is worth it almost entirely for Guns of the Patriots, finally freed from its PS3 exclusivity and looking better than ever — though the missing Online mode and recycled Peace Walker keep this from being a truly complete package.

The Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 is a collection that successfully brings together three very different experiences without making any of them feel out of place within the package. Metal Gear Solid 4 is naturally the main highlight, especially because it is finally available on modern platforms, but Peace Walker and Ghost Babel also have enough qualities to justify their inclusion. Beyond Ghost Babel itself, the collection offers an interesting amount of bonus content, ranging from additional camouflage options to a digital soundtrack, concept art, and complete digital books containing information about the story, characters, and other elements of the games. In the end, we have three different ways of telling stories within the same franchise, each with its own level of density and structure, yet all capable of entertaining and engaging players in different ways.


It becomes clear that the purpose of the Master Collection Vol. 2 is much closer to preserving and adapting these experiences than rebuilding them according to modern standards. Improvements to resolution, performance, controls, and accessibility make the games more comfortable to play on modern platforms, but many older elements remain. Some of these characteristics are part of the games' identities and help preserve their original experience, while others could have received more careful treatment in this new version. Even considering that we are dealing with a remaster, there were opportunities to improve certain visual, technical, and presentation aspects, making the package even more consistent without necessarily changing the essence of the games.


Regardless of which of the three titles you choose, there is a unique experience waiting for the player, and I find it particularly interesting how such different approaches can work so well when placed side by side. Metal Gear Solid 4 remains an extremely solid and dense experience, Peace Walker is particularly surprising thanks to its combination of short missions, management, and multiplayer, while Ghost Babel demonstrates how the essence of Metal Gear could be adapted even to hardware as limited as the Game Boy Color.


The core experience of these games remains strong enough to deliver an extremely satisfying result and, above all, preserve three distinct moments from one of the most important franchises in video game history.

Even with less content than its predecessor, Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 is a dream come true, bringing the climax of Solid Snake’s story to modern platforms. On top of that, it includes Big Boss’s excellent portable chapter and an obscure Game Boy Color classic, so the quality more than makes up for the quantity. Konami did a solid job porting these games, with plenty of customization options on PC while leaving their core intact.

While short on additional content, flawlessly adapts MGS4 and brings back another game from the franchise that had been lost in time (Ghost Babel). Added to this is the inclusion of Peace Walker and other content such as guides and scripts, giving it added value for both new players. However, it's important to note that—with the exception of the Game Boy game—prior knowledge of the franchise is required to fully enjoy the two canonical games included in this collection.

Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 is a valuable preservation package that brings together three very different chapters of the series, with strong variety, archival extras, and a clear appreciation for Metal Gear's history.

But for those of you who have played through the contents of volume 1, even in the past, before they were bundled in a modern volume, then get it. We all know you want it.
