Metal Gear Solid Master Collection: Volume 2 is yet another sign that Konami is coasting on Snake’s legacy, relying on a brand that keeps shining despite everything. The three included games remain heavyweight works, still capable of telling a crucial chapter of gaming history, but the package around them is so lazy it makes the already modest Volume 1 look almost committed. The bare‑bones upscale, recycled assets, blurry cutscenes, and total lack of meaningful enhancement reveal an approach focused more on the logo on the box than on the quality of the offering. The material deserved far better, and while die‑hard fans will fill the gaps with their affection for the series, everyone else is left with the sense of a missed opportunity — a tribute that could have celebrated a legendary saga but merely resells it, without conviction, hoping it’s enough.

Konami brings back three very different pieces of Metal Gear, from Solid Snake’s emotional finale to Peace Walker’s tactical foundations and Ghost Babel’s handheld curiosity. Not everything is remastered equally, but the historical value of the package is huge.

Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 preserves better than it modernizes. That phrase probably best summarizes my experience with the collection. The stories remain excellent and represent some of the most important moments in Metal Gear. Especially Metal Gear Solid 4, which finally ceases to be limited to the PlayStation 3 after so many years.

Overall, "Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2" is a well-rounded package. For the first time, it's possible to play "Metal Gear Solid 4: Guns of the Patriots" outside of its original release platform, while "Peace Walker" offers a different gameplay experience than most installments in the series thanks to its numerous different content options.
Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 is another home-run release by Konami, which continues to do a great job of making its back catalog available on modern systems.
Excellent, Konami: Age hasn't slowed you down one bit.
Metacritic user score 8.5/10 (1408 ratings).

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is easily a contender for game of the year, as it blends merciless action with skill-based combat in a near-seamless way. The story and visuals complement the ridiculously sharp gameplay extremely well, and though the camera can be a little problematic on rare occasions, that shouldn’t stop you from experiencing Capcom’s latest banger.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a visually stunning revival that successfully brings Capcom’s classic franchise into the modern era using the RE Engine. Musashi injects a refreshing sense of personality into dark fantasy Kyoto, especially during the game’s intense and cinematic boss fights. This is definitely an action adventure game of the year contender.
As rewarding as it is difficult, Onimusha isn’t just one of the best games of the year; it’s one of the best action games ever made.

For as long as I can remember, I have wanted to be perfect for 10 seconds. Onimusha: Way of the Sword understands that desire. Each time I landed a perfectly timed Issen, pulled off a risky deflect, or landed a combo at just the right time, I felt like I had accomplished something. I had put myself to the test, and I’d succeeded. It’s a testament to Way of the Sword’s combat that I could beat it without using some of the systems designed to help you progress – not because you don’t need them, but because it leaves room for you to truly understand its action and overcome their absence through sheer determination. Even if I hadn’t intentionally made things harder for myself, though, I still would have loved spending time with Okuni, Takamura, Murasaki, Shizuka, and nearly all the denizens of this world. I still would have thought that Musashi himself is one of the coolest, most interesting protagonists in any video game, and I would have loved going on this journey with him. I still would have savored the creative fights against Ganryu and Benkei and a dozen others I won’t spoil here. My journey reflected Musashi's, and Onimusha made that possible. The best part of life is the challenge. You have to learn to love the fight.

Onimusha is a criminally underrated series, and while it was not a series I was expecting to be revived, I am delighted to see it make a comeback. And with the sheer quality that Capcom has pumped into Way of the Sword, I have no doubt that this is a game that is going to sell like hotcakes, and I'm already getting my hopes up for another new Onimusha title, In a competitive field, Onimusha: Way of the Sword is hands-down the best action-adventure title of the year so far. Its combat system is as electrifying as it is challenging to master, and it's backed up by a great story and characters, and a lovely little world to explore. Capcom can probably scarcely believe how well its 2026 is going. Here's hoping its new golden age continues for many years to come.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword isn't just an excellent series revival from a company that has seemingly mastered them, taking a proper understanding of the early entries' appeal and matching it perfectly to modern sensibilities. It's also just plainly the best action game this year, and probably for the past few years.

Onimusha is back and ready to claim the highest honors. Content,
quality, fun – the full package is right here.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword marks a triumphant return for Capcom’s samurai action series, combining spectacular visuals with deep, demanding combat built around precise parries, the classic Issen technique, and a varied arsenal of Oni weapons. Strong performances, memorable boss battles, rewarding progression, and an excellent recreation of feudal Japan make it one of Capcom’s most accomplished action games, while repetitive sub-bosses and a few minor presentation issues do little to diminish an outstanding experience.
Onimusha: Way of the Sword proves Capcom can't go wrong in 2026, offering combat that stands out with every swing of the blade and fascinating characters.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword masterfully revives the franchise with gameplay rich in mechanics and variety, full of boss battles that could make even FromSoftware fans envious. The story is like an incredible shonen anime. Musashi is a captivating and funny protagonist, accompanied by a cast of equally interesting supporting characters and antagonists who come together to create one of the best journeys Capcom has ever crafted.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword sets a new standard when it comes to reviving long-forgotten IPs. The series returns with a vengeance in the RE Engine, where Capcom has shown clear improvements in overall optimization and presentation. And to top it off, the game offers some of the most intuitive combat designs in an action game, which, paired with well-crafted boss fights, creates a memorable experience in multiple ways. After 20 years of dormancy, it feels like the franchise is getting its Resident Evil moment, and we’re sure to see more of the IP in the near future.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is such a refreshing action game, with focus on its combat systems and cinematic narrative. In those respects, it sets a high standard for all other video games. The only critiques some could make is that it’s a very linear game, and that could be a problem for some. It’s also maybe 20 hours long, and once the story’s finished, there isn’t a breadth of post-game modes. Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a cinematic action game, and Capcom exceeded any expectations people could have in that regard. It just lacks some kind of score mode, or Bloody Palace to keep players invested beyond the main story. I loved Onimusha: Way of the Sword, and I think it will be celebrated as a modern action classic.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is not just the best possible comeback for a franchise that hadn't seen a new installment in 20 years; it is the starting point for what could become Capcom's most epic IP of the coming decade. The game has it all: spectacular combat, incredible graphics and animations, and a magnificent story driven by unforgettable characters.
Some writing and delivery issues are about the only flaws present in an otherwise incredible Onimusha experience. Capcom’s rich vein of form continues.

Despite some repetition, an overlong finale and an occasionally frustrating camera, Onimusha: Way of the Sword delivers a remarkable experience. Its highly addictive gameplay, rewarding progression, striking atmosphere and Musashi’s incredible charisma make this long-awaited comeback a resounding success.
The way of the samurai shines bright in Onimusha: Way of the Sword, marking a triumphant return for Capcom's long-running action RPG series.
A stylish title with incredible combat, Onimusha: Way of the Sword is easily one of the best action-adventure titles of the year and one that you shouldn't miss.

With Onimusha: The Way of the Sword Capcom doesn't seem to have wanted to completely reinvent the franchise. Instead, it took what made the retro games special and combined it with a more modern combat system, spectacular presentation, and some ideas that bring the experience closer to the Soulslike genre. Way of the Sword stands out as one of the most interesting revivals of a classic franchise and continues to mark one of Capcom’s best years.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword marks a successful return for the legendary series, one that wisely steers clear of the current trend of turning action games into ‘soulslikes’. The game shines with its brilliant, gory combat system, exemplary Sekiro-esque parrying, charismatic characters (the superbly animated Musashi!) and fantastic bosses. It retains the series’ atmosphere and beautiful visuals, and the optimisation for the PS5 is flawless. The overly passive common enemies are a slight disappointment, and unfortunately there aren’t enough interesting puzzles; even so, it remains a highly satisfying power fantasy and a wonderful tribute to the series’ entire legacy.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a triumphant revival that rewards patience with exceptional combat, demanding boss fights, and surprisingly strong level design. Its slow narrative buildup and uneven side content hold it back, but once its systems fully open up, Capcom delivers a deeply satisfying action game worthy of the Onimusha name.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a fantastic return for one of the most promising franchises in the entire industry. With an excellent story and exceptional combat, Capcom hits the mark once again, delivering a title that is a true spectacle. Capturing the best of its blend of samurai and horror, it transforms into an exciting and action-packed experience that should be remembered as one of the best of the year.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword brings the samurai saga back in full force, delivering a distinctive combat system alongside challenging and memorable boss encounters. Its highly polished execution makes it a strong return for the franchise, offering an experience that welcomes longtime fans and newcomers alike.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is an often outstanding action game that bears all the hallmarks of a modern Capcom masterpiece. Its combat is clearly the main draw and it's a superb system once it gets rolling. The boss fights in particular are some of the best you'll find on PS5. But even beyond the sword-swinging skirmishes, Way of the Sword impresses with great characters and eye-popping cutscenes. This is a fantastic revival of a franchise that's been sleeping for far too long.
Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a welcome return for the series, and Capcom has been doing an incredible job with the action genre this year.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword marks a successful return for a series that had been absent for far too long. The combat system—precise and heavily reliant on timing—is undoubtedly the highlight of this new entry in the Capcom franchise, while the atmosphere of a Kyoto overrun by the Genma miasma creates truly evocative moments. Although some limitations regarding side activities and a degree of repetition prevent the adventure from achieving true excellence, Musashi and his journey amidst samurai and demons still manage to leave a lasting impression. It is a compact, spectacular experience that remains, above all, faithful to the spirit of the Onimusha franchise.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword’s cast, quest, numerous asides, and the evolution of techniques and combat throughout this adventure have the weight and depth to make you roar in triumph, groan in agony, and hit most of the feelings in between along the way. And that’s exactly what I want out of my demon-slaying samurai action-adventure.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a fantastic return for a franchise many thought Capcom had left behind. Even when I thought combat had hit its peak, the game kept layering on deeper mechanics, richer upgrades, and thrilling boss encounters that demand your absolute best. In a stacked month of massive releases, Musashi’s journey isn't just worth your time—it's an absolute must-play for action fans.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword may be the best game in the series and by quite a large margin. Definitely start out on Story difficulty to find your feet and get used to the game’s pacing of enemy attacks, but once you’re in the zone, it is a genuinely wonderful game from start to finish.

This triumphant revival delivers a deep, rewarding combat system and a stunning cinematic presentation despite a sluggish start. While the Kyoto hub feels slightly padded and sub-bosses are occasionally recycled, the breathtaking RE Engine visuals and exhilarating boss encounters ensure a top-tier experience. It successfully modernizes the classic formula without losing its identity to the soulslike trend.

After a 20-year wait, Onimusha returns in spectacular fashion. Way of the Sword delivers a fantastic combat system, stunning visuals, and a compelling story that welcomes both veterans and newcomers, making it easily one of the best action games of the year.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword marks the triumphant return of Capcom’s classic franchise. With fluid, beautifully choreographed combat, charismatic characters, creative bosses, and spectacular art direction, the game modernizes the series without losing its essence. Its low difficulty and less-inspired side content are minor flaws in an otherwise exceptional adventure.
Onimusha: Way of the Sword finally ends the 20-year wait. The thrilling samurai fights we've been looking for, combined with a fun and engaging story, are now livening up our PlayStation 5 console.

Amid a sea of mediocre Soulslikes, Onimusha: Way of the Sword arrives as a much-needed breath of fresh air. Capcom has delivered a top-tier action title with remarkable depth and variety, keeping you fully engaged from start to finish. While a few minor flaws exist, they do little to dull the game's overall excellence. It is a triumphant comeback for the series, positioning Onimusha to reclaim its spot as a dominant force in the action genre.
A fantastically self-assured reboot of Onimusha, which is significantly better than any of the previous games, with excellent combat, plenty to see and do, and some engaging storytelling.

Capcom’s willingness to return to old franchises is continuing to pay off, because Onimusha: Way of the Sword is yet another banger from a developer that just cannot stop winning. It’s easily the best game that it’s released this year, which includes behemoths like Resident Evil Requiem and Pragmata, and if you’re an Onimusha fan praying that this new game will finally revive the series, you should be very excited about the future. Now do Dino Crisis next, Capcom.

The very identity of Onimusha is back in full force, so it’s time to wipe the grit from your blade and assume the role of a legendary sword savant, comforted in the knowledge that you’re in store for a spellbinding and endlessly rewarding samurai action adventure opus.

Onimusha has repeated boss fights – especially if you complete all of the game’s optional objectives – and that might annoy you if you haven’t dedicated yourself to the Way of the Sword. If you aren’t entering each fight with the intention to do better than before (use fewer heals, take fewer hits), then you’re probably not playing it right. Combat in Onimusha isn’t something to be overcome, but something to savour and improve at, and there’s no way of telling how much better you’ve become without taking on familiar foes.

While you’ll have seen all the various elements of this title in other games before in various forms, Capcom has done a wonderful job bringing it together and forming something that feels relevent and tells a great tale.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword confirms Capcom’s success in masterfully reviving the franchise, pleasing both new and returning fans with its humorous plot, agile combat, and expansive exploration. Although it has its shortcomings—such as excessively tough bosses, limited enemy variety, and minor exploration flaws—these issues do not diminish the brilliance of this excellent title.

The game's linear missions keep the game moving at a solid pace, though the open hub Kyoto area feels out of place and a bit too repetitive. What isn't repetitive, however, is the gameplay, which truly embodies the way of the sword, challenging players to master the katana through an exhilarating combat system built from attacking, parrying, dodging, and breaking enemies. It's all wrapped together in a breathtaking presentation built on the always impressive RE Engine. Capcom walked the way of the sword, and Onimusha: Way of the Sword successfully balances the discipline, strategy, and self-improvement the saying embodies.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a reboot done right. Rather than chase trends, Capcom has updated the gameplay while staying true to its roots. With stellar combat and rewarding exploration, this is one of the best action-adventure games released for the PlayStation 5.

It's hard to imagine how this could be a stronger comeback for Onimusha, and in an already incredible year for Capcom, I can't believe that I'm saying Onimusha: Way of the Sword easily sits at the top of the mountain.

After years of hoping, complaining, and probably bringing up Onimusha more than once when absolutely nobody asked, I can finally say that the series is well and truly back. Way of the Sword feels like a modern version of exactly the kind of game that made me so excited about Onimusha all those years ago.
If you are a fan of titles where combat is the main focus, you definitely have to play this one, as it draws inspiration from the best games on the market while adding its own distinctive touches.

Monsters beware, Musashi is here! One of the best hack and slash titles to come out in some time, Onimusha: Way of the Sword is deliriously fun. When it’s all said and done, Kyoto might be under the scourge of the devilish Genma, but it’s an absolute blast getting lost in it.

Onimusha's return was significant in its own right. But the real value of Way of the Sword lies in the fact that it doesn't simply bring the Onimusha name back. Capcom understood what made the series so beloved and has blended those qualities with the evolution of modern action game design.

Twenty years is a long time to wait for a new Onimusha, but Capcom gave me the return I was hoping for. Musashi is funny, the sword combat feels great and the bosses were some of my favorite parts of the entire adventure. I also really enjoyed playing a focused action-adventure again, one that sends you somewhere for a reason and keeps the story moving without burying it under endless side activities. I had a great time with Way of the Sword, and I really hope Capcom doesn’t leave Onimusha on the shelf for another twenty years.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword rounds out Capcom's phenomenal year in style. It may be the best game the company has released in a year full of instant classics. This is a beautiful reinvention of the franchise and an exceptional game on its own merits, anchored by one of the best combat systems in years. A slow start and some unnecessary padding hold it back, but those are minor complaints. Way of the Sword is easily the best Onimusha game and a celebration of everything that makes the franchise work.

Overall, I am thoroughly impressed by Onimusha’s comeback. In practice, it is yet another Capcom title that more than earns its place among the modern gaming greats, and it is an easy recommendation for fans of action games, particularly thanks to its excellent story and superb combat mechanics. At the same time, I cannot help but wonder how much better it could have been with a little more variety and slightly more thought put into the pacing. That said, these complaints are fairly minor when viewed in the bigger picture. Capcom has once again hit the mark and shown how a proper samurai adventure should be made.
With its outstanding sword-fighting action, Onimusha: Way of the Sword scratches at the very edge of the perfect combat system and is already one of the best action games of 2026.

Capcom forges a new katana with Onimusha: Way of the Sword, successfully reinventing the samurai saga for modern times. There is room for improvement, but if this marks the beginning of a second life for the Oni warriors—and we hope it does—it is a great first step along the path of the samurai.

While repetitive side activities and weak non-combat pacing occasionally stall its momentum, the game completely makes up for it with top-tier counter-based combat and thrilling swordplay. Despite a lack of compelling replayability, it delivers pure satisfaction the moment you draw your blade.

With Onimusha Way of the Sword, Capcom could have easily messed things up, especially after leaving the franchise dormant for so long. But instead of turning it into an open-world game or a Soulslike, Capcom went back to basics and built the experience around what really matters: the sheer pleasure of wielding a sword. Sure, the writing is pretty standard, the open areas can be tedious, and some side content lacks variety, but all of that quickly becomes secondary once the combat kicks in. Chaining parries, landing a perfectly timed Issen, watching souls swirl around Miyamoto Musashi and taking down bosses that force you to master every mechanic is exactly what makes Onimusha feel special again. And then there’s Musashi, a charismatic, funny and slightly arrogant hero who gives the adventure plenty of personality. In short, Capcom absolutely nailed it.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword marks a triumphant return for a series that had been somewhat forgotten by Capcom. Yes, the story is a bit weak, but it inherits the key mechanics that worked for the franchise while introducing interesting gameplay improvements. It is a very entertaining action adventure that offers one of the most satisfying and accessible swordplay experiences in a long time.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword proves that Capcom's franchise still has a place in today's gaming landscape. After nearly two decades without a new mainline installment, the studio could have chosen to completely overhaul the formula to follow popular trends. Instead, they decided to recapture the essence of Onimusha and adapt it to modern possibilities.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a very fun game packed with memorable combat, but the constant reuse of bosses takes a bit of the shine off it, with certain moments in the campaign where the game is simply stalling to make itself seem longer than it needs to be. Even so, it is easily one of the most enjoyable games I played in 2026.
If nothing else, Onimusha: Way of the Sword serves as both a brilliant revitalization of the franchise and an excellent starting point for sequels in the future.

The return of Onimusha coincides with the release of a chapter that looks to the present without forgetting its roots. Way of the Sword undoubtedly modernizes the formula, expands exploration, and builds around Issen a combat system that is as spectacular as it is demanding, one that rewards timing, precision, and a cool head above all. A few shortcomings in the AI and a camera that is not always flawless prevent the game from reaching absolute excellence, but they do not change the bottom line: Capcom has succeeded in bringing one of its most fascinating series back to life without compromising what made it special. And after an absence spanning two console generations, that was by no means a foregone conclusion.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword delivers atmospheric samurai action with a precise, rewarding combat system. Predictable story and recycled bosses hold it back, but it remains a strong modern return to the series.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword's super-fun sword combat really packs a punch and is the star of the show along with the ridiculous game world and cast of characters that'll make things a lot more entertaining if they click with you.

Ultimately, despite its mixed aspects, Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a very good action game that upholds the franchise's signature focus—maintained for over two decades—on refined, powerful combat that prioritizes the clash of blades. Steel against steel, sparks, tension, and deadly edges. While there are questionable design choices—such as the semi-open world, filler content, and the passivity of basic enemies—the game is well worth playing for its spectacular boss battles and exquisite controls. If this marks a reboot, the foundation is there to take the saga into a new era; we hope Capcom takes note of what worked and what didn't, as they have our confidence, and for now, we can simply celebrate the fact that Onimusha is back.

More than twenty years after the last truly original instalment, Capcom isn’t merely delivering a nostalgic comeback with Onimusha: Way of the Sword. Above all, it proves that the series still has something to offer modern action games without betraying what made it unique. It may not be Capcom’s finest title in recent years, but it is a thrilling adventure that will delight fans of Japan.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword may not be the Onimusha sequel I dreamed of, but I can’t feel any real disappointment with a game this damn good. It’s got some of the absolute best sword combat in the business - real top shelf stuff - alongside a roster of unforgettable bosses and a very fun script. If only the game didn’t recycle so much of its own material and it had something of substance to flesh out the side content, it would be an all-timer. As it stands, Onimusha is nonetheless completely back as a series, and that’s not disappointing in the least.
Onimusha: Way of the Sword has one of the best parry systems since Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice. Its excellent combat is somewhat marred by an outdated open world and some issues with enemy behavior.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a polished action-adventure with an excellent combat system built around precise parries, dodges and enemy interactions. Its boss fights are particularly impressive, while its small open world and linear levels feel somewhat conservative. The story is serviceable, but the satisfying swordplay, strong visuals and superb Spanish voice acting make it highly recommended.
Sublime swordplay and spectacular samurai horror make Onimusha: Way of the Sword a thrilling return, despite too much repetitive busywork.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is an excellent revival of Capcom's samurai series. It's a bit more gritty and nitty but it retains the cheesy humour, too. And while combat is exceptional, not everything clicks in place so seamlessly.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a great modern entry into the long-running and long-dormant Capcom series. The combat and story are great, but open-world bloat makes this Capcom's most divisive release in years.
Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a great return for the franchise. Musashi is a fantastic new lead, with a supporting cast that shines.

Capcom's Onimusha reboot successfully combines old-school linearity with contemporary melee mechanics. The result is a throwback action-adventure bolstered by ultra-satisfying and modernised combat, as well as some of the most surprisingly unsettling comedy and horror moments in recent memory.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword perhaps doesn't make the best first impression and takes a little time to warm to, but once all of its systems are in play, it becomes pretty enthralling. Ultimately, it's a game worth picking up - even if only for its spectacular, and challenging, boss fights.

Way of the Sword clearly aims to be a modern take on old-school Onimusha: dark, bloody, linear, and cinematic - and it absolutely succeeds. Rather than chasing open worlds and hundreds of hours of content, it focuses on a brilliantly designed combat system and dynamic, brutal encounters. And sometimes, that’s more than enough.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword successfully revives the series with rewarding swordplay, cinematic combat, and a compelling new protagonist. Uneven pacing, audio problems, awkward movement, and limited accessibility options keep this promising new beginning from reaching its full potential.

Though fairly standard in some ways, at its core, Onimusha: Way of the Sword delivers incredible, best-in-class swordfighting combat, making for an overall package that is well worth the long time that series fans have been waiting for it.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword understands what makes a great action game: combat should challenge the player without turning every encounter into a punishment. Its regular enemies are relatively forgiving, allowing for stylish and spectacular swordplay, while its bosses demand patience, precision and genuine mastery. The combat system is the clear highlight but the exploration feels more like a complement to the action than a defining feature, and some optional activities can become repetitive surprisingly quickly. After all of this Way of the Sowrd is a great action game and the best restart for this sleepy IP.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a great action game with exciting combat and some of the best bosses Capcom has ever created. With its cinematic presentation and challenging yet fair gameplay, each boss encounter feels like a genuine highlight and offers a memorable experience. Unfortunately, everything between those fights is just alright, with the game becoming repetitive due to recurring objectives and the frequent reuse of minibosses.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword lives up to its name by providing intense, complex sword-based combat against a barrage of powerful bosses. In these numerous fights, players can truly test their mettle, potentially coming out unscathed. However, repetitive exploration and side quests make up another sizable portion of the game, often distracting players who hope to wring out more content. Capcom has done players a service by bringing back Onimusha, let’s just hope it’s not another 20 years next time.
While it’s not necessarily a continuation of the series’ plotline, what is certain is that this is one mighty fine Samurai adventure that continues Capcom’s streak of hits.

Twenty years after its last major appearance, Onimusha: Way of the Sword makes a triumphant return, firmly establishing itself as a hardcore action game. With its surgically precise combat system, exhilarating parries, and exquisitely elegant animations, Capcom’s offering truly shines the moment Musashi crosses swords. It is a shame, however, that this technical mastery is undermined by an unnecessarily drawn-out open-zone structure, burdened with dated side activities and repetitive backtracking that disrupt the adventure's pacing. Were it not for these design missteps in Eastern Kyoto, the title would have reached the pinnacle of the genre. Even so, it remains a visceral, spectacular, and highly recommended experience, proving that the saga’s blade has lost none of its luster.

After twenty years, Onimusha returns, reimagined as a modern action-adventure. Way of the Sword shines through its deep, visceral combat, a charismatic Miyamoto Musashi, memorable bosses, and exceptional technical polish. Capcom has given the series a new direction without abandoning the core identity that made it special.

After mastering the art of alternating between Resident Evil remakes and new entries without ever wearing out its welcome, after establishing Street Fighter 6 at the top of the fighting game genre, and after winning the gamble on a new franchise with Pragmata, Capcom is now demonstrating the same level of excellence when it comes to reviving a franchise left dormant for 20 years. For a few hours, however, one could have thought Capcom had lost its way. Compact though it was, this open world felt derivative and uninspired. Doubts that were partly confirmed, as there is undeniably some filler and recycling in the air, alongside a noticeable lack of variety and surprise in level design. But beyond that, Capcom didn't just aim to deliver "the ultimate swordplay game"—they actually did it, or came extraordinarily close. Amidst the sea of action-blade games video games already offer, the soul of Onimusha: Way of the Sword shines with the brilliance of the absolute greats.

Though some of the connective tissue that binds Onimusha: Way of the Sword together is a bit weak, though some of the pacing and padding is a bit thin, Capcom has once again shown us it is a master of its craft here. The developer dares to say 'no' to the ubiquitous Soulslike design and opt for something more unique, and more fitting for its central character, instead. By insisting you play honestly, learn how to wholly embody Musashi and his philosophies, Capcom forces a level of role-playing that merges narrative and mechanical storytelling. The result? There is no game out there that makes you feel more like a swordsman of legend than Onimusha: Way of the Sword.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword should definitely be on the wishlists for action fans. Unlike the last few of the series’ remasters, this new entry feels particularly approachable for newcomers, with its likable cast of new characters and intelligent gameplay overhauls, particularly in the camera department. It’s probably a few hours longer than it needs to be and recycles content more than I’d prefer, but I still had a great time with its deep and challenging combat, and you likely will as well.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is another fantastic release from Capcom and a triumphant return for one of its most beloved franchises. Its standalone story, while still containing references to the wider series, makes it an excellent entry point for newcomers, while its faithful combat and classic Onimusha DNA should delight returning veterans. After more than 20 years of waiting, fans can finally return to this beloved samurai action series, and that patience has absolutely been rewarded. Onimusha: Way of the Sword delivers a modern take on the franchise without losing sight of what made the original games so special, making this one comeback that was well worth the wait.

After two decades, Onimusha Way of the Sword is a turning point for the franchise. It’s a genuinely engaging and engrossing story that sets up for a sequel I’m already itching to play, but is unfortunately held back by a cloud of annoying — and avoidable — pitfalls.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is another win for Capcom. It’s a game with stellar combat that stumbles when it comes to its open-world design and side content. Luckily, when it's time to cross swords, this game is incredibly fun

When it’s all put together, Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a glorious comeback for a series that has been latent for far too long. Musashi has a nice, distinctive sense of humor and personality that is always entertaining, whether bantering with allies or feuding with demonic, manipulative villains. While its open-world structure in Kyoto is a bit bloated and somewhat detracts from an otherwise fantastic linear experience, the side content adequately supports an authentic, interesting setting. But the biggest takeaway is the game’s riveting, intense, and masterful combat design, which ultimately defines the game and, to summarize what Takamura says to Musashi regarding part of his reasons for fighting: “it’s just damn fun.”

The combat can be rewarding and fun, even if the excitement is dulled over time. It’s just that those hiccups keep Onimusha: Way of the Sword from maintaining its best elements. Still, when it wants to, the game can really cut through those basic hangups and deliver a terrific action game.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword has its flaws, but they stop mattering when it comes to the most important thing: Action. It’s excellent, expertly executed, wonderfully balanced, and incredibly addictive. Who cares about a weaker story or the lack of exploration when the combat is this good?

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a spectacular, challenging samurai action game that will put your reflexes to the test in a ruthless way. It isn’t a ‘soulslike’, but it draws on some of its principles to create electrifying combat.

Onimusha triumphantly returns and manages to stand out in the crowded samurai action market due to its cutting-edge, yet elegant, swordplay. If the story and variety of enemy designs showed more ambition, this game might be a certified classic. For now, it's the start of a bright new future for this once-dormant series.

An intense, grueling and addictive experience that thrives on a brilliant combat system, especially in boss fights. Though the game overstays its welcome by a bit, the gameplay and story highs far exceed its problems.

This tight choreography comes a little undone outside of combat due to flabby side-quests and some narrative padding. But Way of the Sword fulfils its goal of convincing you that you’re the greatest swordsman in the world, where success is measured in the split seconds you’re untouchable thanks to exquisite timing of a dodge or parry.

It has a heartfelt story, charming characters, surprisingly manageable sandbox, and excellent combat. Although the pacing suffers a bit and feels drawn-out due to an overabundance of mini-boss battles, “Way of the Sword” is the triumphant resurgence that the series needed.
Onimusha: Way of the Sword shines with thrilling combat, but its level design feels stretched at times.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword marks a fascinating yet overly conservative return for Capcom's iconic franchise, starring the legendary Miyamoto Musashi. While boasting stunning cinematic direction, top-tier voice acting, and rock-solid technical performance on PS5, the game is held back by a passive AI, an overly permissive difficulty curve, and a combat system that pulls its punches. It's a solid, beautiful foundation for a series revival, though it ultimately lacks the necessary bite to truly master its craft.

The central foundation upon which Onimusha: Way of the Sword is built - the combat system on which the entire experience is based - is as solid as bedrock, but everything else, including mission design, enemy variety, world structure, progression, and level design can't quite compete with the titans of the genre. Unfortunately, the game finds itself in a gaming landscape where this sort of experience has been in abundance, and so it really needed to be exceptional in more respects.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword reaches in a few too many directions in terms of storytelling and gameplay, and the edges of its identity blur as a result. Nonetheless, a responsive and rewarding combat system and an occasional sense of humor will carry you happily to the end.

With Way of the Sword, Onimusha is officially back after 20 years. It's not the best possible return the series could have had, but it's well worth it if players can accept its faults. Its combat is truly enthralling, intensive, and gripping. Every single sword clash makes every lackluster moment worth it.
It isn't ruinous, but you can't shake the sense that there's a lethal 15-hour romp in Way Of The Sword, cosplaying as a 25-hour game. [Issue#428, p.104]

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a pristine game that is very often trapped in its attempts to solve the problems that were never really there. Cut out all the fat, streamline the experience, and with the sequel you can get yourself a really outstanding action title. To live is to suffer, and as it stands, you really do have to suffer with some of the parts of Way of the Sword.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword lives up to its promise of being the ultimate sword-fighting experience, delivering a uniquely exhilarating combat system. However, the satisfying sensation of cutting enemies down that once defined the series is nowhere to be found, and the game suffers from numerous glaring flaws, including a severely limited enemy variety, tacked-on exploration elements, and a story that feels abruptly cut short. Nevertheless, as a parry-focused sword-fighting action game, its boss battles rank among the very best the genre has ever seen. Players willing to overlook the shortcomings of its story and much of the experience outside its boss encounters will find something truly exceptional here.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is worth playing for the combat alone, but the game around it doesn't live up to the standards that it sets from a pure gameplay perspective. Full of filler, overlong and focussed on the wrong things, there is a much better game in Onimusha: Way of the Sword if some of the pieces were arranged differently.

I appreciate Way of the Sword for the sheer force of will it pours into finally resurrecting the spirit of Onimusha. Yet, much like this version of Musashi at the beginning of the game – wandering aimlessly, entirely fixated on perfecting his katana prowess – it doesn’t quite yet have a bigger picture in mind.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a frustrating experience that actively undermines its own potential. An often great game that overstays its welcome with enemies acting frustratingly passive for the most part.
A sublime mix of classic Capcom action and weighty physical swordfighting. The only enemy it can't overcome is its own pacing.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword reaches in a few too many directions in terms of storytelling and gameplay, and the edges of its identity blur as a result. Nonetheless, a responsive and rewarding combat system and an occasional sense of humor will carry you happily to the end.

The uninspired semi-open-world is a misstep that doesn’t justify its existence, yet Way of the Sword is still a fantastic and welcome return for the series, led by outstanding combat that firmly places it in the upper echelon of modern action games. Fighting is everything, after all, and there’s nothing else quite like Musashi’s brand of calculated violence.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword properly carries the mantle of the original games. Delivering exciting and satisfying combat swordplay in combination with an engaging story, Way of the Sword continues Capcom’s hot streak through 2026.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a supremely satisfying samurai action game with some of the best video game boss battles this side of Sekiro. Pulling off perfect parries always feels great and makes the few flaws easy to overlook, like the wonky difficulty curve. Time-poor players will also appreciate the game's more approachable size.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a successful revival of Capcom's samurai franchise that pushes its gameplay in an exciting new direction while still retaining its core identity. The slower, more deliberate combat feels great, especially when you manage several deflections in quick succession before slicing your foe in half. Glorious.Not everything works. The English voiceover doesn't quite fit with the overall presentation, while occasional jaunts to and from multiple NPCs threaten to derail the otherwise excellent pacing. These are minor gripes, though; Onimusha is back, baby, and it's better than ever.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword shows flickers of sheer brilliance throughout its beefy campaign. Fantastic characterization, industry-leading facial motion capture with RE Engine, satisfyingly demanding combat, and spectacular visuals have all the makings of a true classic. The game suffers immensely under the weight of its laborious and drab open world, as Capcom still struggles to nail the format — but it's not enough to stop the game being a must-play 2026 title.
Onimusha: Way of the Sword's combat is as sharp as a katana, but unfortunately, that blade is uneven and dull elsewhere.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a remarkably polished parry-focused action game (perhaps the best-feeling of its ilk) with some truly exceptional production values and animations that elevate it well above the average action game.

Sure, some repetition does settle in eventually and the difficulty curve is prone to unexpectedly spiking, but there’s no doubt Way of the Sword is the kind of franchise reboot Capcom’s long-gestating Onimusha series deserved.

After a two-decade hiatus, Onimusha: Way of the Sword delivers a great modernization of the classic series' formulas without losing its identity to the Soulslike trend. While the semi-open Kyoto and narrative aren't memorable, its sharp combat system, excellent enemy design and difficulty balance make the game a triumphant comeback for returning fans and newcomers alike.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is one of those games that reminds us how satisfying a thoughtfully crafted combat system can be. Every exchange of blows, every dodge, and every successful Issen gives the feeling of truly being in control of the fight, while the bosses transform this solidity into spectacular, tense, and challenging duels.
Onimusha is finally back, and Capcom's penchant for sound storytelling and moreish combat shine through a bleak, Genma-infested Kyoto.
Onimusha: Way of the Sword is an excellent title, captivating above all for its art and a combat system that is, without fear of contradiction, among the best in its category.

Capcom dusts off one of its longtime franchises in “Onimusha: Way of the Sword,” featuring fantastic characters and bosses and a fun combat system that balances risks and rewards. It isn’t perfect as the pacing can get uneven once exploration is thrown in. Sometimes, though, you just need a stepping stone to get back on the right track after losing your way. In that sense, I feel quite confident that Onimusha is back on solid ground.
Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a great game with excellent reaction-based combat, and some of the most enjoyable, satisfying boss encounters in gaming.

Overall, Onimusha: Way of the Sword is an absolute triumph. The fast-paced action, engaging characters and story, and sublime visuals combine to create one of my favorite games of the year so far. Yes, it's that good. I highly recommend this game to anyone looking for a slice of adventure. And if you don't believe me, there's a free demo ready to sway you.
To what extent is Onimusha: Way of the Sword a reboot? In other words, what exactly has been booted out? The plot of the first game in Capcom's ser...

Onimusha: Way of the Sword successfully revives the series with rewarding swordplay, cinematic combat, and a compelling new protagonist. Uneven pacing, audio problems, awkward movement, and limited accessibility options keep this promising new beginning from reaching its full potential.

It's hard not to think about what Onimusha: Way of the Sword could've been in the context of prior entries - especially the first game. What is here, though, is still a thrilling action game (once it takes the training wheels off) with a loveable cast of characters and unique identity amongst CAPCOM's other goliath franchises.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword marks a successful return for the legendary series, one that wisely steers clear of the current trend of turning action games into ‘soulslikes’. The game shines with its brilliant, gory combat system, exemplary Sekiro-esque parrying, charismatic characters (the superbly animated Musashi!) and fantastic bosses. The game retains the series’ atmosphere and beautiful visuals, and the optimisation for the PS5 is flawless. The overly passive common enemies are a slight disappointment, and unfortunately there aren’t enough interesting puzzles; even so, it remains a highly satisfying power fantasy and a wonderful tribute to the series’ entire legacy.
All in all, it is an excellent, gorgeous, and addictive hack-and-slash adventure, and a defining new game for the genre mechanically.

For all the variety modern action games offer, the depth of combat still comes down to whether its core experience is satisfying. From that perspective, Onimusha: Way of the Sword delivers exactly what a pure action game should.
It may retain plenty of traditional, even somewhat outdated design choices, while its level structure and progression system offer little that feels new. But Capcom has polished the most crucial part into an almost perfectly cohesive whole.
For an old IP that had nearly faded from memory, this is about as perfect and dignified a return as one could ask for.
After nearly two decades away, Onimusha is back. And thankfully, it still knows which end of the sword to hold.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a satisfying return for the beloved series after a two-decade absence. The game offers solid gameplay mechanics that elevate the core experience and exhilarating boss fights you will keep coming back to.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is not just the best game of the series, but also an incredibly well-designed action game. Ironically, it’s not just combat that makes Way of the Sword stand out from other action games, but also its story and characters.

Onimusha's return was significant in its own right. But the real value of Way of the Sword lies in the fact that it doesn't simply bring the Onimusha name back. Capcom understood what made the series so beloved and has blended those qualities with the evolution of modern action game design.

Way of the Sword is arguably the best entry in the series since its debut. While it suffers from the usual ills of modern projects, like obscure side content and a drawn-out running time, it's a welcome return for Onimusha.

Yes, there’s been the staples with Resident Evil, Street Fighter and Monster Hunter, but Dragon’s Dogma, Pragmata, Kunitsu-Gami and now Onimusha: Way of the Sword show that Capcom’s serious about finding new ideas, too. That they are all landing so well speaks to a developer/publisher riding one of the best waves it has in its entire history.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword never treats gameplay as a mere bridge between cutscenes, nor does it equate cinematic presentation with reducing the player to a passive spectator. Instead, it integrates its cinematic ambitions into the very fabric of its gameplay. Fluid animation, precise character movement, and the deliberate rhythm of combat generate the same sense of spectacle, scale, and dramatic weight that cinematic games often pursue by diminishing player agency and leaning heavily on scripted sequences. Here, cinematic presentation does not come at the expense of interactivity; it emerges organically from it. Onimusha has returned with remarkable force, and Way of the Sword feels less like the conclusion of a long-awaited comeback than the beginning of a new chapter.
Equipped with a unique gauntlet, a samurai stands against the advancing Genma threat in Kyoto'and he does so with great skill. The game offers, above all, superb sword combat.

I kept coming back for more battles and pushing myself to beat the bosses even though I fell over and over again. Onimusha has found its way of the sword by balancing on the edge of this phenomenally well crafted blade. It once again shows that Capcom remains on top of its game.
Young people sometimes use the term ‘bangier’. It suits Onimusha: Way of the Sword perfectly. It’s the very essence of a video game and exactly what I expect from this form of entertainment.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword can be considered another success for Capcom in 2026. While Onimusha is a more niche series compared to franchises like Resident Evil or Devil May Cry, you don’t need any prior knowledge to enjoy its latest entry. If you’re a fan of action games, Way of the Sword has plenty to offer, from thrilling boss fights and a compelling story with an incredibly likable protagonist to its fascinating world.

Even after the credits roll, the game has enough replay value to make at least one more playthrough worthwhile. So if you’re an action game fan, don’t miss out on this Eastern epic, and treat yourself to an adventure worth experiencing.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword marks a fascinating yet overly conservative return for Capcom's iconic franchise, starring the legendary Miyamoto Musashi. While boasting stunning cinematic direction, top-tier voice acting, and rock-solid technical performance on PS5, the game is held back by a passive AI, an overly permissive difficulty curve, and a combat system that pulls its punches. It's a solid, beautiful foundation for a series revival, though it ultimately lacks the necessary bite to truly master its craft.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword was tasked with reviving a dormant series for a modern, globalised gaming community, and it ultimately has everything it needs to fulfil this task. It does away with overly archaic elements, whilst remaining pleasantly old-school at its core. It boasts a deep and entertaining combat system that doesn’t underestimate the player and doesn’t hand out success on a plate. And that’s not all. Just as the fictional Musashi Miyamoto possesses a gauntlet imbued with the souls of demons, so Onimusha embodies the spirit of captivating horror folklore. I wouldn’t be at all surprised if it sparked an interest in Shinto and yokai amongst players outside Japan, much as Miyazaki’s *Spirited Away* once did. Although there is, of course, considerably more blood and dismembered bodies in Onimusha.

A perfect return to the once-forgotten series, Onimusha: Way of the Sword blends old school nostalgia with modern sensibilities. Action-adventure fans will get comfortable quickly enough, whilst the returning fans will hit the ground running. It looks beautiful, and whilst the English dubbing might be off-putting to some, it's all part of that classic Capcom charm.

Onimusha: Way of the sword left us with contrasting feelings: while the game has for sure great elements, the progression and the choice of expanding the formula by adding mechanics and activities that deviates from the linear structure of the original games are somewhat puzzling, leaving us the feeling the series has lost its original identity.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a fantastic comeback to a classic franchise. Its story is darker and at the same time funnier than I expected, Musashi is a protagonist I genuinely grew to love, and the combat is a real highlight: methodical, demanding and incredibly rewarding once its systems click, with bosses that are as memorable as they are fun to fight. It’s not without flaws, but none of the negatives take away from what matters most. Whether you’re coming back after twenty-odd years or picking up your very first Onimusha, this one is well worth drawing your sword for.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a welcome return of the dormant series that also barely resembles it. Most of the changes are good, like the more aggressive, reaction-based combat and the quality voice acting and animations. Some are questionable, like the bland semi open world and its unappealing side quests. But if this Oni gate can stay open long enough, Way of the Sword is a great first attempt at dragging this series out of purgatory with a lot of potential for greatness.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword takes Capcom’s classic action franchise to new heights thanks to one of the most reactive melee combat systems seen in recent memory, although its blade is dulled slightly by overly complex progression systems.

It’s just that those hiccups keep Onimusha: Way of the Sword from maintaining its best elements. Still, when it wants to, the game can really cut through those basic hangups and deliver a terrific action game.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is an action hack-and-slash game with enormous potential: it's built on a deep and layered combat system, offers a fantastic take on Miyamoto Musashi's character, and projects Capcom's artistic vision into the future, especially in its direction, animation, and production design.
Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a good action game that sets a solid foundation for the series, but its combat needs more offensive options.
Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a worthy return for a series that was popular among many fans. It also honors the name of Miyamoto Musashi—no small feat when dealing with such a major legend.

Onimusha is back, and with a strong entry to make its case as one of Capcom’s best. With responsive combat and great flow between animations, it’s a great time for fans of action games. While some aspects of the original franchise might be a little weak, Way of the Sword managed to build its own identity without feeling too derivative of other titles like it. It starts strong and can only grow from here.

The amount of effort seen here gives me hope for Capcom’s future attempts at reviving classic titles, as Onimusha: Way of the Sword, the latest title of the once dormant franchise, comes back in the best way possible as it very well might be my game of the year contender.
Onimusha: Way of the Sword presents a decent story that’s held up by its absolutely stellar combat.

I may not have expected much from Onimusha: Way of the Sword, but it still found ways to pleasantly surprise me. It’s one of the most enjoyable games I’ve played this year. And much of that is because it’s just so much fun. The game knows what it is and leans into the samurai theme instead of trying to replicate a formula that may have worked for some other developer. When I do get the time, I’ll definitely be chasing every Steam achievement for this game.

It’s for this reason that I give it the Thumb Culture Platinum Award!

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a successful comeback for the long-dormant series. Its fluid combat makes one-on-one duels the game's strongest moments, even if chaotic fights against groups, linear levels and some needless backtracking hold it back.

I really wanted to love this game. Especially because every now and then brilliant highlights shine through showing what could have been. I thoroughly enjoyed the linear sections and the boss fights in particular were so outstanding that they made battling through the rest of the game worthwhile on their own. However Onimusha: Way of the Sword gets so bogged down in extra content that it seems to lose sight of its own strengths, ultimately dragging on for at least 15 hours too long.

Despite its flaws, Onimusha is one of the most fun games of the past nine months, in all its imperfections. This is thanks to a well-structured, well-built combat system, incredible direction, and a damn charismatic protagonist we already miss.

Onimusha Way of the Sword is an extremely solid hack and slash action packed game with a lot of button bashing combat in between the far more technical boss battles (which can be brutally punishing on the normal difficulty setting). Casual gamers might struggle here while seasoned veterans of Soulslike games like Sekiro or Bloodborne will love this.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is an incredible, imperfect game. When it’s good, it’s excellent, and I ended up having a fantastic experience with a series that, until a week ago, meant absolutely nothing to me.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a robust game and a great addition to the Nintendo Switch 2 library. Even with some graphical and performance limitations, particularly when playing in docked mode, the game still delivers a solid experience in handheld mode.

The repetition, some extremely linear sections, and a campaign that feels a bit stretched out do weigh the experience down, but they don’t take away from the fact that this is still a good game. It’s a great choice for longtime fans of the series, as well as anyone who enjoys a good hack-and-slash game, sword-based combat, and a samurai setting mixed with supernatural elements.

It’s not a game I would consider revolutionary in any particular aspect, but it does a good job of keeping you entertained for several hours, even with all the repetition mentioned above.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword delivers a spectacular return for the series, combining deep, fluid sword combat, outstanding boss fights, brutal finishers, and a surprisingly engaging story with a charismatic Miyamoto Musashi. Its excellent main missions, striking atmosphere, and expressive character animations shine, but repetitive side activities, unnecessary grinding, limited enemy variety, and an overly stretched campaign prevent this otherwise fantastic action adventure from reaching its full potential.

Its highs are so high I think it’s well worth traversing the valleys to get there. But those valleys are wide and they’re not getting any narrower. Every once in a while you need to remember that the cookie is every bit as important as the cream in an Oreo, that you need something solid to chew on to enjoy yourself. Onimusha is a tasty cookie, I just wish I could scrap some of the filling out.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a fantastic game. Following Resident Evil Requiem, Monster Hunter Stories 3, and Pragmata, Capcom has achieved a "four out of four" with this game, creating a great series in 2026.
It’s a huge step beyond anything the series did before, and yet it still feels like an Onimusha game in all the right ways.
In an absolutely stacked year so far for Capcom, Onimusha: Way of the Sword is my favorite by a mile.

We can say it loud and clear: this is yet another success for Capcom. Onimusha is back in the spotlight after so many years, and fans will be delighted with the final result. The combat is so fantastic that it carries the entire game. Combined with the boss battles, these are the highlights of the adventure. Not all the elements are perfect—including the use of the semi-open world and the side missions. But that doesn’t stop you from finishing the game with a satisfied smile. And while that may sound simple, it was the goal for a series coming back from the dead.

Even amongst the glut of so many samurai-themed games over this past several years, Onimusha: Way of the Sword stands tall above many of them thanks to its unique tone, style, and exemplary modern approach to hack and slash combat.

Way of the Sword was destined for greatness either way. Its combat is gorgeous both in how it looks and how it plays, its boss encounters are electric, I don't remember the last time I spent time with a cast as magnetic and memorable, and genuinely, I struggle to imagine a game more deserving of its moniker. But the early Onimusha titles were short and sweet. They had backtracking and puzzles and exploration, yet they were tight-knit experiences that still hold up 25 years later because they weren't wasteful. Playing through Way of the Sword's filler, seeing how it pads its runtime, I have to wonder what an absolute juggernaut it would have been had Capcom thought to trim the fat.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword keeps the spirit of the originals while bringing the combat and presentation firmly into the modern era.
.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword upgrades the franchise from the previous era, making for a much more technically challenging game. Instead of fighting fixed camera angles, you are fighting fast enemies with move sets that require precision to overcome. This could easily feel like anything or everything else on the market, but instead, thanks to a clever skill tree of robust abilities, you get a vast amount of tools that require timing to master. It is enough that you can choose which ones to emphasize practicing if others aren’t working out the way you need them to. This elevates the title’s combat from simple hack-and-slash to something creative and enjoyable.
Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a comeback that, personally, I've really enjoyed.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword makes a particularly convincing comeback. Its excellent combat system, memorable boss battles, and polished presentation make this new adventure an incredibly enjoyable action game. Repetitive side activities, frequent backtracking through Kyoto, and a few slower sections keep the experience from reaching true greatness. Still, none of these issues are enough to spoil the pleasure of seeing the return of a franchise that clearly still had plenty to offer.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword marks a triumphant revival for a franchise that has remained in the shadows for far too long, demonstrating how a classic formula can evolve without betraying its original essence. While it stumbles over the typical weaknesses of modern blockbusters—such as an overly convoluted hub and side activities that feel like filler—Capcom’s game shines brightly thanks to a consistently satisfying combat system. Musashi’s commanding presence, the choreographed tension of the epic duels, and the sumptuous art direction powered by the RE Engine crown this return as a must-play for fans of pure action.
A testament to Capcom's years of refining action gameplay, Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a game any action fan can pick up and love — series veteran or not.
A stylish return to classic action, blending feudal Japan’s mysticism with fast-paced combat and cinematic flair.
So what do we make of Onimusha: Way of the Sword? Well, it’s a solid game. The core of its gameplay isn’t groundbreaking: it’s classic, knows what it’s doing, and does it well.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword gets it right that the best moments are putting a sword in your hand and fighting an ever more intriguing series of monsters. Onimusha is back after over two decades, and it’s a game worthy of the name. It’s not flawless, but it’s great combat, great bosses, an amazing presentation, and a great samurai feel, making it one of Capcom’s most successful reboots.

Onimusha Way of The Sword is a return to form for a dormant Capcom franchise, boasting an incredible combat system, albeit one held back by a lack of difficulty options to really take advantage of it, and a middling open ended Kyoto area that overstays its welcome towards the end.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a home run for Capcom. It’s an amazing way of bringing the series back into the forefront of gamers' minds. The series has always had a bit of a struggle with its identity, often just resembling a samurai version of Resident Evil or even, confusingly, a Smash Bros clone at one point. I think Capcom drawing influence from the soulslike style of game couldn’t have worked better; it has all the cinematic flair you would come to expect from the developer while not doing the obvious thing of just copying and leaning on a certain Dante-led series.

​Much like a rose, Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a beauty with a few barbs. The difficulty is going to be mixed for some, and the fluff of the open world can really do a number on the pacing. But all in all, Capcom has once again put the gaming world on notice with a very strong contender for Game of the Year 2026 and has done an amazing job of resurrecting another long-forgotten franchise. I can only hope that one day I can see them bring back another of their dormant series as spectacularly as they have with this one.

Its vague open world in no way detracts from a spectacular combat system, a more-than-interesting story, magnificent and varied boss battles, dreamlike graphics and optimization, and much more. Don’t miss the chance to revisit one of the most important hack-and-slash franchises in history—one that even served as inspiration for the first *God of War* on the PS2—in what is likely a once-in-a-lifetime year for the great Capcom.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword manages to impress at times thanks to its fluid animations and deep mechanics. While it could have benefited from more focused project management to fully realize its potential, it is still a game that demonstrates that things are going in the right direction at Capcom.

This is how you revive a dormant series. Capcom did not rely on nostalgia or imitate every modern action game around it. It found an identity in the physical clash of swords, then built a funny, bloody, surprisingly heartfelt adventure around that foundation. I started with no history with Onimusha and finished convinced that Way of the Sword belongs beside Capcom's very best work.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a successful revival of a franchise that had been dormant for 20 years, thanks to its utterly addictive and rewarding combat, a cast of characters that really captivated me, and superb animations that raise the bar for games in this genre. Whilst there is still room for improvement in a potential sequel, this is nonetheless an action title that continues the winning streak for the Japanese studio, which had already enjoyed a historic year full of successes with players, thus adding yet another hit to its portfolio.

Powerhouse Capcom has been knocking it out of the park with its releases this year, and Onimusha: Way of the Sword is no exception. This game has it all: stunning cutscenes and character models, phenomenal Japanese voice acting, impressive performance on the Switch 2, and an incredibly smooth combat system that makes it hard to put the controller down. So, free up your schedule and sharpen your swords, because there is Genma to slay!

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is an excellent revival of Onimusha. The strengths of the franchise's modernization easily stand out, elevating the game to a level that makes it a great title in its genre. The combat system's potential is formidable, turning challenging boss battles into moments of pure tension that deliver immense satisfaction upon completion. Musashi is also one of the series' best protagonists; his mannerisms are entertaining, and his character development is a major highlight of the narrative.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is an excellent and bold reinvention of Capcom’s iconic franchise. The game more than rewards fans for the long wait with one of the most impressive and satisfying combat systems the series has ever seen, complemented by a superb technical presentation and a charismatic, deeply engaging reinterpretation of its story.

Way of the Sword is a game with great fighting, exciting boss fights, an interesting lead character, and great presentation, the kind of game that can keep you riveted to the screen despite its limitations. If you ask me what’s the most important thing about this new Onimusha, my answer is simple: this game knows sword fighting.

Capcom essentially "issen"-ed its way back into every action gamer fan's heart with this fifth mothership samurai-versus-demons-and-soul-vacuuming action entry. With a likeable protagonist, beautiful aesthetics, spot-on controls and fighting, and memorable boss encounters, there's never a better time to get into Onimusha than with this big-budget samurai supernatural combo.
Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a truly excellent comeback, as it demonstrates once again how purely action-oriented games can evolve without losing their soul.

Capcom has another solid title on its hands. Onimusha: Way of the Sword sounds at odds on paper. A goofy rice bun eating samurai amidst a sea of dead villagers and ferocious Genma sounds like tonal whiplash but Capcom nails this balance. Musashi is now one of my favourite protagonists in the action genre and the moment to moment combat, despite a slow start, builds into some of the best boss battles I’ve seen in some time. There is some run of the mill padding that detracts from the spectacle and visuals that don’t hold up outside of cutscenes. But these issues don’t get in the way of what Onimusha does best: a goofy character that I’ll continue to follow into hell, with my own rice bun in hand.
With sharp combat and a story mixing humor and weight, Onimusha: Way of the Sword is the kind of well-written, stylish revival fans have waited decades for.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a masterclass of action, blending fast-paced swordplay with graceful character movement for an experience that feels both fantastical and grounded. Rather than sticking to the formula of its predecessors, it takes bold risks and delivers an unforgettable story about the greatest swordsman who ever lived. Capcom couldn’t have closed out its stellar year on a higher note.
Onimusha: Way of the Sword shines with excellent combat, fantastic bosses, and a Musashi full of personality. Some sections slow the pace down, but when it gets good, it gets really good.

No longer slumbering, Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a fully realized successor to Onimusha that makes it more than it ever was. CAPCOM has managed to reinvent and reinvigorate the series for new and old fans. Onimusha: Way of the Sword offers excellent soulslike combat and systems within a character action game, representing a new hybridization of game design I’m all for. Parries carry the game to make the combat exciting, deep, and rewarding. As Takamura Ono says, “Just sublime, boy.”

Onimusha: The Way of the Sword lowers the barrier to entry with relatively easy parrying, while still delivering that satisfying combat feel for veterans through the series' signature 'Issen' mechanic. Furthermore, it attractively reinterprets familiar narratives by weaving bizarre occurrences at historical locations into captivating 'ghost stories'.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a fantastic revival of the franchise that once again proves that Capcom can seemingly do no wrong this console generation. The sheer quality of the blade-to-blade combat, the gorgeous visuals, and the epic storytelling make it impossible to put the controller down, with Onimusha: Way of the Sword offering a deeply rewarding adventure that honours its PlayStation 2 roots whilst carving out a brilliant new path for the franchise.
Manages to effectively straddle the line between quicker action and deeper satisfying sword combat

Onimusha: Way of the Sword opens up a bright future for the series, providing plenty of room to refine existing ideas and introduce new solutions. Ultimately, it may move away from what defined the original game, but it does so in a way that can appeal to both new and longtime fans through a polished, high-quality structure.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword delivers exhilarating swordplay built around intricate clashes and counters, while the charismatic Miyamoto Musashi and a strong emotional cast keep the journey compelling. Its open world can feel tedious and parts of the story fall short, but none of that dulls the brilliance of its combat—an experience so satisfying that simply fighting is reason enough to keep playing.

I haven’t embraced its open world map quite as much as Capcom probably hoped I would, but those are minor issues. All in all, despite my already sky-high expectations, Onimusha: Way of the Sword ended up being even better than I could have anticipated. By borrowing elements from pretty much every acclaimed samurai game out there, it somehow manages to create a gameplay loop that feels entirely like its own thing. It’s got heart, it’s a feast for the eyes, and it boasts one of the best combat systems I’ve experienced in recent memory.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a very good action game that suffers from a fair amount of unnecessary repetition. Despite this significant flaw, it offers plenty of enjoyable gameplay that’s both spectacular and challenging, especially on higher difficulty levels. If you’re a fan of this kind of gameplay, you’ll find plenty to keep you entertained for hours.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a triumphant return for the series, with Issen-based combat that rewards precision and risk like few action games before it, anchored by a magnetic protagonist and genuinely moving storytelling.

Capcom’s long-awaited return to the Onimusha series after 20 years lives up to the name. Starring Japan’s legendary swordsman Miyamoto Musashi, Onimusha: Way of the Sword delivers sword combat worthy of its protagonist, showcasing katana-based action at its finest.

The game’s deliberately slower combat pace may sound awkward on paper, but thanks to its high-quality animations and finely tuned combat system, it instead becomes one of the game’s greatest strengths. Musashi himself, brought to life with the facial likeness of Toshiro Mifune, is also charismatic enough to carry the story and makes it easy to become invested in his journey.
Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a well-crafted, atmospherically dense comeback that impresses with solid combat mechanics, strong presentation, and a polished German localization.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword marks a successful return for a series that had been absent from the spotlight for a long time. Capcom has managed to modernize the formula without losing the unique character that made Onimusha stand out, with the combat system undoubtedly being its greatest strength.
Onimusha: Way of the Sword delivers an excellent combat system and epic boss battles, but its game structure stretches itself unnecessarily, resulting in too much repetition.
Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a superb samurai action game with exceptional combat, memorable bosses, strong characters, and a striking horror tone.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is one of those games where, whilst playing, I found myself thinking time and again: “Blimey, this is phenomenal.” The combat, in particular, left a lasting impression on me. The combination of parries, dodges, Issen attacks and spectacular boss battles ensures that you’ll want to draw that sword time and time again. The Japanese atmosphere, music and visual splendour also make this a particularly atmospheric adventure. Unfortunately, the repetitive Malice and Rift missions, recurring sub-bosses and the inevitable back-and-forth running mean the game doesn’t quite reach perfection. But I thoroughly enjoyed it. Even when I got thoroughly beaten as Musashi, I found myself staring at the screen with a smile. Following Resident Evil 9: Requiem and PRAGMATA, Capcom proves once again that it still knows how to deliver top-class games. With Onimusha: Way of the Sword, the company has hit the bullseye once more.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a spectacular, challenging samurai action game that will put your reflexes to the test in a ruthless way. It isn’t a ‘soulslike’, but it draws on some of its principles to create electrifying combat.

That kind of comeback after twenty years makes up for the wait. The dynamic combat and boss fights are the best thing that happened to action games this year. It’s just a shame that, in between them, the game makes you do the exact same thing for a few hours too long.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword delivers a truly immersive experience, featuring breathtaking visuals that vividly bring its fantastical world to life, alongside engaging gameplay that keeps players captivated throughout. Its compelling storyline adds depth and emotional weight, showcasing Capcom's skill in creating a masterpiece that stands as a strong contender for Game of the Year.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a successful comeback for a series that has been absent for far too long.
