The combat system is precise and entirely built around timing, undoubtedly representing the greatest strength of this new chapter in Capcom's franchise, while the atmosphere of a Kyoto overrun by Genma malice manages to deliver some truly evocative moments. Some limitations in the side activities and a certain degree of repetition prevent the adventure from reaching excellence, but Musashi and his journey through a world of samurai and demons still manage to leave their mark. A compact, spectacular experience that remains, above all, faithful to the spirit of the Onimusha franchise.

​Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a bloody and satisfying return for a series that has been missing for far too long. The brutal sword-fighting, interesting story, incredible environments and entertaining dialogue kept me hooked, even when the camera decided to fight me harder than the Genma. Onimusha is finally back, and it was well worth the wait.

If you’re a fan of action games, samurai, Japanese history, demonic fantasy, or simply great sword combat, Onimusha: Way of the Sword should definitely be on your radar. An excellent comeback that further confirms Capcom’s impressive form.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a must-play because Capcom has managed to recapture its essence and adapt it to the modern era. The combat system is undoubtedly its greatest strength, delivering some spectacular moments. Add to that a fantastic setting, memorable boss battles, and top-notch audiovisuals. Not everything is on the same level, but it proves that the franchise has an excellent foundation for the series’ future.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is an action-packed welcome back that’ll give fans both new and old something to be excited about. It’s a game that respects the past with its familiarity while also inserting its own flavor to make it stand on its own against other single player narrative games while even paying homage to action games that more or less could’ve replaced it.

Capcom has modernised the formula without sanding off its personality, combining deliberate swordplay, grotesque demons, and a rather rollicking adventure marked with dark twists and turns. The end result is a bloody, stylish and surprisingly amusing-in-spots slasher that understands the appeal of cutting through Genma demons with increasing degrees of supernatural bullshit. It’s not trying to be Warlords again. It’s forging its own blade. And after nearly two decades of waiting, I’m more than happy to be storing it up on my katanakake with the older ones.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword offers a solid foundation in certain aspects, particularly with its protagonist, Musashi. In addition to the combat system and several distinctive ideas in its boss encounters. However, the game did not utilize these elements well due to a lack of enemy variety, an overly easy difficulty curve, lackluster level and quest design, and shallow exploration. These shortcomings held the experience far below its true potential, ultimately rendering the game a wasted opportunity on all fronts.

Rebooting a classic franchise is never an easy task, but Onimusha: Way of the Sword pulls it off with precision, delivering a fun, action-packed samurai adventure that will appeal to both veterans and newcomers to Capcom’s saga. The fact that even its occasional difficulty spikes don't prevent a recommendation proves it is well worth wielding the Oni Gauntlet and putting an end to the demonic hordes as Miyamoto Musashi. And, fortunately for us, the Switch 2 is a great platform for doing just that.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword not only rescues the franchise but elevates it to a new level, positioning itself as one of the best games in Capcom's recent history. The edge of the sword has been sharpened with perfection, patience, and respect for the source material. Without a doubt, one of the best releases of the year!
Way of the Sword borrows just enough from that genre to feel current without losing its own identity, making it approachable even for players who normally avoid Soulslikes.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is one of the best action games you'll play in 2026 - Capcom is once again at the top of its game with thrilling combat, boss fight spectacles, and a charismatic, endearing protagonist in Musashi.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword successfully modernises the series without losing its identity, pairing precise combat and satisfying Issen mechanics with strong historical fantasy storytelling. The semi-linear structure and mundane side activities occasionally disappoint, but polished presentation and rewarding mastery make this a confident revival.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a game that has surprised us immensely. It manages to adapt the franchise to modern standards without losing its identity or its dark fantasy atmosphere. The depth of its combat system, the spectacular nature of its boss fights, and the meticulous work on the animation and Japanese folklore more than compensate for minor aspects such as the repetitiveness of some side quests. Despite this, Onimusha: Way of the Sword—unexpectedly—is easily one of the best games we've played in 2026.
Onimusha - Way of the Sword delivers great Action and boss battles, but stumbles over itself. The modernising, soulless way of the open world has dulled this warrior's blade.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is Capcom's best game of 2026—a title featuring cutting-edge visuals, a protagonist who ranks among the company's finest, and combat that will leave players jaw-dropped. A triumph.
Capcom is on a roll and continues to be so with a great revival of Onimusha. Way of the Sword feels great to play, the action is slick and tense, while the story is fun but a bit campy as well.
Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a rare kind of comeback — deep, demanding combat wrapped around genuine charisma, honoring twenty years of legacy while welcoming newcomers with open arms.

With "Onimusha: Way of the Sword," Capcom successfully continues its impressive series of great video game adventures, delivering one of the biggest highlights of 2026 for fans of hardcore sword-fighting action.

In the end, the return of Onimusha through this release proves Capcom's serious effort to revive one of its most venerable franchises in a style that blends the spirit of the past with modern-day challenges, smartly drawing inspiration from combat mechanics in games like Sekiro. While the game shone by delivering intense and challenging boss battles, alongside a stable technical performance that serves fast-paced movement, it faced a few clear obstacles. The weak AI of regular enemies and the dullness of the linear design for main missions negatively impacted the adventure's pacing, in addition to a drab visual tone that dimmed the luster of the game's world. Nevertheless, the experience remains an enjoyable and worthwhile stop for fans of the series and samurai game enthusiasts, provided you overlook a few missteps in balance and overall difficulty level.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword shines with fantastic gameplay, which, thanks to its abundance of parries and defensive mechanics, can even rival Sekiro. The mix of dark, grotesque themes and a slightly naive sense of humor has been successfully wrapped in a modern presentation and, together with the compelling story and wide variety of boss fights, makes for a highly enjoyable experience.

Unfortunately, the sheer number of bosses, along with the somewhat average NPCs, starts to wear thin fairly quickly. Combined with the uneven difficulty curve, this is the game's biggest weakness. However, if you can live with these shortcomings, you're getting one of the best action RPGs of recent years.

Things like a slow start or some of the protagonist’s highly repetitive lines during battles detract a bit from the overall experience, but the boss battles are a clear highlight of Onimusha: Way of the Sword. With about 20–25 hours of gameplay, the title also offers a satisfying length, and some special boss battles will require you to use all your skills. An absolute must-have for fans of the series, and for fans of action-adventure games, the demo alone should be enough to win you over.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword returns after 20 years with an impressive boss-battling experience, featuring deep combat mechanics and cinematic encounters. While its story and exploration fall short of expectations, the game is still worth experiencing, especially for fans of sword-based combat, Souls-like games, and hack-and-slash titles.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a triumphant return for the series, delivering a combat system that is both intricate, deliberate, and immensely satisfying, with extreme highs. Every duel demands precision, timing, and awareness, rewarding players who master its mechanics with exhilarating victories. Battles feel like true tests of skill rather than simple button‑mashing encounters, giving players a risk‑reward tension from the Issen counters to the tactical depth of stamina management and Blade Barrages.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword marks a strong comeback for Capcom’s series, modernizing itself without losing its gritty, blood‑soaked charm. With a magnetic lead like Musashi, memorable foes, and a combat system built on precision and reading the opponent, the adventure stays engaging throughout. Despite some flaws — uneven progression, recycled enemies, and basic side missions — the overall experience remains solid, fun, and surprisingly inspired. Its striking aesthetics and excellent Italian voice acting elevate the whole package, and when a game makes you crave a second run right after finishing it, you know it hit the mark. Onimusha is back, sharp enough to leave a lasting cut.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is some damn good fun, providing an action packed adventure I thoroughly enjoyed. Musashi's journey may obviously detour from his real life exploits, but the bond of strength he has with Ganryu makes for a compelling rivalry that sets this game apart from its peers. From compelling combat to a fantastic cast of characters and bosses, Way of the Sword was well worth the wait, and I can’t help but want more.
Some issues with repetition aside, Onimusha: Way of the Sword's phenomenal combat and compelling characters make this a worthwhile samurai romp.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a fantastic return for Capcom's classic samurai action series. Its brutal and satisfying combat, excellent pacing, strong writing, and cinematic presentation make it feel like a true Onimusha game, even after twenty years away. While some visual inconsistencies hold it back slightly, Way of the Sword is an excellent action game and a welcome reminder of why this series was so beloved.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword takes its time to show you what it does best, but once it does, there's a lot to love. Satisfying samurai combat, superb storytelling, and a beautifully grim world make this long-awaited action adventure a great title for newcomers and longtime fans alike.
Onimusha: Way of the Sword returns with a bloody new adventure that cuts deep with satisfying combat, a charismatic protagonist, and a supernatural world that’s claw-some from start to finish.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword proves that a franchise doesn't need to return exactly as we remembered it to remain recognizable. Capcom modernizes its combat, expands its exploration, and builds one of the most attractive art directions of this new era without losing the souls, the Genma, and the dark fantasy that have always defined the series. Its story may not always carry the same weight and its soundtrack might fly slightly under the radar, but once the katana leaves its sheath, it's hard not to celebrate Onimusha's return among us. A brilliant, solid comeback with scars that, far from hiding the passage of time, end up becoming part of its new identity.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a fantastic revival the series has needed for a while. Its satisfying combat is the obvious highlight, with Issen, parries, deflects, and Oni abilities giving you plenty of ways to approach enemies and show off, while the excellent latter bosses constantly push you to master the core kit. Musashi is also a surprisingly likable protagonist, and I was genuinely impressed by how invested I became in the story and its side characters. The game does take a bit too long to properly challenge you, and its exploration is a bit unambitious, but these are relatively minor complaints. With fantastic animation work, a rewarding combat system, memorable bosses, and a surprisingly engaging story, Way of the Sword feels like exactly the kind of comeback Onimusha deserved.
Onimusha: Way of the Sword is an excellent choice for both veterans and newcomers to the series, and it succeeds in revitalizing the series’ reputation, making it feel fresh and modern.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a spectacular revival built around sublime, ever-evolving combat, striking Genma design and memorable boss battles. Repetitive side activities dull the blade slightly, but little else gets in Musashi’s way.
Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a real triumph for Capcom. They've modernized the franchise and offered fans of cinematic action games a title you simply can't miss.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is the modern revival that fans have been waiting decades for. It exudes charm through its comedy and fantastic cast of characters, while delivering intense combat and swordplay. While the console version does have some issues with lighting outside of cutscenes, and its story and side content could’ve done a better job matching the spectacle that the combat brings, it makes for a fun and entertaining action title.
Capcom pushes all boundaries once again with Onimusha: Way of the Sword by delivering a compelling narrative alongside one of the most reactive and engaging combat systems in the genre.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is not just a tribute to a classic franchise, a legendary character, a memorable actor, and a rich culture like the Japanese one. It feels much more like the beginning of a new phase. If this is indeed the path Capcom intends to follow, bring on more demons.
Way of the Sword brings Onimusha back with exceptional combat, but not quite the consistency to make its return truly great.

"A powerful comeback for a legendary series"
Onimusha: Way of the Sword proves that classic series can keep up with the times without losing their identity, thanks to a deep and fluid combat system, a distinctive Japanese horror atmosphere, and a stunning visual world. 
While the numerous mechanics might take some getting used to, the experience remains powerful and perfect, worthy of the Onimusha name.

After Resident Evil Requiem and Pragmata, I was expecting a Capcom hat trick. It didn't quite work out. *Onimusha: Way of the Sword* is a very good game, but it lacks the very quality that most recently set the developer apart from the competition: focus.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is an excellent action game and a worthy rebirth for the series after decades of absence. Its combat system is deep and, above all, rewarding, even if it takes some patience to master, while the fights have a strong, realistic feel and the story has a cinematic impact. Too bad for the repetitiveness of the final hours and the sometimes excessive difficulty, but it's a title worth trying if you are looking for a stimulating action game.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword delivers an enjoyable and well-rounded samurai experience worthy of the legendary historical figure Miyamoto Musashi, whether in terms of gameplay, overall design, performance, or technical stability. However, it stumbles slightly in its storytelling, which may not appeal to everyone. Nevertheless, it remains a strong return for the series and a standout experience for fans of samurai games.

stalker-2-heart-of-chornobyl-cost-of-hop.title: S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2: Heart of Chornobyl - Cost of Hope

reviews.excerpt: Metacritic user score 8.3/10 (145 ratings).

If you haven’t played S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2, ‘Cost of Hope’ marks the perfect time to jump in. Though be warned, this is a story expansion that requires you to have nearly completed the main campaign. It is seamlessly blended into the progression of the story, and it is fantastic. Genuinely scary moments abound, with the title’s trademark gunplay feeling better than ever. Consider playing in the native VO, and lose yourself in the zone.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2 returns to the Zone with The Price of Hope and, above all, an "Update 2.0" that significantly refines the experience. The DLC expands the rivalry between Duty and Freedom with new missions and two endings—preserving open-world freedom—though it suffers from narrative consequences that remain confined to the expansion itself. The update improves lighting, A-Life mechanics, fog effects, balancing, and difficulty customization, while adding new weapons, optics, and binoculars. The result is a more vibrant, solid, and complete adventure, even if some content arrived noticeably late and we will likely be stuck with certain minor enemy AI quirks forever.

STALKER 2's Cost of Hope expansion represents the next generation of a beloved franchise, but this time, it sets the stage for the most major evolution we've ever seen. It's a haunting, emotional, and twisting expansion that might not be perfect, but comes damn close.

Stalker 2 has received its first major expansion—as well as its biggest update to date—and the game is moving in a very positive direction. The foundation was solid at launch, but through successive fixes, improvements, and new content, it is increasingly becoming the game it was always meant to be.

As you wander through the Iron Forest, the care put into its reconstruction is immediately apparent—matching the level of detail found in the locations from the main adventure. The same holds true for the other areas: the aforementioned power plant and the Space Bubble. The latter is a surreal, labyrinthine setting that hosts one of the game's most intense and evocative levels, featuring staircases suspended in the void, rooms reminiscent of Piranesi’s *Imaginary Prisons*, and a generally unsettling atmosphere. This backdrop sets the stage for the plot's pivotal turning point, where Skif, the protagonist, is forced to pick a side. Regarding choices, the experience remains close to the base game: both factions have their own valid reasons and moral ambiguities. In gameplay terms, "choosing" also means following one of two branching paths, which differ in specific missions and narrative moments. In this respect, *Cost of Hope* offers genuine replayability for those who want to see absolutely everything. The themes are also classic, centering on whether or not to exploit the Zone for a greater good—even at the cost of sacrificing many lives and permanently destroying relationships that were already incredibly fragile.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2: Cost of Hope is a fantastic expansion that builds on what made the base game so compelling, even as its slow-burn pacing and punishing gameplay remain largely unchanged. Its strong narrative on two of the series’ popular factions, as well as its deeper dive into the convoluted science-fiction mythos makes it a worthwhile return to the Zone. The addition of Update 2.0 and two new explorable regions, including the iconic CNPP, gives longtime fans more than enough reason to soak in the Roentgens and smell the irradiated roses.
An almost perfect story DLC, even if I have to grit my teeth a little.

Cost of Hope works because it understands that S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2 did not simply need more land, but places, encounters and choices that make exploration meaningful again. Iron Forest, the Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant and the Space Bubble succeed where the base game could sometimes feel too spread out. Duty and Freedom bring back one of the series’ defining conflicts, even if the characters remain weaker than the ideas they represent. The bestiary plays it safe, but stronger mission design and denser spaces make up for it. Update 2.0 improves the whole experience, but it should remain separate from the DLC’s value.

STALKER 2: Cost of Hope DLC is an excellent story expansion that delivers a new route for Skif to either contain/destroy or explore the Zone. The introduction to the two new major factions feels impactful, and the main characters from each of these factions are likeable. Not only does this DLC expand on the Story, but also on the Zone itself. You get to explore two new regions in the Zone, including the long-awaited CNPP. There are new weapons, new secrets, and new Artifacts to help you in this new chapter of the story.  On top of this new content, Update 2.0 makes the whole game even better with the engine rework.

The best version of S.T.A.L.K.E.R 2, whether you’re a new player or returning veteran. Update 2.0 and Cost of Hope’s DLC missions combine to deliver an impactful experience that is brutal, rewarding, and best when it lets humanity shine.

I can say straight away the expansion is good; it explores classic factions, offers new areas, and new characters. It also features new dangers, weapons, and new equipment. Although there are significantly fewer missions than in the base game, they are of a relatively much higher quality in terms of mission design and level design, and they'll particularly appeal to those of you who really enjoyed the first game and its expansions. I still think it's worth it for new players as the story is gripping, the weapons are quite useful for the rest of the adventure, the mutants offer more variety, and the binoculars are brilliant for the flatter, open environments you explore in the base game. The expansion could have included a few more new missions, radio tracks, and additional mutants, but overall it expands the world in a good way and all the fresh content fits seamlessly with the main campaign. If you're playing S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2, I think you should snap this up.
I persisted in spite of the horrors, because the rest of what’s on offer in Cost of Hope is so stellar and well worth picking up.
S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2 has finally been tidied up enough.

While S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2: Heart of Chornobyl was already a great open-world game, Update 2.0 and Cost of Hope have pushed it even further, regardless of whether you’re a franchise die-hard or a new player.

STALKER 2: Cost of Hope is an excellent expansion thanks to its engaging story centered around beloved factions, deeper worldbuilding, and some of the most memorable missions in the game. It could easily stand on its own as a shorter spin-off. Its substantial amount of content gets off to a somewhat slow start, but then builds steadily toward a grand finale. It’s just a shame that it ultimately has no more significant impact on the world itself. If you’ve been hesitant about another trip to the Zone, though, it’s never been in better shape.

The expansion Cost of Hope offers the perfect opportunity to dive into the world of Stalker 2. For just under 30 euros – or for owners of the Ultimate Edition – you get a very intense and extensive campaign that tells a gripping story. At the same time, the new patch delivers numerous visual and technical improvements, ensuring that this atmospheric shooter is more playable than ever before. However, you should still expect a few rough edges when it comes to presentation and performance. Furthermore, ‘Cost of Hope’ repeatedly gets in its own way with clumsy gameplay elements.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2: Cost of Hope left me with mixed emotions. On one hand, it is the best of S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2, with iconic new areas to explore and a return to the franchise’s sense of mystery and horror unlike anything else in the base game. However, it is hard to escape the feeling that much of the DLC is content from the main game, repackaged and sold for an additional price. While I would highly recommend any S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2 fans give the DLC a try, I would understand if they were left feeling a bit jaded by the cost of entry.
Metacritic user score 8.8/10 (107 ratings).

I’m left feeling thoroughly satisfied with this grand new addition to a game I already loved. If you’re someone who’s been starving for Dragon’s Dogma content for a few years, then this is just about everything you were hoping for, and if you’re someone who bounced off the base game, then a lot of the more notable points of friction have been eased. Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen is a tighter and more focused DLC that still manages to bring in very nearly everything about what made the base game such an incredible experience.
Dark Arisen has not only made Dragon’s Dogma 2 a must-play RPG, but it’s also one of Capcom’s best games in years.

Returning to Dragon's Dogma II is a treat in itself, but tack on a couple dozen hours of fantastic new content in a harsh but beautiful new region, and this is the best the game has ever been. Dark Arisen's unique loot cycle and challenging encounters work alongside a compelling new story to make it worth every penny.

If you love the idea of a grand fantasy adventure and experience a truly unique and immersive single-player game where you feel as if you’re actually accompanied by real players going on treacherous adventures together, with great moment-to-moment gameplay, then please, please play Dragon’s Dogma 2, then continue your adventure into Dark Arisen DLC and the cold lands of Norgan.

Dragon's Dogma 2: Dark Arisen is often Capcom's open world RPG at its absolute peak. It's one hell of a meaty expansion, delivering a surprisingly involved story, joyous exploration, and deeply compelling combat. A transformative DLC.

Whether you’re a lapsed Arisen returning to the world of Dragon’s Dogma or a curious newcomer finally taking the plunge after Capcom’s stellar track record convinced you it was worth it, Dark Arisen proves to be an absolute delight. It builds upon the excellent foundation Capcom’s been polishing for the past two years, with sharp combat and engaging exploration. It challenges you with brutal new trials, all the while making the grind less unbearable. It cements Dragon’s Dogma 2 as an unforgettable experience.

Dragon’s Dogma II: Dark Arisen does what the original expansion had accomplished and set the bar with 20 hours more. With both Dark Arisen’s original premise and the Lost Rites challenges, there is more things to do, fight, and see, within the world even before deciding to end it at the finishing fight. While some things do remain the same from its 2024 base, the effort and vastness make up for it doesn’t demand a slow crawl, but a satisfying slow pain-and-gain run. For those who could tear themselves away from Crimson Desert, this Action RPG might be for you.

The Dark Arisen expansion for Dragon’s Dogma 2 adds a ton of new content to the base game, along with much-needed quality-of-life improvements that make the overall experience the most definitive one yet. If you enjoyed the base game, Dark Arisen is a must-play.

Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen is an excellent expansion that builds on the base game's strongest elements while ironing out enough of the friction its weaker parts caused upon release. It advances the foundations of its exploration and combat loop, making it feel like the definitive version of those systems and something worth diving into right away.

Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen is what expansions are truly about. The wholly distinct and dangerous region of Norgan sends players to explore the treacherous cold for new threats. What will be uncovered is a rich story, phenomenal encounters, and a wealth of new content that pushes Dragon’s Dogma 2 into the territory of an unforgettable journey.
Dark Arisen may not quite be perfect, but as a whole package, Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen is easy to recommend to anyone hunting for their next grand adventure.

Dragon's Dogma 2 Dark Arisen is an expansion that makes returning to this fantasy world well worth the effort, introducing a new region with harsh weather conditions and formidable enemies, alongside a series of fresh challenges in the base game that reward players with exciting loot. It provides a compelling reason to revisit the adventure while serving as an excellent addition that should not be missing from the collection of longtime fans or newcomers experiencing the game for the first time.

Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen breaks new ground, takes risks and doesn’t settle for offering more of the same. Capcom has delivered a very special DLC, featuring unique and imperfect ideas that redefine and transform this massive and unique RPG.

Dragon's Dogma 2: Dark Arisen is an amalgamation of coolness thanks to a superb base game, impressive new area, and lots of challenges that'll really test your mettle as well as put all your swanky new gear through the wringer.
Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen is an excellent addition to an already meaty game. If you liked the base game, Dark Arisen offers even more difficult challenges alongside even greater rewards.

Dark Arisen is a solid expansion that expands Dragon's Dogma 2 with new challenges, plenty of exploration, and systems that make progression more interesting. Despite the lack of new vocations and some uninspired side quest choices, the expansion fulfills its purpose and reinforces the feeling that the franchise still has a lot of potential.

Dragon’s Dogma 2 Dark Arisen is a thoroughly enjoyable expansion to what was already one of my favourite action RPGs, thanks to a smart new loot system and an entirely new region to explore and fight in.

Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen might not be the ultimate expansion, but it is a substantial one. The new content is excellent and there’s even more for mid-level and post-game players to enjoy. New players get the benefit of recent updates, but they’ll need to have a couple dozen levels of time invested to survive any of the new stuff. Of course, getting there will be a pleasure. Dragon’s Dogma 2 Dark Arisen is a must-have expansion for current players already enjoying one of the best ARPGs on the market.

Dark Arisen is a substantial expansion that does more than just pad the runtime; it actively refines and elevates the core Dragon's Dogma 2 experience. By weaving in sweeping additions, from a dynamic new weather system and refined traversal tools like the grappling hook and fast travel, to challenging dungeons, boss fights, and fresh skills, the expansion successfully broadens the world and delivers the kind of compelling new hurdles that make returning to the journey entirely worthwhile.

Dark Arisen marks the point at which Dragon’s Dogma 2 should reach the apex of its mainstream appeal with action RPG players, having been strenuously polished and consistently putting its best foot forward. One of this generation’s greatest adventures beckons players back with a cold twist on its formula that fully exploits its wintry conceits.

Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen is an expansion that adds an interesting twist to the base game. It builds on the main adventure with a new region, an overhauled loot system, more challenging quests, and memorable bosses. While it leaves a few existing flaws untouched, it remains a DLC well worth considering.
An engrossing expansion full of interesting new characters and vibrant enemies.

Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen is a fantastic new expansion that improves the base game in many ways. While some of the base game’s worst parts impact the overall experience, the negatives aren’t enough to overshadow its amazing elements.

Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen is an excellent expansion packed with over 40 hours of new adventures, spectacular boss battles, rewarding exploration, and a densely designed new region. Its uneven difficulty, relentless encounters, and inventory-cluttering loot system can be frustrating, but Norgan is still an essential journey for every Dragon’s Dogma 2 fan and a compelling reason to return for those disappointed by the original launch.

Dark Arisen may not add a whole lot to Dragon's Dogma 2 in terms of new ideas and mechanics, but the icy tundra of Norgan is a joy to explore and the frictional systems of the game shine through just as strongly as ever.

Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen serves up a new land with a surprising amount of content. The move to the chilled north adds hours for returning players and sands off many of the rough edges the base game had. The downside, though, is that much of the friction is gone, and as much as I like streamlined experiences, I never once thought Dragon’s Dogma needed it. The campaign is a surprising blast, with Norgan offering an excellent new land, a new loot system, and challenges to overcome.

Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen is an excellent expansion that makes an already enjoyable RPG all the better. It does have its shortcomings and doesn’t fix all the original’s problems, but they rarely overshadow its accomplishments. More importantly, Dark Arisen understands what makes Dragon’s Dogma special: the freedom to venture into an unfamiliar world and discover adventures through exploration. Returning players will find plenty of reasons to jump back in, while those disappointed by the original game’s difficulty and progression may finally discover the experience they wanted. It doesn’t fix everything, but Dark Arisen is a fantastic adventure that makes the game worth playing again or for the first time.

Dragon's Dogma 2: Dark Arisen was the final piece needed to bring this sequel to its peak; however, I believe the quality of the narrative and side quests could have been handled better. On the other hand, the expansion delivers a beautiful, challenging new realm, offering an exploration experience that truly captivates thanks to its distinct atmosphere.

If you liked Dragon’s Dogma 2, you will certainly love the expansion as well. The expansion delivers more linear storytelling with decent characters, without the necessity of a complex political story running the plot in the background. You’ll encounter new creatures that can put up a fight and challenge your capabilities, but it also stimulates the player to explore the region in order to find these new relics that can help with upcoming battles along the way. This expansion offers a lot of new equipment and weapons with randomized abilities that can help with developing the perfect build for your adventure. It stimulates you to be adventurous, and that’s a good thing. New abilities for your vocations are also a big plus. This expansion is aimed at fans; if you wanted something different from this expansion, you’ll move on to another RPG. You won’t miss out on anything groundbreaking.

We missed having some substantial new features—such as a new vocation or an additional system to spice up combat. Instead, just like in the original title, having a well-balanced party—featuring a healer and a mage capable of casting devastating spells like Meteor Shower, backed by a couple of tanks or DPS—is enough to overcome even the toughest foes. The constant hunt for more powerful gear might appeal to a certain type of player, but once you reach a power level sufficient to handle any threat, there isn't much left to do. Or rather, something is missing to make facing yet another... compelling.

I wanted to like Dragon's Dogma 2 more than I did, but I can't say the same about Dark Arisen's new content. I just have a twinge of disappointment. What started as an exciting return to an underappreciated series sadly turned into a bit of a slog, with fight after fight starting to feel like little more than button mashing.

Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen is a substantial upgrade to an already enjoyable RPG, adding a new adventure in Norgan while improving many aspects of the base game. The new story is a major improvement over the base game’s narrative, while the addition of new vocation skills, expanded weapon skill slots, Relic Appraisal, and the Lost Rites dungeons makes this the definitive version of Dragon’s Dogma 2. On the other hand, some of the original game’s problems remain, with repetitive enemies and pacing issues holding it back. Fans of Dragon’s Dogma 2 will find plenty to enjoy here, but those who struggled to connect with the original game may not find enough to change their minds. For RPGamers looking for a strong sense of adventure and an absolutely beautiful world to get lost in, Dark Arisen is worth considering.

A meaty DLC that continues the game’s strong points, and with the recent improvements to the game provides a smoother experience than ever before. Not radical enough to recommend without reservations, but to those who can’t get enough of the game it’s a pleasant diversion.
With a new landmass to explore and new creatures to tackle, Dark Arisen presents a stern challenge even for high level players, in this enjoyably challenging new expansion.

Control Resonant is the portrait of a bolder studio. Remedy is never scared of taking risks, and that shows through many ways in this game. Bizarre, inventive and extremely fun to play, Control Resonant will probably be running for all the prizes it can by the end of the year.

Control Resonant gambles on a new genre and it pays off. A stellar cast and some of the strongest art direction you'll find in a game this year make for a sequel that builds on the promise of the original, and delivers even more special moments. Make time for Control Resonant this year. You won't regret it.

With its incredibly fun traversal mechanics and edge-of-your-seat action gameplay, the end result is one of the most imaginative action RPGs I’ve played in years and Remedy Entertainment’s best work yet.
Control Resonant is a shining example of what a studio like this can do when given time and patience, and it's surprising and entertaining at every single turn. An astounding game.

Control is one of the best action RPGs ever made. The game combines an emotional story and rock-solid world-building with deep, satisfying combat and delightful movement. Add a breathtaking, open-ended world to the mix, and you have an absolute masterpiece that will stay with players for a long time to come.

Control Resonant proves unequivocally that Remedy understands the medium. Somehow, in crafting its most video-game-ass video game to date, it's managed to not just retain but amplify its own, peculiar and fascinating brand of storytelling. This is not only an excellent Control sequel, but a damned good character action game in its own right.
Few studios are capable of so consistently capturing that feeling of the new and awe-inspiring, and perhaps none can match Remedy's mastery of it. Resonant indeed.

Resonant is the rare sequel that dares to demand something different from the player of the original, rewiring the gun combat into crunchy melee with style. It’s perhaps more conventional than the 2019 game but executed with such flair that it’s irresistible.

Control Resonant takes the series in a different direction without losing Remedy's identity. The new melee combat is excellent and offers countless build possibilities, while the exploration of Manhattan, the secrets, and the side missions expand the universe beautifully, although enemy variety could be much better and some open-world activities are uninspired, but the overall package is excellent, making Control Resonant one of my favorite games of the year.

Control: Resonant proves that Remedy remains one of the most creative studios in the industry. Its combat, progression, and narrative strike a balance with audiovisual elements that make every setting and melody an integral part of the experience. Remedy doesn’t just build a world to explore—it creates one that invites us to pause, observe, and discover a meaning that continues to resonate long after the credits roll, proving that video games can also be art.

Control Resonant is a shockingly massive game but none of it feels like misused space. One might argue that Remedy was at the top of its game with Control in 2019, especially after lukewarm reception to Quantum Break. But it’s with Control Resonant that Remedy feels at its artistic peak. This is a culmination of the developer’s phenomenal body of work over the last few decades. Rather than being a condensed exploration of established themes, Remedy decided to go all out. Few games burn this proudly and confidently across so much real estate. Control Resonant never relinquishes–a brilliant work that is awe-inspiring, thought-provoking, and at the apex of creativity.

Remedy deliver another hit, boasting enigmatic and visceral combat, an incredibly stylish, mind-bending, kaleidoscopic cityscape, and a surrealist yet utterly captivating narrative. Control Resonant ranks amongst the best of 2026, and absolutely has to be experienced.

You can never quite tell where Resonant is going, which gives it the storytelling power of great film or television. It’s got enough authorial decisions through customization and exploration to make you feel like you’re in “Control,” but it also contains remarkably confident writing, not just in plot but dialogue and character work as well.

Control Resonant is the natural, and very welcome, sequel to the
experience that captivated the world seven years ago. More artistic.
Bolder. More complete. And much, much more challenging.

Remedy has channeled its madness and boldness into gameplay that defies
the laws of physics. And while the story didn’t quite win me over, it’s
in the combat and movement mechanics that the new heart of these Finnish
virtuosos truly beats.

Control Resonant is one heck of a follow-up to Control, with a setting twisted by a paranatural force that's perverted Manhattan into a supernatural playground. Remedy's somehow taken what makes them so unique in the industry and applied it to an open world that becomes what I can describe as a paranatural rollercoaster throughout Manhattan. What unfolds is unlike anything else you'll play this year. Without a doubt, Resonant delivers a memorable return to the world of Control.

Control Resonant has a solid grasp of the elements that made the first game stand out and finds interesting ways to expand upon them. The distorted Manhattan, gravity shifts, and agile combat create an engaging adventure, though enemy repetition, customization limitations, and some uninspired content hold the game back from reaching its full potential.Ultimately, Control Resonant is a great experience and an excellent expansion of the universe created by Remedy. It may not be the reinvention its premise might have led us to expect, but it is a sequel that finds new ways to play with the strange and demonstrates that there is still plenty of room to explore within this universe.

CONTROL Resonant takes a lot of risks, and almost all of them pay off. It features a new protagonist, a very different feel to its action, and a far larger game that keeps taking audacious chances throughout. Still, it feels like a Control game in all the most important ways, building beautifully on the original. It sits comfortably among the best games of 2026.
Control Resonant ambitiously reframes its predecessor's gameplay to mixed results, but Remedy Entertainment's undeniable style still captivates.

A sequel that expands the world of Control through Dylan's story and fast-paced melee combat. Confusing navigation and repetitive puzzles can be tiring at times, but its bizarre, twisted vision of Manhattan can only be described as a work of art.

CONTROL Resonant is an excellent sequel that expands the universe of the first game, changing and adding things in a unique way without losing the essence we knew and loved. You can spend hours delving into the text and audio files scattered across the map to better understand the story. The musical elements are very appealing, making the gameplay even more immersive, as are every visual detail in the environments, some perhaps irrelevant, but still satisfying. On the other hand, the difficulty can make the experience frustrating, causing the player to feel stuck and have to leave some things behind until later. In any case, it's a must-have title for fans of the first CONTROL.
A stunning paranatural epic with fantastic combat, Remedy's latest offers a compelling new narrative wrapped up in its signature weirdness.

Control Resonant is an ambitious sequel that feels fresh and exciting while still retaining much of the same tone and feel as its predecessor. Moving from ranged to melee combat is a gamble; moving from a semi-open world to a full open world with some extended linear sections bolted on is a huge leap. However, Remedy has accomplished this tall order with aplomb, creating a game that still feels firmly rooted in the same world as the original Control, with the same dry, Lynchian sense of humour and a surprisingly heartwarming tale about forgiveness and finding your place in an increasingly nonsensical and hostile world.

Despite those shortcomings, however, I couldn’t help falling in love with Resonant the more I played. The bizarre paranormal world of Control is on full display in this sequel, and it shines through in both the Escher-esque world design and amalgamation of side stories that are a joy to discover. Resonant feels experimental in a lot of ways, like Remedy pushing at the bounds of what it’s known for. But the bumps along the way are more than worth it for the astronomical highs Control Resonant reaches.

Remedy Entertainment has delivered a wonderful experience. The game is not without its issues, but its strengths overshadow its flaws. Control: Resonant is not just the next chapter in this universe; it is a sensational adventure that everyone should play in 2026. It is something you cannot afford to ignore.

Control Resonant might frustrate you at times, especially in its early hours, but the more you dig into it the more enjoyable and rewarding it becomes. Weird in the most wonderful of ways, its creativity makes it one of the highlights of the year.

When Alan Wake 2 turned out to be one of the best survival horror games around, despite Remedy having never made anything in the genre before, I thought that the developer would never be able to surprise me again. I was wrong, as Control Resonant turned out to be one of the best action RPGs I have ever experienced. Most of all, it is certainly one of my favorite titles that Remedy has ever created, and further cements them as one of the best developers operating today. Even if I have to wait for another 7 years until the next Control game, the many replays I have planned for Resonant will almost definitely keep me busy for the years to come.

The Board's ways may be inscrutable, but one thing is certain after playing Control Resonant: Remedy has once again proven its mastery of video games. By swapping third-person shooting for a fast-paced and deep action system, the studio has revitalized its formula without losing the strangeness and richness that define Control’s identity. With an endearing Dylan, particularly satisfying combat, extensive exploration, and a world that remains as fascinating as ever, Resonant is an adventure that’s as surprising as it is polished.

Control Resonant is killer. Plain and simple. It takes (not always successful) chances with the combat, occasionally stumbles technically, and sometimes makes things easier than they need to be. Yet none of those shortcomings prevented me from disappearing into it for an entire week, exploring Manhattan, and getting more lost than Clark in the basement of his furniture store. It’s a sequel that completely earns its place beside the original. More importantly, it’s proof of two things: Remedy is still capable of making games that feel unlike almost anything else out there, and nobody tells a story quite like them. It’s easily a must-play, top-10 game of 2026.

Control: Resonant is Remedy at its finest: strange, ambitious, and hard to compare to anything else. Its fantastic hack-and-slash gameplay takes a while to reveal its full potential and can feel somewhat repetitive at times, but it ultimately delivers frantic, flexible, and incredibly addictive combat. Its extraordinary mobility, the strength of its narrative, and a Manhattan capable of creating one-of-a-kind images and sensations make this sequel one of the most unique games of the year.

Control Resonant is a blend of qualities that overcome its own flaws. Remedy Entertainment shows that the sky’s the limit for them and has created an incredible hack-and-slash game with an excellent narrative, great combat, a sublime soundtrack, and compelling missions. When people say that video games are art, Remedy is undoubtedly one of the Leonardo da Vincis of the industry.

A down-to-earth sequel? Not with Remedy! Control Resonant not only matches the quality of its impressive predecessor but actually surpasses it with an even more ambitious concept—one that is executed brilliantly for the most part. Defying the laws of physics, in particular, remained a sheer delight for me right to the end; this made it easy to overlook occasional repetitive content and dusty technology. Few studios excel at creating atmospheric, surreal worlds, mysterious narratives, and uniquely presented experiences quite like Remedy Entertainment. We can never have enough projects like this, especially given a AAA landscape increasingly defined by uniformity. Keep up the great work, Remedy team.

Control Resonant once again showcases Remedy Entertainment's creativity and ingenuity with a memorable experience built around an inventive, unconventional story, satisfying combat that can be tailored to different playstyles, and mind bending environments. Although exploration can occasionally feel confusing, it remains a highly compelling and easy to recommend experience.

Remedy once again expands its interconnected universe with Control Resonant, sparing no expense in the process. The game stands out as a brilliantly written, remarkably bold action-adventure that pushes the studio’s signature storytelling and kinetic gameplay to new heights. By refining what made the original so compelling while introducing ambitious new mechanics, it marks a massive leap forward for the franchise. Ultimately, Control Resonant delivers a thrilling experience while signaling a bright, highly promising future for Remedy Entertainment.
Control Resonant remarkably maps its protagonist’s inner life onto his movement through the game’s open world.
Control Resonant is a lot of fun, with stunning visuals and a remarkable narrative style. The battles can get repetitive, but they don't quite detract from this new masterpiece from Remedy.

CONTROL Resonant is a prime example of how a sequel can realise the full potential of a formula. While Remedy had undeniably succeeded in building a remarkable world with the first game, its many shortcomings arguably limited that world's impact. With this second instalment, however, the Finnish studio pushes past what we could have imagined, not only fixing most of its predecessor's flaws but also bringing in just the right amount of new ideas. The result is an adventure that is at once distinctive, gripping and impressive ; the kind that confirms Remedy as one of the most creative studios in the industry.

I have mentioned before how I adore developers who take risks, and Remedy are the founding fathers of this approach. Control Resonant is a vastly different prospect to the original title, yet somehow, they have pulled it off. An engaging story full of weird and downright bizarre moments is propelled by a wonderful protagonist. A solid combat system and mind bending level design make this game truly unforgettable. Play this game and experience it for yourself. Yes, the final act and some repetitive combat moments grated on me by credits roll but ultimately, this is a game like no other, made by a team like no other. Inception meets Twin Peaks meets Alan Wake. Long live Remedy!

Control Resonant leaves the series’ shooter roots behind in favor of brilliantly crafted melee combat that takes the franchise to new heights and lays an excellent foundation for future adventures in this fascinating universe.

Control Resonant brilliantly reinvents Remedy’s formula with more moving storytelling, an engaging Dylan and a remarkably rich universe. Its melee combat is immensely satisfying, its bosses are spectacular, and its level design plays with gravity in impressively inventive ways. Striking art direction, inspired side quests and excellent use of the DualSense further enhance immersion. However, the sheer number of documents, overly repetitive encounters towards the end and occasional frame rate drops disrupt its momentum. Despite these shortcomings, this ambitious sequel confirms Control’s potential and leaves us eager to discover how much further Remedy can take this distinctive universe.

Remedy’s choice to bet on themselves is another one worth making. CONTROL Resonant is a stellar sequel that risks everything yet succeeds in nearly every area it touches. Certain design choices and a slow start aside, Resonant has the heart of CONTROL inside it with a beautiful story that reaches your soul, vicious combat, and a spectacular world to explore that only they could build. Shaking things up usually works best with Shake 'n Bake, but Remedy cooks with Resonant's shift from the status quo.

By turning a relatively contained adventure into a much bigger game, Remedy took a real risk. Completely reinventing Control without losing what made it special was no easy task, but the Finnish studio pulled it off. The hand-to-hand combat is up there with the best in the genre, while exploration makes great use of supernatural movement, open and highly vertical environments, and gravity-bending mechanics. The story and atmosphere also stay true to the original and to Remedy’s unique style. There are a few technical hiccups during in-game cutscenes and some dated mechanics, but they’re easy to overlook. Remedy delivers an ambitious, bold sequel that takes the franchise to the next level.

CONTROL Resonant expands Remedy's universe with changes that work both in gameplay and atmosphere, all without losing that strange, captivating blend of sci-fi, horror, and surreal storytelling. Fans of the studio and the franchise won't be disappointed by the shift toward melee combat, the fresh setting, and a narrative that maintains Remedy's trademark depth.

Control Resonant makes your last LSD trip feel like a shot of cough syrup. New York is a true work of art, with buildings twisting into each other in ways that are impossible to put into words. This is Remedy at its absolute best: in storytelling, visuals and, finally, combat too. [Issue#375, p.56]

CONTROL: Resonant is the kind of sequel that swings for the fences, and for the most part, it lands. Remedy has taken everything that made the original Control special and expanded it into something bigger and stranger, filled with otherworldly level design that feels pulled straight from an alien’s mind and brought to life. Dylan’s melee-based combat is also a welcome shift, creating satisfying encounters that complement its semi-open world with focused, fast-paced action. Still, many things need addressing, from performance issues during crowded encounters to a deeply underwhelming ending that leaves more questions than answers. Overall, these faults don’t take much away from the experience, which is packed with Remedy’s visual and audio splendor. With just a few imperfections, it remains an otherwise mesmerizing science-fiction story that breaks the traditional Pattern of what videogames can be.

Control Resonant strays quite far from the formula of the first Control, opting for an open world and combat focused more heavily on melee. While this change may disappoint those expecting a more straightforward sequel, Remedy once again demonstrates its talent for creating fascinating worlds, environments, and paranormal situations. It doesn’t surpass its predecessor, but it does succeed as a remarkable sequel with a personality of its own.
CONTROL Resonant had a frustratingly obtuse start and an incredible ending. It is a worthy successor to a similarly flawed but great game.

Control Resonant is yet another piece of evidence that we need to protect Remedy Entertainment at all costs. The studio understands and openly embraces its identity, one that smells of coffee and creative weirdness, and this sequel proves they know how to reinvent themselves without losing an ounce of their soul.

Control Resonant is great hack-and-slash fun packaged into an intriguing science fiction package. The world is hard to get a grip on, but it's endlessly interesting. The combat is challenging in the best way. A Game of the Year contender for sure.

After a few years of silence, Remedy returns with Control Resonant with two stated goals: expanding the lore and structure of the first game and appealing to a wider audience. The latter goal, however, remains unfulfilled: Resonant is a sequel through and through, offering little in the way of a welcoming entry point for those who haven't played—and fully grasped—the original, and featuring a somewhat convoluted opening phase (lasting 4–5 hours). Once past that hurdle, however, the game unfolds into an extraordinary narrative crescendo, keeping players hooked for 40–50 hours of gameplay—spanning the main story, side quests, and the studio's signature rich emergent storytelling (documents, audio logs, and environmental dialogue). In terms of gameplay, it is an open-world action title with RPG-like progression: Manhattan is divided into macro-areas that level up alongside Dylan, creating a stimulating structure that rewards exploration. Combat, however, can easily devolve into mindless button-mashing if you aren't into crafting builds, echoing the repetitive nature of the first game. The real weak point is the technical execution—with character models, lighting, textures, and detail falling short of the studio's usual standards—though this is redeemed by the highly inspired art direction. All in all, Control Resonant is a quintessential Remedy game—unapologetically true to its own identity.

Depending on how much you engage with Control Resonant’s offerings, it will either be an oppressive action game with great narrative beats and presentation or just a pretty tough action game with all the worldbuilding fixins. Remedy mostly nails its first attempt at stylish action, but the misses are apparent and disappointing. The remaining package has me eager to uncover every remaining secret even after rolling credits. As someone most excited to be awash in Control’s lore again, I’m glad that aspect of this sequel resonates most effectively.

Control Resonant trades the Oldest House for a warped, sprawling Manhattan, and the Service Weapon for a shape-shifting melee arsenal. Yet somehow it still feels unmistakably like Control. The combat is a blast (once I chilled it out a bit), the traversal is fantastic, the boss fights are gloriously bizarre, and the soundtrack is as good as ever. Assist Mode is a ground-breaking, best-in-class accessibility system. Dylan is slow to win you over, the pacing struggles to balance the story against a mountain of side content, and the plot occasionally drifts into the fog. But this is a big, confident sequel that fixes nearly everything that initially held the original back.
A game full with personality and surprising art design. It will challenge what you take for granted in action adventures, but some technical flaws lessen the overall experience.

Control Resonant is absolutely worth the wait. Some of the open-world aspects put strain on the exploration but, there’s enough curiosities and compelling events both in that world and in the combat design to recover every time fatigue begins to set in.
It took us a long time to really get to grips with Control Resonant. But once we’d mastered its quirks, we had a lot of fun with this wacky action game from Remedy.
A mind-bendingly beautiful world that stumbles at the finish line due to shallow characterization and gameplay that is fun, but ultimately too simple.

Control Resonant is an impeccably confident and tantalising sequel that has all the hallmarks of a Remedy classic. It’s endlessly stylish and playful; it looks gorgeous, especially on the PS5 Pro, and it manages to address many of the woes that I had with the original Control. Repetitive combat is the big hitch, however, holding the game back from true greatness. Ultimately, though, it's not enough to overrule all that Remedy is doing right with this sequel.

Any game that lets you execute a bus, or stamp on windows to direct a cat to attack a woman called Sandra is a winner in my books. Remedy should be credited for taking their time and making a very different sequel, rather than more of the same, and also for throwing a lot of ideas into the game. However, for me, it's a little too unfocused and padded.
Remedy's follow-up to 2019's Control moves to action combat in an open world and tells a more character-focused story with its paranatural edge intact.

Control Resonant’s Manhattan is a stunning and mind-bending distortion of 3-D space, with the boss fights feeling less like reflex challenges than visual spectacles. But the game’s narrative layer, again infused in science-fiction tropes, feels small and far away as I hurtle into that urban chasm.

Control Resonant expands Remedy's surreal world with a fascinating new setting, compelling story, and stunning art direction, but repetitive combat and enemy encounters hold it back from reaching loftier heights than its predecessor.
Strange, ambitious and often frustrating, Control Resonant pushes Remedy’s formula to its limits. It won't appeal to everyone, but its strong personality makes it hard to forget.

Just as Dylan and Jesse are brother and sister, Control Resonant and Control share a 50/50 genetic heritage that emphasizes often labyrinthine yet impactful level design, spectacular set pieces, and a narrative that in the sequel becomes even more grounded in emerging elements. Sure, the two games have different personalities; the combat system is revolutionized, and it's surprising that such a bold choice actually works well, despite some limitations that become increasingly evident. And speaking of limitations, the technical side of things experiences equally dramatic highs and lows: the price to pay for such an open structure, yet made all the more sweeter by the many gems, surprises, and inspirations of a remarkable artistic direction.

Even without the composure and playful and artistic balance of the first Control and Alan Wake 2, Resonant leaves its own recognizable mark on the industry. It has the drive to do so much, to offer so much, and to stimulate as much as possible. Its exuberance is contagious but unbalanced, especially in its balancing of challenge and the diversification of the combat system. Resonant's diversity and diversity, however, come together in a blend that only Remedy can blend so coherently. A charismatic melting pot of the most disparate influences, the second Control entertains for dozens of hours and can appeal to fans of the weird with a unique and bizarre personality that is worth surrendering to.

Despite his structural limitation, which weighs most heavily during the longer boss fights, Control Resonant remains an experience worth seeing through to the end, because its ability to astonish through exploration and writing is rare enough to make almost every flaw tied to its more purely action-driven side forgivable. A flawed work, but undeniably memorable.

CONTROL Resonant is a standout experience, and uniquely so. It is enigmatic and occasionally paradoxical. But that’s kind of the beauty of it. Its intricate, painstakingly crafted world is so beautifully surreal, but it’s also relentless, oppressive, and kind of scary. Its incredibly detailed story is always riveting and novel but wildly disorienting and even frustratingly bewildering at times. Its combat and deep RPG systems, later balance woes aside, always remain engaging. At the end of the day, though it’s not a perfect experience, it’s unusual and exceptional, and in one aspect or another, RPGamers are sure to find something here that deeply resonates.

It’s an incredibly artistic world dripping with style and that classic Remedy aesthetic, and the more linear sections are the studio at its absolute best. While there are some open world fumbles that kind of drag the overall quality down, the rest of Control Resonant is so spectacular that they’re worth putting up with. It’s another great entry in the Remedyverse, and I’m all in on what the studio wants to do next.

Dylan’s melee gameplay evolves at a nice pace over time as his powers and weapons diversify, keeping the title feeling fresh. And newcomers won’t feel overwhelmed by not playing the original as it stands on its own feet separately.

Billed as Remedy's most ambitious game to date (until the next one?), Control Resonant lives up to the claim in almost every department. By letting us step outside the Oldest House, Remedy has above all thrown wide open the doors of perception. To the studio’s usual flashes of artistic brilliance, Control Resonant adds a level design expertise no one saw coming. This open world like no other (because it truly is one) delivers dizzying moments and phantasmagoric visions that sweep you in and disorient you—a pleasure made all the deeper because Remedy never holds the player's hand. Plenty of great games are coming out right now, but let's make sure Control Resonant isn't the casualty of this autumn slate: now more than ever, Remedy is an auteur-driven studio whose vision deserves support, and one that still has room to polish its remaining weaknesses in combat and cinematography.

A true anomaly in the highly structured world of action-adventure games, Control is fascinating for both its strengths and its flaws. By fusing unstructured brawler mechanics, gravity-defying platforming, and deep action-RPG elements, Remedy has created a work of immense ambition and generosity. However, the game pays a price for this boldness through constant friction in its quests and combat that feels a bit too chaotic. If you are willing to embrace the demands of its complex rules, you will take great pleasure in navigating this electrifying, "altered" experience.

Control Resonant is a bold sequel precisely because it doesn’t simply try to be a bigger version of Control. Swapping Jesse for Dylan, moving away from firearms as the main focus, emphasizing melee combat, and shifting the action to an open, warped Manhattan works. But the larger scale also works against it. There are too many similar encounters; certain enemies and patterns are repeated ad nauseam; the start is unnecessarily difficult; and on top of that, the game’s length stretches certain narrative and gameplay ideas beyond their sweet spot.

Control Resonant is packed with familiar ingredients that combine into something completely unique. Inception-like level design, a mix of different media woven into the gameplay, and writing that twists the everyday into the abnormal add up to a one-of-a-kind experience. That experience is, however, held back by a fairly run-of-the-mill combat system.

Control Resonant, just like its predecessor, is an incredibly aesthetic and stylized spectacle that both enchants and baffles. What a brilliant game this is. The overall vibe, style, and art direction: wow. In terms of atmosphere, this is top-notch. But while the world continues to surprise, the combat gets a bit monotonous, and unfortunately, the game ultimately isn’t without its flaws. But anyone who loves bizarre sci-fi detective stories with the apocalypse at stake will overlook that.

Control: Resonant fascinated me and practically sucked me into its universe and systems. And while the sometimes overly long combat encounters can get frustrating, I happily cut down on sleep to unravel its mysteries and experience what mind bending visuals Remedy would come up with next. And if you can get a father of three to voluntarily miss precious hours of sleep, you’re at the least doing something very right.

Control Resonant is far from being a bad game. In fact, its open game world offers even greater gameplay variety, placing a stronger emphasis on exploration and platforming. However, parts of the game do feel somewhat arbitrary or even generic, clearly distinguishing it from its predecessor, which had a much more focused direction. Furthermore, Jesse’s adventure offered a superior narrative and was significantly more tightly crafted, not just in terms of storytelling. Even so, viewed on its own, Control: Resonant still delivers a story that's still high above the average level in games, an atmospheric open world, and, last but not least, a cool combat system, if you enjoy spectacular, fast-paced, and at times frenetic action. Yet even if that is the only aspect that appeals to you, you still might not be overwhelmed, but certainly not disappointed as well.
Control Resonant is fun and it's visuals are amazing, but overall the content within the open world feels repetitive.

The story and gameplay of CONTROL Resonant seem at odds with each other—starting strong, then grinding to a halt in the late game. Combined with the rote, repetitive gameplay, underwhelming powers, and a weaker Remedy music moment, this feels like the weakest Remedy game in over a decade.

Control Resonant doesn't quite reach the heights of the first Control, but this doesn't detract too much from an experience that is unmistakably viewed through the surreal and "paranoid" lenses of Remedy. We could have done with a bit more linearity in its levels, as the open-world segments are often repetitive, while the melee combat doesn't fare particularly well when compared with the genre's masters, such as Bayonetta and Devil May Cry, among others. Be that as it may, the audiovisual pandemonium, utterly satisfying and fast-paced platforming, and some truly imaginative areas will definitely satisfy fans of Remedy.
Control Resonant is another masterclass in storytelling from Remedy Entertainment, but its potential for greatness is hindered by a completely detached open-world experience.

Control Resonant isn’t a bad game, but it’s not the Control successor that people were left wanting after the original game. While Remedy’s habit of zigging when fans think they will zag is one of the studio’s greatest strengths, this is one of the rare times when it hasn’t fully paid off. Repetitive combat encounters that lack depth, a dated open-world environment, and a dull story fail to captivate in the same manner as the original.

Control Resonant hits a vibe I haven’t felt in a while in an action melee. Dylan’s super-powered nature makes for a fun ride through the paranormal, chaos-filled streets of Manhattan, and the palpable fear of him by normies and his general awkwardness make for an interesting dynamic through the game as he tries to help others while also chasing Jesse (whom everyone tells him they liked more). Control Resonant isn’t an airtight experience. Besides running into a little too much repetition hours in, the bugs are sometimes as weird as the narrative, and the visuals, while atmospheric, are sometimes a harsh assault on the senses with no options for alleviation. However, between bizarre side encounters, mind-bending traversal, and a compelling main quest, there’s more than enough here to keep it moving.

For those willing to tolerate its quirks and accept the rough edges, Control Resonant offers much to admire. It's unlike anything else you'll see this year, perhaps even next year and the many more after that, and that counts for something.

Control Resonant has a lot going for it. It's a technical and artistic achievement, with amazing visuals, memorable characters, and a lot of platforming... but it fumbles with the combat. Sadly, fighting is incredibly boring and repetitive, and fighting is something Dylan does a lot. The most frustrating and disappointing aspect of Resonant is that it's a brilliant idea that's executed so utterly flatly.

Where Control evoked an oppressive feeling of distorted reality, here there’s a more conventional tale about a man on a mission of redemption, and there’s even the odd moment of human warmth in Dylan’s interactions with his bureau colleagues and his elusive sister. Just like the gameplay, the story has made a tonal shift towards easily digestible mainstream convention, and while there’s nothing inherently wrong with that, I’m left craving the original’s more hallucinogenic vision of the action-RPG.
A brave but foolhardy pivot from ranged to melee combat turns the Control sequel into a repetitive slog, brightened only by some impressively surreal visuals.

Whereas that 2019 title was a splendid synthesis of Remedy’s signature strengths, Control Resonant‘s many failures make it seem as though it came from a different studio altogether. Its melee combat is bafflingly hollow, relentlessly repetitive, and poorly balanced across the board. Dylan’s quest to save the day lacks inventive concepts that stretch the mind and ends up being a fairly one-note story with an unearned ending. By failing to engage the fingers or brain, Resonant is not just a disappointing sequel; it betrays the very notion of what it means to be a Remedy game.

Control Resonant is another excellent addition to Remedy Entertainment's connected universe project.
