Control Resonant continues the Remedy tradition of offering an ambitious experience filled with incredible ideas. The game controls beautifully, the combat is fun and flexible, the side stories are strong and the presenation is, of course, excellent. But repetitive encounters, beautiful but underwhelming boss battles and an uneven open-world structure all make Resonant feel uneven. Regardless of its flaws, Control Resonant is both bold and enjoyable, though it doesn't reach the usual heady heights established by the illustrious Remedy canon.

CONTROL Resonant is a fantastic follow-up that expands on almost everything that made the original great. Dylan becomes a compelling protagonist, melee combat offers impressive depth, traversal is a joy, and Remedy’s signature weirdness is as strong as ever. Some uneven difficulty, limited enemy variety, and occasional visual clutter hold it back slightly, but this is still one of Remedy’s strongest games.
CONTROL Resonant spreads the Oldest House across Manhattan and hands the lead to a Dylan Faden who is finally himself.

I'm still blown away by the environment design and art direction in CONTROL Resonant. The work here is nothing short of masterful. Honestly, we probably won't see another game that delivers a comparable experience for years to come. Remedy's signature strengths of artistry, visuals, and storytelling are practically dialed up to eleven in this entry. As for the combat and player guidance, there are still a few minor hiccups, but they certainly haven't taken a step back. If anything, they are actually a solid improvement over the first game.
Control Resonant is exactly the kind of game we want to see from a studio like Remedy: strange, ambitious, and totally out of control .
Control Resonant proves once again that Remedy doesn't need to follow the industry's usual patterns to create a distinctive experience.

Control Resonant embodies Remedy's tried and true tropes and risky experiments that you must find a connection with. But once you connect with the game, you'll be inseparable until the end credits roll.

Control RESONANT feels like an AAA production infused with the creative spirit of an indie game. In Control, surrealism was something you merely witnessed, but here, thanks to innovative level design, creative mechanics, and clever puzzles, it is something you can actually experience. Expanding the game’s world to Manhattan also creates room for a richer narrative backdrop, allowing it to explore even stranger concepts. Nevertheless, the game cannot escape the common shortcomings found in Remedy’s works. The combat gradually becomes repetitive, some surprises feel formulaic, and the narrative slowdown is difficult to overlook. Resonant stands as one of the most distinctive experiences in today’s AAA landscape, yet it still suffers from Remedy’s familiar shortcomings.

Remedy has managed to create fun mechanics in a genre they are trying for the first time. When you add in the story, which continues from the first game, the result is a really great experience. I just wish the combat encounters in the second half of the game had been less repetitive...

Control Resonant is Remedy's boldest experiment yet, successfully bringing its distinctive style to the open-world action RPG genre. Its story, characters, world design, exploration, customization and atmosphere are excellent, while the combat is merely decent and holds the experience back. Despite some compromises, its unique world and wealth of content make it difficult to put down.

The biggest obstacle is the combat's difficulty, particularly when enemies attack from outside your view or provide unclear tells. You can either adapt to the game's demanding combat or use the extensive assist options to tailor the experience to your preferences. Either way, Resonant successfully expands what a Control game can be while retaining the strange atmosphere that made the original stand out.

Control Resonant is a bold sequel in which Remedy has rebuilt the foundations of its predecessor, rather than simply offering more of the same. Brilliant combat, excellent development of Dylan’s abilities, satisfying exploration and a Manhattan brimming with abstract ideas make it hard to tear yourself away from this adventure lasting over 30 hours. Not all plot threads maintain the same pace, and the visuals aren’t as rich in detail as Alan Wake 2, but ultimately the Finnish developers have stepped out of their comfort zone and delivered an even better game.

Topping the first Control is no easy feat, and while it’s debatable if it has, the fact remains this is one of the most unique experiences, a game that trusts you enough not to spoon feed you everything and rather give you enough breathing space to figure things out yourself.

Resonant is creating its own moments that remind me that this isn’t just a hack-and-slash. It’s a journey through the paranormal, alongside a journey of self-discovery and redemption. And it's bloody brilliant.

"Throughout Remedy's history, you won't find any game quite like Control Resonant. With this title, they've created something that could make anyone unfamiliar with the studio fall in love with them. Blending RPG elements with close-quarters, hand-to-hand combat wasn't what we expected from them, and Remedy has pulled it off in the best way possible. While there are weaknesses in the story, it still delivers a clear and purposeful experience."

Control Resonant achieves the hardest feat for a sequel: justifying its own existence without merely replicating what worked before. Dylan, Manhattan and the Aberrant change the tone and pace of the experience, while Remedy's identity remains recognizable in every impossible building and every unsettling detail. The combat has enough ideas and tools to be exhilarating, but the opaque progression and the repetitiveness of the last part keep it from consistently reaching the heights of the artistic and narrative side. On PS5 Pro it remains a remarkable action adventure, recommended above all to those who want a more dynamic and experimental sequel, not simply another trip through the corridors of the Oldest House.

Control Resonant boldly swaps hero, genre and setting, delivering satisfying melee combat, a flexible Assist Mode and a surreal Manhattan that is a work of art, even if its story is Remedy at its strangest and its atmosphere never quite reaches Alan Wake 2.
While Control Resonant hasn’t quite reached the catharsis of their last title, it’s easily the Remedy game I’m most likely to come back to in the near future on the strength of it’s gameplay.

Delivers a fantastic, atmospheric story with excellent voice acting, enjoyable combat, and a memorable soundtrack. Unfortunately, its rather average open world and underwhelming RPG mechanics often get in the way of what makes the game truly special. Beneath these shortcomings lies an outstanding narrative experience that would have benefited from a more focused approach.

Control Resonant marks a risky genre shift for the franchise, one that comes with both improvements and downgrades, resulting in a sequel that, while enjoyable, isn’t able to reach the heights of its predecessor.

CONTROL Resonant finally puts Dylan Faden at the center of the story. One of the franchise's most enigmatic characters, Dylan spent much of the first Control under the care of the Federal Bureau of Control, while his sister Jesse tried to understand the paranatural phenomena threatening the Oldest House. Throughout that journey, it was hard not to wonder what would happen when he finally awakened and what role he would play in the events to come. Now, Remedy turns that anticipation into a new adventure, taking the franchise in a different direction. Rather than remaining confined to the Oldest House, the story expands into a Manhattan consumed by paranatural phenomena, where Dylan must confront the consequences of his past while trying to find Jesse.

CONTROL Resonant is one of the most impactful, immersive, and enjoyable games I have played this year. Changing the protagonist, overhauling combat, and expanding exploration were decisions that could have distanced the sequel from what made the original so special, but Remedy turns these changes into its greatest strengths. The first Control remains one of my favorite games, but Dylan's journey won me over with its freedom, mechanics, and the importance of its story. More than simply repeating a successful formula, the sequel demonstrates that a franchise can expand by exploring new directions, as long as its defining qualities remain intact. It is an exceptional adventure that leaves me even more curious about what Remedy will develop next.

You may find other action games that play better than Control Resonant, but you’ve never played an action game that’s quite like Control Resonant. At a time where players desire fresh and unique takes on familiar ideas, I can’t imagine a better exhibit for that desire.

Control Resonant is a game dramatically torn in half, a title defined by stark contrasts. On one hand, it represents the artistic and narrative pinnacle of Remedy Entertainment: an exceptionally designed "weird New York" warped by impossible brutalist architecture, where defying gravity is a joy for both the eyes and the mind. The writing of Dylan Faden and the desperate portrayal of a crumbling FBC deliver an unforgettable, auteur-driven sci-fi experience.

On the other hand, the gameplay framework—specifically its action—collapses under the weight of poorly calibrated game design. A tedious combat system, bullet-sponge enemies, and progression broken by level scaling turn encounters into a repetitive chore. If you are willing to make this compromise purely for the sake of the story and exploration, you will uncover a uniquely mesmerizing world that only Remedy could ever craft.

The thing I really like about Control Resonant is that it feels so distinct from most recent AAA games. It’s always bringing new methods to travel, explore, fight and design the environment, from start to finish.
Control Resonant delivers an excellent blend of paranormal action and exploration, though a few underdeveloped mechanics keep it from fully realizing its potential.

Control Resonant is the pinnacle of what Remedy Entertainment has achieved in the action genre, and one of the best games they have ever made! It tells a mysterious, masterfully told story, paired with a very enjoyable hack-and-slash style of combat that might just be the studio's best combat system yet. This is complemented by an iconic level design that ranks among the best I have seen in a long time. All of these elements came together to form an exceptional game, and one of the best games of the generation.

Remedy's Control Resonant trades guns for Dylan Faden's fluid melee combat in a beautifully twisted Manhattan. Blending deep ARPG action with stunning visuals, this masterful sequel is easily their best game yet.

Control Resonant is a bold sequel that doesn’t simply repeat the formula of the first game. The shift from a third-person shooter to a melee combat system, the multifaceted abilities of the Aberrant, and the open-ended exploration ensure a distinctly more varied experience. It features several interesting moments, though they may not necessarily resonate with those who loved the first Control, but in any case, Control Resonant remains an intriguing prospect.

CONTROL Resonant takes a bold step beyond the Oldest House, putting Dylan at the center of a paranormal crisis in a warped Manhattan. Some encounters grow repetitive, and the city can’t quite match the original’s claustrophobic atmosphere, but Remedy’s willingness to experiment makes this a memorable evolution of CONTROL.
Control Resonant is an ambitious sequel that dares to challenge almost everything that worked in its predecessor.

Control Resonant is a worthy and solid sequel to the original. Building upon the world introduced to us in Control and expanding it tenfold. The game design is tight, sharp and easy to get into. This title has even managed to scratch my openworld power fantasy, not fulfilled since my [Prototype] playing days and made the Control  games my second favourite series (still wanting a Quantum Break sequel one day if you’re reading this and are somehow able too Remedy), and although the Alan Wake games are still my personal favourites within the ‘Remedyverse’, Resonant feels like a well polished, thought out and solid entry into the ever expanding series of interconnected games this developer seems to be building. Control Resonant is an ambitious and visually staggering action role-playing game. Taken as a part of the whole, Control Resonant delivers an emotional first draft of a far more interesting shared world. Control Resonant is an exceptional reminder that Remedy are the masters of their craft. Control Resonant isn't as confidently executed as its predecessor, but the game's trippy visuals, gripping story and surreal world design put it in a league of its own, flaws and all.

Control Resonant is an excellent sequel. Control Resonant is a game where its awe-inspiring visual experience outweighs its gameplay shortcomings — if you can stomach the repetitive combat, confusing navigation, and dense walls of text, it delivers an even more satisfying experience than its predecessor.

Control Resonant is bigger and better than its predecessor, shedding much of the original’s clutter in favor of a clearer vision, renewed art direction, greater ambition and a remarkable ability to celebrate art both within and beyond video games.

CONTROL Resonant shows us that Remedy is definitely still at the top of its game and can tackle any genre. Control: Resonant expands on its predecessor with an ambitious open world, fast-paced melee combat, and deeper progression. Dylan’s supernatural abilities and challenging boss fights deliver an engaging experience, although labyrinthine level design and some empty areas affect exploration. Despite these flaws, Remedy offers an exciting paranormal adventure that builds on the original’s strengths.

CONTROL Resonant takes a real risk by throwing out a formula that worked for Remedy and building something almost unrecognizable in its place. It comes out the other side as one of the studio's strongest overall efforts, even with a navigation system that fights you more than it should.

Overall, Control Resonant takes everything that made the original special and elevates it with incredible melee combat, breathtaking artistic visual design, and a deeply emotional story. While the early difficulty curve and less traditional RPG systems might not suit everyone, the overall experience is nothing short of extraordinary.

It is stranger, faster, more physical and considerably more willing to throw its toys out of the pram. Most importantly, it feels like Remedy actually had something to say with the sequel beyond “here’s more Control.” It’s a sequel is that’s willing to take a big, weird swing, and it mostly connects.

After nearly 30 hours, I can say I really enjoyed my time with Control Resonant, but I feel it has one too many superfluous elements that only serve to unnecessarily complicate a gameplay that was already strong. It is a very good game and worth playing, but when I eventually want to dive back into Remedy's connected universe, I think I’d prefer to replay Alan Wake 2 or the original Control rather than this one.

There is a lot to like about Control Resonant. I genuinely respect how Remedy opted to make this sequel the yang to Control’s yin. Remedy Entertainment has created another absolute triumph with Control Resonant. Despite some big bugs, that doesn’t stop the momentum that Remedy Entertainment has built with Control Resonant.
f you enjoyed CONTROL, absolutely. CONTROL Resonant successfully expands the original game’s world while giving Dylan his own identity, combat style and story.

I couldn’t recommend Control: Resonant enough, especially to those coming off either Alan Wake 2 or Control. This sequel captures Remedy’s unique specialty in the video game space, as there’s no other studio that can deliver a sci-fi world like Control.

CONTROL Resonant was an excellent game in my opinion. There wasn’t really anything I can complain about, but I don’t feel like it’s perfect, so I would hesitate to give it a 10/10, but know that I did contemplate the idea.

Overall my experience with Control Resonant ended with me being very pleased with everything involved, as the combat was very in-depth and was constantly shifting, allowing for new gameplay styles and combinations.

Control Resonant is an absolute masterpiece of game design. I had my worries after seeing that the follow-up to Control was essentially an entirely different game. A new genre, a new protagonist, and basically an entirely new story. But Remedy is a studio that isn’t afraid to answer that door, kick it wide open, and invite whatever multidimensional nightmare is waiting on the other side directly into the living room. That’s why so many love them: they refuse to stay inside the creative lines, which often leads to some of the most memorable, bold experiences in modern gaming—and Control Resonant is no exception.

Control Resonant is one of thosegames that is difficult to explain in words, because a big part of what makes it special comes from experiencing it yourself. Its level design, direction, world, and ideas make it a unique experience. Despite some flaws and its high difficulty, Remedy’s signature is still very clear, constantly making you wonder: “How did they think of this?!”

While it’s a slow start at a discordant pitch, Control Resonant quickly tunes into the right frequency and hums with humanity. Its frayed edges can sometimes become apparent; its characters, writing, world, and sheer originality vastly outweigh any downsides.

Control Resonant is a bold and ambitious open‑world action‑horror experience that builds on the foundation of Control and expands it in every direction. Its sprawling Manhattan sandbox, layered combat systems, and dense lore crack open the series’ paranatural universe and let it spill freely across a chaotic New York, leaving players to explore, survive, and master it.
It’s been a long time since I was as excited to play a game as I was for this one, and I can say that Control Resonant delivered that in almost every way that mattered.

CONTROL Resonant sees Remedy confidently master the action genre, drawing inspiration from Japanese action classics to deliver challenging, satisfying, varied, and deep gameplay. Essential for fans of the original Control and highly recommended for anyone seeking fast-paced action in the vein of Devil May Cry.
Control Resonant is a top class action RPG, with some of the most mind bending imagery you've ever seen. The story isn't as strong as its predecessor, but the gameplay more than makes up for it.

I will say, though, that Remedy still maintains its strong core identity with Control Resonant, with its strong narrative design and refined combat, where it’ll go down as one of this year’s best action games.

CONTROL Resonant is a bold sequel that refuses to simply recreate the original. It’s one of the best, most emotionally arresting action games of 2026 and an easy game of the year contender.

Control Resonant is a showcase, and that’s because few developers have shown the kind of courage that Remedy has demonstrated in recent years with the titles it has released—and just how different they are from one another.

High peaks and deep valleys, but that’s also why we’ll still be talking about Control Resonant for many years to come.

The story of Control - Resonant is not bad, but coming from Remedy it is disappointing and so the Control sequel lacks a key charme of their games. But I also enjoy fast paced, frantic combat and for that that alone this trip to New York was worth it.

For their very first game, Wych Elm have blown it out of the park. I recommend Silver Pines to everyone: fans of horror, Metroidvanias, and detective stories. Silver Pines is a cerebrally divine love letter to David Lynch and all the narrative trademarks he was known for, from the cult classic Twin Peaks to Blue Velvet and Lost Highway. It digs even deeper to its spiritual successor Silent Hill, from the fog-filled streets to the nightmares that lurk with bared teeth, and embraces all those inspirations with the utmost grace and respect while still very much telling its own story. Combat can take a bit to get used to, but feels satisfying after a while with plenty of options at Walker's disposal. For their very first attempt, Wych Elm have knocked it out of the park. The influences from the masterworks of Lynch, Remedy and Silent Hill, the thriller steeped in ’90s Americana, the discovery of the city’s secrets, and that sense of unease and anticipation about what we’ll encounter every time we step into a new area, blended together in an unforgettable experience.

Silver Pines is a horror search-action game that borrows concepts from established games in the genre and uses them wonderfully to strengthen its own gameplay. Compelling, atmospheric, and brilliant, Silver Pines is a dive into mystery that's hard to put down and even harder to let go. It makes you feel like a detective, an action hero, and a man on the brink of uncovering horrifying darkness all at once.

Silver Pines is a great survival-horror that came just at the perfect time. Silver Pines is an atmospheric game, a Metroidvania-style survival horror title that draws heavily from genre classics like Silent Hill, Resident Evil, and Alan Wake, as well as from television and film, such as Twin Peaks, The X-Files, and The Shining. However, these inspirations don’t reduce Wych Elm’s work to a mere collection of references; thanks to excellent storytelling, they allow the game to carve out its own path between nightmare and mystery. Solid gameplay underpins the experience, reinterpreting the genre’s conventions without forcing a radical overhaul. It’s also impossible not to mention the excellent art direction, featuring rotoscoped animations, and the soundtrack, with atmospheric music that heightens the tension. Silver Pines is a haunting adventure, a glimpse into the mystery of identity that straddles the line between reality and imagination.

Silver Pines is a glorious revival of the 90s survival horror formula. Fans of the early Silent Hill and Resident Evil games will be thrilled by a title that perfectly distills those classics' formulas, opting for 2D gameplay with strong Metroidvania elements.

Silver Pines is a sharp, moody debut. It mixes survival horror and Metroidvania design with real confidence. The hand-drawn art is gorgeous. All in all, the atmosphere is thick and unsettling. Silver Pines is a metroidvania survival horror game developed by Wych Elm and published by Team17. In his quest to find the missing musician Eddie Velvet, private detective Red Walker travels to Silver Pines, a small town in the United States that is practically deserted due to a severe weather alert that forced everyone to evacuate. Searching for clues to Eddie Velvet's whereabouts, Red Walker scours the town and soon realizes that something dark hangs over it. Strange and aggressive creatures roam the area, making the detective's life difficult. He must investigate the case of the missing musician while trying to unravel the mystery of Silver Pines, all while attempting to survive the town's dangers.

Silver Pines brings a breath of fresh air to survival horror games, with a new visual and perspective approach, while maintaining the standard characteristics of the genre. Its deliberately slow pace is essential for building tension, along with excellent sound and visual appeal. The story is initially intriguing, but loses momentum over time. The controls, while serving their purpose in the narrative, didn't appeal to me as much, being a bit frustrating at times. The exploration and investigation, as well as the puzzles, are the highlight for me. Even though I'm seeing everything in third person and with a side camera that allows me a wide field of view, you really feel scared and apprehensive about moving forward without knowing what's coming. Silver Pines shows that it's possible to be innovative even in genres that seem to need nothing new.

Silver Pines is a standout indie survival horror experience, blending haunting atmosphere, compelling mystery, and clever Metroidvania exploration. Despite some clunky combat and confusing navigation, its distinctive style and psychological tension make it one of 2026’s best indie horror games.

Silver Pines blends survival horror, investigation, and Metroidvania exploration into a compelling adventure filled with mystery and suspense. Despite these shortcomings, its fascinating world and strong investigative elements make it a memorable horror experience.
For me, Silver Pines is less the Metroidvania it's marketed as and much more a classic survival horror game set in a large, interconnected world. And as such, it works brilliantly.

While the 2D platform aspect can be quite limiting, the developer has squeezed every inch out of it. For such a small development team, Silver Pines is a little gem. I reviewed this on Xbox, but it’s also available on PS5, Switch, and Steam. Go check it out; you won’t be disappointed.
Visit Silver Pines, it’s got great coffee, a cozy mystery, and gooey monsters to boot. Call in and book your room now!

Silver Pines nails that classic survival horror game vibe, all whilst adding some impressive modern touches to exploration across its Metroidvania-style world. I had a really good time uncovering its world, solving its satisfying puzzles, and unravelling its unsettling narrative (even if it is guilty of being a bit derivative in places), whilst the gorgeous visuals really do give it a distinct sense of style.
It’s just a really, really good game - horror fans have truly been spoilt lately, and Silver Pines is another release they won’t want to miss out on.

Silver Pines is a fascinating blend of classic survival horror and Metroidvania that stands out for its intriguing narrative, extraordinary art direction, and an atmosphere evocative of the genre's greatest icons. Although its gameplay leaves room for improvement and its influences occasionally wear on its sleeve, Wych Elm succeeds in crafting an experience with a distinct identity that will thoroughly delight fans of psychological horror.

Silver Pines: is an atmospheric horror adventure that combines a surreal mystery reminiscent of Twin Peaks with disturbing creatures and elements inspired by Silent Hill and Resident Evil. Exploration, cleverly designed puzzles, and a practical photography system for documenting clues are among its biggest strengths, while the lack of clear guidance can occasionally make progression frustrating. Despite a few shortcomings, it's a compelling choice for psychological horror fans who enjoy uncovering the secrets of a world where nothing is quite what it seems.

​Silver Pines is an excellent addition to the horror genre and a great choice for Halloween 2026. It’s quirky, immersive, terrifying, and thought-provoking. It succeeds where many games with larger budgets fail, earning its place among the best recent survival horror titles.

The only horrifying aspect of the game is that it doesn’t have a more distinct identity and chooses to lean a little too strongly on its inspirations. The upside, however, is that it serves as a fantastic gateway drug into the surreal world of David Lynch’s brand of horror. The owls may not be what they seem, but Silver Pines absolutely is: it could be the next great horror game in your collection.

Silver Pines is a somewhat unconventional addition to the survival horror genre. However, it makes excellent use of tried-and-tested mechanics and beloved genre tropes, making it a definite hit with any fan of the genre. Were it not for a few minor shortcomings, it could have been a truly perfect and unique experience.
I loved my time with this game and even amongst an impressive crop of horror titles I feel confident that Silver Pines can go toe to toe with the best of them. Silver Pines is well worth a visit.

Silver Pines is an entertaining game that plays it safe by following tried and tested methods from the psychological horror playbook. However its unique art style in a metroidvania presentation make it an interesting combination to explore all it has to offer. horror fan or not, Silver Pines has something to offer you.
Brings a new and distinctive feel to the eShop, blending what would normally feel like an adventure game with horror to create a satisfying and creepy experience

Silver Pines rarely nudges you to charge in without thinking. Instead, you read your surroundings, hold onto clues, stretch your supplies, and slowly figure out how the whole town fits together. Puzzles and exploration matter more than fighting, and the mood and story give you a good enough reason to put up with the awkward moments.

Silver Pines is an incredibly ambitious first entry from new developer Wych Elm. Yes, it deliberately takes the addictive Resident Evil inventory system and Silent Hill’s imprecise but unnerving combat. The narrative itself percolates Twin Peaks and The X-Files to a perfect distillation of them, but never losing its identity. Wrapping it up in a metroidvania layout that dukes it out with the best of them, and you have a wicked formula for success. Red may be having the worst night of life, but you most certainly will enjoy one of your best.

Silver Pines is an excellent game, built on the genre’s core foundations and successfully translating its defining mechanics into a 2D, Metroidvania-style structure without ever feeling disjointed. Where it falls short, however, is originality: there isn’t a single idea that feels truly unique or distinct. This applies not only to the gaming landscape, but also to its cross-media influences, which the developers seem to have mined with all the subtlety of a stick of dynamite.

For their very first attempt, Wych Elm have knocked it out of the park. The influences from the masterworks of Lynch, Remedy and Silent Hill, the thriller steeped in ’90s Americana, the discovery of the city’s secrets, and that sense of unease and anticipation about what we’ll encounter every time we step into a new area, blended together in an unforgettable experience.

Silver Pines proves that the survival horror and Metroidvania genres were made for each other. It isn't particularly scary and enemy encounters could be better, but its mysterious *Twin Peaks*-inspired narrative, excellent atmosphere, and superb map design make it an unmissable experience.

Silver Pines is a beautiful homage to David Lynch, Angelo Badalamenti, and Alan Parker; it draws upon the influences of these masters to craft its own story which, within the classic survival horror framework, stands as one of the genre's finest examples and one of the best games of the year.

This chilly yet atmospheric little town has everything it takes for a fantastic horror experience, provided you’re willing to make a few concessions. If you can accept this, an incredible game awaits you, one that has everything it takes to make the hairs on the back of your neck stand on end and drown you in melancholy. For a restless dream of a Metroidvania, Silver Pines is the perfect final destination.

Silver Pines is a wonderfully surreal metroidvania-survival horror hybrid that excels through its Lynchian atmosphere, rewarding exploration, constant sense of progression, clever environmental puzzles, excellent soundtrack, and a mysterious story that leaves plenty of room for interpretation. Frustrating encounters with multiple enemies, fairly simple boss fights, restrictive inventory management, and some intrusive survival mechanics occasionally disrupt the flow, but they do little to diminish an experience that is remarkably easy to get lost in. jsemgamer.cz

Every corner of this rain-battered town tells its own story in an effective, mature manner, uniting environmental storytelling, immersive sound design, and exemplary fidelity to the foundations of survival horror and metroidvania. The result cements Silver Pines as a remarkable debut for Wych Elm, delivering an intriguing, authentic investigation that honors its classic inspirations while forging a memorable artistic identity of its own.

Silver Pines proudly wears its darkened, beating heart right on its sleeve, and it is in that unabashed love for its influences that it emerges a confident, distinct experience for survival-horror fans both new and old. Its central mystery will keep you awake and desperately thinking for an answer, while its old-school horror gameplay is a fun, uncompromising love-letter to the genre that remains compelling despite the rough edges. It’s an acquired taste that’s a lot like black coffee: strong, bold, and deeply engaging. To that end, Silver Pines is a damn, fine cup that’ll keep you wired for days.

Silver Pines evokes the likes of Resident Evil, Silent Hill and Twin Peaks. Fans of those, or of a strong metroidvania, should treat this as a must-play. In a year as stacked as 2026, it’s difficult for games to get the time they deserve, but it would be criminal to let this one slip through your fingers. One of my favourite horror games this generation.

Resident Evil, Silent Hill and even Dead Space are among the greatest survival horror classics that can easily be seen as inspiration for Silver Pines. Rather than just being a love letter to this era, Silver Pines strongly carves out its own identity with Metroidvania inspired level design without the backtracking pitfalls. Like many survival horror, combat is the weakness, especially at the bosses, and coincidentally, it suffers the same problems that Prince of Persia had due to its visual style with a lack of precision. Outside of that and a few other minor complaints, Silver Pines is one of the most unique survival horror games in years and an absolute must for fans of the 90’s and early genre icons.

The dark visual style, the Lynchian atmosphere, the clever puzzles, and the map that slowly opens up and rewards exploration. Silver Pines is one of the big surprises of the fall, and in many ways I enjoyed it even more than Silent Hill: Townfall – despite the considerable differences in the size and budgets of the teams behind them. For its price point, Wych Elm’s debut is a highly recommendable thriller for fans of the genre, and it certainly doesn’t lack atmosphere.
Silver Pines delivers a heavy story, blending classic and modern noir elements into an experience worthy of a podium finish at major gaming awards.

Silver Pines feels like a true work of art, but it does have one minor drawback, and that is that you sometimes have to persevere a bit to find your next key to success by navigating the map. However, that also has its charm. Especially in the beginning, you really stand there with your mouth open, gazing at the style of this title, and I find that admirable. The world opens up with every step you take and every item you find. The dialogues are short enough and not long-winded, meaning you practically never skip them, making you genuinely want to and try to keep following the story, no matter how many hours you’ve already put into the game—and that is certainly at least fifteen by the end. Furthermore, you don’t necessarily have to discover everything, but you do want to. For that reason alone, Silver Pines might well be one of the most surprising games of this autumn, and there are still quite a few top titles to come. As far as I’m concerned, this game deserves a great deal of respect, even though many people probably haven’t seen this title pass by in the crowded lineup yet.

I went in hoping for a clever blend of two genres and came away with one of my favorite games of the year. The bosses can be punishing, and the Xbox Ally X has occasional dips, but neither issue took much away from the mystery, the remarkable art, or the simple joy of finding a new way through Silver Pines. I loved every minute of the 14 hours it took me to complete. An essential game!

Silver Pines is one of the biggest surprises of the year. Its blend of Metroidvania and survival horror works wonderfully thanks to well-crafted exploration, an intriguing story, and an atmosphere that draws you in from the start. The combat is a bit clunky and doesn't quite measure up to the rest of the game, but it doesn't detract from an adventure that comes highly recommended, especially if you're a fan of Resident Evil.

Silver Pines is an atmospheric game, a Metroidvania-style survival horror title that draws heavily from genre classics like Silent Hill, Resident Evil, and Alan Wake, as well as from television and film, such as Twin Peaks, The X-Files, and The Shining. However, these inspirations don’t reduce Wych Elm’s work to a mere collection of references; thanks to excellent storytelling, they allow the game to carve out its own path between nightmare and mystery. Solid gameplay underpins the experience, reinterpreting the genre’s conventions without forcing a radical overhaul. It’s also impossible not to mention the excellent art direction, featuring rotoscoped animations, and the soundtrack, with atmospheric music that heightens the tension. Silver Pines is a haunting adventure, a glimpse into the mystery of identity that straddles the line between reality and imagination.

The greatest compliment that I can give to Silver Pines, is that if David Lynch envisaged a Twin Peaks game, I expect it’d look something like Wych Elm’s sensational Metroidvania. The collision of a Twin Peaks-like town, 2D survival horror gameplay and Castlevania exploration was an ambitious project, but I’m delighted to say it has comfortably delivered. The town of Silver Pines is a wonderfully sinister place to explore, it’s story deep and intriguing, and presentation a horrific delight. Silver Pines is the best horror game you can play for Halloween 2026.

Silver Pines is a decent Metroidvania game that plays like a solid survival horror title. However, its poor combat can detract from the overall experience, although fans of the genre should still have this on their radar.

Silver Pines is an excellent survival horror game. Although it falters in some aspects of its narrative development, the game masterfully leverages its greatest strength: adding Metroidvania-style exploration to a combination of ideas that were already very good on their own.

The Blood of Dawnwalker is one of the most impressive games I’ve played this generation. The sprawling world and multifaceted story are wonders to behold, while the combat walks the perfect line between complexity and accessibility. Though there is a little bit of open-world jank to contend with, you’d be missing out by choosing not to play this game, as it may already be the best release in an extremely competitive September.

Rebel Wolves may have built the game on familiar open-world RPG foundations, but The Blood of Dawnwalker ultimately establishes an identity entirely its own. Its ambitious storytelling, rewarding combat and excellent vampire mechanics make it a genuine Game of the Year contender, and an absolute must-play for RPG fans.

Ultimately, I loved exploring the world Rebel Wolves has built with The Blood of Dawn Walker. While Coen and his companions often feel a bit too young and beautiful for the gritty story they inhabit, Vale Sangora feels rich within the limits of its mountain range. The directional combat was a lovely change from simple three-button combos and a pleasure to master, while the time resource management mechanic helped me maintain focus without feeling overly pressured. If you have ever enjoyed Skyrim, The Witcher, or a Red Dead game, I suspect there is a lot here you will love. My family will soon be complaining that I’m busy saving Coen’s family too often as I run through multiple playthroughs over the coming weeks.

Simply exploring the world counts as a free action for those who just want to see what’s around and discover what they can find, while finding secrets and transforming your Coen as a result is an engaging blast. The scenario writing and character work deliver on all the expectations from The Witcher 3, with plenty of morally tricky propositions for the player to uncover and crack. It’s the sort of game that you want to revisit as soon as you set it down. Strong graphics, great storytelling, and solid gameplay all come together to deliver one of the best games of the year. If you like games like The Witcher 3 or Elden Ring, Blood of the Dawnwalker is a must-play experience. Even if you don’t like those games, the strength of the execution in Rebel Wolves’ first game is worth checking out and admiring.

Supported by sharp combat, deep day-night synergy, a fantastic score, and a lived-in world, the game delivers on its ambitious promises. Minor hiccups like stiff facial animations or initial calendar anxiety do nothing to diminish what Rebel Wolves has achieved here. The Blood of Dawnwalker isn't just an outstanding RPG; it is a landmark statement in game design that proves restraint, atmosphere, and meaningful player agency beat mindless scale every single time. An absolute, brilliantly executed dark fantasy masterpiece.

Most Western RPGs have been overshadowed this year by an incredible run of JRPGs, both those already released and several more looming on the horizon in the coming months. Against that backdrop, The Blood of Dawnwalker might genuinely be one of the best games 2026 has to offer. It has it all and then some, constantly surprising with consummate professionalism and polish.

The Blood of Dawnwalker is a game that lays its ambitions bare at the beginning, and one-by-one pays off all those ambitions in remarkable ways. It’s a game that grips you early on, and sinks its teeth into you more with every passing hour.

The Blood of Dawnwalker understands something that most open-world RPGs seem to forget. You cannot experience everything. Time is always moving forward, and how you spend it is important. Having to make those sacrifices initially frustrated me because I wanted to see everything the game had to offer, but eventually it became the reason I enjoyed the journey so much. It also makes The Blood of Dawnwalker highly replayable, because there will always be things you left behind to discover on another playthrough. And with that, I am off to play it all again.

The Blood of Dawnwalker does almost everything right that you'd expect from an action role-playing game. Exceptional gameplay, a story full of twists and turns, and an immersive gaming experience make Rebel Wolves' debut a contender for Game of the Year.
The Blood of Dawnwalker is a fantastic RPG worthy of diving and sinking your fangs into again and again.

Ladies and gentlemen, without mincing words or beating around the bush, The Blood of Dawnwalker is simply a great video game. Rebel Wolves hits the mark perfectly and delivers a debut that confidently enters the club of the best action RPGs on the market. Never predictable and capable of breathing new life — or rather, new blood — into the vampire mythos, The Blood of Dawnwalker offers adrenaline-fueled combat, deep and customizable character progression, solid technical performance, and an interesting story capable of engaging the player, also thanks to the possibility of making choices that have a real impact on events. Sure, some elements could have used a little more polish, and some mechanics can feel cumbersome, but that doesn't change the fact that Coen's adventures will entertain you and keep you glued to your controller. The Blood of Dawnwalker is one of the biggest and most interesting surprises the 2026 gaming year could have given us.

The Blood of Dawnwalker deserves to be a new AAA mainstay, and I’d gladly join Coen on future ventures. Rebel Wolves’ debut outing is everything you could want from the former director of The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt, but it’s also something entirely new. Its time mechanic is risky - and a nightmare for completionists - but it adds a brilliant sense of urgency into the open-world. The Blood of Dawnwalker is all about consequence. Which quests should you tackle? As a human or a vampire? It’s entirely what you make of it, offering up a bold and engaging formula that I’d be glad to see walk away with 2026’s GOTY trophy.

The game goes a step beyond merely being a homage, and perhaps borrows a few too many gameplay elements from the legendary The Witcher 3, but it's hard not to be quite considerably impressed by what Rebel Wolves has achieved here. The Blood of Dawnwalker offers innovative solutions to well-established design challenges that far larger, more experienced studios have been unable to resolve, and it does so with flair, character, and enthusiasm.

The Blood of Dawnwalker has a familiar DNA, yet manages to carve out a distinct identity as an RPG. Its time-based system forces players to carefully consider their next move, giving greater weight to every decision they make. Strong writing, engaging combat, and rewarding exploration showcase the expertise its developers have refined over the years, resulting in a compelling and confidently crafted role-playing experience.
The Blood of Dawnwalker is an excellent open-world fantasy RPG with some unique, interesting ideas.
The Blood of Dawnwalker is an impressive, bloody cocktail of interesting ideas and well-written characters, making it one of this year’s best open-world RPGs.
The Blood of Dawnwalker is a fascinating action-RPG, where every choice to save Coen’s family feels rightly consequential.
The Blood of Dawnwalker is an excellent, albeit imperfect, starting point, but one that Rebel Wolves has used to forge its own path. If you love decision-making RPGs, you won't be disappointed.

The Blood of Dawnwalker is going to be one of the most memorable RPG experiences of the year. Not because it has a movie-like budget, but because it executes its ideas brilliantly and makes the most of what it has
Blood of Dawnwalker features a great setting, a brilliant dual gameplay loop, and satisfying combat in a world I want to see much more of.

Rest assured: The Blood of Dawnwalker is more than just "The Witcher with vampires." Rebel Wolves weave together proven action-RPG staples with an incredibly organic time-management mechanic and engaging, hybrid day-night gameplay. The result is a genuine RPG-gem; while it still has some technical kinks to iron out, in terms of both gameplay and narrative, it need not shy away from the genre’s heavyweights. I can hardly wait for a sequel already.

The Blood of Dawnwalker from developer Rebel Wolves is a great starting point for what could become a bigger series. It delivers a strong story, entertaining gameplay elements, and plenty of quests to keep the journey going.

A fantastically designed game that, with its unique time-flow mechanic, brings a true evolution to the open-world RPG genre. For many players, this will be an experience that reminds them of the best moments from The Witcher 3, and it will surely become a favorite modern RPG for many.

The Blood of Dawnwalker is a fun race against time that effectively introduces a universe teeming with vampires and even worse threats. While there are some technical issues and enemy balancing could be improved, that doesn't change the fact that Rebel Wolves has delivered one of the best RPGs of 2026.

The Blood of Dawnwalker makes an excellent start for Rebel Wolves. Their first game possesses great writing all around, with well-realised characters and deep lore. The combat also has a good foundation, and hopefully it will be developed further in future instalments, alleviating some of its rigid animations and limited enemy variety. However, the high quality of all the other elements more than makes up for these shortcomings, delivering an RPG that we hope will continue to expand in the future.

The Blood of Dawnwalker is a masterclass in how to make an actual RPG, and it poses itself as one of the best vampire games ever. With its stellar writing, interesting time-based mechanics and open-ended story approach, it overshadows many of its peers despite a few, very minor hiccups on the gameplay side.

Taking your time with The Blood of Dawnwalker isn’t a choice, it’s a requirement, and it’s one that you’ll be all too happy to oblige thanks to an engaging combat and a free form approach to questing that’s equal parts stressful and rewarding.

Blood of Dawnwalker is much more than just another Witcher-like RPG. Its dark vampire setting, meaningful choices and strong storytelling give the game its own identity. The combat is challenging but flexible, while the time system and the differences between day and night add welcome depth. Some issues with controls, camera work and technical polish remain, but they rarely overshadow the overall experience. In short, Blood of Dawnwalker is one of the first major RPG highlights of the second half of 2026.

The Blood of Dawnwalker is a confident dark-fantasy RPG from Rebel Wolves that wears its The Witcher 3 influences proudly. While its barebones combat and mediocre visual presentation leave more to be desired, the fantastic writing coursing through its veins and novel 30-day time limit prove that it’s more than just a shadow of its silver-haired, monster-hunting inspiration. With a sequel confirmed to be in development, there’s plenty of room for Coen’s journey to sink its teeth deeper into fans of this fresh-blooded IP boiling with so much potential.

Its strong narrative alone helps The Blood of Dawnwalker stand out in a crowded field of open-world RPGs. Add layered, nuanced combat and separate day and night skill systems, and you’re well on the way to something special. The innovative 30-day clock sounds like a better idea than it turns out to be, thanks to an inconsistent and somewhat punishing implementation. There’s also a fair amount of repetition in the loop of questing and fighting. Still, the positives far outweigh the negatives, and The Blood of Dawnwalker is an engaging and entertaining experience.

The Blood of Dawnwalker is a fantastic open world RPG with a sharply written story, great characters and meaningful choices throughout. It wears its Witcher 3 inspirations on its sleeve, but isn't afraid to add some twists to keep it fresh.
A gripping vampire-RPG with tough choices, strong dialogue, and a cool parry system, but a formulaic open world.

In a month packed with big-name releases, The Blood of Dawnwalker might be one of the best games of the bunch. It's a well-crafted adventure with an engaging story, an enjoyable world, interesting powers and a genuinely compelling approach to player choice. The time limit gives every decision weight. The open-ended storytelling makes exploration meaningful. The day/night system gives Coen two distinct ways to interact with the world. Most importantly, the game trusts you to make choices without constantly telling you whether you've made the "right" one.

While it suffers from rough graphics and repetitive combat, The Blood of Dawnwalker delivers a deeply engaging narrative shaped by meaningful choices under a 30-day time limit. Driven by compelling characters and solid storytelling, it stands out as a rare gem among story-driven medieval RPGs.

The Blood of Dawnwalker manages to avoid becoming a mere repetition of familiar formulas and finds an identity of its own, thanks to a combination of reactive storytelling, meaningful exploration, and a time mechanic that alters how every decision is approached.

With incredibly well-written missions, captivating characters, and a variety of three skill trees that enhance the average combat, The Blood of Dawnwalker features a great storyline filled with memorable moments and gameplay brimming with sublime freedom.

All of this is as fun as it sounds, a few graphics glitches aside, but what’s most remarkable about “Dawnwalker” is the storytelling. Vale Sangora is a detailed setting with fascinating characters throughout. While you’re mostly a lone warrior, the story of “Blood of Dawnwalker: requires Coen to make allies, and they are not just bland NPCs but fully considered supporting characters with arcs and backstories of their own that feel complexly written.

The Blood of Dawnwalker is more than an outstanding debut IP for Rebel Wolves. It comes with its own very well-executed ideas, a decision system with tangible consequences, and one of the most satisfying combat systems in the genre. It is not a 'The Witcher with vampires'; it is an adventure with its own personality that fans of action RPGs and medieval fantasy will love.

The Blood of Dawnwalker is an ambitious RPG that manages to step out of The Witcher 3’s shadow thanks to its clever use of time, meaningful choices, and the duality between human and vampire. On PS5, Quality Mode delivers impressive visuals while maintaining a solid 30 FPS, backed by excellent audio and a narrative structure where choices and their consequences genuinely matter.

Although it has some flaws in combat, The Blood of Dawnwalker delivers a solid and characterful experience. Its time management system, the freedom to explore, and the choices that shape Coen's journey are its greatest strengths and make Rebel Wolves' RPG stand out from other games in the genre.

A little less revolutionary than we might have imagined in our wildest dreams, The Blood of Dawnwalker is still a must-play for vampire fans and anyone who enjoyed The Witcher 3. It blends a fairly classic approach, especially in its visuals and open-world design, with some welcome ideas like its time-based structure and directional combat. But where it really shines is in what matters most for an RPG: its storytelling, exploration and meaningful player choices. The foundations of a great series are here, and we can’t wait to see where Coen’s journey takes him next, potentially across several games and centuries, all the way to the modern era.

The Blood of Dawnwalker bears all the hallmarks of a project crafted by brilliance, particularly through its top-tier storytelling and tight combat mechanics. Yet while its core identity as an Action RPG is rock-solid, the surrounding package lacks the high-end production polish needed to elevate it further. It’s an undeniable achievement, but one constantly shadowed by the obvious strain of a limited budget and workforce.

The Blood of the Dawnwalker is an impressive debut from Rebel Wolves, with challenging combat and choices that shape the story around you. It breathes life back into a tired genre of vampire action RPGs, using time as a resource and allowing the player to shape the world around them. Despite relatively benign issues that can easily be rectified, it is certainly one to watch within the world of RPGs.
The Blood of Dawnwalker impresses with its world-building, characters, and time-driven choices. Despite dated visuals, it’s an ambitious and compelling RPG debut.

The Blood of Dawnwalker is an ambitious, choice-driven vampire RPG with an intricately connected world, satisfying directional combat, and meaningful player agency throughout most of its journey. Repetitive enemies, technical issues, and a surprisingly rigid finale keep Rebel Wolves’ debut from reaching its full potential, but its compelling characters and nonlinear storytelling make it a promising start to a new RPG universe.
An original, macabre horror story with a strong setting, central narrative, and characters, though Coen is no Geralt.

The Blood of Dawnwalker is excellent, if not quite successful in everything it tries. It's fun to teleport around in a cloud of smoke and bats or walk on ceilings, but the story is also fantastic. It's probably even darker and grimmer than you're expecting, and it gripped me throughout and was complimented by equally fascinating side quest stories that I had to choose between. If you like RPGs, vampires, or great stories, you won't want to miss The Blood of Dawnwalker.

The Blood of Dawnwalker is a solid RPG with an intriguing time-based system and a compelling story filled with memorable characters and numerous paths to explore. However, issues with its combat and technical performance prevent it from fully realizing its ambitious vision. Even so, it remains a highly entertaining and worthwhile experience that is easy to recommend.

The narrative might be subservient to the mechanics, and not as thematically evocative as I might like, but excellent writing does combine with quality, well-executed mechanics to give us the equivalent of a pulp fantasy page-turner, and like the stories of dark pulp fantasy writer, Robert E. Howard, it’s really (really) difficult to put down.
The Blood of Dawnwalker is a fantastic first outing from Rebel Wolves and the clear start of a franchise. It's full of smart ideas that have the making of another classic RPG franchise.

The Blood of Dawnwalker is both what was expected and what was feared: an RPG anchored in familiar structural mechanics that attempts to break new ground with a couple of fresh design ideas. The signature style of Rebel Wolves—a team largely hailing from CD Projekt Red—is most evident in the writing; the world-building, lore, and plot are compelling and satisfying, keeping players glued to their controllers for hours. Centered on Coen, the game features a "sandbox" spirit and a 30-day mechanic—two gambles that pay off in terms of replayability and a sense of consequence, even if the promised freedom is only partially realized. The result is an enjoyable debut that is magnetic at times, yet suffers from the flaws typical of a first outing.

Overall, The Blood of Dawnwalker is an incredibly ambitious, deeply interesting first game from Rebel Wolves. Not every good idea lands and not every envelope is pushed as far as it could be, but the potential of the game is vast, and there’s a huge amount to lean into and love. And it’s all bolstered by excellent writing that makes for one of the deepest and most interesting game worlds I’ve run across in some time. The Blood of Dawnwalker is the kind of RPG that feels great to get lost in, that digs into your mind and stays there, and which is worth scouring and savoring.

A stellar opening bite from Rebel Wolves, The Blood of Dawnwalker demonstrates it can claw and battle with the toughest of the vrakhir. While it's not quite at the level of the very best in the genre, it delivers a superb open world adventure, filled with intrigue and compelling combat. Give it enough time to feed and this Dawnwalker could grow into a titan, and I can't wait to see what blood feast will come next.

The Blood of Dawnwalker is a flawed game, but the heart at the centre of it is strong. Rebel Wolves certainly has work to do in this post-release period with balance, performance, and quality-of-life updates – but once this work is done, I feel this will be the first entry in what becomes a beloved saga. For all its faults, The Blood of Dawnwalker has sold me on its world and characters, and I am eager to take up my sword as Coen in the future.

The final assessment of our experience with The Blood of Dawnwalker is undoubtedly positive. Aside from a few flaws in the gameplay systems (likely due to the development team's relative immaturity), the game is easily one of the best action RPGs currently available, thanks in part to a masterfully written story and superb worldbuilding. The only disappointment is a few glitches in the navigation systems, which ultimately dilute the sense of immersion in the universe created by Rebel Wolves, but Coen's adventure in this dark fantasy world bodes well for the developers' future.

There’s plenty to do in The Blood of Dawnwalker, and I’ve already spent a great deal of time wondering how different decisions might have shaped the outcomes, enough so that I will be playing through it again straight away. For a game I wasn’t entirely sure about at first, I’m happy to be walking away with a new addition to my lineup of favorite RPGs, and one that I’d love to see influence the genre.

Playing The Blood of Dawnwalker is like attending a live rock concert: it's often uncomfortable, the music is sloppy, it's incredibly loud, but the energy and passion knock the walls down. There are numerous technical issues, the execution is far from flawless, many mechanics are poorly refined, the animations often leave much to be desired, and there's a widespread shortage of original assets. On the other hand, Rebel Wolves have staked everything on their historical strengths, on their ability to create unique worlds and develop deeply fleshed-out characters, weaving a web of choices and consequences that pays homage to the great role-playing games of the past, finding the perfect setting for an experience of this genre to shine. A competent, courageous experience, tied to unique gameplay, which unfolds its enormous potential within a framework that is certainly not one for grand occasions, at least not in this pre-launch version. Take it or leave it: the heart of true role-playing games beats in Coen's story, but to perceive it you have to lower the little finger of the form.
A spirited and open-ended action role-player that blends vampire lore with authentic European history, while introducing an impressive new swordplay and magic-based combat system.

Don't mistake this for selective amnesia regarding the various flaws addressed by the reviewer: however annoying some of these limitations may have been, they ultimately pale in comparison to the masterful achievements showcased here. Admittedly, the visual presentation sometimes feels anachronistic, and we find some of the major shortcomings of the talented team behind The Witcher 3 (awful inventory, a slight lack of variety in attack patterns and the bestiary, among other things). Despite these drawbacks, they cannot overshadow the incredibly deep and branching narrative presented here, aided by a successful combat system, superb art direction (both visually and in terms of sound design), and a cast of wonderfully endearing characters. The Blood of Dawnwalker is essentially a salutary and completely timely reminder: the key to any game's success is, above all, to embrace its own identity.

The Blood of Dawnwalker was a very engaging experience during the 18 hours it took me to reach the credits—though it would take much longer if you were to use all the available days and complete more missions. Its strong narrative component helps make the combat challenges feel less tedious.

Like a vampiric sire turns a hapless mortal to their own purposes, Rebel Wolves have taken the body of a modern-day RPG classic and turned it into something strange and new. The Blood of Dawnwalker’s few flaws come from a team biting off more than it can chew, and I would never fault a vampire game for that.

The world is also exceptionally well-realized. Although it is a fantasy setting, the developers have done an excellent job of making it feel like a believable fantasy—something that could actually have happened.

By the end of The Blood of Dawnwalker, the developers' passion for the title is undeniable. All the care poured into the narrative, the characters, and this twisted vampire world proves that it's no coincidence the studio's leadership was behind The Witcher 3. There is a genuine heart embedded within it, yet a persistent question lingers: given a few more months of development, it might have achieved something close to perfection.
The Blood of Dawnwalker is an RPG through and through, featuring a gripping storyline and world that make it a must-play for fans of the genre—and, of course, of The Witcher.
The vampire may have taken centuries to assemble; here you have 30 exhilarating, memorable days. [Issue#429, p.102]

Please don't turn The Blood of Dawnwalker into another The Witcher; instead, see it for what it is: an ambitious debut game that dares to make bold choices and has its own unique identity. We can only encourage that originality and boldness.

The Blood of Dawnwalker is a compelling action RPG with solid directional combat, engaging time management, and an intriguing duality between human and vampire abilities. Repetitive activities and technical issues hold it back, but Rebel Wolves delivers a promising and enjoyable debut.

The Blood of Dawnwalker is a rock-solid debut for Rebel Wolves. The story, the characters, the extensive RPG systems and the enjoyable combat all work, and they keep you glued to the controller for dozens of hours. Unfortunately, my playthrough was thoroughly soured by technical problems that even affected my progress. That's a real shame, because in almost every respect The Blood of Dawnwalker is a diamond that just needs some polishing here and there.

The Blood of Dawnwalker stands as a highly promising first step for the Rebel Wolves team. It delivers a deep story, finely crafted characters, and an enjoyable combat system. However, the lenient execution of time pressure, repetitive enemy design, and frustrating technical issues make the game feel like a vampire stepping out before sunset.

The Blood of Dawnwalker is narratively brilliant, but the activities in the Sangora Valley don’t live up to its story and characters. An imperfect but promising debut. Let’s hope it lays the foundations for a great saga.

The Blood of the Dawnwalker is full of good intentions in every respect: the time-management gameplay, the human/vampire duality for the RPG elements, the directional parry system in combat, and the impact of player choices. However, each of these aspects is held back by mediocre execution—whether it’s the overly limited bestiary, the rudimentary writing, or inconsistencies in game design. In its determination to follow in the footsteps of The Witcher 3, the game never truly dared to stray from the beaten path. By focusing too much on its role model's feet instead of fixing its gaze on its own horizon, it often ends up stumbling. Yet I know it will get back up—and hopefully, this time, it will be to forge its own path.
While The Blood of Dawnwalker and its dark fantasy vampire setting is well worth exploring, best wait for a few patches before exploring its vast open world.

The Blood of Dawnwalker offers a role-playing formula that hits the mark in terms of narrative, but falls short when it comes to combat, world-building and polish. Rebel Wolves is a little too ambitious, despite demonstrating that there is tremendous potential in this role-playing universe featuring vampires.

According to Rebel Wolves, The Blood of Dawnwalker is just the first instalment in a planned series. And honestly, that's what it feels like: a starting point. Fans of vampire fiction or choice-driven RPGs should still gel with Dawnwalker based on the strength of its world building, characters, and deliciously dark tones. But you'll need to stomach some of the most serviceable, yet frustratingly stunted gameplay I've encountered in quite some time.

Despite my mechanical gripes, I remained invested in Coen’s story to the end. The final confrontation encapsulated the many decisions and paths I took and had me face their ramifications one after the other. I may have been unfazed by the time mechanic’s pressure, but the limitation did shape my adventure. The Blood of Dawnwalker shows that curating a massive RPG rather than pursuing every single quest holds immense potential. The ending made me realize that having all the time in the world would have prevented inner ambitions to finally come to broad daylight.

The Blood of Dawnwalker has an interesting core, but it throws too many obstacles in your way before you can get to it. Rebel Wolves builds a rich universe with many stories worth discovering, but its clunky mechanics and various issues with its main systems are hard to ignore.

The Blood of Dawnwalker has a brilliant reactive story and some genuinely clever ideas, but its basic combat, familiar open world and underdeveloped vampire fantasy stop it from becoming the game it threatens to be.

While Rebel Wolves shows a lot of promise with some narrative highlights and a handful of compelling quests in its vampiric open-world RPG, The Blood of Dawnwalker unfortunately struggles under the weight of its ambition thanks to a bloated open world and mechanical misfires in combat.

A repetitive open world, encounters that quickly lose their excitement, clunky traversal, systems that sound more interesting than they actually are, and a time mechanic that too often feels arbitrary might have been easier to overlook when games like The Witcher 3 were helping redefine what an open-world RPG could be. In 2026, they stand out considerably more. There is a version of The Blood of Dawnwalker buried underneath all of that I'm sure I would love, and I sincerely hope Rebel Wolves gets the chance to dig it out someday. As it stands, though, this feels less like the next step forward for the genre and more like a game arriving after the world it was built for has already moved on.

The Blood of Dawnwalker is an ambitious first title that delivers an intriguing narrative experience well worthy of the studio's pedigree. Held back only by limited replayability and somewhat simplistic combat, it's still well worth the purchase for RPG fans
CD Projekt Red alumni create a familiar dark fantasy adventure, but one with bold and provocative ideas of its own, that's mostly, enormously successful.
The Blood of Dawnwalker is a resolutely miserable horror RPG with some great ideas of its own, though it doesn't always have the courage to follow them through.
For an RPG that keeps telling me that it matters I've been cursed to be a vampire, it feels all too frictionless and forgiving.

The Blood of Dawnwalker is a dark, brilliantly written vampire RPG with a superb prologue, a memorable cast and inventive powers. It's dragged down at times by repetitive combat, a rough performance, and an insipid lead. A flawed, fascinating debut with cult classic written all over it - one that needs some post-launch patches, but kept me hooked regardless.

The Blood of Dawnwalker is an ambitious project that occasionally wears both the best and worst aspects of its inspirations on its sleeve. Where it shines is in allowing players to make their own choices and learn from their own mistakes. It’s incredible fun to play in a world where the clock is ever-ticking, and the results of our actions and words have real consequences not just for us but for those around us.
The Blood of Dawnwalker has strong ideas and a compelling story, but repetitive design, uneven systems, and constant jank hold it back.

The Blood of Dawnwalker is not the worst game, but it doesn't amount to a revolution in the genre. Perhaps if the timer had been stricter, things would have been different. Then you'd really have to make agonizing choices, cutting off entire quest branches with a careless phrase. 
As it stands, the end result feels too soft and even unnecessary. As if at some point at Rebel Wolves they got scared that audiences wouldn't like the restrictions, and then reworked the timer. So every plus comes with a minus.

The Blood of the Dawnwalker is the rare game created by a studio of decorated ex-AAA veterans that actually gets very near to its original inspiration. With an intriguing setting, a one-of-a-kind narrative sandbox approach, fantastic writing, and solid combat, this may well be the first installment in an epic saga that will accompany gamers for decades to come.

While The Blood of Dawnwalker is a competent enough action RPG, it also leaves something to be desired: the characters are well written and well acted, but its roleplay elements feel weaker than they might look at first glance; and the combat is snappy, but enemy variety is extremely poor; the game is visually pleasant and well optimized at 1080p, but gameplay is capped at 60 fps and cutscenes at 30. It did leave me wanting for a sequel, though.
Rebel Wolves’ debut game The Blood of Dawnwalker is a triumphant achievement in the art of telling rich, raw, human stories set with a more fantastical backdrop.
Engaging vampire RPG with weighty choices, strong dialogue, and a cool parry system, but a formulaic open world.

The Blood of Dawnwalker is a brilliant debut for Rebel Wolves. It inflicts weight on every decision with its time mechanics, yet still lends you enough freedom to embrace those small moments that make us human. It pushed me into agonizing situations, uncomfortable choices, and ridiculous asides, all interwoven with a simple yet tremendously satisfying combat system. Small gripes about overused enemies and dated animations aren't enough to keep this from being one of my favorite RPGs in years.

The final assessment of our experience with The Blood of Dawnwalker is undoubtedly positive. Aside from a few flaws in the gameplay systems (likely due to the development team's relative immaturity), the game is easily one of the best action RPGs currently available, thanks in part to a masterfully written story and superb worldbuilding. The only disappointment is a few glitches in the navigation systems, which ultimately dilute the sense of immersion in the universe created by Rebel Wolves, but Coen's adventure in this dark fantasy world bodes well for the developers' future.
Rebel Wolves delivers a dark fantasy RPG that can hold its own against its illustrious cousin and is a firstborn that we hope will produce other gems in the same vein in the future.

There's real ambition here from Rebel Wolves, but the the game needed more time for technical polish along with some major overhauls to the repetitive combat. Still, there's a compelling story to be told here.
Rebel Wolves' debut project is an instant classic, and one of the best RPGs of 2026
It's clear from the off that there's a strong RPG pedigree at work in The Blood of Dawnwalker. The work of Rebel Wolves, a studio founded by forme...

The Blood of Dawnwalker is an incredible RPG that sinks its fangs into you from the moment you start playing, signalling an incredibly strong start for Rebel Wolves. Choices feel meaningful, combat is satisfying, and the time system makes you stop and think about just what you're doing when you play games. While some quests drag and there were some technical hiccups along the way, nothing made me want to stop playing this adventure that trades breadth for depth. As such, The Blood of Dawnwalker is easily one of my favourite RPGs in years and well worth a taste.

The Blood of Dawnwalker is an excellent dark fantasy RPG that combines meaningful choices, a clever time-management system and satisfying combat with a world that constantly encourages another playthrough. Rebel Wolves wears its Witcher 3 influence proudly, but this is a game with a strong identity of its own.

The Blood of Dawnwalker from Rebel Wolves is a grim RPG which, at its best, rivals The Witcher 3 story-wise. The game charms with an excellent prologue, a grounded, down-to-earth atmosphere, mature choices in shades of grey, and memorable characters. Unfortunately, after a brilliant start, the experience suffers due to repetitive, Ubisoft-style open-world activities that you have to plough through to uncover the narrative treasures. It is an ambitious and successful, albeit uneven, title – a must-play for fans of atmospheric games who are willing to overlook some of the rough edges typical of a debut title.
Otherwise, however, Dawnwalker is an excellent starting point for a potential successful dark fantasy saga.
The Blood of Dawnwalker is a concept that has yet to fully mature—perhaps it will in a future installment.

While the initial experience might feel a bit rough around the edges, and mechanics like gear score and open-world design even give off a slightly cookie-cutter vibe, Blood of the Dawnwalker is an excellent title that keeps revealing its brilliance once you fully sink your teeth into it. It does an outstanding job with its choice-driven content and delivers quite a few genuinely unexpected moments.
Easily one of this year’s best games, The Blood of Dawnwalker also makes a strong case to position itself among the best action RPGs ever made.

Rebel Wolves' story-driven RPG is clearly built on the role-playing ethos established by The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt, but it's the breadth and depth of original ideas at play that make the game stand on its own merits.

The Blood of Dawnwalker feels more like a sandbox adventure where you make your own story rather than play one that’s been predetermined by the writer. It’s different, but not necessarily better or worse than what we’re used to.

An original and, in many ways, unusual action RPG that challenges you to take a fresh look at a familiar genre. This universe has great potential, and we can't wait to see how these bold ideas are developed in the already confirmed sequel.

The Blood of Dawnwalker, despite it shortcomings, managed to meet a significant portion of my expectations. The game boasts notable strengths in world-building, atmosphere, music, character development, and combat system design,making it especially appealing to those who have long awaited a dark, medieval-themed RPG. On the other hand, one cannot overlook its technical issues, stiff animations, certain visual weaknesses, and the less-than-ideal implementation of the time-limit system. Rebel Wolves' effort to craft a game that draws from the legacy of The Witcher 3 without merely copying it is commendable. In many ways, The Blood of Dawnwalker proves that there is still room for a story-driven, atmospheric, and engaging RPG,and if you approach it with the expectations of an AA title, it just might become one of the more beloved and distinctive experiences the genre has to offer.

The Blood of Dawnwalker is the kind of ambitious RPG that invites you to lose yourself in its world, where your choices play a major role in shaping the story and allow you to experience it on your own terms. This freedom is the game’s biggest strength, while its deep RPG mechanics and engaging combat complement the experience nicely.
Despite some shortcomings, Dawnwalker ultimately delivers a satisfying and memorable experience. With plenty of replay value and different paths to explore, it’s a game you can return to and experience in a whole new way. If you’re a fan of open-world RPGs with deep stories and meaningful choices, The Blood of Dawnwalker is a journey worth taking.

The Blood of Dawnwalker is an excellent start to a new universe, one that draws on the experience of the creators of The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt, but which, thanks to the 30-day system, Coen’s transformation and the consequences of your decisions, quickly finds its own identity. The game’s greatest strengths are its superbly written quests, interesting characters and a world you’ll want to return to in order to experience completely different versions of events. The underdeveloped combat and technical issues can be irritating, but they do not detract from the fact that Rebel Wolves has created a large, ambitious RPG that is well worth checking out.

You will enjoy spending time with the vampire hero as he demonstrates his power, engaging in combat and exploring a perilous open world. With dozens of hours of battles, moving scenes and conversations, the game is sure to win you over.
