A bit too much grinding, a structure prone to repetition, and a narrative that falls short of the game world's full potential keep the title from achieving perfection. Yet, Raiders proves something important: Splatoon is not merely a brilliant competitive arena, but a world still brimming with possibilities. And this spin-off is concrete proof that Nintendo was right to explore them.

Splatoon Raiders is an amazing evolution of the series, perfectly expanding and improving the Salmon Run-mode. Especially the gameplay-feeling when fighting against the wicked salmonids sucked me right in and captivated me for hours on end.

Splatoon Raiders is more than a spin-off; it's an incredible launching point for a new branch of more single-player adventures, combining some of the best parts of the original Splatoon trilogy and turning it into something that feels fresh. Upgrading your arsenal as the Mechanic as you go from island to island, splatting hoards of Salmonids, is even more satisfying than it looks, and though the story isn't too deep, the gameplay couldn't be richer. Not only is Splatoon Raiders an essential addition to your Switch 2 game library when it launches 23rd July, it's a splat-tastic reason to own Nintendo's latest system in the first place.

Splatoon Raiders successfully transforms Splatoon's signature gameplay into an engaging single-player adventure. Excellent enemy design, rewarding progression, and deep customization make every expedition satisfying, while its polished PvE systems feel like a natural evolution for the series. More than a spin-off, it's a strong blueprint for Splatoon's future.

Splatoon Raiders is great. Putting more of a focus on solo and co-op for this game has led to an adventure with a really satisfying progression as you level up, grind stages for experience and gear, and build up your loadout to tackle the next big challenge.

Splatoon Raiders is an amazing action RPG with an expertly executed loop. It has fantastic new powers with crazy upgrades that are worth chasing, tough battles that force you to put care into your build in order to overcome them, and a huge variety of fun level types to jump between. The pacing, balance, and difficulty curve are very impressive: I always had to work to get better, but none of the campaign ever felt like grinding or needless padding. Raiders stays fresh by constantly introducing deeper ways to customize my abilities that spark new ideas for creative combinations. I reached the credits more than 20 hours ago, but thanks to an overpowered endgame worth coming back for and the option to seamlessly play with friends online, I’ve got plenty of raiding left to do. This is the best Splatoon campaign yet and one of the top games on Switch 2.

Splatoon Raiders may be missing the series’ iconic Turf War, but what we have here is possibly the most variable and exciting game the series has ever offered. Regardless of your skill level or personal play styles, the game is able to cater to practically any taste, and all whilst delivering one of the most enjoyable gameplay loops on the console. It looks good, runs fantastically, and you can play practically the whole thing with friends if you wish. Not only that, but Nintendo’s flogging it for a bargain price. It may not push any boundaries within the genre per se, but it’s difficult to find anything negative to say about it, it really is a must-play for almost anyone.

Splatoon Raiders builds upon the most enjoyable elements of the series and transforms them into a polished, challenging, and highly entertaining PvE adventure. Its gameplay loop of exploring, fighting, gathering resources, and upgrading equipment is consistently engaging, supported by a progression system that rewards patience and encourages experimentation with different weapons, gadgets, and playstyles. Although it can occasionally feel like Salmon Run taken to the extreme, and its story falls short of its full potential, the game makes up for it with fluid action, excellent pacing, outstanding visual presentation, and a compelling amount of content for its price. It does not reinvent Splatoon, but it clearly proves that the franchise can successfully support a single-player experience with a distinct identity.

I was disappointed Splatoon Raiders was revealed as a single-player spin-off, but I was dead wrong. It is incredible, playing like a brilliant mix of Ratchet & Clank meets Helldivers that hooked me instantly. Teaming up with the Deep Cut crew, the loop of raiding Salmonid hordes for loot and upgrades is deeply satisfying. The overhauled movement adds a sense of verticality that the main games desperately need, and progression actually feels rewarding rather than a slow grind. Even with a more atmospheric than catchy soundtrack, this is an absolute must-play. Take it from a skeptic: Splatoon Raiders might just be the best game in the whole franchise.

Splatoon Raiders is a brilliantly moreish extraction shooter, whose ink-based gameplay helps make a well-trodden genre feel fresh and interesting. A great time alone, assisting others or grouping up with three friends, Splatoon Raiders proves there’s far more to be done with this series, and I, for one, cannot wait for where we go next.
An exceptionally entertaining single player adventure, Splatoon Raiders is expertly designed, full of content, and just a fantastic time.

Splatoon Raiders successfully transforms the core idea of Salmon Run into a full-fledged single-player adventure. While it doesn't quite match the creative level design of the main series' campaigns, its addictive gameplay loop, flexible build system, and atmospheric exploration make it one of the strongest Splatoon experiences to date. Fans of the series should definitely give this spin-off a try.

Splatoon Raiders surprised me in the best way possible. I expected a fun solo experiment, but Nintendo turned it into a surprisingly deep spin-off with raids, smart loadout choices, great bosses and a fun co-op system. Some raids might feel repetitive after a while, but the constant stream of weapons, gadgets, mods and upgrades kept me hooked from start to finish. This isn’t just something to play while waiting for Splatoon 4, it’s proof that Splatoon can work really well outside of its usual multiplayer comfort zone.

Nintendo’s more single-player-focused spin-off from their unique multiplayer shooter retains its excellent mechanics, and makes for a consistently challenging good time, even if sometimes a grindy one.

Splatoon Raiders maintains its infectious ink-shooting core but remixes it into a loot-driven, gadget-enhanced adventure RPG. It sacrifices competitive multiplayer for deeper single-player/co-op depth, customisation, and narrative focus, offering a fresh direction that complements rather than replaces the mainline games. After a trilogy of Turf Wars, it feels good to finally work together with other players on an adventure on such a grand scale. Splatoon 3 isn't going anywhere, and even Splatoon 2 is still active, making Raiders absolutely a justified experience.

Splatoon Raiders is a gorgeous, brilliantly fast-paced shooter that looks and feels excellent to play. The shooting systems are lovely, and each raid feels like a bite-sized chunk of energetic fun. Some of the optional challenge maps feel a bit like bloat, and there's a certain sense of familiarity that creeps in the further you go, but Splatoon Raiders is still a stellar experience that you'll want to check out if you have a Switch 2.
Splatoon Raiders continues Nintendo’s hot streak on the Switch 2 and, for the first time, I’m excited about whatever comes next in the world of Splatoon.

Splatoon Raiders transforms the franchise's formula into a PvE experience focused on combat, exploration, gear collection, and build crafting. With quick missions and a wide variety of weapons, gadgets, and customization options, the game offers a fun and addictive gameplay loop. Despite some repetitive objectives, it was a very pleasant surprise for me.

Splatoon Raiders proves once again that a franchise can reinvent itself and explore new directions without sacrificing its essence. Its focus on PvE and cooperative play, combined with a roguelike approach, creates a solid and highly addictive gameplay core. It is a fresh experience, supported by a visual presentation that takes advantage of the Nintendo Switch 2 hardware. And although it can become somewhat repetitive, it never stops being fun. Recommended for both veterans and newcomers ready to sweat ink.

Splatoon Raiders is the Splatoon gameplay experience perfected. While the narrative and visuals take a backseat, and there are moments where it does not feel like a Nintendo Switch 2 game, the emphasis on character work, charm, customization, satisfying combat, and replayability more than make up for these shortcomings. Even if Raiders does not recapture the magic that I felt with the very first Splatoon, if this is the foundation that future entries will build on, then Splatoon 4 is in great hands.

It's not perfect, but Splatoon Raiders is still an exceptional game. It's impressive how chaotic the missions can become with zero slowdown of any kind, and the core gameplay combined with the rewarding progression makes it a must-have for Switch 2 gamers, especially if they have someone to play co-op with. Splatoon Raiders is a high point for the franchise and will hopefully inform the story mode content in future Splatoon games.

Through laser sharp design in its progression and combat mechanics, Splatoon Raiders offers one of the best shooter campaigns of the year. It takes all of the learnings from its predecessors and expertly adapts them to an addictive looter shooter that’s packed to the gills with content and wrapped in a delightfully endearing package.

Despite its occasional repetition and a progression system that can occasionally discourage experimentation, Splatoon Raiders works as a fast, colourful and consistently entertaining shooter. Its short missions make it ideal for quick sessions, yet its upgrade loop is compelling enough to keep you playing far longer than intended. Whether you are tackling raids solo, teaming up with friends or jumping in for a brief burst of action, the game really delivers a steady stream of energetic fun.

Splatoon Raiders has ditched PvP in favor of single-player or co-op
gameplay, and that’s definitely a good thing. I haven’t played a better
shooter this year.

Overall, Splatoon Raiders is a breath of fresh air for the franchise. Not that it really needed it, but after three entries, it’s great to see this world of interesting characters expanding. The only remaining question is what’s next: Splatoon Raiders 2 or Splatoon 4?

The amount of weapons and gear, as well as the customisation options for characters and materials and the variety of enemies that we encounter all contribute to make this a very addictive experience, and it only becomes more enthralling as we go on and unlock more possibilities and a more demanding difficulty level. Truly a marvellous adaptation of the Splatoon name and experience.

Splatoon Raiders is a worthy addition to any Switch 2 library. From the customization of builds and playstyles to the story with Deep Cut and multiple maps while trekking the island, it makes for quite the trip to the islands. The option to play either multiplayer or single-player is a worthy addition. Completionists will find this game worth the price, but be warned of the expected grind fatigue for new weapons and mods. Be it a fan or newcomer, Splatoon Raiders is a solid addition to the series.
Though Splatoon’s single-player content has always been underappreciated, Splatoon Raiders makes it impossible to ignore, shining a bright light on the series’ oft-slept-on side.

Splatoon Raiders successfully transforms Salmon Run into a full-fledged PvE adventure. Its addictive progression, satisfying combat loop, and rewarding customization make it one of Nintendo's most compelling multiplayer experiences. While repetitive environments and a less memorable soundtrack prevent it from reaching perfection, this spin-off proves that expanding a great idea can be just as exciting as creating a new one.

Splatoon Raiders can be considered a success in the way it reimagines parts of the main series to deliver an alternative experience, moving away from competitive multiplayer to focus on its other strengths. With a wide variety of enemies, plenty of build-crafting possibilities, and breathtaking action sequences, this spin-off has earned the right to stand on its own merits.

Nintendo dips a "tentacle" into the looter-shooter genre with Splatoon Raiders, and the result is one of this summer's most refreshing surprises. It is the perfect vacation game for Nintendo Switch 2 and an ideal entry point for both newcomers and veterans alike.

Splatoon Raiders is such a fun action platformer that it's really hard to put down, especially as you keep unlocking new features and gadgets that make the incredibly entertaining combat even more personal and engaging. Plus, it's so stylish that you'll feel cool just for playing it.

Splatoon Raiders builds upon its core loop to deliver addictive gameplay driven by challenges, loot, and strategy, all wrapped in an art style that truly shines in its weapon designs and environments.

Splatoon Raiders is a fresh, fun, and highly recommended spin-off for both fans of the series and those looking for an entry point into this inked world. It is a light multi-genre experience that will keep us glued to the controller. It is one of those games you expect little from, but it ends up surprising you with its premise.

Splatoon Raiders isn't the grand single-player campaign the series has been begging for, yet it hides the smoothest, most brilliant gameplay Nintendo has ever put together. Its looting loop is addictive and co-op rounds out an adventure only held back by a tangled difficulty system and modest long-term content.

Splatoon Raiders is a fantastic spin-off that serves as a welcoming entry point for newcomers, while offering existing fans a clever looter-shooter expansion of Salmon Run. It is a highly satisfying treat that perfectly captures the franchise's signature charm.

Splatoon Raiders proves just how absurdly effective the shooting of this Nintendo Switch-exclusive series can be when an expanded take on Salmon Run is combined with enemy grinding and loot hunting. Its controls and combat feedback, paired with well-developed loot, progression, and build systems, make it incredibly difficult to stop playing once you start. However, as the gameplay reaches its later stages, both the amount of content and the depth available for experimentation begin to fall off.

Splatoon Raiders adds a solid looter-shooter formula to the fun of Salmon Run, making it hard to put down your Switch 2. For those who love Splatoon’s one-of-a-kind visuals but find PvP a bit intimidating, this spin-off may be the perfect companion.
A fun, fresh, and thoroughly convincing adventure that makes Splatoon Raiders a safe bet for fans of the series, who will feel right at home with this new spin-off installment.

Splatoon Raiders is exactly what I wanted from the franchise. As a fan of the single-player content from the previous entries, this builds on those foundations, elevating the experience. The addition of looter shooter mechanics adds replayability, urging you to experiment with the systems to create different builds. While some fans may miss the PvP aspect of the series, the PvE elements are excellent, providing plenty of ways to play together. More importantly, it proves that Splatoon can thrive beyond its competitive roots, creating an adventure that's every bit as colourful, inventive and addictive as its multiplayer counterpart.
Splatoon Raiders is proof positive the series can evolve past its competitive multiplayer roots, creating a fun and engaging ARPG experience that’s hard to put down.

Splatoon Raiders is a looter shooter wrapped in Nintendo's kid-friendly world, but it's not to be slept on. While not as deep or complex as some other games in the genre, its charm, loot chase, and satisfying gameplay loop make it one of my favorite games of 2026 so far.

While it doesn't quite escape some of the issues of its inspirations, Splatoon Raiders is a novel spin-off of one of Nintendo's most creative franchises. This is a no-brainer recommendation for fans of Salmon Run, and is one of the best co-op experiences on the Switch 2 thus far.

Splatoon Raiders is a partially refreshing spin-off with new gameplay aimed at rich loot, fast combat system and vast customization making this hunt for treasure refreshing even after 15 hours. The co-op or multiplayer components cannot be denied, but if you want to honor your Splatoon skills in different ways, this is one charming title to do so.
Splatoon Raiders is a fantastic shooter that surprises with the depth of its systems and challenge.

Splatoon Raiders successfully takes the series in a bold new direction without losing sight of what made it special. Its single-player adventure remains engaging from start to finish, with only the endgame showing a few rough edges that could be smoothed out through future updates. Splatoon fans, as well as players looking for a more unconventional take on the looter shooter formula, will find an accessible and compelling experience here. The foundations for a strong new spin-off series are all in place. Now it's up to Nintendo to build on them in the months ahead.

For fans of the franchise who have been wanting a single-player experience, I’m sure this spin-off is an excellent choice. It’s also a great opportunity for those who have never played Splatoon but would like to try a title from the series—or simply want something other than online matches. If you only enjoy the multiplayer mode found in the main games, you might want to make sure the cooperative mode suits your preferences.

If you've spent all these years caught up in the ink-covered battles between Inklings, Octolings, and the rest of the sea-dwelling cast, we're confident that Splatoon Raiders will be one of the standout experiences on your Nintendo Switch 2 in 2026. Likewise, if you've never given the series a chance because of its multiplayer focus but have always been intrigued by it, now is the perfect time to jump in. Nintendo may not be delivering the year's biggest blockbuster, but it has once again brought us an experience overflowing with fun—one that's so well crafted and thoughtfully designed that, from the very moment you pick it up, it's incredibly hard to put down.

Splatoon Raiders has turned out to be a highly entertaining game that solo players can easily pick up. If you only play through the missions, you'll see the end credits roll after about thirty hours, but in many ways, that's when Splatoon Raiders really begins.

It is rare to change one’s mind between the preview and the final review. Yet, that is exactly what happened with Splatoon Raiders. It is not just after an hour and a half of play, but rather over the long haul, that this first entry in the franchise—exclusive to the Nintendo Switch 2—reveals its full potential. By adopting the conventions of Borderlands-style "shooter-looters," Splatoon Raiders delivers an addictive adventure driven by varied levels, a satisfying sense of progression, and gameplay that is more exhilarating than ever. With a wealth of customization options, there is something here for everyone as they tackle the many demanding challenges this content-rich experience has to offer. Now, I hope Nintendo gives *Splatoon Raiders* the same level of ongoing support seen with Splatoon *, ensuring this excellent foundation continues to receive regular updates.

It delivers a masterclass in looter-shooter progression, blending addictive ink-based combat with deep customization. This loop remains consistently rewarding despite repetitive mission structures and lackluster environmental variety. Although the soundtrack fails to hit previous heights, the seamless performance and robust cooperative integration define a surprisingly essential experience.

A single player Splatoon game that makes a splash. With lots of variety in gameplay, teammembers, weapons and mods and lots of content, this is a full package for who wants to experience the world of Splatoon without getting dirty in Multiplayer. All the chaos is still there, which results in many hours of splattering good fun.

A bold first spin-off that hits the mark, paint in hand. Although held back by a forgettable storyline and repetitive environments, Splatoon Raiders compensates with a solid, addictive, and surprisingly deep PvE infrastructure. A title that trades narrative plot twists for hours of tactical challenges, captivating and thoroughly inking anyone who decides to give it a chance.

Addictive, easy to learn, difficult to master, Splatoon Raiders scratches that looter shooter itch, and even provides some surprising survival horror vibes along the way. It’s only brought down by some uninteresting environments, middling aesthetic customization and a dearth of voice-acting. A solid spin-off to the Splatoon IP that I’ll be playing for months to come, no doubt.
Splatoon Raiders is primarily a single-player title, but it still delivers a highly addictive game loop. Plenty of content and charm make it fun from start to finish. It is pretty ink-redible.

With its focus on the solo campaign (which also supports co-op play), Splatoon Raiders sets itself apart significantly from its predecessors. The game compensates for the potential downside of lacking a competitive aspect with its spectacular mass battles, diverse weapons, cool gadgets, and motivating progression system. All in all, it delivers a high-quality experience that action fans on the Switch 2 will find hard to pass up.

Splatoon Raiders successfully transforms the franchise into a cooperative looter shooter while preserving its unique identity. The signature ink-based mechanics blend naturally with exploration, character progression and fast-paced missions, creating an addictive gameplay loop. Excellent performance on Nintendo Switch 2, charming visuals and a rewarding upgrade system make the experience consistently enjoyable, even if repetitive mission design occasionally sets in. The lack of Brazilian Portuguese localization is disappointing, but it doesn't overshadow what is ultimately a creative and refreshing new direction for the Splatoon series.

Splatoon Raiders is a genuinely great twist on the Splatoon formula. Going in, I wasn’t sure what to expect but as I left the tutorial, I knew this is a game that I find far and above more my jam than the mainline games. It might not have the deepest story, but what Splatoon Raiders does have is sense adventure and the island hopping in search of treasure does just enough with its story and characters to keep you entertained through to the credits.

Splatoon Raiders is a lot of fun. The gameplay loop is addictive and it becomes more fun the harder it gets and the more powerful you become; with very deep customization options, from the character, the weapons, the gadgets and upgrades that truly make you feel that your decisions mattered; it looks decent and runs super smoothly; and is equally fun even if you play solo or with friends.

If you've had a hankering for a solo twist on the loot shooter genre, you'll love this, as it does that extremely well. A successful non-PvP outing for the series, Splatoon Raiders has room for improvement, but nonetheless offers a fun adventure that's not quite like anything else.
Splatoon Raiders offers up a new twist on the decade-plus old formula, but could have gone further.

Splatoon Raiders succeeds in its goal of expanding the series, delivering an excellent action game full of customization options with a focus on single-player gameplay. You will spend many hours exploring, fighting, gathering resources, and upgrading your character and equipment. Switch 2 owners are getting a rich game with fantastic value, and we recommend they give it a try.

I would be surprised if Splatoon Raiders supplants the main Splatoon titles. The series is a big success for Nintendo, so clearly the competitive ink-splattering multiplayer has found an audience. But Splatoon Raiders shows a new degree of flexibility for the franchise, with a single-player campaign that’s much more satisfying than its past attempts to inject a story campaign into the main games. I hope this new looter shooter sub-series gets to live alongside the main series, because it’s loads of fun already, and the concept could be pushed even further.

Splatoon Raiders shows that Nintendo's online multiplayer series works just as well in an offline solo setting. It's very much a game with a single, simple loop  – shoot everything, die, upgrade, shoot everything again – but it delivers this loop with such engaging, enjoyable action that you don't need to worry about repetition creeping in, you'll happily open the front door and invite it in for dinner.

As far as experiments go, Splatoon Raiders is certainly successful at bringing something new and different to the table. It's a game that revels in its freedom from competitive play, offering new perspectives and concepts that recontextualise classic Splatoon gameplay into something that feels both familiar and fresh. While it does wear thin towards the end of its runtime, it never fully runs out of gas, offering a presentational leap for Nintendo that bodes well for the future of the Switch 2.
This series offshoot is a hectic, often overwhelming delight.

Despite being a single-player experience, Splatoon Raiders still has heaps of great frantic gameplay moments that can be found in a mainline Splatoon game and a great cast of characters to boot. While it is lacking in some of the style options of the series, there is still a lot of amazing weapon customisation to be found, and many different gameplay styles to embrace. The addition of PvE multiplayer is also a great addition, even though the game is still a blast without it. I will surely be staying trapped in the Spirhalite Isles for a long time coming. Catch ya later!

Splatoon Raiders builds upon the Salmon Run modes from Splatoon 2 and 3 in a clever way, resulting in a looter-shooter with varying objectives. It can 100% be played and enjoyed solo, but I had the most fun playing with others and suspect that will prove a highlight once folks get their bearings and start perfecting their weapon, tank, and gadget loadouts. However, I will note that because it is primarily focused on taking on Salmonid hordes with things like time limitations and egg requirements, it may not have the broader appeal of the mainline games’ campaigns.

Splatoon Raiders sets its sights on inking Salmonids to such a singular degree that the game can sometimes feel a bit one-note, but a solid array of different mission variants and a gratifying dopamine-dispensing progression system has that “just one more raid” effect. While Splatoon Raiders doesn't offer as much variety as earlier entries in the franchise, it does its one thing quite well, and those who jive with this new looter-shooter approach will likely find themselves caught in this game's net for some time.

Splatoon Raiders does exactly what Splatoon has always done: deliver instant fun in a colorful shooting festival. Your reflexes and understanding of the mechanics are constantly put to the test in an ingeniously simple design that celebrates Nintendo’s philosophies, as interpreted here by its newest generation.

Splatoon Raiders pulls off the hardest trick of all: turning one of Nintendo's most iconic multiplayer series into a single player adventure without losing its identity. The gameplay remains incredibly fun, the progression is surprisingly deep, and the customization system offers far more freedom than expected. Exploring the Spirhalite Isles and the constant hunt for new gear make every mission enjoyable, while co-op adds extra longevity without overshadowing the game's single player nature.

Ultimately, Splatoon Raiders is a valuable piece of the series' broader picture—a shift in perspective rather than identity. It is a complementary experience that enriches the saga's lore while simultaneously pointing toward a new direction. With its ability to reinvent itself, this new Splatoon is poised to broaden the series' horizons without betraying its core principles; it would come as no surprise if Nintendo chose to pursue this path further in the future. After all, there remains significant untapped potential and room for improvement—whether through the lens of adventure or along mysterious, uncharted paths that offer something new for both veterans and newcomers alike as they step into this vibrant, colorful world.

Ultimately, it’s much more than just a tutorial that’s been expanded. Splatoon Raiders is a fully-fledged game in its own right and will appeal to fans of the main series as well as those who were clamouring for more single-player content, although we can also explore it with others if we wish.
If you’re looking for a 4-player PvE looter shooter with a unique ink based battle system look no further than this well made and addictive game that can be played in short bursts if you desire.

What initially feels like a rather simplistic shooter quickly blossoms into something with real depth. Importantly, compared to other looter shooters that Splatoon Raiders riffs on, you can hop in and out here generally without needing to commit an obscene amount of time. I had my doubts about Splatoon Raiders when I saw it was yet another looter shooter, but who’s got ink all over their face now.

I realise that I’m not the target audience for Splatoon Raiders, and I’m sure those that are the target audience will get a great deal of value out of the depth of its systems. And from Nintendo’s point of view, it’s a relatively low-cost project to fill the release schedule until the next big thing (Fire Emblem) comes along. I do, however, suspect that just about everyone, from the diehard fans to me on the spectrum of Splatoon advocacy, will ultimately wish that the first proper single-player outing for the franchise were a bit more than it turned out to be.
Splatoon Raiders is an excellent spin-off that centers the experience around a fun gameplay loop and a high level of challenge, all enhanced by excellent performance.
There's treasure out there for those looking for an entertaining looter shooter. You won't have to dig very far to find a good time, especially if you've got some friends with shovels handy.

Splatoon Raiders isn't the definitive story mode fans have been chasing for years, but it’s honestly more fun and ambitious than it needed to be. The gadget system is one of the freshest ideas the series has ever seen, the bosses remain memorable and the presentation is a remarkable leap in quality for Nintendo. It lacks a narrative that matches its mechanical ambition, as well as some trimming down of the repetition in its final hours, but as a first attempt at bringing Inkling ink into loot-and-explore territory, it proves to be a winning formula, one that deserves further exploration from Nintendo's creative minds.
A blast of fast-paced action, whether you're running solo or in co-op. Tons of upgrade options and challenging levels will definitely keep you hooked.

Splatoon Raiders successfully proves that the series can thrive outside its multiplayer roots, delivering a rewarding single-player adventure built around progression and player expression. Although a shallow narrative and an uneven mid-game progression keep it from reaching greater heights, its satisfying gameplay loop and excellent customization systems make those shortcomings easy to overlook. Whether you're a longtime Splatoon fan or simply looking for a fun action-adventure, Splatoon Raiders is a worthwhile expedition that confidently charts a new course for the series.

Splatoon Raiders is a fun looter-shooter with chaotic fights against hordes of enemies. While difficulty spikes and some slight repetition in specific stage formats may make the experience unfavorable for some players, there’s a lot to dig in at your own pace. The different take on Splatoon has paid off as a solid new experience for solo players and those who want to enjoy these stages in co-op with friends alike.
Splatoon Raiders reinvents Nintendo’s ink-based shooter as an addictive looter with superb co-op and technical polish.

Splatoon Raiders tries something new with one of Nintendo’s somewhat more recent long-running series, to largely great success. Though a bit more variety in terms of missions and character customization options would have been ideal, the numerous weapon and gadget combinations and unique approach to Splatoon’s core gameplay craft an exciting spin-off that’s worth your time.
The latest Splatoon title eschews its multiplayer DNA for a single-player spinoff that is, in many ways, a more compelling package than the series that spawned it.
A great gameplay loop blends well with a game fiercely challenging. Even in solo mode, Splatoon stays fresh.

Splatoon Raiders is a great addition to the Splatoon brand, with the transition from competitive multiplayer to a primarily single-player game being done very well. The gameplay is great, and the abilities and upgrades you unlock in Splatoon Raiders are a fantastic addition to the Splatoon franchise. This title serves as an excellent entry point for new Splatoon players, while also offering seasoned fans an opportunity to expand their experience with the brand.
How thrilling it remains nonetheless - and how remarkable that all these reheated ingredients should result in something so fresh. [Issue#427, p.110]

Splatoon Raiders brings an intense, fun cooperative looter shooter to the Nintendo Switch 2—one that I think the system really needed! While the core gameplay loop can sometimes become tedious, the weapon and enemy variety paired in with Splatoon’s signature movement makes for incredibly intense horde survival battles. Explosive even.
Fans of the original Splatoons may be nonplussed by how Nintendo has changed the narrative with Raiders but the ink has marked out some interesting new territory and shouldn’t be written off.

Splatoon Raiders is my favorite game in the franchise and a wonderful trek into a new genre. I am glad Nintendo finally created a game that can be enjoyed without having to play online. I have always enjoyed the idea of Splatoon, just not its format. Playing with friends only enhances the experience, but it is just as fun when raiding solo. Definitely pick this one up, one of the best Switch 2 exclusive games so far.

Instead of competitive multiplayer, Splatoon Raiders has you take on fishlike enemies with an array of weapons and gadgets. It’s all fun enough, as a playground with well-designed jungle gyms and monkey bars.
Splatoon Raiders has an incredibly engaging core gameplay loop, an always-engaging style, and plenty of heart. It just can’t overcome a lack of gameplay variety and some heavy-handed dialogue.

Splatoon Raiders is a game that consistently delivers plenty of fun, thanks largely to its excellent core gameplay and technical polish. The mission pacing and looter-shooter structure make the title ideal for short play sessions, while massive bosses lend the campaign a real sense of scale. At the same time, the game lacks variety - both in terms of locations and mission types - which quickly leads to a sense of repetition. Furthermore, limitations within the online mode restrict the kind of freedom that is absolutely crucial to this genre.

Despite how enjoyable and devilishly moreish it can be, Splatoon Raiders does feel like a seismic rinse and repeat. The levels are lavish, the challenges are plenty, the compulsive qualities are undeniable, and its whimsy is as wonderful as always, yet it is hard not to feel like something more ambitious was left on the cutting room floor and Raiders really could do with more variation to keep the sense of monotony at bay.

Splatoon Raiders is Splatoon through and through: the core gameplay, controls, and movement are as enjoyable as ever, while tanks, gadgets, and a Monster Hunter-inspired structure add a fresh twist. Yet beneath that solid foundation, repetitive missions, uninspired level design, and a lack of standout moments keep it from leaving a lasting impression. Like returning to the same campsite in France every summer, it's fun while it lasts, but familiar enough to fade from memory not long after the trip is over.
I just don’t feel much of a drive to play more of Splatoon Raiders. I had fun drowning all of those salmonids in ink. But just like them, I’ve had my fill.

It is a shame that the experience becomes far too repetitive for long stretches—especially when, at a couple of points, you are forced to do a bit of grinding just to be ready for the challenges of the adventure's final act. The sense that something is missing becomes even more apparent when contrasted with a couple of levels where the developers clearly aimed for more, creating non-linear environments that offer activities beyond the simple run-and-gun gameplay characterizing the rest of the campaign.

Ultimately, as a first spin-off, Splatoon Raiders gets the job done by drawing inspiration from the Salmon Run mode while adding its own unique twist to the franchise's already excellent gameplay—though a more substantial story would have been welcome. That said, there is plenty of replayability thanks to various difficulty levels, which encourage players to aim for 100% completion or experiment with the many possible builds. Now, the question remains whether it is worth the €50 price tag. It all depends on what you look for in a Splatoon game. If you are after competitive multiplayer, this spin-off might not be for you; however, if you are interested in a single-player or cooperative experience, this title could certainly be worth your while.

As it stands, this is a solid and mechanically fun adventure game with some really clever, joyous battles to find across its layered map. A love for Splatoon will elevate the action significantly, with its light delivery of lore tidbits creating a string to pull yourself along. For those new to the Splatoon series, there might be more friction in its introduction, but the game’s best ideas are charming regardless, and its Octolings are quick to cement a spot in your heart.

A spin-off that's both substantial and slight, Splatoon Raiders is a novel experiment that will please both fans and newcomers hoping for this colourful shooter to cater to better solo players, even if at times it feels like it's been cobbled together from last season's washed-out fashions.

Splatoon Raiders is a decent spin-off to the main series, aiming to deliver a single-player experience. Visually, it is up there with other great Switch 2 titles, and the gameplay remains fun in single-player. However, we believe it would have made more sense as an expansion of Splatoon 3 rather than a standalone title, as the reuse of assets is obvious, while the repetition of environments creates a sense of déjà vu. The necessity of grinding also becomes tiresome, rather than serving as a fun mechanic to add longevity.
There's a lot of positive things that can be said about this spinoff, like the frantic and fun action. But the end result could have been also so much better.

Splatoon Raiders ditches PvP for a PvE dungeon-crawling looter-shooter. You explore the mysterious Spirhalite Islands armed with an arsenal of weapons, three distinct ink-tank "talent trees," and swappable special gadgets. It's a well-designed and varied departure for the series, with really good, WoW-raid-like boss fights and a solid co-op mode.

Splatoon Raiders is a game for everyone to have fun with, mainly thanks to the delightfully fluent gameplay and large number of options. Unfortunately, all that freedom doesn't make for a mechanically interesting game.

The systems governing Splatoon Raiders are better than Splatoon Raiders itself. It features a rich enough well of progression and a wide enough variety of playstyles that the less exciting gameplay might feel worth slogging through. While combat’s entertaining at times, the miserable level design and an overall lifelessness really lets it down. Whether you’ll like Raiders ultimately comes down to how deeply you get into its fine tuning options, but the elements most pertinent to a videogame really struggle to hold up their end.

Salmon Run remains one of the great co-op experiences of the modern age but only a minimal effort has been expended in turning it into a single-player game, as Splatoon Raiders struggles to justify its existence.
By removing Turf War and transitioning to something pretty close to a first-person shooter, Nintendo has taken what makes the franchise unique and discarded it with Splatoon Raiders.

I’ve never quite fully gotten to grips with the motion control move-the-Switch-around-to-aim system on top of the thumbstick physical in-game character movement. But it does its jobs well enough in this title not to be a complete nuisance.

In spite of some drawbacks, there’s still plenty of enjoyment to be had with Splatoon Raiders. Its fast-paced combat and short levels make Raiders a great game to play in brief bursts, which is particularly ideal for those who play Switch 2 while on the go. Nintendo has found with Raiders that it can absolutely expand the Splatoon IP outside of its trappings as a competitive multiplayer series with ease, but there’s still plenty of room for improvement and ingenuity if this spin-off were to get a sequel of its own in the future.
Greed, not art, is the motivating force behind your actions throughout Splatoon Raiders.
This is the biggest surprise about Splatoon Raiders: it is pedestrian. If you’ve played one of dozens of modern cooperative action games, you’ve played this.

If you've had a hankering for a solo twist on the loot shooter genre, you'll love this, as it does that extremely well. A successful non-PvP outing for the series, Splatoon Raiders has room for improvement, but nonetheless offers a fun adventure that's not quite like anything else.

Splatoon Raiders successfully trades competitive PvP for an addictive, looter-shooter loop packed with bite-sized raids, deep crafting, and thrilling co-op. While a few late-game missions hit mild repetition, the top-tier movement, gorgeous Switch 2 visuals, and rock-solid 60 fps performance keep the momentum going strong. Whether you're playing solo or with friends, it's a phenomenal spin-off that no Splatoon fan should miss.

Splatoon Raiders trades the PvP-focus of the other games in the series for an addicting action-RPG adventure that's an absolute blast in co-op.
Splatoon Raiders is the exact type of game that appears simple enough on the surface but soon reveals a flabbergasting level of mechanical depth as soon as you scratch beneath it.

Splatoon Raiders is a refreshing take on the Splatoon formula, stripping out the PVP from the mainline games while adding replayable stages with loot shooter mechanics. This Splatoon spinoff is definitely geared toward co-op, which is great news for folks who want more cooperative gameplay and a multiplayer campaign. The music can be polarizing but production values are solid overall and the writing also remains hilarious and cheeky. I also wish the co-op had more options to make it more accessible to families such as split-screen and game sharing. If an extended Salmon Run with loot shooter mechanics sounds like a swimmingly good idea to you, Splatoon Raiders will float your boat.

Splatoon Raiders is ultimately a valuable addition to the series' larger picture, a shift in perspective but not in identity; it's a complementary experience that enhances the saga's imagery while also pointing to a new direction.
Splatoon Raiders is a worthy addition to any Switch 2 library.

While it doesn't quite escape some of the issues of its inspirations, Splatoon Raiders is a novel spin-off of one of Nintendo's most creative franchises. This is a no-brainer recommendation for fans of Salmon Run, and is one of the best co-op experiences on the Switch 2 thus far.

Thanks to an addictive gameplay loop, stellar third-person shooting, exceptional performance, and a large collection of challenging, diverse stages, it's immediately one of the best games on the platform.

Splatoon Raiders is a real tonal shift for the series, and it works far more often than it falters. Splatoon Raiders holds its own alongside the grind-heavy RPGs it draws from, but there are still a few blank spots to fill before it can claim a spot at the very top.

Splatoon Raiders is more than a spin-off; it’s an incredible launching point for a new branch of more single-player adventures, combining some of the best parts of the original Splatoon trilogy and turning it into something that feels fresh.

Splatoon Raiders is a partially refreshing spin-off with new gameplay aimed at rich loot, fast combat system and vast customization making this hunt for treasure refreshing even after 15 hours. The co-op or multiplayer components'cannot be denied, but if you want to honor your Splatoon skills in different ways, this is one charming title to do so.

Splatoon Raiders proves that the world of Splatoon works just as well outside of online competition. Nintendo has created an incredibly satisfying action game with very well-designed progression, although it lacks greater mission variety and a more engaging story. If you enjoy fast-paced combat, character progression and the distinctive atmosphere of this series, the Japanese developers’ latest release should provide you with plenty of fun.
Splatoon Raiders is an excellent spin-off that centers the experience around a fun gameplay loop and a high level of challenge, all enhanced by excellent performance.

Splatoon Raiders successfully breaks away from the series' multiplayer-first routine by delivering a dedicated single-player campaign in the looter-shooter genre, all while keeping the franchise's signature fast-paced gameplay intact. It also stands out with a great variety of enemies and bosses, paired with rewarding loot that keeps you running more raids to upgrade your weapons and abilities. So overall, it's a strong, promising start for a new Splatoon spin-off.

Splatoon Raiders is peak character design and one of the best looking Nintendo Switch 2 games to date. As said before, each level is unique and the graphics beautiful. The base itself is very detailed, even when you ink around a workstation and then use the station, the ink is still visible. The workstations themselves have a lot of detailed parts and items laying around giving it that lived-in feel. Overall the world detail, Salmonid visual upgrades, and the equipment you hold all look great and give Splatoon Raiders a top spot graphically on the Switch 2.

Splatoon Raiders is not only a truly successful spin-off of the series but also - thanks to its varied mechanics, engaging gameplay loop and elements of randomness - an extremely entertaining and at times challenging game. Whether you play alone, with friends or online with others, you will almost certainly quickly find yourself hooked, thinking to yourself "Just one more round." after every finished treasure hunt.

Splatoon Raiders places Deep Cut at the centre of a fantastic adventure and gives the series’ ink combat a rewarding campaign structure that can be played solo or cooperative multiplayer. I loved following the group across the Spirhalite Islands, improving my ink arsenal, and taking on increasingly-challenging Raids with higher stats and better loadouts. The colourful setting and energetic soundtrack exude Splatoon’s personality, and it's one of the best presentations yet for a Nintendo Switch 2 game.
Splatoon Raiders trades competitive matches for fun expeditions where smart builds and stronger gear always give you a reason to jump back in.
Splatoon Raiders has achieved a very successful conversion of the Splatoon series to single-player. Fun raids, swift weapons, and extensive crafting options!

Splatoon Raiders has surprisingly become my personal GOTY, thanks to extremely well-structured gameplay mechanics that focus on the ultimate goal of any video game: entertaining the player. And this is precisely where Raiders succeeds, keeping us entertained for hours on end without us even realising it, reaching remarkable heights of playability, delivering frenetic action and extensive customisation, while also maintaining a consistently well-balanced level of challenge. Highly recommended for anyone looking to spend hours playing without a care in the world, and ultimately finish their session with a smile.

Splatoon Raiders is the culmination of 11 years of work on the franchise, resulting in its most fun and interesting entry yet, boasting a both addicting and rewarding gameplay loop focused on getting more and better loot as we move along the narrative.
Splatoon Raiders offers enough new ideas to feel fresh without throwing away what made the series so enjoyable in the first place

Splatoon Raiders is the kind of game that the Splatoon series had always been missing before this point. As a fan of single-player games over multiplayer games, it naturally wound up appealing to me more than the mainline games do. Without the typical baggage of Splatoon’s online play such as map and game mode rotations, the end result is something that feels more focused and considered towards single-player and cooperative play. The surprisingly high skill curve and daunting enemy designs also makes it one of the toughest Nintendo games in a while, with a real mean streak that allows the customization elements to be fully leveraged. This in conjunction with a surprisingly long main campaign makes for a game that’s easy to enjoy fully with friends or by your lonesome. Pretty much the only issue with it is that it’s somewhat wanting for variety, as all its got going on is the core Splatoon gameplay, which is as good as ever, but potentially not a good sell for everyone without the multiplayer or live service elements that help define it. While I don’t think the end result is quite as strong as it perhaps could have been, it’s very much a worthy entry in the Splatoon series.

Splatoon Raiders is the first major spin-off in the series and focuses on a more single-player-oriented experience, with enjoyable combat and some good ideas, but struggles to hide its multiplayer foundations.

Even though I was sceptical at the beginning, Splatoon Raiders successfully strips away the competitive multiplayer, and succeeds as a phenomenally addictive single-player looter-shooter experience. An incredibly satisfying gameplay loop, familiar gunplay, fluid mechanics, and deep build customisation make it a brilliant new direction for the franchise.

Splatoon Raiders is precisely what fans of the series have been waiting for. It features excellent shooting mechanics and a huge variety of weapons and gadgets to choose from. All that’s left to do is grab a roller and start painting.

Splatoon: Raiders is a bold and entertaining experiment that transforms the series’ familiar formula into a loot-driven action game with excellent shooting, satisfying weapons, strong enemy design and plenty of build experimentation. Unfortunately, repetitive environments, a weak story, overpowered abilities and a shallow endgame gradually undermine the core Splatoon identity, making it feel more like an enjoyable side experiment than a true successor to Salmon Run.
Splatoon Raiders is the definition of a “summer” game for me. Light, fun, colorful, it plays carefree and relaxed, despite its intense action nature. And this paradox is what makes it so unique.
The new title delivers exactly what I expected, bringing the franchise's vibrant and colorful gameplay to a single-player format.
The game brings a fresh sense of excitement to the Splatoon franchise and makes this new direction feel like a natural evolution.
Splatoon Raiders manages to reinvent the saga’s classic formula by embracing an extraction-and-survival structure that proves highly addictive.

Splatoon Raiders uses the best elements of the Splatoon franchise as the foundation for an experience worthy of the finest looter shooter games. With diverse enemies, highly unique builds, and addictive gameplay, the game offers a fun campaign and a vast amount of post-game content.

Despite the slow start, Splatoon Raiders eventually becomes a fun and engrossing experience. Creative level design, different dungeons, intriguing boss battles, fluid fighting, and excellent replay value make it one of the best spin-offs the Splatoon franchise has produced.

Splatoon Raiders could have easily been a simple spin-off that relied solely on the popularity of the franchise. Instead, Nintendo has delivered something that genuinely expands the Splatoon universe in meaningful ways.
Splatoon Raiders does exactly what a good spin-off should do: it respects the essence of the franchise while introducing enough new ideas to justify its existence.

Splatoon Raiders is a solid PvE-only title from the franchise. The shooter gameplay flows smoothly here as well, with support for both stick and motion controls. Enemies are varied and the levels offer good diversity.
Splatoon Raiders is a colorful third-person shooter with paint instead of bullets. The game is well-executed and promises a lot of fun for both young and older players.

I firmly believe that this is the best Splatoon title since the very first. It’s got degrees of complexity and madness that the most hardened minmaxer can appreciate, but it’s also crazy approachable in presentation, explanation and fun. It lets you focus on what you want: what weapons, how your base looks, your fashion and your burgeoning relationship with Shiver. This becomes your game. And, as such, it’s easily one of my favorites of the year.

Splatoon Raiders, for the most part, does what it sets out to do. Whether it will be a successful entry point for players who want to start inking everything in sight, I cannot say, but it should be. There is an interesting experience in here, collecting long-forgotten treasures and bursting Salmonids. This is also a great game to play with friends, which you really need. The issue is the game never grabbed me the way I was hoping it would. Some points were downright frustrating, and not in a challenging way.

Splatoon Raiders successfully reinvents the series with rewarding cooperative gameplay, satisfying progression, and excellent performance. Repetitive environments, limited incentive to experiment with its broader toolkit, and a weak narrative prevent it from reaching the creativity and variety of the mainline games.

Splatoon Raiders shines when it mixes the spirit of Salmon Run with action RPG progression, co-op support and a constant hunt for better loot. It does not need a complex story to hook you, because its pace, challenge and technical polish work extremely well.

Splatoon Raiders feels like a natural evolution for the series. Rather than simply delivering another multiplayer-focused package with a short campaign attached, Nintendo has fully embraced what made those previous single-player modes enjoyable and expanded them into a complete adventure. The exploration is rewarding, the progression keeps you constantly unlocking exciting new toys, and the familiar ink-based gameplay remains every bit as entertaining as ever.

Will it convert players who have never enjoyed Splatoon? Probably not. If the core shooting mechanics have never appealed to you, Raiders is unlikely to change your mind. Likewise, players who only ever cared about competitive multiplayer may still prefer the mainline entries. But if, like me, you’ve always found yourself wishing Nintendo would make a proper single-player Splatoon adventure… Well, this is exactly that.

It’s colourful, funny, packed with personality and incredibly easy to lose yourself in for both quick sessions and longer evenings. Add in flexible difficulty options, satisfying progression and Nintendo’s usual level of polish, and you’ve got a fantastic new direction for the franchise. I genuinely loved my time with Splatoon Raiders, and I sincerely hope this isn’t the last time Nintendo lets the series venture into dedicated single-player territory. For me, this is an easy recommendation.

Splatoon Raiders proves that breaking from the norm can produce something unique for a franchise that might have easily relied on iteration. This bold move adds dimension to the Splatoon universe and sets the stage for further spin-offs. Raiders, alone or with friends, is a vivid, satisfying, and shockingly rich adventure that fits alongside Nintendo's best recent releases.

Splatoon Raiders is yet another surprising first-party addition to the Nintendo Switch 2’s catalogue. Its mission-based hunt for gold and power might not be for everyone, but Nintendo’s first step into the looter shooter space is confident and robust.

A bold first spin-off that hits the mark right on target. Although held back by a forgettable script and repetitive environments, *Splatoon Raiders* makes up for it with a solid, addictive, and surprisingly layered PvE framework. It’s a game that forgoes narrative twists to offer hours of tactical challenges, captivating and thoroughly immersing anyone who decides to give it a chance.

Splatoon Raiders proves that a spin-off doesn’t necessarily have to live in the shadow of the main series; on the contrary, it stands on its own as a solid experience that works perfectly even without the cornerstones that made the franchise famous in the first place. With a more polished and cinematic narrative, an extremely engaging gameplay loop, and a surprisingly well-executed and addictive looter shooter structure, the game easily becomes much more than just a passing diversion while we wait for Splatoon 4. In short, Splatoon Raiders is fun, surprisingly deep, and one of the best titles available on the Nintendo Switch 2, and we can confidently say it will be one of the games that keeps us entertained all summer long.

Splatoon Raiders is a solid entry in the series, but in my opinion, it’s designed solely for fans and won’t be able to draw in anyone from outside the series. However, if you loved the previous Splatoon games, you’ll feel right at home here—just without the intense competition.
The latest Splatoon title eschews its multiplayer DNA for a single-player spinoff that is, in many ways, a more compelling package than the series that spawned it.

Splatoon Raiders had me hooked on the treasure hunt. While there’s repetitiveness to the formula, the game had me saying “just one more” constantly. For the prize hoarders like myself, Splatoon Raiders really puts the “loot” in looter shooter.

Splatoon Raiders is a winning bet when it comes to spin-offs – and beyond – as it successfully applies the franchise’s formula to a more linear experience, underpinned by a storyline which, whilst not exactly phenomenal, is satisfying enough to carry me through the 11 hours until the credits roll. The addictive and satisfying gameplay, the constant sense of progression with every raid completed (or not), the excellent optimisation and a final challenge that firmly seals the mark of quality are more than enough reasons to justify a visit to the Spirhalite Islands. It’s a title with a simple core, but one that’s executed superbly, easily captivating fans of the genre without leaving the curious behind – a game I consider to be my favourite Switch 2 title of 2026 so far.

With an addictive gameplay loop and excellent performance on Switch 2, Splatoon Riders hits the mark by reinventing the franchise with a memorable solo campaign, falling short only due to the lack of Brazilian Portuguese localization and limited outfit customization.

As a newcomer to the franchise, Splatoon Raiders has managed to draw me deeper into the game than I’d expected. It challenges you to constantly tweak your load-out, but not to the point of tedium. The mix of raids and dungeons provides just the right dopamine rush, making it hard to put Splatoon Raiders down. It takes you on a colourful adventure that’s perfect as a quick bit of fun. A must-play to add to your list.

Splatoon Raiders shows that Nintendo has managed to transform its shooter franchise into a surprisingly fun action and progression-based experience. With an addictive gameplay loop, a great variety of weapons, tanks, and builds, the game offers dozens of hours of content for players who enjoy constantly developing their character. Despite stumbling with a simplistic story and a multiplayer system featuring some questionable decisions, the overall result is extremely positive, making this one of the franchise’s most interesting spin-offs and an easy recommendation for fans of games focused on cooperation and grinding.
Splatoon Raiders drops the competitive scaffolding, keeps the ink, and loses less than you would expect. What is built on top is a good action RPG and the most fun I have had with Splatoon in years.

Had the level design and island art direction been at all interesting, I’d be ready to sing this game’s praises from the fire escapes of Splatsville. Because the shooting mechanics are unbeatable, legitimately the best Splatoon has ever played. But Splatoon is more than just its mechanics. This series has an aesthetic and vibe all its own. Without that, or even an attempt at a substitute fit to the sub-tropical setting, Splatoon Raiders ends up as all substance, no style.

We had a fantastic time with Splatoon Raiders and certainly aren't ready to send Team Deep Cut back to Splatsville just yet. Splatoon Raiders is all about pure, chaotic fun—and it delivers that in spades. Anyone wanting to play Splatoon but put off by the intensity of multiplayer action will find Splatoon Raiders to be a perfect fit.

This is a fantastic Splatoon game, and that’s exactly what me and millions of other fans were looking for. If you’ve been wanting to experience this series but wanted a single-player focused experience, this is where you’ll want to start.

Splatoon Raiders comes highly recommended because it clearly demonstrates that the franchise has much more potential beyond its competitive side. Nintendo has successfully adapted familiar gameplay mechanics into an exploration title that can be enjoyed both solo and in co-op. Although there are some areas for improvement, the result is a spin-off that keeps Splatoon’s identity intact while still feeling distinct enough.
Splatoon Raiders is an enjoyable single-player spin-off that should delight fans whilst they wait for a new, more traditional instalment.
Splatoon Raiders proves that the series can be much more than “just” a great competitive online game, and I hope this is the first of many single-player-focused spin-offs the franchise will bring us.

In spite of some drawbacks, there’s still plenty of enjoyment to be had with Splatoon Raiders. Its fast-paced combat and short levels make Raiders a great game to play in brief bursts, which is particularly ideal for those who play Switch 2 while on the go.

Overall, it's fun, but most of the levels lack the verve and experimentalism that the single-player structure would have granted the series, finally moving away from the formalism that is essential in multiplayer battles.
Splatoon Raiders is a big drop from Nintendo that stands on its own. With an addictive single-player experience and the addition of online co-op, a new vice is born with this fresh catch.

When the lights go out on the Spirhalite Islands and the base returns to rocking silently on the sea, you’re left with the feeling that you’ve stumbled upon something rare, because what I feared would be mere filler turned out to be a profound, generous, and surprisingly vast adventure, one that weaves a treasure hunt into a progression that offers no respite.

Setting aside technical aspects that could have been more daring and a few somewhat lackluster early islands, you find yourself caught up in a loop that’s as simple as it is hypnotic, where every run promises new loot and every piece of loot drives you toward the next, making it almost impossible to put the game down.

Whether you’re a seasoned veteran or setting sail for these waters for the first time, my verdict remains the same: Splatoon Raiders is a treasure in every sense, and I can’t wait to see where this new series will take us next.

Splatoon Raiders successfully pivots the franchise into a single-player focus, delivering an incredibly addictive loop powered by bite-sized missions, flawless performance, and a vast array of weapons and gadgets. While its narrative takes a backseat and the visual palette is surprisingly muted compared to the series' usual vibrancy, it remains a standout, hard-to-put-down adventure that proves Splatoon can thrive far beyond traditional multiplayer.
Splatoon Raiders is an absolute triumph for anyone who ever wanted a dedicated, pressure-free PvE spin-off from Nintendo’s colourful shooter franchise.

Splatoon Raiders manages to tick a lot of the right boxes by bringing its oft-forgotten single-player mode to the forefront. It’s a fantastic way to introduce new players to the series who were put off by its multiplayer focus, while still challenging the returning players. The fact that it’s such a great game makes it all the more disappointing that it seems to lack any additional accessibility options, especially as motion sickness seemed to be such a problem for some people in Splatoon 3. Hopefully, they might add them in later, as it mars what would have been an otherwise perfect game.

Splatoon Raiders successfully expands the franchise beyond its competitive roots, delivering a surprisingly deep cooperative adventure packed with customization, rewarding progression, and plenty of personality.

Splatoon Raiders effectively reinvents Nintendo's colorful shooter with satisfying growth, great action, and unlimited build variety. With little repetition, it’s engaging, and it’s one of the best PvE journeys in the franchise.

Splatoon Raiders reshapes the series into a genuinely satisfying looter shooter, with deep Gadget customization and chaotic Salmonid encounters that prove the franchise can thrive outside competitive multiplayer.

Splatoon Raiders is a fun, deep single-player adventure, with an art direction that once again stands as one of its greatest strengths. Its clever progression system, exploration, and environmental storytelling make this spin-off much more than an experiment: it is, in all likelihood, the best entry point for discovering everything Splatoon has to offer beyond its multiplayer.

Splatoon Raiders takes the series' most beloved elements and points them in an entirely new direction, delivering a satisfying loot loop and genuine cooperative depth that make it one of Nintendo's boldest spin-off experiments yet.

Splatoon Raiders feels like an easy home run for Nintendo. The single-player story will please fans of the original games (particularly Splatoon 3), and the detailed progression system with collectibles, upgrades and treasure does enough of the heavy lifting to keep you coming back again and again.

Nintendo has taken one of its brightest multiplayer franchises and confidently marched it into completely different territory without losing its identity along the way. That’s a remarkably difficult balancing act, yet Splatoon Raiders makes it look effortless for most of its runtime.

Splatoon Raiders successfully expands the Splatoon universe with a content-rich adventure that blends exploration, customization, and satisfying loot-driven progression. Its colorful world, strong sense of discovery, and polished gameplay make it feel like a natural evolution for the franchise. While a few repetitive moments prevent it from reaching its full potential, it’s an excellent spin-off that proves Splatoon can thrive beyond competitive multiplayer.

Splatoon Raiders delivers the fast-paced, satisfying combat the series is known for, with a solid selection of weapons, gadgets, and customization options that make battles against Salmonid hordes enjoyable. However, its campaign becomes repetitive, underuses its most interesting mechanics, and relies heavily on grinding, which hurts the overall pacing. While it lacks the creativity of previous entries, the game remains an entertaining and content-rich experience, particularly for players interested in tougher challenges or multiplayer, making it a competent, if somewhat uninspired, addition to the Splatoon universe.

Splatoon Raiders got great shooter qualities. It''s a perfect game for turning my head off after a long day and just splat away. But I would be more happy, if I could raid a treasure island that got more moments that stick out besides cool boss fights and well made cutscenes that are few and far between.
Splatoon Raiders manages to maintain the high standards of this successful franchise.

Nintendo succeeds, once again, its bet on a solo adventure for the license carried by the Tridenfers. Splatoon Raiders offers a dynamic adventure, with a bluffing tactical depth and a significant choice of weapons. If we add to this a bestiary inspired by multiple dangers and a curve of controlled difficulty, we obtain a captivating gaming experience that will please both novices and regulars of the license.

Whether playing solo or with others in co-op mode, we had a blast with "Splatoon Raiders" thanks to the spectacular mass battles, diverse weapons, cool gadgets, and motivating crafting and other upgrade options.

Splatoon Raiders does exactly what Splatoon has always done: deliver instant fun in a colorful shooting festival. Your reflexes and understanding of the mechanics are constantly put to the test in an ingeniously simple design that celebrates Nintendo’s philosophies, as interpreted here by its newest generation.

Splatoon Raiders is the PvE-focused Splatoon adventure fans have been waiting for: a fast, colourful, and remarkably deep shooter packed with satisfying loot, flexible builds, inventive levels, and the series’ unmistakable charm. Its frantic Salmonid battles and rewarding raid loop kept me chasing one more upgrade long after I should have stopped, while its solo campaign proves Nintendo can make Splatoon shine just as brightly outside of PvP. Whether playing alone or eventually with friends, this is one raid well worth joining.

Splatoon Raiders is a solid looter shooter with brilliant core gameplay. Blasting enemies with ink, swimming through it, and aiming with precise gyro controls feels fantastic. A wide range of weapons, gadgets, perks, and mods also encourages experimentation. Unfortunately, repetitive level design and increasingly grind-heavy progression drain much of the initial excitement. Its drab, dated visuals also fall short of what I expect from a Switch 2 exclusive. Splatoon fans may still enjoy it, but newcomers are better off starting with Splatoon 3.

Deep Cut finally has their own game, delivering an entertaining, quintessentially Splatoon take on a loot-level-optimize gameplay loop that should hit the spot for many — and might even convince newcomers to check out the main games.
Metacritic user score 8.1/10 (49 ratings).
Granblue Fantasy Relink: Endless Ragnarok adds so much to not just the endgame but the whole experience that it feels like a 2.0 release.

I greatly enjoyed my time with Granblue Fantasy: Relink, and I’m fortunate to finally have gotten the chance to try what’s a truly delightful adventure with Endless Ragnarok. This is definitely an expansion I’d wholeheartedly recommend both returning players and newcomers to try out. If what exists here in Granblue Fantasy: Relink – Endless Ragnarok is any indication, then I truly believe there’s endless potential for future Granblue Fantasy games of this ilk.

Granblue Fantasy: Relink - Endless Ragnarok answers a lot of the complaints I had with the base game and adds a ton more to do in the game. If you haven’t played Granblue Fantasy: Relink before, this is the perfect time to get the game and the expansion, as it is still an amazing experience.

Granblue Fantasy: Relink - Endless Ragnarok is a great expansion to an already excellent action RPG. The new additions add thoughtful challenges and new strategic options that are helpful when it comes to surviving the onslaught of endgame content. It’s important to keep in mind, however, that this is the kind of addition that is meant for those who have already dug deep enough into the experience and those who haven’t yet will not get much out of it without some hours of grinding to get there.

Granblue Fantasy: Relink - Endless Ragnarok is a commendable expansion, offering more of the same engaging gameplay, which is a compliment here. It revitalizes both early and endgame content with new challenges. The expansion introduces boss-focused encounters with unique mechanics and roguelike Confluence missions that blend combat, platforming, and memory tests, adding variety beyond traditional arenas. While the cinematic presentation and character progression are strong, the intense grinding, especially for new players facing a significant power gap, can be a drawback.

The new Endless Ragnarok expansion, as its name suggests, brings a massive amount of new content to Granblue Fantasy: Relink, Cygames’ colorful action RPG originally released in early 2024. The update introduces new abilities, higher difficulty levels, additional characters to unlock, and even a brand-new roguelike mode, significantly expanding the game’s longevity. While its story, built around many familiar genre clichés, may not leave a lasting impression, the real highlight is its refined combat system. Deep, fast-paced, and spectacular, it draws inspiration from the very best action JRPGs, delivering dozens of hours of engaging gameplay whether you’re playing solo or with friends.

If Granblue Fantasy: Relink had your attention before but you never took the plunge, there legitimately isn’t a better version of the game to play than Endless Ragnarok. If you just want the main story, you won’t get the most out of the game, but if you’re in it for the long haul, Cygames has you covered with an absurd amount of fun and an enjoyable game.

The Endless Ragnarok expansion picks up seamlessly where the main game left off, telling a solid story that promises around 20 to 25 hours of additional gameplay while introducing exciting new features. Whether it’s the "Conflux" roguelike mode, the summoning mechanic, the six new party members, the new Master Trait system, or the numerous new bosses, fans are sure to be satisfied. The long-awaited addition of crossplay also earns a thumbs-up. However, the fact that local co-op is exclusive to the Switch 2 version – and that the Conflux mode doesn't support co-op at all – is baffling.

Granblue Fantasy: Relink - Endless Ragnarok is an excellent expansion that makes the game even more fun, while improving the brutal endgame grind. By introducing a brilliant single-player roguelite mode alongside the most challenging content to date, game-changing character traits and giving Lyria an active role in combat, Cygames has exceeded expectations once again, delivering a must-get for newcomers and veterans alike.

A massive expansion for Skyfarers returning to the endless skies. The overhauled farming mechanics and the introduction of the Summons system add new depth to combat, while six highly distinct new characters and challenging new bosses shake things up. However, a progression system still heavily reliant on the Damage Cap and a boss lineup mostly consisting of familiar faces from the base game leave something to be desired.

Granblue Fantasy: Relink – Endless Ragnarok takes a good game and makes it even better. The reworked and expanded cast are a ton of fun to use, the story is a blast, and the summons and master traits truly change up combat and party composition.

As a whole, Endless Ragnarok feels like more Granblue Fantasy: Relink, and I mean that as a positive. The story is decent, the characters are charming, and all play incredibly well, and there's seemingly an incredible amount of content here that I'm still yet to dive into. If you're fond of Relink, I can't recommend Endless Ragnarok enough, but it's definitely not going to change your mind if it didn't interest you initially.

Endless Ragnarok is very much worth playing through, not only because of characters like Fediel and Maglielle, who will have you rethinking how you tackle the game’s encounters entirely, but also because of the flashy new fights and new grinds available, as well as the extremely fun summoning system.

Endless Ragnarok builds on what Relink was already good at, making it even better. It adds nearly double the content of the base game, giving players more enemies to beat and materials to grind for. While the narrative is forgettable, the added gameplay systems, combined with its great overall presentation, make it one of the best co-op action RPGs on the market right now, and it’s well worth the price.

If you loved Granblue Fantasy: Relink, Endless Ragnarok gives you plenty of reasons to jump back in, with playable summons, deeper character builds, a fun roguelite mode, new characters, and cross-platform multiplayer that make the endgame far more engaging. The story doesn't quite recapture the charm and pacing of the original campaign, but the gameplay upgrades more than make up for it.

Granblue Fantasy: Relink - Endless Ragnarok is arguably the definitive version of Cygames’ action JRPG, an expansion that does more than simply add content; it significantly enhances the core of the experience. Avernus makes farming less repetitive, while Mastery Traits and Weapon Transcendence vastly expand the possibilities for customisation, and the new co-op mechanics further enhance a combat system that remains amongst the best in the genre. At the same time, however, Endless Ragnarok is content designed exclusively for veterans: the entry barrier is extremely high, and those who haven’t already invested dozens of hours in the base game may feel left out. Furthermore, the narrative element remains peripheral, and some long-standing issues - such as the lack of variety in bosses and the tendency for more advanced battles to turn into endurance tests - have not been fully resolved. Ultimately, then, this is a rich and clever expansion that takes Relink to its full potential without transforming it into something different from what it already was.

Granblue Fantasy: Relink — Endless Ragnarok is more of what I wanted from Cygames, and its expansion is meaty with tons of thoughtful decisions made that make sense. Whether I'm exploring the Sky Realm while learning six new characters or entering The Conflux to grind out new materials and gear, I'm consistently having a blast with this game. Even if the main story isn't up to par with the base game, it warrants a return because the gameplay really is that good and even now, 100-plus hours later, there's something new to discover. And thankfully, all the new bosses provide a real and hard-hitting challenge — which will have you itching to get back into the fight with every loss.
