With impressive graphics and exceptional performance, it updates the arcade experience for modern times and expands the narrative with new cutscenes, brilliantly localized and dubbed in our language. Despite the new modes, however, it remains a relatively short game.

Throughout this entire review, playing hour after hour on Corneria with the orchestral soundtrack filling the headphones and General Pepper speaking with an authoritative accent in perfect Brazilian Portuguese, Kazin kept thinking that the phrase applies to the whole game. James McCloud would be proud.

Star Fox on Nintendo Switch 2 brings back the classic foundation of Star Fox 64, recreating Fox McCloud and the Star Fox team’s mission against Dr. Andross in the Lylat System. The game opts for a more modern presentation, with revamped visuals, voiced dialogue, a more powerful soundtrack, new camera modes, and updated controls for the Switch 2. The campaign remains short and very familiar, but it works well thanks to its fast-paced arcade action, alternate routes, and the fun feeling of getting back into the Arwing. Battle Mode and Challenge Mode help extend the game’s longevity, even though the main experience is still clearly centered around the campaign.

Star Fox soars back into players' hands with gorgeous visuals, high-paced arcade action, and plenty of replay value. There’s room for the series to grow, but this solid reboot gives long-time fans and newcomers an adventure worth taking to the skies.

Star Fox for the Switch 2 is this game in its best form to date. It looks and sounds better than ever, with the most ways to play, and characters get more love and attention than ever before. Whether you’ve played the previous versions or not, you’ll have a great time. I haven’t been this excited for a potential full sequel since 1997 – surely it’s written in the stars by now!

Star Fox on the Switch 2 is certainly the definitive version of the single-player game. The controls, visuals, sounds, and overall experience are impeccable. It has quality for any enthusiast of rail shooters and aerial combat games, and fans of the original have a real treat in their hands. On the other hand, the playtime is quite limited by current standards. Four to six hours are more than enough to exhaust the campaign content.
While we haven’t had much Star Fox, this entry is the best to date. Hopefully, this spawns into something rooted in this experience without remaking Star Fox 64.

Star Fox on the Nintendo Switch 2 is exactly the kind of remake fans have been hoping for. It stays true to what made the Nintendo 64 classic so memorable while introducing enough visuals, audio and gameplay improvements to make it feel fresh for a new generation of gamers.

Star Fox clearly isn’t trying to reinvent the wheel, and perhaps that is precisely its greatest strength. Nintendo has chosen to modernise a classic without losing the original’s identity. The gameplay remains wonderfully addictive, the alternative routes invite you to take off again and again, and technically, everything runs exceptionally smoothly on the Nintendo Switch 2. Yet it remains difficult to work with a team that offers more commentary than actual help during the missions. But every time I thought, “just one more mission”, I realised that Star Fox had gripped me all over again. And that is perhaps the greatest compliment I can pay to this remake.
Star Fox is a gorgeous and solid remake that brings this classic arcade shooter into the present.

Star Fox is another remaster of a beloved classic. Fans were undoubtedly hoping for more, but it’s still an enjoyable experience. It’s just a bit too short, especially since the multiplayer mode fails to deliver.

At the end of the day, Star Fox’s biggest strength and most fatal flaw are one in the same: It’s just Star Fox 64 again. On hand, that’s why it’s so much fun to play. It is a pretty good remake of a borderline perfect video game. But it also has to measure up to a borderline perfect video game, which it simply doesn’t in some important regards. I’m satisfied with what I’ve played, but also beyond ready for an actual new Star Fox game.

If you have never played Star Fox 64, then I highly recommend it because it is a timeless masterpiece of the genre. If you have now played the original game and are not particularly curious about this new aesthetic implementation, then it has nothing essentially new to offer you.
Star Fox on Nintendo Switch 2 redefines what a modern remake should be, delivering an adventure capable of winning over any player wanting to discover and expand the Star Fox universe.
Star Fox on Switch 2 is therefore a wonderful reminder of what Nintendo did best when it set out to refine an idea to perfection.

Star Fox proves that not every remake needs to reinvent a classic to be memorable. By respecting the original’s essence while introducing meaningful improvements, it delivers a fun, immersive, and highly addictive experience. Its short campaign is more than compensated by outstanding replay value. A title that showcases the Nintendo Switch 2’s potential and reminds us why this franchise should never be forgotten.

This gorgeous Switch 2 remake masterfully captures the responsive, high-speed magic of Star Fox 64 with stunning 60 FPS performance and cinematic flair. While some new narrative choices underwhelm and the bare-bones multiplayer falls flat, the replay-dense campaign and stellar single-player challenge mode offer a spectacular entry point for newcomers.

Star Fox may just be a by-the-book remake, but it hits all the right notes, encapsulating what we loved about the original three decades ago. It's time to take to the skies again in a wonderful trip that is worth the price of re-admission.

Star Fox for Nintendo Switch 2 is a successful revival of a classic Nintendo franchise. It respects the original while giving it the visual upgrade, cinematic presentation, and online Battle Mode needed to feel relevant again.
The gameplay may be showing its age, and the lack of modern control options holds it back slightly, but the overall package is still strong. The cutscenes make the story more engaging, the graphics are great, the music is fantastic, and Battle Mode gives the remake something new and exciting.
Most importantly, this feels like a strong new beginning for Star Fox. Hopefully, this is only the start, because Fox McCloud and the rest of the Star Fox squad deserve to blast off again very soon.

Nintendo preserves the legacy of Star Fox while updating it with impressive cinematics, a strong Spanish dub and outstanding audiovisual work. More Landmaster and Blue-Marine stages would have been welcome, but Fox McCloud’s return still lands with real impact.

Star Fox is a fantastic remake of a game that made history on the Nintendo 64, although, once you reach the end of this adventure, a question naturally arises: was a third reimagining of Lylat Wars really necessary? We’re sure Nintendo did its homework, banking on a title that’s already excellent in its own right and that could capture the attention of new players after Fox McCloud and his team have been off the screens for so long; at the same time, we hoped that for this occasion, the Big N would have planned to expand the universe of a title that left its mark nearly 30 years ago. It’s a solid effort—a well-crafted remake complete with fun and successful online play (though not without its limitations)—but we’re certain they could have done a bit more to truly set it apart.

My honest opinion is that Star Fox for the Nintendo Switch 2 is, by far, the best game in the franchise. It features the best gameplay, story, and levels; and while much of this stems from the legendary original game being remade, it is also impossible not to give credit to the talented team at Velan Studios for everything that was recreated, reimagined, and added.

Star Fox successfully modernizes a Nintendo classic with stunning visuals, refined controls, and an engaging presentation while preserving the fast-paced arcade gameplay that made the original memorable. The new content and replay value give players more reasons to return, even if the adventure remains relatively short. Overall, it's a faithful and polished remake that marks a welcome return for Fox McCloud and his team.

Star Fox returns with a remake that features excellent controls and a visual and cinematic ambition befitting the year 2026. It’s a straightforward, intense, and highly replayable arcade experience that introduces some truly tough new challenges and a surprisingly fun multiplayer mode. The campaign might feel short if you’re just looking for a quick playthrough, but the game is much more than that.

Star Fox is a solid remake that brings the N64 classic into the modern era with gorgeous visuals and sharper controls, even if it still struggles with the original’s limited content and familiar repetition.

This is as close to a perfect 1:1 remake as you could ask for. Star Fox feels and looks exactly how my brain remembered the game back in 1997. Every detail has been touched up to make for a modern experience while leaving the core gameplay loop intact. I would prefer if we had more shiny new toys to play with but when they refreshed the old toy this good, it’s hard to complain. The new cutscenes and dialogue bring the characters to life like never before. The orchestral arrangements of the legendary soundtrack are chef’s kiss. This is also a surprise graphical showcase for the Nintendo Switch 2. Velan Studios did an amazing job, and I hope to see them stick with the franchise the way Grezzo has with Zelda and MercurySteam with Metroid. Star Fox is back. Next time, let’s take him to new heights.

Star Fox for the Nintendo Switch 2 is the ultimate way to experience this gem from the 1990s, revitalised thanks to its superb visuals and cutscenes that take the storyline to a whole new level – one that no other version even comes close to. Although the gameplay hasn’t received the same level of attention, and is starting to show its 30 years a little, and whilst the campaign’s length may not appeal to players simply looking to see the credits roll, this is a successful reboot that provides a fresh launchpad for Fox McCloud and the rest of the Star Fox squad to blast off towards stardom with several hours of solid fun.

Star Fox 64 is not the best rail-shooter ever made (that distinction belongs to Sin &a; Punishment: Star Successor), but it is up there. I have no idea how well you personally will agree with that, but I do know that sitting here replaying it again, I remember how much fun that original game was. It kind of makes me happy that someone who had never even heard of the N64 original could feel like that today.

Star Fox on Switch 2 is a faithful and well-crafted remake of one of Nintendo's classics that does a wonderful job of bringing a classic into the present without sacrificing its essence. Beautiful graphics and overall thoughtful changes have made this the best iteration of Star Fox yet.

I was one of the first to bemoan a remake of Star Fox 64, despite how much I love the original. But with amazing upgrades to the visuals and music, the fleshing out of the main cast, and great challenge modes, Star Fox will likely become one of my most-played games this year, despite wanting a bit more from the rest of the cast and the online multiplayer.

Velan Studios has done something remarkable: rebuilt one of Nintendo's most beloved classics piece by piece with respect and skill, adding enough new content to make it more than a nostalgia trip. This is the definitive version of Star Fox — and if this is truly the beginning of a new chapter for Fox McCloud, the Lylat System's future has never looked brighter.
The Star Fox remake gives Nintendo’s furry ace a slick new coat of paint, but you’ll be (barrel) rolling credits before you’ve even had time to settle into the cockpit.

It occurs to me that if Star Fox Zero never happened, I’d probably be a lot kinder to this remake. A lot of Star Fox 2026 is what I want from a proper remake of Star Fox 64, but it’s still Star Fox 64. Again. Some of the rough edges are sanded down, but they’re still there. Even $50 is pushing it for what it has to offer. To anyone at Nintendo or Valen Studios who would listen, I beg of you. No more remakes. Take what you have here and build on it with a new installment. Let this franchise finally step out of Star Fox 64‘s shadow again. Or, if you must do another remake, do Star Fox 2. That game needs a remake even more than Star Fox 64 did. Or bury the franchise for good. At this point, I don’t care which.

I have a huge amount of admiration for Star Fox; the graphics and music are truly stunning and worthy of accolades. However, this is not a movie, and whilst some missions are good fun to blast through, the repetition eventually starts to feel draining. Ultimately, this is a game I will barrel roll into now and then for a quick shoot ’em up, rather than chill out with for a long, dedicated gaming session.

Star Fox (2026) absolutely proves that the Lylat System is still worth saving, whether you’re completely new to the franchise or revisiting it after one of its many past iterations. It pairs incredibly fun flight gameplay with modern visuals to create a more than worthwhile experience.

While each individual run is short, the branching paths and other differences between each campaign provide plenty of replayability and ensure that the path to Venom feels different each time. On top of that, it comes packed with additional challenges and modes to play.

It isn’t entirely flawless, of course. Teammates that act more like flying targets at times and how the alternate vehicles feel to control are downsides. But they remain fairly minor issues in the grand scheme of things.

Star Fox is the glorious return of a childhood classic. With gameplay that is just as smooth as ever, a new Challenge Mode to take on, and an expanded cinematic story, it is exactly the game fans of the series have been waiting for. While a few minor issues hold it back, it is still a must-play, and the perfect entry point for newcomers. 

Welcome back Star Fox Team! We missed you!

Star Fox is about to get a lovely tribute on Nintendo Switch 2 with one of the best achievements in interactive video game history. Velan Studios has created the ideal arcade experience, fiercely nostalgic and excitingly contemporary, by refusing to dilute the mechanical purity that made the original design universally beloved.
Velan Studios delivers the definitive version of a timeless classic — stunning visuals, expanded narrative, and the same irresistible formula that made Star Fox 64 legendary in 1997.

Star Fox on the Nintendo Switch 2 is a remake with two faces. For players who have never played the original, this is undoubtedly the best way to get acquainted with one of Nintendo's most unique franchises. Despite its age, the gameplay still feels surprisingly fresh, the arcade setup works excellently, and the audiovisual presentation is among the best the Switch 2 currently has to offer. For fans, the story is slightly different. The remake is so faithful to the original that there are hardly any surprises to be found. Everything that once made Star Fox 64 great is still present, but virtually nothing goes a step further. Nevertheless, it remains a high-quality Nintendo production that shows why Star Fox 64 has been considered a classic for nearly thirty years. Not an instant classic in itself, but certainly the definitive version of a timeless classic.

Star Fox is the worthy remake of Lylat Wars, the most popular game in the franchise featuring the adventures of McCloud and its crew. A campaign that will look short if you only plan to make one run, but will find interest in its replayability. Different branches to explore other alternative planets and script sequences, abounding challenges that bring challenge and that will feed the most complete veterans, and content in cooperation or 4v4 that will boost the dynamics of the game. Nintendo has just delivered, irreproachably, an example to revive a classic in its catalog

Star Fox for Nintendo Switch 2 is a meticulously crafted, spectacular, and immensely enjoyable remake that perfectly understands what made the Nintendo 64 classic so special. It doesn't reinvent the franchise, nor does it turn its story or multiplayer into its biggest selling points, but it makes up for it with magnificent gameplay, an outstanding audiovisual presentation, and that rare ability to feel exactly like the idealized memory many of us kept of the original.

Star Fox brings Fox McCloud and the Arwing back in a short arcade shooter that makes more sense the more you replay it. The campaign is brief, but medals, hidden exits, and better stage outcomes gave me a reason to keep improving instead of stopping at the credits. The biggest issue is that Star Fox sticks very close to Star Fox 64. Joy-Con 2 mouse controls are interesting, but I kept going back to traditional controls because the Arwing felt better there. Star Fox fans who still enjoy short replayable missions should have the easiest time with it, and newcomers just need to know the campaign is short by design.
Star Fox serves as a welcome reminder that elegance never goes out of style

With "Star Fox," Nintendo has delivered a successful remake on the Switch 2, boasting stylish graphics, fun firefights, snappy dialogue, and cool boss battles. However, the gameplay mechanics remain very close to the original.

Starfox is faithful remake of the classic that also brings new modes and mechanics to the experience that will no doubt excite fans. Not only does it push replayability more than ever before, but it is crammed with unlockables, enjoyable multiplayer modes, and hidden challenges.
For fans who have been playing this game for decades now, the fresh coat of paint and reinvigorated multiplayer more than justifies the price of admission here.

Star Fox is an impressively faithful remake of the Nintendo 64 classic, brought into the modern era with a fresh coat of paint. For some players, that alone will be enough, but it's hard not to feel a bit disappointed by the fact that the package doesn't include even a single new level.

Star Fox 2026 is a game straight out of 1997, with all the personality and simplicity that entails. It’s a game you can finish in an afternoon, but the gameplay is fun and unique enough to make every hour rewarding.

Recommended for both newcomers and veterans alike, Star Fox elevates Nintendo’s charismatic franchise to new heights on the Switch 2, introducing welcome new features while delivering a spectacular reimagining worthy of the 1997 classic's legacy. So, if there was ever any doubt, it is now gone: redesigned and revitalized for the current generation, young McCloud and his crew have a very promising future ahead, and the decision to unite past and present through a remake has proven to be a brilliant move.

‘Star Fox’ remains a fantastic action game with no real competition. Where else do you get to battle flying monkey heads whilst a space frog shouts tips at you? The remake stays true to the original, but gives the graphics a massive overhaul and sensibly modernises the controls.

Not only has Nintendo pulled off a perfect reboot of the Star Fox series, but we’ve also been treated to yet another must-have title for the Nintendo Switch 2. Now all that’s left is to wait for a truly new installment in the Star Fox saga.
Even if it’s just “reheated food” for Nintendo’s most hardcore fans, there could hardly be a better foundation on which to build the future of the Star Fox series.

Visually and acoustically, Star Fox impressed us across the board. The overall atmosphere is more intense, more immersive, and still retains that essential sense of nostalgia for longtime veterans. All the more disappointing, then, is the lack of additional missions to expand the relatively short single-player campaign. While the Challenge Mode is a nice extra for achievement hunters, full-fledged missions or even a second campaign would have added significant value to the remake. The multiplayer mode also suffers from a limited number of maps and mission types, even though the core gameplay is enjoyable. We hope that Star Fox marks a reboot of the series and that this high level of quality can be maintained in future installments.
Metacritic user score 8.4/10 (185 ratings).
A gorgeous and cleverly designed two‑player co‑op adventure that turns retro anime nostalgia into smart, heartwarming puzzle‑driven storytelling.
Another brilliant, and incredibly varied, co-op title to enjoy with a friend, with a gobsmackingly-good and highly-memorable visual style.

I had high hopes for Orbitals after seeing that beautiful 80s anime style, but I didn’t expect the co-op to be this creative. We had a lot of fun figuring out the puzzles while messing around with all the different tools and discovering whatever strange idea the game had waiting for us next. I also love that it doesn’t really care who does what, swap tools, switch roles, and figure it out together works incredibly well, whether you play games every day or barely touch them. There really isn’t much I would change here; Orbitals is exactly the kind of co-op adventure I love to play.

Ultimately, Orbitals is a standout exclusive on the Nintendo Switch 2, one more indicative of a first-party release than a debut title from a new studio, making it an absolute must-play for owners of Nintendo’s latest hybrid console.

It feels like we’re still just scratching the surface of what co-op only games can be with the likes of A Way Out, Split Fiction, and now Orbitals. Orbitals is full to bursting with incredible ideas, more than it can properly execute on, but it remains an incredible, fun, and charming experience the whole way through.
Whether it’s due to the visuals, a puzzle’s solution, or from bumping into a screaming alien creature, Orbitals is awe-inspiring.
Orbitals is an absolute must-play for the discerning co-op sickos among us, pairing fiendishly clever puzzle design with a crisp, gorgeous retro anime aesthetic.

Orbitals is a dazzling audiovisual achievement and a brilliantly designed co-op adventure, combining the spirit of classic ’80s and ’90s anime with a constant stream of inventive ideas. Its only real flaw is that such a wonderful journey ends far too soon.

After playing it in local multiplayer on a single console, Orbitals is shaping up to be one of the most interesting co-op games coming to Nintendo Switch 2 this year. Its biggest strength is that all of its different elements seem to work together toward the same goal. The anime-inspired aesthetic isn’t separate from the gameplay, co-op doesn’t feel like an afterthought, and everything fits together seamlessly.

Orbitals is a fantastic game that uses its inspirations to the highest degree. The art design and aesthetic are a true triumph. Interlacing the cooperative video game genre with the themes of 80’s mecha anime series is executed well.

The important thing is that its runtime is a blast from start to end. You and your co-op partner are going to have a hard time putting Orbitals down and will always be excited to discover the next challenging puzzle and gorgeous destination. We used to dream about games looking this good. Even after beating it, I still look at Orbitals with wonder.

My main complaint is that I wanted much more of it, and while the gameplay itself feels perfectly paced, the somewhat abrupt ending only reminded me that I wished we had spent a little more time establishing the stakes and motivations of the story. Ultimately, Orbitals is a truly phenomenal co-operative title and one of the best ways to spend an evening with a friend this year. With its phenomenal visuals, thrilling mechanics, and the brilliant characters and story, this is the new high bar for co-op games.

Orbitals is an absolutely stunning love letter to classic anime, perfectly capturing a beloved 20th-century aesthetic and delivering an engaging and beautifully told narrative to boot. Beyond its visuals, it lets you and a mate explore an intriguing intergalactic universe and wield a fun array of space-tech to get through each of its tight puzzle-platforming sequences. It’s joyful, stylistic, heaps of fun, and doesn’t outstay its welcome – a perfect excuse to cuddle up on the couch with a loved one.

Orbitals may lean heavily into its retro vibes, but it never uses them as a crutch. The co-op adventure is still the focal point, and each level feels unique. Whether that's by using some unlocked ability or playing through sections that suddenly turn gameplay on its head, there are plenty of surprises along the way. Honestly, I'm just amazed that in 2026, a game can borrow so many elements from the past but still feel original today. That's a monumental feat in its own right, and it's even more impressive that Orbitals is both fresh and fun.
Orbitals combines fantastic gameplay with stunning retro animation to make a great multiplayer co-op game.

A wildly successful fully cooperative experience, Orbitals is an absolute essential purchase for Switch 2. It is demanding for non-gamers, but also highly rewarding, dishing out challenge, fun, and laughs both scripted and emergent. Definitely the most perfect recreation of an 80s anime gaming has ever achieved.
A well crafted adventure that shows real charisma and an excellent level designs for two. One of the most interesting games of the year for Switch 2.

Orbitals draws inspiration from It Takes Two, but manages to forge its own identity thanks to excellent level design, cooperative mechanics that truly require communication, and spectacular art direction inspired by 1980s anime. Its puzzles are easy to understand but grow increasingly complex as you progress, while the game's brisk pace keeps the adventure from feeling repetitive. However, the space sections between levels are uninteresting, and the battles against powerful enemies could have made much better use of the cooperative mechanics. Despite these shortcomings, Orbitals is a charming cooperative adventure and one of the most interesting offerings in the genre in 2026.

Orbitals is a fantastic tribute to classic anime and, above all, a magnificent cooperative video game. Shapefarm combines nostalgia, personality, and some truly ingenious gameplay ideas in one of the most appealing exclusives in the Nintendo Switch 2 catalog. Find a partner before you blast off: this space journey is designed for two.

Despite its short campaign, Orbitals wins players over with a wealth of references and diverse gameplay optimized for two people. Its original story and anime-inspired universe ensure a unique experience for fans of games like It Takes Two and Split Fiction.

Orbitals is a beautifully crafted cooperative adventure that blends the spirit of Hazelight's couch multiplayer with the visual language of classic Japanese anime. The real surprise, however, is its gameplay. Rather than locking players into predefined roles, Orbitals allows both characters to freely exchange tools and responsibilities, making communication and improvisation the heart of its environmental puzzles.
Orbitals is a visually spectacular co-op game that kept me smiling from start to finish, with loads of clever ideas for you and a friend to experience.

Orbitals stands out with its nostalgic retro-anime style and colorful co-op mechanics. Its puzzles and platforming may feel somewhat ordinary, but coordinating roles and timing with a friend makes up for it. Best enjoyed together in the same room, it reminds us that sometimes games are fun not because you play well, but simply because you play together.

Orbitals is a love letter to anime series from the 1980s and 1990s. It uniquely blends varied cooperative gameplay with fantastic presentation. The fact that I regularly couldn't tell the difference between the impressive cutscenes and the actual gameplay makes Orbitals an incredibly impressive game to look at. For an asking price of €40 digitally and €50 physically, I just wish there had been a lot more to play.

Orbitals delivers a stunning 'playable anime' experience with a retro aesthetic that captures the essence of 90s classics. Although long cinematic sequences occasionally disrupt the narrative flow, the brilliant cooperative puzzles and flexible character roles provide a deep, rewarding challenge. It stands as an essential co-op title, despite some unoriginal mechanics and a steep learning curve.
With Orbitals, Shapefarm has made an extremely strong start in the league of co-op games.

Ultimately, Orbitals is another successful co-op adventure in the vein of Hazelight titles like Split Fiction. However, thanks to its gameplay and especially its appealing retro-anime aesthetic, it is far from a cheap knock-off; instead, it retains its own unique character while matching the quality of its inspirations. For Switch 2 owners who love 80s anime and have even a passing interest in adventure-like co-op gameplay, Orbitals is essentially a must-play.

Orbitals is a charming Switch 2 co-op adventure that combines inventive puzzles, rewarding exploration, and a striking '80s anime-inspired world. Its story can struggle to land its emotional beats and progression sometimes limits exploration, but the consistently creative cooperative design makes communication, experimentation, and shared discovery the heart of the experience.

A fantastic cooperative action-adventure game that follows in the footsteps of Hazelight’s genre-defining titles, yet carves out its own distinct identity thanks to its artistic direction inspired by Japanese animation and the wonderful sense of freedom it offers in controlling the two characters.

Orbitals is the exact opposite of what the industry asks video game products to be lately. No open world. No store. No pre-order skins. No countless hours of gameplay. No ranks or levels or skill trees. Then, how is it that it was one of the most galvanizing and "alive" experiences of recent memory?

Orbitals is one of the most interesting cooperative experiences available on Nintendo Switch 2. While it doesn’t always match the narrative depth of the titles that clearly inspired it, it makes up for this with imaginative puzzles, carefully crafted cooperative gameplay, and exceptional art direction. Short yet intensely enjoyable, Maki and Omura’s journey proves once again that the best cooperative adventures aren’t necessarily those with the toughest puzzles, but those capable of turning the act of solving them into a shared memory.

Orbitals is simply a brilliant title that fully lives up to the pedigree of where it comes from. While it doesn’t quite reach the same heights in terms of design that we saw in Split Fiction, it constantly manages to surprise us with fresh gameplay ideas that make it clear just how special it is to design a video game entirely around the concept of two players cooperating. Add to that visuals we haven’t seen before in a video game, which also deliver exactly what they set out to do, and you have an unmissable title for anyone looking to have a great time with someone by their side.

It’s clear that ShapeFarm has a project on its hands that could become one of the cooperative surprises of the year—and perhaps even of this generation. The influence of Josef Fares’s work is evident, but the studio has managed to forge its own identity around its anime aesthetic, a story centered on friendship, and mechanics that prioritize cooperation over difficulty—resulting in an experience that perfectly recreates the warm and fun feeling of watching a retro anime.

Orbitals is proof that there’s space in the co-op adventure genre for other teams to create something truly special. Its incredible art direction and fantastic moment-to-moment gameplay make this an engaging adventure from start to finish. Although the main plot sometimes fades into the background and you’ll hit the credits sooner than expected, it’s still a memorable experience, one that stands out through its creativity, charm and sheer sense of fun.

With a campaign that lasts less than 10 hours, Orbitals offers an accessible and straightforward cooperative experience that you can power through in just a few sessions. The game is well worth it on the Nintendo Switch 2 for delivering just the right dose of nostalgia, creativity, and fun.

Orbitals is a charming cooperative adventure that combines a beautiful aesthetic inspired by 1980s and 1990s anime with mechanics designed to keep both players constantly engaged. Its puzzles could offer a greater challenge, and the story loses some momentum toward the end, but the freedom to exchange tools, its excellent soundtrack, and the charisma of its protagonists make it an experience that is remarkably easy to enjoy with a partner.
Orbitals is visually distinctive and plays a lot like It Takes Two. While it still falls some way short of the genre's greats, it is nevertheless a very solid two-player co-op game.

While it may not quite reach the heights of the best modern co-op games, Orbitals takes that same formula, dresses it in a unique personality, and—with the same magic found in 80s and 90s anime—reminds us how wonderful it is to discover something together.

Some of the best moments in Orbitals came from my friend and me just stopping to smell the roses. We had a great time figuring out its puzzles together, especially when a simple gadget led to a solution neither of us expected. That sense of discovery carries through the adventure, helped along by a world that is as strange as it is gorgeous. The problem is that some of its best ideas barely have time to develop throughout its 10-hour runtime, whether they come from the story or the mechanics. For all the things we wanted more of, though, we never stopped having fun with the game.

Orbitals is another must-play for co-op lovers and those looking for a good time with a friend or significant other. While a bit too short in many areas, there’s no denying the charm and fun puzzles deliver on all fronts. It keeps you engaged and emphasizes teamwork, leading to great memories. I hope there’s more in store for Maki and Omura, as I (and Matty) are ready to explore space again at a moment’s notice.

Orbitals is an easy recommendation if you’re looking for a new co-op game on Switch 2. It’s close to being best in class at what it does and properly feels like a cartoon come to life. It’s hard to imagine anyone not having a good time with it, the co-op gameplay, standout anime presentation, and riveting story making for a game you’ll enjoy from start to finish.

My partner and I had a really nice time with Orbitals, and while it doesn’t quite reach the couch co-op excellence tier that Hazelight has set for the rest of the genre, it’s still a journey worth embarking on. The incredible ‘80s/‘90s anime artwork and music are the clear standouts, with so much love and charm drawn into every inch of this experience. It is pretty brisk, and there is an occasional feeling of repetition in the gameplay that isn’t always the most interesting action in the world. Even so, Switch 2 owners have another very nice exclusive on their hands. Orbitals is a lovely game to spend with your playing partner over a weekend.

Orbitals' overall identity is closely tied to its aesthetics, and that's fine. Fortunately, the studio has designed a range of solid puzzles, a series of satisfying mechanics and versatile level design, which keep it entertaining right through to the end. I would have liked to see a bit more effort put into the overarching narrative, but we were smiling all the way through, and that's saying something.

Orbitals is a brisk, enjoyable interstellar romp that will perhaps, at the end of the day, be more fondly remembered for its authentic approach to vintage Japanese animation than its ability to bring friends together. That’s not to say it doesn’t succeed as a co-op puzzler—it does—although I think it falls a hair short of its contemporaries in terms of chaotic creativity and scope.

The creativity and visuals are stunning, the characters have a ton of heart, the soundtrack is an absolute banger, and the atmosphere immediately transported me to the cozy feel of an ’80s–’90s anime. If this is only the beginning for Shapefarm, the future of co-op games is bright.

Orbitals is an enjoyable co-op adventure amongst the stars. If you have fondness for older anime series and movies, this game captures the look, sound and spirit of a fun movie from a different time and age. If you’re looking for a cooperative game to share with a friend or loved one, I definitely recommend checking out Orbitals.

Orbitals pulls a lot of interesting and familiar elements into a tidy package with a charming pair of heroes and a lengthy array of challenges to put their friendship to the test. The obstacles we faced were an incredible gauntlet of amusing sci-fi navigation and repair work as we pushed forth into the unknown in our modest little ship, but ultimately, it’s the friendship Maki and Omura share throughout the adventure that kept it heartwarming and compelling - just kids doing their best and having fun along the way. And that vibe extended to us as we guided them through their trials, doing our best as well. Orbitals has kind of a whimsical feeling to it in that way, and that whimsy makes it a trip for two well worth taking.

In an era where many video game experiences seem to want to convince us of their greatness through expansive worlds, increasingly complex systems, and endless amounts of content, Orbitals decides to take a completely different, more intimate path: it takes two people by the hand, places them in front of the same screen, and reminds them that, sometimes, the most memorable adventure isn't the one you experience alone, but the one that happens when two players turn to each other and, with a nod of understanding, realize they've experienced something that today, practically, almost no longer exists.

Orbitals is a charming co-op adventure that stands out thanks to its stunning retro-anime aesthetic and a great variety of puzzles that steadily increase in difficulty. While its story isn't quite as compelling as it could have been, it delivers a polished, carefully crafted experience that proves you don’t have to reinvent an entire genre to make something genuinely good.

Despite its strengths, the game isn't well-balanced and suffers from pacing issues. While the adventure can be completed in under ten hours, allowing for short, well-paced sessions for two players, I constantly counted the disorienting backtracking between the same doors, the maintenance tasks, and the engine repairs, all against the backdrop of a storyline that struggles to truly establish itself. It's not until the third act that the adventure finally takes off, offering some sublime moments, a lengthy animated sequence, and a handful of particularly well-executed boss fights. A consistency we wish had been present much earlier. Despite these design flaws, the charm works its magic and the enjoyment of the game remains undiminished from beginning to end. An imperfect but generous offering, proving that passionately crafted cooperative gameplay still has a bright future.
It promises a game that emulates a vintage anime, then delivers exactly that: Orbitals is an authentic artistic achievement.

Despite its late-game stumbles, Orbitals is an utter joy that captures the nostalgia and innocence of classic anime, turning it into an inventive, thoroughly enjoyable co-op adventure. With brilliant puzzles, a gorgeous setting, and lovable protagonists, Shapefarm has delivered a trip down memory lane worth taking. It’s a stacked month of releases, but if you’re a Switch 2 owner, this needs to be in your orbit. (Not proud of that one).

Orbitals is just a pure delight, every episode of its adventure presenting us with something new and exciting to accomplish together that kept the smiles firmly plastered on our faces. It goes without saying, but the presentation is magical, heaped in nostalgia and taking me right back to the Saturday mornings as a child watching cartoons all those years ago. Maki and Omura’s journey through space did feel a little shorter than I’d have liked, but as far as these types of cooperative asymmetric adventures go, Orbitals ranks top in my book.

Orbitials has the uncanny ability to pull out long dormant memories of my childhood watching anime – memories I wouldn't come to fully appreciate until adulthood – giving that nostalgia a playable form for me and a friend. Its familiar but entertaining puzzles and striking art style make it a strong addition to any co-op library, and one that asked me to continually keep my curiosity piqued, if only to have it answered with a fun, fleeting interaction that put a smile on my face for a moment. It does lose some momentum toward the end, but this world is always exciting to get lost in – if for nothing else, just to let the synthetic soundtrack and whimsical characters wash over you like a warm Saturday morning. This adventure might be over, but I'm excited to see what Shapefarm does next.

Like It Takes Two and Split Fiction, Switch 2 exclusive Orbitals is a co-op only experience that demands players work as a team. And while it's not quite as finely-tuned or inventive as Hazelight's titles, it's still a great deal of fun to play.

Orbitals is one of those perfect games you finish in an afternoon with the right person. It’s not particularily ambitious, but it doesn’t need to be; rather, it delivers a great co-op experience that’ll take you across the stars in a bid to save a space colony in your trust. Sitting down to play Orbitals will likely serve as a catalyst for your childhood of watching anime on weekends, and its stunning animation is hard to ignore.

Orbitals is a short adventure with a predictable narrative that can be completed in under 10 hours. Even so, it is undeniably a cooperative experience that draws inspiration from retro anime to deliver a magical space journey, featuring Brazilian Portuguese localization and an equally captivating soundtrack.

Orbitals' commitment to its retro anime aesthetic makes this one of the most gorgeous Switch 2 exclusives yet, with two eternally optimistic leads that ensure a charming time, though having a dependent gaming partner is on you.

While it may stumble slightly in its narrative and controls, Orbitals succeeds wonderfully as a cooperative experience. The game’s striking retro-anime visuals and high-quality German voice cast, combined with deeply rewarding teamwork mechanics, culminate in a memorable multiplayer adventure.

Orbitals is a charming co-op adventure that stands out thanks to its fantastic 90s anime presentation and attention to detail. While its gameplay variety doesn't quite reach the heights of It Takes Two or Split Fiction, the clever gadgets, enjoyable puzzles and strong focus on teamwork make exploring the galaxy together a lot of fun. Some potential may have been left in orbit, but co-op and anime fans should definitely give Maki and Omura's adventure a chance.
Orbitals is a game for fans of co-op split-screen adventure who’ve fallen in love with Hazelight’s games. With its anime-style visuals and accessibility, it’s a lovely experience to play with anyone.

The new split-screen experience is one of the most satisfying on the market today, with its retro anime aesthetic, music, and basic yet easy-to-learn controls taking center stage. While the two characters are charismatic, the main appeal is not their relationship, but rather how the game plays and how easy it is to step into this world without knowing anything about video games. The difficulty can ramp up too quickly throughout this nearly 10-hour adventure, but the journey is always better with company.

Orbitals stands out right away thanks to a very captivating retrofuturistic art style that resembles a 1980s anime movie with a sci-fi theme, but the gameplay experience too is a remarkable feat beyond all doubt. This two-player cooperative adventure with puzzle-solving and platforming elements will see the protagonists coordinating closely to approach each challenge in a slick, smart and pragmatic way that keeps players with their wits on at all times. The controller implementation and the satisfaction resulting from every solved challenge all but leaves the question in the air: why couldn't Orbitals be longer?
For younger audiences and those who still cherish the couch co-op experience, Orbitals is one of the must-buy titles of the year.

No game has managed to fully bridge the divide between video games and anime like Orbitals. It is a game that fools you into thinking it's a hand drawn cartoon, while simultaneously providing brilliant co-op fun.

Orbitals is a stunning co-op adventure for retro anime fans (and others too, why not?) that keeps you engaged throughout the entire journey. If there’s ever a sequel, better pacing, a longer runtime, and clearer visual hints would be nice. Even so, this was quite a joyful experience.

Orbitals is an excellent game. It gets a lot of things right, starts and ends exactly when it should, and delivers a thoroughly enjoyable time for those willing to cooperate and work together. While it may not match the depth or quality of Hazelight Studios' titles, it is a delightful space-themed treat for genre fans, absolutely worth experiencing if this style of game appeals to you.
Gorgeous and inventive, and nostalgic with its VHS-filtered anime aesthetic, this game is a delight from start to finish and a must-try for Switch 2 owners.

Orbitals masterfully captures the nostalgic vibe of 1980s anime while delivering highly satisfying asymmetric co-op gameplay. Although its weak story and lack of side content are disappointing, it remains a deeply rewarding experience if you have a partner to play with.
Orbitals is an audiovisual spectacle with unforgettable protagonists, but its repetitive gameplay and short length keep it far from co-op greatness.
Orbitals is a charming, visually striking co-op adventure. It takes a while to get off the ground, but when it does, it really sticks the landing.

Although its artistic direction and gameplay are both a lot of fun, the fact that it never properly explains why any of this is happening unfortunately keeps Orbitals from becoming a truly memorable game. That said, I think the team has a very bright future ahead of them. If they don't hit the jackpot this time, I'm sure they'll knock it out of the park next time.
Clearly inspired by It Takes Two, Orbitals tries to bring the cooperative split-screen formula to an 80s anime setting, which works well in many ways and flaws in others.

Orbitals doesn't quite crash and burn, but its execution leaves a bit to be desired. That said, even after a lukewarm ending, returning to the game to hear the title theme and see the smiling protagonists once more makes me undeniably sentimental. I wish I connected more to Orbitals' story and systems, but I can't deny its playful, cozy vibes.

Orbitals injects sci-fi charm and 90s anime nostalgia into the growing genre of modern couch co-op games. While the story is a little slow, it oozes style and is a relaxing and entertaining way to spend some time with a friend.
Stunningly beautiful in its recreation of 80s and 90s anime, Orbitals is a fun co-op adventure that doesn’t quite match the best of the genre thanks to its more constrained gameplay.

Playing Orbitals is like stepping into a classic anime, packed full of the soft tones and expressiveness of the era. With strong animation credentials and traditional processes behind the concept, there's a genuine heart and authenticity to this world. Clever co-operative play, fun set pieces and a curious mystery at the heart of the story tie this sci-fi tale together well. Slightly rushed and occasionally fiddly at times, but certainly worth blasting through to discover the fate of these new protagonists. Grab a friend, pop the TV on and live out those Saturday morning shows in style together.

Orbitals gives Switch 2 owners a new It Takes Two and Split Fiction style co-op game that also experiments with bringing the 2D 1980s anime aesthetic into a 3D world. There are some satisfying challenges here and a few occasions where there’s clever level design. It also features a camera that often doesn’t feel quite right in certain situations, moments that will leave you spending 5-15 minutes wondering what exactly it is you’re supposed to do, and storytelling that expects you to care about characters without showing you why them and their situations should matter. Orbitals is interesting and could prove a fun follow-up for folks who have been playing Hazelight Studios multiplayer games since A Way Out, but there are some times when this experiment doesn’t always work out.

Orbitals is a game that clearly wants to do well, there's no doubt about that. Whilst Shapefarm truly excels in its visual design, the studio certainly isn't lacking in ambition when it comes to offering fresh co-op gameplay, even if it struggles to fully convince us. Although its approach is still a little too shy, it's certainly not running out of ideas. It was the storytelling in particular that left us slightly cold, as it rushed things a bit too much. We simply would have liked to see more, both in terms of the game's world and the gameplay innovations. But regardless, we'll be keeping a close eye on the studio's future releases.

Orbitals knows exactly what it wants to be: a co-op adventure built around teamwork, with enough freedom in gadgets and player roles to give it an identity beyond its obvious Hazelight influences. While unclear puzzle instructions, a linear structure, limited exploration, and lengthy loading screens occasionally slow the adventure down, its accessible puzzles and flexible gameplay make it easy to enjoy with players of all skill levels. Above all, Orbitals shines through its lovingly crafted nineties anime presentation, resulting in a charming space adventure that may not redefine the genre but is absolutely worth taking with the right co-op partner.

The aesthetics and overall vibe of Orbitals carry the game immensely. This is, without doubt, the most appealing part of this anime-infused cooperative action title, focusing on a beautifully rendered world with creative tools. Unfortunately, where Orbitals falters is in its story and gameplay departments. Because this is a short, four-hour-long adventure, characters can’t develop properly, and the plot is as basic as they come. That’s not to mention, as enjoyable as the tools are, there’s very little challenge when it comes to the puzzles, being overly simplistic with only a handful of standout mechanics. In the end, Orbitals is a quirky, enjoyable anime adventure that falls short of expectations.

Orbitals delights with its retro-anime aesthetic, excellent voice acting, and wonderful music, but the gameplay relies too heavily on the same items, preventing the variety from being as satisfying as it could be. There are plenty of fun sequences, and a smile will rarely leave your face (since playing with someone else naturally brings one on), but there is no denying that the balance of engagement between the two players could be better—too often, one person faces a challenge while the other simply tags along.

Visually, Orbitals is a resounding success. The decision to pay homage to 1980s Japanese animation is executed masterfully, in terms of both visuals and sound. It is a shame, then, that the plot fails to convince—much like the spaceship sequences, which drag down a cooperative gameplay experience that is otherwise engaging, not necessarily due to complexity, but thanks to its freshness.
Immaculate anime stylings aside, Orbitals doesn't bring an awful lot to the post-It Takes Two co-op renaissance, but switch to Japanese and it's never a bad hang.

Orbitals has few issues reminding you what you're doing, but it struggles with the why. Like those 80's shows, it doesn't make us want to switch over, but seems destined to fade from memory. [Issue#429, p.112]

Despite its gorgeous anime-inspired presentation, Orbitals never quite manages to reach the heights it desperately aims for. There is an undeniable passion stitched throughout each piece of the game, but a lack of difficulty and lackluster narrative leave me mixed. Younger players could have a great time with Orbitals, but I struggle to recommend it to anyone looking for anything more than a surface-level experience.
With Orbitals, Shapefarm has made an extremely strong start in the league of co-op games.

Orbitals is a game that wants to do well, there's no doubt about it. While Shapefarm excels in its graphics, the studio clearly aims to offer fresh co-op gameplay, even if it struggles to fully captivate us.

In an era where many video game experiences seem to want to convince us of their greatness through expansive worlds, increasingly complex systems, and endless amounts of content, Orbitals decides to take a completely different, more intimate path: it takes two people by the hand, places them in front of the same screen, and reminds them that, sometimes, the most memorable adventure isn't the one you experience alone, but the one that happens when two players turn to each other and, with a nod of understanding, realize they've experienced something that today, practically, almost no longer exists.
Orbitals is a great bite-sized adventure that lures you in with nostalgic anime and then captures you with a wide variety of puzzle-solving gameplay.

Orbitals is a fantastic game that uses its inspirations to the highest degree. The art design and aesthetic are a true triumph. Interlacing the cooperative video game genre with the themes of 80s and 90s mecha anime series is executed well.

Orbitals is a brisk, enjoyable interstellar romp that will perhaps, at the end of the day, be more fondly remembered for its authentic approach to vintage Japanese animation than its ability to bring friends together. That's not to say it doesn't succeed as a co-op puzzler-it does-although I think it falls a hair short of its contemporaries in terms of chaotic creativity and scope.
Unfortunately, at least for Orbitals, art alone doesn't guarantee excellence. Despite its spectacular sci-fi production design and anime aesthetic, the game falls just short of greatness.

Although its artistic direction and gameplay are both a lot of fun, the fact that it never properly explains why any of this is happening unfortunately keeps Orbitals from becoming a truly memorable game. That said, I think the team has a very bright future ahead of them. If they don't hit the jackpot this time, I'm sure they'll knock it out of the park next time.

Orbitals is a thoroughly enjoyable co-op adventure which, rather than constantly bombarding players with new mechanics, places greater emphasis on puzzles, communication and working together to find solutions. The gameplay is simpler and less varied than in It Takes Two or Split Fiction, but the ability to swap roles freely, the brilliant world design and the inventive use of the available tools mean that two players can have a really good time together. It’s just a shame that the adventure ends so quickly and doesn’t offer much in the way of replay value, as Shapefarm has created a very solid offering for fans of co-op games.

A fantastic cooperative action-adventure game that follows in the footsteps of Hazelight's genre-defining titles, yet carves out its own distinct identity thanks to its artistic direction inspired by Japanese animation and the wonderful sense of freedom it offers in controlling the two characters.

Orbitals is a visually stunning cooperative adventure that captures the magic of classic 1980s anime through its beautiful hand-drawn art style, memorable soundtrack and excellent Spanish voice acting. Its two-player gameplay offers enjoyable puzzles and creative ways to work together, but an underdeveloped story, limited gameplay variety and a universe full of untapped potential hold it back from reaching its full promise. It's still a charming experience worth sharing with a friend, especially for fans of classic anime.

Orbitals is proof that homage, when made by people who truly know the subject, can become language instead of citation. The reconstruction of the aesthetics of '80s and '90s anime is the most convincing seen in a video game, not because it imitates drawings but because it has understood their inner mechanics – the sampling of the animation, the analog photography, the role of the sung theme song – and reproduced them with rigor. Around this scaffolding, Shapefarm has built an intelligent asymmetric co-op game, generous with ideas, supported by two protagonists who are a pleasure to accompany. It is not a masterpiece, and it would be unfair to sell it as one: the second half burns through its concepts too quickly, the bosses are not up to the puzzles, the camera betrays you at the wrong moments and the compressed ending leaves on the table the emotion it had built. But it is a game that knows exactly what it wants to be, that does not waste your time and that, if you have someone to share the couch with, will give you back one of those evenings you remember. In the still young catalog of Nintendo Switch 2, it is one of the best reasons to turn on the console for two.

A wildly successful fully cooperative experience, Orbitals is an absolute essential purchase for Switch 2. It is demanding for non-gamers, but also highly rewarding, dishing out challenge, fun, and laughs both scripted and emergent. Definitely the most perfect recreation of an 80s anime gaming has ever achieved.

Despite its presentation, Orbitals fails to live up to the high expectations set when we first encountered it; nevertheless, it fulfills its purpose as a cooperative game designed to be enjoyed with friends. We found the story somewhat dull and certain mechanics feel overly simplistic, but the cooperative gameplay provided enough great moments to make the 8-to-12-hour adventure an enjoyable experience.

Orbitals is enjoyable to play, looks good, and features puzzles that are all quite manageable. It is, however, a game that requires you to play with someone else. If that’s not an issue for you, then you’ll get a lot of enjoyment out of it. It should be noted, though, that the story isn’t always particularly engaging. Otherwise, it’s a really great game to play on the Nintendo Switch 2.

Orbitals is a stylish co-op adventure that shines through creative two-player mechanics, smooth movement, strong retro-anime presentation, and consistently varied cooperative gameplay. Its weak story, underdeveloped characters, overly simple puzzles, sparse environments, and repetitive soundtrack keep it from reaching its full potential, but the core co-op experience remains highly enjoyable.

Orbitals is simply the perfect couch co-op title for the upcoming autumn. With its great visuals, charm and heart the game captivates you from the very first minute and makes you lose track of time. The gameplay is equally entertaining for experienced and less skilled players alike, making it fun for everyone regardless of skill level. So grab a friend, hunker down together on the next rainy weekend and dive into this ultra-cool space adventure.

Orbitals is a short, straightforward cooperative adventure. At times, I felt we could have explored this crafted cosmic world a bit more—perhaps precisely because its meticulous design leaves you wanting more. The animations and overall aesthetic elevate the entire package, making it a must-play two-player adventure—whether you’re looking to spend quality time with someone else or want to feel like you’ve stepped back in time to watch an anime from your childhood.
Orbitals is a charming cooperative adventure and an excellent example of what a strong art direction can bring to a game, even if repetition and some of its objectives hurt the overall pacing.
Orbitals may struggle with shallow puzzle mechanics, an uneven final stretch, and a story that never fully explores its ambitious ideas, but its strengths ultimately make the journey worthwhile.

Orbitals is a playable love letter to classic Japanese anime, built on a remarkably well-crafted asymmetric co-op design and a stunning art direction. The bond between Maki and Omura, the creative use of its limited toolset, and the flawless presentation all shine throughout the adventure. It stands as one of the most special experiences in the Nintendo Switch 2 library and deserves the attention of anyone with someone to share the controller with.

Orbitals has a charming art direction in every detail, along with delightful gameplay that uniquely relies on co-op mechanics. However, the experience isn't without its flaws! Most notably, the level design, which is unfortunately hit or miss. Alongside the rushed storytelling and the lack of variety in music. Even so, Orbitals remains a solid co-op game that adds a welcome variety to the Switch 2's library.

With the soundtrack by Falk &a; Klou and features like GameShare and Global Friend’s Pass, we have a co-op title that may not measure up to the best in the genre, but it knows exactly who its target audience is and generously gives them what they want.

I don’t say this often, but if there are games that are ‘required playing’ for Switch 2 owners. Orbitals would find itself alongside Switch 2 greats like Donkey Kong Bananza and Pokopia for me. The story and world is charming and nostalgic while also feeling new and different for the console.

Orbitals makes cooperation the heart of a space adventure filled with clever puzzles, minigames and constant coordination between Maki and Omura. Its biggest limitation is clear: you absolutely need another person to experience the game.

I really, really liked Orbitals. There’s something slightly strange about how few games we get that are built around this sort of co-op experience. When it works, there’s nothing quite like sitting with someone and solving problems together, laughing when you get something completely wrong and celebrating when everything finally clicks. The puzzles are varied, the characters are lovely, the anime-inspired presentation is beautiful and, most importantly, it consistently gives both players something meaningful to do.

Whether you play locally with a partner, with a friend or online with someone on the other side of the world, I can easily see Orbitals creating some lovely gaming memories. For me, this is a reminder of why co-op games can be so special. An absolute essential Switch 2 purchase if you have someone to play with.

Let’s have some fun with a nice comparison. Orbitals is like a gorgeous birthday cake. It’s beautiful, it makes your eyes sparkle, and you’re happy to eat it. However, you shouldn’t have a second slice because, despite its tempting appearance, it’s still a huge amount of sugar. And that’s not good for your health. Orbitals won’t harm your body, but it’s easy to draw a parallel. Thanks to flawless art direction and plenty of humor, the game is worth your attention. Its playtime might put some people off—and with good reason, since the final playtime clocks in at around seven hours. Still, it’s a very enjoyable cooperative adventure that can be recommended to everyone, ages 7 to 77!

A co‑op gem wrapped in stunning anime‑style visuals.

Orbitals is packed with personality, clever ideas, and a beautifully crafted Japanese anime‑inspired visual style that gives every moment a vibrant, expressive charm. Its co‑op focus, evolving story, and heartfelt presentation make it an easy recommendation for anyone looking for a meaningful shared adventure.
Fans of co-op-only games can definitely dive straight into Orbitals with confidence, as it delivers a brilliant adventure from start to finish.
While I would have loved a little more of the story throughout, along with some extra opportunities for combat, there’s no denying how good Orbitals looks, on top of how fun it is to play.
The story would have benefited from a little more breathing room.

Orbitals is an entertaining co-op game that clearly takes its cue from Hazelight Studios. Whilst the game certainly won’t be the best co-op title of 2026, it does manage to win you over with its colourful anime style and catchy music. The varied level design helps you quickly forget the puzzles’ shortcomings, and the stunning cutscenes are a real treat. If you can find a partner in crime, the game is well worth spending an evening on the sofa playing.
Orbitals delivers exactly what I wanted from a co-op game: a great time shared with someone else, backed by lovable characters, a memorable story, and fantastic retro-anime style.
Orbitals is like a fun, short anime series you start watching with someone - just when it gets the most interesting, you suddenly realize it’s already over.
Orbitals charms with its nostalgic retro anime-inspired presentation, strong co-op gameplay, and lovable characters, even if the story runs a bit out of steam towards its final stretch.
Orbitals is a game for fans of co-op split-screen adventure who’ve fallen in love with Hazelight’s games. With its anime-style visuals and accessibility, it’s a lovely experience to play with anyone.

Orbitals is one of those adventures that fully understands what it wants to be and never strays from that vision for a single second. Its cooperative gameplay turns communication, trial and error, and player camaraderie into an essential part of the experience, while its art and sound direction achieve something extraordinarily difficult: rather than merely mimicking late-80s anime, it recaptures its texture, expressiveness, and unique vision of the future. It’s not a title for everyone, but if you buy into its premise and have the right co-op partner by your side, it’s remarkably easy to get swept away in its galaxy for hours on end.
Orbitals delivers smart co-op, varied puzzles, strong anime-inspired presentation, and a memorable world, though its story and final stretch leave some potential unexplored.

I can confidently say that Orbitals is a must-play multiplayer experience on the Nintendo Switch 2, offering charm, polish, and plenty of fun. Creativity and attention to detail shine through in every aspect of the gameplay, and it is hard to ask for anything more from a great game.

Shapefarm has created something magnificent, if challenging, and it’s a clear invitation to fans the world over.  It’s a change, but a wonderful one. As Sadie Williams said, “I have loved the stars too fondly to be fearful of the night.” So let’s venture into this new dark together. It’s unknown, but we have each other, and that means the whole damn universe.

Orbitals isn't interested in being purely an 80s anime tribute; instead, it aims to recreate the feeling of seeing a work of art for the first time and immersing in it, alongside a good friend. It's a multiplayer triumph in visuals and gameplay, but lacks a little in the story.

Orbitals is a split-screen multiplayer game that follows the structure of titles like It Takes Two and Split Fiction. With absurdly striking visuals reminiscent of 1980s anime, fun and accessible gameplay, and a campaign that leaves you wanting more, this is an excellent Nintendo Switch 2 exclusive.

Orbitals is one of the most interesting cooperative experiences available on the Nintendo Switch 2. It doesn’t always match the narrative depth of the games that openly inspired it, but it makes up for it with imaginative puzzles, carefully crafted co-op gameplay, and exceptional art direction. Short but intensely enjoyable, Maki and Omura’s journey proves once again that the best cooperative adventures aren’t necessarily the ones with the hardest puzzles, but those that turn solving them into a shared memory.

Orbitals recaptures the magic of pure cooperative gaming on Nintendo Switch 2. With stunning visuals inspired by 80s anime and addictive gameplay, it is a charming, must-play space journey to share with a partner or friends.

"Orbitals" is another successful co-op adventure in the vein of Hazelight games like "Split Fiction." In terms of gameplay, and especially its appealing retro anime style, it's not a cheap imitation, but rather a game that retains its own unique character while meeting the quality standards of its predecessors.

Orbitals’ only suffering comes from its own success. It’s such a delight to play through and just exist in this world with Maki and Omura that I wish me and a friend could do it for much longer. However, what is here is a constant delight, extremely fun, and one of the Switch 2’s very best titles.

It's just over six hours of extremely enjoyable co-op, presented like an anime we can control, and accompanied by one of the best soundtracks I've heard recently in a game of this type. It doesn't need to be the new Split Fiction. Being Orbitals already works quite well.

Orbitals took me completely by surprise. It is charming, creative, visually gorgeous, and constantly fun to play with another person. While its story is a little too familiar at times, nearly everything else, from the music and animation to its clever puzzle tools and varied levels, comes together beautifully.
If you want a co-op game that captures the feeling of watching a beloved retro anime with a friend while still delivering fresh, satisfying gameplay, Orbitals should absolutely be on your radar.

Orbitals is a stunning tribute to 80s anime, wrapped around an asymmetric co-op concept that constantly surprises with creative, character-driven puzzle sequences. The presentation is pitch-perfect down to the film grain, the soundtrack is a genuine earworm, and the humor lands more often than not. A missable-collectibles system and single-save-slot limitation hold it back slightly, but this is nonetheless a co-op essential that easily stands alongside genre heavyweights like It Takes Two and Split Fiction.

I do wish that plot details in Orbitals were a little more obvious from a storytelling perspective, but the amount of fun you’ll have in this short six-hour sci-fi adventure hardly makes you think about any of that. Orbitals is just a good time to spend with a friend, and that’s all you should really want from it.
Metacritic user score 8.2/10 (931 ratings).

Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy enshrines Asobo Studio’s deep passion and expertise at delivering emotional narratives that are wrought with tension and adventure. As the pieces fall together and players have made the laborious journey along with her, Sophia does not come out unscathed. However, she emerges as one of the rawest, most emotive protagonists in memory. This harrowing spectacle full of constant surprises, daunting vistas, and moving passion is truly a thing of beauty, an unforgettable adventure.

A haunting, emotional story is paired with fantastic combat, exploration, and puzzle-solving. Resonance: A Plague Tale solidifies the franchise as one of the best franchises of the modern era and shouldn't be missed.

Although Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy doesn't tell the story of Amicia and Hugo, it manages to offer a different perspective to the player. Not only are the graphics impressive, but also the combat, setting, and puzzles which, while becoming tiresome at times, prove to be intelligent and well-developed. This is, without a doubt, one of the best titles of the year.

Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy is a great game with a compelling and excellently performed story. There are still ties back to the original series for fans, and still plenty of tense stealth sections, but this is more action adventure with combat that offers a decent challenge. A new way to adapt the mythology of the Minotaur is the cherry that tops this experience.

Putting you in control of a popular character from A Plague Tale: Requiem and letting you experience an important chapter of their life, Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy exchanges rats and stealth for combat and puzzles, and is captivating from beginning to end. As long as you don't mind puzzles that involve reflecting light, anyhow.

The next step in a clear path from Innocence, through Requiem, Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy confidently switches to a full on action-adventure in the vein of Uncharted. A good combat system, simple story-serving design choices and a great story, make this a joy and to play, even as the dread mounts and you descend into the heart of darkness towards scenes every bit and terrifying and memorable as that tsunami of rats.

Between the stunning visuals, emotionally resonant storytelling that spans centuries, and satisfyingly varied gameplay loop, Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy impressed me from beginning to end. It ran well with basically no technical issues during my playthrough, and I just had a truly great time playing it. It’s a story and a gameplay experience I’ll be thinking about for quite some time, and that’s really saying something. Whether you’re a longtime Plague Tale fan or new to the franchise, Resonance is well worth picking up if you like a good action-adventure game with a strong narrative at its core.

Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy successfully fulfills the mission of expanding the franchise's universe without feeling like an expendable chapter. By swapping the Rune siblings for Sophia, Asobo Studio takes a risk with a new protagonist and a more overt approach to combat, yet retains what has always defined the series: a rich narrative, well-crafted characters, and impeccable art direction.

Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy represents one of Asobo Studio’s boldest gambles. It is not simply the third chapter in the saga. It is not Requiem 2. Above all, it does not attempt to replicate Amicia and Hugo with different characters. It is a new starting point. Sophia changes the pace of the experience, combat radically transforms the gameplay, the Greek-Mediterranean setting gives Asobo completely new material to work with, and the mythological component further expands the series’ narrative universe. The risks, however, are just as evident: some mechanics feel less original, the puzzles can disrupt the pacing, and moving away from certain iconic elements could alienate those who primarily loved the stealth-focused gameplay and distinctive atmosphere of the first two chapters. But perhaps that is precisely the point of Resonance. Asobo does not want to repeat A Plague Tale. It wants to find out how far it can push the series. We can say this having played it ourselves: the direction it has taken is surprisingly solid. Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy seems determined to prove that a series does not necessarily have to remain static in order to stay true to itself. Asobo has taken what worked, questioned what risked becoming repetitive, and built around Sophia an experience that suits her perfectly—a more vertical game, and one closer to the grand cinematic action-adventures. It may not be the Plague Tale that fans were expecting, but perhaps that is exactly why it could be the one the series needed.

Asobo Studio has delivered a fantastic adventure, leagues ahead of A Plague Tale: Requiem, and a clear demonstration of how much the team has grown. Unique, story-driven single-player experiences like this don't come around nearly as often these days, so this isn't one to skip. Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy is absolutely worth playing.

With Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy, Asobo Studio has not only added another major title to its catalog, but may have created its best game to date. Offering a grand adventure, this prequel reminds us of some of the finest moments in Uncharted and Tomb Raider, without losing sight of everything that makes Asobo and A Plague Tale so strong and unique. This new installment delights as much as it mistreats, impresses as much as it provokes thought, and thus leaves an indelible mark once the journey comes to an end. An exceptional game that showcases, more than ever, the talent and identity of our developers in Bordeaux.
Part-Uncharted and part-Assassin’s Creed, Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy is an absolutely fantastic adventure.
Beautiful, creative and constantly surprising, Resonance takes A Plague Tale in new directions and evolves the series wonderfully. One of the year's best games.

Resonance has everything the previous Plague Tale games had: a strong story, compelling characters, and a visually impressive supernatural twist. On top of that, it adds surprisingly fluid, polished action and a more streamlined gameplay experience. Asobo Studio has done it again.

Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy does not try to recreate Innocence or Requiem with a different character. It takes their sensitivity, darkness and obsession with shattered destinies, then ventures into new territory. Seeing Asobo take that risk—preserving the saga’s identity while allowing it to evolve—clearly deserves praise. And I can tell you this: like a grand mythological Indiana Jones adventure, I loved every moment I spent alongside Sophia. Immersion, adventure and mystery are the key elements I look for in a video game, and throughout the twenty or so hours it took me to complete this thrilling journey, the game delivered in spades. Yes, Asobo has earned its place at the table of kings!
Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy is the nearly perfect sequel that builds on the narrative strengths of its predecessors and finally complements them with great gameplay.

Asobo Studio succeeds in creating a truly excellent spin-off sequel with Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy. While the story didn't quite captivate us as much as Amicia's tale the connection to Greek mythology and the likable heroine kept us engaged right to the end. In terms of gameplay, however, we actually prefer Resonance. The impactful, fast-paced combat is just as enjoyable as the overall well-crafted puzzles, and the platforming elements, particularly during the dramatic escape sequences, are a welcome addition. All in all, we feel Asobo has maintained the high standards of the previous titles while even making slight technical improvements. If you enjoyed the earlier games and don't mind the significantly increased focus on direct action, you can certainly pick this one up with confidence.

With Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy, Asobo Studio partially distances itself from the previous installments in the series - not from a narrative standpoint, which remains, rich, compelling and features mature writing full of plot twists, but in terms of gameplay. The strong stealth element of its predecessors has been relegated to specific parts of the adventure, while the rest is a delightful mix of exploration, puzzle-solving (often quite original), and combat, built on a well-crafted, varied, and sufficiently deep combat system. It’s a sort of captivating Uncharted/Tomb Raider hybrid, with faint horror undertones, that fits perfectly into the franchise’s timeline.
Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy executes familiar genre staples and delivers a moving story starring a charismatic pirate on what may be the most impactful and tragic adventure of her life.

Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy is a fantastic game with top-notch world design, art direction, and narrative; everything that we expect from A Plague Tale. What I didn’t expect was a game that also boasts well-balanced, aggressive combat.
