Perhaps some systems could be improved upon; Asobo is out here flexing their creative muscles, going outside their comfort zone, while still maintaining their identity- you love to see it.
A Plague Tale: Resonance boldly reinvents the series with a fresh setting, strong new protagonist, and engaging exploration. Despite minor flaws, it’s the refreshing new beginning the series needed.
Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy is well worth playing whether familiar with the previous games or not, telling a captivating story with some wonderful gameplay.

Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy is a striking and unsettling title that intelligently steers the franchise toward ambitious new horizons. Enjoyable for both *A Plague Tale* veterans and newcomers alike, it offers a fast-paced journey featuring puzzles, evocative exploration, and a narrative that intertwines the Macula with the myth of the Minotaur—all while incorporating a combat system that is basic yet aggressive and fun. It is a dark game brimming with ideas that is unlikely to disappoint.

Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy is a strong adventure that delivers a clever twist on Greek mythology rather than the games its spun off of. It combines strong combat, exploration and atmosphere with some gnarly creature encounters in a clever way, though the puzzles are uneven and the mechanics are largely derivative. Regardless, Sophia's journey is intriguing from beginning to end, making Resonance a memorable adventure even if its resemblance to the Plague Tale games are fleeting.

Replacing high-profile suffering with fun combat and adding loads of puzzles did breathe new life into this series. And while Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy is undoubtedly a good game, it also feels like it’s time to take a step forward, instead of dancing backwards and around.

The final output is an oddball that struggles even harder to straddle the line between product and art; a creative vision from another land trying to find its feet in the gaming analogue of Hollywood, making concessions to focus tests and market research while still struggling to grip tightly enough to a core essence as to remain true to itself. The craftsmanship here is impressive, and the two halves have fused well together. As such, both are cromulent, but neither can quite shine as an absolute triumph.

Resonance shifts gears to deliver a blockbuster-style adventure that offers few gameplay innovations compared to other similar AAA titles, yet perfectly captures the spirit of adventure, providing a captivating narrative and a well-balanced mix of action, puzzles, stealth, and platforming.

Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy follows in the footsteps of previous titles in the series, whose strong narrative component remains present. However, it introduces some interesting changes such as its new, deeper, and more dynamic combat system that gives more prominence to the action. There are some minor graphical flaws that are barely noticeable, but nothing that ruins the experience.

If you're a fan of A Plague Tale, you'll find it essential to return to its world with Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy. And for those of you who might not be as keen on the series or aren't familiar with it, its more balanced blend of action and puzzles also makes it a very appealing solo adventure, as you don't need to know the series to enjoy it. An excellent adventure to bid farewell to the summer with.

Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy successfully takes the series in a new direction, blending treasure hunting, puzzle-solving, and close-combat action into a visually stunning addition. While its combat and story lack depth at times, the beautiful world, engaging exploration, and strong sense of adventure make for a fresh and entertaining addition to the A Plague Tale universe.

Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy isn’t Plague Tale, and that’s actually a good thing. Resonance is a highly action-oriented adventure with a fun, accessible combat system built on proven principles. Its scenery and performances are breathtaking, while the standout use of a unique monster ensures that stealth still has a place. It’s explosive and exotic, occasionally brutally mature in its cutscenes, but in gameplay it feels more like a Hollywood thrill ride that starts repeating itself rather quickly and fails to make full use of some of its more interesting systems.

Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy is a captivating adventure, full of heart and charisma, capable of bringing well-developed characters to life on screen and telling a story that will undoubtedly win you over. It is narrated with skill and backed by highly sophisticated technology, which has enabled the team at Asobo Studio to deliver an experience that isn't afraid to evolve while remaining faithful to the style and atmosphere that have made A Plague Tale one of the most compelling productions of recent years.

A compelling and well-designed third person action role-player with a re-telling of the Minotaur legend at its core, that reinterprets the themes of the Plague Tale franchise in a more combat orientated prequel.

Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy leans more heavily into action in a series known for its stealth. It's the change we didn't know we needed. It offers a charming world, clever puzzles, fluid combat, and a story packed with mystery, tragedy, and even horror.

Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy leans into action and melee combat, departing from the formula of its predecessors. While the combat system lacks depth, the exploration and puzzles work really well. Its greatest strength lies in its spectacular setting, complemented by outstanding graphics and art direction. It doesn't surpass Innocence or Requiem, but it remains a highly enjoyable and recommended adventure.

Rarely does changing the genre work so well as in Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy. Asobo Studio managed to do what Naughty Dog no longer does with their Uncharted series and delivered an exciting adventure.

As a prequel to Asobo Studio's pair of popular A Plague Tale games, Resonance takes the risk of not only introducing a new protagonist, but significantly switching up the franchise's enduring gameplay formula. Forgoing the stealth, survival, and relentless rat swarms the series is known for, Sophia's story is a swashbuckling one, packed with fast, action-focused combat and plenty of puzzles to solve and ancient artifacts to uncover. Aside from an occasionally clunky combat camera, this fresh approach works brilliantly, although faithful fans craving another foreboding trek through the Black Death might find its new formula a bit too safe and familiar.

Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy is more than a spinoff; it’s reinventing the conventions and removes the classic stealth gameplay to introduce its first interesting combat system. A system that could be more fleshed out but this doesn’t take away that the story, breathtaking environments, and excellent sound design pave the way for something fresh that still feels like the quality of game we’ve come to expect from Asobo Studio. It’s Plague Tale’s most action-packed adventure set in mystery and mythology. A great game to pick up whether or not you’ve played the others before, it stands on its own.

Resonance is a welcome addition to the Plague series that tries, and largely succeeds, in offering something different from its established gameplay and aesthetic. It succeeds thanks to its satisfying combat system and the beautiful scenery of Crete, although the puzzles are slightly lacking in comparison.

Yet if the glue holding Resonance together is a known formula, its pieces are uniformly exquisite, aligned with near-unparalleled craft, and they don't often make them like this any more. [Issue#428, p.96]

Resonance is another mighty fine entry in the Plague Tale series, proving that there’s plenty of scope to take this endlessly-interesting world to new places and explore new types of gameplay. Combat and puzzles could have been a touch sharper, and it has some genuine issues on base PS5 consoles, but overall this is another unforgettable journey.

The emphasis is much less on sneaking around than in “Innocence” and “Requiem.” It takes some getting used to, but it does work, and the combination with clever puzzles provides plenty of variety. When, after a while, you encounter an enemy from whom you have no choice but to flee, the familiar “Plague Tale” experience is back in full force. Add to that the beautiful graphics and a compelling, surprising plot, and you have a strong new installment in a series that’s quickly becoming indispensable.

When developers take a bold new direction in an already successful franchise, I will always applaud the courage to take that risk. Whilst uneven combat and puzzles can take some shine off, there are still plenty of positives to find in Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy. A thought provoking genre bending origin story, full of great moments and characters. Stunning visuals and superb audio design and soundtrack, make this a worthy entry in this beloved franchise. Asobo Studio, I hope you continue to innovate and take chances; this is what more developers should do!
Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy is a great prequel. It's adventure style shines as exploring this mysterious world. The biggest downside is the repetitive combat and some situations.

Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy could have been so much more. It could also have been so much less. It's a title that envelops you with its incredible atmosphere, flatters you with the quality of its cutscenes, enchants you with music reminiscent of Homeric myth, then after a few hours brings you back to reality with an almost too-stultifying structure. The team at Asobo Studio demonstrates its mastery of creating linear narrative experiences, but this very pedigree prevents them from fully embracing it. The transition from stealth to action is seamless, but it further highlights how the studio struggles to let go of the player. Yet the path is the right one; you just need to have the courage to follow it to the end.

Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy does its best to enrich the gameplay with its puzzles and combat. That mostly adds more action and variety, but it's never groundbreaking. The show is still stolen by the rock-solid storytelling and believable characters. On top of that, the pacing has been elevated to an art form.

Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy is a two-speed game, and it deserves to be judged by honestly acknowledging both sides of the coin. It's not a blind day-one purchase, especially in such a crowded release period, but it's still a production worth picking up at a calmer pace in the months ahead, especially for anyone who loved Innocence and Requiem and wants to keep exploring this universe.

Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy is an agreeable set of straightforward action-adventure environments and gameplay to the point that it ends up feeling like a shadow of the emotionally devastating, narrative-driven stealth series that founded it. Fortunately, the stunning visuals and intricate designs of the island’s many landscapes, tremendous music, an engaging central mystery, and the delectable challenge it offers on its higher difficulty levels more than make up for the parts that left me soured.

Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy delivers a focused linear adventure without trying to reinvent the genre. Its exploration, puzzles, combat, visuals, atmosphere, and story keep players engaged throughout the journey. While some puzzles can feel repetitive and the combat is fairly simple, the game remains a competent and enjoyable experience. Fans of A Plague Tale will especially appreciate the opportunity to learn more about Sophia and explore an untold part of her story.

Ultimately, Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy stands out as a solid title and a rewarding experience for anyone wishing to delve deeper into the world surrounding Amicia and Hugo’s adventures. While the story takes a while to get going, it truly comes into its own during the second half of the journey. The Asobo Studio team demonstrated great respect for Greek mythology while allowing themselves a few necessary narrative liberties. These adjustments blend seamlessly into the game's overall formula, offering a cohesive expansion of the franchise. However, you may be disappointed if you are primarily looking for a pure action game or particularly deep gameplay mechanics. The attempt to shift the formula toward more dynamic combat is only partially successful; the stiffness of the encounters and a lack of mechanical variety prevent the title from taking the next step in terms of the actual gameplay experience. It is a journey alongside Sophia in Crete that remains enjoyable for its atmosphere and setting, yet quickly reveals its limitations once the controller is in your hands.

By pivoting away from the gameplay that defined its predecessors, Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy takes a significant gamble. The end product is an uneven experience that doesn't always hit its mark, yet the effort is far from a misstep. If anything, this new direction demonstrates that the universe has rich, untapped potential capable of thriving well beyond the tragic journey of Amicia and Hugo.

Overall, Resonance A Plague Tale Legacy is a pretty paradoxical entry. Asobo Studio takes some risks with Sophia, the Minoan mythology and a new approach to gameplay, but at the same time, it tries to spice up the formula by borrowing pretty heavily from Uncharted. In 2026, climbing, big cinematic set pieces and chase sequences are no longer enough to feel fresh, especially since the studio doesn’t always handle this formula perfectly. Thankfully, whenever Asobo goes back to its own universe, Resonance finds a real sense of identity again. The Macula, the dual timeline and the light-based puzzles are the game’s best ideas, backed up by some really strong art direction and a great soundtrack. Resonance: A Plague Tale – Legacy does a good job of taking players back in time to explore this world further while also providing a welcome twist on the formula from previous games. Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy is a prequel spinoff that takes a lot of interesting chances with the series, following a new protagonist, refocusing its encounters around melee combat, and even introducing a whole new way to haunt your dreams. Some of these experiments pay off, like the new foe you eventually find yourself against and the overarching story about the ancient civilization you’ll explore the ruins of, but many more of them fall flat. That includes a significantly less compelling journey for its main character, battles that get repetitive way too fast, and light-manipulation puzzles that provide a dim flicker of amusement more often than a roaring flame. There’s still quite a bit to enjoy about Sophia’s origin story, especially if you’re just happy to be spending more time in this depressing but oddly hopeful setting – but it never came close to knocking my socks off the same way either of Amicia and Hugo’s adventures have.

Sophia may traipse a path similar to that of countless treasure-hunting, action-adventure video game classics – but for all the overfamiliar design choices, there is enough verve in the beguiling presentation and lively, compellingly drawn characters to elevate this beyond mere retread. Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy succeeds, in large part, because of Sophia, a heroine who confronts history head on, before finally breaking free of it in apocalyptically spectacular style.

Overall, I liked Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy. I think it adds a valuable chapter to the overall mythos of the series, and manages to carve out its own identity in several places without continuing to rely on fan-favorite Amicia or the terror of contending with waves of rats. But you have to be such a fan of the series already to enjoy it to the same extent as I did, and even then, shortcomings in combat and the companion system hold the game back, especially in a latter half that seems to drag as you get closer to the conclusion. I want people to play Resonance, but I can’t ignore that any game that requires doing homework beforehand to enjoy is a bit lacking. Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy is a surgical operation on a beloved franchise: Asobo Studio had the courage to remove almost completely the stealth, the hordes of rats and the linear structure that had defined Innocence and Requiem, replacing them with a rhythmic, vertical action adventure deeply tied to the myth of the Minotaur. A myth boldly reinterpreted, intertwined with the mysteries of the Macula and creating an experience that is at the same time a tribute to classical mythology and an original evolution of the saga. For fans, the Minotaur becomes the key to understanding the origins of the Macula and the destiny that binds Sophia, Theseus, Amicia and Hugo in a single, terrible legacy. The most evident transformation concerns the gameplay: the combat, based on parries, dodges and heavy blows, is demanding but – at the same time – highly rewarding. Sophia, with her arsenal of sword, dagger and grappling hook, is a more autonomous and capable character in combat than Amicia, while Theseus offers a more brutal and aggressive approach. The Minoan Sphere, besides being essential for solving puzzles, becomes a survival tool against the creature hunting Sophia through the shadows, creating a coherent experience where light is both a tool for solving and for protection. The level structure, with its vertical design, intricate labyrinths and temporal duality, represents a significant evolution compared with previous chapters, offering denser, more coherent and more interconnected exploration. The puzzles, based on the refraction of light and environmental manipulation, are more complex and require genuine observation and reasoning, maintaining the tradition of the saga while evolving it significantly. All of this is accompanied by a sumptuous art direction, a soundtrack, once again entrusted to Olivier Deriviere (without a shadow of a doubt among his best works), with an epic Mediterranean flavor that fits the Cretan setting perfectly, and a well-optimized technical side on PS5 Pro. The result is a game that renews the formula without betraying its soul and that represents one of the best action adventures – not only of 2026 – but of recent years.

Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy takes a big risk as a prequel by overhauling the combat system, introducing a new protagonist, and delivering a dual-sided story rooted in Greek mythology. Yet nearly every risk pays off, resulting in the best entry in the series to date one that cleverly uses environmental storytelling, dialogue with enemies, and even its stunning music as tools to deliver an exceptional narrative.

Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy is not A Plague Tale: Requiem. That distinction is worth making from the outset, because Asobo Studio has little interest in retracing the path of Amicia and Hugo. Instead, it takes a character who was once little more than a supporting presence and places her at the heart of a story that is very much her own. Rather than living in the shadow of what came before, Resonance attempts to build a new identity from its foundations.

Sophia is the reason that approach works. Her journey gives the game a clear emotional centre, while the writing surrounding her remains one of its strongest qualities. The narrative also takes greater risks with its structure, bringing past and present into increasingly close contact as Sophia’s visions begin to reveal connections between people, places, and events separated by centuries. What initially feels fragmented gradually takes shape as a larger mystery, giving the story a sense of momentum that extends well beyond the simple search for answers.

The same willingness to change direction can be found in the gameplay. Resonance moves away from the stealth-heavy design of its predecessors and gives Sophia a far more direct relationship with danger. Its combat system is not sophisticated enough to compete with the genre’s dedicated action games, but it does not need to be. Parrying, dodging, and counterattacking are responsive enough to make encounters satisfying, while their relative simplicity keeps combat from overwhelming the broader adventure. It is a change that feels driven by the character rather than imposed upon her.

Asobo Studio’s visual work remains equally impressive. The game’s environments have a strong sense of identity, from the crowded streets of Venice during Carnival to the quiet, enigmatic spaces of the island, while its lighting frequently serves a purpose beyond presentation. Strong art direction and confident cinematic staging allow some of Resonance’s most memorable moments to emerge naturally from the world around Sophia rather than simply placing spectacle on top of it.

The experience is not without weaknesses. The island’s puzzle-heavy structure can become repetitive, particularly during its first half, where the frequency of environmental challenges occasionally works against the pace of exploration. Some combat encounters are more punishing than their mechanics justify, and not every escape sequence reaches the same level of direction or intensity as the game’s best set pieces. On Xbox Series S, there are also occasional frame-rate drops during the more demanding late-game sequences. More difficult to overlook is the runtime itself: just as several characters begin to develop into genuinely compelling parts of the story, the credits are already approaching.

Even so, those shortcomings do not define the experience. What ultimately gives Resonance its value is the confidence with which it allows Sophia to exist independently of the characters who came before her. Her story is not about replacing Amicia, nor about recreating what made the previous games resonate. It is about confronting a past that has been deliberately obscured and discovering that the truth can be just as difficult to live with as the uncertainty that came before it.

Beneath its plague, its rats, the Macula, and the lore surrounding them, Resonance remains interested in something much more recognisable: what people do with loss, guilt, fear, and the parts of their history they would rather leave behind. Its world may be filled with extraordinary forces, but its emotional core is grounded in people trying to understand what happened to them and deciding what to do with that knowledge once they finally have it.

That is why Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy works best when it stops trying to answer the question of what comes after A Plague Tale: Requiem and starts asking a different one: what can A Plague Tale become when someone new is given the chance to tell its story? The answer is Sophia. This is not Amicia and Hugo’s journey. It is hers. And by the time Resonance finds its own voice, it has done more than continue a familiar story—it has earned the right to tell a new one.
